title: Knickerbocker Group named to Forbes’ best-in-state residential architects list
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Knickerbocker Group’s design team has been recognized by Forbes for its “excellence in design, a deep mastery of residential practice and meaningful contributions to their communities and landscapes.”
The invitation-only selection process for the 2026 list of America’s best-in-state residential architects included evaluation by Forbes editors along with a seven-member advisory board of professionals in architecture, design, sustainability and architectural history.
Firms that participated submitted one “exemplary” home completed since 2021, which was evaluated alongside the firm’s full body of work.
Knickerbocker’s team submitted its Honeymoon Cottage project, which was also a recipient of an honor award in the residential design category at the 2025 AIA Maine Design Awards.
The home was built as a group of three elevated linked pods and was designed to minimize its foundation footprint to protect the native landscape.
Professional presentation and reputation were included in the Forbes’ selection process, as well as a project’s “stability, utility and beauty, along with its approach to siting, materials, craftsmanship, spatial design, technology, sustainability and environmental responsiveness.”
“We are deeply honored to be recognized by Forbes among America’s best-in-state residential architects,” said Danielle Betts, president of Knickerbocker Group.
“At Knickerbocker Group, good design begins with listening — to our clients and to the land,” Betts said. “Each home is personal, shaped around how our clients want to live and thoughtfully connected to its unique place. This recognition celebrates the creativity of our team and the collaboration that brings each client’s vision to life.”
Knickerbocker Group is a 77-member employee owned design-build firm, founded in 1978, with offices in Portland and Boothbay.

title: Foxcroft Academy football’s family connections leading to outstanding season
text:
DOVER-FOXCROFT, Maine (WABI) - The Foxcroft Academy football team features family connections this season.
F.A. is 5-1 and in the middle of the Class C race.
Head coach Danny White’s son, Owen, has helped lead the charge.
“I think it’s just a special opportunity that most kids don’t have their fathers coaching them. I know what he’s thinking because I’m just around him a lot, so I know what he needs out of me and what he expects,” said Owen White, sophomore tight end, wide receiver, running back, defensive back.
“I’m just really taking advantage of each and every day and practice that we get to spend together. It’s a unique situation that not a lot of people get to experience,” said Danny White.
Offensive coordinator Austin Seavey won a state championship as Ponies quarterback during his career at F.A.
Now, his brother Evan, is under center.
“The experiences I’m going through, he’s gone through them. The game hasn’t changed a tremendous amount since he was in high school. He can communicate to me in a way that I’ll understand it because he’s gone through these experiences. Over the past four years, I’ve definitely grown to know how special it is,” said Evan Seavey, senior quarterback, defensive back.
“I would say I was a lot faster than he is. He’s definitely a tougher runner. I was much more just like pre-snap getting the ball out of my hands as fast as I could. He dissects the game a lot better than I ever did, and he has actually a lot more arm talent than I ever did. I can still out-throw him when we’re throwing spots though,” said Austin Seavey.
The Ponies explained why having family on the team can lead to winning football games.
“Football is the greatest ultimate team game so the bonds are very tight,” said Danny White.
Foxcroft Academy hosts Hampden Academy on Saturday at 1 p.m. before traveling to Brewer and Leavitt to close out the regular season.
Danny White’s nephews Thomas Day and Jacob and Jaedon Haack also play for Foxcroft Academy.

title: 10 years of Jackson Lab science shows the lifesaving power of genome-matched cancer treatment
text:
Edison T. Liu, MD, is president emeritus of The Jackson Laboratory.
Though I am known to many as a genetic scientist, my origins were in medicine, specifically cancer medicine. So, every question I pursued as a fundamental biologist was anchored with a single goal: “How can I use my findings to better treat my cancer patients?”
Over the years, I have seen how the impact of biomedical research has grown exponentially. Never in history has science been more powerful. Paradoxically, however, the limiting factor today is not the rate of discovery, but the difficulty that talented medical practitioners have in understanding and deploying powerful, but complex, technologies to benefit their patients.
Despite the quality of the physicians and nurses in our rural state, I saw, when I arrived in 2012, that they too were struggling with interpreting the genomic tests of their patient’s cancer. Over the next few years, The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) grew to become a major scientific center for modern cancer genomics, the key technology in clinical decision making for precision oncology.
We had the technical knowledge, and we simply could not let our neighbors flounder when we could help.
JAX’s executive vice president at that time, Chuck Hewett (also a Mainer), and I put our heads together and came up with an idea that would provide advanced genomic testing for cancer patients in Maine, and, importantly, also help guide how these results can be interpreted.
Backed by an $8.4 million initial donation from the Harold Alfond Foundation, the Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative (MCGI) was launched 10 years ago this week, with Bangor oncologist Jens Rueter, MD, leading the effort.
Molded by the three of us, the structure of the MCGI took form: JAX would provide the genomic test for patients who enroll in the MCGI cohort study and establish the computational analytics that linked the mutations with clinical action. JAX set up the statewide genomic tumor board where Maine physicians could present their most difficult cases to their peers, and to genomic experts from across the world. These recommendations became the basis of a treatment plan.
The results were stunning. Nearly all oncology practitioners in Maine participated in the MCGI. Over 1,600 Maine cancer patients were enrolled in the cohort study and, over the past decade, the MCGI touched the lives of more than 4,000 patients and their families.
The genomic tumor boards advised the best treatment for patients tailored by the results of the tumor’s genomic configuration. Patients who received targeted
therapies recommended by the board survived longer with their cancer.
Doctors benefited, too. We found that the participating physicians reported increased self-confidence in interpreting and using genomic reports, which previously seemed confusing. This local success was recognized by our national scientific peers. In 2022,
the National Cancer Institute asked Dr. Rueter and the MCGI to lead a national 18-institution trial to test whether our genomic tumor board would increase the use of targeted therapeutics across all cancers.
Thus, our small rural state became a national leader in “implementation sciences” — the discipline of crafting optimal system-wide approaches to disseminate complex technologies toward improving health outcomes. In the process, we had a discernible impact on the lives of Mainers with cancer.
Ten years on, as we celebrate the Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative’s decennial, that impact continues. But more work lies ahead. We are engaging genetic counselors to help patients navigate any underlying genetic susceptibility to cancer. We have dramatically improved the efficiency of the genomic tumor boards, as well as the depth of the mutational analysis. We are expanding outreach to other hospital systems.
There are many lessons from the MCGI story. One is that community counts, and that mutual support and collective learning leave a powerful and lasting legacy. Perhaps the most pertinent is that “small is mighty.” We are a rural state with a small population distributed across a vast geography, which has demonstrated to the nation how advanced genomic technologies can be effectively distributed to benefit all cancer patients.

title: In Rockland, artists now have an innovative, creative space to live and work
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Some might say that what it takes to create a thriving community of artists is funding. Others might argue it’s housing, or spaces for creatives to do their work in. Still others would say it takes inspiration. Architect Matthew Baird, the vision behind the newly reimagined mini-campus of Rockland’s Ellis-Beauregard Foundation, says it takes all of the above — plus a dinner party.
“We would always meet with the trustees on Thursdays at 4 o’clock, and (Foundation executive director Donna McNeil) would always stop the meeting at 5:30 and say, ‘OK, all of you please come to my house for dinner.’”
There, he and members of his New York-based firm would sit down and eat with everyone from curators at the Center for Maine Contemporary Art and the Farnsworth Art Museum to the Camden Film Festival and local artists.
“Those conversations meant that by the time we got halfway through the design, we really had an understanding of the local community and what was meaningful to them,” he says. “Donna knew that if she threw a great dinner party and brought all of these interesting people together, that it would inevitably inspire a great process.”
The result of that five-year process is Rockland’s latest addition to its cultural institutions, intended to further cement the area as an arts destination. The Ellis-Beauregard Foundation provides resources and support for artists and sustains the legacy of its founding artists, Joan Beauregard and David Ellis. Two innovative, net-zero energy structures have been built adjacent to the original building where Beauregard and Ellis once lived. The new buildings, built by Mussel Ridge Builders in Rockland, include residence and studio units for four visiting artists, plus performance and exhibition spaces, at a total cost of about $6.2 million.
In June, the new campus was inaugurated after the foundation’s preexisting visiting artists program was reignited in January. (Alumni include the Reggie Burrows Hodges, whose residency there is credited with first getting his work noticed; painter Anne Buckwalter; and photographer Dylan Hausthor.)
CONVERSATIONS WITH ARTISTS
Those visiting artists introduce new perspectives and voices to Rockland, says McNeil. “One thing we provide that neither the Farnsworth nor the CMCA do is we bring in a national group of artists to engage in the conversations,” she says. “It brings an outside voice to the community that residents seem to enjoy, and certainly the other institutions respect and value.”
And while Baird’s design for the new campus could easily have been a throwdown meant to match the creative works it houses and exhibits — his roster of high-profile projects, after all, includes the likes of the Woodmere Art Museum in Philadelphia and the New York Studio School — he’s quick to explain that he wanted just the opposite.
“A lot of times, I think architects brought onto arts projects feel the need to make something artistic themselves,” he explains. “But this is not a moment for the design to take center stage. What you want to do is create a neutral backdrop for art, so anyone can bring their vision and not find the architecture is in the way.”
Instead, he focused on those conversations he was having with artists in the community including many who’d already been through the program. “We spoke with 30 or more,” says McNeil, who accepted the post of executive editor after coming out of retirement from an illustrious career that included helming the Maine Arts Commission. The artists’ requests ranged from wanting lots of natural light (northern light — prized for its indirectness and consistency — pervades the buildings) to high ceilings. “And they definitely didn’t want to sleep in the studios,” recalls Baird. “If you were painting with oil paints, (you’d be) sleeping with that smell.”
ARTISTIC SPIRIT AND SUSTAINABILITY
Aesthetically, he aimed to turn the buildings’ minimalism and functionality into something familiar to the artists — to echo “the gritty loft living and the kind of places where people were making art in lower Manhattan and Brooklyn,” he says, and to “capture that spirit in Rockland.” That’s also reminiscent of the New York lofts where artist founders Joan Beauregard and David Ellis lived and worked before moving to Maine. “We wanted to make a building that’s ultimately utilitarian, and that finds beauty in its utility.”
And then there was the sustainability effort, which was about “making a building that the artists would be proud to be a part of because it was so responsible environmentally,” he says. That’s manifested in elements like the green roof, which has a reservoir that can retain rainwater. “It’s like a sponge up on the roof, so we protect the harbor from all the runoff that some buildings can create,” he says. It’s equally evident in other groundbreaking systems — several of which were the product of a $100,000 grant from the Helen Frankenthaler Foundation. “It was the first project where we’ve taken solar power, used it to run heat pumps, and have those produce hot water that we’ve run in a slab to create radiant heat. So in the wintertime, the artists are in bare feet in the studios and they love it.”
Other innovations extend to the new second building. “We built an exhibition and performance space, and they can use that space to hang an exhibit, invite a curator, to have a performance, or screen a film,” says McNeil. “We put in a sprung floor for dance because we love choreography here, and it’s attracted a lot of applications.”
“It can be a choreographer, a composer, a theater person, a novelist, an essayist, a visual artist, a sculptor. The overarching concept was sort of Bauhausian omni conversations across genres,” she says. It highlights “different ways of knowing and looking and working and tackling information for everybody, and it expands the work. The artists love having those conversations across genres.”
And the community is also brought in, via regular public events at local bars. “It’s so much better because everybody’s relaxed,” she reflects. “They’re having a drink. It’s dark. They’re commingling. If you create the proper setting, the barriers come down. And the exchange of ideas is more fluid and informal, and people become friends, not just colleague-to-colleague or workmate-to-workmate. It just becomes a conversation among people.”
Which has echoes of the dinner parties McNeil threw for the design team. “I think it’s more fruitful that way. Something happens around a dinner table that doesn’t happen in a meeting,” she says. “So yeah, I believe in the dinner table.”
Alexandra Hall is a longtime New England lifestyle writer who lives in Maine.

title: Overboard cruise ship passenger rescued after 20 hours in the water, officials say
text:
(Gray News) – A woman who went overboard from a cruise ship was rescued after 20 hours in the water, Greek authorities said in a press release.
The news release states the woman fell into the water early Friday. A “local emergency plan” was activated and searches began with the help from the Hellenic Coast Guard.
A video shared by the Hellenic Coast Guard shows the moments leading up to the 44-year-old Salvadoran woman’s rescue.
You can see the woman floating in the water inside a lifebuoy and hear someone say, “Are you OK?”
A rope was thrown to the woman and she pulled herself toward the rescue vessel. She received first aid once she was pulled onto the ship, according to the press release.
While the press release did not identify which cruise ship the woman was aboard, USA Today reported she was on Royal Caribbean’s Odyssey of the Seas.
CruiseMapper shows the ship was on a weeklong cruise that departed from Civitavecchia, Italy on Oct. 4. It was scheduled to return on Oct. 11.

title: Parents charged with murder after their young children died in RV fire
text:
LIBERTY COUNTY, Texas (KHOU) — The parents of two young children who died in an RV fire in Texas are in custody and facing murder charges, authorities said.
The fire happened Aug. 11, when authorities said the travel-trailer the children had been left in caught fire with them still inside.
Skylar Jane, 3, and Maverick, 4, died in the fire.
Parents away from trailer when fire started
Family members who spoke anonymously at the time said the children’s parents, Matthew Chambers and Meaghan Herrod, had stepped away to visit another home on the property when the fire happened.
“They had walked from their trailer to my daughter’s house and just opened up the door, and one of the neighbors over here started screaming, ‘There’s a fire. Call 911.’ So, naturally, they all ran back to the trailer,” a family member said.
Couple charged with murder
The Liberty County Fire Marshal’s Office confirmed Chambers and Herrod are now charged with murder in connection with the children’s deaths.
The investigation and additional questioning ultimately led to both being taken into custody.
Authorities haven’t said what caused the deaths, only that the children’s remains were found inside the trailer.
It’s not clear when Chambers and Herrod are expected back in court. Each has a $1 million bond.
The cause of the fire is still not known.

title: A.J. Brown returns to Patriots practice after high ankle sprain
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown is a step closer to returning to game action.
Brown was back on the practice field on Wednesday for the first time since being placed on injured reserve last month because of a high ankle sprain.
He became eligible to return after missing the last four games. He now must be activated within 21 days or placed on season-ending IR.
Cornerback Christian Gonzalez also practiced after missing the last two games because of a shoulder issue. In addition, offensive lineman Marcus Bryant (ankle) returned after being placed on injured reserve during the preseason.
Brown was injured in the second half of New England’s season-opening 13-10 loss at Seattle on Sept. 9. He left the game early in the third quarter following an incomplete pass from quarterback Drake Maye. He was falling to the turf as he tried to make the catch, and Seahawks cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett’s knee made contact with Brown’s ankle, pushing it against the ground. Brown had three catches for 26 yards before the injury.
“I think he’s stayed engaged,” coach Mike Vrabel said. “I think it’s difficult sometimes to stay engaged. I think his routine was really good, his ability to be around guys in the meetings and then also focus on rehab. He’s just treating everything as a pro, being where he’s supposed to be and working hard to get back.”
During the portion of practice open to the media Wednesday, Brown could be seen smiling at times as he went through some light drills with his right ankle heavily wrapped with tape.
“It’s a warm welcome in the huddle to have him back in there,” Maye said. “You can see how closely he’s been watching the games. Little things he picks up on, you can tell he really watching and really cares. …There’s not many like him that are around here in this league.”
Patriots safety Kevin Byard said Brown’s return brings instant energy to the sideline.
“Huge boost. He’s a receiver (No. 1),” Byard said. “Very talented guy as far as the pass game. Obviously, the last couple of weeks our pass game has been playing really well. So, he’s obviously just going to add another dynamic to that. And hopefully we’ll continue to have a good passing game with A.J. in there.”
Brown’s fellow receivers – Mack Hollins, Romeo Doubs, Pop Douglas, Kyle Williams and Efton Chism – have stepped up without him, accounting for six touchdown catches in his absence, and the Patriots have gone 3-1 with Brown on the shelf. Maye is coming off passing for a season-high 374 yards and four touchdowns last week against the Las Vegas Raiders.
Brown’s potential return to the lineup is perfect timing, with Hollins going on injured reserve last week because of a calf injury.
But Maye said Brown returning to the mix gives him another option to spread the ball around in the passing game.
“We have a lot of guys that can make plays. So it’s going to be tough on defenses,” Maye said.

title: These trading posts swap plants and produce to help the community
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (InvestigateTV) - Producing fresh food in cities from coast to coast, urban farming is taking root across the country.
“I think it’s just good for you. I think humans are supposed to be at least somewhat in nature,” Curtis said.
Curtis started gardening when he was a kid, thanks to his dad, who inspired him to grow food.
“Just eating fresh food from your garden is way healthier than the stuff that we get at the store. Tastes better, it’s more sustainable,” Curtis said.
Now at 28 years old, Curtis noticed something missing in his generation.
“I feel like in my generation has kind of been shot. People just don’t talk anymore, which is really weird. It’s not good,” he said.
The concept
Three years ago, Curtis started a project called Pineal Trade Stations.
“The concept is take a plant, leave a plant,” Curtis said.
People build their own Pineal Trade Station and then get uploaded to the Pineal map by purchasing the activation kit.
The trade stations are community-run hubs where neighbors can trade and share plants, seeds, houseplants and other urban homesteading goods.
“There is so much extras if you’re growing a garden, like you have to thin out your plants all the time,” Cutirs explained. “And most of the time it just goes in the trash or the compost pile. But somebody could just have it and it, you know, saves people money, but it also kind of just brings that human back to community. Like people are actually real people.”
Community response
Deanna O’Connell saw Curtis on Facebook and called him up. This will be her third summer to host a station.
“I saw Noah on Facebook, called him up, thought it’s a great idea,” O’Connell said.
“With gardening, you always have extra zucchini, tomatoes, all that stuff,” she said.
“Some of our neighbors have even put extra groceries in it at times, and the neighborhood has utilized that also,” O’Connell said.
Instead of a price tag, the stations run on trust. Take what you need. Leave what you can.
Curtis said the project addresses a larger need in 2026.
“I think everybody kind of feels it in 2026 that everybody just hates each other. And that’s crazy. I think, yeah, it’s like, you know, if half the country hates half the country, it’s not going to end well, like for anybody,” he said.
The stations offer a reason to slow down and show up.
“Cycle of good that you can put yourself in,” Curtis said.
“It’s a little goodness in the world, you know, to give back, and without expecting anything in return,” O’Connell said.
Curtis chose the name Pineal Gardens for a reason. Pineal is not a plant but a gland deep in the middle of the brain. Its job is to secrete the hormone melatonin, which helps regulate the body’s sleep-wake cycles.
There are about 100 Pineal Trade stations across 15 states. For more information click here.

title: Whitewashing history is no path to peace
text:
It is hard to imagine a more vacuous and willfully one-sided column than Douglas Rooks’ Oct. 8 piece (“‘Genocide’ or not, US must seek an end to the suffering in Gaza”). In more than 760 words ostensibly offering a solution to Gazan suffering, Rooks places blame entirely on Israel — by my count, he mentions either Israel or Netanyahu by name 24 times while mentioning Hamas but twice.
Whitewashing history provides a weak foundation for peace; serious problems require acknowledging inconvenient facts. It was Hamas that militarized Gaza’s civilian infrastructure and embedded its war-making apparatus among the people it purported to represent. It was Hamas that initiated this war with its murderous Oct. 7 attack, then sheltered its fighters in tunnels while leaving Gazan civilians above ground to endure the foreseeable Israeli response. And, it was Hamas’ continued captivity of Israeli hostages that prolonged the conflict, compounding Gazans’ suffering.
Exploiting civilians — Gazan and Israeli — is integral to Hamas’ strategy. Yet the column never confronts Hamas as an obstacle to resolution. It contemplates Netanyahu’s removal through Israeli democratic elections without considering whether Hamas’ removal from power would advance the cause of peace. Wouldn’t an honest assessment of peace prospects examine the governing entities on both sides?
Lasting relief requires an honest and serious reckoning with the conduct and responsibilities of all parties to the conflict. Ignoring Hamas while focusing solely on Israel is neither honest nor serious and provides no path to peace.
Daniel Kagan
Lewiston

title: New research on psychedelics could have big impact on mental health patients
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (InvestigateTV) - Millions of Americans take prescription medications for mental health conditions, but those might not be enough for people with severe depression or post-traumatic stress disorder.
Relief for some can be found in treatments that use drugs that produce psychedelic-like effects. After President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at speeding up research on several psychedelic drugs, it could open the door to similar therapies.
For 25 years, Logan Curtis says he struggled with anxiety, depression and panic attacks tied to childhood abuse.
“I carry a lot of these deep wounds with me,” Curtis said.
Curtis said he tried talk therapy and spent years on antidepressants, including SSRIs, but wanted more than simply managing symptoms.
“I don’t want to just exist,” Curtis said.
Three months ago, Curtis said he watched a documentary that opened his eyes to different treatments. It led him to Derive Health in Charlotte’s Dilworth neighborhood for ketamine treatments. Ketamine is currently the only legal psychedelic medicine in North Carolina and is used in clinical settings for conditions including treatment-resistant depression.
“Ketamine itself is a very safe medication, but it does do best with some medical monitoring or support,” said Dr. Jonathan Leake, who has treated patients with ketamine for a decade.
Leake said ketamine is administered by prescription through an IV over a series of sessions, with medical supervision and therapeutic support.
“You really are seeing people that have suffered, and then over six weeks, they’re kind of transforming before your eyes,” Leake said.
The FDA is now fast-tracking review of three other psychedelic drugs for PTSD, major depressive disorder and treatment-resistant depression, according to advocates tracking the federal actions. The president’s order would loosen research restrictions on psychedelics, including ibogaine.
Both ketamine and ibogaine can produce psychedelic experiences, but the drugs are used very differently.
Ketamine is a type of anesthetic used in small doses that can give you an “out of body” experience. Treatments last around an hour and done in a series over several weeks.
Ibogaine is often used a single, intense all-day session. Researchers also say it carries more serious heart risks with it.
Most psychedelics are illegal on a federal level, but states like Oregon and Colorado have legalized certain therapies. Several of the psychedelic drugs are being studied in trials for mental health conditions.
Gina Giorgio, with the North Carolina Psychedelic Coalition, said the federal push could move approvals faster, but states will play a major role in how research and treatment are carried out.
“This expedites approval through the federal government, but it’s really the states that will be carrying out this type of research and this type of treatment,” Giorgio said. She added that building training protocols for therapists would be essential.
Giorgio said more study is still needed on safety and effectiveness, but she believes the policy shift broadens what could become available for patients who have not found relief through other treatments.
“We’re not saying that this is for everyone,” she said. “But we’re saying it should at least be an option if people are not experiencing relief elsewhere.”
If the drugs are found safe and effective, some approvals could come later this year. Any treatments would be administered in a clinical setting under medical supervision, not taken at home.

title: Happy to do as Trump says
text:
President Trump is saying at his rallies to “Just close your eyes and pretend that I’m on the ballot.” I think everyone should do as he says.
Look at where the U.S. stands with an endless war, high gas and grocery prices, heating oil through the roof and a president whose family has generated billions of dollars in income and profits from various business ventures since he returned to the White House.
When one goes to vote, just imagine that every Republican is Trump. Great idea.
Peyton Higgison
Brunswick

title: Woman accused of killing husband, 3-year-old son at Great Wolf Lodge in Pennsylvania
text:
Woman accused of killing husband and 3-year-old son at Great Wolf Lodge in the Pocono Mountains
A woman is accused of killing her husband and 3-year-old son at a popular resort in the Pocono Mountains in Northeastern Pennsylvania.
The Pocono Township Police Department and a district attorney have confirmed a double homicide occurred Monday night in a guest room at the Great Wolf Lodge, a resort and indoor waterpark in Scotrun, Pennsylvania, which is outside of Tannersville and is located between Scranton and Allentown.
"This was a violent domestic tragedy in which two people, the boy and the father, lost their lives," Monroe County District Attorney Mike Mancuso said in a news conference on Tuesday. "There are charges filed now against the woman who was actually the caller."
According to court documents obtained by sister station WGAL, 27-year-old Metallica Harrison of Towanda, Pennsylvania, is accused of killing her 3-year-old son and her husband, who has been identified as Charles Harrison.
Charles Harrison suffered multiple stab wounds, while the child suffered a single stab wound to the chest.
Metallica Harrison was taken to the hospital for self-harm and told dispatchers she wanted to die to be with her husband and son. She is facing two counts of criminal homicide.
Police say this was an isolated domestic tragedy and there is no threat to the community.
Officials say the investigation is ongoing.
"There's a lot more testing. There are post-mortem examinations yet to be conducted. There's a review of various items of evidence. All of that will be unfolding over the course of the next several months, so this is only the first stage in a long process," District Attorney Mancuso said.

title: Father sentenced for killing 9-year-old daughter after claiming she was abducted while on vacation
text:
ELIZABETHTOWN, N.Y. (WCAX/Gray News) - A Montreal man was sentenced Wednesday to 25 years to life in prison for killing his 9-year-old daughter and concealing her body in New York.
Luciano Frattolin, 45, was convicted by a jury in August for killing his 9-year-old daughter, Melina, in Ticonderoga on their way back from vacation in July 2025.
New York State Police said Warren County 911 received a call from Frattolin reporting that his 9-year-old daughter was missing in a possible abduction, which led to an AMBER Alert being issued.
Hours after the alert was issued, Melina was found dead. Her body was found north of Lake George Village, near the state border with Vermont.
Investigators said the pair had been traveling through parts of the Northeast together for the last week and were headed back to Canada when Frattolin allegedly killed his daughter and dumped her body.
“You tried to show her how much fun you could have with her, and something happened, and no one other than you will be able to tell us what happened. Like everyone that has heard of this story, everyone wants to know why,” the judge said.
During the trial, prosecutors said cellphone and car data placed Frattolin in the Ticonderoga area the night Melina was killed, even as he insisted she was kidnapped and denied being there.
The district attorney also pointed to notes Frattolin wrote mentioning “ending the madness” and making a decision about Melina, who he claimed was mentally ill.
The judge handed down a sentence of 25 years to life for second-degree murder and a consecutive sentence of one to three years for hiding Melina’s body.
“We continue to suffer deeply since the day Melina was brutally murdered. Nothing can bring Melina back, but we are relieved that this chapter is over,” said Essex County District Attorney Michael Langey.
Despite being satisfied with the sentence, Langey said he’d like to see changes in the state’s criminal justice system regarding who can be charged with first-degree murder, which carries the potential for longer sentences and no eligibility for parole.

title: Jury returns mixed verdict after NFL star Tyreek Hill’s estranged wife accuses him of abuse
text:
MIAMI (AP) - A Miami jury on Tuesday found Tyreek Hill liable for two counts of battery but not liable for the eight remaining claims made by Lakeeta Vaccaro — ending the high-profile civil trial involving the NFL wide receiver and his estranged wife.
Hill, who has played for the NFL’s Kansas City Chiefs and Miami Dolphins, was found liable for two counts of battery — one stemming from an incident in January 2024, and another from April 2025. The jury awarded Vaccaro $500,000 in compensatory damages but did not award her punitive damages.
The jury found Hill, 32, not liable for eight other counts that included battery, assault and continuing domestic violence.
The trial involved allegations of abuse made by Vaccaro, 30, who on the stand described instances in which Hill allegedly pulled her hair and “treated me like I was, just, a man.” Hill took the stand last week and mostly denied what he called “false allegations” made by his estranged wife, while saying in one instance he shoved Vaccaro and “created a hole in the wall.”
Hill, wearing a dark polo shirt on Tuesday, embraced one of his attorneys and shook hands with others following the verdict before leaving the courtroom by himself.
It wasn’t immediately clear what the verdict means for Hill’s return to the NFL. He is still working his way back from a dislocated knee and torn ligaments suffered in September 2025 while he was with the Dolphins, but his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, has indicated that he could be ready to play by November.

title: Death Notice: Caleb R. Keune
US halts prosecution of former CIA analyst accused of aiding South Korean intelligence
text:
US halts prosecution of former CIA analyst accused of aiding South Korean intelligence
The U.S. Justice Department has agreed not to prosecute a former CIA analyst who in 2024 was accused of serving as a secret agent for South Korea’s intelligence service, according to court documents filed Tuesday.
Related video: Body camera footage shows police officers confronting, arresting Luigi Mangione inside McDonalds
Federal prosecutors said Sue Mi Terry had shared nonpublic government information, facilitated access for South Korean officials to U.S. officials and accepted luxury gifts in exchange for advocating South Korean government positions during media appearances.
The Justice Department agreed Tuesday to put her prosecution on hold for a year, and then drop the charges altogether if Terry stays out of legal trouble. The deal comes weeks before Terry was set to stand trial in a Manhattan federal court on charges of acting as an unregistered foreign agent.
Prosecutors did not explain in court documents why they decided not to move forward with her case, saying only that they determined that the interests of both Terry and the U.S. "will be best served by deferring prosecution.” The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York declined to comment.
Terry had maintained her innocence. Her attorney, Lee Wolosky, said Tuesday that Terry had “served her country loyally for many years” and was pleased with this result.
“We have consistently maintained that her interactions with South Korean officials were conducted in furtherance of U.S. interests and her work as a leading American specialist on North Korea and East Asia,” Wolosky said in a statement.
As part of her deal, Terry signed a document agreeing to certain facts of the case, including that she had shared notes with a South Korean intelligence officer from an off-the-record meeting she attended with then-U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken in 2022.
The document also said she accepted designer handbags and coats from South Korea’s intelligence service for her work, which were collectively valued at about $9,245.

title: Construction finally underway at Lewiston’s massive Continental Mill housing development
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON — Seven years after New Hampshire-based Chinburg Properties purchased the hulking Continental Mill on Cedar Street, work is underway to redevelop the property into nearly 400 apartments and commercial space.
Preliminary work began earlier this year, described by Chinburg officials as cleanup and stabilization of the historic mill buildings, with removal of old materials such as rotted wood and paint. The scope of the construction will ramp up in the coming months, the developer said.
The Continental Mill was built to produce textiles between 1855 and the 1890s in phases, and is actually 16 interconnected buildings, varying in height from one story to six.
In late September, the city approved the first phase of the project, with an estimated cost of $32.5 million. The total redevelopment will cost an estimated $80 million.
Chinburg has broken the redevelopment into two phases, roughly along north-south boundaries of the complex.
“So, the first phase here we’re calling Project South, and it’s going to encompass 179 units and approximately 20,000 square feet of commercial space,” said Paul Goodwin, director of commercial development for Chinburg.
Completion of the first phase is expected in early 2028, Goodwin said.
In all, the redevelopment will produce some 377 studio, one- and two-bedroom units and 45,000 square feet of commercial space. Rents will be based on the prevailing market rate.
Planned amenities include a club room, a lounge, gym, business center, and bike storage. Goodwin said the center courtyard will be a focal point outside, with a patio area, fire pits and grills for residents.
As far as the look of the apartments, Goodwin said the two driving factors are historical requirements and working with existing components like beams and columns within the structures.
One aspect of the building that will be very noticeable is all the windows. “Historic factory-style windows,” Goodwin pointed out. “We have high, exposed ceilings, so brick-and-beam architecture is going to be prominently featured in the units. The floors are going to be hardwood.”
Construction of a 287-space parking lot will happen next year and an additional 280 spaces will be leased from the city’s Chestnut Street parking deck.
Goodwin said the property fronting Cedar and Lincoln streets will have the biggest visual impact.
A single-story structure at the entrance to adjacent Picker House Lofts, known as the mill No. 5 building, will be ready for tenant buildout in the first quarter of 2027, with the hope it will host a restaurant or similar establishment. The building is about 5,000 square feet.
Picker House Lofts was developed by a different developer, The Szanton Company, over 17 months, with tenants moving in starting in January 2025.
Chinburg officials also hope to attract an eatery or pub and other businesses to 20,000 square feet of space in the first phase. An additional 15,000 square feet of space is planned for phase two of the redevelopment.
The Continental Mill has more than 500 feet of river frontage and Chinburg granted the city of Lewiston an easement to extend the city’s Riverwalk past the mill, with work expected to begin next year.
Chinburg has 40 years of adaptive reuse projects in Maine, New Hampshire and Massachusetts, with the Continental Mill being among the biggest such projects the developer has undertaken.
“We know the transformative power of returning these historic buildings back to productive use for communities,” Goodwin said, “so we are incredibly excited about the opportunity for Continental Mill, and what having all of these new residents in the downtown, on the waterfront, is going to contribute to the community and the economic impact of that.”
Goodwin made the point that buildings like the Continental Mill are not built anymore, and that the redevelopment project represents a unique moment in history as the grand industrial buildings are returned to use.
When both phases of construction are complete, the entire complex will be a net space of 375,000 square feet.

title: Pres. Trump urges Alaskans to vote for the real Dan Sullivan
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Gray Media’s White House correspondent Jon Decker interviewed President Donald Trump in Wasilla, Alaska, as the US Senate race between Republican Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola comes down to the wire.
Jon Decker:
Mr. President, welcome to Alaska. You have done exceptionally well in Alaska, won the state three times. You won by 13.5 points in 2024. And yet in this Senate race, it’s exceptionally close. Why do you suppose that is and why did you travel seven hours for this campaign event?
President Donald Trump:
Well, I think maybe the people don’t know what a great job Dan Sullivan does. Senator Sullivan is a great senator, respected by everybody. And I think I have to tell the people I did 1 to 3 times the fact I got the highest vote in the history of Alaska. So I said, I better come out here and explain, because Dan Sullivan is great and they have a fake Sullivan in here. They put the Democrats, put a guy named Sullivan who never did anything only because of his name, hoping to confuse people, which I thought was disgraceful. So I came out here for that too. We can’t let them get away with that.
Jon Decker:
It is so expensive to live in Alaska. You know that, Mr. President. Gas is so expensive here. Going going to the grocery store. Also very expensive is affordability. Whatever you want to call a cost of living. A big issue as to why. Dan Sullivan, Senator Sullivan is not performing as well as he’d like to right now.
President Donald Trump:
Well, affordability is big, but it was caused by the Biden administration. We’re bringing it down. I’ve only been here a little more than a year and a half, and we’re bringing it way down. Groceries have come way down. Everything is coming down, and all will be coming down as soon as I finish with Iran, which is going to be very soon. They’re defeated in every way. Their military is gone. Their navy, their air force, everything’s gone. They have the highest inflation of any country in the world. They have no money. They have no leadership. Their leadership was gone. The second phase is gone. They have some people we don’t even know. I mean, frankly, who are we dealing with? Nobody’s exactly sure. Nobody wants to be the leader. So Iran is in is going to fail very shortly. And when they do. Gasoline is going to be tumbling down and other costs are going to be tumbling down. But affordability is a nice word. But as everyone knows, and really, Jon, you know, we inherited that from the Biden administration. He had the worst inflation in the history of our country. And we took it over and we brought everything down. And last for the last three months, we’ve been at 1.7% inflation.
Jon Decker:
You and Senator Sullivan, you see eye to eye on virtually everything, almost to 100% voting record that Senator Sullivan has with you. You don’t see eye to eye on one issue in particular. Mr.. Mr. president, and that is the issue of Russia and President Putin. Senator Sullivan is called President Putin a dictator, an authoritarian, a mafia regime leader. He’s against that diesel deal that you announced last week. Why, Mr. President, are you right? And Senator Sullivan is wrong on this. Well, look, I have to make deals with people so I don’t go around calling them names. I’m a deal maker. I’ve always been a very good deal maker. I became very rich because of deals. So I don’t go around mocking people. You know, part of the reason you have that war in the first place is Biden went around mocking Russia and mocking everybody else and didn’t know what he was doing. That was a war that should have never started. If I were president, if that election wasn’t rigged and it was rigged, you wouldn’t have had a war with Ukraine and with Russia. So I also feel it’s not all coming to us and it’s diesel. What you need. I feel that it’s great because it’s it’s released to the world. It’s not released us, it’s released out to the world, and it’s going to bring down the price of diesel, all very substantially.
Jon Decker:
Mr. President, I want to thank you so much for taking the time and, your time here in Alaska.
During his speech, President Trump revisited many of his favorite themes and stories. He also urged Alaska voters to vote down “ranked-choice voting”.

title: In Bangor, Mike Johnson calls Paul LePage’s race ‘top 5’ in the country
text:
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
House Speaker Mike Johnson made his second trip to Maine for former Gov. Paul LePage on Wednesday, calling his 2nd District race “a top five race in America right now” as forecasters increasingly see Democrats winning the House.
The Republican in danger of losing his leadership post in the November election spoke to supporters at a meet-and-greet event at Sea Dog Brewing Co., telling them control of the chamber will come down to about 22 districts.
The speaker struck an upbeat tone even as his party’s national picture worsens. His own super PAC is pulling money from Republican incumbents elsewhere. The 2nd District, being vacated by four-term Democrat Jared Golden and won three times by President Donald Trump, is one of the few places where Republicans are playing offense.
“What you do here is not just for Maine,” Johnson said. “It’s for the entire country and the future of freedom.”
Decision Desk HQ, the BDN’s election results partner, gives Democrats a 77% chance of winning the House, up from 59% in July. LePage’s odds against State Auditor Matt Dunlap, the Democratic nominee, have held fairly steady throughout the campaign and now sit at 61%.
Republicans seem to be responding to that picture. The Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Johnson, is cutting off funding to help incumbents and moving $10 million into 16 other districts, including Maine’s 2nd, The New York Times reported Tuesday.
The 2nd District is another story. Republicans and their allies hold a $13.5 million to $10.1 million edge in general-election ads, according to AdImpact. The leadership fund and a group tied to President Donald Trump’s political operation have put about $10.7 million behind LePage, while House Majority PAC has $9 million backing Dunlap.
Johnson told the crowd to discount polls showing Republicans behind, arguing that GOP voters no longer answer pollsters. He also acknowledged the history working against him. A president’s party has gained House seats in his first midterm only twice in 90 years.
“Let’s run like we’re 10 points behind,” he said.
LePage tied his race to U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and asked the crowd to vote for both. He said he wants to join her as “the only Republican out of New England” in the House. The region has had none since Golden unseated two-term incumbent Bruce Poliquin in 2018.
“We need Susan back in Washington,” LePage said of the senator in a crucial race against Democrat Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president.
Dunlap’s campaign pointed to Johnson’s record. The speaker steered last year’s Republican tax-and-spending law, which cut federal Medicaid funding, through the House. LePage backed key parts of that law, including work requirements for Medicaid recipients. House Republican leaders have used procedural rules to block votes on ending Trump’s tariffs.
“Paul LePage will be a rubber stamp for his party bosses in DC,” Harry Burke, Dunlap’s campaign manager, said in a statement.

title: This 78-year-old Vermont logger is also a lawmaker, polo umpire and former pilot
text:
MIDDLESEX, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Jed Lipsky, 78, still works alone cutting down pine trees, a job he has done for 55 years.
A logging career that started young
Lipsky started cutting trees at age 15 in his native Massachusetts, where he also built ski trails.
“So I started cutting when I was 15 and loved it,” Lipsky said. “Very challenging.”
Lipsky uses cutting and wedging techniques to control where a tree falls.
Asked where his crew is, Lipsky said, “You’re looking at him.”
Logging is considered the most dangerous profession in North America, Lipsky said. He has had multiple surgeries and broken bones during his 55 years in the profession.
From skiing to polo
Lipsky has also worked as a competitive skier, a pilot and a professional polo player.
“I’ve had a pretty complex life. Pretty wonderful life,” Lipsky said.
Lipsky now serves as the sole umpire for the Sugarbush Polo Club in Shelburne.
In his early 30s, Lipsky played professional polo, including in the All-Ireland Championships, the Dominican Republic, Hawaii and Texas. During that time, his logging business and his marriage suffered.
“I consider it a quest for glory,” Lipsky said. “And it was a false quest.”
Logger turned legislator
Lipsky, now 78, said working alone gives him time to reflect.
“Every single day you learn, and you generally learn the most from your mistakes,” Lipsky said.
He now serves in the Vermont Legislature as an independent representing Stowe.
“I’m definitely the only logger in the Vermont Legislature,” Lipsky said. “I feel very fortunate.”

title: Bennett, Charles and Pingree to take part in WMTW debate

text:
Rick Bennett, Bobby Charles and Hannah Pingree face off in Maine gubernatorial debate on WMTW
With less than three weeks to go until Election Day, the three chief candidates for Maine governor faced off in an hourlong debate hosted by Maine's Total Coverage on Wednesday. The debate between independent State Sen. Rick Bennett, Republican candidate Bobby Charles and Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree aired on WMTW Channel 8. Below is a summary of how the candidates responded to the questions they were asked during the debate.
A recap of the debate from Maine's Total Coverage political reporter Jackie Mundry and analysis from the In the Arena podcast team is featured in the video player at the top of this page.
You can watch the entire debate in the video player embedded below, or on the WMTW YouTube channel.
Charles and Pingree both won their respective primary races, which each featured crowded fields of candidates. Both primary races also needed to be decided by a ranked-choice voting tabulation. Bennett, meanwhile, was the only independent candidate who secured enough signatures to appear on the ballot for the Nov. 3 general election.
Bennett, a longtime Republican, served in the Maine House of Representatives (1990-94) and has had two separate stints serving Oxford County in the Maine Senate (1996-2004, 2020-present). The former State Senate president (2001-02) left the GOP last year and has centered his campaign around people over party. Bennett has said he wants to tackle housing, energy, childcare and healthcare.
Charles has a campaign slogan of "cut crime, cut taxes, no nonsense." A former assistant U.S. secretary of state under Colin Powell, Charles wants to deal with the drug crisis, eliminate the state income tax and cut property taxes.
Pingree served in the Maine House from 2002 and 2010, and she was elected House Majority Leader (2006-08) and Speaker of the House (2008-10). In January 2019, Gov. Janet Mills appointed Pingree as director of the Office and Policy Innovation and the Future. Pingree held that role until she resigned from the position in May 2025. She then announced her gubernatorial campaign a month later. Pingree said she wants to address housing, climate change and improving outcomes for Maine students.
All three candidates have made affordability one of their top priorities.
The Maine Secretary of State's Office previously announced that there are two declared write-in candidates in the governor's race: independent Jon Glowa and Republican Randy Wilcox.

title: Could GLP-1 drugs be anti-aging medications?
text:
Could GLP-1 drugs be anti-aging medications?
Could GLP-1 drugs be anti-aging medications?
GLP-1 medications for weight loss and diabetes appear to slow the body's aging processes, a sign that the blockbuster drugs could ultimately help people live longer.
Video above: GLP-1 drugs may cut asthma and COPD attacks, study suggests
The idea that these medications may extend lifespan isn't exactly far-fetched; it's more of an extension of what they've already been shown to do. Studies have found that along with helping people shed fat and control blood sugar, GLP-1 drugs improve the health of many different parts of the body, lowering the risk of heart, kidney and liver disease, for example, and reducing sleep apnea and inflammation, which contribute to loss of health and function as people age.
"Aging is the biggest risk factor for many diseases, and if we can target aging itself, we might be able to treat all kinds of diseases that are associated with aging," said Dr. Danica Chen, a professor at the University of California at Berkeley who studies calorie restriction and aging.
Now, scientists have turned their attention to biological markers of aging to better understand exactly how GLP-1 drugs may affect the aging process.
The new research conducted in mice and people is early, and scientists say they don't know whether the benefits apply only to people who are overweight or have diabetes when they start taking the medications, or if they could also slow aging in people who are normal weight and otherwise healthy.
For that reason, experts say it's too early for people to use this medication solely in the hopes of living longer.
"There are people who are 'biohacking' and taking these agents who are not either diabetic or obese, and the question there is what happens in lean younger non-diabetic individuals, especially over the long term," said Dr. James Kirkland, who directs the Center for Advanced Gerotherapeutics at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. "My concern is that people could overread some of this stuff."
Kirkland says the metrics used in the new studies – which are based on measurements of epigenetics, the way genes are turned on and off in the body and the measures of proteins our bodies make over time — are still in development, and although they're useful for studies in larger groups of people, they're not very informative for individuals, though many companies have begun marketing these types of tests to curious consumers.
"They can vary tremendously from day to day within a person," Kirkland said.
Video above: New study suggests GLP-1s may protect against serious infections
Measuring biological clocks
Still, these early findings are generating excitement.
"We're seeing a reduction in age," somewhere around three to six years, said Dr. Kevin Duffin, vice president of aging research at Eli Lilly. Lilly makes tirzepatide, which is sold as Zepbound for weight loss and Mounjaro for diabetes management.
"It's not the panacea. It's not like we're going to reduce age by 30 years or something, but it's a significant reduction," Duffin told a packed audience at the recent Aging Research and Drug Discovery conference in Boston.
Duffin presented new data from Lilly's Surmount V clinical trial, which randomly assigned more than 700 adults who were overweight but did not have diabetes to use either tirzepatide or semaglutide for 72 weeks. The aging study looked at a group of 71 participants from the study who were on tirzepatide and over the age of 50.
By measuring how certain genes in their blood were turned off and on during the course of the study, the researchers were able to look at changes to so-called epigenetic clocks, which reveal the biological age of their organs and tissues, as opposed to their calendar age.
Over the course of the study, Duffin explained, they would have expected a person to age 1.38 years in chronological time. But in the small group of study participants who were using tirzepatide, biological clocks advanced more slowly. Across different types of epigenetic clocks, the researchers saw an average change of between 1.1 years and 0.7 years in biological aging. Some biological clocks actually went backward, suggesting that some organs and tissues were acting younger than when people started the study.
Duffin acknowledged that the study has limitations. There was no placebo group that was not using any weight loss meds to compare against the people on tirzepatide, for example, and the follow-up was relatively brief.
From what the researchers could see, the anti-aging effects seemed to get stronger over time, however, so they hope to follow people for longer in the next trial.
"Be very interesting to see what happens at four or five years after treatment with a GLP-1," Duffin said.
It's also not yet clear whether the slowing of biological aging is due to weight loss or if there could be some effect of the GLP-1 drugs independently. There's a lot of good evidence, for example, that eating a calorie-restricted diet — cutting calories by about 25% — has anti-aging effects and extends the lifespan of many types of animals.
Studies have shown that weight loss surgery, which helps people drop significant amounts of weight, slows biological aging, too. But it's very hard to achieve weight loss or cut calories that much through willpower alone, making the role of medications and surgery critical.
In one of the first questions after his talk, an audience member asked Duffin whether he had repeated the experiment in someone who was not overweight, to see if the effect was a result of weight loss or something else the drug was doing.
"We get this question all the time," Duffin said. "The bottom line is, these drugs work through [blood sugar] reduction and through weight loss, and the effects we're seeing are mostly due to that."
Benefits beyond weight loss
The drug semaglutide, which is sold as Wegovy and Ozempic, shows many of the same anti-aging benefits, according to new research from drugmaker Novo Nordisk.
By measuring changes to proteins in the body over time in people using semaglutide, the company's scientists found that it reduced the heart's biological age by two to four years compared with a placebo, and it reduced the age of organs such as the lung, kidney, brain and pancreas by one to four years. The study was published as a preprint, ahead of peer review.
The researchers said the effects were not completely explained by weight loss, blood sugar control or inflammation.
Study author Dr. Alejandro Aguayo-Orozco, senior global director of cardiometabolic research and development at Novo Nordisk, said the benefits of GLP-1 medications had thus far been measured one disease at a time — but what if the effects were bigger than that?
"If we're touching so many diseases, are we actually also touching something that is systemic across these diseases? Is it aging? Is it health span?" he asked at the recent Aging Research and Drug Discovery meeting.
Recent research in mice tried to answer some of these questions more directly. Mice typically live about two years, so it's easier to follow them throughout their lifespan than it is to do the same for humans.
Scientists at the University of California at Berkeley took 20-month-old mice — roughly the age equivalent of 60-year-old humans — and gave them injections of semaglutide or a placebo for the rest of their lives.
They were roughly the same body weight at the start of the study. But the mice on semaglutide ate less and lost weight, and they lived longer than the mice that got placebo injections. The semaglutide-treated mice had an average lifespan of 834 days, about the same as 80 human years, while the mice injected with placebos lived 742 total days, or roughly 75 human years.
To test whether it was the weight loss or the drug specifically that was responsible for the benefit, researchers next reduced the amount of calories fed to another group of mice by 25% — about the same amount of reduction seen in mice on semaglutide.
Like the GLP-1-treated mice, the calorie-restricted mice lived longer, but there were some differences between the two groups, said Chen at UC Berkeley, who helped lead the research, which was published in the journal Nature.
For many tissue functions the group looked at, especially related to muscle function and mobility, the semaglutide-treated mice and calorie-restricted mice performed about the same.
But mice on semaglutide showed some advantages. They functioned better at thinking and at finding their way out of a maze, and they were better able to manage their blood sugar than mice on calorie restriction alone.
"So that just means that it's more than just a calorie restriction and has additional benefits," Chen said.

title: Toys R Us opening soon in the Auburn Mall as store brand comes back to life
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUBURN — The toy store that many people thought was gone for good is making a comeback nationally, and getting ready to open its doors inside the Auburn Mall.
Toys R Us has leased a 3,600-square-foot space next to the women’s clothing store Maurices. Inventory is being stocked, but no employees were present Wednesday. It’s unclear when the store will open.
According to management at the mall, which has been aggressively recruiting new businesses, Toys R Us has committed to being open year-round. Efforts to contact the company were unsuccessful.
The chain filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2017 and closed all its stores by 2018. WHP Global, a brand management firm based in New York City, acquired a controlling stake in 2021 and has been steadily regrowing the brand.
Toys R Us partnered with retail giant Macy’s and now has stores-within-stores in more than 400 Macy’s locations, including at the Maine Mall in South Portland.
An additional 160 stand-alone stores are coming online through a partnership with Go! Retail Group. Some of its stores are seasonal.
In 2018, Toys R Us stores in South Portland and Bangor were closed as part of the company’s bankruptcy filing.
Toys R Us used to be known as the “big box” of toy stores, but the new format features smaller footprints, collectibles, LEGO sets, and interactive Creator Studios.

title: Worried on behalf of heating oil customers in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Department of Energy’s statistical arm, the Energy Information Administration, announced that total winter heating bills, for households using heating oil, are projected to be 21% higher on average this winter compared to last winter.
The price of heating oil is forecast to average $5.26 per gallon, a 34% increase nationwide. A slightly milder winter in the Northeast is going to slightly lower consumption by about 9%, which will help to soften the total bill increase down to 21%.
I attended college in Maine and lived in Portland and Gorham in the mid-’90s. I have friends in Maine who have been struggling over high energy prices. This winter’s heating bill will require them to make difficult budgetary sacrifices elsewhere.
George Albrecht
Warwick, R.I.

title: South Portland police investigating embezzlement allegations related to Strikers youth soccer club
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - South Portland Police Chief Dan Ahern confirmed that the police department is investigating allegations of embezzlement related to the South Portland Strikers, a popular youth soccer club.
Hundreds of local children are involved with the Strikers, who play home games at the Wainwright Recreation Complex.
The president of the club, Gabe Harp, sent an email to parents Monday night, saying: “The South Portland Strikers Board of Directors is aware of an ongoing matter that involves the potential unauthorized use of club funds in 2025 and 2026 by a former member of our board.”
Ahern would not provide any additional information about the case, including who is being investigated or the amount of money that was embezzled.
“We take our fiduciary responsibilities seriously, have engaged an external financial professional, and are implementing improved financial controls and governance practices,” Harp said in his email to parents.
Harp’s email to parents went on to say that because this is an active legal matter, the organization will not share specifics, and the priority is to cooperate with law enforcement.
The Cumberland County District Attorney’s Office said it could be two to three weeks before the case ends up in the DA’s office and charges are filed.

Northern Light Podiatry is pleased to welcome foot and ankle specialist Justin Garvin, DPM, to Northern Light Podiatry at Sebasticook Valley Hospital. Dr. Garvin joins James Fullwood, DPM, at the Pittsfield podiatry practice.
Dr. Garvin specializes in limb salvage and reconstructive surgery and provides the full spectrum of podiatry care, including diabetic foot care, sports injury care, and conditions involving the ankles, arches, heels, Achilles tendon, plantar fascia, and more.
Dr. Garvin decided to pursue podiatry after having foot reconstruction surgery in high school.

Letter: Matt Dunlap will work for us
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When I think about this coming election, I want to vote for someone who has leadership skills, compassion for voters and taxpayers, and insight into a national economy that is dominated by people who don’t care how their decisions affect everyday families and workers. I want to vote for someone who is not only unlike the president, but someone who will resist the president’s worst policies and attitudes. I want someone who will work for us, not downsize, fleece, or deport us.
Matt Dunlap lives in Old Town, not in a Florida mansion. He is our state auditor, a great way to get to know the reality of Maine’s economy and our needs. Jim Owen
Belfast

title: Federal complaint filed after thousands of dead fish found in Brunswick
text:
Federal complaint filed after thousands of dead fish found in Brunswick, Maine
Friends of Merrymeeting Bay filed a complaint with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) regarding a massive fish kill along the banks of the Androscoggin River in a 1/2-mile stretch near Pinette Landing Park.
In the complaint written to Secretary Debbie-Anne Reese, the environmental conservation non-profit explains they were made aware of thousands of dead young-of-the-year alewives on Sunday, Oct. 11. The fish appeared to have been decapitated or killed by concussive strikes and barotrauma caused by the dam's turbines.
Ed Friedman, chair of Friends of Merrymeeting Bay, wrote that they were in contact with Brookfield, and company officials said they were alerted to the migration Friday morning. The complaint says a public works crew told the company the fish were released from Sabattus Pond.
Brookfield officials say a nighttime shutdown was initiated Friday to allow for safe passage, but around 10 a.m. Saturday fish techs noticed a small number of dead fish. By 2:15 p.m. company officials had initiated a 24-hour shutdown and remained shut down through Monday afternoon.
"Clearly what they did wasn't enough," Friedman told Maine's Total Coverage. "So, we have thousands and thousands of dead alewives on the shore." He's hoping the complaint will lead to infrastructure changes amidst the re-licensing process.
He wrote, "In normal conditions, the only way for migratory fish to pass downstream at Brunswick is through an 18" pipe with a grate over the upstream end and flows of 40 cubic feet per second." Friedman says this passage is situated between turbines and is not easily navigated by migrating species.
"It's kind of like Russian roulette," he said. He believes the health of a river is comparable to the human body. Friedman questioned, "Do you want plaque in your arteries? That's what dams do. A dam with no passage is the same as blocking off your artery, and you have a heart attack, right?"
Friends of Merrymeeting Bay wants all safe passage possibilities to be thoroughly vetted.
Brookfield Renewables did not respond to Maine's Total Coverage's request for comment.

title: Series of suspicious deaths along river trail sparks serial killer fears
text:
LANSING, Mich. (CNN) - A series of suspicious deaths along a Michigan river trail is stoking public fears of a possible serial killer.
Five suspicious deaths have happened along a river trail in Lansing, Michigan, since last October. Four of them were between July and September of this year, all within weeks of each other. The victims were men, ranging in age from 22 to 70 years old.
“One question that we are being asked. Do we have a serial killer in Lansing?” Lansing Police Chief Robert Backus said. “We are looking at the idea or the possibility that these may be related cases.”
Backus says one link is that the victims were all homeless, possibly sleeping outside. The attacks appeared to take place in the early morning hours, roughly 3 to 4 a.m.
A suspect has been arrested and charged in connection with one of the homicides, which took place in late August. He remains in custody without bond and is expected to undergo a mental health evaluation, according to court records.
“Is this a suspect for all the incidents? That is a challenging question to answer,” Backus said.
As the investigation continues, police are stepping up patrols in the area, adding more security cameras and working with local homeless groups to spread awareness.
