title: An engineer’s 41-acre Maine compound of unique homes he built himself is for sale
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Housing
This section of the BDN aims to help readers understand Maine’s housing crisis, the volatile real estate market and the public policy behind them. Read more Housing coverage here.
A 41-acre compound with four separate, unique homes — one of which has 24 sides — located a 35-minute drive from downtown Bangor is on the market for $750,000.
Kosciusko Drive in Stetson holds the four homes that collectively offer roughly 7,500 square feet of living space with eight bathrooms and roughly a dozen bedrooms.
Each is unique in its structure and shape, but all can be lived in year-round, as they have heat, water, septic and electricity, according to Ashleigh Rolfson of Real Broker, the listing agent for the property.
“Each building is so unique and has these little surprises as you look around,” she said. “You really have to see it to understand it.”
The mastermind behind the estate, Dennis Kosciusko, was a mechanical engineer and bought the property in 1973. At the time, it covered 48 acres, but he sold off a few plots to others before beginning construction the following year, Rolfson said.
The first house, known as the Oval House, is a two-story structure covering more than 2,800 square feet with at least five bedrooms and two bathrooms. The property was built in 1974, then an addition with an indoor pool in the basement was created in 1980, according to Rolfson. In 2013 the pool was filled and more bedrooms were added to the home.
Today, the building’s shape resembles an overlapping oval and square, which Kosciusko chose to let in plenty of natural light, Rolfson said. The property is full of unique features, such as swinging couches, a large stone hearth and a porch on one side.
In 1996, Kosciusko built the 1,364-square-foot Tall House, which offers an apartment-style living space on the second floor. The one-bedroom, one-bathroom building has a large circular window, a cavernous car port that Kosciusko used to renovate an old school bus, a covered patio and a greenhouse, Rolfson said.
Kosciusko completed a third yurt-style house in 2006 that appears circular, but actually has 24 sides, making it an icositetragon. The single-story home has one bedroom, two bathrooms and nearly 2,900 square feet of living space.
The building has a circular living space in the middle with the home’s other rooms forming a ring around it. Aside from the home’s unique shape, the building has a deck and a small loft space in the middle, which is accessible via a pull-down ladder.
Kosciusko once held retreats on site and the 24-sided home was used as a gathering place, as some flooring can be removed to reveal a fire pit in the middle of the living room, Rolfson said.
Finally, in 2013, Kosciusko added a 465-square-foot tiny home on the land for his aging father-in-law to live in, according to Rolfson.
“[The homes] are a little dated, but charming, very solid and in great condition,” Rolfson said. “They’re not going anywhere.”
Rolfson said the number of bedrooms across the buildings is flexible, as some rooms now used as offices could become bedrooms if needed.
Kosciusko’s daughter and granddaughter have been the caretakers of the property since his death earlier this year, Rolfson said. They’re now selling it hoping someone new will enjoy the property in full, rather than chop up the land into subdivisions.
The property is exceptionally private, as it’s set back from the main road, and contains fields, two ponds and fruit trees, according to Rolfson.
The site hit the market earlier this month with a $750,000 price tag. The listing hasn’t garnered much interest yet, which Rolfson credited to its unorthodox setup.
“It’s so unique, so the buyer pool for it is pretty small,” she said. “We’re mostly looking for an investor or maybe someone who wants a family compound.”

title: 10 years of Jackson Lab science shows the lifesaving power of genome-matched cancer treatment
text:
Edison T. Liu, MD, is president emeritus of The Jackson Laboratory.
Though I am known to many as a genetic scientist, my origins were in medicine, specifically cancer medicine. So, every question I pursued as a fundamental biologist was anchored with a single goal: “How can I use my findings to better treat my cancer patients?”
Over the years, I have seen how the impact of biomedical research has grown exponentially. Never in history has science been more powerful. Paradoxically, however, the limiting factor today is not the rate of discovery, but the difficulty that talented medical practitioners have in understanding and deploying powerful, but complex, technologies to benefit their patients.
Despite the quality of the physicians and nurses in our rural state, I saw, when I arrived in 2012, that they too were struggling with interpreting the genomic tests of their patient’s cancer. Over the next few years, The Jackson Laboratory (JAX) grew to become a major scientific center for modern cancer genomics, the key technology in clinical decision making for precision oncology.
We had the technical knowledge, and we simply could not let our neighbors flounder when we could help.
JAX’s executive vice president at that time, Chuck Hewett (also a Mainer), and I put our heads together and came up with an idea that would provide advanced genomic testing for cancer patients in Maine, and, importantly, also help guide how these results can be interpreted.
Backed by an $8.4 million initial donation from the Harold Alfond Foundation, the Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative (MCGI) was launched 10 years ago this week, with Bangor oncologist Jens Rueter, MD, leading the effort.
Molded by the three of us, the structure of the MCGI took form: JAX would provide the genomic test for patients who enroll in the MCGI cohort study and establish the computational analytics that linked the mutations with clinical action. JAX set up the statewide genomic tumor board where Maine physicians could present their most difficult cases to their peers, and to genomic experts from across the world. These recommendations became the basis of a treatment plan.
The results were stunning. Nearly all oncology practitioners in Maine participated in the MCGI. Over 1,600 Maine cancer patients were enrolled in the cohort study and, over the past decade, the MCGI touched the lives of more than 4,000 patients and their families.
The genomic tumor boards advised the best treatment for patients tailored by the results of the tumor’s genomic configuration. Patients who received targeted
therapies recommended by the board survived longer with their cancer.
Doctors benefited, too. We found that the participating physicians reported increased self-confidence in interpreting and using genomic reports, which previously seemed confusing. This local success was recognized by our national scientific peers. In 2022,
the National Cancer Institute asked Dr. Rueter and the MCGI to lead a national 18-institution trial to test whether our genomic tumor board would increase the use of targeted therapeutics across all cancers.
Thus, our small rural state became a national leader in “implementation sciences” — the discipline of crafting optimal system-wide approaches to disseminate complex technologies toward improving health outcomes. In the process, we had a discernible impact on the lives of Mainers with cancer.
Ten years on, as we celebrate the Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative’s decennial, that impact continues. But more work lies ahead. We are engaging genetic counselors to help patients navigate any underlying genetic susceptibility to cancer. We have dramatically improved the efficiency of the genomic tumor boards, as well as the depth of the mutational analysis. We are expanding outreach to other hospital systems.
There are many lessons from the MCGI story. One is that community counts, and that mutual support and collective learning leave a powerful and lasting legacy. Perhaps the most pertinent is that “small is mighty.” We are a rural state with a small population distributed across a vast geography, which has demonstrated to the nation how advanced genomic technologies can be effectively distributed to benefit all cancer patients.

title: ‘Steel Magnolias’ at Lewiston’s Public Theatre leans into ‘laughter through tears’
text:
“Steel Magnolias,” the 1987 play by Robert Harling, became a perennial favorite after the movie version hit the big screen a couple of years later. The play’s nearly perfect mix of comedy with some serious themes earned a reputation that continues to draw audiences to theater stages everywhere.
The Public Theatre in Lewiston will be opening its new season with a new production of the play running Oct. 23 to Nov. 8, and Dolly Parton’s recent passing will no doubt add a slightly melancholy touch to the show.
Parton’s character in the film, Truvy Jones, runs the hair salon where a multi-generational group of Southern women bond together through laughter and tears while also getting their hair done.
Heather Dilly, who will play Truvy, is known for her many roles at the Public Theatre over the years, as well as in movies and TV. She was cast in the Public Theatre production before Parton’s death and admits she cried when she heard the news of her passing. Dilly says she feels “lucky that I get to honor her in this way.”
Having family members from the South helped the actress, who’s originally from the Midwest and said she caught the acting bug at the age of 3, to appreciate the power of a good Southern accent.
“Southern accents make a joke land in a way that I will always love,” she said. Most importantly, though, she wants to put a lot of heart into her role — like Parton did.
Both Dilly and director Janet Mitchko cited Truvy’s line about “laughter through tears” as their favorite emotion and the key to fully appreciating the play.
While she didn’t initially plan to direct this production, Mitchko was ultimately drawn to the task after she cast many of her favorite actresses in her role as the Public Theatre’s artistic director. She couldn’t resist the opportunity to “spend time with them in the rehearsal room,” she enthused.
Dilly, in turn, reflected that she finds the director to be a “true partner” and “a trusted guiding light” for her actors.
The veteran of over 30 years of directing at the theater, Mitchko has long found “Steel Magnolias” “very, very funny and also very, very moving — sometimes both at the same time.” She notes that it’s interesting that a male writer could have had such insight into “the humor, heart and strength of women.”
The original 1980s period and “Southern sensibility” within the play will be maintained, though.
“The story itself is quite timeless,” Mitchko said.
Mitchko notes that “Dolly Parton’s passing might make people a little nostalgic to revisit the play.” But she said the story will live on in the hearts of people through the “wonderful foundation of love and friendship” she hopes to bring to life again onstage in Lewiston.
“Steel Magnolias,” Oct. 23-Nov. 8, The Public Theatre, 31 Maple St., Lewiston. Tickets $42, with discounts available. For more, thepublictheatre.org or 207-782-3200.

title: Lewiston shooting victims demand accountability from MCF
text:
Lewiston mass shooting victims demand accountability from Maine Community Foundation
Survivors of the Lewiston mass shootings slammed the Maine Community Foundation (MaineCF) over how funds were handled following the tragedy in October 2023.
A group of survivors held a news conference Wednesday afternoon and said they are still being left in the dark about some of the funds distributed by MaineCF, claiming they have been silenced by the Government Oversight Committee, and that no action has been taken on an investigation.
After the shootings on Oct. 25, 2023, two different funds were created. One fund was created for the survivors and the families of those who were killed, and the other for nonprofit organizations in the Lewiston-Auburn area.
The shooting survivors claim that they were originally told all funds would go to them and the victims' families, and they take issue with the fact that $1.9 million was given to nonprofits. The survivors also claim some nonprofits that received money did not help the victims at all.
"True accountability means that no other family or individual will have to go through what we have in the aftermath of a tragedy at the hands of an unethical nonprofit," said Amy Sussman, whose nephew was killed in the shootings.
"This distribution of funds is not right. We can do better than this. This is not left or right, it's about right and wrong," said Jennifer, a shooting survivor.
Survivors said they have not received any meaningful assistance from Gov. Janet Mills or her staff.
MaineCF maintains that all donations were properly distributed.

title: Scarecrow making popular at annual Apple & Pumpkin Day in Rumford
text:
RUMFORD — On a sunny, brisk day on Oct. 10, it was all about all fun things fall during the annual Apple & Pumpkin Day at the Rumford Center Meeting House.
Among those attending were Erica Damon of Scarborough, with her daughters, Penny, 6, and Evelyn, 3, as well as grandmother Dawna Green of Cumberland.
Erica said they were returning after attending last year’s event. They were here for the scarecrow making. “You just don’t hear about scarecrow making in other places,” she said.
Everything from the wood frame to support the skeleton, clothing, hay and stuffing, hats and more were available.
Other events included a trailer with pumpkins to be used on site for carving and painting, and a hands-on apple cider press for squeezing and fresh cider tasting.
Inside the 1828 meeting house were seasonal fall foods, including pumpkin/squash soup.
This event was hosted by the Rumford Center Village Improvement Society. All proceeds from the event support the ongoing physical and functional restoration of the historic Rumford Center Meeting House.
The next RCVIP fundraiser will be a wreath-making workshop Saturday, Nov. 14, from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the Meeting House, 1352 Route 2.
Cost is $15 per wreath, all materials provided. They will also have coffee, tea, cocoa and mulled cider for sale.

title: Lawyers for NY man shot by ICE say officer fired into car without warning
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Lawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son in New York said in a court filing Wednesday that the agent who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.
The account by lawyers for Oscar Belgal contrasted sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials. They have said officers opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers.”
The Legal Aid Society, in a petition filed in Brooklyn federal court seeking Belgal’s release, said he had picked up his son from school and was stopped in front of a fire hydrant, looking for a parking spot, when “an anonymous, masked man” stormed up to the vehicle with his gun drawn, followed by other masked men with guns.
“The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way,” Belgal’s lawyers wrote. “Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat. One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed.”
New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn’t conclusively resolve the dispute about how the shooting happened.
The video shows a man wearing a sweatshirt and a red hat running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. The window shatters on the second blow.
A second officer comes into view alongside the car and draws his gun. Belgal then pulls into the street, away from the two officers. The car pulls out of view of the camera, with the officer in the red hat in pursuit.
Whatever happened next didn’t appear on the NYPD’s security cameras, but the chase ended just a moment later, with Belgal’s damaged car resting against a concrete barrier with bullet holes in its windshield and a rear window.
Video from bystanders and NYPD body camera footage show that ICE officers handcuffed Belgal and tended to a gunshot wound to his neck as he sat on the pavement outside the car. NYPD officers took Belgal to a nearby hospital.
DHS didn’t comment Wednesday on the claims by Belgal’s lawyers, saying the incident remains under investigation. But DHS officials have maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger.
Belgal’s lawyers said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital. They say he remains detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where he has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his neck. They also say he has lost sensation on the left side of his face and is suffering from impaired hearing.
The Federal Bureau of Prisons, which manages the jail, didn’t immediately comment.
“Mr. Belgal’s detention was unlawful from its inception. ICE officers shot him in the neck in front of his five year-old son, failed to provide him with immediate medical assistance, and now continue to hold him in a facility notorious for medical neglect,” said Perry McAninch and Elyssa Williams, the lawyers representing Belgal.
At a news conference last week, Marcos Charles, the head of ICE’s enforcement and removal operations, said Belgal refused orders to exit his vehicle and then accelerated and smashed into two government vehicles as ICE officers tried to block him from driving away.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has maintained officers didn’t know a child was in the car and blamed Belgal for putting his son’s life in danger.
___
Associated Press reporter Valeria Gonzalez in McAllen, Texas contributed to this story.

title: US stocks drop to their worst day since July as inflation worsens
text:
US stocks drop to their worst day since July as inflation worsens
U.S. stocks dropped to their worst day since July on Wednesday following the latest signal that inflation is getting worse.
The S&P 500 sank 1.1% for a fifth loss in the six days since setting its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 48 points, or 0.1%, and the Nasdaq composite slid 1.9% as stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry led the way lower.
Stocks felt pressure from rising yields in the bond market, where worries grew after a report said U.S. consumers had to pay prices for fuel, food and other costs of living last month that were 3.7% higher overall than a year earlier. That means inflation accelerated from its 3.4% rate in August and was worse than the 3.6% that economists expected.
Inflation has remained more painful than anyone would like since the economy catapulted out of the crevasse created by the COVID-19 pandemic. It's accelerated recently in part because of jumps in fuel prices caused by the war with Iran, and the price for a barrel of Brent crude added 0.4% Wednesday to $106.06.
That has added to the longstanding worries about fast-rising debt loads for governments, signals that the U.S. economy is still growing and other factors that have sent bond yields to their highest levels in years.
The centerpiece of the U.S. bond market, the 10-year Treasury, saw its yield briefly jump above 5.32% from less than 5.17% just before the inflation report's release. It eventually gave back much of the gain.
Yields on shorter-term Treasurys had even bigger leaps as traders raised their expectations for coming hikes to interest rates by the Federal Reserve, though they also moderated as the day progressed.
The Fed recently raised the interest rate that it controls, which affects very short-term loans, for the first time in three years in hopes of reining in inflation. Higher rates do that by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money and slowing the overall economy.
Traders now see a nearly 35% chance the Fed will raise the federal funds rate at its next meeting in two weeks, up from the 22% probability seen a day earlier, according to data from CME Group.
Part of what's keeping inflation high is that Americans overall are continuing to spend, which encourages businesses to keep raising prices for their products and services. As Americans become more "price-sensitive" and the economy also benefits from greater productivity by workers, Vanguard Senior Economist Adam Schickling said inflation should slow, but "patience will be required."
Much of Wall Street's pain on Wednesday was due to drops for companies riding the AI frenzy to huge profit growth and stellar stock gains.
Higher bond yields making borrowing money more expensive could make it more difficult for companies to raise cash to build data centers and fill them with AI chips. Drops of 3.2% for Nvidia, 3.1% for Broadcom and 5.7% for Advanced Micro Devices were among the day's heaviest weights on the S&P 500.
CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, tumbled 15.5% for its worst day since February. GE Vernova, which is hoping to electrify power-hungry data centers, dropped 6.2%, and Oracle sank 8.8%.
Smaller companies also feel the bite of higher interest rates because many need to borrow to grow. The Russell 2000 index of the smallest U.S. stocks fell 1.9%.
Higher yields in the bond market push downward on prices for all kinds of stocks, and the main way companies can offset that is by delivering bigger profits. That's exactly what analysts are expecting, and it's how the S&P 500 has been able to set records despite the many challenges weighing on Wall Street.
But the high expectations also mean companies will likely get punished if they fall short of targets for growth.
Bank of America dropped 4.8% after reporting weaker profit and revenue for the summer than analysts expected. The profit would have failed to meet expectations even if the U.S. Treasury Department had not announced $1.2 billion in fines late Tuesday for alleged violations of anti-money laundering and sanctions laws by the bank.
State Street sank 4.1% after reporting weaker revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected, even though its profit was slightly above their forecasts.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 86.51 points to 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 48.62 to 51,621.48, and the Nasdaq composite sank 511.51 to 26,692.87.
In stock markets abroad, indexes ticked higher in Europe following a weaker finish in Asia. They rose 0.7% in London and fell 0.9% in Shanghai for two of the world's bigger moves.
___
AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

title: Prosecutors urge life sentences for Alexander luxury real estate brokers in sex trafficking case
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Federal prosecutors on Wednesday urged a New York judge to send two of the nation’s most successful luxury real estate brokers and their brother to prison for life for drugging and raping dozens of women over a two-decade stretch, while defense lawyers recommended 15-year terms.
The lengthy written submissions by both sides precede the sentencing later this month of twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 39, and Tal Alexander, 40.
The brothers were convicted in March of multiple charges including sex trafficking, which carries a mandatory minimum penalty of 15 years in prison.
“As the evidence makes clear, the defendants are serial rapists who violated woman after woman and girl after girl for years upon years,” prosecutors wrote. They said they had identified at least 70 victims who were raped or sexually assaulted by at least one of the defendants.
Defense lawyers said the brothers apologize to the women they insulted or offended for conduct they admit was “insensitive toward the feelings of certain women at certain times,” but they added that all three “steadfastly maintain their complete innocence of these awful charges.”
Oren and Tal Alexander, once known as real estate’s “A Team” for their high-ticket sales and celebrity clientele, face sentencing Oct. 27 along with Alon Alexander, who ran their family’s private security company.
Prosecutors said the brothers began sexually assaulting women as early as 2001 or 2002, when they were in high school. As the years passed, the government said, they developed a pattern of drugging and raping women who they enticed to join them on luxury getaways.
“The defendants felt empowered to take whatever they wanted from any woman or girl who agreed to get on a plane, go to a party, or sit at their table at a nightclub,” prosecutors said.
Once sexual assaults began, the brothers “seemed to prefer — when the women protested, struggled to get free, or lay lifeless in front of them,” prosecutors said.
Eleven women testified at their trial, with many of them describing being raped or sexually assaulted after they became disoriented and lost control of their bodies after being given a drink by one of the brothers.
Prosecutors noted that the Probation Office has recommended that each defendant serve 15 years for each victim they raped, which would result in 180-year sentences for Alon and Tal Alexander and 195 years in prison for Oren Alexander.
Defense lawyers described the brothers as “dedicated husbands and fathers” and said they had all lived “lives very different than what was portrayed at trial” for years prior to their 2024 arrests. They have been jailed ever since.
The defense submission projected confidence that the brothers will do well on appeal, saying the evidence was “remarkably weak” on critical points and that the men faced “overwhelming prejudice” as a result of Judge Valerie E. Caproni’s decisions about what evidence the jury saw.
“We fight against injustice,” they wrote.
The lawyers also urged Caproni to see the brothers as “human beings, not the monsters falsely portrayed in Court and in the media.”

title: Join the 14th annual UMaine March Against Domestic Violence Friday
text:
ORONO — The 14th annual March Against Domestic Violence will take place at 5 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 16 starting on the steps of the Fogler Library at the University of Maine.
The march will proceed around the Mall and end in the area near an information booth in the Memorial Union. Following the march, Renate Klein, UMaine associate professor of human development and family studies; and speakers representing Partners for Peace, the UMaine Counseling Center, Triota and other organizations will share insights on domestic violence and ways to detect it to improve safety.
A remembrance ceremony will also be held for lives lost to domestic violence recently. Community resources will be available for those who need them.
For more information about the event, contact Nory Jones at njones@maine.edu.
More one in three women nationwide have experienced contact sexual violence, physical violence and/or stalking by an intimate partner during their lifetime, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

title: Appeals court will hear arguments on Trump's National Guard deployment in the nation's capital
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — More than 14 months after National Guard members began patrolling the streets of the nation’s capital, a federal appeals court on Wednesday will hear arguments over whether they should be sent home.
Oral arguments are scheduled in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. The hearing comes months after the court paused a lower court’s ruling that the deployment was illegal.
President Donald Trump deployed the guard in August 2025 as part of what he said was a crime-fighting mission in Washington, D.C. The force, which rose to a peak of about 5,000 troops over the summer, has supported arrest operations, patrolled city streets and neighborhoods and participated in cleanup efforts.
Trump’s Republican administration says the deployment has contributed to a decrease in crime in the city, where crime was already on the decline before the National Guard arrived. Officials and activists in the overwhelmingly Democratic city say the deployment is a waste of taxpayer money and has normalized the militarization of a major American city.
The case is about whether the president has the authority
At the heart of the court case, brought by D.C.’s attorney general, is whether the president has the authority to deploy the National Guard to the city, which, as a federal district, has limited autonomy over its own affairs. The U.S. Constitution gives federal lawmakers authority over the District of Columbia, while the Home Rule Act of 1973 lets residents elect a mayor, a council and neighborhood commissioners.
The city has argued that the mobilization is an illegal use of the military for domestic law enforcement.
Last December, the three-judge panel that paused the lower court’s ruling said Trump might prevail in his argument that the president “possesses a unique power” to mobilize the guard in Washington.
The court went on to say in a unanimous 32-page ruling that other factors also favored the Trump administration, including the “disruption to the lives of thousands of service members,” as well as what it said was the president’s interest “in the protection of federal governmental functions and property within the nation’s capital.”
The judges found that the district “has not identified any ongoing injury to its statutory interests.”
Even if D.C. wins at the appeals court level, the Trump administration will undoubtedly go to the U.S. Supreme Court, which has already shown deference to the president in a number of cases.
Legal experts look at the arguments that could be made
Syracuse law professor William Banks said D.C. might have a slim argument under its home rule, questioning whether National Guard units can be deployed to the city when it isn’t authorized by local law.
But, he said, outside of that argument “there is no overarching federal principle that would bail out the district in this case.”
Because D.C. is not a state and because the president is commander in chief, there’s a “tremendous amount of leeway and discretion for the president” to control or delegate control of the local National Guard and out-of-state units, Banks said.
Margaret Hu, a professor at the William and Mary School of Law, said one issue to look for was raised by states supporting the deployment in court briefs. They argued the president was reacting to an emergency. Hu said the open-ended manner of the deployment might allow a challenge to that.
“Some argue that the indefinite nature of the deployment means that there’s no emergency justification here,” she said.
A judge said Trump couldn’t unilaterally deploy the DC National Guard
U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb concluded last November that Trump’s military takeover in Washington illegally intrudes on local officials’ authority to direct law enforcement in the district.
Cobb found that while the president does have authority to protect federal functioning and property, he can’t unilaterally deploy the D.C. National Guard to help with crime control as he sees fit or call in troops from other states. She put her order on hold for 21 days to allow the appeal by the Trump administration.
The appeals court stayed the order and has allowed the guard to remain in place while the case is pending.
The mobilization, extended until January 2029 by the Defense Department, has taken on a sense of permanence, despite the court case.
The federal government awarded a $292 million contract to a private company to provide members of the Joint Task Force-D.C. with apartments. The numbers have grown as well, ballooning to around 5,000 during the height of the semiquincentennial celebration. As of last week, that number had dropped to about 2,900.

title: Social Security recipients to get 3.6% cost of living boost, an average of $75 per month
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities — including about 400,000 people in Maine — will go up by 3.6% next year.
Some say it’s not enough to offset soaring prices.
The adjustment, which accounts mostly for inflation, translates to an average of $75 extra per month for the 73 million people nationwide who receive monthly Social Security benefits and the nearly 7.5 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
In all, the cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries will add about $360 million to Mainers’ pockets next year, and the Social Security Administration’s commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.”
But most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices. The adjustment for this year was 2.8%, following 2.5% in 2025, 3.2% in 2024 and a historically large 8.7% jump in 2023.
And these are top issues for older Mainers, a key, high-turnout demographic in the upcoming midterm elections: Another AARP poll of older Maine voters found that their top concerns were affordability and Social Security and Medicare.
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits facing many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — 1 in 5 have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last,” AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan said.
AARP Maine State Director Noël Bonam said there is a flaw in the Social Security annual adjustment system, which is based on year-on-year measures by the Bureau of Labor Standards: It simply does not account for the true cost of living.
The recent national AARP poll found that almost 40% of Social Security recipients planned to reduce their expenses on everyday needs, including groceries and medication. The more accurate annual increase, those respondents said, would be 5% to 8%.
The cost of goods such as heating oil have rocketed well past the pace of inflation since the start the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran this spring. Those costs reached an all-time high last month, and the Natural Resources Council of Maine found families in Maine will spend an additional $1,200, at least, this winter filling their tanks.
Jess Maurer, the executive director of the Maine Council on Aging, said it cost 60% more to fill her tank this year than it did last fall.
That’s untenable for the one-third of Mainers age 65 and older who have no major savings or other income than Social Security, she said. Many, Maurer said, will have tough decisions to make this winter: medication or food or fuel.
“A 3.6% cost of living increase for people who already don’t have enough money to meet their basic needs — $75 a month isn’t going to cut it,” Maurer said. “It may, in fact, cover the increased cost of food, but it won’t cover the increased cost of goods and of fuel oil for the winter.”
Maurer said older women, especially those living alone, will be among the hardest hit by the disconnect between increases in Social Security benefits and the cost of living. Maine women, she said, are more likely to have worked in lower-paying careers or to have left work to become caregivers. That often means they paid less into Social Security over their working years.
“It is definitely women who get caught in that circle more than men, and it’s been women who have fewer resources later in life,” she said. “They’re the folks who are getting squeezed right now.”
Meanwhile, the Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old-age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Massachusetts, and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. The COLA is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
Treating all income the same “would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” Warren and Moreno wrote in The New York Times. The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the cap would add roughly $3 trillion to the program over the next 10 years.
The solution will require tons of new money, Maurer said — but it’s necessary.
“It is about survival, not thriving, at this point for a lot of older Mainers,” she said.
This story contains reporting from The Associated Press.

title: ‘It’s a forever change’: supporting aging parents through loss of a child
text:
(Aging Untold) — Losing a child is something no parent expects to face, no matter their age.
The Aging Untold experts are talking candidly about why this grief is so often overlooked in older adults and how families and caregivers can help.
An “unnatural” loss, no matter your age
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, pointed out a troubling pattern she’s seen in her work with older adults.
“One of the saddest things I see is when we have our aged community and they lose their child, and it’s not treated the same,” Cradduck said. “If you’re my age and you lose a child, everybody rallies around and they’re there for you. But when an aged person loses their child, it’s like, ‘Well, you’re old. What do you expect?’ ... I think that is such an unfairness that we have allowed ourselves to do.”
A story from the nursing home
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, shared a personal memory from her time as a nursing home administrator that illustrates how older adults’ grief could go unacknowledged.
“I greeted a new resident, went into the room, sat at the bedside and we were just talking, and all of a sudden she started telling me about her daughter who had died of cancer. It broke my heart,” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke described how her team responded.
“We got activities, we got social services, we got the chaplain, got everybody together, and I said we’re going to keep an eye on her. Let her talk, let her grieve. Let her say her daughter’s name. Let her share the memories, look at the photos and remember her so you can create some history with her,” O’Rourke said.
A grief that never fully resolves
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said there is a prolonged grieving process for a parent mourning the death of a child.
“I’ve had a couple of friends and colleagues and your heart just hurts for them. But to see how they can sometimes get stalled is very hard to get over,” Rogers said.
A shift in perspective helped Rogers’ friends and colleagues while navigating loss.
“I listened to them and they said, ‘You know, hey, I had to remember the time that they were here and concentrate on the good, not look at this loss, and celebrate the life,” Rogers said.
She said that helped the people she knows stay intact physically, emotionally and spiritually.
Cradduck added that acceptance — not resolution — is the realistic goal.
“I think you have to assume that you’re always going to grieve this loss,” Cradduck said. “You can make it to acceptance, which is the goal. But I don’t think you ever will ever not be grieving that child. I believe that’s just something that’s significant and it stays forever. And I think you have to go into it knowing that this is a forever change.”
Staying connected helps everyone heal
O’Rourke shared an example from a neighbor who lost her daughter but chose to stay close to her son-in-law and grandchildren.
“She faced the fear of being there without her daughter, but she said it was one of the best things that she did, because when they talked about the daughter, it helped her heal,” O’Rourke said.
Cradduck noted the ripple effect of that choice.
“It helped her son-in-law, and it helps those grandchildren to keep that memory alive and keep that person alive,” Cradduck said.
You don’t need the right words — just presence
Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, offered guidance for friends and family who aren’t sure how to support a grieving parent.
“Don’t feel like you need to have the right words — just your presence is enough, just being there,” Ambrose said. “Also giving people permission to not be OK, and that there’s no time limit, there’s no comparison on how long you feel a certain way. People can grieve for the rest of their lives.”
Finding purpose in the pain
Several hosts pointed to purpose and legacy as paths toward healing.
Rogers observed that many grieving parents find a way to honor their child by helping others.
“When they have a loss of a child, they find another purpose to help you maintain the memory of that person,” Rogers said. “That’s a healthy way of doing it.”
Cradduck shared a personal connection to this idea, describing a close friend whose son was an organ donor.
“She knows where some of his organs went to,” Cradduck said. “I’ve watched the change in her, and I know that it’s a forever change for her, as it is for her entire family. But there is a peace that can come, and I think that has to be recognized. There can be a peace that comes in finding the purpose for that pain and doing something with it.”
Cradduck closed with a message for anyone going through this kind of loss.
“If you’re going through it, please find a way to make that pain purposeful and let that legacy live on,” Cradduck said.

title: Struggling UMaine football prepping for Bryant with new offensive coordinator
text:
The University of Maine’s struggling football team, now 1-5 and the loser of five straight games, is preparing for Saturday’s contest against visiting Bryant University with new offensive coordinator Sean Green trying to improve an offense that is one of the worst in the conference.
Green, who had previously been the running backs coach, replaced Mikahael Waters, who was fired on Oct. 5. Waters was also the quarterbacks coach.
In the Coastal Athletic Association conference alone, the Black Bears are last among the 13 teams in points scored (14.5), total yards per game (270.17) and touchdowns (9). They are 12th in passing yards per game (174.17) and pass completion percentage (52.04), and 11th in rushing yards (96) and average yards gained per rush (3.11).
Fifth-year head coach Jordan Stevens said he has been pleased with how the players and coaches have responded to the change while adjusting to Green, who is in his first year at UMaine.
Stevens said when it comes to reshaping the offense, the team isn’t going to make any major changes.
“We aren’t in a position where we’re changing the terminology or anything like that with the players,” explained the head coach.
“For us, we just want to continue to find a way to be more balanced in what we’re doing in the run game and pass game. Being better in situational football,” Stevens said. “We have a very talented group on offense starting at the quarterback position down to our offensive line.”
Green will be calling the offense against Bryant, Stevens added. Green has called plays in the past and Stevens is confident in his ability.
As a head coach, Green led Portland and Cape Elizabeth High Schools to state championships and he has also been the quarterbacks coach at the University of New England in Biddeford, where he was involved in the offensive play-calling.
In their last game, a 24-16 loss to Sacred Heart, UMaine alternated quarterbacks Eddie Buehler and Caden Drezek throughout the game until Drezek engineered a six-play, 69-yard scoring drive early in the fourth quarter that cut the lead to 21-16. Drezek played the rest of the snaps.
This is Buehler’s first season in which he has started every game.
Stevens said he didn’t know what their approach will be with the quarterback position on Saturday. He said both did well in the previous game.
“They weren’t the root of our shortcomings against Sacred Heart. We are working through the quarterback position and how we are going to manage it this week,” Stevens said.
Buehler completed one of five passes for 13 yards against Sacred Heart and Drezek completed 12-of-28 for 141 yards.
Buehler has connected on 54.6 percent of his passes (84-for-154) for the season for 828 yards and four touchdowns with six interceptions. Drezek has completed 17 of 40 for 201 yards and a touchdown. He hasn’t been intercepted.
While UMaine is 1-5 overall and 1-2 in the CAA, Bryant is 4-2 and 2-0 in its third season in the conference. The teams play at 1 p.m.
Stevens said redshirt junior tight end Elijah Smalls, who is fourth on the team in receptions with eight for 80 yards, is expected to be back sometime this season after injuring his knee hurdling a Pioneer in the Sacred Heart game. Smalls landed awkwardly out of bounds and didn’t return.

title: Lawsuit alleges Hannaford improperly markets some salmon products as sustainable
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A class-action lawsuit filed this week alleges that Hannaford and its parent company display “misleading sustainability guarantees” in the grocery chain’s seafood sections.
The complaint, filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York, narrows in on salmon products that it claims are not sustainably sourced, as in-store signage suggests.
A Hannaford spokesperson said Wednesday that the company does not comment on pending litigation and that neither the Scarborough-based grocer nor its Dutch parent company, Ahold Delhaize, had received the complaint.
The suit states that Hannaford stores all contain signs that indicate their seafood products are sustainably sourced, including ones reading, “We sell only high-quality, traceable and sustainably harvested seafood,” and “Every fish has a tale. Ours you can trust.”
“In reality, Hannaford sells industrially farmed salmon whose production inflicts grave harms on pristine marine ecosystems and has caused the destruction of marine life around the world, from Canada to Chile,” the lawsuit says.
The 76-page complaint includes numerous pictures of signage at Hannaford locations and products in question.
The lead plaintiff in the suit is Kathleen Boyle, of Queensbury, New York. It states she purchased at least some of the products cited at Hannaford stores in New York throughout 2025 and 2026, believing they were “sourced from suppliers whose practices did not harm marine ecosystems” and were otherwise sustainable.
The lawsuit includes as class members anyone who bought any of the products in question in New York within the statute of limitations. The complaint says that the plaintiff believes there are thousands of people who fit this description.
The suit focuses on salmon products predominantly sourced overseas, though some stem from Maine and elsewhere in the United States. It argues those products are not truly sustainable, citing reports of mass mortality events, and details many regions’ salmon farming practices — especially in Chile, where it says some suppliers have histories of overproduction and farming in sensitive or protected areas.
The lawsuit notes that if Hannaford’s products are truly traceable, then it would be aware of some of these “destructive” practices. If not, “their sustainability promises were nevertheless empty and false” when it comes to those products, the complaint says.
The plaintiff is seeking a jury trial and monetary relief.

title: Don’t close the door, Mom, I’ll be back
text:
Abdullahi Ahmed, Ed.D., of Portland is a naturalized citizen who came to the U.S. as a refugee from Somalia. He has worked for the Portland Public Schools since 2001.
When I left Somalia, I did not think I was leaving my country. I thought I was leaving for a while. I can still imagine the moment of departure. The uncertainty of the journey was real, but so was the belief that I would return. Somewhere in my mind, I was already planning my way back. I did not know how long I would be gone, but I did not imagine that the distance between me and home would grow into years, decades and eventually most of my adult life.
Perhaps this is one of the quietest and most powerful dreams of an immigrant: I will come back. People leave their homes with a suitcase, a few belongings, memories and a promise to themselves and to the people they love. They leave believing that the door they walk through is not a door that closes behind them. It is only a door they will walk through again.
That is why I imagine telling my mother, “Do not close the door. I will be back.” I did not say those exact words, but they describe what I carried in my heart. I was not saying goodbye to Somalia, to Mogadishu, the city I love. I was saying, “Wait for me.”
Like many immigrants, I thought my absence would be temporary. I imagined returning to the streets I knew, to familiar voices, familiar food, familiar smells and the landscape that had shaped my childhood. I imagined sitting with family again, telling stories about the places I had traveled and the things I had learned. But immigration has a way of changing the meaning of time.
A year becomes several years. Several years become a decade. Children grow up. Parents grow older. Friends move away. Neighborhoods change. The streets you remember remain in your memory, but sometimes they no longer look the same even when you return. Eventually, you realize that you have been away longer than you ever imagined.
Yet something strange happens to an immigrant during those years. While I am away from my country, my country is never completely away from me. I could not continue living in Somalia, but Somalia continued living in me. I carried Somalia into Pakistan. I carried it with me when I came to America. I carried its language, its stories, its hospitality, its struggles, its humor, its faith, its food, its memories and the voices of the people who raised me. In many ways, my country did not carry me. I carried my country.
That may be one of the great contradictions of immigration. We leave because circumstances, opportunity, education, safety, family, war, poverty or hope push us beyond our borders. We cross oceans and continents looking for another life. But crossing a border does not mean leaving everything behind. The country we leave often becomes even more present inside us. We become immigrants, but we also become living memories of somewhere else.
I became an American. I built a life in Maine. I became an educator and educational leader, a husband, a father and a member of communities that welcomed me. America became home in ways I could never have imagined when I first arrived. But becoming part of a new country did not erase the old one. There is a Somali tradition that captures something about this experience: wherever you travel, you carry your identity with you. That is what immigrants do. We build new homes while carrying old ones and identities inside our hearts.
When I think about that imaginary door, I understand now that the promise to return was about more than geography. It was a promise to remain connected. I may not have been able to live in Somalia, but Somalia has continued to live in me. Perhaps this is why so many immigrants keep saying, in one form or another, “I will be back.” We leave believing we are going for a short time. We leave with hope in our hearts and return tickets in our minds. But life has its own plans.
Still, somewhere inside the immigrant heart, the door never completely closes. We continue to look back. We continue to remember. We continue to carry. And even after decades away, a part of us is still standing at that door, telling our mothers: “Do not close it. I will be back.”

title: Social Security will jump 3.6% next year. How far does that really go in Maine?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities — including about 400,000 people in Maine — will go up by 3.6% next year.
Some say it’s not enough to offset soaring prices.
The adjustment, which accounts mostly for inflation, translates to an average of $75 extra per month for the 73 million people nationwide who receive monthly Social Security benefits and the nearly 7.5 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
In all, the cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries will add about $360 million to Mainers’ pockets next year, and the Social Security Administration’s commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.”
But most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices. The adjustment for this year was 2.8%, following 2.5% in 2025, 3.2% in 2024 and a historically large 8.7% jump in 2023.
And these are top issues for older Mainers, a key, high-turnout demographic in the upcoming midterm elections: Another AARP poll of older Maine voters found that their top concerns were affordability and Social Security and Medicare.
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits facing many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — 1 in 5 have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last,” AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan said.
AARP Maine State Director Noël Bonam said there is a flaw in the Social Security annual adjustment system, which is based on year-on-year measures by the Bureau of Labor Standards: It simply does not account for the true cost of living.
The recent national AARP poll found that almost 40% of Social Security recipients planned to reduce their expenses on everyday needs, including groceries and medication. The more accurate annual increase, those respondents said, would be 5% to 8%.
The cost of goods such as heating oil have rocketed well past the pace of inflation since the start the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran this spring. Those costs reached an all-time high last month, and the Natural Resources Council of Maine found families in Maine will spend an additional $1,200, at least, this winter filling their tanks.
Jess Maurer, the executive director of the Maine Council on Aging, said it cost 60% more to fill her tank this year than it did last fall.
That’s untenable for the one-third of Mainers age 65 and older who have no major savings or other income than Social Security, she said. Many, Maurer said, will have tough decisions to make this winter: medication or food or fuel.
“A 3.6% cost of living increase for people who already don’t have enough money to meet their basic needs — $75 a month isn’t going to cut it,” Maurer said. “It may, in fact, cover the increased cost of food, but it won’t cover the increased cost of goods and of fuel oil for the winter.”
Maurer said older women, especially those living alone, will be among the hardest hit by the disconnect between increases in Social Security benefits and the cost of living. Maine women, she said, are more likely to have worked in lower-paying careers or to have left work to become caregivers. That often means they paid less into Social Security over their working years.
“It is definitely women who get caught in that circle more than men, and it’s been women who have fewer resources later in life,” she said. “They’re the folks who are getting squeezed right now.”
Meanwhile, the Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old-age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Massachusetts, and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. The COLA is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
Treating all income the same “would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” Warren and Moreno wrote in The New York Times. The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the cap would add roughly $3 trillion to the program over the next 10 years.
The solution will require tons of new money, Maurer said — but it’s necessary.
“It is about survival, not thriving, at this point for a lot of older Mainers,” she said.
This story contains reporting from The Associated Press.

title: Cony girls soccer surges past Lincoln in second half
text:
AUGUSTA — It was a situation that might have caused concern for the Cony girls soccer team if it had happened a month ago.
Instead, the Rams responded with a flourish.
After falling behind in the second half, Cony scored two goals in the final 20 minutes to beat Lincoln Academy, 2-1, in a Class B game Wednesday afternoon at Fuller Field.
The Rams (8-4-1) are in a title battle with Hermon, Skowhegan and Belfast for fourth place in the Class B North Heal points standings as they continue their climb after starting the season with three losses in their first four games.
“That was huge, that was a really big game for us,” said Cony junior forward Kya Douin, who had a goal and an assist. “We knew (Lincoln Academy) was a really good team and we had to work hard in the last few practices and just grind it out.”
Here are some other takeaways from Wednesday’s game:
How did it happen?
After a scoreless first half, Lincoln (8-4) took the lead when sophomore Dory Westhaver pushed the ball into the net from a scrum in front of Cony senior keeper Charlotte Gearhart off a corner kick.
Cony responded less than four minutes later when Douin sent a kick from 17 yards that bent to the left and over the head of Eagles keeper Natalie Hanna.
“You could see, from that moment, we felt like we were going to win,” said Cony coach Michael Sweeting.
Four minutes later, Douin sent a perfectly placed ball up the middle of the field to junior forward Riley Miller, who took off on a breakaway and knocked a low shot past Hanna.
What does it mean?
After a 3-7-4 record a season ago, Cony has already secured its best season under Sweeting. In the last two weeks, the Rams have a victory over Class B North rival Erskine Academy and a tie against Class C South contender Hall-Dale.
“We’re not just a boot-it-and-run team anymore,” Sweeting said. “We still play forward fast, we still try to be aggressive, but it’s with a purpose now.”
Not only will the Rams be in the playoffs, but with Wednesday’s win, they’ll likely host a preliminary-round game.
“This team has really done a good job of getting together and playing for each other,” said Sweeting, who is in his third year leading the program. “It’s been a little bit of a journey for this team … It looks like we’re going to have a home playoff game next week, and it’s been a minimum of 16 years since (the program) has had that.”
Lincoln entered the match ranked No. 5 in Class B South, with a season sweep over Erskine on its record.
Unsung hero
Playing in her final regular-season game at Fuller Field, Gearhart made six saves for the Rams and was a vocal leader for a defense that allowed just three shots in the second half.
“Our defense is our rock right now,” Douin said. “We have so much faith in them in the back. I don’t worry about them at all.”
Gearhart was one of the two Cony seniors honored before the game, with midfielder Kelsie Huard.
“They really deserve (this win),” Sweeting said of his two seniors.
Statistical leaders
Cony: Kya Douin (1 goal, 1 assist), Riley Miller (1 goal), Charlotte Gearhart (6 saves)
Lincoln Academy: Dory Westhaver (1 goal), Natalie Hanna (7 saves)

title: Matt Dunlap will work to protect Mainers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I am writing to support the candidacy of Matt Dunlap for Congress from Maine’s 2nd Congressional District.
As a senior citizen, I appreciate that one of Matt’s priorities is to protect Medicare and Social Security so older Mainers can depend on the benefits they have earned over their working lives. As the cost of living continues to soar for all of us — especially for food and heat — we need a representative who will work to eliminate the tariffs and the war in Iran, which are hitting families very hard.
Finally, as a mother of two adult daughters, I strongly support Matt’s position to always support a woman’s right to make decisions about her own healthcare. I am voting for Matt because he will work to protect the rights and welfare of all Mainers.
Susan Staples
Bryant Pond

title: Bicyclist hit, killed by freight train
text:
BILOXI, Miss. (WLOX/Gray News) — A man riding a bike was hit and killed by a train while trying to cross the tracks in front of it, according to police.
The Biloxi Police Department reported the man was hit and killed by a freight train at about 8 a.m. Tuesday on the tracks near Eisenhower Drive.

title: Reports of discolored tablets lead FDA to recall Amazon-branded acetaminophen bottles
text:
Amazon-branded acetaminophen recalled after reports of discolored tablets
Reports of discolored tablets found inside bottles of extra strength acetaminophen sold on Amazon has led to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issuing a nationwide recall.
Related video: How to stay ahead of recalls
The FDA said in an enforcement report that Aurobindo Pharma USA Inc., based in New Jersey, issued the recall on Sept. 18, which covers 112,932 bottles of 500-milligram acetaminophen caplets sold through Amazon.
Extra Strength Acetaminophen sold on Amazon in 200, 500, and 1,000-count bottle are affected. The affected medication lots and expiration dates are listed as follows:
- 200-count bottle
  - Lot ACD125040A, expiration date Sept. 30, 2027
- 500-count bottle
  - Lot ACD124036A and ACD124030A, expiration date Sept. 30, 2027
  - Lot ACD124042A, expiration date Oct. 31, 2027
  - Lot ACD124048B, expiration date Nov. 30, 2027
  - Lot ACD125010A, expiration date Feb. 29, 2028
- 1000-count bottle
  - Lot ACD124048A, expiration date Nov. 30, 2027
The medication recall comes after the company said it received complaints from consumers of tablets inside being discolored.
It is unclear, at this time, the risk the discoloration may pose if the tablets are taken.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Acetaminophen is an over-the-counter medication used to temporarily relieve pain and reduce a fever. It is available in different forms including tablets, capsules, liquids, and powders.

title: CHINA: Uncontested races, referendum questions on Nov. 3 ballot
text:
China voters have uncontested local elections (with room for write-ins on the ballot) and four local referendum questions to answer at the polls on Nov. 3.
Polls in the portable building behind the town office will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Registered voters may also vote in person at the town office during office hours through Thursday, Oct. 29.
The candidates for select board are incumbents Edwin Bailey, Blane Casey and Thomas Rumpf. Town Clerk Sydney Laird said as of Oct. 13, there are no declared write-in candidates.
Art. 3 on the Nov. 3 local ballot asks voters to authorize the select board to spend up to $750,000 to buy a new fire truck, to be owned by the town and used by the China Village Volunteer Fire Department. Money to pay for the truck will include the $200,000 voters appropriated at the June 9 town meeting and any grants or gifts received.
Art. 4 asks voters, if Art. 3 is approved, to authorize the select board to borrow up to $550,000 to finish paying for the fire truck.
The select board recommended approval of Art. 3 on a split vote, three in favor and two opposed. Its members unanimously recommend approval of
Art. 4. The budget committee recommends approval of each article, with five members in favor and one, who is also a fire department member, abstaining.
A short article in the Oct. 3 issue of the town’s China Connected newsletter explains why the department needs to replace an existing truck, advantages of a replacement and specifically advantages of a new truck over a used one.
Art. 5, unanimously recommended by the select board, asks voters to replace the current China solid waste ordinance with a new one titled “Solid Waste Management and Resource Recovery Ordinance.”
This ordinance is on the China website, chinamaine.org. The Elections tab on the right side of the main page opens a list of ordinance amendments, with Solid Waste at the bottom.
Its 56 pages are less dismaying than they sound; the text doesn’t begin until page 10, and each of the 10 sections starts on a new page, providing partly-blank pages between most of them.
At the Oct. 5 select board meeting, Town Manager Rebecca Hapgood said the new ordinance is a complete rewrite of the old one. The new one, she said, is more clearly arranged; it is updated, for example by adding electronic waste (which is eligible for a resource recovery program, under Section 6.2) and strengthening provisions for inspecting loads being brought in (Section 5.11; Section 5.12 lists grounds for rejecting a load of waste).
The final Nov. 3 warrant article, also recommended by all five select board members, asks voters to approve specified amendments to four sections of China’s Land Development Code, those covering phosphorus control, flood plain management, appeals and definitions.
These changes are also on the town website, under elections and listed right above the new solid waste ordinance.
The major changes to the phosphorus control section are additions of references to state Department of Environmental Protection standards.
Amendments to the floodplain ordinance are more varied. Some of the substantive amendments add a provision that utilities (as well as buildings and other man-made things) be at least a foot above the base flood level; and add provisions for a variance from floodplain ordinance requirements.
If a property-owner receives a variance, the ordinance says that “the applicant agrees in writing that the applicant is fully aware of all the risks inherent in the use of land subject to flooding, assumes those risks, and agrees to indemnify and defend the municipality against any claims filed against it that are related to the applicant’s decision to use land located in a floodplain and that the applicant individually releases the municipality from any claims the applicant may have against the municipality that are related to the use of land located in a floodplain.”
Amendments to the appeals section are consistent: wherever there is a time limit for action, the words “unless this time period is extended by agreement [or sometimes “by written agreement”] of both parties” are added.
The definitions section has one updated reference and three added definitions, of “agricultural structure,” “containment wall” and “qualified professional.”
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!
