To help, please visit our online donation page or mail a check payable to The Town Line, PO Box 89, South China, ME 04358. Your contribution is appreciated!

title: Roller coaster rider's death puts spotlight on the safety of ever more thrilling rides
text:
The horrific death of a man who was ejected from a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia is drawing attention to the safety of amusement park rides that have become increasingly faster and steeper in their quest for the biggest thrill.
Even so, deaths on roller coasters are still extremely rare, and Georgia officials have said little about what happened Monday when Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, was thrown from his seat while riding the Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia before striking other patrons and then landing below the ride.
Goliath uses a sheer drop from 200 feet (61 meters) to reach top speeds of 70 mph (112 kph) and focuses on velocity and downhill plunges rather than turning riders upside down through loops or corkscrews. It has operated at the park for two decades.
Six Flags temporarily closed nine similar coasters across North America following the death, saying it was doing so out of an abundance of caution.
Ride manufacturer Bolliger & Mabillard said it is “actively investigating the incident and will not comment further until we have a better understanding of what happened.”
The US has a patchwork of rules regarding rides
In the U.S., roller coasters and other rides at major amusement parks such as Six Flags are not regulated by the federal government. That responsibility falls to states.
Some say this has led to an inconsistent patchwork of rules where some states have strict regulations and others have little to no oversight.
U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has repeatedly introduced legislation to close what he calls a “loophole” in federal law that allows U.S. safety officials to regulate mobile rides, but prevents the Consumer Product Safety Commission from overseeing stationary rides like those at major amusement parks.
Brian Avery, a University of Florida professor and amusement ride safety expert, agrees that more federal regulations are needed.
“Who’s watching those in these organizations to ensure that they are adequately trained, that they are compliant, that they are monitoring these rides to the level in which the standards have established?” Avery said.
Georgia’s Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which oversees annual ride inspections in the state, is “conducting an in‑depth and comprehensive review” of what happened Monday at Six Flags, said Garrison Bennett, a spokesperson.
Amusement park industry has set its own safety standards
Amusement park operators worldwide generally adhere to what are known as ASTM standards set by industry experts, which cover everything from ride design and construction to how much acceleration and force each rider is allowed to experience.
The industry has multiple layers of inspection, said Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group. Park operators are under pressure from insurance carriers that could face a hefty payout if something goes wrong.
“With the checks and balances that are put in place, theme parks are really one of the safest places to be on the planet,” he said in a phone interview Tuesday.
The trade group said the chance of being seriously injured on a U.S. amusement park ride is 1 in 15.5 million rides taken.
Martin Lewinson, a roller coaster expert and a professor at Farmingdale State College, said it was difficult to imagine there being a mechanical malfunction on a roller coaster such as Goliath because of its design.
The ride features a pull-down lap restraint, called a “clamshell,” that works with a ratchet mechanism that makes clicking sounds as you press it down over your hips. These have multiple disks to ensure redundancy if one fails, Lewinson said.
“They’re dependable. They’re not so technically advanced that theme parks have difficulty with operations,” Lewinson said.
The operator then has a safety system that displays a green “go” light for every seat on the train before it can be dispatched. The train should theoretically not be allowed to proceed unless all restraints are locked, Lewinson said.
But few things are 100% safe.
In 2022, a 14-year-old Missouri boy fell to his death from an Orlando amusement park ride when the harness didn’t lock properly due to his size. In 2013, a 52-year-old Dallas woman was killed when she slipped out of her seat on the Texas Giant ride at Six Flags Over Texas. Six Flags has since added redesigned restraint-bar pads, seat belts and a coaster seat at the ride’s entrance so guests can check before they get on whether they fit safely into the cars.
Nick Mendenhall, who has been on the Goliath more than a dozen times in recent weeks, said he saw Six Flags staff check the restraints each time he rode it.
“There are two employees, one on either side of the train, and with their hands they push down and they make sure it locks every time. I’ve never seen them not do it,” Mendenhall said.
States handle oversight in different ways
In California, the state Department of Industrial Relations approves new rides and rides that have been modified. State officials either directly inspect them and how they are being operated each year or rely on an annual inspection by the owner, according to the department’s website.
Florida’s largest theme parks, on the other hand, are exempt from state safety inspections, unlike smaller venues and fairs. Instead, the largest theme parks like Walt Disney World and Universal conduct their own inspections and have their own protocols, but they must report to the state any injury or death. Texas, similarly, relies on inspections carried out by private inspectors hired by park operators or their insurance companies.
Arizona, where Six Flags Hurricane Harbor Phoenix is located, does not have a state-level agency that regulates amusement park rides or conducts safety inspections at all. The law requires an annual private inspection, with enforcement largely by local government.

title: Showers and wintry weather later this week
text:
Showers and wintry weather later this week
Showers and wintry weather later this week
Rain moves back into Maine on Friday as low pressure strengthens to our west. Rain will spread into western Maine around noon, bringing another beneficial soaking with rainfall totals expected around three-quarters of an inch. Because this system moves quickly, rain should last about eight to 12 hours in any given location.
Wintry precipitation is possible at higher elevations Friday morning, with cooler northwest winds arriving Friday night and bringing a better chance for snow showers across western Maine's mountains and foothills.
A sharp shift to winter-like conditions arrives Saturday behind a strong cold front. High confidence points to a blustery weekend with temperatures well below normal for mid-October. Northwest winds gusting over 40 mph could lead to isolated power outages from downed tree branches, especially along the eastern slopes of the mountains, and a wind advisory may be necessary.
Wind chills will make it feel like winter, and conditions above the tree line in the mountains will be dangerous, making fall hiking unsafe. Cold weather will continue through the weekend with subfreezing temperatures possible Saturday and Sunday nights.

title: Cornell president admits he never followed up on gang rape allegation
text:
Cornell president admits he never followed up on gang rape allegation ahead of no-confidence debate
Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff knew in 2024 that a student had reported being gang raped at a fraternity house, but never followed up to learn what had happened to her or whether any of the accused students had been punished.
Video above: 'You deserve to be safe': bipartisan campus safety bill promises help for survivors
In an interview with The New York Times published Tuesday, a day before Cornell’s Faculty Senate was set to begin debating a no-confidence resolution in his administration, Kotlikoff acknowledged that he did not know until recently that the woman had dropped out of Cornell or that students had been expelled or suspended over the incident.
Kotlikoff publicly addressed what he called “deeply disturbing” allegations involving drug use and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house in a November 2024 message to the Cornell community, saying criminal and university investigations were underway.
He subsequently convened a presidential task force to examine how Cornell handles sexual assault, but said this week that he never followed up to learn the outcomes of the criminal or Title IX investigations into the woman’s allegations.
Video below: Attorney of the former student who alleges she was raped speaks to CNN
Case has drawn national attention, roiled campus
The case has drawn national attention since the woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints.
On Tuesday, Kotlikoff announced a ban on fraternity parties through the end of the academic year and plans to give state police a role in investigating sexual assault reports.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten initially declined to pursue charges after reviewing a summary prepared by Cornell University Police, but later said it omitted key details. He reopened the investigation after the lawsuit was filed. Gov. Kathy Hochul subsequently removed him from the case, appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor and ordered an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the allegations.
The Cornell Faculty Senate's proposed resolution, declaring no confidence in the administration's ability to handle reports of sexual assault on campus, reflects growing concerns among some faculty members that people who report sexual misconduct face institutional barriers and fear retaliation. Some have called for Kotlikoff’s resignation, while others have urged patience as independent investigations proceed.
Kotlikoff was scheduled to address the Faculty Senate on Wednesday before members begin debating the resolution. Debate was expected to continue Oct. 28, followed by electronic voting by the Faculty Senate, which has approximately 130 voting members. A simple majority is required for passage.
Professor who reported harassment says it nearly cost her career
For Ariana Kim, an associate music professor at Cornell and co-sponsor of the resolution, Kotlikoff’s acknowledgment that he had not followed up on the woman’s case was deeply troubling.
“I mean, that’s appalling in and of itself, right?” Kim said. “That you don’t know about a student who faced an alleged horrific crime, that you don’t think to check in.”
Kim, a Grammy-nominated violinist, said she was motivated to take action after being struck by Jane Doe's story, as well as her own personal experiences on campus since she started at Cornell a decade ago as a young academic in her 20s. She said when she experienced bullying and sexual harassment by senior colleagues, Cornell failed to properly document her complaints and that she was never clearly informed what disciplinary action, if any, had been taken.
“I was asked what I had done to provoke the situation,” she said.
Kim said she continued to be expected to work alongside colleagues involved in the dispute. She believes reporting the misconduct later affected her tenure review.
She spent 18 months appealing an adverse tenure decision, a process during which she lost 20 pounds (9 kilograms) and struggled to eat or sleep. A university appeals board ultimately overturned the original decision, and she secured tenure.
Now seeking promotion to full professor, Kim said she recognizes that publicly criticizing university leaders could again jeopardize her career.
“I’m speaking out publicly against this administration that may very well deny my promotion,” she said.
Kim said she has considered leaving Cornell many times over the years but is determined to stay and make the university safer for those who come after her.
“If by me fighting, it helps move the needle a little bit so that my female students aren’t going through this in 10 years or my female colleagues aren’t going through this in five years, then maybe it’s worth it.”
Faculty members question whether Cornell can investigate itself
Anne Marie Brady, a senior extension associate at Cornell’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations and another co-sponsor of the resolution, questioned whether Cornell University Police can independently investigate serious allegations of sexual misconduct.
“There doesn’t seem to be independence between the administration and the Cornell Police Department,” Brady said. She pointed to its handling of campus protests as one reason for her concerns and said serious criminal allegations should be investigated by outside law enforcement agencies.
Brady welcomed Kotlikoff’s announcement that state police would take on a role in sexual assault investigations, saying it showed the administration was listening to faculty concerns. But she questioned the timing, a day before the Senate was scheduled to begin debating the no-confidence resolution.
“I’m happy that they are listening — we need a dialogue,” she said. “We need to debate and discuss this. But I also feel it’s a bit disingenuous that it comes out just before the resolution.”

main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Design-Build firm Knickerbocker Group has been named to Forbes’ 2026 list of America’s Best-in-State Residential Architects.
The recognition celebrates residential architecture firms that demonstrate excellence in design, a deep mastery of residential practice, and meaningful contributions to their communities and landscapes. Greg Norton, Director of Design, shared: “We tend to be stewards of Maine for our clients as well, which is a very important aspect of how we do things. We take that honor and responsibility seriously in our work. Thank you, Forbes, for the recognition, congratulations to our peers on the list, and thank you, Maine, for providing the perfect backdrop for what we get to do.”
The invitation-only selection process included evaluation by Forbes editors and an independent advisory board of experts in architecture, design, sustainability, and architectural history. Firms submitted one “exemplary” home completed since 2021, which was evaluated alongside the firm’s broader body of work. Evaluations considered professional presentation and reputation, as well as a project’s stability, utility, and beauty, and its approach to site, materials, craftsmanship, spatial design, technology, sustainability, and environmental responsiveness.
“We are deeply honored to be recognized by Forbes among America’s Best-in-State Residential Architects,” said Danielle Betts, president of Knickerbocker Group. “At Knickerbocker Group, good design begins with listening—to our clients and to the land. Each home is personal, shaped around how our clients want to live and thoughtfully connected to its unique place. This recognition celebrates the creativity of our team and the collaboration that brings each client’s vision to life.”
About Knickerbocker Group.
For nearly 50 years, Knickerbocker Group has designed, built, and cared for homes, buildings, and properties across Maine. Bringing together real estate and land use planning, architecture, interior design, landscape architecture, preconstruction, construction, and property care—Knickerbocker Group guides projects seamlessly from initial concept through long-term stewardship, across
scales from focused renovations to full property development.

‘Salter Saturday’ in Freeport to celebrate new life for Maine’s sea-run brook trout
text:
Maine’s native sea-run brook trout, which spend part of their lives in saltwater before returning to coastal freshwater rivers to spawn, will be spotlighted and celebrated at a full-day event that includes a book launch, a river walk outing, presentations and networking sponsored by the Merrymeeting Bay chapter of Trout Unlimited.
The public is invited to attend the free “Salter Saturday” from 1-4 p.m. Saturday at the Freeport Community Center, 63 Depot St.
Event highlights include:
• Tom Pero reading from his new book “Salter,” published by Wild River Press and the first comprehensive book ever written about sea-run brook trout.
• A presentation by Francis Smith about the restoration of Quashnet River on Cape Cod.
• A panel discussion including Merry Gallagher, biologist with Maine IFW Maine, and Trout Unlimited members including Nate Hicks discussing sea-run trout river projects in Maine.
• Table top presentations by Trout Unlimited chapters from across Maine showcasing their conservation projects.
“Salter Saturday” will kick off at 10 a.m. with a free walk along Frost Gully Brook to view former dam sites removed by the Merrymeeting Bay chapter in partnership the Freeport Conservation Trust. Removing the dams enables the return of sea-run brook trout to downtown Freeport. The walk is hosted by Hicks and Matt Streeter, professional consultant to environmental organizations and immediate past president of the Maine council of Trout Unlimited.
Walkers will meet at Burr Cemetery parking lot at 56 Durham Road, and should wear tick protection and knee-high rubber boots.
Contact Gene McKenna at 207-512-5610 or [email protected] for more information about the event. Contact Hicks at 207-756-9364 or [email protected] for more information about the river walk.

also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hannah Pingree was the youngest ever female speaker of a U.S. state house, now she wants to be Maine governor
Pingree was in second place after primary night before winning the Democratic race in a ranked-choice tabulation
Hannah Pingree was the youngest ever female speaker of a U.S. state house, now she wants to be Maine governor
Pingree was in second place after primary night before winning the Democratic race in a ranked-choice tabulation
Hannah Pingree was the youngest woman in the country to serve as a state house speaker. Now, the Democrat seeks to become Maine's second female governor.
Pingree was in second place in the Democratic field at the end of primary night back in June before eventually beating front-runner Nirav Shah in the final round of the ensuing ranked-choice voting tabulation.
"I think ranked choice was a very positive process," Pingree said. "It ended up being a race where we talked about the issues. There were not a lot of negative attacks. And after the race was over, all four of my primary opponents have supported me. They've been helping me in my campaign."
Pingree is a former legislator. She served as the Speaker of the Maine House and was the director of Policy Innovation and the Future in the Mills administration, an office created by Gov. Janet Mills.
Pingree wants to succeed her former boss, but history is not on her side.
The Blaine House typically changes parties after each administration, in fact, the last time a governor was succeeded by a governor of their own party was in 1959.
Pingree has been campaigning for more than a year, focusing on the issues.
"Day one I'm ready to roll up my sleeves and work with school districts all across the state of Maine to implement this," Pingree said talking about implementing the science of reading. "We also know that things like universal pre-K really help kids to be ready to learn when they get to kindergarten. There's much more we need to do."
On education, she wants to look at other parts of the country and see what's working and to implement it here.
Another priority of Pingree's is housing. She wants to get every homeless veteran off the street in Maine and cut red tape so projects can get off the ground faster. She also wants to invest $100 a year in affordable housing. 
"It's not in one kind of housing. It's everything from affordable homeownership to rural rentals to senior housing to actually funding the infrastructure that connects housing so private developers can can expand and build, but they have that little funding that they need to actually make a project work," Pingree said.
She has been criticized by her opponents, Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett, for being tied to Mills and the housing crisis Maine is facing, which is a policy area she oversaw in her last job.
"I am different than Governor Mills. I'm appreciative of some of the issues that I've been able to work on, but I won't govern in the same way she has," she said. "There are major differences on issues like tribal sovereignty, where I will take a very different approach. But when it comes to housing, you know, we have actually made some good progress in Maine."
That progress includes making it easier to build accessory dwelling units on your property and the increase in housing production.
Pingree wants to keep the Blaine House in the same party for the first time in 67 years.
"We need to feel good about Maine's future again. I've spent my entire career working across the aisle to deliver for Maine people. I'm ready to do that as governor. And I'm ready to work with anybody who cares about Maine's future. And again, I'm ready to get the job done," she said.
Bennett, Charles and Pingree will face off on November 3.

title: Katie Zacharia’s White House debut raises new questions about the press secretary’s job
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump’s new press secretary stepped to the podium, the eyes of a packed room of journalists — and many in their audiences — upon her. She smiled broadly at the sea of faces both probing and friendly. With that, Katie Zacharia went live and became the official voice of the world’s most powerful person.
Fourteen minutes and just three questioners later, she was done. In the aftermath, it was clear that the former Newsmax commentator accomplished at least one thing: She put the “brief” back in briefing.
In her debut Tuesday, Zacharia looked downward and often read directly from a script. She paused and grinned when she uttered the words “Department of War.” She stumbled on a question about her background and mixed up the words “husband” and “president.” The few questions she took were nonconfrontational and from media outlets that have been sympathetic to the Republican president. In short: She made no memorable impression — or at least, to hear some tell it, not the one she likely wanted.
This would not be an easy job under any circumstances. Trump most frequently serves as his own spokesman. And his antagonism toward the media has created a new layer of tension. Zacharia is finding out on day one that she, too, will be under constant watch. Some — including a few of those who have stood in her shoes — didn’t think it went all that well.
In fractured times, in a national media scrum unimaginable just a few decades ago, what is the proper way to approach a job like this? How do you speak effectively when your boss speaks for himself so often that he commandeers the news cycle multiple times a day — and sometimes late into the night — with remarks provocative, unexpected and sometimes incendiary?
For one, you realize for whom you work: not your audience of millions but your audience of one, and the absolute need for his approval.
“I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people,” Zacharia said. Nowhere did she mention the task of disseminating accurate information to Americans.
The press secretary role has been many things
Over the nearly 10 decades since former journalist George E. Akerson made his and the office’s debut as Herbert Hoover’s press secretary in 1929, the job has served many purposes: deliverer of information, amplifier of policy, jouster with journalists, protector of the presidential reputation and, sometimes, overlord of obfuscation.
Under Trump and his second-term press secretary so far — Karoline Leavitt, who resigned in August — the job has been primarily one of acting as the immovable object against an irresistible, and in Trump’s eyes sometimes treasonous, force.
Leavitt got to know this terrain well in her 17-month tenure. She took a smiling but combative stance against a press that was increasingly coming under Trump’s criticism for coverage — and was named in at least one lawsuit about White House media access. She was not shy about interdicting what she considered media bias. “What a stupid question,” she said to one reporter at a briefing last year.
Trump, outside the White House on Tuesday shortly after Zacharia’s briefing, praised her debut as “excellent.” She was standing behind him at the time.
Other early reviews were more critical. MS NOW quoted one unnamed White House official as saying of the performance: “She needs to get much better fast, otherwise she’ll break Scaramucci’s record.” Anthony Scaramucci, an early White House communications director for first-term Trump, lasted 11 days in 2017. Said Scaramucci on X Tuesday afternoon: “I hope she makes it.”
Joe Biden’s former press secretary, Jen Psaki, now the host of a show on MS NOW, put it more succinctly, posting on X: “Well that briefing was basically an SNL skit….except it wasnt.”
Talking up Trump but taking few questions
While Zacharia’s performance — and of course, that’s what every briefing is — may have been bumpy to some, it was also mostly content-free except for news she broke about the White House asking U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to quit, which she immediately did.
Predictably, also like Leavitt before her, Zacharia spent a great part of her opening monologue praising Trump and giving an “up ‘til now”-style update on his second term’s priorities and accomplishments so far. Talking points included a “booming economy,” “his historic boom in energy production” and “a great relationship with Venezuela.”
She was also fond of superlatives, a trait that likely will resonate with a president whose remarks are often equally if not more expansive: “President Trump is working to secure the Western Hemisphere for centuries to come.”
When it came to questions, though, she was downright parsimonious. She allowed three questioners, then answered an additional one as she prepared to depart. The three called on during the briefing were Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail, all of which have been friendly to Trump in varying degrees during periods of his two terms. And she said she would continue Leavitt’s policy of bringing “new media” in — which has often meant outlets more sympathetic to Trump.
“We love new media and we want to be able to embrace it,” she said. Currently, three major outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — are fighting to regain White House access after Trump banished them last month, saying he didn’t like their coverage and calling it “fake news.”
How will Zacharia fare in coming days and weeks and, if it lasts, months? That, like so much else, depends on one thing: Donald Trump.
The late U.S. Sen. Howard Baker once famously said that, when being asked difficult things, handle it something like this: If you don’t like the question being asked, just answer a different question. On Tuesday, a half-century later, Katie Zacharia found a different way in — pick three nonconfrontational questioners, then defer to your boss and say: The End.

title: Woman escapes after man slashes her throat, police say
text:
FAIRMONT, W.Va. (WDTV/Gray News) - A man has been arrested on an attempted murder charge after police said he slashed a woman’s throat.
Benjamin Mayfield, 50, of Fairmont, has been charged with attempted murder, according to the Fairmont Police Department.
Police say the victim arrived at a home on 14th Street on Sunday, which she previously shared with Mayfield, to get her belongings, and while she was there, the pair got into an argument.
During the argument, Mayfield grabbed a bread knife from a box in the home, grabbed the victim in a chokehold and slashed her throat with the knife, court documents say.
The victim sustained a severe laceration to her throat but was able to escape, police say. She was transported to Ruby Memorial Hospital and had multiple lacerations on her left hand from trying to defend herself, court documents say.
Mayfield is currently in the North Central Regional Jail with bond set at $1 million.

title: Six Flags Over Georgia rides were inspected before season, commissioner says after fatal fall
text:
ATLANTA (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — The Georgia Insurance and Fire Safety Commissioner said his office is investigating the death of a man at Six Flags Over Georgia.
“Our very professional inspectors have inspected every one of those before the park season even started, and they’re currently on the ground looking at every nook and cranny, conducting interviews and conducting a thorough review of what happened,” Commissioner John King said during an Atlanta Press Club-sponsored debate broadcast on Georgia Public Television.
Cobb County police also investigating
The Cobb County Police Department’s major crimes unit is also investigating the Oct. 12 death of Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, who fell from the Goliath roller coaster, according to the department. Investigators said he was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction.
King is facing a reelection challenge from Democrat Keisha Sean Waites, and ride safety at amusement parks was the first question that came up during the debate.
Candidates respond to park reopening
Waites said Six Flags Over Georgia is set to reopen Friday.
“Prior to that opening, I would ensure that all of the amusement park rides have been inspected thoroughly to make sure that this will never happen again in Georgia,” she said.
The commissioner’s office is charged with inspecting, permitting and regulating amusement parks throughout the state.
“Clearly, this is one of our primary duties when it comes to safety,” King said.
King said his office’s inspectors inspected the rides before the park season started and are now on the ground investigating.
“It’s a little premature to be making a whole lot of comments about this. Obviously, this is an ongoing investigation, but I look forward to being able to report back to the Georgia public that these rides are safe, they will continue to be safe and we will continue inspecting them from top to bottom,” King added.
Waites, a three-term state House member and former Atlanta City Council member, said she would have ensured “there’s an inspection at that particular facility as time permits, in addition to that, to ensure that any challenges that we’ve had in the past, that they were investigated thoroughly.”
Election context
All of Georgia’s constitutional offices and House and Senate seats are on the ballot for the Nov. 3 midterms. Early voting began Oct. 13 and runs through Oct. 30.

title: Don’t close the door, Mom, I’ll be back
text:
Abdullahi Ahmed, Ed.D., of Portland is a naturalized citizen who came to the U.S. as a refugee from Somalia. He has worked for the Portland Public Schools since 2001.
When I left Somalia, I did not think I was leaving my country. I thought I was leaving for a while. I can still imagine the moment of departure. The uncertainty of the journey was real, but so was the belief that I would return. Somewhere in my mind, I was already planning my way back. I did not know how long I would be gone, but I did not imagine that the distance between me and home would grow into years, decades and eventually most of my adult life.
Perhaps this is one of the quietest and most powerful dreams of an immigrant: I will come back. People leave their homes with a suitcase, a few belongings, memories and a promise to themselves and to the people they love. They leave believing that the door they walk through is not a door that closes behind them. It is only a door they will walk through again.
That is why I imagine telling my mother, “Do not close the door. I will be back.” I did not say those exact words, but they describe what I carried in my heart. I was not saying goodbye to Somalia, to Mogadishu, the city I love. I was saying, “Wait for me.”
Like many immigrants, I thought my absence would be temporary. I imagined returning to the streets I knew, to familiar voices, familiar food, familiar smells and the landscape that had shaped my childhood. I imagined sitting with family again, telling stories about the places I had traveled and the things I had learned. But immigration has a way of changing the meaning of time.
A year becomes several years. Several years become a decade. Children grow up. Parents grow older. Friends move away. Neighborhoods change. The streets you remember remain in your memory, but sometimes they no longer look the same even when you return. Eventually, you realize that you have been away longer than you ever imagined.
Yet something strange happens to an immigrant during those years. While I am away from my country, my country is never completely away from me. I could not continue living in Somalia, but Somalia continued living in me. I carried Somalia into Pakistan. I carried it with me when I came to America. I carried its language, its stories, its hospitality, its struggles, its humor, its faith, its food, its memories and the voices of the people who raised me. In many ways, my country did not carry me. I carried my country.
That may be one of the great contradictions of immigration. We leave because circumstances, opportunity, education, safety, family, war, poverty or hope push us beyond our borders. We cross oceans and continents looking for another life. But crossing a border does not mean leaving everything behind. The country we leave often becomes even more present inside us. We become immigrants, but we also become living memories of somewhere else.
I became an American. I built a life in Maine. I became an educator and educational leader, a husband, a father and a member of communities that welcomed me. America became home in ways I could never have imagined when I first arrived. But becoming part of a new country did not erase the old one. There is a Somali tradition that captures something about this experience: wherever you travel, you carry your identity with you. That is what immigrants do. We build new homes while carrying old ones and identities inside our hearts.
When I think about that imaginary door, I understand now that the promise to return was about more than geography. It was a promise to remain connected. I may not have been able to live in Somalia, but Somalia has continued to live in me. Perhaps this is why so many immigrants keep saying, in one form or another, “I will be back.” We leave believing we are going for a short time. We leave with hope in our hearts and return tickets in our minds. But life has its own plans.
Still, somewhere inside the immigrant heart, the door never completely closes. We continue to look back. We continue to remember. We continue to carry. And even after decades away, a part of us is still standing at that door, telling our mothers: “Do not close it. I will be back.”

title: Gardiner residents seek clarity in expanded archery season
text:
GARDINER — Helen Stevens can tell you about the animals living in the woods behind her Dresden Avenue home — the fox and its kits that appear in the spring, the owls and crows that battle for treetop dominance and the raccoon that recently moved into the big oak at the front of the house.
Pointing to the large pine trees in the forest, Stevens said her backyard feels like you have stepped into a state park, even though you are still in the city.
It’s the deer that concern her the most, and maybe not for the reason you’d think.
About every other year, Stevens said a bowhunter will ask permission to hunt on the land behind her home, something she has not agreed to. The homes of Stevens and her neighbors sit on about 30 acres of land just south of Gardiner’s downtown. Their backyards are heavily wooded, with steep slopes and deep gullies.
The wooded area is “patchwork quilt of property owners,“ Stevens said. “None of which owns enough property to say ‘sure you can hunt on my property, that’s OK.’”
In Maine, areas like Stevens’ neighborhood, a mix of residential and wooded areas, are open to an expanded archery season for deer in the fall to help keep populations in check.
State wildlife officials say in developed areas deer can cause problems like deer-vehicle collisions and spread ticks that carry Lyme disease.
While Stevens and her neighbor Lisa St. Hilaire don’t oppose hunting, they think the high density residential zone where they live is not suitable for it and would like Gardiner city officials to ban it in that area.
WHERE THE DEER ARE
Some hunters prefer archery, although it has its challenges.
Brent St. Clair is a bowhunter from Fayette. While he hunts both with a bow and firearms, he prefers hunting with a bow. He hunts for both recreation and food, explaining that “we seldom eat beef anymore.”
“It’s just more of a challenge, there’s a lot of finesse involved with it, and you’re probably more of a stalking hunter in the woods than you would be if you had a rifle,” he said.
Lee Robinson of Audette’s Hardware in Winthrop is a bowhunter who hunts during the expanded archery season. He said the hardest part about the expanded season is getting access from landowners.
About three decades ago, the state established an expanded archery season around the state’s urban areas and neighboring towns and along the coast, beginning in mid-September and ending in mid-December.
This season was an addition to the regular monthlong October bowhunting season and comes with a requirement for an archery permit and its own bag limit.
The expanded season was established to manage deer population in areas where the use firearms is difficult or not permitted. Much of the land in these areas is privately owned, and hunters must get permission to hunt there. They cannot hunt within 300 feet of a dwelling unless they have permission.
“It’s developed areas such as towns, suburban areas as well as the outskirts of urban areas,” Mark Latti, communications director for the Maine Department if Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, said. “Where there are high deer numbers, high instances of Lyme disease, higher number of deer-vehicle collisions, and complaints from property owners such as deer eating their shrubs, or farmers dealing with excess deer in their fields.”
So far this year, the Maine Department of Transportation has counted 3,773 deer-vehicle collisions, and most are in the state’s more populated areas, from Kittery to Bangor and along the coastline.
Bob Humphrey, a bowhunter from Pownal, said during the expanded archery season, hunting becomes more of a challenge, beginning with getting permission from landowners, and then navigating hunting on more developed and smaller parcels of land.
Despite the challenges, the demand for the sport has remained steady for about a decade. According to Latti, there are approximately 15,000 licensed bowhunters in Maine, and 9,070 expanded archery permits were sold last season.
LIMITS ON HUNTING
In early September, Stevens and St. Hilaire went to the Gardiner City Council, asking for a hunting ban in the area behind their houses.
They said while the city code does not allow firearms or slingshots, it has no mention of crossbows or bowhunting.
Some cities and towns have put in place limits on discharging projectiles like bullets, arrows and bolts.
Portland, for example, has banned the discharge of firearms and archery hunting equipment inside city limits, including the coastal islands.
Lewiston’s expanded archery area covers most of the land within the city’s boundaries, except for the northern portion of the city near No Name Pond.
Jonathan Connor, the director of planning and enforcement for Lewiston said the city follows state laws, and does not have local ordinances pertaining to bowhunting.
The Parks and Public Works departments are looking into prohibiting archery hunting in public parks within the expanded archery zone. The departments are also contacting neighboring municipalities in the zone to learn whether they have adopted or are considering similar regulations.
In Augusta, about seven miles north of Gardiner, the city code includes regulations for archery.
According to its city code, “no person shall shoot a bow and arrow or any other projectile instrument within the compact section of the city, as such is defined by the Maine Department of Transportation, without first acquiring permission to do so from the Police Chief.”
Jesse Brann, Augusta’s deputy chief of police, said if someone wants to hunt in a compact zone, or an expanded archery zone, hunters can fill out a discharge permit request. If they want to hunt on private property, they must provide evidence of permission from the landowner before the permit is granted.
Brann said in an email he cannot recall any recent concerns about hunting in high-density residential areas from Augusta residents.
In Waterville, hunters can contact the Waterville Police Department for information on ordinances that govern using or possessing a bow or arrow inside city limits.
When it comes to concerns about bowhunting in urban areas, Latti said, “we get far more complaints about issues arising from high deer numbers than we do about complaints about the season.”
A QUESTION OF SAFETY
Because the wooded area behind their Gardiner houses makes it hard to distinguish property lines, Stevens and St. Hilaire worry about stray arrows and wounded animals traveling onto land where the property owner did not give permission to hunt.
Latti said he has heard the concern about wounded deer traveling outside of permitted hunting areas. “If that happens, certainly someone can contact the Maine Warden Service and they could retrieve that deer,” he said.
Latti emphasized the safety of hunting, especially bowhunting, explaining that incidents are very rare.
“I cannot think of the last time that we had a bowhunting or crossbow incident,” he said. “Hunting is a very safe sport. We have over 240,000 hunters in the state, and last year I think we had two or three hunter incidents, or injuries related to hunting. I can’t even think of the last time we had a bowhunting incident. I do not believe we’ve ever had a bowhunter injure another party.”
Humphrey said oftentimes, hunters are shooting from elevated tree stands, so if the arrow doesn’t hit the target, it will hit the ground.
For Stevens and St. Hilaire, their request will be sent to the Gardiner Ordinance Review Committee, and will not be changed for this hunting season, which is already underway. St. Hilaire said she assumes it will not be changed for the next either. In the meantime, she recommends residents post their land if they would not like hunters on it.
“It seems like in a high density, residential zone, any kind of hunting is potentially a safety hazard,” St. Hilaire said. “This is not anti hunting … it’s not to say that anybody is wrong, it’s just that we want the city to look at it.”

title: Obituary: Stanton M. Whitaker
text:
AUGUSTA – Stanton M. Whitaker, 93, passed away on Oct. 10, 2026, surrounded by his family at his home in Augusta, where he has lived since 1965.
Stanton was born on March 23, 1933, in Belfast, the son of C. Maynard and Christabelle Fuller Whitaker. He grew up on the family farm in Windsor and graduated from Cony High School in 1951. Before beginning his career with Central Maine Power Company in 1953, he worked on the farm and drove logging and gravel trucks. Stanton worked for Central Maine Power for 38 years before retiring in 1991, and he returned temporarily to help during the ice storm of 1998.
On June 18, 1955, Stanton married his beloved wife, Donna M. Cooper. They shared 58 wonderful years together until her passing in 2014.
Stanton enjoyed working with his hands and was always willing to lend his skills to friends and family through construction projects, mowing, and other acts of service. He generously gave of his time to help at Christian Life Fellowship Church in Chelsea and the Washington Advent Christian Campground, where he was a member and regular attendee. He also was a member of the Eastern Star, and the Capital Area Wheels chapter of Good Sam as he loved spending time camping with friends and family.
Stanton was predeceased by his beloved wife, Donna; his brother, Jerry Whitaker; his sister, Priscilla Clark; his toddler grandson, Tyler Allen; and his baby great-granddaughter, Brooke Whitaker.
He is survived by his son, David Whitaker, and his wife, Jennifer, of Presque Isle; and his two daughters, Diane Smith, and her husband, Scott, of Hudson, N.H., and Pamela Allen, and her husband, Curt, of Hallowell.
He is also survived by his 10 grandchildren: Greg Whitaker and his wife, Erica, of Mapleton; Joel Whitaker and his wife, Elizabeth, of Presque Isle; Aaron Whitaker and his wife, Chelsea, of Mapleton; Timothy Smith and his wife Marie of Hudson, N.H.; Rebecca Johansen and her husband, Austin, of Tyngsboro, Mass.; Michael Smith and his wife, Alicia, of Hudson, N.H.; Chad Allen and his wife, Clarissa, of Bedford, N.H.; Laura Brooks and her husband, Joshua, of Waterville; Emily Allen of Winthrop; and Katie Allen of Winthrop. He is also survived by 14 great-grandchildren, who brought him tremendous joy.
He leaves behind his prized 26-year-old green GMC pickup truck.
The family extends its sincere gratitude to MaineGeneral Medical Center and Hospice, Gray Birch Rehab, and especially, the home care team, who provided compassionate care and support to Stanton and his family over the past couple of weeks.
Relatives and friends are invited to a visitation at 1 p.m., followed by a celebration of Stanton’s life at 2 p.m., on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, at Hope Baptist Church on Route 202 in Manchester. His burial will take place at Resthaven Cemetery in Windsor, at a later date.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to Washington AC Camp, in care of Pam Allen,

title: Varsity Maine Week 6 high school football picks
Acclaimed cartoonist inks in New England’s queer history
text:
During queer graphic novelist Tillie Walden’s tenure as cartoonist laureate of Vermont, she encountered a story close to home, set centuries before. The account of openly gay Charity Bryant and Sylvia Drake, who lived in Weybridge, Vermont, in the 18th and 19th centuries, is a tale of two women who did not fit neatly within the lines drawn up by society. They built a home together at a time when women could not own property, and started a successful tailoring business allowing them to live with independence and authenticity.
Through the sepia tones of Walden’s prolific pen, “Charity & Sylvia” transforms the silhouettes of two lives framed by historical archives into living, breathing neighbors, elders and lovers on the page.
‘Charity & Sylvia’ takes place during the early years of the United States, surrounded by revolution and conflict. How does their life together fit in with these other rebellions?
I think their life was a very quiet, very subtle rebellion compared to those around them. While Charity and Sylvia were different from their Vermont neighbors — they were lesbians — they never experienced discrimination to the degree of, say, the Indigenous people who lived on the land before them. But this is what’s so interesting to me about American history, and why I loved writing about it. All the violence, complexities and small victories are contained together. Charity and Sylvia achieved something grand and historic, even if it was quiet.
Charity and Sylvia wrote extensively — you mention reading over 900 of their letters. What was your guide in giving voice to their history?
The archive at the Henry Sheldon Museum held my hand while I walked through the past. There was an enormous amount to read and I tried to sift through the archive with little judgment about where the story should lead. Ultimately my guide was Sylvia. Her journals gave me the most evocative and descriptive information about their lives, but it was painful to know that what I was seeing was only part of the story. The truth of their life together is something that only they knew. This book is my attempt at interpreting that truth.
There were also many other resources that helped. Rachel Hope Cleves wrote a wonderful book about them. I also read a lot of the fiction of the era to try and inhabit the language of the time, like “Pamela” by Samuel Richardson.
Sylvia grapples with her faith throughout her life, struggling to reconcile her relationship with Charity with her religion. Did her thinking evolve? How did you come to the line, ‘If you are to go to hell then I should like to come with you’?
Ah, I forgot about that line. I like that line! I don’t have an exact timeline of their faith journey. I have blips, moments. I have an excessive amount of information from the 1820s and ’30s but little from later decades. Most of what I read in Sylvia’s journal is a record of shame. She clearly felt conflicted about her queerness. But the fact is, despite the shame, they lived 44 years together. They never left each other’s side. That tells me that clearly there was some other force holding them together, one fighting back against feelings of sin and shame.
How did you organize the narrative?
I was baffled at the start with how to structure the book and went through a few different versions. I’m drawn to flashes of memories but I had to ground the story to make it work for readers. I hacked it mostly by drawing in a very free-form way with a lot of loose pages scattered all around me. While drafting, I was still going to the archive every week, so the two started working together. To be honest, I had no idea if it was going to work. It was only when I started inking the final pages that I felt like I had done something interesting.
You often play with negative space on the page. Were gaps in the archives telling to you as you drafted?
Oh yes, absolutely. The gaps were riveting. I was just as moved by what I knew as what I didn’t. Sylvia was very coy with me in her journal, and would often drop a bomb, like she did when she wrote, “Charity says we should never know one another’s true thoughts.” Like, excuse me? Go on! But then she didn’t — she just stopped, moved on to talking about church and neighbors and tailoring. The gaps were visual too. I had to find ways to fill in drawings when I had no idea what was actually there. I ended up leaning a lot on logic: the materials they had, what was likely available, what was similar to what I already knew. I drew a lot of logs.
Many of Charity and Sylvia’s struggles and successes are familiar to LGBTQ+ people and other marginalized folks living today. 250 years later, how do you hope this book speaks to the contemporary queer experience?
I hope it expresses that truth about history — that every time, every era that people have experienced, was once the present. None of us start out as the past, it’s something we become even when we’re not ready. I hope the book helps people think about history, and about how varied queer lives are. Charity and Sylvia were conservative, devout women. They were lovely people and also prejudiced people. Part of what I’m proudest of in telling this story is being able to share that complexity; to get to the end of their lives and ask the question — what do they deserve? What do any of us deserve?
Rylan Hynes is a queer transgender writer living in central Maine. Their debut novel, “Grafting,” was published by Islandport Press in 2026.

title: Person killed, two others in the hospital, after morning fire in Bangor
text:
Person dead, two others in the hospital after house fire in Bangor, Maine
One person is dead and two others were taken to the hospital after a fire at a home in Bangor on Wednesday morning, fire officials tell Maine's Total Coverage media partner WABI.
The two who were taken to the hospital were being treated for smoke inhalation.
The Bangor Fire Department said the two-alarm fire at the corner of Second Street and Cedar Street was reported at about 6:30 a.m.
At about 8:30 a.m., the fire department said crews were still at the scene, people should expect delays in the area for the rest of the morning.
The cause of the fire was under investigation.
Officials did not immediately release the name of the person who died.

title: New England Cancer Specialists offering highly personalized blood treatment
text:
New England Cancer Specialists offering highly personalized blood treatment to Maine patients
New England Cancer Specialists (NECS) is now offering CAR-T cell therapy, a highly personalized blood cancer treatment, to its patients in Maine.
CAR-T is short for chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy. The three-week process begins with the collection of a blood cancer patient's T cells. They are then shipped to a specialized laboratory to be genetically modified.
The T cells are re-engineered to recognize a specific target on cancer cells. The treated blood is then shipped back to NECS in Westbrook and re-infused into the patient. The modified cells can identify and attack the cancer.
NECS doctors say CAR-T has produced responses in patients whose cancers have persisted or returned despite other treatments.
Patients previously had to travel out of state for this type of cell therapy. Travel, expenses, and caregiver requirements are a few of the challenges that limited access for many patients in Maine.
Yoni Resnick, vice president of pharmacy at NECS, adds that patients are also often hesitant to work with new nurses and doctors at an unfamiliar healthcare center.
"Some patients don’t want that change in their care. They want the comfort of their team, their nurses, their patient care coordinators, their physicians, and that’s what gives them the most hope for their disease," Resnick said.
Resnick is on the team advocating for this treatment in Maine. He anticipates a slow rollout but hopes to reach an increasing number of patients in the coming years.

title: VETERANS CORNER: You have a right to file a claim: Don’t let fear syndrome come into play
text:
First, I’ll answer those who have asked for increases or are trying to but don’t know how to do it. There are so many veterans that have what I call fear syndrome, and that is not at all necessary as you have a right to file a claim and one that has no way to come back and bite you. Fear has kept many good men and women from applying for a pension, or asking for an increase. Let me help you eliminate some of that unnecessary fear. Some veterans fear they will be punished for asking for a pension because of a possible service connected or aggravated injury. If you were hurt in anyway while doing anything legal you have a right to file for a disability, irrespective of what the causation was. You have entered into a contract with the military from bombs to basketballs, if you were injured.
Once again I will say, a good VSO, such as VFW, American Legion, Maine Vets, Paralyzed Veterans of Foreign Wars or Am Vets and DAV all have someone who will help you. You can walk in or call for an appointment. VA’s main number is 207-623-8411 push “0” and a live person will direct your call. All these agencies will help you fill out necessary forms in the formulation or your claim. They will defend you to the best of their ability. They all have great training and expertise in case development.
I personally go directly to VBA in bldg. 248. They have a very large trained staff that is always available to help you feel comfortable and help with the development of your first claim. There is nothing to fear and everything to possibly gain. Problems other than claims can be assured as well including veteran burials and DIC questions. That is Dependency and Indemnity Compensation, regarding our loved ones. When you go bring your DD-214 and any other relevant paperwork such as any possible medical records and Entrance and Exit Exams if you have them. If you are record deficient your adviser will help you with how to obtain them.
So, many veterans are under the misconception that in order to file a claim they had to see action, but such is not the case. Don’t let the backroom lawyers confuse you. If you were hurt in any way while serving your country, your country accepts that responsibility. Age is not a factor and how and what happened causing injury, of any sort, is possibly compensatory. I have seen basketball injuries; bar room fights and slipping on ice receive a percentage and a payday. Like I have stated before, the only thing that is not acceptable is fraud. Tell the truth and that will never be an issue. No one is out to trap you or take something away from you. If you already have a small percentage don’t worry about losing it. No one wants to harm you. Some of those who will work with you are veterans themselves. They have a rule book that they must live by. (Follow)
One veteran said to me, “I am afraid that they will take something away from me”. Once again, I state if what you are claiming is based in truth, you have nothing to fear and no one will take anything from you. The purpose is to increase not to decrease. You’re doing this for you and your family and when you signed that contract with the U.S. Military you agreed to defend your country and they agreed to protect you and yours if you were injured in anyway. I’ve seen basketball, car accidents; contaminated living conditions causing lung, heart and stomach conditions. I’ve seen those affected by fear. If your entrance said you were 100 percent fit and your ETS exam told a different story, then you have a case on paper right there.
Sexual issues, which most everyone doesn’t want to talk about can cause some very serious emotional problems. If there is someone you would feel comfortable talking to and that person will be supplied. You earned that right. Just speak to your Primary Care Provider. (PCP) and if that is not the person you want to talk to then they can refer you to someone you would feel comfortable with. Under this administration you are allowed to go outside of the VA system.
Just ask the PCP’s here at Togus and they will get you where you need to go. The human body is very complex and there are many times our needs can not be met at Togus. So, you just ask to go outside. Now, not all doctors will take Togus Veterans so you might not have the exact doctor you seek but a comparable is always available. In many situations there is even the availability of free transportation. Just explain you have no way of getting to where you are scheduled and most likely transportation will be supplied. Also, our “Fisher House” has been condemned because of poor planning but other places can be supplied and paid for by the VA. Also, you don’t have to accept an appointment that is a great distance from your home. Travel expenses are available with tolls included. There are many opportunities available, just ask and fill out the necessary paper and keep receipts. You might need to include hotel and food.
I will mention some general items regarding cases of time. Many of us older veterans have cases that have been on the books for some time. So perhaps it’s time to revisit them. if you have ratings that are 20 years old they can’t be reduced below current level, except because of that nasty word Fraud – 38CFR 3.95(b). if you have above 20 years, your cases are locked by the 20-year protection rule.
If your cases are over 10 years old they cannot have service connected severed, again except for fraud. Also, a question I get very often is, if my condition is “0%” does that mean it’s worthless? Far from it, it means you have been recognized as service connected but not granted enough to be compensable. 38 CFR 4.31 and protected under 38CFR 3.105. Filing a general request for an increase does not open you to a reduction, if your wording says” increase” only, say nothing else. The danger only comes if you file for a “decrease”. Who would do that? You can even ask VBA to do a general overview due to time and possible addendums to your low percentages or even “0” percentages. They can’t play with you because the law protects you.
During the history of your injury, pain and connections may provide for increases as well. Sometimes conditions will merge that were rated separately in their original form. If this occurs than you can ask for that union to be considered to move a law rated percentage upward and possibly a service connected “0” percent to elevate as well. Consult your VSO if time and other conditions may have changed your previous ratings. Never ever say “I give up”! That will get you nowhere.
Well, I guess that is enough for Columbus so let’s see what you do with this advise. Ask for a reevaluation if time has gone by but your percentage hasn’t grown. God bless you all, and don’t forget the election is near, VOTE. Vote for the most realistic veteran champion. Have a safe and happy week. Short ones are great unless you are getting old like me and Roland.

title: Pope Leo XIV shares first message following lung cancer diagnosis
text:
(Gray News) - Pope Leo XIV released his first message since undergoing surgery for lung cancer in Rome.
“As you know, I have been unable to be among you during these days,” Leo wrote in a statement. “I thank you warmly for your prayers and for the work you have done together. Your sharing of experiences and attentive listening are indeed a gift to the whole Church.”
The pope’s message was issued to Catholics who were meeting to celebrate the 10th anniversary of Amoris Laetitia, a document written by Pope Francis about the church’s work with couples and families, CNN reported.
”It is my hope that families will always be active participants in the life and mission of your local churches," his statement continued. “I ask you please to pray for me, as I pray for you.”
Pope Leo underwent surgery on Tuesday in which doctors removed a cancerous mass from his lung.
The 71-year-old pope was said to be recovering normally following the procedure, according to his doctors.
“The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room. He resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch,” Dr. Luigi Carbone, the pope’s personal doctor, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the head thoracic surgeon at Gemelli Hospital, said. “Recovery is proceeding as planned.”
Doctors said the surgery confirmed that Leo had lung adenocarcinoma, a common type of lung cancer, with surgeons removing the lower lobe of his right lung.
The Vatican hasn’t announced any changes to the pope’s planned trip to South America in November.

title: Former T.J. Maxx employee accused of hiding camera in dressing room facing new charges
text:
MACHESNEY PARK, Ill. (WIFR/Gray News) - A former T.J. Maxx worker accused of hiding a camera in the women’s dressing room at the store faces new charges.
Jeffrey Wallin, 37, of Loves Park, was charged in March with unauthorized video recording and live video transmission, unlawful video of a residence and obstruction of justice.
Authorities said the investigation began Feb. 28 after a customer alerted store employees to a lens in a ceiling tile.
At the time, detectives asked the public to come forward to locate any further victims.
As a result of the ongoing investigation, Wallin now faces the following charges:
- 5 counts of unauthorized video recording with a victim under 18 years of age
- 4 counts of unauthorized video recording and live video transmission
- Obstructing justice/destroying evidence
- Burglary
Wallin was arrested on the new charges on Oct. 14.

title: Cumberland to add 24 acres to Twin Brook park
text:
Cumberland will purchase a 24-acre parcel abutting Twin Brook Recreation Area, expanding the town-owned park’s size by about 10%.
Town Manager Matt Sturgis said that the land’s owners approached the town to see if their property could be added to the park and preserved for the public to enjoy.
The parcel consists primarily of woods, rolling hills and streams, said Sturgis, adding variety to the recreation area’s many fields.
After some negotiation, the landowners and town agreed on the price of $85,000. It will be paid using the town’s land acquisition fund, which is generated by impact fees. Having discussed the acquisition previously in executive session, the Town Council authorized Sturgis to execute a purchase and sale agreement on behalf of the town at a meeting Tuesday night.
“It’s going to be something we only have the opportunity to get once,” said Councilor Geoff Michalak.
Twin Brook Recreation Area is a 224-acre, four-season park that offers 4 miles of trails for hiking, which are groomed for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing in the winter. It also contains 22 acres of athletic fields for soccer, baseball and softball, as well as a disc golf course.

title: Student dies after accidental injury at school involving scissors, officials say
text:
UNIVERSITY CITY, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) — A Missouri high school student died Tuesday after suffering an accidental injury at school last week.
The injury happened at University City High School near St. Louis.
School district officials said a student was accidentally injured with a pair of scissors at the district’s high school on Oct. 5, which prompted a lockdown.
On Tuesday, officials said that student died from his injuries.
School district officials and police said there was an internal investigation following the injury, and no foul play was suspected.
Police did not reveal exactly how the student was injured with scissors.
The district said it is making crisis counselors available to students and staff.
“The wellbeing of our University City students, staff, families and community remains our highest priority,” the district wrote in a release. “Comprehensive crisis counseling and mental health support services are available at all district schools for any student or staff member in need of support. The School District will also have additional counselors and wellness resources at University City High School to respond to student needs. We thank you for your patience and understanding as we have honored the confidentiality and privacy of the family.”
Further information was not yet available.

title: Surry training business helps ‘salty’ pups build skills for 10 years
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SURRY, Maine (WABI) - Helping dogs navigate the human world is the goal of Surry business now celebrating a milestone: Salty Dogs Obedience & Adventure is marking a decade of trainings, treats and tail wags!
“I think like most trainers, I got into dog training by having a difficult dog myself,” shares Salty Dogs owner and head trainer Whitney Thurston. “So I ended up working with another trainer at the time named Lane Fisher, and she became my mentor. And she helped me get started in understanding working with dogs and people, and then we had Salty Dogs!”
Offering private and small-group sessions, they specialize in working with pups, as the name suggests, with saltier personalities.
“A big part of what we also do, we call Maine Canine Academy, similar to a daycare, but it is all training focused,” Thurston explains. “So, we actually end up taking a lot of dogs who wouldn’t be successful in a daycare or who struggle maybe with appropriate social behavior or have a hard time with new people and we put them in a stable social group.”
For Thurston, training is translating dog behavior to human expectations, helping owners and their furry friends understand each other.
When she adopted her now 15-year-old Husky mix Lana 13 years ago, she was reactive to people and other dogs.
Thurston says she discovered through training that anxiety was the basis of Lana’s behavior. After working on building her confidence, Lana now lives happily with Thurston, her husband and children, and their other dog, Tessa.
“A lot of times if we see a dog like that, we might say that they’re trying to be dominant or they’re trying to be the alpha, but a lot of times they’re just underconfident or don’t know what’s expected of them,” Thurston describes. “I want those dogs to be able to have full lives, and I want the people who find that they’ve adopted this dog that now has problems they weren’t expecting, I want them to know that they’re not alone, and we actually have a support group for that. I want them to know, like, this is not their fault, this is not their dog’s fault, that it actually is so common.”
With a decade under its belt, Thurston and her four other trainers have worked with more than 7,000 dogs. It also hosts events for pet parents and workshops that bring dogs out into the community.
Thurston says the milestone represents the reach of their work: “It’s really incredible to know that we’ve been able to help so many dogs and so many owners.”

title: Homeless man accused of breaking into locked storage units in Shapleigh
text:
Man accused of breaking into locked storage units in Shapleigh, Maine
A man police say is homeless is accused of breaking into several locked storage units in Shapleigh.
Deputies from the York County Sheriff's Office were called to the U-STORE Storage facility on Emery Mills Road at about 6:30 a.m. on Tuesday for reports of a suspicious person.
When deputies arrived, they say they found Jason Desruisseaux, 38, behind one of the storage units. Police say they then discovered that several units had been broken into and that Desruisseaux was on current conditions of release.
Police say Desruisseaux had a grinder and bolt cutters.
As deputies continued to investigate, they found a motorcycle that they say Desruisseaux stole from one of the units.
He was charged with burglary and violation of conditions of release. He was held without bail at the York County Jail and was due in court on Wednesday.

title: Auburn woman sentenced for tax fraud

text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - An Auburn woman convicted of tax fraud was sentenced in federal court Wednesday.
The Department of Justice said Rakiya Mohamed, 30, was sentenced to 5 years probation.
Mohamed was also ordered to pay restitution to the IRS in the amount of $51,000 dollars.
According to court documents, Mohamed filed false income tax returns for her language interpretation business between 2018 and 2019.
