title: Who's behind The Maine Independent?
text:
Less than a month before the midterms, a large dark money group is sending copies of a partisan newspaper to thousands of Maine voters.
The Maine Independent is nondescript. Its masthead is plain in black and white. It includes crosswords and recipes among its 12 pages. But the paper has no explanation of who’s behind it, no statements about its mission, and no reason why it wound up on voters’ doorsteps.
Despite its moniker, it is far from an independent local news organization, both in its funding and its politics.
The paper is one of about 20 nearly identical publications created in swing states across the country over the last decade by American Independent Media, a subsidiary of a similarly named, large dark money group closely tied to Democratic super PACs, politicians and campaign operatives.
From Alaska to Florida, the American Independent Foundation has propped up outlets created to boost Democrats ahead of crucial state and federal elections. They present themselves as independent local news organizations, mailing 12 pages of ideologically slanted stories to voters who never subscribed to the outlet.
Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson “will fight for universal healthcare and lower drug prices,” one Maine Independent headline reads. “Susan Collins says she’s pro-choice, but her Senate votes helped end Roe,” says another.
In addition to its printed paper, the outlet has reached hundreds of thousands of people through more than $47,000 worth of social media ads, according to the Meta Ad Library.
None of The Maine Independent’s content is flatly untrue or blatantly misleading. But all of their stories omit important nuance in support of Democratic politicians.
“It’s an attempt to mimic journalism by providing information that might, in fact, be accurate, but is framed in a partisan manner,” said Michael Socolow, a journalism professor at the University of Maine and board member of the Maine Press Association.
The Maine Independent is one of many so-called “pink slime” news outlets established in Maine by both liberal and conservative dark money groups in the lead up to the 2026 midterm elections. The term, an allusion to ultra-processed meat products, is used in a news context to refer to outlets run by partisan interests posing as local and independent news.
NewsGuard, an organization that tracks misinformation and rates news outlets’ credibility, said American Independent Media and its local sites “generally fail to maintain basic standards of accuracy and accountability” by infusing opinion into their reporting and failing to disclose the partisan interests behind the operation.
“That’s what makes these publications so pernicious,” said Sam Howard, politics editor at NewsGuard. “They threaten to undermine what’s left of the trust that news consumers have in the media, particularly local media. Because these publications are framed as local, seemingly independent, seemingly nonpartisan publications.”
Joe Conason, the Independent’s editor-in-chief, did not respond to interview requests or questions about their reach and operations in Maine.
SLIME-SWAMPED MAILBOXES
Mailing newspapers to voters en masse has been a hallmark of American Independent Media’s operation for years.
In 2021, the organization mailed papers to Virginia voters ahead of a tightly contested gubernatorial election. In the run up to the 2022 midterms, the Independent mailed faux-local papers to more than 2.5 million people in Wisconsin, Michigan and Pennsylvania, The Washington Post reported.
Ahead of this year’s midterms, they have has expanded to at least five more battleground states with pivotal Senate races: Florida, North Carolina, Iowa, Alaska and Maine.
Those state branches have each spent tens of thousands of dollars on social media ads, according to the Meta Ad Library. But their main business is still sending physical papers through the mail, according to Chiara Vercellone, a senior analyst at NewsGuard.
“They’re trying to prove their credibility, and we know that there’s a lot of junk out on the internet or on social media,” she said. “Creating a seemingly innocent-looking newspaper that people receive in their mails touts their supposed credibility.”
American Independent Media micro-targets its print papers toward moderates and women in swing states, The Washington Post reported in 2022. At that time, the organization mailed monthly copies to some 3.2 million voters nationwide, making it one of the country’s largest print media operations.
Spreading pink slime through the mail could prove more effective in Maine than elsewhere, said Socolow. The state’s population of only 1.3 million residents is comparatively small and skews older, on average, than anywhere else in the country.
“People still read the newspapers that pop into their mailboxes,” Socolow said. “I think it’s a smart strategy to reach older people.”
THE OPERATION
The American Independent Foundation describes its mission in business and tax filings as spreading “increased public awareness of progressive values.”
Among the foundation’s owners are Conason, a longtime journalist and liberal commentator, and Matt Fuehrmeyer, former director of research for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. Its media arm similarly has been run by Jessica Floyd, a longtime operative for Democratic campaigns and super PACs, and Ari Rabin-Havt, deputy director of Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders’ 2020 presidential campaign.
Both organizations are tax-exempt nonprofits. The foundation is a 501(c)(3) organization, which are prohibited from political activity by law. American Independent Media, however, is a 501(c)(4) — meaning it has legal leeway to be more political.
Neither group is required to disclose its donors or financial backers, placing them each in the realm of so-called dark money groups that are dumping tens of millions of dollars into Maine’s Senate race.
Together, they operate The American Independent News, which acts as a national news source and syndicate for its local outlets’ content.
Both the foundation and its media arm have contracted with a number of progressive consulting firms and media groups, their tax filings show, including a marketing firm called Mission Control, which describes itself as “the most successful direct mail firm working in Democratic politics today” — hinting at the Independent’s mailing strategy.
Unlike many other pink slime outlets, The Maine Independent’s articles include real people’s bylines on their stories, many of whom were reporters at traditional newspapers prior to joining the partisan outlet.
But despite the dozens of Maine-centric stories the outlet has published, none of its staff appear to be based in the state.
Only a few of The American Independent’s reporters and editors have publicly available contact information. Neither they nor the publication’s general contact lines responded to questions about The Maine Independent or its parent organization.
A GROWING ECOSYSTEM
The Maine Independent is not the only pink slime site created here by national partisan groups in the months prior to this November’s pivotal midterm elections.
Conservative dark money groups and super PACs have similarly established several outlets masquerading as local Maine news sources ahead of the November elections.
Those operations have primarily used social media as a means to spread their message. The Independent, however, is taking a markedly different approach by mailing printed copies directly to voters.
It’s not uncommon for swing states to be inundated with political ads ahead of important elections. But Socolow, the UMaine professor, said the influx of misleading news outlets in Maine highlights how much stake national interests have in winning the state’s U.S. Senate race — and how they can use a shifting media ecosystem to do so.
“You would think you would see this kind of proliferation in a much larger audience area,” Socolow said. “But I think the reason that so many of them are here is that it’s cheap. We’re a small and easily influenced voter base, through social media and micro-targeting.”
Partisan news isn’t a new phenomenon, Socolow noted. Prior to the last hundred years or so, political parties often sponsored newspapers to toe the party line. Even today, local outlets like the Maine Beacon and Maine Wire are run with the stated goal of pushing particular political agendas.
What is new is national groups seeding swing states with slanted faux-local news, Socolow said. And with the advent of social media, those efforts have become more widespread than ever.
What remains to be seen, however, is how effective the strategy will be.

title: An AI chatbot tipped off police about an unsolved murder, but the tip wasn’t real
text:
PHILADELPHIA (CNN) - The Philadelphia Police Department said an Anthropic AI model gave it a false tip about a murder investigation in July.
The department said the tip came in through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com but was flagged as spam.
Anthropic told the Philadelphia Police Department about the incident this month, the department said.
The department said it’s “unacceptable” that the company took so long to detect and report what happened.
Anthropic said it has been investigating, “Claude submitting a sensitive form on a real website when it should not have.”

title: Waterville school evacuated, canceled Wednesday after bomb threat found on voicemail
text:
WATERVILLE — Waterville Senior High School was evacuated Wednesday morning after school personnel discovered a bomb threat left on voicemail.
The Waterville Police Department identified the caller as a juvenile who left a message with the school late last night and Maj. Jason Longley said the police do not believe it to be a credible threat. The caller has been charged with terrorizing, a felony, Longley said.
Superintendent Peter Hallen canceled school after students were evacuated, with the high schoolers initially moving to Mount Merici Academy on foot before being discharged.
The police department dispatched bomb dogs to the school, and Longley said the department is “taking all the necessary steps,” but that he believes this to be a “localized issue” and not a credible threat.

title: Augusta water district sues paper mills for PFAS contamination
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Greater Augusta Utility District is suing the owners of four paper mills on the Kennebec River for allegedly contaminating one of its drinking water wells downstream with toxic “forever chemicals.”
The district said that per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS, discharged at the mills and nearby landfills were carried by the Kennebec into one of its drinking water wells.
The district had to close one of its riverside wells in 2024 after it recorded PFAS levels above the state safety limit of 20 parts per trillion.
In the lawsuit, the agency says the mill owners should be solely responsible for all PFAS remediation costs.
The utility district did not respond to an interview request Tuesday. It wants the companies to pay for current and future water treatment and remediation.
The lawsuit names the Sappi Mill in Skowhegan, Huhtamaki plant in Waterville, a defunct mill in Winslow owned by Kimberly-Clark and a former facility in Augusta owned by now-bankrupt American Tissue Mills of Maine.
In a statement, Sappi said that it was in the process of reviewing the complaint and was in compliance with all environmental regulations and its state and federal discharge permits.
“Sappi does not knowingly use PFAS containing materials in any of its products,” spokesperson April Jones said.
The lawsuit alleges that pollution from the mills has contaminated the Kennebec River, as recorded by elevated chemical levels in fish tissue recorded by the Maine Department of Environmental Protection.
“Maine DEP has reported PFOS contamination in aquatic species collected from multiple locations along the river, including Hinckley, Fairfield, Gardiner, Augusta, and downstream locations,” the utility said.
Only one of its wells hydrologically connected to the Kennebec River showed elevated levels of PFAS chemicals, according to the utility district. Other drilled wells have shown no contamination, it added.
The well that was taken offline two years ago was restored last week after the district added a $2 million PFAS treatment system, according to news reports.
Emily Carey Perez de Alejo, executive director of Maine environmental group Defend our Health, said Augusta’s lawsuit was the first of its kind in Maine.
While landowners have sued paper mills over PFAS contamination from wastewater sludge sprayed on their land and water districts have pursued manufacturers in U.S. court, Carey Perez de Alejo said the case may be a unique example of a public utility coming after PFAS users.
“The information on the hazard of PFAS chemicals has been available for years, and there is significant business risk in choosing to produce or use hazardous chemicals,” Carey Perez de Alejo said.
“Industries choosing to create or use PFAS in spite of that should not be surprised when consumers, regulators, and other impacted groups (like water and wastewater utilities) seek compensation for the harms generated by those PFAS,” Carey Perez de Alejo added.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: More than 2,000 pigs killed in barn fire
text:
SIBLEY, Iowa (KTIV/Gray News) - Hundreds of pigs were killed in a barn fire in Iowa.
According to the Sibley Fire Department, a hog barn caught fire late Monday night into early Tuesday morning. The building was destroyed before firefighters got to the scene.
“It’s always a scary first few moments but we got the fire knocked down,” the fire department said in a post on Facebook.
About 2,400 pigs were killed. No one was injured.
The Sibley Fire Department said its crews worked to protect two nearby gas cylinders and to keep embers from spreading to a cornfield.
Osceola County Emergency Management said multiple fire departments worked to contain the fire. The Sibley Fire Department said the Ashton Fire Department, Little Rock Fire Department and George Fire Department were among those that assisted.

title: 7 haunted halls, tours and more set for central Maine this month
text:
KENNEBEC CREEPS & CRAWLS
A tour of all things creepy in Hallowell is set for 3 p.m. Sunday, Oct. 18 and 25, at Hallowell Cemetery, 447 Water St.
Participants can learn about the city’s history, victorian funeral customs, explore cemetery symbolism, try your hand with the dowsing rods, and listen and learn more about the 16 girls who passed away at the Industrial School for Girls.
Tickets cost $30, to reserve a spot or for more information call 207-542-3701.
SHADOWS IN THE HALL
The third annual Shadows in the Hall is set to return from 6-9:30 p.m. Friday and Saturday, Oct. 23 and 24, at Johnson Hall Opera House, 280 Water St., Gardiner.
Those who attend can expect ghostly stories, unexpected scares and characters from another time. More than 50 community performers, ages 6 to 83, plan to bring the building to life through a series of short scenes inspired by different moments in time.
Guests can travel through Johnson Hall in small groups, moving from scene to scene as stories unfold. Some are eerie, some are unsettling, some may make you laugh and you never know what might be waiting around the next corner.
The full experience lasts approximately 30 minutes.
Shadows in the Hall is not intended for young audiences. The experience includes frightening scenes, sudden scares and mature themes; viewer discretion is advised.
Tickets cost $14.44; johnsonhall.org.
HALLOWEEN PARANORMAL EVENT
Central Maine Ghost Hunters are set to host a Halloween Paranormal Event Saturday, Oct. 24, at Giberson Funeral Home, 18 River St., Bingham.
A meet-and-greet begins at 6 p.m., a four-hour ghost hunt is set for 7-11 p.m., and a two-hour private investigation after the event is set for midnight-2 a.m.
Tickets cost $40 or $60 for the VIP investigation experience.

Planned events include Trunk or Treat from 4 to 6 p.m. on Main Street and Castonguay Square. Donations accepted; lightsupskowhegan.org.

title: Portland police to participate in Drug Take Back Day
The Latest: Battle lines as Republicans retreat from front-line House districts
text:
Republicans are retreating from a handful of battleground U.S. House races, while Democrats are racing to raise money to boost candidates who seemed like long shots earlier this year. The strategy in the final three weeks of midterm campaigns points to an increasingly defensive posture by Republicans, who have already trimmed their expectations in U.S. Senate races, and new aggression from Democrats, who are trying to capitalize on President Donald Trump’s weak approval ratings.
Kamala Harris is building out her final fall campaign blitz on behalf of other Democrats, completing a midterm schedule that by Election Day will have taken her to multiple early presidential primary states on Democrats’ 2028 calendar as the former vice president mulls whether to seek the White House again.
A federal judge on Tuesday extended an order blocking Trump’s administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, a pivotal operational development for the organizations as the extraordinary case — pitting the president against the media that cover him — makes its way through the legal system.
The Latest:
White House press secretary’s debut raises new questions about her job
Katie Zacharia, now the official voice of the world’s most powerful person, put the “brief” back in briefing during her initial White House press conference, reading from a prepared text before answering just four questions.
“I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people,” Zacharia said.
Nowhere did she mention the task of disseminating accurate information to Americans.
How will Zacharia fare in coming days and weeks and, if her tenure lasts, months? That, like so much else, depends on one thing: Donald Trump.
Pricey gas and rising AI costs likely pushed inflation higher in September
U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes, and air fares got more expensive just as Americans prepare to vote in elections focused on affordability.
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. Monthly costs showed the biggest gain in five months.
The figures reflect the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and surging investments in data centers and artificial intelligence. Core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month, well above the Federal Reserves’s 2% target.
The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found just 17% of U.S. adults approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, and only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Trump says oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is set to begin. It’s not that simple
Trump said “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in “our new and beautiful Greenland ” early Wednesday.
It wasn’t immediately clear what exploration or developments the U.S. president was referring to in his post, and Greenland is a self-governing territory of Denmark, rather than a part of the United States.
Rising energy prices — a direct result of Trump’s war in Iran — are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for America’s working class ahead of the midterm elections next month. Trump’s comments Wednesday are likely aimed at addressing voters’ concerns before they head to the polls.
But despite Trump’s optimism, resource exploration and extraction in Greenland has stymied companies for decades thanks to the island’s harsh climate, lack of key infrastructure and difficult geology. Previous efforts to extract so-called rare earth minerals, as well as oil and gas, have never progressed beyond the exploratory stage.
Judge extends order blocking Trump from banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from White House
A federal judge on Tuesday extended an order blocking Trump’s administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, a pivotal operational development for the organizations as the extraordinary case — pitting the president against the media that cover him — makes its way through the legal system.
In a victory for media organizations at a time when tension between the White House and journalists is high, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in their constitutional free speech and due process claims.
“Still,” he added in his late-night order, “no one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”
But Kelly agreed with the plaintiffs that the national security arguments came after the fact and were unsupported by the administration.
Kamala Harris adds stops to her final midterm campaign stretch. Her decision about 2028 comes later
Kamala Harris is building out her final fall campaign blitz on behalf of other Democrats, completing a midterm schedule that by Election Day will have taken her to multiple early presidential primary states on Democrats’ 2028 calendar as the former vice president mulls whether to seek the White House again.
Spanning from Oct. 21 to Oct. 30, Harris’ expanded closing stretch will now include New Hampshire, Wisconsin and Mississippi, along with a virtual event in Florida, according to a schedule her office shared first with The Associated Press. Harris already had announced late October stops in Georgia and Nevada.
Harris has said in multiple recent interviews that she’s focused on helping Democrats win in November. But she’s not ruled out another presidential campaign after losing the 2024 general election to Donald Trump.
Her late October tour focuses on nominees for governor and U.S. Senate, including pairings that put the first Black woman to serve as vice president alongside potential history-making candidates.
Democrats eye opportunities as Republicans drop spending in some House races
Republicans were retreating Tuesday from a handful of battleground U.S. House races while Democrats were racing to raise money to boost candidates who seemed like long shots earlier this year.
The Congressional Leadership Fund, the leading House Republican super PAC, canceled spending in four races from the Midwest to the East Coast and increased its investment in 16 other races from Texas to Pennsylvania. Another super PAC allied with President Donald Trump is cutting back in a battleground district in the Las Vegas area.
Meanwhile, Democrats’ House campaign committee is eyeing openings in Republican-held districts and hoping to raise millions of dollars in the next week to fuel a late round of advertising that they say could net at least a half dozen more seats.
The shifting money in the final three weeks of midterm campaigns points to an increasingly defensive posture by Republicans, who have already trimmed their expectations in U.S. Senate races, and new aggression from Democrats, who are trying to capitalize on President Donald Trump’s weak approval ratings.

title: High schools Wednesday: Skowhegan girls soccer takes down Bangor
text:
A goal by Mae Dubois with 3:02 remaining propelled Skowhegan to a 2-1 win over Bangor in a Class A North girls soccer match Wednesday in Skowhegan.
Charlotte Libby also scored and Lydia Herrick set up both goals for the River Hawks (10-1-1). Skowhegan keeper Chloe Cyr made five saves.
Bangor (7-4-2), the reigning Class A champion, got a goal from Callen Pooler and 13 saves from Emily Caulkin.
FIELD HOCKEY
WINSLOW 2, ERSKINE ACADEMY 1: Delana Ferran assisted on Adriana Lombardi’s tying goal in the second quarter, then scored the go-ahead goal in the third as the Black Raiders (6-5-1) edged the Eagles (4-7) in Winslow.
Erskine’s Rachel Grant opened the scoring in the first quarter, assisted by Ayla McCurdy.
Emma Fales assisted on the winning goal.
Winslow goalies Silver Picard and Emma McCaslin combined for three saves, while Audrey Tibbetts of Erskine stopped nine shots.
WINTHROP/MARANACOOK 5, OAK HILL 1: Evelyn Mortimer scored three goals to pace the Ramblers (12-1) to a win over the Raiders (4-8) in Wales.
Natalie Irwin and Ella Giles each chipped in with a goal and an assist. The Ramblers broke the game open with three goals in the third quarter after leading 1-0 at halftime.
Madalyn Sikora scored for Oak Hill.
SKOWHEGAN 3, CAMDEN HILLS 2: Faith Pease tied the game late in the third quarter, then set up the winner by Kaitlyn Dufour early in the fourth as the River Hawks (12-1) completed their comeback from an early two-goal deficit against the Windjammers (10-2) in Rockport.
Camden Hills grabbed a 2-0 lead on goals by Carly Fitzpatrick, on a rebound off a penalty corner, and Alanna Smith. Charlotte Haynie started Skowhegan’s comeback midway through the second quarter, converting a penalty corner with an assist from Dufour.
Skowhegan goalie Michelle Williams finished with eight saves.
BOYS SOCCER
BUCKFIELD 2, MT. ABRAM 1: Nate Thomas stood tall in goal with 22 saves for the Bucks (6-5-2) in their win over the Roadrunners (6-5-2) in Salem Township.
Nolan Litchfield and Evan St. Pierre provided a goal apiece for Buckfield.
Brennan Mitchell scored for Mt. Abram off an assist by Will Swain. Goalie Ben Beaulier made two saves.
HALL-DALE 3, MOUNTAIN VALLEY 0: The Bulldogs (12-1) defeated the pesky Falcons (5-5-2) to earn their 12th straight victory in a Class C South matchup in Rumford.
Hall-Dale broke through 20 minutes into the game when Davis Madore sent a nice through ball to Kayden Reith for the first goal. Kayden Ferguson added another first-half goal, poking in a cross by Collin McArthur. McArthur finished the scoring by heading in a cross from Colby Keene with six minutes remaining in the game.
Mountain Valley goalie Gabe Hall finished with 14 saves, while Hall-Dale’s Landon Gilbert stopped two shots.
MONMOUTH ACADEMY 7, WINTHROP 0: Zane Foyt and Bryce Fletcher scored in each half, leading the Mustangs (11-0) to a win over the Ramblers (3-8-2) in Winthrop.
Jake Harmon and Noah Schultz added to Monmouth’s lead during a five-goal second half that included an own goal.

title: Crash causes backups on Maine Turnpike southbound in Scarborough
text:
Maine Turnpike crash causes backups on Interstate 95 south in Scarborough
Two of three travel lanes were closed for a time
Maine Turnpike crash causes backups on Interstate 95 south in Scarborough
Two of three travel lanes were closed for a time
Drivers experienced delays on the southbound side of the Maine Turnpike late Wednesday morning following a crash in Scarborough.
Turnpike officials first shared a traffic alert about the crash on Interstate 95 south shortly before 10:15 a.m. Wednesday, stating that the left lane at mile 41 in Scarborough was blocked.
In an update shared shortly after 10:30 a.m., the MTA said the left and center lanes were blocked as a result of the crash.
Shortly after 10:40 a.m., the center lane had reopened to traffic but the left lane remained blocked.
Shortly before 11:15 a.m., officials said that the crash scene had been cleared, but they also warned drivers that heavy traffic remained between Exit 42 in Scarborough and Exit 36 in Saco.
A photo shared with Maine's Total Coverage shows there were heavy backups on that stretch of the turnpike.
The MTA lifted the crash alert shortly before 11:30 a.m.
Turnpike officials have not shared additional details about the crash.
Another photo shared with Maine's Total Coverage shows a red Toyota Tacoma pickup truck was being towed away from the scene.

title: Police investigate fight at youth football game in Livermore Falls
text:
Livermore Falls police are reviewing a recording and interviews related to a fight that occurred Saturday between parents and a coach at Griffin Field in Livermore Falls.
Video of the altercation, which took place on the sidelines of an Area Youth Sports football game, was disseminated widely on social media.
Once the police investigation is concluded, police Chief Abe Haroon said, the report will be given to the Androscoggin County district attorney for review to determine if any charges will be lodged against participants.
No summonses have been issued and no arrests have been made, he said.
One of the men involved is Cpl. Dylan Rider, an Androscoggin County Sheriff’s deputy, an Area Youth Sports football coach and a county commissioner. Rider was off duty.
In accordance with the organization’s bylaws and code of conduct, the AYS board of directors has initiated a formal review of the incident, AYS President Nixon Ortiz wrote in an email.
“Area Youth Sports (AYS) is aware of the recent incident and video circulating on social media,” Ortiz wrote. “The safety, well-being, and sportsmanship of our youth, families, and community are our highest priorities.”
“Pending the outcome of this thorough investigation, all involved parties have been asked not to attend any practices, games, or AYS events for the balance of this season,” Ortiz wrote. “This interim measure ensures a fair and complete investigative process can play out so that the Board can make informed, appropriate final determinations.”
William Gagne, chief deputy of the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office, said Tuesday that his office is aware of the situation. “It was brought to our attention and we are actively looking into the matter internally,” he said.
A short video recording of the altercation was posted on Facebook by Donna Jewell, who accuses Rider of assaulting her and her husband.
The video shows Jewell going up to Rider with a puppy in her arms. It appears she makes contact with Rider, who turns toward her as her hands go up toward Rider’s face. He grabs Jewell’s arms and pushes her to the ground as he makes his way toward a fight between two men. One of those men was Rider’s father.
Rider’s son also plays on the youth football team. Jewell is the parent of an athlete as well.
Rider wrote on his Facebook post that he was punched and scratched by Jewell, and that his father was allegedly punched in the stomach by the other man.
Jewell, whose post of the video has more than 1,300 comments, did not return a request for comment. In a Facebook post, she said an attorney had advised her and her husband to not discuss the issue in public anymore.
Rider’s attorney, Andre “AJ” Hungerford, wrote in an email, “Because there is an investigation of events on Saturday, October 10, 2026 involving various parties, including Dylan Rider, I am withholding comment until a more appropriate time.”

title: Social Security will jump 3.6% next year. How far does that really go in Maine?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities — including about 400,000 people in Maine — will go up by 3.6% next year.
Some say it’s not enough to offset soaring prices.
The adjustment, which accounts mostly for inflation, translates to an average of $75 extra per month for the 73 million people nationwide who receive monthly Social Security benefits and the nearly 7.5 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
In all, the cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries will add about $360 million to Mainers’ pockets next year, and the Social Security Administration’s commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.”
But most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices. The adjustment for this year was 2.8%, following 2.5% in 2025, 3.2% in 2024 and a historically large 8.7% jump in 2023.
And these are top issues for older Mainers, a key, high-turnout demographic in the upcoming midterm elections: Another AARP poll of older Maine voters found that their top concerns were affordability and Social Security and Medicare.
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits facing many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — 1 in 5 have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last,” AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan said.
AARP Maine State Director Noël Bonam said there is a flaw in the Social Security annual adjustment system, which is based on year-on-year measures by the Bureau of Labor Standards: It simply does not account for the true cost of living.
The recent national AARP poll found that almost 40% of Social Security recipients planned to reduce their expenses on everyday needs, including groceries and medication. The more accurate annual increase, those respondents said, would be 5% to 8%.
The cost of goods such as heating oil have rocketed well past the pace of inflation since the start the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran this spring. Those costs reached an all-time high last month, and the Natural Resources Council of Maine found families in Maine will spend an additional $1,200, at least, this winter filling their tanks.
Jess Maurer, the executive director of the Maine Council on Aging, said it cost 60% more to fill her tank this year than it did last fall.
That’s untenable for the one-third of Mainers age 65 and older who have no major savings or other income than Social Security, she said. Many, Maurer said, will have tough decisions to make this winter: medication or food or fuel.
“A 3.6% cost of living increase for people who already don’t have enough money to meet their basic needs — $75 a month isn’t going to cut it,” Maurer said. “It may, in fact, cover the increased cost of food, but it won’t cover the increased cost of goods and of fuel oil for the winter.”
Maurer said older women, especially those living alone, will be among the hardest hit by the disconnect between increases in Social Security benefits and the cost of living. Maine women, she said, are more likely to have worked in lower-paying careers or to have left work to become caregivers. That often means they paid less into Social Security over their working years.
“It is definitely women who get caught in that circle more than men, and it’s been women who have fewer resources later in life,” she said. “They’re the folks who are getting squeezed right now.”
Meanwhile, the Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old-age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Massachusetts, and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. The COLA is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
Treating all income the same “would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” Warren and Moreno wrote in The New York Times. The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the cap would add roughly $3 trillion to the program over the next 10 years.
The solution will require tons of new money, Maurer said — but it’s necessary.
“It is about survival, not thriving, at this point for a lot of older Mainers,” she said.
This story contains reporting from The Associated Press.

title: The Best New Movies to Watch at Home This Weekend
text:
The Best New Movies You Can Watch at Home This Weekend
New movies are coming to streaming this week and every week, at a faster pace than ever before. As always, ScreenCrush has your back, with a weekly guide to the latest releases on streaming (and digital rental or purchse) that deserve your attention. Sit back, relax, and check out what’s coming to a TV or computer (or, sigh, a phone) near you.
Then you’ve got all weekend to watch up with these titles. The theater is still the best, of course, but some weekends you just can’t muster the energy to get off the couch and haul yourself to the multiplex.
New Movies Streaming This Week and Weekend
This week you can watch Anya Taylor-Joy try to throw Chris Evans in a volcano, plus documentaries about Norm Macdonald and the most valuable hip-hop album in history. Or how about a drama starring Hugh Jackman as old Robin Hood? This is one of the wildest weeks on streaming in a while.
If these titles don’t do it for you, you can also check out some other recent streaming releases here. Or just keep scrolling, and see the new movies you can stream or rent on digital at home this weekend.
Sacrifice
In Sacrifice, Anya Taylor-Joy plays a cult leader who believes that the only way to avoid the apocalypse is by sacrificing Chris Evans by tossing him into an active volcano. Anya, Ghosted was bad but it wasn’t, like, that bad. The dark comedy also stars Vincent Cassel, Sam Richardson, John Malkovich, Salma Hayek-Pinault, and Charli xcx.
Where to watch Sacrifice: Premieres on October 16 on Netflix.
The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable
The story of the Wu-Tang Clan’s famous album Once Upon a Time in Shaolin — of which only one copy has ever been (or will ever be) made or sold — is the subject of this Netflix documentary, which also focuses on (per Netflix) “Dutch-Moroccan rapper and producer Cilvaringz, who transformed himself from the group's most devoted fan into the unlikeliest of disciples to his childhood heroes, including The RZA, whose mentorship shapes the odyssey that follows.” Unlike Once Upon a Time in Shaolin, The Disciple will be widely available to anyone with a Netflix account.
Where to watch The Disciple: Premieres on October 16 on Netflix.
The Death of Robin Hood
Hugh Jackman’s latest gritty action movie about an aging hero comes from Michael Sarnoski, the director behind the excellent Pig and A Quiet Place: Day One. Jackman plays a man who, once upon a time, was known as Robin Hood. Now he’s an old warrior haunted by a past far less heroic than the modern legends about him. Can be be redeemed?
Where to watch The Death of Robin Hood: Premieres on October 16 on HBO Max.
Norm: The Tale of Norm Macdonald
Saturday Night Live alumni Norm Macdonald passed away in 2021 at the age of 61 after a long but private battle with leukemia. His life, career, and unique sense of humor are the subject of the latest documentary from Judd Apatow, whose previous non-fiction films about standups include George Carlin’s American Dream and The Zen Diaries of Garry Shandling.
Where to watch Norm: Premieres on October 16 on Netflix.
Buddy
Remember “Too Many Cooks,” the astoundingly and hilariously strange Adult Swim short film that mocked the tropes of ’80s and ’90s sitcom schlock? That was created by Casper Kelly, who makes his feature directorial debut with Buddy, a horror comedy about the dark side of a Barney-style children’s television show of the 1990s.
Where to watch Buddy: Prime Video, Apple TV, Fandango.

title: QUINN QUESTIONS: Imaginary quotes
text:
A historian once suggested “great triumphs should be recorded.” Since then, when anyone did something important, a reporter wrote it down.
Then audio and video got invented. After that, the newsperson simply pointed a microphone or camera at famous people.
If the celebrity said something good, it made the nightly news. If the quote was something unexpected, it might become a “blooper,” and could be replayed frequently…sometimes even at parties.
Here’s the point: If we had current technology a long time ago, we could have recorded these famous sayings. (Unfortunately, since we didn’t, I had to make them up.)
“Excuse me…is this East Texas?” – Columbus, on discovering the Bahamas.
“Honey, I’m starving. You heat up the stove, and I’ll ask the neighbors over for dinner.” – Melvin the Cannibal
“So, while I was asleep under the tree, an apple fell on my head. I shall call it ‘concussion.'”—Isaac Newton, before he thought of the word “gravity.”
“How about we just eat ducks? I can’t get these dang turkeys in the pot.” – Pilgrim chef.
“Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered weak and weary, over some old catalog I had tossed out once before…”—first draft of The Raven.
“What do you think this is? A quick-print shop?” – Gutenberg, to an early printing customer.
“C’mon, masked man. Let’s duel. On guard! Hey…where’s my nose?” – Zorro’s fencing partner.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: A Wyoming grad student who allegedly poisoned a colleague has been arrested fleeing to China
text:
A Wyoming grad student who allegedly poisoned a colleague has been arrested fleeing to China
A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations that she poisoned the tea of a fellow student who had pending patents and with whom she didn't get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested Oct. 6 at Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in research similar to what she once did in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim's wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
U.S. officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.

title: South Berwick adopts data center moratorium
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
South Berwick has become the latest Maine town to pass a data center moratorium amid a nationwide debate over the impacts of unregulated, large-scale data processing facilities.
The Town Council decided Tuesday night to adopt the 180-day pause retroactive to July 14 — the date that the town’s planning board originally consulted a lawyer so it could begin drafting ordinance language.
That means any data centers proposed from that date are on pause, though councilors said in September that they didn’t know of any.
Like several municipalities across the state, including nearby Sanford, South Berwick’s moratorium is meant to give officials time to conduct in-depth studies about what a data center could mean for the town. The planning board will use those findings to draft ordinance language and set permanent guidelines — or outright bans — for future proposals.
Planning board member Tony Palazzetti, who is also a candidate for Town Council, said the board originally reviewed a proposal that would permit facilities under 100,000 square feet. But officials decided it would be best to follow in the footsteps of municipalities like Sanford, which have significantly smaller thresholds.
“We reduced that to 10,000 (square feet), thinking that was more appropriate for this town and the level of industry that’s here currently,” Palazzetti said Tuesday, adding that larger data centers have the potential to significantly impact the small town’s resources like water and electricity.
Councilor Joel Martin said regardless of what the planning board is working on, the town will also use the state’s recommendations for large-scale data center developments, which are set to be released by Jan. 29, 2027.
Officials noted that the town’s moratorium will expire nearly three weeks before then. But so long as the planning board can show that it has made progress on drafting an ordinance, the Town Council can easily extend that deadline.
“We recognize we’re on a very tight window to do that, and we’re ready to pursue,” Palazzetti told the council.
The council voted 4-0 to pass the moratorium. Vice Chair Mallory Cook was absent.

title: Burglary suspect jumps through closed window to escape deputy
text:
OKLAHOMA COUNTY, Okla. (KOCO) - A dramatic escape was caught on body camera video after a suspected copper thief in Oklahoma jumped through a closed window.
“This is an experienced deputy; he’d never seen anything quite like it before, and by the time that he got outside, our suspect was long gone,” Aaron Brilbeck with the Oklahoma County Sheriff’s Office said.
The video shows the moment a suspect dove through a closed window to escape a deputy. The deputy was investigating a burglary at a vacant home in Oklahoma County on Oct. 1.
“This is a vacant property. Our deputy went up to the back door; he saw the back door had been forced open,” Brilbeck said.
Brilbeck said the suspect was allegedly stealing copper from the appliances and the walls inside the building.
According to the official report, the deputy tried to track down the suspect in his patrol car and then launched a drone to try to find him, but the deputy had no luck.
A nearby residence was also searched, but the suspect was nowhere to be found.
Then, a key piece of evidence was found along with a bicycle: an ID card.
“He was good enough to leave behind his backpack, and inside his backpack was his driver’s license, so it made it really easy to identify him,” Brilbeck said.
The suspect does have a history in Oklahoma County.
“A lot of theft, drug-related stuff, he’s got an assault charge in there,” Brilbeck said.
Despite leaving his driver’s license behind, the suspect remains on the run.

title: 'Affordability is the issue': Inflation climbs ahead of midterm elections
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
'Affordability is the issue': Inflation climbs ahead of midterm elections
With less than three weeks until the midterms, two major economic indicators released Wednesday show affordability remains a top concern for voters.
'Affordability is the issue': Inflation climbs ahead of midterm elections
With less than three weeks until the midterms, two major economic indicators released Wednesday show affordability remains a top concern for voters.
The Social Security Administration announced Wednesday that nearly 72 million Americans will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) beginning in January 2027. The increase averages $75 per month after accounting for inflation, according to the Get the Facts Data Team.
However, a Consumer Price Index (CPI) report released the same day shows inflation outpacing the COLA increase, with prices rising 3.7% in September compared to last year.
Researchers say the shortfall is adding to already tight household budgets, especially for those on Social Security.
AARP says previous increase have forced many members to cut back on essentials like food and medicine.
"If people are going to have to skip meals or skip their medicines and stop taking the pills that their doctors have prescribed for them, the implications to that for people are dire," Bill Sweeney, AARP senior vice president of Government Affairs, said. "That's why it's so important that we protect and strengthen Social Security for years to come to ensure that people can continue to put food on the table and keep a roof over their heads."
Social Security insolvency remains another looming issue, with projections showing the program could become insolvent by 2032.
Sweeney says lawmakers elected during the 2026 midterm cycle could face tough decisions to address the problem.
To fix the program, some lawmakers have already proposed changing COLA calculations to alternative measures of inflation or switching to a flat-rate COLA. However, Sweeney warns that any plan to cap or trim COLA could cut thousands of dollars from a person’s lifetime benefits.
On the campaign trail, President Donald Trump has attempted to address voter concerns on affordability and rising prices.
"Your prices are going to come tumbling down. They already are," President Trump said in a rally speech in Alaska Tuesday.
President Trump also recently introduced a $90 government payout for some Medicare recipients to help offset rising Medicare Part B premiums.
But political analysts say the one-time checks may do little to address rising costs and growing voter frustration.
"Affordability is the issue, and people are getting really tired of high prices," Todd Belt, a professor and analyst at George Washington University, said. "The real difference and why we're seeing this change is they're now putting this at the feet of the president."
Trump has also campaigned on additional measures, including $5,000 dividend payouts if Republicans maintain control of Congress and a $500 Affordable Care Act refund check for some enrollees, aimed at boosting voter turnout ahead of the midterm election.

title: Ellsworth Public Library, Ellsworth Chess Club to host Dick Powell Memorial Chess Tournament
text:
ELLSWORTH — The Ellsworth Public Library and Ellsworth Chess Club will host the Dick Powell Memorial Chess Tournament on Saturday, Oct. 17 from noon to 5 p.m., bringing chess players from across the region together to honor a man who devoted decades to the game and to the young people he taught. The memorial tournament offers former students, fellow players, friends and chess enthusiasts an opportunity to remember Powell through the game he loved.
For decades, Powell was a familiar and influential figure in Maine’s chess community. He helped organize the Ellsworth Chess Community and founded the chess program at Deer Isle-Stonington Elementary School, where he coached for 28 years and helped build a remarkably successful program. During his tenure, the team won 39 state championships and competed in national tournaments. In 2014, the Maine Legislature recognized Powell upon his retirement as a teacher for his extraordinary commitment to the youth of Maine. Richard Aldrich “Dick” Powell of Ellsworth died on Oct. 1, 2025, at the age of 82.
“There are no ‘secret formulas’ that I used along the way. Keeping their interest and having fun were the cornerstones for me,” Powell in an interview with ChessMaine.net in 2014 said. He went on to explain his own motivation: “The fact that I could play [chess] wherever I happened to be — Madagascar, New Zealand, Brazil, Guatemala, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, etc. — was what kept me interested.” Powell was an avid traveler who spoke French, German, Spanish and Portuguese.
Registration: Players and community members interested in participating or learning more can visit the library’s event page. Preregistration is encouraged at https://easypairchess.com/public/tournaments. The tournament is beginner-friendly.
In October 2025, the Ellsworth Chess Club and the Ellsworth Public Library hosted a National Chess Day Tournament with the help of MDI Chess, which drew players of all ages from communities including Machias, Lewiston, Bangor, Glenburn, MDI, Ellsworth, Thorndike and Winthrop.
Ellsworth Public Library is an open, welcoming and safe space where people come together to learn, connect and grow. It is a vibrant hub of curiosity and community where everyone is invited to participate through every chapter of life. The library believes that strong communities begin with equitable access to knowledge, meaningful connections, and lifelong learning and that literacy, especially early literacy, is a vital foundation for the well-being of all community members. Learn more at ellsworthlibrary.net.

also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - One local flower shop spent Wednesday afternoon bringing joy to strangers in downtown Bangor.
For the fifth year, Bangor Floral took part in the nationwide event known as ‘Petal it Forward’.
In West Market Square, florists offered two flowers to strangers.
One flower to keep, the other to be given to somebody to make their day brighter.
Bangor Floral says that it’s just one way to give back to a community that has supported them for more than a century.
“I just I love the look on people’s faces when they realize that the flower is free and they get to keep it and they get to give it to a loved one or a friend. I’ve had people cry. I’ve had people hug me. I love it. It’s my favorite day of the year,” said Heather Murray, office manager at Bangor Floral.
Bangor Floral was one of seven flower shops in Maine taking part, joining more than 700 shops around the United States.

title: OBITUARIES for Thursday, October 15, 2026
text:
DANAL A. GERRARD
WHITEFIELD – Danal A. Gerrard, 61, aka Blondie, Duck Soup, Grampa Dan, passed away on Thursday, September 24, 2026, following a one-and-a-half-year long courageous battle with cancer.
He was born in Augusta on July 2, 1965, son to Norma Gerrard. He was a comedian until the very end. Danny attended the Augusta school system, and had his own rules, which did not coincide with school policies. He left school at the age of 13, and later in life, returned to obtain his GED.
At 14, Danny started his journey with the love of his life, Robin, in their first apartment on Mill Street, in Augusta. Dan had a new role as a provider, family friends, Gerine Ferris and Jim Martin, provided guidance and opportunity for odd jobs, such as mowing lawns and cemetery maintenance. These experiences gave Dan lifelong knowledge, skills, and abilities which contributed to his growth and career path.
Dan’s longest role was as foreman of Augusta Parks, Recreation and Cemeteries for over 30 years. In this position, Dan was responsible for maintaining and decorating the city for all festivities. He helped organize the Fourth of July parade during his years with the city. He would often joke that his job was to plant trees and people. Later in life, he loved working at the Margaret Chase Smith House as a maintenance man for the elderly residents; always going above and beyond to put a smile on their faces. His last role, which Dan felt was his most fulfilling throughout his lifelong career of helping others, was as head custodian at Whitefield Elementary School. Where not only his own grandchildren, but teachers and students alike, called him Grampa Dan.
Dan the man had a heart of gold, he was a family man through and through and took pride in carrying on family traditions. He loved to host family holidays and made sure everyone was cared for, especially “The Aunts”, Aunt Joan and Aunt Nancy. Dan enjoyed planning family events and activities from huge camping trips, hikes, beach trips, cliff jumping, to the annual Mother’s Day bash. He was a coach, a certified girl scout, a jack of all trades and master of none. His motto was “the more the merrier”. Although he was a safety-first kind of guy, he liked to push himself and other to the limit. He liked to march to the beat of his own drum. Dan had a zest and passion for life and adventure which often found him in dangerous situations. His main purpose in life was caring for his wife and children. Shhh… don’t tell anyone, but his grandchildren were his pride and joy. He never missed an event for his children or grandchildren and continued to show up even in his last days. Grampa Dan, the man, the myth, the legend.
Dan was an organ donor and when he was diagnosed with cancer, he learned he was no longer eligible. Disheartened by this news, he set out to find an alternative way to give back. Dan learned of the University of New England’s anatomical donation program for orthopedic research. A lifelong educator, he was thrilled by this option. Once the research process is complete, his remains will contribute to the “Ashes to Ash Trees” program bringing his work of planting trees full circle when he becomes one to help oxygenate the planet.
Dan was predeceased by his grandparents; his mother Norma; his sisters Deborah and Diana; his infant son Shawn; and his sister-in-law Candy. He is survived by his wife of 43 years Robin, their daughter Kellie Coates and her daughters River and Indie and their father Christopher Coates; his daughter Danielle Gerrard and her children Allianna, Kristianna, Jaxson, and Piper and her fiancé Jake Michaud; his brother Darrell Gerrard and fiancée Melanie Bridges; his sisters Deana Tardiff, Darcie Verrill and partner Chris Smith; his sisters-in-law Tammy Kincaid and husband Brian, Tracy McKenney and husband Mike; nephews and nieces, Amanda, Richie, Eric, Josh, Zach, Mitch, Brian, Ashley, Jesse, Jason, Sasha, Kayla, and their families as well as several great -nieces, nephews, aunts, uncles, and cousins
A celebration of life was held on Saturday, October 10, 2026, at Whitefield Elementary School.
In lieu of flowers, please make donations to his daughter Kellie for final expenses.
SALLY F. HOTHAM
ALBION – Sally (Fletcher) Hotham, 76, of Albion, passed away on Sunday, September 27, 2026, following a long battle with Parkinson’s.
Sally was born on August 29, 1950, in Benton, to Byron and Rosella Fletcher. She graduated from Lawrence High School, in Fairfield, in 1969 and shortly after married her high school sweetheart Steve, who went on to enjoy 57 years of marriage together. They settled in Albion where they raised their two children, Dina and Travis.
Sally held several jobs over the years where she met many of her life-long friends, but her main focus was raising her children, making sure they made it to every practice, game and event without ever being late. After retirement she enjoyed “puttering around” with her sisters and being a proud Mimi to Avery and Bennett, where she could always be found at a field, court, event, or with them having a sleepover at Mimi’s house.
Sally is survived by her husband Steve; her daughter Dina (Brad) Giggey; her son Travis (Katie); her grandchildren Brad, Damien, Samantha, Ryan, Avery and Bennett; great-grandchildren Zachary, Elise and Grace; her sisters Karen (Linwood) Doughty, Donna (Blaine) Bunker and Beth Stanhope; sisters-in-law Judy Hotham and Charleen Grotten; many nieces and nephews. She was predeceased by her parents, her brother David and her twin sister Sandra.
A celebration of life will be held on Saturday, November 7, 2026, at the MacCrillis-Rousseau VFW Post #8835, in Winslow, from 1 to 4 p.m. To celebrate Sally please wear a pop of color or some “bling!”
GAY P. MAHEU
WINSLOW – Gay P. Maheu, 90, of Winslow, passed away on Wednesday, September 30, 2026.
She was born on August 15, 1936, in Waterville, the daughter of Wilfred and Gilberte (Roy) Rancourt. Gay was the eldest of four siblings (Ann Gilbert, deceased, Jeanette Leblanc of Florida, and William Rancourt of China, Maine).
Upon graduating with honors from Waterville High School in 1954, Gay entered the work force and worked a wide range of office jobs.
She was married to Donald A. Maheu (deceased) on July 4, 1960. They celebrated 54 years of marriage and five children, Deborah Carr and her husband Michael, Susan Perry and her husband Colonel (Ret.) Warren Perry, James Maheu and his wife Kristen, Vera Maheu, and Robert Maheu and his wife Dawn. She is also survived by five grandchildren, Matthew, Erin, Katie, Michael, and Sam; and four great grandchildren, Dalton, Grant, River, and Margot.
Mrs. Maheu was a member of Corpus Christi Parish, Waterville/Winslow, and served as a volunteer there during coffee hours. As a life member of the Women’s Auxiliary Post #8835, of the Winslow VFW, she worked organizing the children’s Christmas parties. She used her love of sewing to construct quilts for Aids babies and to dress teddy bears at Christmas for the Salvation Army. Gay could be found assisting at any school event her children were involved in including sports, band, and religious education. In her free time Gay enjoyed ballet, opera, reading, and coloring.
A funeral Mass was celebrated Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at Notre Dame Parish, 116 Silver St., Waterville. Burial took place at the Maine Veterans Memorial Cemetery, at 143 Blue Star Avenue, in Augusta. Funeral arrangements are under the care and direction of Veilleux Funeral Home Waterville, Maine.
In lieu of flowers, Gay asks that you donate to your favorite charity.
PATRICIA H. LYFORD
WATERVILLE – Patricia “Pat” Helm Lyford, 88, passed away Wednesday, September 30, 2026, at 12:15 p.m., at Bedside Manor, in Oakland.
Pat was born in Woonsocket, Rhode Island, on November 21, 1937. Her parents were George Theodore Helm and Marjory (Ward) Helm. She graduated as valedictorian of Burrillville High School, in Harrisville, Rhode Island, in June 1955. She attended the University of Rhode Island (URI) and graduated Bachelor of Arts with “highest scholastic honors” in June 1959.
While at URI, Pat met Gordon G. Lyford, from Dover-Foxcroft, Maine. They married on July 25, 1959, in Slatersville, Rhode Island. Their first home together was in Chepachet, Rhode Island, and Pat was a first grade teacher for two years at the local elementary school.
In 1961, Pat and Gordon moved to Maine. Their first child, Peter, was born in March 1962, in Portland, Maine. Moving to Waterville later in 1962, Pat became a lifelong homemaker. Their second child, Kimberly, was born in August 1963 in Waterville, followed by Nancy (December, 1966) and Christopher (October, 1968).
Pat and Gordon joined the First Congregational Church of Waterville in 1962, and she continued as an active member until her passing. She served the church in many capacities: Sunday School teacher, Sunday School superintendent, president of Evening Fellowship, president of Women’s Fellowship, member of the Board of Deacons (three terms), and 16 years as clerk. She was a member of the Evening Sandwich Program for 30 years.
Pat was a faithful blood donor at Red Cross Blood drives throughout her life. She volunteered as a Girl Scout leader, a Cub Scout den mother, a member of Thayer Hospital Auxiliary, a member of Board of Directors of Sunset Home, and a member of Waterville AAUW. Pat received the Micah Award from the Kennebec Valley Organization in 2014 for her many services to her church and her community.
Family was central to Pat’s life, and she hosted many family events here in Waterville, on Cape Cod, and at the family camp in Sebec. Pat’s cookies, bars, brownies and rum cakes are remembered fondly and will be greatly missed by all.
Pat was predeceased by her husband Gordon on May 3, 1983. Her parents, George and Marjory Helm, predeceased her in 2003 and 2007 respectively. She is survived by her children, Peter Lyford and wife Lee Kimberly Lyford, Nancy (Lyford) Hale and husband Steve, Christopher Lyford and wife Cari; her six grandchildren, Zachary Hale and wife Katelynn, Helm Toler, Seamus Toler, Noah Lyford, Caleb Lyford, and Harper Lyford); and three great-grandchildren, Grayson, Delaney, and Elijah Hale; her siblings, Ted Helm and wife Judy, Jeffrey Helm and wife Kathy, Jennifer (Helm) Geurtsen and husband John; eight nephews and nieces, John Helm, Michael Helm, Kelly Helm-Pullar, Brent Helm, Kala Helm Campbell, Melissa Geurtsen Norwood, Kerry Geurtsen Jerin, and Andrew Geurtsen.
A memorial service and celebration of life will take place on Saturday, October 31, 2026, at 1 p.m., at St Mark’s Episcopal Church, 60 Eustis Parkway, in Waterville. The service will be followed by a reception at the same location. Pat specified there be no visiting hours and a private committal service.
In lieu of flowers, memorial gifts may be made to First Congregational Church of Waterville, United Church of Christ, 21 College Ave., Waterville, ME 04901.
TRAVIS S. RICH
CLINTON – Travis Scott Rich, 35, passed away on Monday, October 5, 2026, following a courageous battle with cancer.
A funeral service honoring and celebrating the life of Travis Scott Rich will be held on Friday, October 16, 2026, Valley High School, in Bingham. Doors will open at 2:30 p.m., with the service beginning at 3:30 p.m.
In lieu of flowers, the family kindly requests that memorial donations be made to The Travis Rich Children’s Legacy Fund, established in memory of Travis to help provide for the future of his three children. Donations may be made directly at any Skowhegan Savings Bank – The Travis Rich Children’s Legacy Fund.
GWENDOLYN H. CUNNINGHAM CASEY
WINDSOR – Gwendolyn H. Cunningham Casey, 91, passed away on Saturday, September 19, 2026, while she was in her own home.
She was born April 25, 1935, in Vassalboro, the third of 10 children to Montie Senior and Marguerite Rainey Cunningham. She was married to her husband Glendon Casey for 68 years. Together they had seven children, Brian and wife, Alice; Glenda and husband, David; Keith; Dawn and late husband Jim; Jeffrey, and wife, Rhonda; Heidi and husband David; and Bobby; also two stepchildren, Joshua and Heather. She was the proud nana of 17 grandchildren, 18 great-grandchildren, and 2 great great grandchildren.
She was a long time active member of the North Windsor Baptist Church. She became a member of the church in 1978. She was a kind, caring, loving, and faithful Christian woman. She was known as a true prayer warrior. She was a true example of what faith in Jesus means.
Her employment included, waitressing, Bureau of Motor Vehicles title examiner, and a jury officer for Kennebec County and many others. She really enjoyed knitting and every year she presented several knitted dish cloths to all. She enjoyed the Sunday dinners with anyone and everyone who showed up. She loved bird watching out her dining room window, although she didn’t enjoy the squirrels so much. She really enjoyed camping and fly fishing at Round Pond. She was an avid Boston Red Sox fan.
She was predeceased by her husband Glendon, her sons Keith and Bobby, and her stepdaughter, Heather, by both parents, and four brothers, one sister, two grandchildren and three nephews.
A graveside service will be held at 11 a.m., on Saturday, October 24, 2026, at Village Cemetery, in North Vassalboro.
NORMA NIVISON
OAKLAND – Norma Nivison, 80, was born on January 11, 1946, the daughter of Leland “Bud” and Maefred (Thomas) Thing. She attended Waterville High School, graduating with the class of 1964. Norma went on to work at Thayer Hospital, where she dedicated nearly 40 years of her life before retiring in 2011.
In 1966, Norma married Melvyn D. Nivison. Together, they enjoyed many years of marriage and shared a number of adventures and special memories. They loved snowmobiling, taking long trips together on their trike, and accompanying Mel as he performed with his band, “The Entertainers.” Norma also enjoyed ceramics and was known for cooking wonderful holiday dinners for her family and extended family, creating traditions and memories that would be cherished for years to come.
Norma was a devoted mother, grandmother, sister, and friend. She will be remembered for the love she had for her family, the joy she found in spending time with those close to her, and the many memories she created throughout her life.
Norma was predeceased by her parents, Leland “Bud” and Maefred Thing; her husband, Melvyn; and her sister, Nancy Thing. She is survived by her daughter, Margo Nivison; her son, Kurt “Bubba” Nivison; her granddaughter, Sarah Briganti; her brother, Robert “Bob” Thing and his wife, Shirley; her brother-in-law, William “Bill” Nivison; her cousin, Charlene Mushero; and her lifelong friend, Paula Mitchell.
The family will be holding a private burial in the coming weeks.
RUSSELL L. BRAGG
LEE – Russell ” Rusty ” Lynn Bragg, 65, passed away unexpectedly on Tuesday, September 29, 2026 at his home in Lee. He was born January 26, 1961, in Waterville, the son of Nancy Bragg Violette and Wayne Bragg { deceased}.
Rusty graduated from Winslow High School in 1979 and went on to attend Vermont Technical College where he received a degree in Mechanical Engineering. He worked as a Geotechnical / mechanical engineer for S. W. Cole Engineering for over 40 years,” retiring” at the age of 58. He then worked for Owen J. Folsom and other private consulting firms. His work combined with this technical intellect and his love for the Earth he built a professional legacy defined by precision and dedication.
Rusty was a passionate basketball player throughout his years at Winslow High school. He dedicated countless hours to coaching and teaching the game to younger, upcoming players, passing on not just the skills for the court but lessons in sportsmanship and teamwork.
Rusty enjoyed being out in nature hunting, fishing, playing golf, reading and learning history.
Some of Rusty’s most treasured times were when he was hunting alongside his father, his grandfather ” Bampie”, his brothers Greg and Ryan and his uncles.
He served two terms as selectmen in his home town of Lee. He was deeply committed to his community demonstrated by his strong sense of civic duty and integrity. He was extremely witty and fluent in sarcasm. He had a presence and was such a force in life. He could command a room. He enjoyed sharing his knowledge with anyone who would listen.
Above all else, he enjoyed spending quality time with his only daughter Melinda ” Mindy” Crawford and his grandson Aden Bragg.
Rusty is survived by his mother Nancy Bragg Violette and husband Robert Violette; his only daughter, Melinda “Mindy” Crawford, his grandson Aden Bragg; his brothers Greg Bragg, wife Marne Bragg, Ryan Bragg wife Tonya; many aunts and uncles; Dale and Priscilla Abbott, Sherry and Roger Deschaine, Brenda and Mark Lint, Sandra Bragg, Joyce Patrick, Carla Dumont, Pam and Nimer George, Brenda Bragg, Carl Bragg II; many nieces and nephews. Rusty touched so many lives it would be impossible to name them all, know that you are loved. If you received random calls to just “check in” know that you were a friend.
Rusty’s life was rich with enduring friendship. That stood the test of time. During his formative years he and his best friend, Marc Maheu shared countless adventures with legendary stories that were meant to be kept between the two of them. He shared a lifelong friendship with Judy Tibbetts beginning at the age of 13 years old. She remained a devoted constant friend throughout his lifetime sharing many of his special times. He often teased her that she had “thrown him off the bridge”. Years later he tried to find that wooden bridge where their initials were carved into the beams. He wanted to build another bridge that he would never be thrown off from.
He was predeceased by his only sister Lisa Cunliffe, his father Wayne Bragg, his grandparents who influenced the essence of Rusty’s love of the outdoors and passion for reading. Harold” Bampy” Abbott and “Nana “Mildred” Abbott, as well as Carl Bragg and Thelma Bragg, Glen Dumont and Natalie Buker Brooks, mother of Melinda Crawford.
Funeral services will be held on Thursday, October 15, 2026, at 3:30 p.m., at First Church of Waterville, 1 Park Street, Waterville, Maine. Reception to follow at Governor’s Restaurant, 376 Main Street, Waterville, Maine.
Private interment will be held at a later time.
Should you wish to send flowers, the church address is 1 Park Street, Waterville, Maine.
In lieu of flowers Rusty had a passion for St. Jude’s Childrens Research Hospital.
Donations can be made at donors@stjude.org or call 1-800-822-6344.
To share condolences and memories online visit www.bowersfuneral.com.

title: Charlie McAvoy scores in return to help the Bruins beat the Sharks
text:
SAN JOSE, Calif. — Charlie McAvoy scored in his season debut after serving a six-game suspension and the Boston Bruins beat the San Jose Sharks 6-3 on Tuesday night.
McAvoy missed the first six games of the season as punishment for slashing Buffalo’s Zach Benson late in Game 6 of the first round of the playoffs last season when the Bruins got eliminated.
He didn’t take long to make an impact as he got in front of the crease and knocked in a pass from JJ Peterka late in the first period to give Boston a 2-1 lead.
Fraser Minten scored two goals and Matthew Poitras and Pavel Zacha also scored for the Bruins, who have won three straight games. Will Borgen added an empty-net goal.
Jeremy Swayman made 35 saves.
Ivar Stenberg scored his first career goal for San Jose. Macklin Celebrini and Jacob Trouba also scored for the Sharks. Yaroslav Askarov made 20 saves.
Stenberg, the No. 2 overall pick in the draft in June, tied the game at 2 early in the second period when he tapped in a perfect back-door pass from Celebrini on the power play.
Poitras put Boston back in front midway through the second when he got the puck alone in front of the net and beat Askarov. The Bruins extended the lead when Zacha scored with 3 seconds remaining in the period when he finished a two-on-one with Morgan Geekie.
Celebrini scored on the power play early in the third to make it a one-goal game but Minten’s second goal of the game midway through the period restored the two-goal lead.
Up next
Bruins: Visit Anaheim on Friday night.
Sharks: Visit Nashville on Thursday night.

FOR YOUR HEALTH: Carbs Are Not the Enemy – Diet Culture Is
text:
by Kate Rhéaume, ND.
Carbohydrates have become the nutritional villain of the social media era – banished, feared, and blamed for everything from weight gain to brain fog. But like most things in nutrition, the truth is far less dramatic and far more nuanced. Carbs aren’t the enemy. In fact, they’re fundamental to how our bodies and brains function.
Let’s start with what carbohydrates actually do. When you eat carbs, your body breaks them down into glucose, which is the primary fuel for your brain and a major energy source for your muscles. So why the backlash? Influencers often portray carbohydrates as inherently harmful because low-carb diets can lead to quick, visible weight loss. Much of that early drop is water weight, as carbohydrates are stored with water in the body. There’s also a kernel of truth that gets exaggerated: highly processed, refined carbohydrates (think sugary drinks, white pastries, and ultra-processed snacks) are easy to overeat, don’t provide lasting satiety, and promote type 2 diabetes. But that’s a quality issue, not inherent to all carbohydrates.
WHAT ABOUT KETO?
The ketogenic diet, which drastically restricts carbohydrates, can be helpful in specific medical contexts – most notably for managing certain types of epilepsy. It can also be an effective short-term weight-loss strategy for some individuals. But it’s not a universal solution, and it’s not necessary for most people.
In fact, when we look at the most consistently well-supported dietary patterns for longevity and disease prevention, such as the Mediterranean and DASH diets, carbohydrates are a key part of the picture.
These eating patterns typically derive 45 – 60 percent of total calories from carbohydrates, primarily from whole, minimally processed sources. They’re rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, beans, and legumes, and are associated with lower risks of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and cognitive decline.
Do we all need the same amount of carbs? Not even close. A marathon runner will require far more carbo-hydrates than someone who is largely sedentary. Someone with insulin resistance may benefit from moderating carbohydrate intake and focusing on lower-glycemic options. The key is personalization – not elimination.
Carb quality is where the real conversation should be. The body responds very differently to a bowl of lentil soup than to a glazed donut.
High-quality carbohydrates come packaged with fibre, vitamins, minerals, and phytochemicals that support gut health, stabilize blood sugar, and promote satiety. Fibre in particular plays a critical role in digestive health and has been linked to reduced risks of heart disease, certain cancers, and metabolic conditions. Most people don’t get nearly enough of it, and cutting carbs often makes that gap worse.
Your body has sophisticated systems to metabolize carbohydrates, but certain nutrients help those systems run more smoothly. Magnesium plays a key role in insulin signalling and glucose uptake, and low levels are linked with poorer blood sugar control. Chromium is involved in enhancing insulin’s action of guiding sugar out of your bloodstream and into your cells, where it belongs. Fibre – especially soluble fibre from foods like oats, legumes, and flax – slows carbohydrate absorption and helps prevent blood sugar spikes.
There’s also growing interest in compounds like berberine and alpha-lipoic acid (ALA), which may support glucose metabolism. Berberine has been shown in some studies to lower blood sugar and improve insulin sensitivity, often compared to the medication metformin. These nutrients can support healthy carbohydrate handling, but they work best alongside – not instead of – a balanced diet that includes high-quality carbs.
THE BOTTOM LINE?
Carbohydrates are not inherently fattening, inflammatory, or harmful, although poor-quality, ultra-processed foods can be. Instead of fearing carbohydrates, we’re better off upgrading them.
HYDRATE WITH EVERY BITE
