title: Yarmouth dominating, and other Maine high school football storylines for Week 7
text:
As we head into Week 7 and creep toward the end of the Maine high school football regular season, some teams have emerged as state title contenders, while others still have work to do.
Thornton Academy (6-0) and Bonny Eagle (6-0) have all but secured Class A South postseason berths, but can a team like Noble, which is currently on the outside of the playoff picture, find a way to win out and make a postseason run? To do so, the first step for the Knights is getting past South Portland on Friday.
Lawrence and Cony appear to be the favorites in Class B North, but can Skowhegan and Messalonskee make some headway in the division in their final two weeks of the regular season?
Here are three storylines to follow heading into Week 7:
DOMINATION STATION IN YARMOUTH
Yarmouth has been nothing short of dominant this season.
The Clippers (6-0) have outscored their opponents 354-54, tallying 60 points exactly in their last three games and averaging 59 points per game.
They’re first in the Large School South eight-man Crabtree standings and have trounced the other top contenders in the division — Spruce Mountain (4-2), whom they defeated 48-0 on Sept. 12, and Cape Elizabeth (4-2), whom they defeated 82-40 on Sept. 19.
“We’re super excited about this group,” said coach Nick Orsi. “We knew coming into the season it was going to be pretty special. We had a lot of players returning on the offensive side of the ball, including our quarterback, all our wide receivers. We added our running back, Stephen Connolly (54 carries, 940 yards, 14 touchdowns), to the mix this year. He’s a junior from NYA. He’s part of our co-op.”
The Clippers’ passing game is especially prolific, led by senior quarterback Iggy McGrath, who has thrown for 1,227 yards and 21 TDs and has yet to have a pass intercepted.
Even with such a high-performing offense, Orsi believes Yarmouth’s defense is the biggest difference-maker this year. Taking away the game against Cape Elizabeth, the Clippers have only allowed 14 points. Three of their games have been shutouts.
“We’re actually holding opponents to about 150 yards a game in total offense,” Orsi said. “That’s pretty remarkable in eight-man football — there’s so much space on the field, it typically tends to be higher-scoring games. We had a really rough first half against Cape Elizabeth and we gave up an opening-drive touchdown against Lake Region, but outside of that, the starting defense has been virtually flawless.”
On both sides of the ball, Yarmouth has proven itself a contender to win the eight-man Large School state championship for the first time since 2022.
Before then, the Clippers will close out their regular season with games against Orono (3-3) on Friday and Gray-New Gloucester (4-1) on Oct. 23.
HAS WELLS TURNED THE CORNER?
After Leavitt defeated Wells 42-0 on Sept. 26, coach Tim Roche knew his team was at a crossroads, sitting at 2-2 in a competitive Class C division.
“I just said to them, ‘We either step up to this challenge in the next five games, or we just say, ‘Oh … we’re not very good,’” Roche said. “I think we’re good.”
The Warriors (4-2) have won their last two games, defeating Gardiner 47-31 on Oct. 2 and Freeport 28-24 on Oct. 8. With three games remaining, Wells may be on its way to rejoining the field of Class C contenders alongside Leavitt, Greely, Foxcroft Academy and Hermon. Eight teams make the Class C postseason, and the top four host quarterfinals. Wells is currently ranked fifth but could move up if it wins its next three. The Warriors finish the regular season with games against York (2-4) on Saturday, Nokomis (2-4) on Oct. 24 and Hampden Academy (0-6) on Oct. 30.
HIGH-OCTANE HORNETS
Leavitt coach Michael Hathaway said it best after his team’s season-opening 39-8 win over Medomak Valley on Sept. 4: The Hornets don’t want to be reliant on only one component of their offense.
“Really, we just want to spread the ball around,” Hathaway said. “Whether it’s run or pass or whatever, we don’t want to be relying on any one thing. So I think you saw it tonight … a lot of different guys touching the ball.”
With three games to go in the Class C regular season, it’s safe to say Hathaway’s vision for the season has been realized. Leavitt (6-0), No. 1 in the Crabtree standings, is averaging 42 points per game and has had different players step up to play leading roles.
Darren Flagg, for example, scored five touchdowns across the team’s first two games against Medomak Valley and Greely. Then, Landen Reny and Jeremiah McKenzie combined for five touchdowns in a Week 4 win against Wells.
Against Gardiner last week, Flagg was back at the forefront, reaching the end zone five times while exemplifying Leavitt’s quest for versatility: he scored twice on runs, twice on receptions and once on an interception return.
Leavitt plays Nokomis at 7 p.m. Thursday.

title: Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% in sign that prices remain elevated as midterm elections near
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gasoline and many other goods and services became more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before midterm elections that have focused heavily on affordability.
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month.
The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn’t all linked to oil and gas, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month and higher than economists had expected. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed’s 2% target.
Higher inflation will likely put more pressure on the Fed to lift its key interest rate at its next meeting Oct. 27-28. Economists noted that the report showed price increases were spread more broadly across the economy than in recent months.
“The report was worse than expected,” Bill Adams, chief U.S. economist at Fifth Third Bank, said in a note to clients. “Price increases were widespread. ... Consumer demand seems to be holding up better than the downbeat consumer surveys would suggest, helping businesses maintain pricing power.”
Wednesday’s figures are the last major inflation data to be released before the upcoming elections. Ongoing inflation has taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living issue. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Higher prices are eroding Americans’ earnings. The Labor Department also said Wednesday that average weekly paychecks, when adjusted for inflation, shrank last month compared with a year ago for the first time since May.
Gas prices jumped 9.1% just from August to September, the government’s consumer price index report said. Rising gas costs are a highly visible sign of inflation and often drive down measures of consumer sentiment about the economy.
With fuel much more expensive, air fares rose 1.2% last month and have soared 22% compared with a year ago. Hotel prices rose 2% from August to September and are up 4.4% compared with a year earlier.
Consumers saw some relief in grocery prices, which actually declined 0.1% last month and are up just 1.8% from a year ago. Ground beef prices fell 0.8% in September, though they are still up 5.4% from last year.
The cost of toys, new and used cars, sporting goods, and shoes all rose at a rapid clip last month, the government said.
The government also said Wednesday that Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% cost of living increase, based on the inflation figures.
The Middle East and Russia-Ukraine conflicts have also sharply inflated the cost of diesel fuel, which is used by long-haul trucks. Higher diesel prices will increase shipping expenses, which in turn could push up prices for a range of goods.
Ralph Newhouse, CEO of Chefman, which makes countertop appliances, said that rising diesel prices could force him to raise prices in the coming months.
The Mahwah, N.J.-based company, which makes milk frothers, air fryers, blenders and other appliances in China, last increased its prices in 2024. This year, it has used its $20 million in tariff refunds to offset the rise in fuel costs, but may not be able to do so much longer.
“We’re at the point right now that if we continue to see any additional rises in (diesel) prices, then these conversations are going to be forced upon us. We just day by day, hope and pray that we don’t have to have this conversation.”
Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn’t moving quickly enough back to the central bank’s target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9%.
Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year.
Still, Wednesday’s report has led many Wall Street investors to project that the Fed will now act in two weeks. The odds of a rate increase at the central bank’s October meeting have doubled, though remain at just 50-50, according to futures pricing tracked by CME Fedwatch.
Stock prices fell slightly after the report, while greater expectations for rate hikes pushed up bond yields, which will raise borrowing costs throughout the economy.
By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war’s disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can’t address those bottlenecks.
Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It’s already pushed up the price of air fares about 22% from a year ago.
Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients.
The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones.
Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge.
On September 1, Nintendo increased the price for its Switch 2 gaming system by 11% to $499.99. And Apple’s newest iPhone, the iPhone 17, cost about 10% more than its previous upgrade, though some of that likely reflects greater capabilities.

title: Maine governor candidate profile: Bobby Charles
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Republican candidate for Maine governor Bobby Charles says integrity in government and affordability are two of the biggest challenges Mainers face right now.
WABI sat down with Charles and the other gubernatorial candidates to talk about some of the most pressing issues in the state.
Charles says if elected, he would tackle those issues by addressing property taxes, including a homestead exemption, income taxes, especially to encourage young Mainers to stay, live and work in Maine, as well as high energy costs.
Charles also says dealing with addiction in Maine is a major reason he decided to run for office for the first time.
He hopes every Mainer gets out and votes in November.
“This is our one chance. And, when I say one chance, Maine absolutely, unequivocally needs change. If we do not get change now, we’re in a tailspin in all these areas we’ve talked about. We are in a tailspin. I don’t wanna auger in. I don’t wanna see people losing their homes. I don’t want to see people dying because they can’t get into the healthcare they need. I don’t wanna see people paying taxes that they just can’t afford. I don’t want your grandchildren or your children to be leaving the state. I don’t want you to have to leave the state. I want you to feel so good about Maine that you say, ‘God, I not only love the state cause it’s naturally beautiful but I finally trust my governor and my legislature and I know they’re working for me and they’re working hard and I don’t have to look. When the lights go out they’re still in there thinking about how can we possibly help the average Mainer,” Charles said.
Full interviews with Democratic nominee Hannah Pingree and independent nominee Rick Bennett are available on our website, streaming apps and YouTube page.

title: Notice of Violation issued to Golden Anchor following 'unpermitted' cruise ship disembarkation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BAR HARBOR — Officials announced late last week that a Notice of Violation was issued to Golden Anchor L.C., owners and operators of the pier at 55 West St., for disembarking cruise ship passengers without what the town considers to be the proper permit for that activity. The incident marks the first challenge to the town’s cruise ship ordinance following the latest court ruling, which limited the timeframe during which the law could be enforced.
According to a press release sent by the town, as well as the text of the NOV obtained by the Islander, a ship called the Scenic Eclipse, with a lower-berth capacity of 228 passengers, called at Bar Harbor on Thursday, Oct. 1. While Harbormaster Chris Wharff, following federal anchorage regulations, informed the ship, which was not one of the few grandfathered reservations from before the passage of the ordinance, that there was an available anchorage for the ship to park itself, the town stressed that anchoring does not authorize the use of what it deemed an “unpermitted property” for passenger disembarkation.

title: Colton Walker’s courageous journey: From leukemia diagnosis to a bright future
text:
What began with a mother’s concern in the spring of 2019 became a life-changing journey for Colton Walker and his family.
Colton had just turned four when his mother, Ashley Horne, noticed dizzy spells, a loss of appetite and energy, and unusual paleness. Blood work revealed a dangerously low count, prompting an urgent trip to Portland for a blood transfusion.
The Maine Children’s Cancer Program arranged a consultation and bone-marrow biopsy. Although doctors initially believed cancer was unlikely, the biopsy on July 2 led to news the following day that changed everything: Colton had B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, known as B-ALL.
The diagnosis marked the beginning of more than two years of treatment. Colton completed treatment on September 7, 2021, and rang the bell a week later on September14, celebrating a milestone his family had eagerly awaited.
Now a fifth grader, Colton is looking toward another important moment. This October, he is expected to return for his final blood work visit. His family hopes for an excellent blood count and the words they have long waited to hear: Colton is cured.
He will choose his last “poke box” toy and say goodbye, closing a remarkable chapter in his young life.
Along the way, the family has found support from many caring people. They extend special thanks to the Oakland, Winslow and Waterville fire departments for participating in Colton’s Make-A-Wish Day and helping create lasting memories.
Horne also hopes to organize a local childhood cancer walk to raise awareness and support other families facing similar journeys.
For Colton and his family, this October represents more than a final appointment. It is a chance to celebrate how far he has come – and the bright future ahead.

title: 'Not your typical find': Police recover WWII-era grenades found in box purchased from estate sale
text:
'Not your typical find': WWII-era grenades found inside box purchased from estate sale
"Not your typical estate sale find—" police recovered an atypical object that was purchased from an estate sale in Texas, prompting the presence of one department's bomb squad.
VIDEO: Scene shows police, bomb squad at Texas estate sale
In a post from the Austin Police Association, a resident bought some boxes at an estate sale and, while going through them, found what appeared to be World War II-era grenades.
The bomb squad confirmed the grenades were "live and active."
"Huge thanks to our patrol officers, who quickly secured the scene, set up a perimeter, and kept neighbors safe while they waited for EOD," the police association said in the post. "Handling 80-year-old explosives with unknown stability is dangerous, precise work, and they do it with the professionalism this city counts on. The devices were safely seized and removed."
Authorities said no charges were filed, but the incident serves as a reminder that if you come across "old military ordnance, contact local officials" and don't handle the objects on your own.

title: Pope Leo XIV shares first message following lung cancer diagnosis
text:
(Gray News) - Pope Leo XIV released his first message since undergoing surgery for lung cancer in Rome.
“As you know, I have been unable to be among you during these days,” Leo wrote in a statement. “I thank you warmly for your prayers and for the work you have done together. Your sharing of experiences and attentive listening are indeed a gift to the whole Church.”
The pope’s message was issued to Catholics who were meeting to celebrate the 10th anniversary of Amoris Laetitia, a document written by Pope Francis about the church’s work with couples and families, CNN reported.
”It is my hope that families will always be active participants in the life and mission of your local churches," his statement continued. “I ask you please to pray for me, as I pray for you.”
Pope Leo underwent surgery on Tuesday in which doctors removed a cancerous mass from his lung.
The 71-year-old pope was said to be recovering normally following the procedure, according to his doctors.
“The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room. He resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch,” Dr. Luigi Carbone, the pope’s personal doctor, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the head thoracic surgeon at Gemelli Hospital, said. “Recovery is proceeding as planned.”
Doctors said the surgery confirmed that Leo had lung adenocarcinoma, a common type of lung cancer, with surgeons removing the lower lobe of his right lung.
The Vatican hasn’t announced any changes to the pope’s planned trip to South America in November.

title: Obituary: Muriel Arlene Michaud
text:
AUGUSTA – Muriel Arlene Michaud, 85, of Windsor, passed away peacefully at Glenridge Nursing Home during the predawn hours of Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. True to her nature, she was always an early bird!
Muriel was born on Aug. 20, 1941, on the family homestead in Liberty.
Muriel was the seventh oldest of 18 children born to Arthur and Lucy Whitaker. During her childhood, Arthur moved the family to a large farmhouse in South China, where Muriel continued her education.
She eventually graduated from Erskine Academy High School.
As you can only imagine, being raised in such a large family took patience and you learned a good work ethic at a young age! Muriel was no exception to that rule! She could be seen tending to her younger siblings or outside working in the family vegetable garden and attending the farm animals. In addition to family chores, she and her siblings had the responsibility of planting and raising endless fields of string beans. The kids were expected to harvest them to be sold to the Monmouth Canning Company, located at that time in Liberty, Maine.
While attending high school, Muriel also traveled to Aroostook County with her sisters, Elaine and Marie, where the three spent six weeks picking potatoes. These early experiences were a testament to the strong work ethic, perseverance, and sense of responsibility that came with growing up in a hardworking farm family.
On Aug. 19, 1961, she married John Michaud Jr., from Windsor. They would eventually settle down in Windsor and raise three children.
During those early years, Muriel stayed home to raise her family, devoting her time and energy to caring for her children. Of course, with two young boys, there may have been moments when she wondered if joining the workforce might have been the easier job!
Once her children were grown, Muriel returned to the workforce, eventually completing her working career as a baker at Shaw’s Supermarket in Augusta. Her years spent raising a family and working hard were a reflection of the determination and strong work ethic that had been part of her life since childhood.
Muriel loved the outdoors and enjoyed camping, fishing, and even hunting! But her favorite activity of all was spending time with her family.
Her legacy will be that she made the world a better place simply by being kind, caring, and quite plainly, a good human being.
She instilled those values in her children, and grandchildren are following in her footsteps. The kindness she shared and the values she passed down will continue to live on through the generations.
That is her legacy-a life well lived, a family well loved, and a world made better because she was in it.
Muriel was predeceased by her parents, seven of her siblings, her beloved husband, John, and her granddaughter, Kara.
She leaves behind 10 surviving siblings; her three children, Tim and his wife, Sandy, of Topsham, Jeff and his wife, Michelle, of Vassalboro, and Tammy and her husband, Nelson, of Windsor; four grandchildren; and six great-grandchildren.
A graveside service will be held on October 17, at 11 a.m., at the Rest Haven Cemetery in Windsor. Immediately following a “celebration of life reception” will be held at the Boynton -Webber American Legion Hall Post 179, at 79 Legion Memorial Drive, South China. This is the same location that Muriel and John re-wed in the year 1993. It seemed only fitting to gather there once more to celebrate Muriel’s life, share memories, and honor the love and kindness she brought to those around her.
Arrangements are under the care of Funeral Alternatives 82 Western Ave., Augusta, Me 04330

title: Susan Collins floats Mitt Romney to chart a long-term fix for Social Security
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins said Wednesday that a bipartisan group of financial experts, potentially led by former U.S. Sen. Mitt Romney, should recommend how to shore up Social Security days after she said high earners should pay more into the program.
“I believe that we should appoint a bipartisan group of financial experts that would be headed by someone like Mitt Romney, who has a lot of expertise and could give us recommendations of what should be done,” Collins told reporters after she was endorsed by the Maine Fraternal Order of Police in Bangor.
The comments were her first since last week’s debate on WMTW, when Collins said the cap on income subject to Social Security taxes should be “adjusted.” That broke from most Republicans, and it came hours after NBC News said her campaign stated no position on the idea and pointed to her support for a commission.
Collins, a Republican seeking a sixth term in a pivotal November race with Democrat Troy Jackson, did not say whether she would lift the $184,500 cap entirely, raise it or tax income above a higher threshold. She said a movie star earning $40 million a year shouldn’t pay the same in Social Security taxes as someone at the cap, adding one caution.
“Now we have to be careful about how small businesses are treated, and this is going to take some work to make sure that we do it correctly,” she said, adding that “there’s all different ways that it can be structured.”
Romney, a Utah Republican who left the Senate in January 2025, a former Massachusetts governor and the 2012 presidential nominee, pushed for a bipartisan fiscal commission to tackle the national debt and entitlement programs while in office. Social Security’s trust fund is projected to run short in late 2032, which would trigger an automatic 22% cut in benefits unless Congress acts.
Jackson, a former Maine Senate president from Allagash, wants to scrap the Social Security cap and use the money to expand benefits. Jackson said in Thursday’s debate Collins had “rejected time and time again” changing the cap.
“Troy is committed to protecting Social Security from cuts and ensuring that Mainers receive the secure retirement and benefits they’ve paid into and earned,” a campaign spokesperson said.
In Bangor, Collins also touted the Social Security Fairness Act, the 2025 law she co-wrote that restored full benefits to retired teachers, police officers and other public employees whose pensions had reduced them. Fixing it has helped Maine recruit and keep law enforcement officers, she said.
Jackson and Collins meet for their final debate Thursday at the Gracie Theater in Bangor, in the only debate with a live audience and questions from voters.

title: Maine hospital faces termination from Medicare due to lack of infection control
text:
Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston could lose its ability to participate in Medicare over concerns that it’s not providing adequate, safe care. The hospital was investigated after complaints in August about lack of infection control.
A state inspection found that surgical trays at the hospital were contaminated with an unidentified orange or yellow colored substance. Hospital staff told inspectors it was a prevalent issue that had been known for three years.
Inspectors also noted in their report that the hospital failed to ensure patient care areas were maintained in a “sanitary and serviceable condition.”
In a review of hospital board minutes, the inspectors found there were no discussions about infection control concerns during 13 meetings from July 2025 to July 2026.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services sent a letter to Central Maine Medical Center CEO Allen Stefanek on Oct. 8, notifying him that although the hospital no longer poses an “immediate jeopardy” following improvements, it is still out of compliance. The hospital must submit a plan of correction. If it doesn’t achieve compliance, it could be terminated from Medicare by Jan. 6.
A spokesperson for CMMC said there’s no evidence that any instrument used in patient care was nonsterile or contaminated. The hospital said it takes the findings seriously and has made improvements to its policies and processes.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: Who's behind The Maine Independent?
text:
Less than a month before the midterms, a large dark money group is sending copies of a partisan newspaper to thousands of Maine voters.
The Maine Independent is nondescript. Its masthead is plain in black and white. It includes crosswords and recipes among its 12 pages. But the paper has no explanation of who’s behind it, no statements about its mission, and no reason why it wound up on voters’ doorsteps.
Despite its moniker, it is far from an independent local news organization, both in its funding and its politics.
The paper is one of about 20 nearly identical publications created in swing states across the country over the last decade by American Independent Media, a subsidiary of a similarly named, large dark money group closely tied to Democratic super PACs, politicians and campaign operatives.
From Alaska to Florida, the American Independent Foundation has propped up outlets created to boost Democrats ahead of crucial state and federal elections. They present themselves as independent local news organizations, mailing 12 pages of ideologically slanted stories to voters who never subscribed to the outlet.
Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson “will fight for universal healthcare and lower drug prices,” one Maine Independent headline reads. “Susan Collins says she’s pro-choice, but her Senate votes helped end Roe,” says another.
In addition to its printed paper, the outlet has reached hundreds of thousands of people through more than $47,000 worth of social media ads, according to the Meta Ad Library.
None of The Maine Independent’s content is flatly untrue or blatantly misleading. But all of their stories omit important nuance in support of Democratic politicians.
“It’s an attempt to mimic journalism by providing information that might, in fact, be accurate, but is framed in a partisan manner,” said Michael Socolow, a journalism professor at the University of Maine and board member of the Maine Press Association.
The Maine Independent is one of many so-called “pink slime” news outlets established in Maine by both liberal and conservative dark money groups in the lead up to the 2026 midterm elections. The term, an allusion to ultra-processed meat products, is used in a news context to refer to outlets run by partisan interests posing as local and independent news.
NewsGuard, an organization that tracks misinformation and rates news outlets’ credibility, said American Independent Media and its local sites “generally fail to maintain basic standards of accuracy and accountability” by infusing opinion into their reporting and failing to disclose the partisan interests behind the operation.
“That’s what makes these publications so pernicious,” said Sam Howard, politics editor at NewsGuard. “They threaten to undermine what’s left of the trust that news consumers have in the media, particularly local media. Because these publications are framed as local, seemingly independent, seemingly nonpartisan publications.”
Joe Conason, the Independent’s editor-in-chief, did not respond to interview requests or questions about their reach and operations in Maine.
SLIME-SWAMPED MAILBOXES
Mailing newspapers to voters en masse has been a hallmark of American Independent Media’s operation for years.
In 2021, the organization mailed papers to Virginia voters ahead of a tightly contested gubernatorial election. In the run up to the 2022 midterms, the Independent mailed faux-local papers to more than 2.5 million people in Wisconsin, Michigan and Pennsylvania, The Washington Post reported.
Ahead of this year’s midterms, they have has expanded to at least five more battleground states with pivotal Senate races: Florida, North Carolina, Iowa, Alaska and Maine.
Those state branches have each spent tens of thousands of dollars on social media ads, according to the Meta Ad Library. But their main business is still sending physical papers through the mail, according to Chiara Vercellone, a senior analyst at NewsGuard.
“They’re trying to prove their credibility, and we know that there’s a lot of junk out on the internet or on social media,” she said. “Creating a seemingly innocent-looking newspaper that people receive in their mails touts their supposed credibility.”
American Independent Media micro-targets its print papers toward moderates and women in swing states, The Washington Post reported in 2022. At that time, the organization mailed monthly copies to some 3.2 million voters nationwide, making it one of the country’s largest print media operations.
Spreading pink slime through the mail could prove more effective in Maine than elsewhere, said Socolow. The state’s population of only 1.3 million residents is comparatively small and skews older, on average, than anywhere else in the country.
“People still read the newspapers that pop into their mailboxes,” Socolow said. “I think it’s a smart strategy to reach older people.”
THE OPERATION
The American Independent Foundation describes its mission in business and tax filings as spreading “increased public awareness of progressive values.”
Among the foundation’s owners are Conason, a longtime journalist and liberal commentator, and Matt Fuehrmeyer, former director of research for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. Its media arm similarly has been run by Jessica Floyd, a longtime operative for Democratic campaigns and super PACs, and Ari Rabin-Havt, deputy director of Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders’ 2020 presidential campaign.
Both organizations are tax-exempt nonprofits. The foundation is a 501(c)(3) organization, which are prohibited from political activity by law. American Independent Media, however, is a 501(c)(4) — meaning it has legal leeway to be more political.
Neither group is required to disclose its donors or financial backers, placing them each in the realm of so-called dark money groups that are dumping tens of millions of dollars into Maine’s Senate race.
Together, they operate The American Independent News, which acts as a national news source and syndicate for its local outlets’ content.
Both the foundation and its media arm have contracted with a number of progressive consulting firms and media groups, their tax filings show, including a marketing firm called Mission Control, which describes itself as “the most successful direct mail firm working in Democratic politics today” — hinting at the Independent’s mailing strategy.
Unlike many other pink slime outlets, The Maine Independent’s articles include real people’s bylines on their stories, many of whom were reporters at traditional newspapers prior to joining the partisan outlet.
But despite the dozens of Maine-centric stories the outlet has published, none of its staff appear to be based in the state.
Only a few of The American Independent’s reporters and editors have publicly available contact information. Neither they nor the publication’s general contact lines responded to questions about The Maine Independent or its parent organization.
A GROWING ECOSYSTEM
The Maine Independent is not the only pink slime site created here by national partisan groups in the months prior to this November’s pivotal midterm elections.
Conservative dark money groups and super PACs have similarly established several outlets masquerading as local Maine news sources ahead of the November elections.
Those operations have primarily used social media as a means to spread their message. The Independent, however, is taking a markedly different approach by mailing printed copies directly to voters.
It’s not uncommon for swing states to be inundated with political ads ahead of important elections. But Socolow, the UMaine professor, said the influx of misleading news outlets in Maine highlights how much stake national interests have in winning the state’s U.S. Senate race — and how they can use a shifting media ecosystem to do so.
“You would think you would see this kind of proliferation in a much larger audience area,” Socolow said. “But I think the reason that so many of them are here is that it’s cheap. We’re a small and easily influenced voter base, through social media and micro-targeting.”
Partisan news isn’t a new phenomenon, Socolow noted. Prior to the last hundred years or so, political parties often sponsored newspapers to toe the party line. Even today, local outlets like the Maine Beacon and Maine Wire are run with the stated goal of pushing particular political agendas.
What is new is national groups seeding swing states with slanted faux-local news, Socolow said. And with the advent of social media, those efforts have become more widespread than ever.
What remains to be seen, however, is how effective the strategy will be.

title: Lena Dunham to bring back 'Girls' for a 5-episode run on HBO 10 years after its finale
text:
Lena Dunham to bring back 'Girls' for a 5-episode run on HBO 10 years after its finale
The show will begin production in 2027
Lena Dunham to bring back 'Girls' for a 5-episode run on HBO 10 years after its finale
The show will begin production in 2027
"Girls," the show that was the voice of its generation — or at least a voice of a generation — is coming back.
HBO announced Tuesday that creator and star Lena Dunham and nearly all of the core cast will return for a limited five-episode run a decade after its finale.
Relayed video above: Selma Blair appears in court after airplane altercation
Dunham, now 40, will again play her aspiring writer and sort-of alter-ego Hannah, along with Allison Williams as Marnie, Jemima Kirke as Jessa, Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna and Andrew Rannells as Elijah.
Judd Apatow will return as executive producer. The announcement makes no mention of Adam Driver returning.
The show will begin production in 2027, 10 years after the finale of the series that ran for six seasons from 2012-2017 and was nominated for 19 Emmys, winning two.
"We always said we would only return to GIRLS if there was a specific story we were burning to tell," Dunham said in a statement. "I've missed these characters, but for a long time I couldn't quite picture them in the present day. Then, right around my fortieth birthday, they started talking to me in the shower. And, as you may remember, once this fivesome starts talking it's pretty hard to get them to stop."
The revival is among the first production announcements made by HBO since its parent company Warner Bros. Discovery was taken over by Skydance-owned Paramount.
The show was both a touchstone and a lightning rod for its depiction of a group of millennial young women in New York, with its vocal haters often louder than its many devotees. Affection for it has seen a major surge in the decade since, especially among younger viewers, who see it as aspirational as well as endlessly quotable and meme-able.
In one of its most repeated lines, Hannah, while asking her parents to keep supporting her, tells them, "I think that I may be the voice of my generation. Or at least a voice of a generation."
Dunham has kept making film and television, directing the 2022 movie "Catherine Called Birdy" and co-creating the TV series "Camping" and "Too Much," but none of it has had nearly the cultural impact of "Girls." Her screen appearances have been mostly limited to small guest roles.
Williams has had several memorable movie roles, especially in horror films, including "Get Out" and two "M3GAN" movies.
But while the show was all about the lives of young women, the biggest star it spawned was Driver, who went on to star in a "Star Wars" trilogy and has been nominated for two Oscars.

title: How college students can start building credit the right way
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Managing money is rarely part of the official college curriculum, but WalletHub says one wrong move with fees or credit can cost students more than money — it can set back their credit-building efforts before their careers even begin.
John Kiernan, managing editor at WalletHub, said students need to understand what financial tools are available to them before heading to campus.
Kiernan’s first tip: credit can be built without ever making a purchase.
“One thing I’ll say for parents and students out there to build credit with a credit card, you don’t necessarily have to make purchases,” Kiernan said. “If you get a $0 annual fee card and put it in your wallet for emergencies and never use it, you’ll still get credit for paying on time every month because you don’t have a balance. And so you’ll get a monthly influx of positive information to your credit report, which will help you build credit.”
Kiernan said the next step, once a student begins earning a paycheck, is setting up automatic payments.
“Forgetting due dates is one of the easiest ways to hurt your credit score,” Kiernan said. “And just setting up autopay is one of the easiest ways to make sure you build good credit history.”
For students still searching for the right card, WalletHub has ranked the best credit cards for students to help them get started.
“College is about preparing for adult life,” Kiernan said. “This is one aspect that’s not going to be really covered in the classroom, and it’ll set you up and help lay the foundation for your finances moving forward.”
Beyond skipping annual fees, WalletHub recommends confirming that a card reports to the credit bureaus every month, since that reporting is what actually builds the credit history students will need later for renting an apartment or qualifying for a loan.

title: Blockbuster-era law governing privacy of video rentals gets a fresh look from the Supreme Court
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — In 1988, Congress enacted a law to protect the privacy of video rentals after a journalist published details of Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork’s movie rental history during his Senate hearings. Nearly four decades later, the court is weighing how the Blockbuster-era statute fits into the modern age of digital commerce.
The Supreme Court heard arguments Wednesday in a case exploring the extent to which companies from an array of sectors are obligated to protect the privacy of customers’ video-viewing data. A ruling could resolve a lower-court split over how a consumer qualifies for the law’s protections.
Consumer advocates say the Video Privacy Protection Act of 1988 was broadly written to adapt to inevitable advances in technology and safeguard consumers’ personal information.
Critics of the law view it as a relic that plaintiffs’ lawyers are trying to exploit in a way that Congress could not have anticipated before the internet revolutionized commerce. They are urging the justices to reject an interpretation of the law that deprives companies of a vital source of revenue from targeted online advertising.
The current case was brought by a customer who subscribed to Paramount Global’s online newsletter to view videos on its website 247Sports.com. Michael Salazar claims Paramount violated the law by disclosing his video-watching history to Facebook without his consent, allowing companies to use his personal information to create and display targeted advertising.
Justice Elena Kagan, who said the language of the statute is “relatively clear,” stressed that it is easy for companies to obtain consent from customers to use their digital data.
“Going forward, you have two very simple solutions,” Kagan told Paramount lawyer Paul Clement. “One is to get consent. Easy enough. People do it every day. And the other is to stop selling people’s private information. Take your pick.”
“Yeah, or put everything behind a paywall. That would be great,” Clement responded sarcastically.
“Not the same thing,” Kagan said.
“Well, I think that’s one way that people would try to deal with this,” Clement said.
Congress passed the law a year after a video store clerk provided a Washington City Paper reporter with a list of 146 movies rented by Bork, a federal appeals court judge at the time of his nomination by Republican President Ronald Reagan. The reporter’s publication of “The Bork Tapes,” on the eve of Bork’s hearings in 1987 that ended with the Senate rejecting the nominee, fueled bipartisan outrage and led to the law’s enactment.
Paramount’s lawyers say lower courts have overwhelmingly rejected other attempts to expand the law’s reach, with district court judges dismissing most cases.
“And why do you think that is?” Justice Samuel Alito asked Salazar’s lawyer, Joshua Hammack. “Why do you think these smart lower court judges have rejected the kind of very literal interpretation of the statutory language that you’re presenting to us today?”
“I think there is, unfortunately, some reluctance to believe that Congress actually meant what it said in the context of this statute,” Hammack responded. “It wrote a broad law that is very protective of personally identifiable information.”
Paramount argues that Salazar does not meet the definition of a “consumer” under the law to qualify for its protections.
Rulings in two appeals courts defined a consumer, under this law, as anybody who purchases, rents or subscribes to any good or service from a videotape service provider. Two other appeals courts adopted a narrower definition of consumer limited to goods and services with audiovisual content.
Only the Supreme Court “can resolve the split and bring uniformity to this important area of federal law,” Salazar’s lawyers wrote.
Paramount says Salazar has no basis to broaden the scope of the law. The company says the law merely prohibits video rental stores from disclosing customers’ rental histories without consent.
“Salazar seeks to transmogrify it into a prohibition against targeted advertising on the Internet,” Paramount attorneys wrote.
Paramount says 247Sports is a sports news website that posts video clips with articles and photos free of charge.
“That is a completely different business from renting video cassette tapes. The VPPA does not address it,” company lawyers wrote.

title: Footage of Kelly Clarkson in Brooklyn novelty shop released as store owners say singing bird is now $15 million
Judge extends order blocking Trump from banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from White House
text:
Judge extends order blocking Trump from banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from White House
A federal judge on Tuesday extended an order blocking President Donald Trump's administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, a pivotal operational development for the organizations as the extraordinary case — pitting the president against the media that cover him — makes its way through the legal system.
Related previous coverage above: Judge rules Trump administration must restore access for banned news outlets
In a victory for media organizations at a time when tension between the White House and journalists is high, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in their constitutional free speech and due process claims.
“Still,” he added in his late-night order, “no one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”
But Kelly agreed with the plaintiffs that the national security arguments came after the fact and were unsupported by the administration.
The judge also wrote that without a preliminary injunction the outlets “are likely to suffer irreparable harm, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest tip in their favor.”
An email to the Justice Department, which is arguing the case on behalf of the administration, was not immediately returned. The White House also did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment.
Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the three media organizations, hailed the judge's ruling.
“When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment,” Boutrous said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future.”
Judge says no warning given before banishment
Kelly, who was nominated to the bench by Trump, previously ordered the White House to restore the reporters’ “hard pass” press credentials while he weighed their claims. With that temporary order expiring Tuesday, the judge issued a preliminary injunction that preserves the status quo indefinitely while the case is pending.
Kelly said that, “to put it mildly,” the White House didn’t give the plaintiffs any warning that they were in danger of losing their hard passes before Trump’s Sept. 18 social media post about their bans.
The judge also said the impact of the White House ban goes far beyond a single reporter's ability to do their job.
“The ban threatens to cut off all Plaintiffs’ access to the White House press area—a space open to many of their competitors—thereby restricting their ability to observe happenings there firsthand, immediately report on those activities, and try to engage with government officials,” the judge wrote.
Hard passes give journalists who regularly cover the White House longer term access to its campus without having to get permission ahead of time.
The government asked Kelly to suspend his own decision pending an appeal, but the judge said it didn’t justify that request. Kelly said the bans impacted a total of 78 reporters at the three news organizations.
Earlier judicial action against White House had been only temporary
Trump provided no notice before announcing the bans in a Sept. 18 social media post, which criticized their reporting as “fake news.” Kelly temporarily blocked the bans on Sept. 24 at the request of the news outlets, which jointly filed a lawsuit in Washington, D.C.
Attorneys for the outlets have described Trump’s move as “unprecedented and blatantly unconstitutional” under the First and Fifth amendments. They argued that it’s illegal for Trump to punish the journalists because he doesn’t like the content of their reporting.
“The ban also inflicts an injury on all news media organizations — which now risk a similar fate if they engage in fact-based, independent reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable,” plaintiffs’ lawyers wrote.
Government lawyers argued that access to the White House is a privilege — not a right — and said the president can impose the bans to protect national security and to stem the spread of misinformation.
“The White House is the official residence and workplace of the President,” Justice Department attorneys wrote. “Presidents have had a relationship with the press since the beginning. They have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially from administration to administration.”
___
Associated Press reporter Rebecca Boone contributed.

title: Justice Department threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rolls
text:
Justice Department threatens California with legal action over claim of noncitizens on voter rolls
The U.S. Department of Justice has threatened California with possible legal action over what it says are noncitizens believed to have received mail ballots for next month’s midterm elections.
Video above: How could the Senate race in Texas impact the balance of power in Congress?
A letter sent Tuesday to Secretary of State Shirley Weber from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy U.S. attorney general, says the department has provided officials in Los Angeles County with a password-protected thumb drive with a list of names of people the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election.
California mails ballots to all registered voters.
The letter obtained by The Associated Press gives the state 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are included on the list. For individuals whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received it.
The letter warns that legal action may follow if the state does not meet the 48-hour deadline to review the list.
“If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief,” the letter states.
A separate, similar letter was sent to the registrar's office in Los Angeles County, which the U.S. attorney's office had investigated during the state's June primary.
Neither the California secretary of state nor the Los Angeles County registrar immediately responded to requests seeking comment.
The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.
In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state.
“I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official,” Weber said in response.
That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero.
As part of its project to find noncitizens on the voter rolls, the Justice Department has been seeking detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. Some Republican-led states have turned over the information, which has been run through a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database that has been criticized as inaccurately flagging U.S. citizens.
The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for that information, but so far has lost those cases in court. California is among the states that successfully sued, in part by arguing that turning over the data would violate state privacy laws.
Santa Cruz County Clerk Tricia Webber, who is president of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, said she had not seen the letters but said the 48-hour deadline to vet voters flagged by the federal government was “completely unreasonable.”
She said when there is a report of an ineligible voter incorrectly on the rolls, her office does due diligence to investigate. That involves looking at the voter’s registration history, identifying whether that person had voted before and, most importantly, reaching out to the voter, she said.
“It would take more than 48 hours to even begin to get the full picture,” Webber said. She also questioned how the federal government came up with a list of alleged noncitizen voters since it doesn’t have access to the state's detailed voter information.
Webber added that throughout the course of her decades-long career working for local election agencies, she has “never seen anything that would make me believe that our voter records are filled with fraudulent voters.”

title: Maine's new women's soccer team set to unveil branding Thursday
text:
Maine's new women's soccer team set to unveil branding Thursday
The Portland Hearts of Pine's new USL W League team will reveal it's identity ahead of it's inaugural season in May 2027
Maine's new women's soccer team set to unveil branding Thursday
The Portland Hearts of Pine's new USL W League team will reveal it's identity ahead of it's inaugural season in May 2027
The Portland Hearts of Pine is preparing to unveil the branding behind Maine's new women's soccer team Thursday, ahead of its inaugural season next spring.
The team will compete in the USL W League, beginning play in May 2027.
Gov. Janet Mills has proclaimed Thursday as the second-ever "Maine Day of Soccer" in celebration of the new women's franchise.
"The Hearts of Pine have brought a tremendous amount of pride and energy to Maine during their first two seasons, and I can't wait to welcome their new women's team to Portland," Mills said in a statement Wednesday.
The first "Maine Day of Soccer" came in April 2024 when the men's Hearts of Pine team launched its name, crest and brand identity.
According to Gabe Hoffman-Johnson, founder and chief community officer for the Hearts of Pine, the addition of the women's team has been a vision since the beginning.
"This is a moment we've imagined for a long time, and to see it become real with so much support from people across the state is incredibly meaningful," said Hoffman-Johnson.

title: New York City's iconic horse-drawn carriages expected to take their last trot
text:
New York City’s iconic horse-drawn carriages expected to take their last trot
New York City’s iconic Central Park horse-drawn carriage industry is nearing its end after Mayor Zohran Mamdani and City Council Speaker Julie Menin reached a deal on legislation that aims to abolish the carriage rides.
Menin is expected to bring legislation to the council floor for a vote later this month, a spokesperson told CNN. The ban, which will be implemented in phases, will take effect on June 1, 2028, according to a copy of the legislation reviewed by CNN.
The move comes after years of criticism from animal rights advocates who charge that the horses are overworked, get easily scared and live in inadequate stables with drivers flouting city regulations. Horse and carriage owners have denied the claims, arguing the animals are well cared for and the stables are up to code.
“We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all,” Sneha Choudhary, a spokesperson for City Hall, said in a statement.
New Yorkers for Clean, Livable and Safe Streets, a group that has been pushing for the ban for several years, as well as two mayoral administrations, said the agreement would finally put an end to the “cruel and dangerous horse-drawn carriages.”
“This moment belongs to the advocates and supporters who have spent years fighting with NYCLASS to protect horses and people on our city’s streets,” Edita Birnkrant, executive director of NYCLASS, said in a statement.
Momentum to ban the century-old attraction was renewed following the death of 18-year-old tourist Romanch Mahajan, who was killed after he was thrown from a runaway horse-drawn carriage in Central Park last summer.
Mahajan is believed to be the first person to have died in a carriage accident since the rides were introduced more than 150 years ago, according to the industry’s labor union and the Central Park Conservancy, which manages the park.
“The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable,” Menin said in a statement. “Horse drawn carriages have long been part of New York City’s history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability. Next week, the Council will take decisive action by voting on Romanch’s Law to protect New Yorkers, visitors, and the horses themselves.”
Councilman Chris Marte, the primary sponsor of the bill, told CNN the legislation currently has 29 co-sponsors. Marte said he expects the bill will sail through the council and secure a majority of the votes.
Marte said last-minute negotiations between the city council and city hall also helped deliver a provision outlining what will happen to the horses once the industry is phased out. Horse owners will be required to notify the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare before disposing of the animals, and the bill explicitly forbids that horses are sold or transferred for slaughter or for use in another horse-drawn business.
The decision to ban the practice is a blow to the Transportation Workers Union TWU Local 100, the union that represents horse carriage drivers. The union for years has argued their workers will be left without a way to make a living. In recent years, as scrutiny from critics of the industry intensified, the union has increased training and safety measures for drivers.
“Council Speaker Menin’s bill has no meaningful economic relief for workers. It only says the city should prepare a worker transition plan by April 2027 and include weak measures like job fairs and job counseling,” Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen said in a statement. “Council Speaker Menin used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis. This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families’ livelihoods are being destroyed. This entire situation is reprehensible.”
As part of their negotiation, Mamdani and Menin also reached a deal to include an “industry transition framework,” a spokesperson for Menin told CNN. The framework will require the city to come up with a plan to help workers transition into new jobs.
According to a copy of the legislation, reviewed by CNN, Mamdani will designate a city agency charged with implementing the transition and offer potential jobs and training across different agencies, including the NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission, the MTA, NYC Transit, the Port Authority and hospitality and tourism industries.

title: Concerts for a Cause to present Yard Sauce for October show in Brunswick
text:
Yard Sauce will play old-time, bluegrass, country and folk traditions at the Unitarian Universalist Church of Brunswick at 7:30 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 24. All proceeds will be donated to Tedford Housing and Midcoast New Mainers.
Yard Sauce is a Maine-based, acoustic string trio featuring Chris Moore (mandolins and vocals), Jeff Christmas (guitar and vocals) and Callie Brennan (fiddle and vocals). Their dynamic live performances draw from the group’s eclectic musical tastes, diverse regional traditional music influences and a deep catalog of original songs. Old-time, bluegrass, country and folk traditions (including traditional Shaker music) are all part of the mix in every live set.
Christmas began playing music when he was 6 years old. Since then, he has made his way from pop guitar to musical theater to jazz bands to opera to Americana and just about everything in between. He is equally at home on the operatic stage and in a smoky bar. He also is addicted to that connected feeling we can find when playing music together in a room and works to find and cultivate that feeling with collaborators. Christmas was raised in Burlington, North Carolina, and has lived in California, Massachusetts, Tennessee and South Carolina before moving to Portland in 2015.
Moore grew up in Maine where he studied piano and violin, then pursued a degree in acting from Skidmore College. After college, he moved to New York City, where he worked as a performance artist, musician, puppeteer, and on the staff of the Arts at St. Ann’s in Brooklyn. While in New York, Moore studied with mandolin master Andy Statman, then founded the band Rust Farm and released two albums. New England audiences know him as a mandolinist with The Fogg Brothers bluegrass band. When living in Nashville, Tennessee, from 2003–2013, he founded the band Kindling Stone, featuring original compositions along with 19th-century tunes from the Shaker and Sacred Harp traditions. Moore has composed, performed and recorded music for dance, film, television, theater and visual art projects. He has also performed as a classical soloist and was awarded a Maine Arts Commission Fellowship for songwriting. Moore is currently the director of music education for 317 Main Community Music Center in Yarmouth. His latest solo recording, “Changing Union” (2025) was produced by folk icon Tim O’Brien.
Brennan grew up in Maine and at 18 left the state to study music and travel the world. With a bachelor’s degree in violin performance from the University of Colorado and two master’s degrees in music and violin performance from the Guildhall School of Music and Drama in London, Brennan has performed in orchestras all over the world and at prestigious venues such as the Barbican Stage, Royal Festival Hall, Sydney Opera House, Red Rocks Amphitheater and Boettcher Hall in Denver. She recorded a film soundtrack at Abbey Road Studios and has appeared on stage with well-known artists such as Bela Fleck and The Indigo Girls. Now back in Maine, Brennan plays with the Portland Symphony Orchestra, the Portland String Quartet and as a duo with celebrated pianist Laura Kargul.
Tickets are $25 in advance, $30 at the door and $10 for students/children, and will be available at the church office, Gulf of Maine Books or online at ticketstripe.com/yardsauce.

title: Five for Schmidt, Hat Tricks for Gagnon and Willard
text:
The County Scoreboard: Schmidt Scores Five, Gagnon and Willard Add Hat Tricks
Goals came in bunches across Aroostook County on Tuesday, led by a five-goal performance from Katahdin's Conor Schmidt and hat tricks from Madawaska's Aiden Gagnon and Houlton's Cooper Willard.
Madawaska also picked up a boys and girls sweep of Central Aroostook, while Wisdom edged Van Buren in boys action and Bangor Christian needed double overtime to get past the Lady Pioneers.
Here is a look at Tuesday's County soccer results.
Boys Soccer
Madawaska 7, Central Aroostook 1
Aiden Gagnon was involved throughout a big offensive night for Madawaska, recording three goals and two assists as the Owls defeated Central Aroostook 7-1.
Josh Querze scored twice, while Lucas Pelletier and Owen Gagnon also found the back of the net for Madawaska.
Mitchell Burtt scored Central Aroostook's goal.
Katahdin 6, Southern Aroostook 1
Conor Schmidt had another huge game for Katahdin, scoring five of the Cougars' six goals in a 6-1 victory over Southern Aroostook.
Blake Rush added Katahdin's other goal, while Leighton Rodgerson recorded an assist.
Gage Phillips made seven saves in the Cougar net.
Houlton 5, Schenck/Stearns 0
Cooper Willard recorded a hat trick as Houlton earned a 5-0 shutout victory over Schenck/Stearns.
Will Baillargeon and Beckett Koehler accounted for the Shires' other two goals.
Wisdom 2, Van Buren 1
Wisdom earned a close 2-1 victory over Van Buren.
Cayden Hargrove and Zeek Cyr scored for the Pioneers.
Gavin Cormier had the lone goal for Van Buren.
Washburn 2, MSSM 2
Washburn and MSSM finished even at 2-2 in a game that was stopped because of poor field conditions.
Girls Soccer
Madawaska 1, Central Aroostook 0
One goal was enough for Madawaska in a defensive battle with Central Aroostook.
Dani Pelletier scored from a Lucy Hartvigsen assist to provide the only goal of the game and complete a varsity sweep for the Owls.
Katahdin 3, Southern Aroostook 1
Katahdin earned the girls half of Tuesday's matchup with Southern Aroostook, winning 3-1.
Mia McNally, Joey Richardson and Alaina Rodgerson each scored for the Lady Cougars.
Jazmine Ellingwood scored Southern Aroostook's goal.
Bangor Christian 3, Wisdom 2, 2OT
Wisdom pushed Bangor Christian deep into double overtime before the Lady Patriots escaped with a 3-2 victory.
Moriah Emerson scored twice for Bangor Christian, while Annie Allen also found the net.
Madi Cyr and Ellie Cyr scored for Wisdom.
Penobscot Valley 3, Ashland 2
Penobscot Valley edged Ashland 3-2 in another one-goal girls matchup.
Washburn 6, MSSM 1
Washburn put together a six-goal performance to earn a 6-1 victory over MSSM.

Wednesday, October 14
Girls Soccer
Easton at Hodgdon, 3:30 p.m.
Schenck/Stearns at Houlton, 6 p.m.
Caribou at Presque Isle, 7 p.m.

title: Grad student who allegedly poisoned a colleague has been arrested fleeing to China
text:
CHEYENNE, Wyo. (AP) — A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she didn’t get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested Oct. 6 at Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment — research similar to work she’d done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
U.S. officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your student’s life is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told The Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.
Amateur sleuthing helps campus cops develop case
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “K.T.,” began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.
Wang allegedly was recorded Sept. 27 going through the alleged victim’s desk. On Oct. 1, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
During an interview by campus police on Oct. 5, Wang allegedly said she “had not used acrylamide in years.” A day later she was taken into custody in Los Angeles while in possession of “multiple laptops, multiple portable external digital storage devices, related accessories, physical records and written materials,” according to a request by Wyoming prosecutors to “significantly increase” her $200,000 bond upon extradition.
Wang had no reason to go through the desk of the other student whose federally funded, patent-pending research involved “new technology for cancer, neurological and genetic disease treatment,” according to the affidavit.
Wang “was reportedly working on similar research in China before coming to the U.S.,” the affidavit alleges.
A high-achieving student from Vietnam
Gomelsky described the alleged victim as a highly successful student from Vietnam.
Wang failed her first attempt to defend her dissertation and became envious of her colleague’s success in discovering how to deliver RNA to human cells using bacteria, Gomelsky told The Associated Press.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
Wang had not been doing lab work since June while she worked on her dissertation, he said.
Suspect faces return to Wyoming to face charges
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5 million cash-only.
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.
Best known as a carcinogenic byproduct of cooking starchy food and burning tobacco, acrylamide can be acutely toxic in high doses. It’s used in microbiology research involving proteins or DNA.
Discovery of the substance immediately made Tak Sumaya, an assistant professor who helped identify it in the coffee maker water, suspicious. Acrylamide is “not something you would find in that kind of quantity anywhere,” Sumaya said.
The alleged victim was working on “a pretty promising cancer therapy method,” Sumaya said. Wang, Sumaya added, took photos of every page of a notebook the alleged victim left on his desk.
“You wouldn’t do that with like your office or lab mate’s notebook unless there’s a really good reason, and there wasn’t,” Sumaya said.
Professor says the victim is still experiencing symptoms
The alleged victim went to the campus health clinic in August with worsening finger tingling and numbness, and leg weakness. Suspicion led his wife and others to boil away coffee maker water from the shared office to isolate 63 milligrams of white powder that tested positive for acrylamide, according to the affidavit.
The amateur investigators turned the sample over to university police.
The alleged victim continues to experience symptoms from the poisoning, including not being able to focus, tiring easily and a loss of sensation in his left hand, Gomelsky said.
“Acrylamide is a neurotoxin that cannot be neutralized so it stays in neurons and basically kills them. So it’s unclear if he’ll fully recover or not,” the professor said.
___
Brown reported from Billings, Montana, and Riddle from Los Angeles.
