title: Police: Mother made chilling 911 call from Great Wolf Lodge after killing her husband, son
text:
'They're already gone': Police say mother made chilling 911 call from Great Wolf Lodge after killing her husband, son
A woman accused of killing her husband and her 3-year-old son at the Great Wolf Lodge in Pennsylvania called 911, telling dispatchers, "My husband and son are already gone," according to investigators.
Metallica Harrison, 27, was charged with two counts of criminal homicide in the deaths of her husband, Charles Harrison, and her son, whose name has not yet been released.
She is accused of killing them inside a guest room at the Great Wolf Lodge in Monroe County.
If you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or mental health matters, please call the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 (or 1-800-273-8255) to connect with a trained counselor. You can also text TALK to 741741.
Police respond to lodge room after 911 call
According to the affidavit of probable cause, Pocono Township police officers responded to a Great Wolf Lodge room around 3:13 p.m. on Monday after Metallica called 911.
Police said Metallica told the 911 dispatcher that she needed "help dying" and was "unable to find a vein in her neck to stab."
Officers encountered Metallica in the room's doorway and saw her wrist bleeding and superficial puncture wounds around her neck, according to the affidavit. Investigators said Metallica told officers that "she wanted to be with her husband and son."
Husband, son found stabbed to death, police say
Officers entered the room while checking on Metallica's family and found Charles and her son dead on separate mattresses on the floor, according to investigators.
Police said Charles had suffered multiple stab wounds to the chest. The child appeared to have suffered one stab wound to the chest, according to authorities.
Statements made during 911 call
Investigators reviewed the recording of Metallica's call to 911. According to the affidavit, Metallica told the dispatcher, "I'm too weak to stab my neck" and "I need police."
When the dispatcher asked whether she had any weapons, Metallica said she had knives and added, "That's what I've been using, and it's not working," according to the documents.
When asked whether she was alone, Metallica responded, "My husband and son are already gone in the bed in the living room," the affidavit stated. "They're already gone. I'm sorry," she later said.
Investigators said Metallica did not request assistance for her husband or son at any point during the call.
Statements made during ambulance ride
According to police, Metallica was taken in an ambulance to St. Luke's Hospital–Monroe Campus in Stroudsburg for treatment of her injuries. A Pocono Township police officer accompanied her during the transport.
During the ambulance ride, police said Metallica stated several times that she was "not supposed to be here." According to the affidavit, Metallica said, "I f----- up, I f----- up. I just needed energy and strength."
Investigators said that Metallica questioned why there was not "an easier way" and asked emergency medical personnel how deep the vein in her wrist was so she would know "for next time." According to police, Metallica also stated she had taken medication to thin her blood and expressed frustration that her blood was clotting.
"Every day, I work so hard. To be the best person, the best mother, the best wife," Metallica said, according to the affidavit. "It wasn't supposed to end like this. I was supposed to have my happy family. That's what I envisioned since I was a child," the documents stated.
Two knives recovered from the scene, police say
According to investigators, a large butcher knife was found on the bathroom floor and a smaller knife was found on the bathroom sink. Police said both knives had teal-green handles. Great Wolf Lodge employees told investigators that the knives were not the type maintained by the resort, according to the affidavit.
Police also reported finding several medication bottles throughout the room. Investigators said a plastic container on the floor and a garbage can in the bathroom held a brownish-red liquid believed to be blood.
Surveillance video shows family's last movements
Great Wolf Lodge security personnel told investigators that Charles, Metallica and the 3-year-old checked into the resort on Sept. 21. The family extended its reservation Oct. 5 and was scheduled to check out Oct. 13, according to the affidavit.
Police reviewed surveillance video that showed the entire family entering the room at 6:53 p.m. on Oct. 11, according to investigators. At approximately 8:12 p.m., Metallica left the room and used a microwave in a vending area and returned at 8:16 p.m., the affidavit stated.
Metallica and Charles left the room at approximately 10:43 p.m., went to the resort's arcade and returned at approximately 11:22 p.m., according to investigators.
Police said the surveillance review showed no additional activity at the room's door after the couple returned from the arcade.
Investigators obtain search warrants
Police said search warrants were obtained for the hotel, Metallica and Charles's vehicle, which was parked in the resort's lot.
Investigators met with Metallica at the hospital, advised her of her Miranda rights and asked what had led to her hospitalization, according to officials. Police said Metallica responded that she was "suicidal, not stupid" and declined to speak with them.
Detectives said they collected a buccal swab for DNA testing.
Authorities noted that other than the lacerations to her left wrist and a puncture wound to her neck, Metallica had no other injuries, bruising or apparent defensive wounds.
Police said based on the evidence, Metallica was charged with two counts of criminal homicide and awaits arraignment.
Police call deaths an 'isolated domestic tragedy'
The Pocono Township Police Department said the investigation remains active.
The department described the case as "an isolated domestic tragedy" and said there was no threat to the community.
"Our thoughts and deepest condolences go out to the family and loved ones affected by this tragedy," Pocono Township Police said.
Great Wolf Resorts statement
Great Wolf Resorts shared the following statement with sister station WGAL, saying:
"We are deeply saddened and heartbroken by a tragic domestic incident that occurred yesterday in a guest room at our resort in the Pocono Mountains. It was an isolated family incident, and we’re cooperating fully with local law enforcement as they conduct their investigation. Our thoughts are with the family and loved ones of those affected.
"Out of respect for those involved, as well as the integrity of the investigation, we ask that any further information regarding this matter be directed to Pocono Township Police Department.
"I can tell you law enforcement assessed the situation yesterday, determined it was isolated family incident and verified there was no ongoing security concerns."
About Great Wolf Lodge
Great Wolf Lodge operates more than 20 family-oriented resorts across North America featuring indoor water parks maintained at 84 degrees year-round. Its properties offer lodging, dining, children's activities and other attractions.
The Pocono Mountains location opened in October 2005 as the company's sixth resort and is about 90 minutes west of New York City and two hours north of Philadelphia.

title: Maine’s highest court is leaving people in limbo as they wait years for decisions
text:
For three years, Zachary Borg has been waiting for Maine’s highest court to decide if he will return to prison.
Borg was found guilty of felony aggravated assault, along with several misdemeanors, and sentenced to two years in prison in Penobscot County in 2022. He appealed the ruling and was released on post-conviction bail, having already served about a year prior to his sentencing.
The Maine Supreme Judicial Court heard oral arguments in his case on Oct. 5, 2023. More than three years later, it still has not issued a decision.
“Borg still has this other year of incarceration hanging over his head, not knowing if it’s going to get flipped or not,” said Penobscot County Deputy District Attorney Chelsea Lynds, who prosecuted the case.
Borg’s case is one of many that are pending before the state’s highest court that in recent years has taken longer to issue decisions, data shows. As a result, people are waiting months or even years for verdicts that come with serious ramifications, including ones that could either release them from prison or lock them back up. The decisions could also set precedent in other cases, creating ripple effects through the state’s judicial system.
It took the court an average of 162 days to issue decisions in adult criminal cases in 2025, compared with 59 days in 2020, according to data collected by Maine Indigent Defense Center.
“If they uphold this, then what, he’s just going to be plucked out of his life and go to prison for another year?” Lynds said of Borg’s case. “It’s just not right. How do you even build a life knowing that that’s a potential threat?”
Borg declined an interview. His attorney, Harris Mattson, is now a judge and declined a request for an interview through judicial branch spokesperson Barbara Cardone.
Lynds charged Borg with aggravated assault after his daughter survived a fentanyl overdose in 2021, as endangering a child is only a misdemeanor charge. After Borg’s conviction, other district attorneys filed felony charges in similar cases, Lynds said. Those cases also cannot move forward without a ruling in Borg’s appeal.
“We have all these cases that are just like at a dead standstill,” Lynds said. “We have cases that are two to three years old that cannot move forward because we don’t have a decision on the Borg case.”
The state’s supreme court only hears appeals from lower courts, including everything from divorces to child protective custody to civil disputes to criminal cases. Maine is one of eight states in the country that does not have an intermediate appeals court, meaning the high court is required to hear every appeal that comes forward.
The court does not maintain a list of cases awaiting decisions, Cardone said. It also does not have calendars of oral arguments prior to 2024.
The supreme court heard more oral arguments last week, which meant it was “unlikely to be able to respond to these questions until next week,” Cardone said Oct. 7, the day after she was asked for comment on the decision delays.
Some delays leave people found guilty of crimes sitting in prison or jail for years even when their conviction could be vacated. A Penobscot County man, Derric McLain, was in prison for four years after being convicted on drug charges. Three of those years were spent waiting for the supreme court to decide his case before his conviction was vacated in 2025.
Meanwhile, a case about sexual assault of a child was argued in December 2024 and still has no decision. Another about who has access to Maine beaches has no answer two years later.
One of the highest profile cases that’s still waiting for a ruling concerns the constitutional right to a lawyer. The case, heard in an expedited appeal, was presented in oral arguments on Oct. 7, 2025.
“If you had asked me a year ago, if a year from now there wouldn’t be a decision, I would have naively said, ‘Of course there’s gonna be a decision,” indigent defense attorney Robert Ruffner said.
The issues before the court are whether Mainers’ Sixth Amendment rights to a fair and speedy trial were violated due to how backed-up the state’s court system is and if people accused of committing crimes were unlawfully detained. The court must also decide if low-income people can be released from jail and have charges dismissed if the state is unable to provide a lawyer.
The delay means there is still no relief for the hundreds of low-income people in Maine who are waiting weeks or months without lawyers, which is slowing down the legal process for everyone. If the high court upholds the original order from Kennebec County Superior Judge Michaela Murphy, people stuck waiting for a lawyer can be released from jail or have their case dismissed.
“It appears that the trial court is punting rather than deciding the issue that’s in front of them,” Ruffner said.
A similar crisis in Massachusetts was resolved by its supreme court in about two and a half months in 2004.
Even cases involving children are taking longer than they should. Julian Richter, a lawyer for child protective custody cases, said recent cases he has taken to the supreme court have come back in about four months, without an oral argument.
It’s difficult to tell clients there is no expected timeline, said lawyer Taylor Kilgore, who also works in child protective cases for parents and represents children as a guardian ad litem. Kilgore has had cases take more than six months for a decision.
“I don’t want to call it a black hole, but from our side of things, it kind of is,” Kilgore said. “I send off all of these briefs and this information, and the court says, ‘Thank you, we’ve received them.’ Then I have no idea what that schedule looks like either, and I don’t even get hints of it along the way.”
There are a number of factors likely contributing to the delayed rulings.
One of the biggest culprits is the consistent underfunding of the judiciary, multiple lawyers told the Bangor Daily News.
Maine ranks 45th in the nation for judicial salaries, according to the National Center for State Courts. The state also needs 54 more court clerks, who manage documents and schedules and assist judges, according to a 2022 study. There’s also a statewide shortage of marshals, who provide security. Some positions have been funded, but the full need hasn’t been met, Chief Justice Valerie Stanfill said earlier this year.
Additionally, the supreme court had an incomplete panel of justices for 18 months during the last few years. Working without seven justices can slow the decision process.
Appellate lawyer Rory McNamara blames Gov. Janet Mills for that holdup. Mills knew two retirements were coming and still delayed appointing new justices, he said.
“To me, it shows a disdain, a little bit, for the court,” McNamara said. “Everybody has a quick list of who they want to appoint to the court, go ahead and do it. It doesn’t take much to confirm a judge and to be waiting that long says, ‘Well, it’s not really that important to me.’”
Stanfill questioned why there was a year-long vacancy for one of those seats during her 2025 State of the Judiciary address.
“The Governor has always taken seriously her responsibility to nominate the strongest candidates to the bench,” Mills spokesperson Ben Goodman said. “At times, nominations have been affected by the legislative schedule or circumstances beyond the Governor’s control.”
For example, Mills waited to see if Julia Lipez would be nominated to the U.S. Court of Appeals in 2024, Goodman said. But when it didn’t happen, Mills appointed Lipez to the state’s supreme court and she was confirmed in March 2025.
Chief Deputy Attorney Christopher Taub was appointed to the court by Mills in 2026, after the legislative session ended, so he could fulfill his duties, Goodman said.
Another hurdle lawyers pointed to is the rise in full, high-quality decisions, rather than short memorandums, that the court has issued since Stanfill was sworn in as chief justice in June 2021. All seven justices were appointed in 2020 or later.
“They’ve taken more care to get the law right, and I know that that takes more time,” McNamara said. “But there are ramifications for the system when that happens.”
There is no one fix, lawyers told the BDN. More funding and any amount of transparency would be steps to help, they said.
“I find everyone in the system to be very well-intentioned and trying really hard and acknowledging that the problems exist and trying to come up with the answers the best we can,” Kilgore said. “A little additional transparency on what that process looks like would be helpful to all of us, or an explanation of why it can’t be more transparent.”

title: Charlie McAvoy scores in return to help the Bruins beat the Sharks
text:
SAN JOSE, Calif. — Charlie McAvoy scored in his season debut after serving a six-game suspension and the Boston Bruins beat the San Jose Sharks 6-3 on Tuesday night.
McAvoy missed the first six games of the season as punishment for slashing Buffalo’s Zach Benson late in Game 6 of the first round of the playoffs last season when the Bruins got eliminated.
He didn’t take long to make an impact as he got in front of the crease and knocked in a pass from JJ Peterka late in the first period to give Boston a 2-1 lead.
Fraser Minten scored two goals and Matthew Poitras and Pavel Zacha also scored for the Bruins, who have won three straight games. Will Borgen added an empty-net goal.
Jeremy Swayman made 35 saves.
Ivar Stenberg scored his first career goal for San Jose. Macklin Celebrini and Jacob Trouba also scored for the Sharks. Yaroslav Askarov made 20 saves.
Stenberg, the No. 2 overall pick in the draft in June, tied the game at 2 early in the second period when he tapped in a perfect back-door pass from Celebrini on the power play.
Poitras put Boston back in front midway through the second when he got the puck alone in front of the net and beat Askarov. The Bruins extended the lead when Zacha scored with 3 seconds remaining in the period when he finished a two-on-one with Morgan Geekie.
Celebrini scored on the power play early in the third to make it a one-goal game but Minten’s second goal of the game midway through the period restored the two-goal lead.
Up next
Bruins: Visit Anaheim on Friday night.
Sharks: Visit Nashville on Thursday night.

title: Student dies after accidental injury at school involving scissors, officials say
text:
UNIVERSITY CITY, Mo. (KMOV/Gray News) — A Missouri high school student died Tuesday after suffering an accidental injury at school last week.
The injury happened at University City High School near St. Louis.
School district officials said a student was accidentally injured with a pair of scissors at the district’s high school on Oct. 5, which prompted a lockdown.
On Tuesday, officials said that student died from his injuries.
School district officials and police said there was an internal investigation following the injury, and no foul play was suspected.
Police did not reveal exactly how the student was injured with scissors.
The district said it is making crisis counselors available to students and staff.
“The wellbeing of our University City students, staff, families and community remains our highest priority,” the district wrote in a release. “Comprehensive crisis counseling and mental health support services are available at all district schools for any student or staff member in need of support. The School District will also have additional counselors and wellness resources at University City High School to respond to student needs. We thank you for your patience and understanding as we have honored the confidentiality and privacy of the family.”
Further information was not yet available.

title: EVENTS: A full house for Paul
text:
Lily’s Apple Pie returns to the Vassalboro Grange, bringing a local playwright’s humor to another generation.
When Paul Cates put on a play, Vassalboro showed up. His productions filled the Grange so enthusiastically that, on one occasion, the crowd drew a visit from the fire department. His family remembered the episode in his obituary, a fitting detail for a man who knew how to bring his neighbors together.
This October, there is a new reason to gather there.
Lily’s Apple Pie, the late Vassalboro playwright’s comedy first performed in 2003, returns for two performances benefiting the Vassalboro Historical Society. At the heart of the story is a question with plenty riding on it: Will Lily win the Grange pie contest again?
A hometown comedy, with a family connection
Directed by Arthur and Linda Kingdon, the revival features Vassalboro Historical Society President Janice Clowes as Lily. The new cast also includes Paul’s daughter and granddaughter, giving this production a particularly meaningful connection to its author.
The Society chose the play because it wanted a fundraiser rooted in the town’s own history. Paul’s work offered just that: something created here, remembered here, and ready to be enjoyed, again.
The orchard names in the play draw on real apple orchards. That local detail adds another reason for audiences to listen closely.
From East Vassalboro to a divided Berlin
Many neighbors knew Paul as the “Glad Man.” Beginning in 1970, he grew gladiolus on the Cates family farm and sold flowers from his Volkswagen bus.
His life reached far beyond those fields.
According to his family’s account, Paul carried medicines and documents into East Berlin after the Berlin Wall went up, concealing parcels in his overcoat. Through that work, he met Elisabeth, who became his wife.
For someone discovering local history for the first time, that is an invitation to look closer. What other remarkable lives began on familiar roads?
His Quaker convictions guided a life of service. He taught languages at Oak Grove-Coburn and Erskine Academy, and wrote, produced, and performed in plays often set in East Vassalboro. He died on October 21, 2018, at 93.
His words, their voices.
Paul’s family remembered a man who loved songs, sweets, and his grandchildren. Now, a daughter and granddaughter will help bring his words to life again.
That is a lovely reason to be in the audience.
A performance lets those who remember Paul encounter his humor again. It also gives younger residents a first introduction to someone whose creativity became part of the town’s shared life.
Perhaps it will prompt a conversation afterward: Who was he? Did you know him? What else did he write?
Those conversations are part of how a town keeps its stories.
Come see what Lily has up her sleeve
Bring a friend, invite the family, and choose a Friday evening or Saturday afternoon at the Grange. Enjoy a local comedy while supporting the Society’s work of preserving Vassalboro’s history.
Lily’s Apple Pie
A comedy by Paul Cates
Directed by Arthur and Linda Kingdon
Featuring Janice Clowes, Vassalboro Historical Society President, as Lily
Friday, October 23, 2026, at 6 p.m.
Saturday, October 24, 2026, at 2 p.m.
Vassalboro Grange
353 Main Street, East Vassalboro
Admission: $10 adults • $2 children under 12
Tickets at the door. Door receipts benefit the Vassalboro Historical Society.
Add your memory to the story
Did Paul teach you, deliver flowers to your shop, or make you laugh from the Grange stage? Do you have an old program or a photograph from one of his productions?
Share your memories with the Society at vhspresident@gmail.com or (207) 923-3505.
Lily has a contest to enter. Vassalboro has a playwright to remember. Let’s give his words another good audience.

title: Three community members to host free family-friendly Halloween Celebration this October
Rumford police lift shelter-in-place for area of Waldo Street, Maine Avenue
text:
Maine man wanted after police search Rumford apartment following reports of gunfire
A shelter-in-place advisory was issued for the area of Waldo Street and Maine Avenue
Maine man wanted after police search Rumford apartment following reports of gunfire
A shelter-in-place advisory was issued for the area of Waldo Street and Maine Avenue
Authorities are searching for a Maine man who is wanted on several felony charges connected to an incident that prompted a shelter-in-place advisory in the town of Rumford on Wednesday.
Blake Lachance, 21, of Lewiston, is wanted on one count each of aggravated assault with a dangerous weapon, criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon and reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon.
The Rumford Police Department said officers and members of the Maine State Police Tactical Team executed a search warrant at a first-floor apartment at 209 Waldo St. following an investigation into reports of gunfire and suspected drug trafficking at the home.
Rumford police said that over the weekend, they received information concerning suspected drug trafficking involving locals and people from out of town at the Waldo Street apartment. Police said they also received reports from concerned residents, who told police that people associated with the apartment were armed and had been periodically firing guns in the surrounding neighborhood.
Before sunrise Wednesday morning, Rumford police responded to a report of gunfire in the Waldo Street area. Responding officers determined that the people believed to be involved had been inside the apartment and were potentially still there.
Given the possibility of encountering armed suspects, officers from the Rumford Police Department and Oxford County Sheriff's Office established a perimeter around 209 Waldo St. while investigators prepared applications for search and arrest warrants.
The Maine State Police Tactical Team was called in to help secure the area and execute the search warrant, which was authorized by a court late Wednesday morning.
Police said that as officers prepared to search the apartment, Rumford Public Works crews established temporary road closures and traffic detours in the surrounding neighborhood. MedCare Ambulance paramedics were also staged nearby as a precaution.
In a Facebook post shared shortly before 12:15 p.m. Wednesday, Rumford police said people near the intersection of Waldo Street and Maine Avenue were advised to shelter in place and stay inside.
Rumford police said the Maine State Police Tactical Team entered the apartment shortly before 1 p.m. and determined the suspects were no longer inside. Investigators believe the suspects had fled the apartment several hours earlier, around the time police initially responded to the report of gunfire Wednesday morning.
At 1:20 p.m., Rumford police announced that the shelter-in-place advisory had been lifted and that roads that were closed were being reopened.
According to officials, a subsequent search of the apartment, coupled with information developed during the ongoing investigation, yielded additional evidence supporting the reports that police received from members of the public.
Police said Lachance should be considered potentially armed and dangerous, so members of the public should not approach or attempt to confront him.
Authorities are asking anyone who has information regarding his whereabouts to immediately contact law enforcement.
The investigation in Rumford remains active, and police said more people are expected to face criminal charges as investigators continue to develop evidence and identify those involved.

title: Who’s on the ballot in Cape Elizabeth
text:
Election season is upon us.
Cape Elizabeth residents will vote on town council and school board members.
Early voting will continue through Oct. 29 in council chambers in town hall on Mondays from 7:30 a.m. through 4:30 p.m. and Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday from 7:30 to 4 p.m.
TOWN COUNCIL
There are four candidates running for two open seats on the town council.
Stephanie Anderson has served on the town council since 2023, and before that, as the Cumberland County district attorney for decades and as a state senator in 2022. Her top priorities are building workforce housing, limiting property tax increases and improving cell service across town.
Elizabeth Biermann, an attorney who has lived in Cape Elizabeth for seven years, is running for office for the first time. She plans to prioritize lowering costs by taking a long-term view, making the town affordable and making decisions efficiently.
Christopher Groski, a software engineer, is running for office for the first time, and plans to prioritize infrastructure improvements like road paving, protecting open spaces and supporting the school board.
Timothy Thompson, a retired financial adviser, has been serving on the town council for three years. He’s the council representative to the Maine Municipal Association and represents the town on the county’s budget committee. He believes that property tax escalation is one of the biggest issues facing the town and that the state should provide more financial support to Cape Elizabeth.
SCHOOL BOARD
There are three candidates running for two school board seats.
Elizabeth Goodspeed, who has a background in education and has children in the school district, is running for the school board because she wants the schools to plan thoughtfully about using technology in the classroom and for future infrastructure needs.
Karen Lechner, a retired public school counselor and grandparent of two students in the district, is running for the school board to maximize student resiliency, support educators and make sure schools have enough resources.
Julie Pelletier, an emergency medicine physician and parent of three Cape Elizabeth students, is running for the school board because she wants to support educators. She wants to work with school leaders to come up with a plan for technology use in the classroom, retain and recruit more educators and improve school infrastructure when needed.

text:

A shelter-in-place order issued around 12:15 p.m. was lifted about an hour later.

Following an investigation into reports of gunfire and suspected drug trafficking at a first-floor apartment at 209 Waldo St., Rumford police, assisted by the Maine State Police Tactical Team, executed a search warrant Wednesday.

During the same period, police began receiving reports from concerned residents that individuals associated with the apartment were armed and had been periodically discharging firearms in the surrounding neighborhood.

Shortly before 1 p.m., the tactical team entered the apartment and determined that the suspects were no longer inside. Investigators believe the individuals had fled the residence several hours earlier, around the time police initially responded to the morning report of gunfire. title: The first new sunscreen type in 25 years has arrived on US store shelves
text:
The first new sunscreen type in 25 years has arrived on US store shelves
For the first time in more than a quarter-century, Americans have a new option when shopping for sunscreen: a skin-protecting chemical that's long been a go-to option in Europe and other parts of the world.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved bemotrizinol — sometimes called BEMT — in June. The first sunscreens containing it are now hitting U.S. store shelves, including formulas from Neutrogena and other manufacturers.
Dermatologists say the chemical fills an important market gap by offering broad protection, like the most well-established sunscreen ingredients, but without their cosmetic downsides, including white streaking.
BEMT has decades of safety data behind it, including studies showing it has minimal absorption into the skin. That's been a concern with some older sun-blocking chemicals.
"It's not a brand-new ingredient that you're going to be the first person to try," said Dr. Jennifer Stein, a dermatologist at NYU Langone Health.
Here's what to know:
New ingredient offers broad protection without streaks
To be effective, sunscreens must protect against both forms of ultraviolet light that can damage the skin — UVB rays, which cause most sunburn, and UVA rays that pose the greatest risk of skin cancer and wrinkles.
Sunscreens that block both forms are labeled "broad spectrum protection." Those that don't must carry an FDA warning label.
BEMT is the first chemical-based sunscreen in the U.S. that offers this dual protection. Previously, manufacturers had to mix multiple ingredients to protect against both UVA and UVB light.
"This ingredient provides a solution for what is currently a big gap with respect to providing strong UVA protection," said David Andrews, chief science officer of the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit that advocates for higher sunscreen standards.
A different class of sunscreens, using minerals such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, has long been shown to offer strong protection against both forms of ultraviolet light. These mineral-based formulas work by physically blocking harmful rays from the skin.
But some people — particularly those with darker complexions — tend to avoid them because they cause white streaking and discoloration. In other cases, people don't like their texture or consistency.
"Those are good sunscreens," Stein said. "But for people who aren't so inclined to use them — maybe they don't like how it feels on their skin — this is a nice option."
There's less skin penetration with the new formula
The fact that chemical-based sunscreens are absorbed into the skin means they have to be carefully studied to make sure they aren't building up in the body at unsafe levels.
Last month, the FDA revoked approval of an older chemical ingredient, oxybenzone, after determining it was "absorbed through the skin to a greater extent than previously understood."
That's not a problem with BEMT.
"It's a molecule that's too big to really penetrate through the skin and get absorbed into the bloodstream," Stein said. "The older chemical sunscreens had small molecules."
As part of its safety review, the FDA reviewed studies of BEMT in more than 500 patients conducted by Dutch manufacturer DSM Nutritional Products. Levels of the chemical absorbed into the skin were nearly undetectable, the studies found.
Agency reviewers said research in people who used the sunscreen daily for up to three weeks showed that BEMT "did not cause irritation" or allergic reactions. As a result, the FDA designated the ingredient as "generally recognized as safe and effective," alongside the older mineral ingredients zinc oxide and titanium dioxide.
More than a dozen other ingredients are currently used in U.S. sunscreens, but the FDA has said they will require additional evidence to support their safety and effectiveness. The FDA review is part of an ongoing effort to overhaul U.S. sunscreen ingredients that kicked off in 2019.
More evidence is needed about the impact on coral reefs
Scientists have shown that some sunscreen ingredients can trigger bleaching and damage coral reefs. That's led to bans on two chemical ingredients — oxybenzone, the ingredient recently targeted by the FDA, and octinoxate — in Hawaii and parts of Florida. It's estimated about 25% of the sunscreen people apply to their skin washes off while swimming or wading in the ocean.
The U.S. government doesn't classify the environmental impact of sunscreens, and marketing claims like "reef safe" or "reef friendly" have no standard definition or requirements. The European Union's environmental agency has found "limited evidence of environmental toxicity" with BEMT, but longer-term research is needed.
Mineral ingredients like zinc oxide are generally considered safer for the environment, although some experts recommend staying away from so-called nano formulations. Those products are made with tiny particles that are more likely to be inhaled or absorbed by marine organisms.
Older chemicals were often unstable
Experts say BEMT has one other key advantage, in that it doesn't quickly break down in the sun. That's been a particular issue for avobenzone, the only other chemical-based ingredient that filters UVA light.
"Avobenzone has been known to be particularly unstable on its own, and a lot of work and reformulation efforts have gone into trying to find ways to stabilize it," said Andrews. "BEMT is significantly more stable."
As with all sunscreens, dermatologists say it's important to reapply every few hours — more frequently if you're swimming or sweating a lot.
Also, people shouldn't rely on sunscreen alone when spending time outside, Stein said. Taking breaks in the shade, wearing a hat and sun-protective clothing are all important protections.
"Sunscreen is just one part of an overall sun-protection plan," Stein said. "Clothing is even better."

title: Trump says oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is set to begin. It's not that simple
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trump says oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland is set to begin. It's not that simple
U.S. President Donald Trump said “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in “our new and beautiful Greenland ” early Wednesday.
It wasn’t immediately clear what exploration or developments the U.S. president was referring to in his post, and Greenland is a self-governing territory of Denmark, rather than a part of the United States.
Trump posted on his Truth Social platform following a campaign event Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska, to stump for Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan as he seeks his third term to represent the state in an election against Democratic former U.S. congresswoman Mary Peltola.
Rising energy prices — a direct result of Trump’s war in Iran — are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for America’s working class ahead of the midterm elections next month. Trump’s comments Wednesday are likely aimed at addressing voters’ concerns before they head to the polls.
But despite Trump’s optimism, resource exploration and extraction in Greenland has stymied companies for decades thanks to the island’s harsh climate, lack of key infrastructure and difficult geology. Previous efforts to extract so-called rare earth minerals, as well as oil and gas, have never progressed beyond the exploratory stage.
A recent deal paved the way for more US bases but didn't offer exploration rights
Trump’s comments about the Arctic island come less than a month after he signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic following months of tensions with NATO allies over the U.S. president's repeated demands to take control of the semiautonomous Danish territory. It does not grant the U.S. any special exploration rights, but does place some limits on investments by non-NATO countries in strategic sectors.
The deal also paved the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eased tensions over Trump's repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States. The agreement would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.
Trump has expressed his desire to acquire Greenland since as long ago as 2019 and, during his second term, issued threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a NATO ally.
Representatives of the leaders of Denmark and Greenland did not immediately return requests for comment Wednesday.
Greenland has valuable resources
Greenland has large deposits of the rare earth minerals that are needed to make everything from computers and smartphones to the batteries, solar and wind technologies that will power the transition away from fossil fuels. China currently dominates the world's supply of these critical minerals and the Trump administration is seeking to break Beijing's chokehold on them.
The U.S. Geological Survey has also identified major potential offshore deposits of oil and natural gas.
But tapping these resources could be prohibitively difficult: the rare earth minerals are encased in rock, and the offshore oil and natural gas deposits are covered by Arctic ice.
Trump boasts about Greenland’s strategic spot in the Arctic
Trump's Truth Social post also touted Greenland's strategic location, saying that “from a Security Purpose in the Defense and Offense of both the United States of America, and Europe,” the island is “second to none.”
“Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived," he wrote. "It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!”
The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the U.S. military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO.
Trump said last month that the U.S. would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” including “building two very major military bases.”

title: How college students can start building credit the right way
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Managing money is rarely part of the official college curriculum, but WalletHub says one wrong move with fees or credit can cost students more than money — it can set back their credit-building efforts before their careers even begin.
John Kiernan, managing editor at WalletHub, said students need to understand what financial tools are available to them before heading to campus.
Kiernan’s first tip: credit can be built without ever making a purchase.
“One thing I’ll say for parents and students out there to build credit with a credit card, you don’t necessarily have to make purchases,” Kiernan said. “If you get a $0 annual fee card and put it in your wallet for emergencies and never use it, you’ll still get credit for paying on time every month because you don’t have a balance. And so you’ll get a monthly influx of positive information to your credit report, which will help you build credit.”
Kiernan said the next step, once a student begins earning a paycheck, is setting up automatic payments.
“Forgetting due dates is one of the easiest ways to hurt your credit score,” Kiernan said. “And just setting up autopay is one of the easiest ways to make sure you build good credit history.”
For students still searching for the right card, WalletHub has ranked the best credit cards for students to help them get started.
“College is about preparing for adult life,” Kiernan said. “This is one aspect that’s not going to be really covered in the classroom, and it’ll set you up and help lay the foundation for your finances moving forward.”
Beyond skipping annual fees, WalletHub recommends confirming that a card reports to the credit bureaus every month, since that reporting is what actually builds the credit history students will need later for renting an apartment or qualifying for a loan.

title: Six Flags Over Georgia rides were inspected before season, commissioner says after fatal fall
text:
ATLANTA (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — The Georgia Insurance and Fire Safety Commissioner said his office is investigating the death of a man at Six Flags Over Georgia.
“Our very professional inspectors have inspected every one of those before the park season even started, and they’re currently on the ground looking at every nook and cranny, conducting interviews and conducting a thorough review of what happened,” Commissioner John King said during an Atlanta Press Club-sponsored debate broadcast on Georgia Public Television.
Cobb County police also investigating
The Cobb County Police Department’s major crimes unit is also investigating the Oct. 12 death of Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, who fell from the Goliath roller coaster, according to the department. Investigators said he was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction.
King is facing a reelection challenge from Democrat Keisha Sean Waites, and ride safety at amusement parks was the first question that came up during the debate.
Candidates respond to park reopening
Waites said Six Flags Over Georgia is set to reopen Friday.
“Prior to that opening, I would ensure that all of the amusement park rides have been inspected thoroughly to make sure that this will never happen again in Georgia,” she said.
The commissioner’s office is charged with inspecting, permitting and regulating amusement parks throughout the state.
“Clearly, this is one of our primary duties when it comes to safety,” King said.
King said his office’s inspectors inspected the rides before the park season started and are now on the ground investigating.
“It’s a little premature to be making a whole lot of comments about this. Obviously, this is an ongoing investigation, but I look forward to being able to report back to the Georgia public that these rides are safe, they will continue to be safe and we will continue inspecting them from top to bottom,” King added.
Waites, a three-term state House member and former Atlanta City Council member, said she would have ensured “there’s an inspection at that particular facility as time permits, in addition to that, to ensure that any challenges that we’ve had in the past, that they were investigated thoroughly.”
Election context
All of Georgia’s constitutional offices and House and Senate seats are on the ballot for the Nov. 3 midterms. Early voting began Oct. 13 and runs through Oct. 30.

title: House Democrats plan a first 100-days agenda if they sweep to power in midterm elections
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats are preparing an ambitious 100-days agenda focused on delivering their campaign promises — making life more affordable and conducting vast oversight of the Trump administration — if the party seizes majority control in next month’s elections.
Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker if the party wins power, said the Democrats will be united “right out of the gate” on reinstating Affordable Care Act tax breaks, reversing Republican Medicaid cuts, holding votes against the Iran war and undoing President Donald Trump’s tariff regime.
They expect to launch the agenda in the first 100 hours, once the new Congress is seated in January.
“Fighting for an affordable America — that’s what unites Democrats all across the country,” Jeffries said recently at the party campaign headquarters in Washington.
“That’s our commitment to the American people, because the cost of living is way too high and far too many people who are working hard, playing by the rules, can’t thrive and can barely survive — and are drowning — in the Trump economy.”
It’s a hyper-focused agenda tapping into the voter sentiment that is driving much of the midterm election as Americans wrestle with affordability concerns and inflationary costs from the Iran war and other policies.
The undertaking will also test the ability of the sprawling House Democrats to work together and avoid the chaotic divisions and disruptions that have hobbled Republicans under Speaker Mike Johnson’s leadership.
Democrats have been out of power in the House since 2023. If Jeffries takes the helm, he would be the first Democratic speaker since Nancy Pelosi, leading a new generation of lawmakers that includes a handful of far-left candidates who are aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America.
“The antidote to that is getting things done,” said Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski, who is poised to become chair of the New Democrat Coalition, the largest caucus within the House Democrats. She said the party is determined to show the American people that “Democrats know how to govern.”
A Freedom Caucus of the far-left?
Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said he is often asked if Democrats will be confronting their own version of the Freedom Caucus, referring to the far-right Republicans who often grind the House agenda to a halt.
“It doesn’t work that way,” Casar told The Associated Press in an interview. “The Freedom Caucus breaks things. But if you’re a progressive, you want to pass things.”
Leader Jeffries, Casar and other Democrats have been in touch with the progressive candidates, many of whom are backed by the DSA as the party focuses on shared priorities.
“This notion that because we’ll have new members somehow we’re going to be disjointed — not so,” said Louisiana Rep. Troy Carter, who hopes to become chair of the Congressional Black Caucus. “All those banking on that, save the popcorn for another day.”
The Republicans, who are confronting an increasingly difficult election-year climate to hold onto their majority, portray Democrats as beholden to a far-left socialist agenda.
If Republicans retain power, Johnson has said they would press on with what they have already accomplished alongside Trump, which has been an agenda focused on cutting taxes and federal spending.
“What we would do in the next two years is exactly what we have been doing already,” Johnson said on CNBC’s Squawk Box, “and that is putting the conditions in place for a strong America again.”
Fix healthcare, stop the war, end the tariffs – and investigate Trump
Months ago, Jeffries launched five working groups to tackle the affordability agenda focused on healthcare, housing, groceries and goods, gas and utilities, and care-giving.
Each group is headed by a progressive and a centrist Democrat — the healthcare working group, for example, is run by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama — with the goal of striking common ground on draft policies that all House Democrats can support.
At the same time, Jeffries has tasked the ranking Democrats on the House Oversight and Judiciary committees with preparing investigations. They are focused on Trump, his family and his administration, as part of a sweeping anti-corruption agenda. Impeachment, Jeffries has said, is neither on nor off the table.
“We need to lower the cost of groceries and gas. Two, we need to make healthcare affordable for every single American. Three, we’re going to hold the crooks accountable who’ve visited unprecedented corruption on the American people,” Jeffries said. “Beginning on day one.”
Democrats plan to vote quickly to reinstate the health care tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, which expired in 2025, leaving millions of Americans confronting higher health insurance costs.
Proposals are also ready to reverse the Medicaid cuts that Republicans put in place as part of their “One Big Beautiful Bill” of tax breaks and program cuts, including new work requirements for recipients.
There are measures to reverse Trump’s tariffs as Congress works to claw back power from the White House.
And Democrats, who have forced multiple votes on ending the Iran conflict, plan to pressure the Trump administration to end the military action by pushing forward more war powers resolutions.
Much of the House Democrats’ agenda, if they regain power, would depend on the size of the majority. Details also depend on the Senate, and whether it flips to Democrats.
“We cannot simply go back to the status quo,” said Usamah Andrabi, a spokesman for Justice Democrats, an outside group that supports the far-left progressives.
And Trump, at the White House, has ultimate say, with veto power at the stroke of a pen.
“We’re going to do a lot and we’re going to be very busy,” Carter said. “We will not be able to fix everything overnight.”

title: TikTok creator Bryce Hall charged with felony domestic violence, reports say
text:
TikTok creator Bryce Hall charged with felony domestic violence, reports say
TikTok creator Bryce Hall is denying allegations after he was arrested for felony domestic violence, according to court records.
Related video:
E! News reported Hall, 27, was charged with "coercion constituting domestic violence with threat or use of physical force, and one count of domestic battery, first offense, on Aug. 28."
The incident, however, reportedly occurred a month prior on July 27.
In reference to court documents, the outlet said that an arrest warrant was issued on Sept. 10, and a release order was entered Sept. 12.
Hall's representative told TMZ and E! News the allegations are false, saying, "We look forward to the facts coming out in court. We will be taking legal action against those responsible for spreading false and defamatory claims."
Hall previously encountered trouble with the law in 2022 over a confrontation at a Los Angeles nightclub, though he clarified that he "didn't get charged" after being placed under citizen's arrest.

title: Parents charged with murder after their young children died in RV fire
text:
LIBERTY COUNTY, Texas (KHOU) — The parents of two young children who died in an RV fire in Texas are in custody and facing murder charges, authorities said.
The fire happened Aug. 11, when authorities said the travel-trailer the children had been left in caught fire with them still inside.
Skylar Jane, 3, and Maverick, 4, died in the fire.
Parents away from trailer when fire started
Family members who spoke anonymously at the time said the children’s parents, Matthew Chambers and Meaghan Herrod, had stepped away to visit another home on the property when the fire happened.
“They had walked from their trailer to my daughter’s house and just opened up the door, and one of the neighbors over here started screaming, ‘There’s a fire. Call 911.’ So, naturally, they all ran back to the trailer,” a family member said.
Couple charged with murder
The Liberty County Fire Marshal’s Office confirmed Chambers and Herrod are now charged with murder in connection with the children’s deaths.
The investigation and additional questioning ultimately led to both being taken into custody.
Authorities haven’t said what caused the deaths, only that the children’s remains were found inside the trailer.
It’s not clear when Chambers and Herrod are expected back in court. Each has a $1 million bond.
The cause of the fire is still not known.

title: A new bridge linking China and North Korea will open more than a decade late
text:
New China-North Korea bridge opens after more than a decade of delay
A new bridge linking China and North Korea opened Thursday after more than a decade of delay, signaling deeper ties between the two countries.
Related video: President Trump on Russia diesel deal: 'It's a deal for the world. It's not a deal for us.'
China's official Xinhua News Agency reported that a ceremony for the launch of the New Yalu River Bridge was held in the morning. An online video from state media outlet China News Service showed trucks adorned with the national flags of China and North Korea waiting on the bridge, which was also decorated with the flags.
Beijing expected that the four-lane, 3-kilometer (1.8-mile) crossing, which connects the northeastern Chinese city of Dandong to the North Korean city of Sinuiju, would further promote economic, trade and “people-to-people" exchanges.
During the ceremony, Chinese Premier Li Qiang said in a video address that the crossing would become a new landmark symbolizing the two nations' traditional friendship, Xinhua reported. He hoped both sides would seize the opportunity of the opening to continue to enhance connectivity and explore potential for cooperation in border areas, it said.
“The relations between China and North Korea have entered a new stage, embarking on a new chapter,” he was quoted as saying.
North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song also made a video address, the report added.
Bridge opens after a 12-year delay
The bridge initially was expected to enter use in 2014, when China had apparently completed construction on its side. But the date came with no opening and without North Korea doing corresponding work on its side.
The absence of substantial work in Sinuiju fueled speculation that Pyongyang was wary of becoming more economically dependent on China or displeased with Beijing voting for United Nations resolutions toughening international sanctions on the North over its nuclear program. Some observers suggested North Korea and China also differed over the bridge's location.
The setback over the bridge prompted an unusually sharp report in the Global Times, a newspaper affiliated with the ruling Chinese Communist Party, which quoted Dandong residents expressing frustration over delays in what they had hoped would be an economic boon for their border city.
New link opens a month after launch of Russia-North Korea bridge
Observers said the new bridge would likely boost bilateral trade and enhance logistical efficiency gradually.
It is expected to lessen the burden on an aging bridge on the Dandong-Sinuiju route, which handles more than 70% of official trade between the two countries. That decades-old bridge carries a railway line as well as cars and trucks, but vehicle traffic can move only one way at a time.
The South Korean government said last year there were at least 17 active road and rail links across the porous North Korea-China border, which stretches more than 1,400 kilometers (870 miles).
The new bridge's launch came about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a road bridge as part of their efforts to cement relations. Experts say Chinese officials likely felt uneasy about its opening.
China has long been North Korea’s biggest trading partner and economic pipeline. But in past years, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has prioritized Moscow, sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance.
Kim has recently drawn closer to China with the apparent intent to improve his country's economy and build a front against the United States. China, for its part, wants to restore its unique influence over North Korea. Last year, about 98% of North Korea’s external trade was with China.

title: Gradually Drying Out Today... Sunshine Returns Thursday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The steadier rain has pushed off to our east allowing us to dry things out this afternoon. There is a slight chance of an isolated shower in spots but overall mainly dry conditions are expected through the remainder of the day. There will still be plenty of clouds around so most areas will remain cloudy but some breaks of sunshine will be possible... especially south of the Bangor area. Temperatures will be a bit better today with highs climbing to the mid-40s to around 50° north and 50s to near 60° elsewhere. Skies will clear out tonight as high pressure begins to build into the area. As the high approaches... low pressure will be strengthening as it heads up into the Maritimes. This will cause the pressure gradient to tighten up as the night progresses leading to an increasing northwest wind with gusts to 25-30 MPH possible after midnight.
Drier and brighter weather is on tap for our Thursday with plenty of sunshine expected. Strong low pressure over the Maritimes combined with high pressure to our west over the Great Lakes Region will make for a breezy day with a northwest wind gusting to 25-35 MPH at times. Temperatures will be more seasonable with highs in the 50s. Clouds will move back in Thursday night with another storm system bringing more beneficial rain for Friday and Friday night with another .5” to 1” or so of rain possible. We may see some wet snow or mixed rain and snow across Northern Aroostook County but overall it looks to be a mainly rain event. Rain will taper off Friday night as low pressure moves to our east. Rain and snow showers will linger into Saturday morning otherwise expect drier weather Saturday with brightening skies as the day progresses. The pressure gradient will tighten up again on the backside of our departing storm leading to a strong northwest wind to start the weekend. This northwest wind will also usher some colder air into the region with highs on Saturday topping off in the mid-30s to low 40s north and 40s elsewhere. The northwest wind will gust to 30-40 MPH at times... making it feel even colder. High pressure will bring us plenty of sunshine Sunday with highs mainly in the 40s. It’ll still be breezy too but overall wind speeds will be lighter than Saturday.
Rest of Today: Mostly cloudy. Some breaks of sun possible. Slight chance of an isolated shower. Highs in the mid-40s to low 50s north and 50s to near 60° elsewhere. Northwest wind 5-15 MPH.
Tonight: Clearing skies and becoming breezy. Lows between 35°-44°. Northwest wind 10-20 MPH with gusts to 25-30 MPH possible.
Thursday: Mostly sunny and breezy. Highs in the upper 40s to mid-50s. Northwest wind 10-20 MPH with gusts to 25-35 MPH possible
Friday: Rain likely. Some rain/snow mix possible across the north. Highs in the 40s to low 50s.
Saturday: A few morning rain and snow showers possible across the north and rain showers possible elsewhere otherwise expect brightening skies and breezy conditions. Highs in the upper 30s to low 40s north and 40s to near 50° elsewhere. Northwest winds could gust to 30-40 MPH at times.
Sunday: Mostly sunny and breezy. Highs in the 40s to near 50°.

title: Katie Zacharia's White House debut raises new questions about the press secretary's job
text:
Katie Zacharia's White House debut raises new questions about the press secretary's job
President Donald Trump's new press secretary stepped to the podium, the eyes of a packed room of journalists — and many in their audiences — upon her. She smiled broadly at the sea of faces both probing and friendly. With that, Katie Zacharia went live and became the official voice of the world's most powerful person.
Fourteen minutes and just three questioners later, she was done. In the aftermath, it was clear that the former Newsmax commentator accomplished at least one thing: She put the “brief” back in briefing.
In her debut Tuesday, Zacharia looked downward and often read directly from a script. She paused and grinned when she uttered the words “Department of War.” She stumbled on a question about her background and mixed up the words “husband” and “president.” The few questions she took were nonconfrontational and from media outlets that have been sympathetic to the Republican president. In short: She made no memorable impression — or at least, to hear some tell it, not the one she likely wanted.
This would not be an easy job under any circumstances. Trump most frequently serves as his own spokesman. And his antagonism toward the media has created a new layer of tension. Zacharia is finding out on day one that she, too, will be under constant watch. Some — including a few of those who have stood in her shoes — didn’t think it went all that well.
In fractured times, in a national media scrum unimaginable just a few decades ago, what is the proper way to approach a job like this? How do you speak effectively when your boss speaks for himself so often that he commandeers the news cycle multiple times a day.
Video below: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia: Guilfoyle was asked to resign
For one, you realize for whom you work: not your audience of millions but your audience of one, and the absolute need for his approval.
“I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people,” Zacharia said. Nowhere did she mention the task of disseminating accurate information to Americans.
The press secretary role has been many things
Over the nearly 10 decades since former journalist George E. Akerson made his and the office's debut as Herbert Hoover's press secretary in 1929, the job has served many purposes: deliverer of information, amplifier of policy, jouster with journalists, protector of the presidential reputation and, sometimes, overlord of obfuscation.
Under Trump and his second-term press secretary so far — Karoline Leavitt, who resigned in August — the job has been primarily one of acting as the immovable object against an irresistible, and in Trump's eyes sometimes treasonous, force.
Leavitt got to know this terrain well in her 17-month tenure. She took a smiling but combative stance against a press that was increasingly coming under Trump's criticism for coverage — and was named in at least one lawsuit about White House media access. She was not shy about interdicting what she considered media bias. "What a stupid question," she said to one reporter at a briefing last year.
Trump, outside the White House shortly after the briefing, praised Zacharia's debut as “excellent.” She was standing behind him at the time.
Other early reviews were more critical. MS NOW quoted one unnamed White House official as saying of the performance: “She needs to get much better fast, otherwise she’ll break Scaramucci’s record.” Anthony Scaramucci, an early White House communications director for first-term Trump, lasted 11 days in 2017. Said Scaramucci on X Tuesday afternoon: “I hope she makes it.”
Joe Biden's former press secretary, Jen Psaki, now the host of a show on MS NOW, put it more succinctly, posting on X: “Well that briefing was basically an SNL skit….except it wasnt.”
Talking up Trump but taking few questions
While Zacharia's performance — and of course, that's what every briefing is — may have been bumpy to some, it was also mostly content-free except for news she broke about the White House asking U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to quit, which she immediately did.
Predictably, also like Leavitt before her, Zacharia spent a great part of her opening monologue praising Trump and giving an “up 'til now”-style update on his second term's priorities and accomplishments so far. Talking points included a “booming economy,” “his historic boom in energy production” and “a great relationship with Venezuela.”
She was also fond of superlatives, a trait that likely will resonate with a president whose remarks are often equally if not more expansive: “President Trump is working to secure the Western Hemisphere for centuries to come.”
When it came to questions, though, she was downright parsimonious. She allowed three questioners, then answered an additional one as she prepared to depart. The three called on during the briefing were Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail, all of which have been friendly to Trump in varying degrees during periods of his two terms. And she said she would continue Leavitt's policy of bringing “new media” in — which has often meant outlets more sympathetic to Trump.
“We love new media and we want to be able to embrace it,” she said. Currently, three major outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — are fighting to regain White House access after Trump banished them last month, saying he didn't like their coverage and calling it “fake news.”
How will Zacharia fare in coming days and weeks and, if it lasts, months? That, like so much else, depends on one thing: Donald Trump.

title: Don’t close the door, Mom, I’ll be back
text:
Abdullahi Ahmed, Ed.D., of Portland is a naturalized citizen who came to the U.S. as a refugee from Somalia. He has worked for the Portland Public Schools since 2001.
When I left Somalia, I did not think I was leaving my country. I thought I was leaving for a while. I can still imagine the moment of departure. The uncertainty of the journey was real, but so was the belief that I would return. Somewhere in my mind, I was already planning my way back. I did not know how long I would be gone, but I did not imagine that the distance between me and home would grow into years, decades and eventually most of my adult life.
Perhaps this is one of the quietest and most powerful dreams of an immigrant: I will come back. People leave their homes with a suitcase, a few belongings, memories and a promise to themselves and to the people they love. They leave believing that the door they walk through is not a door that closes behind them. It is only a door they will walk through again.
That is why I imagine telling my mother, “Do not close the door. I will be back.” I did not say those exact words, but they describe what I carried in my heart. I was not saying goodbye to Somalia, to Mogadishu, the city I love. I was saying, “Wait for me.”
Like many immigrants, I thought my absence would be temporary. I imagined returning to the streets I knew, to familiar voices, familiar food, familiar smells and the landscape that had shaped my childhood. I imagined sitting with family again, telling stories about the places I had traveled and the things I had learned. But immigration has a way of changing the meaning of time.
A year becomes several years. Several years become a decade. Children grow up. Parents grow older. Friends move away. Neighborhoods change. The streets you remember remain in your memory, but sometimes they no longer look the same even when you return. Eventually, you realize that you have been away longer than you ever imagined.
Yet something strange happens to an immigrant during those years. While I am away from my country, my country is never completely away from me. I could not continue living in Somalia, but Somalia continued living in me. I carried Somalia into Pakistan. I carried it with me when I came to America. I carried its language, its stories, its hospitality, its struggles, its humor, its faith, its food, its memories and the voices of the people who raised me. In many ways, my country did not carry me. I carried my country.
That may be one of the great contradictions of immigration. We leave because circumstances, opportunity, education, safety, family, war, poverty or hope push us beyond our borders. We cross oceans and continents looking for another life. But crossing a border does not mean leaving everything behind. The country we leave often becomes even more present inside us. We become immigrants, but we also become living memories of somewhere else.
I became an American. I built a life in Maine. I became an educator and educational leader, a husband, a father and a member of communities that welcomed me. America became home in ways I could never have imagined when I first arrived. But becoming part of a new country did not erase the old one. There is a Somali tradition that captures something about this experience: wherever you travel, you carry your identity with you. That is what immigrants do. We build new homes while carrying old ones and identities inside our hearts.
When I think about that imaginary door, I understand now that the promise to return was about more than geography. It was a promise to remain connected. I may not have been able to live in Somalia, but Somalia has continued to live in me. Perhaps this is why so many immigrants keep saying, in one form or another, “I will be back.” We leave believing we are going for a short time. We leave with hope in our hearts and return tickets in our minds. But life has its own plans.
Still, somewhere inside the immigrant heart, the door never completely closes. We continue to look back. We continue to remember. We continue to carry. And even after decades away, a part of us is still standing at that door, telling our mothers: “Do not close it. I will be back.”

title: Trump says ‘massive’ oil, gas and mineral exploration in ‘beautiful’ Greenland is set to begin
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - U.S. President Donald Trump said that “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in “our new and beautiful Greenland,” though it wasn’t clear what developments he was referring to on an island where resource extraction has stymied companies for decades.
Despite Trump’s optimism, the harsh climate of Greenland — a self-governing territory of Denmark, rather than a part of the United States — as well as a lack of infrastructure have foiled all previous attempts to extract so-called rare earth minerals, as well as oil and gas. No efforts have ever progressed beyond the exploratory stage, and a moratorium on new gas and oil permits has been in place for several years.
“Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform following a campaign event Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska.
Trump was stumping for Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is seeking a third term to represent the state in an election against Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola.
Rising energy prices — a direct result of the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28 after the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes — are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for working class Americans before the midterm elections next month. Trump’s comments are likely aimed at addressing voters’ concerns before Election Day on Nov. 3.
Recent deal paved way for more US bases but no exploration rights
Last month, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, following months of tensions with NATO allies over the U.S. president’s repeated demands to take control of the semiautonomous Danish territory. It doesn’t grant the U.S. any special exploration rights, but does place some limits on investments by non-NATO countries in strategic sectors.
The deal also paved the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eased tensions over Trump’s repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States. The agreement would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.
Trump has expressed his desire to acquire Greenland since 2019 and, during his second term, issued threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a NATO ally.
Naaja H. Nathanielsen, who represents Greenland in Denmark’s parliament, told The Associated Press on Wednesday that she wasn’t very surprised — or concerned — following Trump’s post.
“This is just the way the president decides to engage,” she said. “I think we have all come to expect something like that.”
Nathanielsen said that any current projects regarding resource extraction were still years away from potential success. She said that she believes Americans worried about the price of gas were the post’s intended audience, rather than Greenlanders, before the upcoming election.
“I recognize the worry in the U.S., but I think it’s not a quick fix,” she told the AP. “There’s no Greenlandic barrels of oil on ground in any near future.”
Nathanielsen also said that she wasn’t upset by Trump calling the island “our Greenland.”
“I think, of course, it’s somewhat disrespectful,” she said. “But you can also see it as a term of endearment if you wanted to be very generous. Right now, I don’t think much of it.”
Representatives from Denmark’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as from Greenland’s prime minister and the island’s mining ministry, did not immediately return requests for comment Wednesday.
Greenland has valuable resources
Greenland has large deposits of the rare earth minerals that are needed to make everything from computers and smartphones to the batteries, solar and wind technologies that will power the transition away from fossil fuels. China currently dominates the world’s supply of these critical minerals and the Trump administration is seeking to break Beijing’s chokehold on them.
The U.S. Geological Survey has also identified major potential offshore deposits of oil and natural gas.
But tapping these resources could be prohibitively difficult: The rare earth minerals are encased in rock, and the offshore oil and natural gas deposits are covered by Arctic ice. And in 2021, Greenlandic lawmakers said the island would not issue any new oil and gas permits because of the environmental impacts of oil extraction, and a desire to avoid further worsening of the global climate crisis.
Trump boasts about Greenland’s strategic spot in the Arctic
Trump’s Truth Social post also touted Greenland’s strategic location, saying that “from a Security Purpose in the Defense and Offense of both the United States of America, and Europe,” the island is “second to none.”
“Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived,” he wrote. “It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!”
The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the U.S. military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO.
Trump said last month that the U.S. would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” including “building two very major military bases.”
