title: Vassalboro planners approve event center permit on split vote
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After another two hours’ discussion Oct. 6 of Ratesha and Keith Rosell’s planned events center on Webber Pond Road, Vassalboro Planning Board members approved a permit, on a split vote with three conditions (see the Sept. 17 issue of The Town Line, p. 2).
Since the board’s Sept. 1 meeting, a Maine Department of Transportation representative had checked the driveway entrance onto Webber Pond Road.
Codes Officer Eric Currie had used the decimeter the town bought to measure sound levels at different points around the property boundaries while music played in the former airplane hangar that will host events. He also checked wooded buffers for quality – one he described as “puckerbrush to pine trees” – and width.
Garrett Lower, of Pine State Code Solutions, accompanied Currie representing the Rosells. He commented that one buffer was too thick to walk through.
Neighbors’ main concern was noise late at night. They pointed out that although the sound level at property boundaries was within ordinance limits when Currie tested at 10 a.m., noise could carry farther at night.
Ratesha Rosell repeated assurances that events would end at 10 p.m. and noise would be controlled. While music plays, the hangar doors will be closed, she said. The walls are to be insulated, further muffling sound.
Lower added that those hosting and attending evening events would not want open doors letting bugs in.
The Rosells plan to host catered events. Some of the people using their space might hire caterers with liquor licenses, Ratesha Rosell said.
Her vision of a typical ending to an event had guests starting to leave early, so that some cars started before others and good-byes were spaced out. Neighbors’ version had a crowd of perhaps not entirely sober people shouting their good-byes as they all started their cars at once.
Planning Board member Paul Mitnik bought the latter version. The Rosells might be able to control music, but “you can’t control people,” he said.
The three conditions on the Rosells’ permit are:
— An MDOT requirement that there be no street parking on Webber Pond Road;
— Another MDOT requirement that a larger area be paved where the driveway and road meet; and
— A board requirement that during events, traffic warning signs be placed on Webber Pond Road at an appropriate distance from the driveway, both north and south.
The vote to approve the permit with conditions was 4-1, with Mitnik opposed.
After the dozen or more people who attended the meeting to raise their concerns left, planning board members reviewed and unanimously approved the other two applications on the Oct. 6 agenda.
Rodney Simmons, 530 Legion Park Road, has approval to make his non-commercial garage an inspection station. He explained that he is qualified to issue inspection stickers and has decided to make them a part-time job, evenings and two full days a week.
State officials told him he needed a local license to get his state approval, he said.
He intends to make minor repairs when needed, but no major work. His building is set back from the road and from neighbors – “I can’t see my neighbors and they can’t see me.”
Board members found his application was complete and his project met all ordinance requirements except the one they unanimously waived, requiring evidence of financial capacity. Approval was unanimous.
The second application was Adam St. Onge’s preliminary sketch plan for a major – eight-lot – subdivision on Stone Road, between that road and Route 3.
St. Onge explained that he proposes to phase in single-story duplexes, one per lot, on seven of the lots. The eighth, less developable, might be added to an adjoining lot or used as a common lot.
Each apartment will be two-bedroom, one-bath; his intended tenants are not large families. He plans to provide space for four cars per building. Access will be from Stone Road.
St. Onge intends to maintain the access road and the grounds himself; maintenance will be “all included in the rental.”
The woman in the young couple who live across Stone Road said they had come to the meeting because they “want to know what we’re gonna get used to looking at from our front door now, instead of a field full of fireflies.”
Planning Board Chairman Virginia Brackett summarized additional information St. Onge needs to include in the preliminary plan that is the next step toward board approval or rejection.
After unanimously approving St. Onge’s sketch plan, board members briefly discussed other issues, including apparent local violations of permits or ordinances, before adjourning.
Their next regular meeting is scheduled for 5:30 p.m., Tuesday, Nov. 3, in the Vassalboro town office meeting room.

It is also expensive!

title: Small changes in Varsity Maine football polls, but big games on top
text:
Thornton Academy received all of the first-place votes and Bonny Eagle every second-place votes to again garner the top two spots in the Varsity Maine 11-man football poll, which is largely the same as it was last week.
There’s a couple games in Week 7 that could shake up the rankings. First, No. 7 hosts No. 5 Portland on Saturday in what will likely determine the top seed in Class A North. Second is the Class C clash in Cumberland between Greely and 10th-ranked Hermon. It’s likely that Class C’s defining game came in Week 2 when Leavitt took down Greely 30-12. However, Hermon has two chances to make a play for the classification’s top seed. First is this week against the Rangers, and the second is next week when the Hawks host No. 6 Leavitt.
A team that might benefit indirectly from the results of any of those games is eight-ranked South Portland. The Red Riots have played Thornton and Bonny Eagle better than anyone else this fall, and last week they beat then-No. 8 Massabesic. title: ‘Steel Magnolias’ at Lewiston’s Public Theatre leans into ‘laughter through tears’
text:
“Steel Magnolias,” the 1987 play by Robert Harling, became a perennial favorite after the movie version hit the big screen a couple of years later. The play’s nearly perfect mix of comedy with some serious themes earned a reputation that continues to draw audiences to theater stages everywhere.
The Public Theatre in Lewiston will be opening its new season with a new production of the play running Oct. 23 to Nov. 8, and Dolly Parton’s recent passing will no doubt add a slightly melancholy touch to the show.
Parton’s character in the film, Truvy Jones, runs the hair salon where a multi-generational group of Southern women bond together through laughter and tears while also getting their hair done.
Heather Dilly, who will play Truvy, is known for her many roles at the Public Theatre over the years, as well as in movies and TV. She was cast in the Public Theatre production before Parton’s death and admits she cried when she heard the news of her passing. Dilly says she feels “lucky that I get to honor her in this way.”
Having family members from the South helped the actress, who’s originally from the Midwest and said she caught the acting bug at the age of 3, to appreciate the power of a good Southern accent.
“Southern accents make a joke land in a way that I will always love,” she said. Most importantly, though, she wants to put a lot of heart into her role — like Parton did.
Both Dilly and director Janet Mitchko cited Truvy’s line about “laughter through tears” as their favorite emotion and the key to fully appreciating the play.
While she didn’t initially plan to direct this production, Mitchko was ultimately drawn to the task after she cast many of her favorite actresses in her role as the Public Theatre’s artistic director. She couldn’t resist the opportunity to “spend time with them in the rehearsal room,” she enthused.
Dilly, in turn, reflected that she finds the director to be a “true partner” and “a trusted guiding light” for her actors.
The veteran of over 30 years of directing at the theater, Mitchko has long found “Steel Magnolias” “very, very funny and also very, very moving — sometimes both at the same time.” She notes that it’s interesting that a male writer could have had such insight into “the humor, heart and strength of women.”
The original 1980s period and “Southern sensibility” within the play will be maintained, though.
“The story itself is quite timeless,” Mitchko said.
Mitchko notes that “Dolly Parton’s passing might make people a little nostalgic to revisit the play.” But she said the story will live on in the hearts of people through the “wonderful foundation of love and friendship” she hopes to bring to life again onstage in Lewiston.
“Steel Magnolias,” Oct. 23-Nov. 8, The Public Theatre, 31 Maple St., Lewiston. Tickets $42, with discounts available. For more, thepublictheatre.org or 207-782-3200.

title: Woman escapes after man slashes her throat, police say
text:
FAIRMONT, W.Va. (WDTV/Gray News) - A man has been arrested on an attempted murder charge after police said he slashed a woman’s throat.
Benjamin Mayfield, 50, of Fairmont, has been charged with attempted murder, according to the Fairmont Police Department.
Police say the victim arrived at a home on 14th Street on Sunday, which she previously shared with Mayfield, to get her belongings, and while she was there, the pair got into an argument.
During the argument, Mayfield grabbed a bread knife from a box in the home, grabbed the victim in a chokehold and slashed her throat with the knife, court documents say.
The victim sustained a severe laceration to her throat but was able to escape, police say. She was transported to Ruby Memorial Hospital and had multiple lacerations on her left hand from trying to defend herself, court documents say.
Mayfield is currently in the North Central Regional Jail with bond set at $1 million.

title: Analyst weighs in on WABI’s Maine Senate debate
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) - A political expert is weighing in on the Senate debate at WABI, saying Sen. Susan Collins and Troy Jackson demonstrated different strengths as they made their cases to Maine voters.
Colby College government professor and political author Dr. Dan Shea said Jackson brought more energy to Tuesday night’s debate, including in the exchange over Medicare and Medicaid, while Collins shifted the focus to her seniority as a means to get things done.
Shea said the two candidates took different approaches on topics like heating costs, with Jackson drawing on his family’s experience and Collins drawing on her knowledge of federal policy.
“She’s very well-informed, and she wants to convince viewers that she has the experience. So, in that sense, she’s quite credible,” Shea said. “But, you know, Troy Jackson spoke from the heart. He spoke about when he was young and the difficulties his family confronted with fuel, with heating issues. I think good responses aren’t necessarily the most precise. I think they both did a good job.”
Candidates could learn from each other, analyst says
Ahead of their final debate Thursday night, Shea said each candidate can learn from the other’s performance.
Shea said Collins could improve by speaking more personally, rather than focusing so heavily on policy details, while Jackson could draw a clearer connection between Collins, President Trump and Republican leadership.

title: Couple finds out they won a huge lottery prize: It wasn't the first time
text:
A couple found out they won a huge scratch-off lottery prize. It wasn't the first time
Talk about a lucky break.
A Canadian couple won big on a lottery scratch-off in August, snagging the Atlantic Lottery's Set for Life top prize of $675,000. But it's not their first time winning big.
Angelina and Edward Lado, of St. John's, Newfoundland, also won $2.5 million from another lottery scratch-off in 2018.
"I thought maybe she was bluffing when she told me; I really couldn’t believe it," Edward Lado told the Atlantic Lottery. "I told her to calm down, and when I come home, we will see if it is for real."
The couple chose the lump-sum winnings of $675,000; the lottery's Set for Life scratch-off game also gives winners the option to receive $1,000 a week for 25 years.
Want more content like this? Subscribe to our News We Love newsletter here.
The couple told the lottery that they plan to use some of their winnings to help their college-aged children pay for school.
Edward Lado said he hasn't ruled out a third big win, either.
"We play, but modestly, especially now, but if you don’t play, you don’t win," he said.
The scratch-off ticket they purchased cost $4.
He also said they plan to take their time with the win and don't want to make any spur-of-the-moment decisions.
"We don’t want to rush into anything," he said. "Taking our time is the best option, and things will fall into place as life progresses."

title: 23rd annual Maine Chinese Conference to celebrate language, culture and international connections
text:
BANGOR — The 2026 Maine Chinese Conference “Thinking Globally … Acting Locally” will bring educators, students and community members together on Saturday, Oct. 17 from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. at the Dyke Center for Family Business at Husson University. The conference is free and welcomes educators, students and community members.
With the theme “Bridging East and West Through Language Education and Cultural Exchange”, the conference will highlight the value of learning the Chinese language and culture while exploring opportunities to strengthen educational, cultural and business relationships between the United States and China.
“There is so much we can learn from each other, and so much we can accomplish together!,” Jing Zhang, director of the Chinese Language & Culture Center of Maine, said. “I am passionate about helping people discover the value of learning another language and understanding another culture. This opens doors to new friendships, new opportunities, and stronger relationships that benefit us all. That is what makes this conference so exciting!”
The Mayor and Council Chair of the City of Bangor, Susan Hawes; Ms. Sun, Vice Consul General of the Chinese Consulate General in New York; and officials from the Maine Department of Education will speak at the conference’s opening ceremony. A panel of community leaders from across Maine will share ideas on how to strengthen friendship and cooperation between the United States and China by improving Chinese-language education. Professor Ying Zhang of the University of Maryland will lead an AP Chinese workshop for Maine Chinese-language educators. Students will present performances celebrating Chinese language and culture during the opening ceremony.
Conference topics include language education, cultural exchanges and educational and business cooperation between the United States and China. The event provides an opportunity for participants to connect with others who share an interest in language learning, cultural understanding and international cooperation.
The conference is presented by the Chinese Language & Culture Center of Maine and the Bangor Chinese School in collaboration with the Maine Department of Education, the University of Maine and the City of Bangor.
Admission is free. Educators, students and members of the public are encouraged to attend. Advance registration is available at https://forms.gle/P2HL5HS89AN631ty9.
For more information, visit www.bangorchinese.com or call 207-990-0710.

title: A handful of preservationists are keeping Maine’s cemeteries alive
text:
KENNEBUNKPORT — Judson Star chiseled a flaky gray substance from a piece of the broken headstone.
“It looks like someone tried to repair it with some type of goop,” he said. It crumbled in his fingers. A bathroom caulk, he guessed, not the preservation-grade epoxy that he brought in his white pick-up truck and mixed on a paper plate.
The fractured stone in Arundel Cemetery in Kennebunkport captured Star’s attention on a windy October morning. It was still upright when he started working a little after 10 a.m., but it wasn’t stable. The bottom right corner was fractured into three pieces, and wobbled under just a little pressure.
After he gently removed the layer of caulk, Star applied the epoxy with a popsicle stick. He slid the stones together like a puzzle, making sure the lines of the epitaph were flush. He clamped wood planks to the stone to hold it in place while it cured for 24 hours.
Star is a professional gravestone conservator who travels all over the state repairing headstones. He works in about 20 cemeteries a year, typically from May through November (the epoxies and mortars don’t cooperate once temperatures consistently drop below 45 degrees).
In about half of the towns he works in, there are dedicated volunteers who work alongside him tackling simpler tasks like cleaning or righting a leaning stone. They ask him questions, and he is always happy to lend a tool. He likes it when they tell him about the histories of the people buried there.
“There’s a lot of things that you could know about preservation, and there are hundreds of stones that need to be worked on in each town,” he said. He teaches the enthusiastic some of his skills, so they can be a little more self-sufficient with ongoing cemetery maintenance.
NEED FOR REPAIR
There are more than 7,800 cemeteries in the state, including historic and modern burial grounds, family cemeteries and single graves, according to Walter Guptill, president of the Maine Old Cemetery Association.
“People buried their family members up on the hillside,” he said. Over time, roads changed, and some were reclaimed by woods. About 1,200 still haven’t been physically located, and that’s after MOCA volunteers found 500 cemeteries over the last two years.
Many of them are small, with 30 burials or fewer. Sometimes, it’s just a grave or two, or a base in the middle of a field, Guptill said.
The number of professional conservators pales in comparison to the preservation needs. Star is just one of about a dozen in the state, Guptill said.
So it’s often up to municipal employees, cemetery and conservation committees, descendants, historical societies and community volunteers to find and maintain these cemeteries.
“The gap is not a lack of interest or good intentions,” Guptill said. “It’s the shortage of trained people, reliable guidance, funding and organized local stewardship needed to care for thousands of cemeteries across Maine.”
LEARN TO DO NO HARM
MOCA hosts workshops and training to pass on the art of conservation to the people who are trying to keep local cemeteries alive.
Lesson one is to do no harm, Guptill said. Lesson two is to only work within the limits of your training.
There’s an adage among cemetery aficionados, Guptill said. “More damage is done in cemeteries by people with good intentions than by vandals.”
Improper cleaning and repair techniques can cause permanent damage. Despite what one might think, bleach and other household cleaners shouldn’t be used on gravestones, Guptill said. Over time, the residue causes discoloration. And if you don’t use a soft bristle brush on marble, for example, you can take away parts of the surface, a phenomenon known as “sugaring.”
“People are out there trying to make it better, and we want to harness that energy with the right skillset, so that people are not only doing good but doing good in the right way,” he said. There’s a risk in overcleaning, if you can imagine, he said.
To grow the pool of experts in the state, MOCA hosts two types of workshops: a one-day gravestone cleaning class and an annual, four-day repair boot camp. The nonprofit provides the instructor and materials. Towns can volunteer their cemeteries as training grounds, so overdue repair work gets completed.
The group also has training videos and resources for people who have lingering questions.
There are three aspects of preservation work, according to Star: moving and lifting the stone, which he does with an aluminum tripod that can hoist up to a ton of weight; prepping the ground, often with gardening tools like shovels, tampers and loppers; and repairing the actual stone, which requires epoxies, mortar and lime.
Star has spent about $10,000 on equipment over the past six years. He keeps a lot of it in the trunk of his truck. (He owns more than 20 orange Home Depot buckets, and keeps the components, like a plastic container of special sand, ready to mix mortar at a moment’s notice.)
He charges a per diem rate. “To fix a stone costs hundreds of dollars,” he said. “Not thousands.”
Star recognizes that municipalities might not have more than a few thousand dollars for cemetery maintenance in any given year, with most of that budget eaten up by mowing and tree care costs.
But proper cleaning techniques can be taught in a day, Guptill said, and you can see the results instantly.
“Have the courage to start,” Guptill said.
START WITH ENTHUSIASM
Star began as an enthusiastic volunteer. Or rather, he started out as someone who didn’t really think twice about cemeteries.
But that changed when his wife’s parents died in short succession, and both of them were buried in Arundel Cemetery.
“Now that we had family there, there was a lot more connection,” he said. “You’re no longer just driving by.”
He started helping out with fall and spring cleanups, picking up sticks and debris. He realized that cemeteries can be happy places, and that good people take care of them. He joined the board about 10 years ago, and in 2019, started his business, Maintain the Memory, cleaning gravestones locally. His town of Kennebunkport has 75 cemeteries, which kept him busy in the beginning.
On this particular October morning, he worked a stone’s throw away from the first grave he ever repaired, in the same cemetery where he discovered his love of preservation.
About a year after starting his business, he wanted to expand his skillset. He participated in the MOCA four-day workshop. He joined the MOCA board, and slowly acquired specialty equipment, like an aluminum tripod and different kinds of mortars. His business grew by word of mouth.
“There’s something deeper than just fixing a stone,” he said. “There’s an emotional aspect. I hope somebody’s doing this for my stone in a couple hundred years if it needs it.”
BREATHING NEW LIFE
Sometimes the preservation work can be dramatic, breathing new life into what was once dilapidated or unrecognizable.
Wescott Cemetery in South Portland didn’t look like a burial ground for decades. A vandal had knocked over all the stones sometime before the 1980s, and the pieces were stored in a shed until this summer, when the historical society received a $5,000 donation from Peter and Muffet Wright to aid their restoration.
Kathy DiPhilippo, the historical society’s executive director, had been tending to this small family cemetery tucked in a residential neighborhood of Thornton Heights for years. This summer, she went to MOCA’s four-day training with her husband, and connected with Star through the group.
Together with the help of a small group of experienced volunteers, they put nearly 20 stones back together, including one that had been fractured into 13 pieces. Viewed in sunlight weeks later, it glowed like a stained glass window.
“It’s incredible,” DiPhilippo said.
Over the years, Star has worked with a lot of volunteers. He said restorations usually trace back to one or two people who care.
“It just takes someone saying we need to do something,” he said.

title: Jury returns mixed verdict after NFL star Tyreek Hill’s estranged wife accuses him of abuse
text:
MIAMI (AP) - A Miami jury on Tuesday found Tyreek Hill liable for two counts of battery but not liable for the eight remaining claims made by Lakeeta Vaccaro — ending the high-profile civil trial involving the NFL wide receiver and his estranged wife.
Hill, who has played for the NFL’s Kansas City Chiefs and Miami Dolphins, was found liable for two counts of battery — one stemming from an incident in January 2024, and another from April 2025. The jury awarded Vaccaro $500,000 in compensatory damages but did not award her punitive damages.
The jury found Hill, 32, not liable for eight other counts that included battery, assault and continuing domestic violence.
The trial involved allegations of abuse made by Vaccaro, 30, who on the stand described instances in which Hill allegedly pulled her hair and “treated me like I was, just, a man.” Hill took the stand last week and mostly denied what he called “false allegations” made by his estranged wife, while saying in one instance he shoved Vaccaro and “created a hole in the wall.”
Hill, wearing a dark polo shirt on Tuesday, embraced one of his attorneys and shook hands with others following the verdict before leaving the courtroom by himself.
It wasn’t immediately clear what the verdict means for Hill’s return to the NFL. He is still working his way back from a dislocated knee and torn ligaments suffered in September 2025 while he was with the Dolphins, but his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, has indicated that he could be ready to play by November.

title: Isolation is one of the hardest battles for caregivers. It doesn’t have to be.
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
When Cathyann Adams called the Aroostook Area Agency on Aging last winter, she was fast approaching her breaking point.
Her husband, Chris, was in the advanced stages of Lewy body dementia and declining fast. As his full-time caretaker, Adams felt herself slipping, too. She was desperate for a break.
The couple had moved from Vermont to Caribou a few years prior — a homecoming for Chris, who grew up in Fort Fairfield, and a new adventure for Adams.
But Chris’s diagnosis, which came shortly after their move, and his ensuing decline soon became the center of their lives, leaving little room for making friends and building a support system.
“I was alone,” said Adams, 67. “I didn’t know how I was going to go forward.”
As Maine’s population ages, taking care of its older residents is becoming an increasingly urgent issue. From the stress of rural isolation to a shortage of workers to complicated federal Medicare guidelines, this guide helps Mainers learn about the services, technology and resources available to caregivers and the parents, spouses, neighbors and friends they’re caring for.
In a rural state like Maine, the emotional and physical toll of caregiving — known as caregiver fatigue — is compounded by an isolation that aging experts say is all too common, placing both the caregivers and the people they’re caring for at greater risk of depression, illness and death.
Maine has the nation’s highest median age (44.9 years) and the highest proportion of residents ages 65 and older (24.6%), according to the U.S. Census Bureau.
Maine also is the second most rural state — 61.5% of residents live outside designated urban areas — a fact that, coupled with harsh winter weather and a lack of public transportation, makes it harder to access services and foster connection.
But aging experts also say there are ways to minimize isolation and caregiver fatigue.
Making a plan early, leaning on your community, and taking advantage of services like respite care, companionship programs, support groups and classes can all help alleviate the pressure.
RESPITE DAY PROGRAMS
Ruth White has heard many pleas for help like Adams’.
“You have such an array of emotions,” she said, ranging from happiness and pride to frustration, resentment and anger. The emotional whiplash and constant stress are exhausting.
“You don’t want to be in your head. You have to be loving and caring (but) you’re just dying,” said White, family caregiver program coordinator for the Aroostook Agency on Aging. “That’s usually the point when we start to get the people to come in.”
She often suggests they take advantage of the agency’s adult day respite center, where caregivers can leave their loved one for a few hours and step away from the demands of the job. There are similar centers across the state.
Older adult service providers say respite care is one of the most impactful resources for caregivers struggling with burnout.
“It’s so important for them to have that ability to walk away from that caregiving for a little while and get back out into the world and sort of regain a little bit of the life that they put so much thought and effort into,” said Ashley Butterfield, executive director of Bath-Brunswick Respite Care.
The Bath-based center is the only respite day program in the region, Butterfield said. They served about 40 families last year.
“I think every caregiver, no matter what stage they’re in, understands everything that they’re giving up. They understand that they do need to socialize more, they understand that they need to maintain connections, but it’s really hard,” Butterfield said. “And I think that’s really where so much of the social isolation stems from. It’s just easier to not go out into the world.”
DON’T WAIT
Jess Maurer’s No. 1 piece of advice for new caregivers is “make a plan early.”
Do not wait. Figure out now who you can lean on, and how you can get a break. The longer you wait, the harder it will be to see a way out, said Maurer, executive director of the Maine Council on Aging.
Start talking to your friends about what you might need.
Who can make a meal once a week that you can divvy up for your person throughout the week? Who can come sit with them or take them to a doctor’s appointment?
Or, if you’re dealing with more challenging behaviors, who can do your grocery shopping or take your car in for an oil change?
Ask for help with “the basic things of life that get lost,” Maurer said.
“It feels really awkward, because it feels very much like ‘This is my responsibility. I have to take care of my parent. I have to take care of myself. I shouldn’t be asking other people,'” she said. “We really have to get past that in a big way because there are so many people who are really struggling.”
Butterfield, at Bath-Brunswick Respite Care, said caregivers often put off seeking help out of a misplaced sense of guilt: It’s too early to need more solo time; it’s not that bad yet; it’s going to be much worse.
“It doesn’t need to be bad in order for a caregiver to need to maintain their own sense of self,” she said. “No caregiver should need to wait until they’re burnt out.”
A LIFESAVER
The Southern Maine Agency on Aging’s adult day program in Springvale has been a “lifesaver” for Terry Turner.
Her husband, Jack Turner, 75, was diagnosed with dementia three years ago and has been attending the day program three days a week for the last two.
He has been thriving.
“With the dementia scale, I have not seen him go down much,” said Terry Turner, 71. “He thinks he works there. That’s the only thing that gets him going is ‘OK, I gotta go to my job.’ He’s so funny. ‘I’m still waiting on a paycheck,’ he says.”
Turner, meanwhile packs as much as she can into that time.
“I don’t just sit and do nothing,” she said. “I literally use up that time for something that I would really enjoy,” like cardmaking and Bible study with her ladies group.
“I have to socialize myself with my girlfriends, in order to enjoy life, you know?” she said.
The Turners also recently converted their Springvale home into a duplex, where their daughter, 40, lives and can help out.
On days when Jack isn’t at the center, they spend time outside. Jack mows the lawn, Turner tends to her garden, a newer hobby. They dote on their three dogs, who Turner said give Jack purpose. He feeds them carrots.
If she needs to pop to the store, her neighbors or daughter might keep an eye on Jack. For now, things are manageable. She’s happy.
Turner is used to caregiving. She took care of her father, who also had dementia, years before.
“I’m OK with it, because maybe that’s what God wants me to do,” she said. “There are some tough days, and if there are, I might have a cry or whatever, and that’s OK, too.”
RESPITE POP-UPS AND COMPANIONSHIP
Six of Maine’s 16 counties don’t offer day programs. And even in counties where there are programs, some communities are simply too far away to make the trip worthwhile.
The Southern Maine Agency on Aging is trying to fill some of the gaps with a new 12-week pilot “pop-up” respite care program.
Thanks to a nearly $100,000 grant from the Alzheimer’s Association, the agency launched “Dementia Respite Without Walls” last month at the Casco Community Center.
Casco is central to areas like Bridgton, Raymond, Windham and Harrison — communities whose residents are less likely to visit the agency’s centers in Springvale, Biddeford or Portland.
Other families may feel that a day program is not the right fit.
In 2022, the state launched a two-year pilot program called Respite for ME, funded with about $5.1 million in American Rescue Plan funds.
The program, overseen by the Department of Health and Human Services and administered by the local agencies on aging, offered grants up to $2,000 in the first year and just over $5,000 in the second to people providing care to an older adult at home.
The money paid for temporary caregivers to come for a few hours of respite, including in-home care, center visits and overnight stays in a facility. The money could also be used for counseling, training, financial guidance and assistive technology.
The results were promising. While caregiver burden and stress remained at medium or high levels for most caregivers, for people participating in the second year, high stress decreased by 10% and high depression decreased by 14%, according to the pilot’s evaluation. Caregivers reported better relationships with their loved ones and less financial strain and worry.
The state Legislature made the program permanent in July 2025 (with a $2,000 limit on grants) but only allocated $100,000, leaving it effectively unfunded.
Maurer, at the Council on Aging, said advocates will be pushing for full funding for the program next year and encouraging the new governor to make it a budget priority.
A break from isolation doesn’t have to come from dedicated respite care, either.
The University of Maine’s Senior Companion Program, a partnership between the university’s Center on Aging and AmeriCorp, matches homebound, isolated older adults with volunteers ages 55 and older.
There’s also a southern Maine chapter through AmeriCorp and the Opportunity Alliance.
Jennifer Jain, director of the university program, said that while the volunteer program is centered on companionship for older adults, the benefits extend to caregivers by giving them a break.
The pairings are intended to be long-term relationships, not just one-and-done visits, Jain said, and by matching older adults with peers around their own age, they are able to relate to each other on a deeper level.
“I don’t want to say it’s a best kept secret, but it’s something that people do not see us as a program to tap into … but respite is up and rising as more of a need in our state,” she said.
‘A DIVINE APPOINTMENT’
Adams, in Caribou, credits the Aroostook agency with helping her get through the last months of her husband’s disease, which she said was like “being on a very violent rollercoaster.”
She tapped into whatever resources were available.
While he was still well enough to go, she brought Chris to the day program.
For a few hours each week, she had time to do whatever she wanted, not just what needed to be done around the house. She’d get her hair done, go for a long walk, sit and cry when she needed to.
She took their Savvy Caregiver class to learn more about what to expect as Chris’ illness progressed. She took a yoga class and found an online caregiver support group.
White also found her a volunteer with shared interests in music and fellowship who could visit with Chris while Adams worked around the house or ran to the grocery store.
For a few months, she could breathe again. And it allowed her enough room to still find “something joyful to share (with Chris) every day.”
Chris Adams, 71, died on July 23.
“I don’t believe that things happen by accident, so I would say it was a divine appointment when I called that number, and Ruth (White) answered the phone,” Adams said. “In a rural area … you need a community. That’s what the Agency on Aging gave me.”

title: These common infections are linked to 12% of new cancer cases, study says
text:
These common infections are linked to 12% of new cancer cases, study says
Millions of new cancer cases around the world may be caused by infections that are either treatable or preventable, suggesting that the cancer could have been avoided altogether.
That's according to new research published in the journal The Lancet Oncology, which found that roughly 1 in 8 cancer cases around the world may be linked to infections – many of which can be prevented through vaccines, screening or relatively straightforward treatments.
Related video above | Trial offers metastatic breast cancer treatment
"We can intervene before it gets anywhere near cancer," said Gary Clifford, the study's senior author and an epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer.
"We just need the politics and the finances and the buy-in from the public and the communication to get the programs implemented. Prevention works," Clifford said. "It's an awareness-raising issue."
About 2.3 million new cancer cases were attributable to infections globally in 2024, which is equivalent to 12% of all cancer diagnoses, the new study found. And two infections stood out in particular: Helicobacter pylori, commonly known as H. pylori, which was mostly associated with gastric cancers and human papillomavirus, or HPV, which was predominantly associated with cervical cancer. Together, researchers estimate that these two infections accounted for more than 1.5 million cancer cases in 2024.
Other infections contributed substantially as well:
- Hepatitis B or HBV was linked to an estimated 360,000 cancer cases, which were mostly liver cancers.
- The Epstein-Barr virus, or EBV, was associated with about 260,000 cancer cases, of which a head and neck cancer starting in the nasopharynx was the main driver.
- Hepatitis C or HCV was tied to 160,000 cancer cases, mostly liver cancers.
"Some infection-related cancers, such as liver and gastric cancer, generally have poor prognosis, meaning that a similar proportion of deaths from these cancers are likely attributable to infection. For other cancers, including cervical cancer and Kaposi sarcoma, infection is necessary for cancer development," Harriet Rumgay, epidemiologist at the International Agency for Research on Cancer and an author of the study, said in an email.
"However, highly effective prevention measures already exist for four of the five leading infectious causes of cancer, as well as for HIV," Rumgay said, referring to the human immunodeficiency virus. The four infections include HPV and hepatitis B, for which vaccines are available, as well as H. pylori and hepatitis C, for which testing and treatments are available.
Clifford, Rumgay and their colleagues analyzed data from the Global Cancer Observatory's Cancer Today database to estimate the incidence of cancer around the world in 2024. They examined how many of those cancer cases could be attributable to infections and then analyzed each infection-cancer pair in their data set.
The new analysis builds on earlier work published in 2018, but the researchers now have a better understanding of the relationships between certain infections and cancer. The new study incorporated 16 additional infection-cancer pairs compared with the previous 2018 global analysis, including some cancers paired with EBV.
"EBV is one of these agents for which we knew it was related to some cancers. In fact, EBV was the first ever cancer-causing agent of infection to be discovered in Burkitt lymphoma," Clifford said.
"That was like 60 years ago almost, and that was the first realization that a virus could cause cancer. And since then, we've identified it in other cancers, particularly nasopharyngeal carcinomas," he said. "We were already clear about the link with EBV, even back in that 2018 data. So, it was there, but it wasn't really fully addressed because we didn't understand the full extent of the cancer burden that it was causing."
Where the infection-related cancer burden is greatest
The new research also reveals that the burden of infection-related cancers isn't evenly distributed around the world. Low-income and middle-income countries accounted for 77% of all infection-attributable cancer cases, reflecting differences in the prevalence of cancer-causing infections as well as access to vaccines, screening, testing and treatment.
But if health officials know which infections are contributing to cancer, and where those infections are most common, they can focus resources on the strategies that have the potential to save lives.
"Even within the United States, the burden of infection-related cancer is not evenly distributed, and some populations have higher rates of infections such as hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HPV or H. pylori, while others have less access to vaccination, screening or treatment. And these differences can translate into disparities in cancer incidence many years later," said Veronika Fedirko, professor of epidemiology at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, who was not involved in the new study.
"Infection-related cancers are certainly an important issue in the United States," she said, referring to a separate analysis from the American Cancer Society that found in 2019, 3.4% of all cancers among adults 30 and older – which was about 60,310 cases – were attributable to seven infections evaluated: EBV, H. pylori, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, HIV and, the largest contributor, HPV.
"Having a cancer-causing infection does not mean that a person will develop cancer. These infections increase the risk of certain cancers, but most people who are infected will never develop cancer," Fedirko said. "Cancer usually develops only in a small proportion of people, often when an infection persists for many years and together with other factors such as age, immune function, smoking, genetics or other exposures."
How to 'take away' the risk
Cancer is an enormously complicated group of diseases with many different causes and risk factors, including genetics, environmental exposures, aging and lifestyle factors. But the new findings show that infections represent an area where prevention can make a meaningful difference.
Prevention efforts can include vaccination and, when appropriate, testing for and treating infections that increase cancer risk. For some cancers, screening can also identify precancerous changes so they can be treated before invasive cancer develops.
Getting tested and following up with a doctor "almost takes away any cancer risk," Clifford said.
Once infections get diagnosed, "we know how to manage them," he said. "The large majority of these infections will not cause cancer. Some of them will, and we're learning more about which ones, but that's a work in progress. The point is: It doesn't mean that you've got a cancer just because you have the infection."
For instance, people can be screened for hepatitis C and treated if they are infected, thus helping to prevent cancer from developing down the road.
The same is true for H. pylori. The bacterium is relatively common, and many people who carry it may not immediately realize they have an infection. But H. pylori can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and become a major risk factor for stomach cancer. Treating the infection with antibiotics can reduce that risk, giving doctors another opportunity to intervene before cancer may develop.
Additionally, HPV and hepatitis B are examples of how vaccination can help prevent cancer. Hepatitis B infection can damage the liver over time and increase the risk of liver cancer, but there is a vaccine available that can help prevent the viral infection.
HPV is a group of more than 200 related viruses, which can spread through sexual contact. In some cases, HPV infection can lead to six types of cancer: cervical, anal, penile, vaginal, vulvar and oropharyngeal (mouth and throat). But the vaccine can protect against those cancers since it works by preventing HPV infection.
The new research "teaches us the importance of vaccination and how that can prevent different types of cancer," Dr. Nancy Lee, a radiation oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center who was not involved in the new study, said in an email.
"This is no different than getting your flu shot to prevent the flu. The public needs to be made aware and vaccination should be reinforced," Lee said. "Many different types of cancers are caused by infection and if we prevent the infection, the incidence of cancer should be lower."
Other prevention measures that reduce transmission of various cancer-attributable infections include "safe injection practices, condom use, and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis," Rumgay said. "If implemented widely and equitably, these strategies could prevent hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of future cancer cases worldwide."

title: Obituary: Walter Sparks
text:
NORWAY – Walter Sparks, 83, of Norway, passed away peacefully on Tuesday morning, Oct. 6, 2026, in the comfort of his home, with his longtime companion, Patty Perry, by his side.
Walter was born on Oct. 31, 1942, in Huntington, West Virginia, the son of Walter R. and Elizabeth Mae (Pendleton) Sparks. He attended local schools and, following Norway High School, proudly served his country in the United States Marine Corps.
After his military service, Walter settled in Columbus, Ohio, where his family had relocated. Walter and Barbara Shepard were married and raised three sons and a daughter together. While his children were in school he was very involved with their sports and other activities.
Walter enjoyed a successful career as a master electrician, most notably with Jess Howard Electric, specializing in commercial and industrial electrical work.
Following retirement, Walter remained active and involved in his community. He volunteered at the Senior Center in Reynoldsburg, Ohio, and became an avid bicyclist, joining a local cycling group and enjoying numerous group rides throughout the state.
In 2014, Walter returned to Norway, Maine, where he reunited with a former schoolmate and dear friend, Patty Perry. Their friendship blossomed into a loving companionship, and together they shared many wonderful years filled with adventure, laughter, and cherished memories.
Walter continued his love of bicycling, joining a local cycling group and proudly participated in BIKE ME in 2015, fulfilling an item on his bucket list. He also discovered a passion for slot car racing, joining a men’s group where he enjoyed building and racing his cars both in Maine and Florida.
Walter and Patty loved exploring Maine together, often taking trips to discover places they had never visited. For nearly ten years, they spent their winters at their home in St. Petersburg, Florida, where they enjoyed dancing, dining out, socializing and making lasting friendships. Eventually, health challenges brought their winter adventures to an end.
Their Maine summers were spent at Patty’s cottage at Empire Grove Campground, a place that became very special to Walter. He became an active member of the community and served on its Board of Directors.
Family was also an important part of Walter’s life with Patty. He especially enjoyed attending sporting events for Patty’s great-grandchildren, who adored him and lovingly claimed him as their own great-grandfather. He embraced that role with pride and affection.
Whenever his family came to visit, Walter delighted in showing them around Maine, sharing stories of his childhood, and taking them to the places where he had grown up and attended school. When he could no longer travel, he enjoyed receiving family pictures of his great-grandchildren on Facebook and staying up to date through phone calls from his children and grandchildren.
Walter will be remembered for his adventurous spirit, his many interests, his love of family, and the special memories he created with those fortunate enough to know him.
Walter was predeceased by his parents, Elizabeth (Sparks) Wood and Walter R. Sparks; his brothers, Robert and Russell Sparks; and his sister, Lora Margolis.
He is survived by his sons, Rodney, Steven, and David; his daughter, Tina; and her companion, Steve; 15 grandchildren and 11 great-grandchildren all of Ohio; his longtime companion, Patricia “Patty” Perry of Norway and her family. He will also be remembered by his beloved parrot, Jack.
A service will be held at a later date, at the convenience of the family. The time and date will be announced.
Arrangements are in the care of Cliff Gray Cremation, where condolences and tributes may be shared at http://www.CliffGrayCremations.com

title: Lawsuit alleges Hannaford improperly markets some salmon products as sustainable
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A class-action lawsuit filed this week alleges that Hannaford and its parent company display “misleading sustainability guarantees” in the grocery chain’s seafood sections.
The complaint, filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York, narrows in on salmon products that it claims are not sustainably sourced, as in-store signage suggests.
A Hannaford spokesperson said Wednesday that the company does not comment on pending litigation and that neither the Scarborough-based grocer nor its Dutch parent company, Ahold Delhaize, had received the complaint.
The suit states that Hannaford stores all contain signs that indicate their seafood products are sustainably sourced, including ones reading, “We sell only high-quality, traceable and sustainably harvested seafood,” and “Every fish has a tale. Ours you can trust.”
“In reality, Hannaford sells industrially farmed salmon whose production inflicts grave harms on pristine marine ecosystems and has caused the destruction of marine life around the world, from Canada to Chile,” the lawsuit says.
The 76-page complaint includes numerous pictures of signage at Hannaford locations and products in question.
The lead plaintiff in the suit is Kathleen Boyle, of Queensbury, New York. It states she purchased at least some of the products cited at Hannaford stores in New York throughout 2025 and 2026, believing they were “sourced from suppliers whose practices did not harm marine ecosystems” and were otherwise sustainable.
The lawsuit includes as class members anyone who bought any of the products in question in New York within the statute of limitations. The complaint says that the plaintiff believes there are thousands of people who fit this description.
The suit focuses on salmon products predominantly sourced overseas, though some stem from Maine and elsewhere in the United States. It argues those products are not truly sustainable, citing reports of mass mortality events, and details many regions’ salmon farming practices — especially in Chile, where it says some suppliers have histories of overproduction and farming in sensitive or protected areas.
The lawsuit notes that if Hannaford’s products are truly traceable, then it would be aware of some of these “destructive” practices. If not, “their sustainability promises were nevertheless empty and false” when it comes to those products, the complaint says.
The plaintiff is seeking a jury trial and monetary relief.

title: More than 2,000 pigs killed in barn fire
text:
SIBLEY, Iowa (KTIV/Gray News) - Hundreds of pigs were killed in a barn fire in Iowa.
According to the Sibley Fire Department, a hog barn caught fire late Monday night into early Tuesday morning. The building was destroyed before firefighters got to the scene.
“It’s always a scary first few moments but we got the fire knocked down,” the fire department said in a post on Facebook.
About 2,400 pigs were killed. No one was injured.
The Sibley Fire Department said its crews worked to protect two nearby gas cylinders and to keep embers from spreading to a cornfield.
Osceola County Emergency Management said multiple fire departments worked to contain the fire. The Sibley Fire Department said the Ashton Fire Department, Little Rock Fire Department and George Fire Department were among those that assisted.

title: Missing Hampden man presumed dead by family and police
text:
For 55 years Doug Dunphy always brought his wife, Sally, flowers on their wedding anniversary.
In 2009, he started trudging through snow every February to instead bring the flowers to Sally’s grave and sit with her after her death.
This was the first year he wasn’t by her side.
Dunphy, 78, was last seen in early January. His family presumes he is dead, but are left waiting for his remains to be found, his daughter Dawn Dunphy told the Bangor Daily News.
The family’s belief that Dunphy is dead is shared by the Office of the Maine Attorney General and Maine State Police, according to a 45-page document that was leaked by the attorney general’s office on Oct. 8. Dunphy is one of the highest-profile missing person cases in the Bangor area.
Maine State Police took over the investigation in early February and have shared few details about Dunphy’s disappearance, besides asking hunters to “remain vigilant” this fall. The Maine State Police is one of the three agencies in the state allowed to investigate homicides.
Doug and Sally Dunphy have a shared vault so they can be laid to rest side-by-side, together forever, but that can’t happen until he is found, his daughter said.
“He needs to be next to Mom,” Dawn Dunphy said. “I want so badly to find him, to put him next to her.”
Dawn Dunphy said she’s hopeful a hunter will find her dad this fall so the family can hold a memorial.
“Every single day we’re all on edge because we don’t know, are we going to get the call they found him?” Dawn Dunphy said. “We don’t know if we’re going to get the call that somebody gets arrested.”
The leaked document details evidence in ongoing cases, including manslaughter or homicide cases in which suspects, named in the document, have not yet been criminally charged. Dunphy’s case is the first listed.
After the document was mistakenly shared, the attorney general’s office said it notified families of victims that information about the cases may be published.
Doug Dunphy’s family learned of the leaked document from the BDN on Tuesday, Dawn Dunphy said. She said she did not hear from the attorney general’s office, nor did anyone in a 16-person Dunphy family group chat.
The family is “up in arms,” about the lack of communication, she said.
The investigating agency typically works with the family in a missing person case, the attorney general office’s spokesperson Danna Hayes said when asked about the lack of family notification. The office hasn’t developed a relationship with the Dunphy family at the request of state police, she said.
Hayes declined to comment on the investigation because it is pending.
State police spokesperson Shannon Moss had no additional information to share about the investigation, and said media inquiries should be directed to the attorney general’s office.
The state police have a good team investigating Dunphy’s disappearance and presumed death, Dawn Dunphy said. Police talk with the family every few weeks but a backlog within the crime lab means the case can’t move forward, Dawn Dunphy said.
Dunphy’s white Ford Econoline van was recovered a couple weeks after he went missing, state police said previously. There have been a couple searches at a property on Kennebec Road, police said. Hampden tax records show Dunphy lives on that road.
Searches of that property and surrounding areas in February and May failed to locate Duphy, police have said.
Dunphy retired from the BDN in 2015 after 35 years as mechanical superintendent. He is 5-foot-10 and weighs 210 pounds and has gray hair and green eyes. Police don’t know what clothing he was wearing when he went missing, they previously said.
For now, Dawn Dunphy’s hopes remain with hunters this year. They’ve found missing people before because they go deep into the woods where others don’t.
“I feel bad for the hunters, asking that, because that’s traumatizing too for them,” she said. “My hope is that they’ll go someplace that nobody thought to go, and they’ll find him.”

title: Brighter & Breezy Day On The Way Thursday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Low pressure will continue to slide off to our east tonight. Expect a few breaks in the clouds with lows that will range from the mid 30s to the mid 40s. A slight breeze remains as northwest gusts to 25 mph will be possible.
Thursday: Brighter, Breezy
High pressure brings back sunshine for most. Highs upper 40s to mid 50s a few degrees cooler for many, with the exception of the mountains and northern areas. Northwest gusts 20-30 mph, weakening later in the day and into the evening.
Friday: Rain Returns By Midday
Dry start with increasing clouds, then low pressure moves in from the west bringing rain by midday Friday. Far northern tip of Maine could start as snow showers before changing to all rain. Rain ends later Friday night. Highs 40s and low 50s. Rainfall totals for most will average from 0.25″ to 0.75″ with some pockets in the north up to an inch.
As the low departs, the pressure gradient tightens. Increasing winds pull colder air in behind the low.
Saturday: Cold and Windy
Lots of sunshine but cold and windy. Highs in the 40s, but it will FEEL at or below freezing with northwest gusts to 40 mph. Mountains and north could see wrap-around light snow with little if any accumulation.
Lows Saturday night will be down into the 20s, one of our coldest nights so far this season. The breeze will make it FEEL even colder into Sunday morning.
Sunday: Mostly Sunny, Still Breezy
Mostly sunny skies with highs in the 40s and low 50s. Northwest gusts to 25 mph. Warmer and less breezy heading into early next week.
First Alert 7-Day Forecast
TONIGHT: Partly to mostly cloudy skies. Lows will range from the mid 30s to the mid 40s. NW gusts to 25 mph.
THURSDAY: Mostly sunny. Highs in the 40s and 50s. NW gusts to 30 mph.
FRIDAY: Increasing clouds with showers spreading across the region. Highs in the 40s and 50s. SE gusts to 25 mph.
SATURDAY: Mostly sunny skies with snow showers in the mountains. Highs in the 40s and will FEEL colder. NW gusts to 40 mph.
SUNDAY: Cold morning and feels colder due to a breeze. Mostly sunny skies with highs in the 40s and low to mid 50s. NW gusts to 25 mph.
MONDAY: Mostly sunny with highs in the 50s and low 60s.

title: Vatican releases update on Pope Leo XIV following his surgery, lung cancer diagnosis
text:
ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV resumed his regular diet, began walking and celebrated Mass in the hospital Wednesday as he recovered from surgery to remove a cancerous mass from his lung, the Vatican said. Questions remained about whether the cancer had spread, while Peru’s president suggested Leo might have to alter his planned visit to Latin America next month.
Blood tests and a chest X-ray showed the 71-year-old pope was recovering normally, his two doctors said.
“The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room. He resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the pope’s personal doctor, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the head thoracic surgeon at Gemelli hospital. “Recovery is proceeding as planned.”
Tuesday’s surgery confirmed that Leo has lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung.
The right lung has three lobes and the left has two. After one lobe is removed, the remaining lung tissue can gradually compensate, especially in otherwise healthy, physically active people. Leo is known for his interest in sports, including weekly tennis games and swimming.
The Vatican said late Wednesday that the pope had celebrated Mass with his secretaries in the afternoon in a special chapel set up for him on the 10th floor of the hospital.
No word yet on whether the pope’s cancer had spread
Experts said some of Leo’s lymph nodes would also have been removed and tested to determine whether the cancer had spread. Those results have not so far been made public.
If the cancer has spread, test results will guide treatment, said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted therapy, which uses pills to treat cancers with specific characteristics.
Liu, who is not involved in the pope’s care, said that, of the different types of lung cancers, adenocarcinoma has the most favorable prognosis.
“While we know the diagnosis, we now need to know the stage,” Liu said. “We now need to know how big it is, how many spots in the lung are involved. Is it just one nodule, or more than one, and the lymph nodes, are they cancerous?”
Dr. PierCarlo Gentile, head of radiation oncology at Rome’s San Pietro Fatebenefratelli Hospital, said the minimally invasive, video-assisted chest surgery the pope underwent typically requires 15 to 20 days of recovery. Postoperative complications, including infections, are rare, he said.
Doubts over Latin America trip
The Vatican hasn’t announced any changes to Leo’s planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6-17.
But Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori said Wednesday that the pope’s diagnosis and recovery could affect the visit, even as she expressed hope it would go ahead. Leo spent two decades as a missionary in Peru, holds Peruvian citizenship and is beloved by his flock there.
“We understand that this recovery will take several weeks, longer than expected,” Fujimori told reporters. “We also understand that there could be some changes to the schedule of his visit.”
The ambitious itinerary for the longest trip of his papacy covers just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles), with a dozen flights and two helicopter rides across the three countries, as well as a significant change in altitude in Peru.
Fujimori said millions of Peruvians were praying for the pontiff’s recovery and awaiting further announcements from the Vatican.
“We hope his recovery will be swift and that his visit can go ahead, but we will also understand if that is not possible,” she said. “What matters most is that His Holiness regains his health.”
Oncology surgeons often advise patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery.
“If it is Stage 1, he can complete these trips. If more treatment is needed, I would likely advise against the trips,” said Liu.
Doctors took tissue samples before surgery
The pontiff has offered a rare degree of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy.
He revealed the discovery of a nodule, or growth, on his lung during his Sunday noon prayer, announcing it on live television. But Leo did not disclose everything he knew Sunday.
Tuesday’s medical bulletin said preoperative tests had led doctors to suspect cancer, which surgery confirmed. Leo did not use the word cancer in his announcement, though he described the nodule as being at an “early stage” and “circumscribed.”
The Vatican has now said that those tests included a robotic bronchoscopic biopsy, known as an ION broncoscopy, meaning doctors had already taken tissue samples to assess whether the mass was cancerous.
The procedure requires general anesthesia and must be performed in a hospital equipped with one of the advanced machines, said Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, chief thoracic surgeon at the European Institute of Oncology in Milan. He said Gemelli hospital had had one for about a year.
The Vatican did not say when Leo underwent the diagnostic tests, which also included a chest CT scan with contrast and a PET scan.
A PET scan can be used to make sure that the disease has not traveled to other places in the body, said Dr. Brendon Stiles, chief of surgical oncology at Montefiore Einstein in New York. Between the scan and the biopsy, Stiles said, “we can be hopefully reassured that this should be a stage-one cancer.”
Pope breaks with a tradition of secrecy surrounding health issues
The Vatican has long been secretive about the health of popes and tightly controlled any such information — a practice encapsulated in the popular Italian saying, “ The pope is fine until he’s dead.”
St. John XXIII died in 1963, nearly a year after doctors diagnosed stomach cancer that was kept hidden at the time. St. John Paul II died in 2005 after suffering for years from the obvious effects of Parkinson’s disease that the Vatican only confirmed after he died.
Pope Francis seemed more up front about his health problems, giving an Argentine doctor a tell-all interview for a book about his physical and mental health. But in the end Francis, too, tightly controlled the information that was released in his dying months.
As a result, Leo’s decision to announce himself that he had a nodule and was undergoing surgery was significant.
“That was truly a revolution. It was like he was reading a medical bulletin himself,” said Giovanni Maria Vian, a church historian and the former editor-in-chief of the Vatican newspaper L’Osservatore Romano.
Vian, who was part of the Vatican communications team from 2007 to 2018, said the Vatican’s obsession with secrecy was due to both practical and cultural considerations. He noted the Vatican is a 2,000-year-old institution that is culturally European — and Europeans tend to be more guarded about health problems than people in the United States.
___
Barry reported from Milan. Associated Press video producer Paolo Santalucia in Rome and Associated Press writer Lauran Neergaard in Washington contributed to this report.

title: CPKC Holiday Train to return to Maine
text:
HERMON, Maine (WABI) - The CPKC Holiday Train is returning to Maine as part of its mission to support food banks.
Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CPKC) says the Holiday Train program kicks off November 19th in Montreal, beginning a 32-day journey with stops in 182 communities, including three in Maine.
The train will be in Jackman on Walton Street Saturday, November 21st at 7:45 p.m.
Sunday, November 22nd, the train will be at the Coldbrook Road crossing in Hermon at 4:15 p.m.
It will make its final Maine stop in Greenville at the Greenville Junction Depot that night at 9 p.m.
The American Authors and Rafaëlle Roy will provide live performances.
“The CPKC Holiday Train is one of the most special events of the holiday season! Not only are the lights and music spectacular, but it brings people together to give back to their communities and support friends, family, neighbours and those in need,” said Zac Barnett of American Authors. “We feel so fortunate to take part in the celebration that makes such a meaningful impact.”
People are encouraged to bring a cash donation or non-perishable food item to donate to a local food bank.
“Our railroaders take great pride in bringing the Holiday Train through hundreds of communities across our network to support people facing food insecurity,” said CPKC President and CEO Keith Creel. “This year, we are going farther south than we ever have before, visiting 10 communities in Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Missouri for the first time.”
“Through the generosity of the thousands of families and fans who come out to see the Holiday Train and support local food banks, whether for the first time or as part of a long-running holiday tradition, we can spread the joy of the season and support the giving spirit of the holidays,” Creel added.

Historical interest rates
How are credit card rates set?
The typical credit card rate formula is the Prime Rate plus a profit margin set by the card issuer. On average, this margin often runs between 12% and 13%. The Prime Rate is currently 7%. It’s typically 3 percentage points higher than the federal funds rate, which is set by the Federal Reserve’s Federal Open Market Committee.
Essentially, the federal funds rate is the interest rate that banks charge each other for short-term (generally overnight) loans. The Prime Rate is a benchmark for what banks charge their most creditworthy customers. It serves as a basis for many financial products.
Credit cards have a higher markup than other loans, such as mortgages and auto loans, because credit cards represent unsecured debt. That means they aren’t backed by an underlying asset such as a home or car that a lender can seize if the borrower doesn’t pay them back.
How the CARD Act changed credit card rate calculations
The CARD Act, which took effect in 2010, altered the way credit card rates were set. Previously, credit card issuers had much more flexibility in terms of when they could change customers’ rates. Now, the easiest way for them to adjust rates (especially on existing balances) is to tie the rate to an index such as the Prime Rate.
If the Prime Rate changes, almost all credit card agreements are written in a way that the adjustment affects cardholders’ new and existing balances without any special notice required. The exact timing of the change varies. Sometimes the issuer uses the Prime Rate on your statement date. It might also be the first day of the month or the last day of the month or another date of their choosing.
Card issuers can change the rate on existing customers’ new purchases with 45 days’ notice. And they have a lot of flexibility regarding new offers just coming onto the market.
Money tip: The most important thing to know with respect to credit card rate adjustments is that Federal Reserve rate changes (up or down) generally pass through to customers within a month or two. And these Fed rate changes affect new and existing credit card balances.

How do credit card rates affect you?
Most credit cards bill on a monthly cycle. If you pay your credit card purchases in full, you aren’t charged interest and you typically receive an interest-free grace period of at least 21 days. For example, if your billing statement is generated on the 1st of the month, you usually have until at least the 22nd of that month to pay without interest accruing. Depending on when you made the purchase, you might actually have close to two months without owing interest (if you bought something early in the billing cycle).
However, if you carry a balance from one billing cycle to the next, it’s a completely different story. Credit card rates are usually expressed as APRs — annual percentage rates. But taking this a level deeper, what actually happens when you carry a balance is that the card issuer assesses a daily interest rate (typically the APR divided by the 365 days in a year) on your average daily balance during a given billing cycle. The most important thing for consumers to understand is that, when they carry balances, interest is accruing every single day (and usually at a hefty interest rate). That’s why it’s essential to pay down credit card debt as quickly as possible.
Let’s say you have $5,000 of credit card debt and your interest rate is 20% APR. If you only make minimum payments, you will be in debt for about 23 years and you’ll end up paying about $7,723 in interest, according to Bankrate’s calculator.
Keep in mind: An interest-free grace period applies only to purchases. If you’ve made a balance transfer or taken a cash advance, different APRs could apply and there may not be any grace period for those transactions.
-  Our methodology When we refer to the average credit card rate, we mean the average midpoint of the APR ranges assessed by 111 popular credit cards offered by the 50 largest U.S.-based credit card issuers. Most credit cards charge different interest rates to different customers based upon their creditworthiness. A consumer with an excellent credit score, for example, might be charged 14.99%. That same card might charge as high as, say, 24.99% to someone with a lower credit score. In that example, we would use 19.99% (the midpoint between 14.99% and 24.99%) in our average credit card rate calculations.
