title: Bangor Symphony opens Season 131 with Grammy-Award winner Zuill Bailey
text:
The Bangor Symphony Orchestra will present the first Masterworks concert in its 131st Season, Blaze and Brilliance, at 3 p.m. on Sunday, Oct. 18 at the Collins Center for the Arts in Orono. The BSO will be joined by Grammy-Award winning cellist Zuill Bailey performing Michael Daugherty’s Tales of Hemingway, plus orchestral performances of Peggy Stuart Coolidge’s New England Autumn and Robert Schumann’s Second Symphony.
Bailey is widely regarded as one of the premiere cello soloists in the world. Over a career spanning more than 35 years, he has performed with more than 200 symphony orchestras worldwide, in addition to recitals and chamber music appearances on major series and festivals internationally. This concert will be conducted by Grammy-Award winning BSO Music Director and Conductor Lucas Richman. The Masterworks concert is part of the Bangor Symphony Orchestra’s 2026-27 Masterworks Season. Single tickets, starting at $18, are available through bangorsymphony.org or by calling 207-581-2787.
On Thursday, Oct. 15 Bailey will be visiting the Bangor Symphony Youth Orchestras at their rehearsal at Peakes Auditorium at Bangor High School from 6:45 to 7:45 p.m. The participating ensemble will be the BSYO Philharmonic Orchestra.
Bailey will be lecturing at a Strings Class at the University of Maine School of Music on Friday, Oct. 16 at 10:15 a.m., followed by a Cello Masterclass from 10:45 a.m. to noon. Masterclass participants are students at the University of Maine School of Music.
The Bangor Symphony Orchestra’s Chamber Music Series kicks off on Monday, Oct. 19 with a performance at 6:30 p.m. at the Gracie Theatre on Husson University campus in Bangor. This new initiative by the BSO brings together premiere soloists with BSO musicians performing chamber music. Bailey will be joined by BSO musicians Mitchell Newman (violin), Simon Bilyk (violin), Laura Galucci (viola) and Noreen Silver (cello) for a performance which will include music of J.S. Bach, Ludwig van Beethoven and Franz Schubert. The Chamber Music concert is part of the Bangor Symphony Orchestra’s 2026-27 Chamber Music Series. Single tickets, starting at $20 with children under 12 and Husson students free, are available through gracietheatre.com or by calling 207-941-7888.
The Bangor Symphony Orchestra is one of the nation’s oldest continually operating professional orchestras, dedicated to enhancing the cultural landscape of Bangor, Maine, through exceptional live performances, music education and community engagement. The BSO continues to perform and celebrate the transformative power of music.
Single tickets are now on sale through the Collins Center for the Arts Box Oﬃce for all concerts. For tickets or more information, visit bangorsymphony.org or follow Bangor Symphony Orchestra on social media.

title: Worker injured by flying barrel in Maine interstate hit-and-run
text:
Maine State Police are seeking the public’s help identifying a driver who hit several barriers in a construction zone on Wednesday morning, sending a road worker to the hospital.
The hit-and-run crash in a single-lane construction zone in Pittsfield was reported at about 8:17 a.m., according to state police.
A silver pickup truck hauling a black dump trailer hit a concrete Jersey barrier and an orange construction barrel on the right side of the road. The barrel was knocked into 56-year-old Richard Smart of Westfield, who was working for Northeast Construction unloading Jersey barriers, police said.
The male driver of the pickup continued north without stopping, according to police, who said witnesses reported seeing him turn around inside the truck as the crash occurred then speed away.
Smart was taken by ambulance to Northern Light Sebasticook Valley Hospital in Pittsfield with serious injuries that were not considered life-threatening, police said.
Maine State Police are asking anyone who witnessed the crash or has information about the truck or driver to call the Bangor Regional Communications Center at 207-973-3700, ext. 9, and ask for Trooper Klayton Peckham.

title: Learn about Maine’s maritime history at Sunday event in Bath
text:
The Maine-based nonprofit Atlantic Black Box will host on Sunday “The Interco(a)stal Walk: Reading Between the Ribs of Maine’s Maritime History,” a free, daylong journey highlighting Black and Wabanaki maritime histories in one of Maine’s most celebrated shipbuilding cities.
Participants will travel just under 3 miles from Bath’s North End Boat Launch to Maine Maritime Museum, encountering historical interpretation, poetry, music, storytelling, performances and installations along the way. The afternoon will feature a shared meal, performances, and the unveiling and activation of a collective reimagining of the museum’s monumental Wyoming evocation sculpture.
The full-day program has filled up, but registration is still open for the afternoon-only program at abbx.me/intercoastalafternoon. This is is a free event.
Convened by Atlantic Black Box in partnership with The Third Place, Maine Maritime Museum, and Bomazeen Land Trust, Interco(a)stal brings together nearly a year of collaborative research, relationship-building, artistic experimentation and public programming. The initiative is one of 10 projects selected nationally for Monument Lab’s 2026 Re:Generation cohort, which supports community-centered approaches to rethinking monuments and public memory.
The event also builds on Atlantic Black Box’s flagship program, the Walks for Historical and Ecological Recovery (WHERE). In 2024 and 2025, ABB worked with partners in 14 communities across Maine to organize walks inviting participants to explore local histories in relationship to the landscapes around them. This year’s initiative brings that approach to Bath.
The Interco(a)stal Walk invites participants to encounter the Kennebec as Wabanaki homeland and a living ecosystem, recenter Black and Wabanaki maritime histories, and trace Bath’s connections to colonization, slavery and Atlantic commerce, migration and diaspora, labor and industrialization, ecological change, and resistance.
“When I think about Bath and the lower Kennebec, Sagadahoc, in my lifetime there’s always been an assumption that there are no more Indigenous people there. That everybody disappeared with colonialism,” said James Eric Francis Sr., Penobscot Nation tribal historian and Interco(a)stal’s art director. “Through this project, we are really taking back those spaces and honoring our ancestors who lived in those areas.”
At Maine Maritime Museum, participants will gather for a shared lunch featuring foods that speak to the histories and communities encountered throughout the day. The afternoon program will include performances and public participation in the reimagining of Wyoming evocation, the skeletal sculpture evoking the six-masted schooner Wyoming, built in Bath in 1909.
Artists and researchers are developing temporary installations on and around the existing structure, asking: What realities should a monument to shipbuilding and seafaring reflect? Whose histories should be visible there?
The collaboration is changing how new audiences encounter Maine Maritime Museum and how the museum reflects on its own offerings.
“It’s exciting to see new communities visiting the museum and interpreting the land, archives, and collections through important contemporary lenses,” said Luke Gates-Milardo, director of exhibits and learning at Maine Maritime Museum. “It’s bringing fresh life to the museum’s collection and site.”

title: Search for missing pup in Yellowstone is under pressure as winter nears
text:
Search for missing pup in Yellowstone is under pressure as winter nears
A small dog that's been on the loose in Yellowstone National Park for a month has been spotted crossing intersections, strolling through employee housing and entering lodges through automatic doors.
Yet Luna, a Jack Russell terrier from California, has eluded capture. And with winter closing in, volunteers in the search for the dog say time is running out.
Related video above | New webcam at Yellowstone National Park records 'small' eruption from Black Diamond Pool
Katie Boucher, the volunteer helming the rescue effort and a spokesperson for Luna's family, says the dog has good survival instincts. Boucher said that before Luna was adopted, the 10-year-old dog spent the first year of her life on the streets.
So far, temperatures haven't dropped too low, but that could change in an instant. Boucher is hoping the light dusting of snow in the area is enough to make her want to come home.
“Hopefully she has decided that winter in Yellowstone National Park is not a good vacation,” Boucher said.
An escape into the wilderness
On the day she was lost, Luna's family left her in a cabin, with a do-not-disturb sign, while they ventured out to see the park. In what they believe was an accident, housekeeping opened the room door and let Luna out.
“The staff then proceeded to chase her around that area of the park for over two hours before the owners came back and discovered all the chaos and their dog missing,” Boucher said.
Luna's family searched for their pup, but were told it was likely the terrier either died or was eaten by a coyote, Boucher recounted. Days after leaving Yellowstone, Luna's owners were told she had been spotted, and contacted Boucher, the president of the Norris Ark Training and Recovery Center in Norris, Montana, an area just north of the national park.
“I cannot fathom how I would feel if I had been taking the vacation of a lifetime, and looking for all these memorable experiences in one of the most beautiful places on earth, and lost one of my family members there,” Boucher said.
Boucher has been tracking sightings of Luna and says the dog is retracing her family's steps from the day before she was lost, sneaking into eateries or lodges they had visited.
Locals and tourists have called Luna’s name or chased her, triggering her fight-or-flight response and driving the dog further into the park, Boucher said. The volunteers set a humane trap to lure Luna in using the scent of her family, since using food could attract other wildlife like bears.
Time is running out as winter closes in
This might be the last week Boucher will be able to look for Luna, as weather could potentially limit how long she can stay in the park. Right now, she's sleeping at an RV park for seasonal employees that closes next Monday.
Despite the time crunch, she's confident she's close to returning Luna to her family.
“Her behavior pattern suggests to me that she is looking for her family,” Boucher said.
The search for the small pup has rallied locals and tourists visiting the area. Marie Jaskula, a resident in the area that runs one of the park's general stores, has posted signs at every entrance to the park so visitors can look out for Luna too.
“It’s really hard to stress the importance of do not chase,” said Jaskula. “Everybody sees this little dog buzz across the intersection or maybe around their employee housing, and the first instinct is to call her name and chase her.”

title: DNA analysis identifies remains as Georgia woman missing since 1997
text:
ATLANTA (Atlanta News First/Gray News) — Human remains found during a missing person investigation have been confirmed as those of a woman who went missing in Conyers three decades ago, authorities said.
Tammy Fortson vanished in 1997 from the Fox Chase Court area, Conyers police said. The investigation into Fortson’s disappearance grew cold until skeletal remains were found near Christian Circle in 2016, one of the last places Fortson was seen.
In 2019, portions of the remains were sent to the University of North Texas Center for Human Identification for advanced DNA analysis, police said. Detective after detective tried to crack the case, but a positive ID of the remains proved elusive.
In 2024, another detective delved into the case, again enlisting the help of the University of North Texas Center for Human Identification for forensic testing.
Months of DNA analysis revealed that the remains “were approximately 104 million times more likely to be the biological child of Ms. Beckhold than an unrelated individual,” police said in a statement.
With help from the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the medical examiner, authorities this past July were able to positively identify the remains as those of Tammy Fortson.

Now that authorities have identified Fortson’s body, the circumstances around her death remain under investigation, police said.

title: McLean Youth Fund seeks donations
text:
In 2015 John McLean, of Vassalboro, set up the Vassalboro United Methodist Church (VUMC) Youth Fund in his wife, Celeste’s memory. Soon before John’s death, in August of this year, VUMC voted to rename it the “John & Celeste McLean Youth Fund.” Harvey Boatman from the VUMC Finance Committee reported, “Thankfully, we were able to tell John about the name change before he passed, which pleased him greatly.”
“Many Vassalboro kids have gone to Camp Mechuwana on scholarships provided by the McLean Youth Fund over the last 11 years,” said Boatman. “It was John’s way of celebrating Celeste’s life and fulfilling her wish to help youth programs at the church. The fund also supports VUMC youth activities such as mission trips and Christian education.”
Thirteen-year-old Eli Orchard, of Winslow, is one VUMC youngster who attended Camp Mechuwana, the United Methodist Church camp, in Winthrop, last summer. Ian shared with VUMC church members that he had never been to an overnight camp before. “I was a bit nervous,’ he wrote. “I went for five days during the creative arts week in August and made a lot of new friends and discovered wood burning, quilling, and origami. title: Trump may scrap plan to livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution, sources say
text:
FORT HOOD, Texas (CNN) - President Donald Trump and his advisors are debating whether to call off plans to livestream the execution of the Fort Hood shooter, according to sources.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hassan last week.
Democrats and some Republicans raised objections about the idea.
Trump’s position
Sources say the president was not initially aware of Hegseth’s plan but firmly backs the idea of using a firing squad to kill Hassan.
Hassan was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding dozens of others at Fort Hood in 2009.
Law enforcement responded to the attack and shot Hassan in the back. He has been paralyzed from the waist down ever since.
Sources say Trump does not necessarily like the optics of livestreaming the execution of a man in a wheelchair.
Hassan is set to die on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood.

title: Dry time ahead of soaking rain arriving Friday
text:
Dry time ahead of soaking rain arriving Friday
Friday brings rain and breezy conditions.
Dry time ahead of soaking rain arriving Friday
Friday brings rain and breezy conditions.
Today will be partly sunny, with temperatures reaching the mid-60s. Winds will start out light and variable before shifting to the northwest at around 10 mph this afternoon. Wind gusts could reach up to 20 mph, making it feel breezier as the day progresses.
Tonight will be mostly clear, with temperatures dropping into the lower 40s. Northwest winds will continue at 10 to 15 mph, with gusts reaching up to 30 mph after midnight. The cooler temperatures and increasing winds will make it feel chilly overnight.
Thursday will bring mostly sunny skies, with highs reaching the upper 50s. Northwest winds will remain at 10 to 15 mph, with gusts up to 30 mph during the morning. Although skies will be mostly clear, the persistent breeze will make it feel cooler, especially in exposed areas.
Thursday night will start with partly cloudy skies before becoming mostly cloudy later in the evening. Temperatures will fall into the upper 30s, with light and variable winds. Clouds will increase ahead of an approaching storm system that will bring rain and colder weather to Maine on Friday.
Rain will move back into Maine on Friday as low pressure strengthens to the west. Showers are expected to spread into western Maine around noon, bringing another beneficial soaking of rain. Rainfall totals could reach around three-quarters of an inch in many areas. Because the system will move through relatively quickly, steady rain should last around eight to 12 hours in any given location. Temperatures will reach the upper 50s, with southeast winds of 10 to 15 mph and gusts up to 30 mph. Higher elevations may see some wintry precipitation Friday morning as colder air interacts with the approaching system.
Friday night will begin with rain showers before conditions gradually improve. Showers may linger into the evening, with partly cloudy skies developing after midnight. As colder northwest winds move into the region, the chance for snow showers will increase across the mountains and foothills of western Maine. Temperatures will drop into the mid-30s, and some higher elevations could see a transition from rain to snow as colder air settles in.
A sharp shift toward winter-like conditions will arrive Saturday behind a strong cold front. Partly sunny skies are expected, but temperatures will struggle to reach the upper 40s, well below normal for mid-October. Strong northwest winds will make conditions feel even colder, with gusts potentially exceeding 40 mph in some areas. These strong winds could bring down tree branches and cause isolated power outages, particularly along the eastern slopes of the mountains. A wind advisory may be needed if gusty conditions develop as expected. Anyone planning outdoor activities should prepare for blustery conditions and rapidly changing weather.
Saturday night will be mostly clear, with temperatures dropping into the upper 20s. The combination of cold air and lingering winds will make it feel even colder, with wind chills adding to the winter-like conditions. Temperatures below freezing will be possible in many areas, creating a risk of frost and potentially icy spots in colder locations.
Sunday will bring mostly sunny skies, but the cold weather will continue. Highs will reach only the lower 50s, keeping temperatures below normal for this time of year. Northwest breezes may continue to make it feel cooler, particularly in exposed locations. Conditions in the mountains will remain especially harsh at higher elevations. Above the tree line, strong winds, low temperatures, and wind chills could create dangerous conditions, making fall hiking unsafe this weekend.
Sunday night will be mostly clear, with temperatures dropping into the lower 30s. Subfreezing temperatures will remain possible, especially in colder valleys and sheltered areas. Anyone with sensitive plants should consider taking precautions against frost and freezing conditions.
Monday will bring partly sunny skies and a gradual moderation in temperatures, with highs reaching around 60 degrees. While conditions will be milder than over the weekend, temperatures may still feel cool at times. Monday night will be partly cloudy, with lows falling into the upper 30s as chilly air remains in place overnight.
Tuesday will bring partly sunny skies and a further warmup, with highs reaching the mid-60s. Temperatures will return closer to the milder conditions seen earlier in the forecast period, providing some relief after the weekend's cold and blustery weather.
Overall, Maine will experience a noticeable change in weather over the coming days. Mild conditions will give way to widespread rain on Friday, followed by a strong cold front that will usher in much colder air and gusty northwest winds for the weekend. Mountain areas could see snow showers, while strong winds may cause isolated power outages. With temperatures potentially falling below freezing Saturday and Sunday nights, and dangerous conditions expected above the tree line, this weekend will feel much more like winter than mid-October.

title: Read the poem ‘Again today I spoke to no one’ by Lucia Owen
text:
This week’s poem, by Lucia Owen, draws us into a lake idyll tinged by the reality of forest fires to the north. I love this poem’s clarion progression of images, the speaker’s stillness among them, and the quiet candor with which she confronts the terrible loss.
Owen moved to western Maine to teach high school English in 1969 and can’t imagine living anywhere else. She began writing poetry seriously at about the same time she began taking care of her husband of 48 years at home. Since his death and now in her eighth decade, she finds that poetry helps her keep on keeping on. Her work has appeared in a number of journals and anthologies.
Poets, please note that submissions to Deep Water are open now and through the end of the year. Deep Water is especially eager to share poems by Black writers, writers of color, indigenous writers, LGBTQ+ writers, and other underrepresented voices. Find a link to submit credits at mainewriters.org/deep-water
Again today I spoke to no one
wandered from task to made-up task and back,
accomplished nothing but tearful gratitude
this morning sitting in my little skiff
in the middle of the still lake.
Haze and calm. I rest my oars, wait –
five loons surface, chortle to each other,
swim, dive, surface, swim away – vanish
against the far shore as they would have done
had I not been there. Witness unneeded
for the loons, the morning and the sky –
but haze – I do witness it, know it comes
from northern forests burning, know that
knowing is not enough, hardly know what I
can do, here rocking in my little boat,
imagining the perfection of the morning,
knowing the illusion. The wind
picks up and I row home.
– Lucia Owen
Megan Grumbling is a poet and writer who lives in Portland. Deep Water: Maine Poems is produced in collaboration with the Maine Writers & Publishers Alliance. “Again today I spoke to no one,” ©2025 by Lucia Owen, was published as “The second day” in The Healing Muse. It appears by permission of the author.

title: Nash Callahan cares about Augusta
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Years ago, I met Saunders Nash Callahan on a Kennebec County group bicycle ride. He was the leader and I was the slowest one. He was very encouraging and made it fun.
Callahan has channeled his love of bikes into establishing a business, Capital City Cycles in Augusta, the city where he was born and raised.
Callahan gives me hope for the future. He cares about our city so much that he risked starting a business downtown. When he says he wants to better our housing and transportation, it isn’t just talk — because he’s proved he follows through. But that’s not the best part.
The best part is that Callahan is running for an at large seat on the Augusta City Council. Please join me in voting for Saunders Nash Callahan in this important election on Nov. 3.
Dale McCormick
Augusta

title: Sanford City Council closes Heritage Crossing near abandoned mill
text:
Sanford City Council closes Heritage Crossing near abandoned mill
The abandoned International Woolen Mill has long been a concern for residents and a spot for unhoused individuals to seek shelter.
Sanford City Council closes Heritage Crossing near abandoned mill
The abandoned International Woolen Mill has long been a concern for residents and a spot for unhoused individuals to seek shelter.
The Sanford City Council voted on Tuesday night to close Heritage Crossing indefinitely after removal operations at the abandoned International Woolen Mill. On Tuesday, Sanford Police Chief Eric Small announced that six people had been removed from the mill and charged with criminal trespass. Three with outstanding warrants were taken to York County Jail. The mill is marked with signs and purple paint signifying it is a no-trespass zone, but police are still seeing people seeking shelter making their way inside.
"There are 30 ways into the building; if you close the tunnel up, someone is going to go in another way. It is not really possible to secure that building anymore," said Small.
In October of 2025, investigators believe a fire was intentionally set at the mill. That concern is still a major one for residents who live in buildings near the mill. Police and fire personnel in the city have said a fire in the building could be deadly for first responders because of the structure and hazardous materials inside.
It is also impacting business owners like Emily Rand, who owns a hair salon just feet from the old Woolen Mill. Rand said she has dealt with trash and needles near her salon and has even lost clients because they do not feel safe.
"I drive down there every day with my phone in my hand and a pit in my stomach to see what is happening. I feel like every time we put the heat on them, and it becomes public, they put a Band-Aid on it," said Rand.
The city council and police chief said they are working to address the homeless population in the city, adding that it is past time to get assistance for those struggling with homelessness and addiction in Sanford. Rand also added that she would like to see programs to uplift the unhoused population in her home city.

title: Rumford police seek Lewiston man after stand-off with empty apartment
text:
Rumford Police are searching for a Lewiston man after reports of gunfire Wednesday morning led to a stand-off with an apartment their suspect had already left.
The incident started when the department got information over the weekend about suspected drug trafficking in an apartment on Waldo Street involving locals and people from out of town.
During the same time, police also heard from residents who said people associated with the apartment were armed and had been periodically shooting guns in the neighborhood, according to the department.
Before sunrise on Wednesday morning, officers responded to another report of gunfire in the area. They believed the people doing the shooting were inside the apartment and created a perimeter around the building while waiting for a search warrant.
Rumford police called in the Maine State Police Tactical Team to help secure the area and execute a search warrant, which was authorized by the court late Wednesday morning, the Rumford department said.
The department released a shelter-in-place notice on Wednesday, and the town’s public works department temporarily closed roads and detoured traffic in the surrounding area. Ambulance paramedics were staged nearby as a precaution, according to police.
Shortly before 1 p.m., the tactical team entered the apartment but found that the suspects were no longer inside. Investigators believe they fled several hours earlier, around the time police initially responded to the morning report of gunfire, Rumford police said.
Based on the investigation, Rumford Police are seeking Blake Lachance, 21, of Lewiston, who is wanted on multiple felony charges involving the use of a dangerous weapon.
The department said Lachance should be considered armed and dangerous. Anyone with information about his whereabouts is asked to contact law enforcement immediately.
The investigation remains active, and more people are expected to face criminal charges as investigators develop evidence and identify those involved, Rumford police said.

title: A handful of preservationists are keeping Maine’s cemeteries alive
text:
KENNEBUNKPORT — Judson Star chiseled a flaky gray substance from a piece of the broken headstone.
“It looks like someone tried to repair it with some type of goop,” he said. It crumbled in his fingers. A bathroom caulk, he guessed, not the preservation-grade epoxy that he brought in his white pick-up truck and mixed on a paper plate.
The fractured stone in Arundel Cemetery in Kennebunkport captured Star’s attention on a windy October morning. It was still upright when he started working a little after 10 a.m., but it wasn’t stable. The bottom right corner was fractured into three pieces, and wobbled under just a little pressure.
After he gently removed the layer of caulk, Star applied the epoxy with a popsicle stick. He slid the stones together like a puzzle, making sure the lines of the epitaph were flush. He clamped wood planks to the stone to hold it in place while it cured for 24 hours.
Star is a professional gravestone conservator who travels all over the state repairing headstones. He works in about 20 cemeteries a year, typically from May through November (the epoxies and mortars don’t cooperate once temperatures consistently drop below 45 degrees).
In about half of the towns he works in, there are dedicated volunteers who work alongside him tackling simpler tasks like cleaning or righting a leaning stone. They ask him questions, and he is always happy to lend a tool. He likes it when they tell him about the histories of the people buried there.
“There’s a lot of things that you could know about preservation, and there are hundreds of stones that need to be worked on in each town,” he said. He teaches the enthusiastic some of his skills, so they can be a little more self-sufficient with ongoing cemetery maintenance.
NEED FOR REPAIR
There are more than 7,800 cemeteries in the state, including historic and modern burial grounds, family cemeteries and single graves, according to Walter Guptill, president of the Maine Old Cemetery Association.
“People buried their family members up on the hillside,” he said. Over time, roads changed, and some were reclaimed by woods. About 1,200 still haven’t been physically located, and that’s after MOCA volunteers found 500 cemeteries over the last two years.
Many of them are small, with 30 burials or fewer. Sometimes, it’s just a grave or two, or a base in the middle of a field, Guptill said.
The number of professional conservators pales in comparison to the preservation needs. Star is just one of about a dozen in the state, Guptill said.
So it’s often up to municipal employees, cemetery and conservation committees, descendants, historical societies and community volunteers to find and maintain these cemeteries.
“The gap is not a lack of interest or good intentions,” Guptill said. “It’s the shortage of trained people, reliable guidance, funding and organized local stewardship needed to care for thousands of cemeteries across Maine.”
LEARN TO DO NO HARM
MOCA hosts workshops and training to pass on the art of conservation to the people who are trying to keep local cemeteries alive.
Lesson one is to do no harm, Guptill said. Lesson two is to only work within the limits of your training.
There’s an adage among cemetery aficionados, Guptill said. “More damage is done in cemeteries by people with good intentions than by vandals.”
Improper cleaning and repair techniques can cause permanent damage. Despite what one might think, bleach and other household cleaners shouldn’t be used on gravestones, Guptill said. Over time, the residue causes discoloration. And if you don’t use a soft bristle brush on marble, for example, you can take away parts of the surface, a phenomenon known as “sugaring.”
“People are out there trying to make it better, and we want to harness that energy with the right skillset, so that people are not only doing good but doing good in the right way,” he said. There’s a risk in overcleaning, if you can imagine, he said.
To grow the pool of experts in the state, MOCA hosts two types of workshops: a one-day gravestone cleaning class and an annual, four-day repair boot camp. The nonprofit provides the instructor and materials. Towns can volunteer their cemeteries as training grounds, so overdue repair work gets completed.
The group also has training videos and resources for people who have lingering questions.
There are three aspects of preservation work, according to Star: moving and lifting the stone, which he does with an aluminum tripod that can hoist up to a ton of weight; prepping the ground, often with gardening tools like shovels, tampers and loppers; and repairing the actual stone, which requires epoxies, mortar and lime.
Star has spent about $10,000 on equipment over the past six years. He keeps a lot of it in the trunk of his truck. (He owns more than 20 orange Home Depot buckets, and keeps the components, like a plastic container of special sand, ready to mix mortar at a moment’s notice.)
He charges a per diem rate. “To fix a stone costs hundreds of dollars,” he said. “Not thousands.”
Star recognizes that municipalities might not have more than a few thousand dollars for cemetery maintenance in any given year, with most of that budget eaten up by mowing and tree care costs.
But proper cleaning techniques can be taught in a day, Guptill said, and you can see the results instantly.
“Have the courage to start,” Guptill said.
START WITH ENTHUSIASM
Star began as an enthusiastic volunteer. Or rather, he started out as someone who didn’t really think twice about cemeteries.
But that changed when his wife’s parents died in short succession, and both of them were buried in Arundel Cemetery.
“Now that we had family there, there was a lot more connection,” he said. “You’re no longer just driving by.”
He started helping out with fall and spring cleanups, picking up sticks and debris. He realized that cemeteries can be happy places, and that good people take care of them. He joined the board about 10 years ago, and in 2019, started his business, Maintain the Memory, cleaning gravestones locally. His town of Kennebunkport has 75 cemeteries, which kept him busy in the beginning.
On this particular October morning, he worked a stone’s throw away from the first grave he ever repaired, in the same cemetery where he discovered his love of preservation.
About a year after starting his business, he wanted to expand his skillset. He participated in the MOCA four-day workshop. He joined the MOCA board, and slowly acquired specialty equipment, like an aluminum tripod and different kinds of mortars. His business grew by word of mouth.
“There’s something deeper than just fixing a stone,” he said. “There’s an emotional aspect. I hope somebody’s doing this for my stone in a couple hundred years if it needs it.”
BREATHING NEW LIFE
Sometimes the preservation work can be dramatic, breathing new life into what was once dilapidated or unrecognizable.
Wescott Cemetery in South Portland didn’t look like a burial ground for decades. A vandal had knocked over all the stones sometime before the 1980s, and the pieces were stored in a shed until this summer, when the historical society received a $5,000 donation from Peter and Muffet Wright to aid their restoration.
Kathy DiPhilippo, the historical society’s executive director, had been tending to this small family cemetery tucked in a residential neighborhood of Thornton Heights for years. This summer, she went to MOCA’s four-day training with her husband, and connected with Star through the group.
Together with the help of a small group of experienced volunteers, they put nearly 20 stones back together, including one that had been fractured into 13 pieces. Viewed in sunlight weeks later, it glowed like a stained glass window.
“It’s incredible,” DiPhilippo said.
Over the years, Star has worked with a lot of volunteers. He said restorations usually trace back to one or two people who care.
“It just takes someone saying we need to do something,” he said.

title: As small police departments in rural Maine disappear, one town is hanging on
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A hundred miles east of nowhere and one block from the center of town, Ashland Police Chief Michael Montpetit shifted his department’s only dependable cruiser into gear and headed out for his morning patrol.
For a few hours, Montpetit looped up and down the few dozen roads that make up Ashland — which, at more than 80 square miles, is Maine’s second largest town by land area.
Around 1,200 people live there, half what the town’s population was a century ago. The decline follows trends in the logging industry, the economic driver of this sparsely populated region on the edge of the North Maine Woods. Its only grocery store has been closed for months.
But Ashland still has its own police department. Few of Maine’s small towns can say the same.
Farther north, Van Buren closed its department in 2019. Limestone followed suit in 2023. Washburn, where Monpetit once worked, disbanded the next year after its chief, Cyr Martin, stepped down.
At that time, Martin was also both Ashland’s police chief and town manager. After Washburn disbanded its force, he told News Center Maine that he was worried Ashland might be next.
That thought lingers in the current chief’s mind. The department’s $500,000 budget passed by two votes at Ashland’s annual town meeting in March.
“I hope that doesn’t end up being my legacy, being the chief when the town decides to close up,” Montpetit said. “It’s always a possibility.”
A Bangor Daily News analysis of 25 years of law enforcement employment data found that 15 police departments in Maine have disbanded or merged with another since 2000. The trend dates back at least a decade further, experts say, and mirrors a shift toward more centralized models of policing across the U.S.
“The trend in Maine that I see is the tax base disappears and public safety is an expensive endeavor,” Mark Marsolais, professor of criminal justice and security at Thomas College, said.
The reasons a department closes vary, often tied to budget constraints or an inability to recruit new officers. Occasionally, scandal shakes a community’s trust in police. But the outcomes are the same: in Maine’s most rural areas, where the vast majority of closures occur, county sheriff’s offices and the state police have taken over.
“A municipality that cannot afford to maintain a police department of at least 10 full-time officers probably should look at contracting that service with the county sheriff or combining services with neighboring municipalities,” said Noel March, Maine’s former U.S. Marshal and a senior lecturer of justice studies at University of Maine at Augusta.
Larger departments are inherently more efficient and pooled resources allow them to provide specialized services, March and other experts said. Larger departments also typically offer greater pay, benefits and promotion opportunities, which aid recruitment and retention.
Forty-nine of Maine’s 101 municipal police departments operated with 10 or fewer full time officers in 2024 — the last year with available employment data. That includes Ashland.
The town has just three full-time cops — Monpetit included — and five reserve officers. Monpetit himself patrols anywhere from 36 to 70 hours in a given week.
The Ashland Police Department is a single room, less than 250 square feet, tucked between the town office and the fire department. Its officers buy their own handguns because the department doesn’t have the money to purchase them.
In spite of that, Monpetit believes contracting outside policing would be a genuine detriment to the town. Ashland is isolated, more than 20 miles to the nearest service community. Who is going to be there when “grandma locks herself out of the apartment,” he asked. Who will conduct property checks? Could a larger agency build the same kind of rapport?
In Washburn, which has turned to regional policing provided by the Aroostook County Sheriff’s Office and Maine State Police, town manager Donna Turner said the arrangement has worked out well.
“We have been very pleased with the level of service they have provided,” Turner said.
Montpetit, who spent 15 years as sheriff’s deputy, says some residents have told him otherwise, to no fault of the police agencies.
“They’re spread thin,” he said. “You can’t expect a deputy that’s covering 30 towns to show up when you have a barking dog complaint. It just doesn’t work that way.”
Maine has the lowest violent crime rate in the nation, according to FBI data, and its overall crime rate has steadily decreased since 2021. But increases in mental health and substance-related calls have kept small departments busy.
Monpetit rejoined the Ashland Police Department in late 2024 and rose to chief within six months. Since then, data shows the department has been more present in the community and developed a stronger enforcement footing.
In 2025, the department responded to 1,919 calls for service and made 23 arrests, on par or higher than other towns of its size. It’s a stark contrast from the previous year, where officers responded to 764 calls for service and made four arrests.
From Dec. 1 to July 27 of this year, the department had already handled more than 2,000 calls, Monpetit said. He attributed the increase to officers working proactively, especially on drug enforcement, which he’s identified as a priority.
“The drug problem here, man, it was really out of control,” Monpetit said. “When I took over, there was no documented intelligence anywhere that I could find about anything that had been going on. We basically had to start from scratch.”
The department coordinated with the Maine Drug Enforcement Agency on several arrests in drug-related investigations in recent months, a DEA spokesperson said.
Little about the arrests is public. So naturally, most of Ashland knows about them. That’s the cost of doing business in a town with two stoplights. But a public perception of an active police department is a good thing, Montpetit argued.
Ashland has avoided many problems that have doomed other small Maine police departments. It has found creative ways to recruit and retain officers, and hasn’t found itself mired in scandal.
But he knows there’s only so long trust can outweigh expense. A nationwide affordability crisis is raising the temperature on local governments to cut costs, and Ashland has a small tax base. Two of the area’s largest businesses, Irving sawmills in Masardis and Nashville Plantation, are just outside town limits.
It’s always possible that in a community where residents vote on the municipal budget, they could revolt against police spending. It almost happened this spring. It’s difficult to say what would happen next, and that frightens Montpetit.
“At the end of the day, we’re fortunate to even have a PD here,” Montpetit said. “We’re one of the few left. We really are. It’s scary. I’m not scared for myself … It’s not an employment issue. I just know the town needs it.”

title: Northern Maine Community College child care center gives students hands-on training
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - The Northern Maine Community College Child Care Center is bringing new energy to the college’s early childhood education program.
New facility offers campus-based training
For students preparing to work in child care, getting real experience in a classroom is an important part of learning the job. Students at Northern Maine Community College can now get that experience without stepping off campus.
“So I think they’re coming in with an energy and an excitement because they know that they’re guaranteed this placement looking at the different ages that will be in this center,” said Angela Buck, VP / Dean of Academic & Student Affairs, NMCC.
Partnership addresses workforce shortage
The center is a partnership between NMCC and AVEC Community Action. While students get a new place to complete their fieldwork, the partnership is also aimed at addressing a shortage of early childhood educators.
“We’re at a critical level of the workforce shortage right now in early care and education. Being able to partner with the community college, have this right here, not only can we help serve the families and students here, we can also grow the workforce so that we’re not only helping at that level, we’re putting things in place and laying the foundation for longevity of early care and education in the county,” said Maeghan Swanson, education manager, AVEC Community Action.
Center details
The center opened in September and is currently operating with a soft opening as staff work through the logistics of staffing. When fully operational, the center is licensed for up to 49 children, with two infant-toddler rooms and one preschool room.
Students can observe the classrooms without stepping directly into the room.
“We have observation rooms built onto each classroom so that they can come in, observe the students, and we can also allow outside therapists that need to come in for observations or assessments to be able to watch the child or children in a non-invasive way which then gives more accurate results for assessments,” Swanson said.
That means students can focus on what they’re learning while the children continue to play, nap and grow.
“So the program really sets people up for a nice trajectory throughout their career in early childhood,” Buck said.
The goal is to give students a stronger start in the classroom while helping build the workforce needed to keep child care available for families across Aroostook County.
Ribbon-cutting events planned
A ribbon-cutting will be held October 23 to celebrate the new daycare and the partnerships that went into it.

title: Police lieutenant indicted after allegedly using Flock cameras to track person for personal reasons
text:
SHARONVILLE, Ohio (WXIX/Gray News) - A police lieutenant was indicted Tuesday after he allegedly used Flock camera systems to track a person for personal reasons.
Sharonville Police Lt. Walter Cordes, 48, was charged with unauthorized use of a computer, cable, or telecommunications property after he used the Flock camera system 29 times between Dec. 19, 2024, and April 20, 2026, to track a person’s whereabouts for “reasons unrelated to law enforcement,” according to Hamilton County Prosecutor Connie Pillich.
“When technology is misused, it undermines public trust and the important work being done by law enforcement officers every day,” Pillich said.
In June, prosecutors said Cordes self-reported during a department audit of the system and admitted to conducting the searches.
The Sharonville Police Department said on social media that Cordes was placed on administrative leave while the department conducted an investigation. After the investigation, Cordes was charged and faces up to a year in prison.
The Hamilton County Fraternal Order of Police said its members were surprised by the indictment.
“He is a member of our lodge. Many of the people I have spoken to since say they’re shocked by this indictment and that it happened, but at the same time, that’s why we have checks and balances,” said Rich Krummen, president of FOP Lodge 74.
Sharonville Police Department is now requiring additional training for every officer on the use of law enforcement databases and technology.

title: Mother accused of driving off cliff with her 2 children in car, authorities say
text:
CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - A woman in Tennessee is facing several charges after she allegedly drove off a cliff with children inside the car.
According to an affidavit obtained by WVLT News, authorities responded to a crash around 8:30 p.m. on Sept. 7.
Officers found 30-year-old Chase Klinedinst had been driving on Stuart Street and, upon reaching the dead end of the road, continued onto a dirt path leading to Coffey’s Cliff, which is about 20 to 25 feet above a train yard.
Police said she drove around a bend and made a left turn before “driving over the edge of the cliff and falling.”
The car came to rest upside down adjacent to railroad tracks, prompting railroad operations to be suspended on one of the rail lines.
Investigators learned Klinedinst also had her two children in the car.
While both children were in child restraint seats, one of them was taken to the emergency room for treatment and was found to have a fractured forearm and pulmonary contusions.
While first responders were removing Klinedinst from the car and helping her to the top of the cliff, she was allegedly “very combative with the medics” and had “very slurred” speech.
Officers also said they could smell a “very strong odor of an intoxicating beverage” from about 5 feet away, and investigators found an empty bottle of wine and another unopened bottle that “was still cold and covered in condensation.”
Klinedinst was charged with two counts of child neglect, driving under the influence and vehicular assault. Her next scheduled court appearance is set for Nov. 17.

title: LETTERS: New rule threatens healthcare to millions
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
To the editor:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has a dangerous new rule beginning October 22 that will threaten the healthcare of millions of Americans. The rule, “Indefinite Suspension of the De Minimis Exemption for Mail Shipments,” will effectively end Americans’ ability to personally import their prescription medicines.
Importing prescription drugs from licensed international pharmacies is the only lifeline for seniors on limited incomes, people with high-deductible health plans, and the uninsured. That’s why CBP and the FDA have allowed it for decades. Due to the much lower cost of medications in Canada and other countries, imported medicine is their only option.
Many imported drugs can be less than half the U.S. price. These necessary medicines prevent blood clots, treat diabetes, and much more. This CBP rule will cut off access to the only affordable prescription drugs for millions, and that will lead to unnecessary harm and preventable deaths.
I ask readers to immediately call or write our Senators and U.S. Representatives and demand they stop CBP from implementing any rule-making that restricts Americans from importing personal-use prescription drugs from licensed pharmacies in Canada or other countries.
Richard Dillenbeck
Waterville

title: Judge sides with CNN, MS NOW, Politico in White House showdown
text:
(AP) - A federal judge has extended an order blocking President Donald Trump’s administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, broadening his support for the journalists by arguing that the restriction violates their constitutional rights to free speech and due process.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in the extraordinary case pitting the president against the news outlets that cover him. In a victory for the journalists, Kelly expanded a previous, temporary ruling that the administration had violated the news outlets’ Fifth Amendment right to due process.
In a late-night ruling Tuesday, he also sided with a second argument by the outlets: that Trump’s ban breached their First Amendment right to free speech.
Kelly rejected Trump’s reasoning that the ban was driven by policy goals, such as protecting national security. He argued the ban was the result of Trump’s stated belief that the outlets’ reporting was inaccurate and biased.
“Simply put,” Kelly wrote, “That is unlawful viewpoint discrimination” — the government taking action against types of speech or coverage it does not like.
“Still,” he added in his late-night order, “no one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”
The White House called the decision “misguided” and said it plans to appeal.
“The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President’s Oval Office,” the statement said. “The lies they smear are a disservice to the American public and tear at the very fabric of our Democracy. They’re completely capable of reporting from directly outside.”
Trump’s standoff with the press is far from over. Kelly’s order did not address whether Trump can ban the three outlets from the rotating pool of broadcast networks that cover the president in tight spaces and share the reporting.
Stepped-up disputes between the president and the press
The fight reflects Trump’s increasing combativeness against news outlets and reporters whose content he does not like — including sharply curtailing Pentagon access for the press corps that covers the Defense Department. Trump or other parts of the executive branch have also, in policy and in the courts, grappled with The Wall Street Journal, The Associated Press and The New York Times — in addition to using the FCC to target broadcast networks.
The case of the three news outlets is increasingly messy and expensive. After the five-outlet rotating pool stood by CNN and canceled its coverage of Trump, the Justice Department over the weekend announced it was investigating whether those five companies violated antitrust laws in doing so.
Kelly’s ruling stood largely by the news outlets. He wrote that without a preliminary injunction blocking Trump’s ban, the outlets “are likely to suffer irreparable harm, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest tip in their favor.”
An email to the Justice Department, which is arguing the case for the administration, was not immediately returned.
Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the three media organizations, hailed the judge’s ruling.
“When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment,” Boutrous said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future.”
Judge says no warning given before banishment
Kelly, who was nominated to the bench by Trump, previously ordered the White House to restore the reporters’ “hard pass” press credentials while he weighed their claims. With that temporary order expiring Tuesday, the judge issued a preliminary injunction that preserves the status quo indefinitely while the case is pending.
Kelly said that, “to put it mildly,” the White House didn’t give the plaintiffs any warning that they were in danger of losing their hard passes before Trump’s Sept. 18 social media post about their bans.
The judge also said the impact of the White House ban goes far beyond a single reporter’s ability to do their job.
“The ban threatens to cut off all Plaintiffs’ access to the White House press area—a space open to many of their competitors—thereby restricting their ability to observe happenings there firsthand, immediately report on those activities, and try to engage with government officials,” the judge wrote.
Hard passes give journalists who regularly cover the White House longer term access to its campus without having to get permission ahead of time.
The government asked Kelly to suspend his own decision pending an appeal, but the judge said it didn’t justify that request. Kelly said the bans impacted a total of 78 reporters at the three news organizations.
Earlier judicial action against White House had been only temporary
Trump provided no notice before announcing the bans in a Sept. 18 social media post, which criticized the outlets’ reporting as “fake news.” Kelly temporarily blocked the bans on Sept. 24 at the request of the news outlets, which jointly filed a lawsuit in Washington, D.C.
Attorneys for the outlets have described Trump’s move as “unprecedented and blatantly unconstitutional” under the First and Fifth amendments. They argued that it’s illegal for Trump to punish the journalists because he doesn’t like the content of their reporting.
“The ban also inflicts an injury on all news media organizations — which now risk a similar fate if they engage in fact-based, independent reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable,” plaintiffs’ lawyers wrote.
Government lawyers argued that access to the White House is a privilege — not a right — and said the president can impose the bans to protect national security and to stem the spread of misinformation.
“The White House is the official residence and workplace of the President,” Justice Department attorneys wrote. “Presidents have had a relationship with the press since the beginning. They have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially from administration to administration.”
___
Associated Press reporter Rebecca Boone contributed.

title: Burglary suspect jumps through closed window to escape deputy
text:
OKLAHOMA COUNTY, Okla. (KOCO) - A dramatic escape was caught on body camera video after a suspected copper thief in Oklahoma jumped through a closed window.
“This is an experienced deputy; he’d never seen anything quite like it before, and by the time that he got outside, our suspect was long gone,” Aaron Brilbeck with the Oklahoma County Sheriff’s Office said.
The video shows the moment a suspect dove through a closed window to escape a deputy. The deputy was investigating a burglary at a vacant home in Oklahoma County on Oct. 1.
“This is a vacant property. Our deputy went up to the back door; he saw the back door had been forced open,” Brilbeck said.
Brilbeck said the suspect was allegedly stealing copper from the appliances and the walls inside the building.
According to the official report, the deputy tried to track down the suspect in his patrol car and then launched a drone to try to find him, but the deputy had no luck.
A nearby residence was also searched, but the suspect was nowhere to be found.
Then, a key piece of evidence was found along with a bicycle: an ID card.
“He was good enough to leave behind his backpack, and inside his backpack was his driver’s license, so it made it really easy to identify him,” Brilbeck said.
The suspect does have a history in Oklahoma County.
“A lot of theft, drug-related stuff, he’s got an assault charge in there,” Brilbeck said.
Despite leaving his driver’s license behind, the suspect remains on the run.

title: Maine governor candidate profile: Hannah Pingree
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Democratic nominee for governor Hannah Pingree cites housing and health care as her top priorities.
Her platform calls for an investment of $100 million a year in housing and a public health care option.
She said another top priority would be providing immediate winter relief for Mainers facing high home heating costs.
Differences with Mills
While Pingree said it was an honor to lead Gov. Janet Mills’ policy office, she said she does not agree with the current governor on everything. That includes Pingree’s call for legislation on tribal sovereignty within the first 100 days and an AI data center moratorium.
According to the latest polls, Pingree holds a double-digit lead in the gubernatorial race.
When asked why voters seem willing to give the Democratic Party another chance at the governorship given headwinds the state faces, Pingree said:
“I’m running as a mom, as somebody who spent 25 years in public service, I’m a lifelong Mainer, I think people want a hopeful vision the future. And I’ve been out there talking about how we improve education for our kids, how we build the housing we need, how we ensure that Maine people have the health care they can afford. And I think Mainers, they believe in their neighbors, they want to take care of each other. I’ve been running a positive campaign. I’ll just say my opponents, especially Bobby Charles, has not. And I think people are sick of, you know, the negativity. And they do want somebody who cares about our state and wants to move it forward. At the same time, I will also say, I think people are worried about this president, about the impacts he has on women’s reproductive rights, on the price of heating oil, on our ability to actually feed kids. And I think that certainly the president has put headwinds for the Republican Party right now. And I think people want a governor who can stand up to him at a critical time.”

title: Ballots: Their journey
text:
Part 3 of 4 parts
You probably wonder how ballots arrive at their destination and how they are handled after that.
Ballots are printed at printers designated by the Secretary of State. Ballots are then shipped through a secure courier to the city/town clerk. Ballots are then checked for content and counted by two persons, sealed and securely placed in a vault.
On election day, the ballots are delivered at the polling place by the police department, are counted again and sent with a receipt to the warden, who signs off once the count is confirmed. The ballots are then opened, one packet at a time, at the check in tables(s). Ballots are closely monitored during the day to assure there are not too many loose ballots.
After the polls close, the unvoted ballots are canceled by the clerk by making a large “X” with a red magic marker through the ballot. All unused ballots are then sealed in a box by the warden. The sealed boxes are then transported by police to be placed in a vault. Following the retention period, the unused ballots are destroyed.
Voters sometimes aren’t interested in voting some ballot styles. The clerk must provide each voter all ballots to which they are entitled, so all ballots can be accounted for after the election. If they choose not to mark the ballot, it must be cast as a blank ballot. If a voter is not provided with all the ballots to which they are entitled, it will result in more unvoted ballots and the inventory will not reconcile.
If a voter spoils a ballot, they must be issued a replacement, and the spoiled ballot is kept and segregated, and placed in an envelope by the warden, marked specifically for spoiled ballots.
What about voters with disabilities?:
If a voter indicates they wish to use the Accessible Voting Solution (AVS), they will not receive a regular ballot. They are issued a card. The AVS allows voters with disabilities to mark their ballots independently. It is not a tabulator, it is a touch screen or keypad device with audio that marks the ballot card for the voter. The card is then inserted in the tabulator to be counted.
Assistance can be provided.
State law allows a voter to request assistance in reading and/or marking the ballot. There are several ways to do that. A person assisting the voter does not need to be 18 years of age. The voter’s child can assist them in reading or marking the ballot. Election workers can assist the voter but should do so in teams of two. The assistance is limited to reading the ballot to the voter and marking the selection for the voter. In this instance, one worker reads and marks the ballot, while the second witnesses, to make sure the first worker is not attempting to influence the voter.
At the end of voting, all cast ballots are secured in metal boxes, locked with a seal attached for security, and transported to be secured, usually in a vault. Each box is registered with the lock and seal numbers, so the boxes cannot be tampered with.
Roland Hallee has 40 years experience in conducting elections, the last 25 years as warden in Waterville.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

Forgiving the man who killed her son

Millions of Americans take prescription medications for mental health conditions, but those might not be enough for people with severe depression or post-traumatic stress disorder.

Daughter of man detained by ICE at Portland Jetport says he has a clean record
text:
Daughter of man detained by ICE at Portland Jetport says he has a clean record
Nguinamau Celestino was heading to Washington, D.C., when ICE agents allegedly stopped and arrested him at Portland Jetport's security checkpoint.
Daughter of man detained by ICE at Portland Jetport says he has a clean record
Nguinamau Celestino was heading to Washington, D.C., when ICE agents allegedly stopped and arrested him at Portland Jetport's security checkpoint.
Margarida Celestino is the eldest daughter of Nguinamau and Sukombo Celestino. Originally from Angola, her parents brought her and her three younger brothers to the U.S. in 2017.
Margarida lives and works in Auburn; she's the only one in her family who has a green card, but her parents own a house in Saco. Hung up on the walls and displayed on tables are pictures of their family.
"This is Abel, our youngest. He's a very athletic person," Margarida said, referring to a picture of her brother with his arms stretched out after he just scored a point at a basketball game. "My dad specifically has attended almost, if not all, of my brother's basketball games."
Abel is also deaf, and now goes to school in Washington, D.C. That's where Nguinamau was heading when he was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at Portland Jetport.
Margarida said her mom dropped her dad off early at the airport on Oct. 9, but when family members checked his location next, he was at the ICE facility in Scarborough.
Since then, they have spoken to Nguinamau daily over the phone. He told his family that he had seen the ICE agents, but assumed they weren't for him since he thought he had all of his documents in order.
"As he got to the TSA kiosk, they said that they were there for him and took him," Margarida said.
Nguinamau has been transferred to Strafford County Corrections in Dover, New Hampshire, where he now awaits his first immigration proceedings.
According to an ICE spokesperson, Nguinamau entered the country legally, but he violated the terms of his admission into the U.S. and has been in the country illegally for nearly eight years. ICE did not explain how he violated those terms and did not respond to our follow-up for more information.
Margarida said that he had all of his paperwork, including a work permit and Social Security card. He was an engineer in Angola, and continued his education at Southern Maine Community College. He eventually became certified in plumbing, heating and HVAC.
"If they're saying that they're targeting criminals, then they should target criminals. I understand why you want to protect your country from criminals," Margarida said. "I mean, he has a clean background. I don't know what their actual reasoning is."
Portland Jetport isn't the only airport seeing targeted enforcement from ICE. Earlier this year, the Get the Facts data team analyzed data from the Deportation Data Project and found an increase in arrests where an airport was listed as the arrest site landmark or marked as a current duty site.
Maine's Total Coverage reached out to the city of Portland to see what, if any, jurisdiction the city has over ICE activity at the airport. The city has not yet responded.
Since Nguinamau was detained, the Celestino family started a GoFundMe to help cover immigration attorney fees and legal representation associated with Nguinamau's detainment. All three kids went through Portland Public Schools; former teachers and classmates have been reaching out, offering help for the family and writing letters talking about Nguinamau's character.
"I found out yesterday for the first time that he has helped one of my brother's teachers. He went to do free plumbing work. Plumbing work here is expensive, and he's doing that for free. We didn't know that until we read the letter yesterday," Margarida said.
Margarida said her dad's next court date is on Nov. 3 and that her family is working with an immigration attorney to have him released on bail. After hearing stories from others who were detained by ICE with clean records, the family is hopeful that he will eventually be released.
Margarida is graduating this November in California with a bachelor's in public health. She said she's not only worried about him not being able to come, but now her whole family is fearful of traveling.
"I wanted my whole family to be there. And now, if they're catching my dad at the airport, now I know that my parents and the rest of my family can't even come to my graduation," she said.

title: Inflation worsened last month to 3.7% in sign that prices remain elevated as midterm elections near
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gasoline and many other goods and services became more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before midterm elections that have focused heavily on affordability.
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month.
The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn’t all linked to oil and gas, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month and higher than economists had expected. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed’s 2% target.
Higher inflation will likely put more pressure on the Fed to lift its key interest rate at its next meeting Oct. 27-28. Economists noted that the report showed price increases were spread more broadly across the economy than in recent months.
“The report was worse than expected,” Bill Adams, chief U.S. economist at Fifth Third Bank, said in a note to clients. “Price increases were widespread. ... Consumer demand seems to be holding up better than the downbeat consumer surveys would suggest, helping businesses maintain pricing power.”
Wednesday’s figures are the last major inflation data to be released before the upcoming elections. Ongoing inflation has taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living issue. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Higher prices are eroding Americans’ earnings. The Labor Department also said Wednesday that average weekly paychecks, when adjusted for inflation, shrank last month compared with a year ago for the first time since May.
Gas prices jumped 9.1% just from August to September, the government’s consumer price index report said. Rising gas costs are a highly visible sign of inflation and often drive down measures of consumer sentiment about the economy.
With fuel much more expensive, air fares rose 1.2% last month and have soared 22% compared with a year ago. Hotel prices rose 2% from August to September and are up 4.4% compared with a year earlier.
Consumers saw some relief in grocery prices, which actually declined 0.1% last month and are up just 1.8% from a year ago. Ground beef prices fell 0.8% in September, though they are still up 5.4% from last year.
The cost of toys, new and used cars, sporting goods, and shoes all rose at a rapid clip last month, the government said.
The government also said Wednesday that Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% cost of living increase, based on the inflation figures.
The Middle East and Russia-Ukraine conflicts have also sharply inflated the cost of diesel fuel, which is used by long-haul trucks. Higher diesel prices will increase shipping expenses, which in turn could push up prices for a range of goods.
Ralph Newhouse, CEO of Chefman, which makes countertop appliances, said that rising diesel prices could force him to raise prices in the coming months.
The Mahwah, N.J.-based company, which makes milk frothers, air fryers, blenders and other appliances in China, last increased its prices in 2024. This year, it has used its $20 million in tariff refunds to offset the rise in fuel costs, but may not be able to do so much longer.
“We’re at the point right now that if we continue to see any additional rises in (diesel) prices, then these conversations are going to be forced upon us. We just day by day, hope and pray that we don’t have to have this conversation.”
Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn’t moving quickly enough back to the central bank’s target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9%.
Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year.
Still, Wednesday’s report has led many Wall Street investors to project that the Fed will now act in two weeks. The odds of a rate increase at the central bank’s October meeting have doubled, though remain at just 50-50, according to futures pricing tracked by CME Fedwatch.
Stock prices fell slightly after the report, while greater expectations for rate hikes pushed up bond yields, which will raise borrowing costs throughout the economy.
By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war’s disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can’t address those bottlenecks.
Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It’s already pushed up the price of air fares about 22% from a year ago.
Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients.
The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones.
Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge.
On September 1, Nintendo increased the price for its Switch 2 gaming system by 11% to $499.99. And Apple’s newest iPhone, the iPhone 17, cost about 10% more than its previous upgrade, though some of that likely reflects greater capabilities.
