title: ICE rejects suggestion that its officers wear body cameras that automatically activate
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal immigration officials need to ensure that body cameras worn by officers are uniformly activated when needed, a government report released Wednesday said, following a series of contentious shootings and aggressive arrests by ICE officers.
The agency rejected the recommendation, saying that using cameras that automatically activate when an officer pulls their weapon or activates a car siren could risk privacy concerns.
ICE has come under intense scrutiny after numerous incidents where officers have opened fire during enforcement operations and the agency has claimed they were under threat but officers weren’t wearing body cameras. Critics say the cameras could help hold officers accountable and promote transparency at a time when the agency is operating at a high tempo across the country and increasingly accused of excessive use of force. The report by the Government Accountability Office covers the period from February 2025 until September of this year. The report, conducted at the request of Democratic members of Congress, delves into policies governing the use of body-worn cameras by ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection and details improvements both agencies can make to improve their programs. But it did not go into any of the high-profile ICE-involved shootings that have focused attention on the agency’s body-worn camera usage, such as the shooting deaths of Renee Good in Minneapolis or Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston.
A fatal shooting exposed gaps in ICE’s camera rollout
Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem announced in February that every Homeland Security officer on the ground in Minneapolis would be issued body-worn cameras. Noem, who was later fired by Trump, said officers across the country would receive them as funds became available.
The department later received $20 million from Congress to finish the ICE body-camera rollout plan. But then came a shooting in July of Salgado Araujo, when Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers shot and killed the Mexican man who lived in the U.S. for more than 35 years. Those officers were not wearing body cameras, raising questions about why the agency still hadn’t gotten the cameras out to officers in the field. Homeland Security said after Salgado Araujo’s death that body cameras had been deployed to more than half of ICE field offices and that the remainder would get them in the next 60 days. In the GAO report, DHS said all ICE offices had received the body-worn cameras as of Aug. 5 and that officers were being trained on their use.
In a statement Wednesday, DHS said that while they’d purchased devices for all ICE officers across the country, the required training was still ongoing and that they expected to be finished “soon.”
DHS rejects automatic recording, citing privacy concerns
The report recommended ICE take additional steps such as “automated camera activation” that it said would be particularly helpful in situations where “unexpected and unplanned incidents, unrelated to sensitive operations, result in use of force by or against personnel.” The report said this would improve transparency and public trust. But DHS disagreed, saying that cameras that automatically activate could result in “the unauthorized recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims.” The agency said the body-worn cameras are required to be turned on at the beginning of pre-planned enforcement activities.
Confusion over camera rules kept one ICE office from using them
The report also said some of the officers they talked to at both ICE and CBP were confused as to when they should activate the cameras. For example, some officers told the GAO they didn’t know whether to activate the cameras during vehicle searches or when transporting detainees. The report noted that at one ICE office, staff was so uncertain about when they were supposed to use the cameras that they hadn’t begun using them even after they’d been trained.
The report also found that neither agency had updated the plans that oversee their body-worn camera programs even as their staff had grown significantly.

title: Yarmouth dominating, and other Maine high school football storylines for Week 7
text:
As we head into Week 7 and creep toward the end of the Maine high school football regular season, some teams have emerged as state title contenders, while others still have work to do.
Thornton Academy (6-0) and Bonny Eagle (6-0) have all but secured Class A South postseason berths, but can a team like Noble, which is currently on the outside of the playoff picture, find a way to win out and make a postseason run? To do so, the first step for the Knights is getting past South Portland on Friday.
Lawrence and Cony appear to be the favorites in Class B North, but can Skowhegan and Messalonskee make some headway in the division in their final two weeks of the regular season?
Here are three storylines to follow heading into Week 7:
DOMINATION STATION IN YARMOUTH
Yarmouth has been nothing short of dominant this season.
The Clippers (6-0) have outscored their opponents 354-54, tallying 60 points exactly in their last three games and averaging 59 points per game.
They’re first in the Large School South eight-man Crabtree standings and have trounced the other top contenders in the division — Spruce Mountain (4-2), whom they defeated 48-0 on Sept. 12, and Cape Elizabeth (4-2), whom they defeated 82-40 on Sept. 19.
“We’re super excited about this group,” said coach Nick Orsi. “We knew coming into the season it was going to be pretty special. We had a lot of players returning on the offensive side of the ball, including our quarterback, all our wide receivers. We added our running back, Stephen Connolly (54 carries, 940 yards, 14 touchdowns), to the mix this year. He’s a junior from NYA. He’s part of our co-op.”
The Clippers’ passing game is especially prolific, led by senior quarterback Iggy McGrath, who has thrown for 1,227 yards and 21 TDs and has yet to have a pass intercepted.
Even with such a high-performing offense, Orsi believes Yarmouth’s defense is the biggest difference-maker this year. Taking away the game against Cape Elizabeth, the Clippers have only allowed 14 points. Three of their games have been shutouts.
“We’re actually holding opponents to about 150 yards a game in total offense,” Orsi said. “That’s pretty remarkable in eight-man football — there’s so much space on the field, it typically tends to be higher-scoring games. We had a really rough first half against Cape Elizabeth and we gave up an opening-drive touchdown against Lake Region, but outside of that, the starting defense has been virtually flawless.”
On both sides of the ball, Yarmouth has proven itself a contender to win the eight-man Large School state championship for the first time since 2022.
Before then, the Clippers will close out their regular season with games against Orono (3-3) on Friday and Gray-New Gloucester (4-1) on Oct. 23.
HAS WELLS TURNED THE CORNER?
After Leavitt defeated Wells 42-0 on Sept. 26, coach Tim Roche knew his team was at a crossroads, sitting at 2-2 in a competitive Class C division.
“I just said to them, ‘We either step up to this challenge in the next five games, or we just say, ‘Oh … we’re not very good,’” Roche said. “I think we’re good.”
The Warriors (4-2) have won their last two games, defeating Gardiner 47-31 on Oct. 2 and Freeport 28-24 on Oct. 8. With three games remaining, Wells may be on its way to rejoining the field of Class C contenders alongside Leavitt, Greely, Foxcroft Academy and Hermon. Eight teams make the Class C postseason, and the top four host quarterfinals. Wells is currently ranked fifth but could move up if it wins its next three. The Warriors finish the regular season with games against York (2-4) on Saturday, Nokomis (2-4) on Oct. 24 and Hampden Academy (0-6) on Oct. 30.
HIGH-OCTANE HORNETS
Leavitt coach Michael Hathaway said it best after his team’s season-opening 39-8 win over Medomak Valley on Sept. 4: The Hornets don’t want to be reliant on only one component of their offense.
“Really, we just want to spread the ball around,” Hathaway said. “Whether it’s run or pass or whatever, we don’t want to be relying on any one thing. So I think you saw it tonight … a lot of different guys touching the ball.”
With three games to go in the Class C regular season, it’s safe to say Hathaway’s vision for the season has been realized. Leavitt (6-0), No. 1 in the Crabtree standings, is averaging 42 points per game and has had different players step up to play leading roles.
Darren Flagg, for example, scored five touchdowns across the team’s first two games against Medomak Valley and Greely. Then, Landen Reny and Jeremiah McKenzie combined for five touchdowns in a Week 4 win against Wells.
Against Gardiner last week, Flagg was back at the forefront, reaching the end zone five times while exemplifying Leavitt’s quest for versatility: he scored twice on runs, twice on receptions and once on an interception return.
Leavitt plays Nokomis at 7 p.m. Thursday.

title: Maine Gubernatorial Candidates Face Off in WMTW Debate
text:

title: School kids take a bite out of Maine Apple Crunch Day

text:

It’s a fun event getting all the kids here in one gym and doing that countdown and enjoying apples. I think it’s pretty cool.”

title: Current credit card interest rates
text:
Current credit card interest rates
The average credit card interest rate is 19.67%, down from a record-high 20.79% set on Aug. 14, 2024.
Current credit card interest rates
Bankrate Data Center
Since 1976, Bankrate has been the go-to source for personal finance data, publishing average rates on the most popular financial products and tracking the experience of consumers nationwide.
See more
Historical interest rates
How are credit card rates set?
The typical credit card rate formula is the Prime Rate plus a profit margin set by the card issuer. On average, this margin often runs between 12% and 13%. The Prime Rate is currently 7%. It’s typically 3 percentage points higher than the federal funds rate, which is set by the Federal Reserve’s Federal Open Market Committee.
Essentially, the federal funds rate is the interest rate that banks charge each other for short-term (generally overnight) loans. The Prime Rate is a benchmark for what banks charge their most creditworthy customers. It serves as a basis for many financial products.
Credit cards have a higher markup than other loans, such as mortgages and auto loans, because credit cards represent unsecured debt. That means they aren’t backed by an underlying asset such as a home or car that a lender can seize if the borrower doesn’t pay them back.
How the CARD Act changed credit card rate calculations
The CARD Act, which took effect in 2010, altered the way credit card rates were set. Previously, credit card issuers had much more flexibility in terms of when they could change customers’ rates. Now, the easiest way for them to adjust rates (especially on existing balances) is to tie the rate to an index such as the Prime Rate.
If the Prime Rate changes, almost all credit card agreements are written in a way that the adjustment affects cardholders’ new and existing balances without any special notice required. The exact timing of the change varies. Sometimes the issuer uses the Prime Rate on your statement date. It might also be the first day of the month or the last day of the month or another date of their choosing.
Card issuers can change the rate on existing customers’ new purchases with 45 days’ notice. And they have a lot of flexibility regarding new offers just coming onto the market.
Money tip: The most important thing to know with respect to credit card rate adjustments is that Federal Reserve rate changes (up or down) generally pass through to customers within a month or two. And these Fed rate changes affect new and existing credit card balances.

How do credit card rates affect you?
Most credit cards bill on a monthly cycle. If you pay your credit card purchases in full, you aren’t charged interest and you typically receive an interest-free grace period of at least 21 days. For example, if your billing statement is generated on the 1st of the month, you usually have until at least the 22nd of that month to pay without interest accruing. Depending on when you made the purchase, you might actually have close to two months without owing interest (if you bought something early in the billing cycle).
However, if you carry a balance from one billing cycle to the next, it’s a completely different story. Credit card rates are usually expressed as APRs — annual percentage rates. But taking this a level deeper, what actually happens when you carry a balance is that the card issuer assesses a daily interest rate (typically the APR divided by the 365 days in a year) on your average daily balance during a given billing cycle. The most important thing for consumers to understand is that, when they carry balances, interest is accruing every single day (and usually at a hefty interest rate). That’s why it’s essential to pay down credit card debt as quickly as possible.
Let’s say you have $5,000 of credit card debt and your interest rate is 20% APR. If you only make minimum payments, you will be in debt for about 23 years and you’ll end up paying about $7,723 in interest, according to Bankrate’s calculator.
Keep in mind: An interest-free grace period applies only to purchases. If you’ve made a balance transfer or taken a cash advance, different APRs could apply and there may not be any grace period for those transactions.

That same card might charge as high as, say, 24.99% to someone with a lower credit score. In that example, we would use 19.99% (the midpoint between 14.99% and 24.99%) in our average credit card rate calculations.

text:
Design-Build firm Knickerbocker Group has been named to Forbes’ 2026 list of America’s Best-in-State Residential Architects.
The recognition celebrates residential architecture firms that demonstrate excellence in design, a deep mastery of residential practice, and meaningful contributions to their communities and landscapes. Greg Norton, Director of Design, shared: “We tend to be stewards of Maine for our clients as well, which is a very important aspect of how we do things. We take that honor and responsibility seriously in our work. Thank you, Forbes, for the recognition, congratulations to our peers on the list, and thank you, Maine, for providing the perfect backdrop for what we get to do.”
The invitation-only selection process included evaluation by Forbes editors and an independent advisory board of experts in architecture, design, sustainability, and architectural history. Firms submitted one “exemplary” home completed since 2021, which was evaluated alongside the firm’s broader body of work. Evaluations considered professional presentation and reputation, as well as a project’s stability, utility, and beauty, and its approach to site, materials, craftsmanship, spatial design, technology, sustainability, and environmental responsiveness.
“We are deeply honored to be recognized by Forbes among America’s Best-in-State Residential Architects,” said Danielle Betts, president of Knickerbocker Group. “At Knickerbocker Group, good design begins with listening—to our clients and to the land. Each home is personal, shaped around how our clients want to live and thoughtfully connected to its unique place. This recognition celebrates the creativity of our team and the collaboration that brings each client’s vision to life.”
About Knickerbocker Group.
For nearly 50 years, Knickerbocker Group has designed, built, and cared for homes, buildings, and properties across Maine. scales from focused renovations to full property development.

title: Crouse House Roasters to open cafe in downtown Lewiston
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LEWISTON — Vicky and Damon Crouse have partnered with coffee roaster Travis Spear to up their game and open a cafe in downtown Lewiston at 291 Lisbon St.
In a video post to social media, Crouse House Roasters, which opened in early 2024, announced its plans to open the cafe through a Kickstarter campaign to raise $20,000 in the next 60 days.
It will be competing with Forage Market and Blue Jay Coffee downtown, where Fifth Pillar Tea House opened in July. All three market themselves as community spots where people can gather and enjoy a coffee or tea, something the Crouses hope to replicate with their new cafe.
“While downtown Lewiston surely presents its challenges, it’s a community our team cares deeply about. We are so excited to bring a specialty coffee shop to downtown Lewiston,” the Crouses wrote in their campaign pitch on Kickstarter.
Kickstarter is a crowdfunding platform that allows people to fund projects or businesses through donations in a set timeframe (1-60 days). Pledging money gives you access to rewards such as merchandise or discounts, but not equity, shares or financial return on investment.
The Crouses have been connected with The Root Cellar for years, and it’s where they started Common Grounds Cafe in early 2022, in the basement of the nonprofit. The cafe was established to help teens learn what it takes to run a business.
Vicky is the director of operations at The Root Cellar at 88 Birch St., while Damon left the organization in May.
The Crouses hired Travis Spear as their roaster in 2025. He was formerly the head roaster at Side By Each Brewing in Auburn until it closed in December 2024.
Damon Crouse said Wednesday that the plan is to have Spear man the roaster and store they have been running part time at 25 Landry Road in Lewiston, while he runs the new cafe.
The building on Lisbon Street is across from the former police station and just down from Cedar Street. Crouse said the landlord is renovating the building and they will fit out the cafe once that is completed.
But the store requires a change of use permit from the city and must still be permitted and inspected.
Crouse is optimistically hoping for a February opening of the cafe. Plans also call for a small bakery, but funds for that aspect of the business have not been secured at this point.

title: Want more fireflies next summer? Do fewer chores this fall
text:
Want more fireflies next summer? Do fewer chores this fall
Want to see more fireflies next summer? There's one big chore you can skip as leaves begin to fall.
As autumn leaves blanket yards, homeowners can put away the rake and leave some leaf litter in garden beds or along property edges. It turns out those fallen leaves are a perfect environment for fireflies -- and other insects -- to thrive.
Related video above | Pennsylvania fireflies stun viewers at Allegheny National Forest night displays
Like many insects, fireflies go through multiple life stages.
The larvae look almost nothing like the adults that light up the summer sky. They often have a long, almost worm-like body and most do not have any wings or have short wings that they cannot use for flying, according to officials with the National Wildlife Federation.
And for years, those fireflies live out of sight. A prime habitat for them is beneath the leaves.
While each firefly species is different, many fireflies spend their larval stage hiding in damp leaf litter or soil, where moisture helps some breathe and small creatures such as snails provide food.
The blanket of leaves also keeps the larvae warm and hidden through winter, until they’re ready to emerge as adults. Depending on the species, this hidden stage can last several years.
So that layer of leaves isn’t just yard debris — it’s a crucial habitat for the next generation of fireflies.
According to the National Wildlife Federation, fireflies are disappearing across the U.S., and how Americans maintain their yards is a big reason why.
When those leaves are raked and thrown into trash bins, it's getting rid of that leaf layer many fireflies need to survive. Oftentimes, the larvae themselves are put into the waste bags.
"To help save the fireflies, you can avoid the yard-waste bags. Instead, opt to intentionally use the fallen leaves in your yard. You can rake the leaves off your paths and lawn and move them to create a beneficial leaf layer in your garden beds and around the base of trees. Leaving the leaves doesn’t just benefit fireflies, but dozens of other wildlife species that depend on it to survive!" writes Tess Renusch, an environmental educator with the National Wildlife Federation.
Even leaving just a corner of your yard untouched can make a big difference. Not only does it help fireflies, but dozens of other species rely on it to survive.

title: A handful of preservationists are keeping Maine’s cemeteries alive
text:
KENNEBUNKPORT — Judson Star chiseled a flaky gray substance from a piece of the broken headstone.
“It looks like someone tried to repair it with some type of goop,” he said. It crumbled in his fingers. A bathroom caulk, he guessed, not the preservation-grade epoxy that he brought in his white pick-up truck and mixed on a paper plate.
The fractured stone in Arundel Cemetery in Kennebunkport captured Star’s attention on a windy October morning. It was still upright when he started working a little after 10 a.m., but it wasn’t stable. The bottom right corner was fractured into three pieces, and wobbled under just a little pressure.
After he gently removed the layer of caulk, Star applied the epoxy with a popsicle stick. He slid the stones together like a puzzle, making sure the lines of the epitaph were flush. He clamped wood planks to the stone to hold it in place while it cured for 24 hours.
Star is a professional gravestone conservator who travels all over the state repairing headstones. He works in about 20 cemeteries a year, typically from May through November (the epoxies and mortars don’t cooperate once temperatures consistently drop below 45 degrees).
In about half of the towns he works in, there are dedicated volunteers who work alongside him tackling simpler tasks like cleaning or righting a leaning stone. They ask him questions, and he is always happy to lend a tool. He likes it when they tell him about the histories of the people buried there.
“There’s a lot of things that you could know about preservation, and there are hundreds of stones that need to be worked on in each town,” he said. He teaches the enthusiastic some of his skills, so they can be a little more self-sufficient with ongoing cemetery maintenance.
NEED FOR REPAIR
There are more than 7,800 cemeteries in the state, including historic and modern burial grounds, family cemeteries and single graves, according to Walter Guptill, president of the Maine Old Cemetery Association.
“People buried their family members up on the hillside,” he said. Over time, roads changed, and some were reclaimed by woods. About 1,200 still haven’t been physically located, and that’s after MOCA volunteers found 500 cemeteries over the last two years.
Many of them are small, with 30 burials or fewer. Sometimes, it’s just a grave or two, or a base in the middle of a field, Guptill said.
The number of professional conservators pales in comparison to the preservation needs. Star is just one of about a dozen in the state, Guptill said.
So it’s often up to municipal employees, cemetery and conservation committees, descendants, historical societies and community volunteers to find and maintain these cemeteries.
“The gap is not a lack of interest or good intentions,” Guptill said. “It’s the shortage of trained people, reliable guidance, funding and organized local stewardship needed to care for thousands of cemeteries across Maine.”
LEARN TO DO NO HARM
MOCA hosts workshops and training to pass on the art of conservation to the people who are trying to keep local cemeteries alive.
Lesson one is to do no harm, Guptill said. Lesson two is to only work within the limits of your training.
There’s an adage among cemetery aficionados, Guptill said. “More damage is done in cemeteries by people with good intentions than by vandals.”
Improper cleaning and repair techniques can cause permanent damage. Despite what one might think, bleach and other household cleaners shouldn’t be used on gravestones, Guptill said. Over time, the residue causes discoloration. And if you don’t use a soft bristle brush on marble, for example, you can take away parts of the surface, a phenomenon known as “sugaring.”
“People are out there trying to make it better, and we want to harness that energy with the right skillset, so that people are not only doing good but doing good in the right way,” he said. There’s a risk in overcleaning, if you can imagine, he said.
To grow the pool of experts in the state, MOCA hosts two types of workshops: a one-day gravestone cleaning class and an annual, four-day repair boot camp. The nonprofit provides the instructor and materials. Towns can volunteer their cemeteries as training grounds, so overdue repair work gets completed.
The group also has training videos and resources for people who have lingering questions.
There are three aspects of preservation work, according to Star: moving and lifting the stone, which he does with an aluminum tripod that can hoist up to a ton of weight; prepping the ground, often with gardening tools like shovels, tampers and loppers; and repairing the actual stone, which requires epoxies, mortar and lime.
Star has spent about $10,000 on equipment over the past six years. He keeps a lot of it in the trunk of his truck. (He owns more than 20 orange Home Depot buckets, and keeps the components, like a plastic container of special sand, ready to mix mortar at a moment’s notice.)
He charges a per diem rate. “To fix a stone costs hundreds of dollars,” he said. “Not thousands.”
Star recognizes that municipalities might not have more than a few thousand dollars for cemetery maintenance in any given year, with most of that budget eaten up by mowing and tree care costs.
But proper cleaning techniques can be taught in a day, Guptill said, and you can see the results instantly.
“Have the courage to start,” Guptill said.
START WITH ENTHUSIASM
Star began as an enthusiastic volunteer. Or rather, he started out as someone who didn’t really think twice about cemeteries.
But that changed when his wife’s parents died in short succession, and both of them were buried in Arundel Cemetery.
“Now that we had family there, there was a lot more connection,” he said. “You’re no longer just driving by.”
He started helping out with fall and spring cleanups, picking up sticks and debris. He realized that cemeteries can be happy places, and that good people take care of them. He joined the board about 10 years ago, and in 2019, started his business, Maintain the Memory, cleaning gravestones locally. His town of Kennebunkport has 75 cemeteries, which kept him busy in the beginning.
On this particular October morning, he worked a stone’s throw away from the first grave he ever repaired, in the same cemetery where he discovered his love of preservation.
About a year after starting his business, he wanted to expand his skillset. He participated in the MOCA four-day workshop. He joined the MOCA board, and slowly acquired specialty equipment, like an aluminum tripod and different kinds of mortars. His business grew by word of mouth.
“There’s something deeper than just fixing a stone,” he said. “There’s an emotional aspect. I hope somebody’s doing this for my stone in a couple hundred years if it needs it.”
BREATHING NEW LIFE
Sometimes the preservation work can be dramatic, breathing new life into what was once dilapidated or unrecognizable.
Wescott Cemetery in South Portland didn’t look like a burial ground for decades. A vandal had knocked over all the stones sometime before the 1980s, and the pieces were stored in a shed until this summer, when the historical society received a $5,000 donation from Peter and Muffet Wright to aid their restoration.
Kathy DiPhilippo, the historical society’s executive director, had been tending to this small family cemetery tucked in a residential neighborhood of Thornton Heights for years. This summer, she went to MOCA’s four-day training with her husband, and connected with Star through the group.
Together with the help of a small group of experienced volunteers, they put nearly 20 stones back together, including one that had been fractured into 13 pieces. Viewed in sunlight weeks later, it glowed like a stained glass window.
“It’s incredible,” DiPhilippo said.
Over the years, Star has worked with a lot of volunteers. He said restorations usually trace back to one or two people who care.
“It just takes someone saying we need to do something,” he said.

title: Brothers, 3 and 5, found dead in pond after sneaking out of apartment while mom napped
text:
DAYTONA BEACH, Fla. (WKMG) - Police in Florida say the bodies of two young brothers who snuck out of their apartment while their mother was taking a nap were found in a pond nearby.
Two brothers – 3-year-old Kashh and 5-year-old Elijah – were reported missing Saturday before their bodies were discovered in a pond near their Daytona Beach apartment complex. Police say Elijah had autism and noted that many children with autism are drawn to water.
Daytona Beach Police Chief Jakari Young said investigators believe the boys’ deaths were accidental and that there is no indication of foul play.
“This is your greatest nightmare – to lose both of your children in that fashion,” Young said.
According to Young, the brothers’ single mother fed them about 5 p.m. Saturday before lying down for a short nap. When she woke up about 15 minutes later, both boys – along with the family dog – had gotten out of the apartment.
“She does have a child safety lock on the door, so apparently, they figured out how to navigate that child safety lock, and they exited the apartment,” Young said.
Police say surveillance video shows the kids running around then going into the pond. Moments later, their mother is seen on the video coming outside.
“She was trying to do her due diligence to see if she could locate the children before calling 911,” Young said. “But by then, based on what we can see now on the surveillance video, they were already submerged in the water.”
While Young believes the deaths were accidental, the case has been handed over to the State Attorney’s Office, which will decide whether the mother will face any charges.
Neighbors say they hope the apartment complex will put up fencing or other protections at the pond.

title: Six Flags Over Georgia set to reopen on Friday after deadly roller coaster accident
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) — Six Flags Over Georgia is set to reopen on Friday, just four days after a man was killed when he fell off a roller coaster.
Six Flags Over Georgia’s website shows the park will reopen Friday.
In a statement, the park’s management called safety its “highest priority.”
“While we are unable to comment on specifics related to the incident or currently closed rides at this time, we are committed to rigorous ride inspection, maintenance and safety procedures that meet or exceed industry standards,” officials added.
PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Six Flags Over Georgia roller coaster death: Everything we know
On Monday, 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was ejected from the Goliath roller coaster, hitting other patrons on the ride, according to Cobb County police. His body was found underneath the attraction, and the park was evacuated.
The death is still under investigation, with no official cause given yet.
In the wake of the accident, Six Flags temporarily shut down nine rides across six parks that were similar to Goliath. The coaster — which goes up to 70 mph, has a maximum elevation of 200 feet and drops twice — uses clamshell lap restraints to secure passengers.
Kariem was a beloved teacher at Wesley International Academy, a K-8 charter school in Atlanta. Soledad Gomez, one of his former students, described him as a joyful man.
“I always just remember his smile and his glasses, and it’s just like, he never got mad at us. He was always patient with us. He would joke with us,” Gomez said.
In a statement, Six Flags said it’s cooperating with the police investigation.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends, and loved ones. We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected,” a Six Flags spokesperson said. “The park team and local authorities responded immediately, and we are cooperating fully with local authorities as they complete their investigation. Out of respect for the family’s privacy, we will not be sharing additional details at this time.”
Since Kariem’s death, Six Flags has temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six parks “out of an abundance of caution.” Officials said the affected attractions are similar to Goliath, which only uses a lap bar to secure riders.
Though Six Flags Over Georgia will reopen Friday, Goliath will remain temporarily closed. In a statement, the park’s president said Goliath does not have an anticipated reopening date yet.

title: Here’s what’s on the ballot in Augusta
text:
With Election Day coming up Nov. 3 and early voting already underway, it’s timefor voters to start thinking about what’s on the ballot.
On the state and national level, voters will choose candidates for the Maine State Legislature, governor and U.S. House of Representatives and Senate. Locally, school board and City Council seats are up for election, and Augusta voters will weigh in on three referendum questions.
Many of the candidates participated in the Press Herald Voter Guide, where readers can learn more about each race.
Voting is set to take place from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 3, at the Augusta Civic Center, 76 Community Drive, Augusta. Early voting is available through Oct. 29 at Augusta City Hall, 16 Cony St., Augusta.
Here’s what to expect on the local Augusta ballot.
CITY COUNCIL
At-large seat: Daniel Burns, Saunders Nash Callahan
Two candidates are running for an At-large City Council seat currently held by Courtney Gary-Allen, who is not running for reelection.
Saunders Nash Callahan is a lifelong Augusta resident and the owner of Capital City Cycles LLC. His top three priorities are homelessness and housing affordability, improving transportation infrastructure and strengthening community engagement and communication with the community.
Callahan said he wants to help the City Council become “proactive in its decision-making rather than reactive,” saying city officials often don’t anticipate challenges as they arise, thereby delaying solutions and exacerbating issues.
Daniel Burns did not respond to the Voter Guide survey.
Ward 1: Robert Eric Austin
Current Ward 1 Councilor Robert Eric Austin is running unopposed for reelection. Austin, who did not fill out the Voter Guide survey, was first elected in 2023 and is running for his second term.
Ward 4: Mike Karagiannes
Mike Karagiannes is running unopposed to replace Eric Lind, the current Ward 4 councilor. Lind has served three consecutive terms since taking office in 2018, making him ineligible to run this year.
Karagiannes, a soon-to-be retired Maine Department of Environmental Protection employee and lifelong Augusta resident, thinks that issues of homelessness and substance use in Augusta need to be addressed with a “balanced approach” and that taxpayers should be getting value for every dollar they spend. He also wants to see pride and optimism restored in Augusta, making it a place where families want to live and businesses want to build and invest.
SCHOOL BOARD
At-large seat: Colton Brann
Colton Brann is running unopposed to replace current At-large Member Charles Hicks, who is not running for reelection. Brann did not fill out the Voter Guide survey.
Ward 2 seat: Sheldon Hussiere
Sheldon Hussiere is uncontested in his race to replace current Ward 2 Member Susan Parks, who is not running for reelection.
Hussiere, a CGI animator and security guard, says his top three priorities are to build a stronger support structure for educators, to create more opportunities for students and to maintain strong education without “taxing my neighbors out of their homes.” Hussiere also wants to focus on supporting students in finding opportunities after graduation and improving fiscal responsibility within the school district.
Board of Education chair: Martha Witham, William Clardy
William Clardy is running against incumbent Martha Witham, who has served as chair of the school board since 2023.
Witham, who also held the Ward 2 seat starting in 2020, is an educational consultant and a retired school administrator. She hopes to continue leading the school board with a focus on providing high-quality education for all students and raising achievement levels despite funding constraints.
Clardy, a database developer and veteran, formerly ran for the Ward 4 school board seat in 2025 and lost to Bobby-Jo Bechard. He is focused on ensuring the school department becomes fiscally accountable and encouraging transparency, accountability and honest debate between the school department and members of the public.
REFERENDUMS
Question 1: Repairs and improvements bond
Augusta residents will vote on whether to borrow $7.37 million to fund new equipment and a mechanical study for renovations at the Augusta Civic Center; improvements and repairs to the Calumet Park swimming pool, the Hartford Fire Station and Department of Public Works garage; the purchase of a replacement rescue vehicle for Augusta Fire and Rescue; and improvements to streets, sidewalks and related facilities. A yes vote will permit the city to borrow the funds.
Question 2: Farrington School expansion and renovation bond
The Augusta School Department is planning to renovate and expand the Farrington Elementary School, resulting in the closure of the Lillian P. Hussey Elementary School. The referendum question asks voters if they authorize the city to borrow $53.57 million to fund the project. If the referendum passes, the renovation will be fully funded by the state with no cost to Augusta taxpayers.
Question 3: Mobile home park lot rent stabilization
Augusta residents successfully organized a citizens’ initiative for a proposed ordinance seeking to prevent significant increases in mobile home lot rent through regulations, including limiting annual rent increases to 3% or the rate of inflation (whichever is lower). A yes vote means the ordinance will be enacted to further regulate mobile home park lot rents. A no vote means the ordinance will not be enacted.
OTHER RACES
Voters in State Senate District 15 will decide between Amanda Heath, a Democrat, and Kati McCormick, a Republican.
In State House District 59, the race is between Democrat Katrina Ray-Saulis and Republican John Reny.
Democrat William “Bill” Bridgeo is seeking reelection for State House District 60 against Republican Wyatt Beaulieu.
Read more about all of the candidates on the Press Herald Voter Guide.

title: Concerned by pro-Susan Collins and pro-Trump bias
text:
I would like to voice my concern with the subtle manner in which the editors of these papers seem to inject a positive bias toward Sen. Susan Collins and President Donald Trump.
It is not obvious, but on a daily basis on the front page there are banners of Collins being endorsed or quoting her disapproval of a Trump policy, even though it has no bearing on her track record. The same could be said with banners or titles of articles that quote Trump making statements that are factually false or laced with his usual aggrandizement and embellishment, where his track record is one of meaningless promises, fabrication and obfuscation.
It is one thing for the paper to describe factual issues and another to parrot the spin doctor of the current administration and majority party.
One can only feel that the incredible amount of money being funded to this state for this election cycle through dark money organizations/individuals are affecting the information that everyday citizens see when trying to understand their choices this November.
I would suggest that there should be a disclaimer by the paper of large-font statements, if those statement describe a promise or a policy that never will see the light of day or have been repeated multiple times without proof that they reflect reality.
Daniel Robbins
Portland

title: Texas prosecutor says ICE agent appeared to intentionally strike man with vehicle
text:
Texas prosecutor says ICE agent appeared to intentionally strike man with vehicle in Houston
A Texas prosecutor says a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent appeared to use a vehicle to intentionally strike a man who took off running in Houston and that an investigation opened by his office could result in criminal charges.
Related video: New York City police commissioner briefs reporters after ICE shooting
Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, needed surgery for a broken leg after being hit by a car Saturday, said Cesar Espinosa, executive director of FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights organization that is helping the man's family.
The encounter has set off new criticism over immigration enforcement in Houston, where local prosecutors have also investigated a July fatal shooting by a federal immigration officer.
Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, expressed concern over surveillance footage that shows Parra Hernandez and another person jumping out of a white truck and running as a dark SUV pursues them. A vehicle strikes Parra Hernandez, who is seen on the ground seconds later.
“In a case like this, the most obvious criminal charge is aggravated assault with a deadly weapon,” Teare told FOX 26 Houston. “Meaning the car was used as a deadly weapon. And it certainly is what appears to have happened based on the surveillance footage.”
Tim Oberle, a spokesperson for ICE in Houston, said in a statement sent to The Texas Tribune on Saturday that, “As ICE officers attempted to apprehend the illegal aliens, Miguel Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”
Spokespersons for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Tuesday.
Parra Hernandez has been in the U.S. for 34 years and was on his way to work when the encounter began, according to Espinosa. Espinosa declined to share Parra Hernandez’s status.
He said he saw two ICE agents in Parra Hernandez's room while visiting him at the hospital.
“He already had a surgery for the injury under his knee and now we’re waiting for swelling to go down in his ankle to be able to have a reconstructive surgery on his ankle,” Espinosa said.
Teare said ICE and DHS have not cooperated with his office during its investigation.
In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his request for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. The shooting was one of at least 10 deaths involving encounters with immigration officers since the start of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

title: SEA Maine awards grants totaling $1M to critical marine community infrastructure projects
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SEA Maine (Seafood Economic Accelerator for Maine) is pleased to award grants totaling $1 million to five marine community infrastructure projects through the Seafood Infrastructure Adaptation Fund (SIAF). The funds will help improve public marine facilities, help strengthen Maine’s seafood sector, and provide greater resilience to climate-related shocks.
“I’m pleased to see these projects benefit from SIAF funding and am optimistic that this funding will result in a stronger, more vibrant future for Maine’s commercially harvested and farmed seafood resources,” says Togue Brawn, co-chair, SEA Maine & Owner, Downeast Dayboat.
Grants ranging from $75,000 to $300,000 were awarded through a competitive process and will help fund a broad range of critical waterfront infrastructure:
Boothbay Harbor: Harbor Bait: Automated Salter and Upgraded High Producing Ice Machines - $193,406.80. Harbor Fish Pier. Installation of an automated bait salter and high-capacity flake ice machine will provide vital access to bait and ice for Maine’s commercial fishing industry.
Tremont: Tremont Cold Storage Facility Upgrade – $161,500. The project will retrofit a 1,200-square-foot town-owned building. Home to a local bait company as well as the Harbormaster, the building will be outfitted with insulation, weather-tight windows and doors, heat pumps, and electrical improvements. This work will thereby improve energy efficiency, resilience, cold-storage capacity, and year-round usability, while continuing to support working waterfront businesses and the seafood industry.
Rockland: Rockland Commercial Fish Pier: Climate Resilience Assessment, Adaptation Planning, and Infrastructure Investment – $300,000. The City of Rockland’s two-phase project will strengthen seafood supply chain resilience at the Rockland Commercial Fish Pier, serving approximately 100 commercial fishing and seafood operations. In collaboration with fish pier users, Phase 1 will assess vulnerabilities, identify adaptation opportunities, develop a site adaptation plan, and complete engineering designs. Contingent on those findings, Phase 2 will carry out the priority improvements identified, and activate the resulting adaptation plan.
Town of Freeport: Town of Freeport Cove Road - Wharf Restoration and Commercial Float Replacement – $218,400 The Town of Freeport will replace deteriorating docks and floats at three locations along the Harraseeket River: Cove Road Wharf, the Commercial River Floats, and the Freeport Town Dock. The infrastructure supports 60+ municipal shellfish license holders, commercial fishermen, lobster and aquaculture gear storage, and temporary vessel berthing. Much of the existing infrastructure has deteriorated due to storm surge, sea level rise, age, and heavy commercial use. The project will replace the piers, gangway, and floats at all three sites.
Swan's Island: Harbor Road Facility Upgrade - $126,693.20. The Town of Swan’s Island will renovate vacant space near Burnt Coat Harbor for dedicated Harbormaster and Shellfish Warden offices, supporting the island’s commercial fishing and working waterfront. Improvements include weatherization, a transition from fuel oil to heat pumps, and adding solar-powered cold storage for fishermen, clammers, and aquaculture operators. The project will strengthen working waterfront operations while adding climate-resilient, shared seafood infrastructure.
The SIAF program was developed based on the 2024 recommendations in the SEAMaine Roadmap. It is supported by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) through the Climate Resilience Regional Challenge (CRRC) awarded in Fall 2024 to the Maine Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future (GOPIF).
“SIAF is an important component of Maine’s $69 million Climate Resilience Regional Challenge Grant,” said Sarah Curran, director of the Governor’s Office of Policy Innovation and the Future (GOPIF). “This unprecedented Federal grant is helping to strengthen resilience to climate effects, especially extreme storms like those that hit Maine in 2023 and 2024. The Seafood Infrastructure Adaptation Fund’s targeted investments are making the seafood sector more energy efficient and protecting its supply chains for the future, building essential resilience to economic and environmental shocks along the Maine coast.”
Community entities were invited to apply for grants to cover planning, engineering, retrofits, and/or design projects for construction on publicly owned land, tribal land, or land where a public entity holds a lease or easement that ensures public access. Eligible entities included municipal (county, state, tribal), nonprofits, business owners, private property owners, and educational organizations representing publicly owned infrastructure. Grantees will contribute a 5% match of the total project cost.
“The announcement of the projects funded through the Seafood Infrastructure Adaptation Fund could not be timelier, coming on the heels of Maine’s Blue Economy Week,” says Carl Wilson, commissioner of the Department of Marine Resources (DMR). “It is a great example of how investments supporting commercial fishing and aquaculture at the local level can help ensure resilience and drive innovation that will shape the future of Maine’s coast. I appreciate the work done by SEAMaine and the Maine Development Foundation to guide this process and bring these worthy projects to fruition.”
“Investing in Maine’s working waterfront infrastructure is vital to the future of our seafood industry and the coastal communities that depend on it,” says U.S. Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME). “These funding awards will support improvements to public marine facilities that will help Maine’s seafood sector better withstand disruptions and remain competitive for years to come.”
“For generations, the success and sustainability of Maine’s coastal communities have been at the center of our prosperity as a state. When our ‘Blue Economy’ grows and thrives, so does Maine,” says U.S. Senator Angus King (I-ME). “Thanks to this new funding our local fishers and sea farmers will continue to expand economic opportunity, create good-paying jobs, and improve sustainability across Maine’s coastal communities - and be more able to handle any choppy waters they encounter. I am proud to continue our work securing this critical federal funding so that our coastal communities have safe, sound infrastructure that is necessary to continue their important work.”
“Maine’s working waterfronts are vital to our state’s economy, culture, and way of life. But aging infrastructure and increasingly severe storms—like the ones that ravaged so many coastal communities three years ago—are putting more and more pressure on our fishermen, lobstermen, aquaculture operators, and the many businesses that keep our waterfronts working,” says U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-ME). “These grants will help communities make much-needed investments in critical infrastructure so they can continue to provide the products, services, and good-paying jobs our state needs to thrive. I’m grateful to SEA Maine and its many partners for their unwavering dedication to Maine’s working waterfronts and coastal communities, and for helping ensure that Maine’s seafood economy remains strong and resilient for generations to come.”
“My district is home to thousands of hardworking men and women who power some of the most storied and successful fisheries in the world,” says U.S. Rep. Jared Golden (D-ME). “The families and communities that depend on them are worth supporting and protecting. That’s why I’m always pleased to see federal dollars such as these SIAF funds going to support worthwhile infrastructure investments in Maine’s marine resources economy. The funded projects in Tremont and Swan’s Island will help these two working waterfronts meet current and future needs so that fishermen can keep doing what they do best.”
MDF is proud to partner with SEA Maine (Seafood Economic Accelerator) and serve as the program manager for the initiative. The SEA Maine Steering Committee includes over 100 members from across Maine including industry, associations, nonprofits, academia, state agencies, and Maine's federal delegation. In addition to SIAF, SEAMaine is working on other strategies to grow the industry, including the establishment of a Maine Seafood Promotion Council.

title: Former Cumberland County district attorney outraises incumbent in campaign contributions
text:
Stephanie Anderson has outraised incumbent Jacqueline Sartoris in campaign contributions, as both vie to be elected district attorney in Cumberland County.
A quarter of Anderson’s donors are attorneys, records show.
Sartoris, a Democrat from Brunswick, was elected in 2022 and recently won her party’s nomination in a June primary against one of her former prosecutors. As of Sept. 1, Sartoris had raised $35,000, including $15,000 in loans, according to campaign finance records. Most of that was received before June 9 and roughly $4,500 came from eight contributors after the primary election.
Anderson, who was district attorney for 28 years before retiring in 2018, had raised more than $69,000 as of Sept. 14. At least 40 contributions came from practicing and retired Maine attorneys, according to an analysis of campaign finance records and a directory run by the Maine Board of Overseers of the Bar.
“I think that really tells you a lot,” said Jennifer Ackerman, a long-time Cumberland County prosecutor who worked under Anderson for 16 years, including seven years as her deputy.
Publicly, the two candidates have sparred about who is most qualified to prosecute what are known as “quality of life crimes,” like public drug use and disorderly conduct, and about the implementation of progressive reforms.
Inside the courthouse, attorneys who have donated to Anderson’s campaign have complained about Sartoris’ leadership. Anderson said she was approached by prosecutors and defense attorneys, “across the political spectrum,” asking her to run. Anderson is running as an unenrolled candidate.
“I mean, I go by yards with my sign beside Troy Jackson signs,” said Anderson, who was reelected seven times as a Republican. “This is an elected position, but it’s not partisan and it should not be politicized.”
Sartoris has said she is aware of discontent among defense attorneys and several prosecutors who have left the office and spoken out publicly, including Ackerman and Valerie Adams, who lost to Sartoris in the Democratic primary.
Sartoris has said it’s proof that she’s making the changes that she promised voters in 2022. In debates and forums, she’s highlighted her recent efforts through a federal grant to inventory untested rape kits, and a recent revamp of the county’s existing restorative justice options.
“This is not a popularity contest for lawyers, who usually want to preserve the status quo,” Sartoris said in a statement. “I ran to bring long-needed change to the people of Cumberland County. I have more regular people on my side, with more donors and more small dollar donations than Anderson. Soliciting money from defense attorneys seems like a conflict of interest.”
Sartoris’ primary campaign four years ago drew an unprecedented $300,000 from an out-of-state political action committee funded by Democratic donor George Soros. The candidates still have another week before they file their newest campaign finance reports. Anderson said on Thursday she has raised another $14,000 in individual contributions since mid-September.
Anderson also serves and is running for another term on the Cape Elizabeth Town Council. She says she has not fundraised for that race.
ENDORSEMENTS
At least eight individuals who have contributed to Sartoris’ campaign this year are attorneys, according to records from the bar and campaign finance reports.
John Kaminski, who donated to her campaign in September and is an attorney focused on affordable housing, praised Sartoris for her work on homelessness and for directing police to share evidence from bike and pedestrian crashes.
“I think she’s had a solid four years in office and will continue to move things forward when she’s reelected,” Kaminski said.
Rep. Grayson Lookner, a Democrat in Portland, said Sartoris has been supportive of his legislative proposals to improve public safety, particularly for diverting at-risk youth from the criminal justice system. House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, a Democrat in Biddeford, said he endorsed Sartoris because of her opponent’s Republican history.
“We’re seeing this across the state that the Republican brand is so bad, that they’ve decided to put a cloak over that label and have ‘unenrolled’ candidates,” Fecteau said. “Voters should know that we have a very strong Democratic district attorney in Jackie.”
Anderson says she believes Sartoris is using the Democratic nomination to her advantage because she doesn’t have enough to highlight from her four years in office. Anderson also accused Sartoris of distorting her remarks.
At a forum hosted by Scarborough town leaders in September, Sartoris accused Anderson of having expressed a desire to work with federal immigration officials.
“I never said that local law enforcement should cooperate with ICE,” Anderson said in an interview, noting that state law restricts police from working with federal immigration officials. “I think I said there’s been a lot of injustices with ICE and it’s been pretty horrific. And why is that a big campaign issue?”
Sartoris previously stated her intent to prosecute agents who commit violent offenses without cause in her district. She has not charged any agents to date.
Anderson suggested the attorneys supporting her campaign “are the people that are paying attention to what’s going on to the DA’s office and what’s going on in the community regarding public safety.” She also highlighted endorsements from three police unions as evidence of her ability to work with law enforcement on prosecuting cases.
Scot Mattox, an attorney who was a Portland police officer for more than 20 years, said he probably arrested more than 1,000 people whose cases Anderson prosecuted.
“Stephanie recognized that a district attorney’s duty is not merely to secure convictions, but to administer justice fairly,” Mattox said in an email.
Former employees who spoke to the Portland Press Herald said they appreciated Anderson’s mentorship and her knowledge of criminal law.
“We can all agree, despite our different professional experiences, that when people like where they work, they care, they work harder, and the morale is stronger,” said defense attorney Kate Marshall, who interned for Anderson and later returned to the office as an assistant district attorney. “This can only benefit the community to which the office serves.”
CRITICISMS
Ackerman said she resigned less than a year after Sartoris took over. Ackerman, who now works for the state, said she was speaking only on her own behalf.
Adams worked in the district attorney’s office for about nine months. Adams was fired by Sartoris after she and a defense attorney asked Sartoris to consider not running.
Adams and Ackerman have both likened Sartoris’ office to a “ship without a captain.”
“She was very much focused on saying what she wanted to do in terms of policies, but the day-to-day work, and the day-to-day policies that our prosecutors needed, we weren’t getting answers,” Ackerman said.
Others have criticized Sartoris’ work in court, saying criminal cases are languishing and that she has at times gone beyond what they believe to be appropriate for her role.
“For me, that makes life for defendants and people who are caught up in the criminal justice system harder,” said defense attorney Rob Andrews.
On the mental health docket, Sartoris said she has dedicated much of her focus on defendants whose mental health might lead them to be found incompetent to stand trial, or not criminally responsible. Attorney Alison Brauner said Sartoris has pushed for forcible medication and the disclosure of clients’ sensitive health information.
“A criminal defendant doesn’t lose their right to privacy around their medical care,” Brauner said.
In a statement, Sartoris said she “will not apologize for asking a judge to medicate people, always at the request of an expert, when their untreated psychotic disorders are causing repeated criminal conduct.”

title: Juvenile charged after hoax bomb threat leads to evacuation of Waterville school, police say
text:
Juvenile charged after hoax bomb threat leads to evacuation of Waterville High School, police say
The Waterville Police Department says a juvenile has been charged in connection with a hoax bomb threat that prompted the evacuation of Waterville High School on Wednesday.
Police said that officers responded to the high school at about 7 a.m. for a reported bomb threat. The school was evacuated and searched out of an abundance of caution, and the threat was deemed to be a hoax, according to officials.
Authorities identified the juvenile who made the hoax threat, and police said that juvenile was "charged appropriately."
Police said the investigation into the threat remains active, so all Waterville High School students and staff members have been dismissed for the day. The school is expected to reopen as scheduled on Thursday.

Joni Mitchell is now an American citizen, six decades after moving to the US
text:
Joni Mitchell is now an American citizen, six decades after moving to the US
Joni Mitchell has finally become an American citizen, more than 60 years after leaving her native Canada.
Video above: Joni Mitchell honored as MusiCares Person of the Year in 2022
The legendary singer-songwriter posted a picture of herself holding a U.S. flag at the naturalization ceremony on Tuesday, with the caption: “A journey that began 62 years ago.”
In the image shared with her more than 1 million Instagram followers, a smiling Mitchell wore a red beret and sunglasses, and extra stars and stripes pinned to her cardigan lapel.
Mitchell, who turns 83 next month and was using a walking stick, also posted a short video clip from the ceremony, in which she was applauded by others gathered in the room.
Born in Fort Macleod in Alberta, Canada, in 1943, Mitchell will continue to have a Canadian passport as both countries allow residents to hold dual citizenship.
The iconic artist, who was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1997 and won a Lifetime Achievement Award at the Grammys in 2002, is best known for 1970s hits such as “Big Yellow Taxi,” “Blue,” “Amelia” and “Woodstock.”
She studied commercial art in Alberta before moving to Toronto in 1964, where she performed at local folk club and coffee houses. Then, during a brief marriage to folk singer Chuck Mitchell, she lived in Detroit before eventually relocating to New York City. It was there that she made her eponymous album, also known as “Song to a Seagull.”
Mitchell, who has 19 studio albums and six live records to her name, later moved to Los Angeles, where she settled in the city’s Laurel Canyon before later moving to Bel Air.
It is unclear why Mitchell chose this time, when relations between Canada and the U.S. are particularly strained, to become an American. She was widely reported to have taken a swipe at President Donald Trump while performing at the Hollywood Bowl ahead of the last presidential election in 2024.
According to media reports at the time, the noted protest singer encouraged her audience to go to the polls: “Everybody get out and vote. This is an important one. I wish I could vote — I’m Canadian. I’m one of those lousy immigrants.”
Mitchell has suffered from a series of health problems in recent years, including a stroke and a brain aneurysm in 2015.
Her health setbacks did not stop her from performing at the 2024 Grammys, where she won the award for best folk album for her 2023 release “Joni Mitchell at Newport.” This year she also received a Lifetime Achievement Award at the Junos, Canada’s equivalent of the Grammys.
An as yet untitled biopic of Mitchell’s life is said to be in development, with IMDb listing Cameron Crowe as the director and Meryl Streep in the starring role.

title: A Maine hunter just accomplished his lifelong dream in a 12-minute hunt
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
Auburn resident Wyatt Morse has been bowhunting since he was 10. He hasn’t shot a deer with a rifle since.
“Ever since my dad put a bow in my hand, I haven’t looked back,” he said.
Morse, 23, has bowhunted across the country, including in Kansas, Wisconsin, Ohio, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Illinois. But on Saturday, Oct. 10, he achieved a goal he had pursued for years: shooting a Maine deer weighing more than 200 pounds with his bow.
The buck weighed 211 pounds and was taken in Wildlife Management District 21, where 4,372 antlerless permits remained available for purchase as of Oct. 13. The district has high deer numbers, but extensive development and limited public land can make finding places to hunt challenging. For Morse, taking a buck of this size on public land made the accomplishment especially meaningful.
“Every state presents its own challenges,” he said, “but hunting in areas with heavy development and a lot of people can be especially difficult.”
Morse didn’t reach his parking spot until 5 p.m. Saturday, leaving him a mile-long hike to his hunting location as daylight faded.
“I knew where the bucks were likely bedding and feeding in the area, and I figured if I could slip in at the right time and the stars aligned, I might have a chance,” he said.
He climbed into his saddle hunting setup around 6 p.m. and noticed the wind and thermals were working in his favor.
He was hunting along a thick, narrow trail with little room for error. If a buck passed through while he wasn’t paying attention, it could spot him before he had a chance to shoot.
At about 6:05 p.m., he heard what sounded like a tree being thrashed. Moments later, he caught a glimpse of a tail and antlers through the thick cover.
The buck slowly fed closer before moving down the trail toward Morse. When it picked up his ground scent, it froze and stared in his direction.
Morse realized the buck wasn’t going to continue toward him. When it finally turned to head back the way it came, he was already at full draw.
At 6:12 p.m., just 12 minutes after settling into his setup, Morse released an arrow. The buck didn’t make it 10 yards before falling.
“This buck represents so much more than just the weight on a scale,” he said. “It’s the countless miles walked, the hours spent spring scouting, the lessons learned and the dedication to becoming a better bowhunter.”
Recovering the deer took considerably longer than the hunt. With help from a friend, Morse dragged the buck a half-mile uphill and didn’t get home until 1 a.m.
Morse credits his father with playing a major role in his development as a bowhunter. The two have traveled across the country together to pursue whitetails.
His next goal is to harvest a Boone and Crockett-class buck with his bow.
Morse also is part of Maine Whitetail Tactics, a bowhunting group that helps hunters develop their skills and find success in Maine’s woods. The group shares scouting strategies and public-land hunting tactics, with a particular focus on getting more young people involved in the sport.

title: Lawsuit alleges Hannaford improperly markets some salmon products as sustainable
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A class-action lawsuit filed this week alleges that Hannaford and its parent company display “misleading sustainability guarantees” in the grocery chain’s seafood sections.
The complaint, filed Tuesday in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York, narrows in on salmon products that it claims are not sustainably sourced, as in-store signage suggests.
A Hannaford spokesperson said Wednesday that the company does not comment on pending litigation and that neither the Scarborough-based grocer nor its Dutch parent company, Ahold Delhaize, had received the complaint.
The suit states that Hannaford stores all contain signs that indicate their seafood products are sustainably sourced, including ones reading, “We sell only high-quality, traceable and sustainably harvested seafood,” and “Every fish has a tale. Ours you can trust.”
“In reality, Hannaford sells industrially farmed salmon whose production inflicts grave harms on pristine marine ecosystems and has caused the destruction of marine life around the world, from Canada to Chile,” the lawsuit says.
The 76-page complaint includes numerous pictures of signage at Hannaford locations and products in question.
The lead plaintiff in the suit is Kathleen Boyle, of Queensbury, New York. It states she purchased at least some of the products cited at Hannaford stores in New York throughout 2025 and 2026, believing they were “sourced from suppliers whose practices did not harm marine ecosystems” and were otherwise sustainable.
The lawsuit includes as class members anyone who bought any of the products in question in New York within the statute of limitations. The complaint says that the plaintiff believes there are thousands of people who fit this description.
The suit focuses on salmon products predominantly sourced overseas, though some stem from Maine and elsewhere in the United States. It argues those products are not truly sustainable, citing reports of mass mortality events, and details many regions’ salmon farming practices — especially in Chile, where it says some suppliers have histories of overproduction and farming in sensitive or protected areas.
The lawsuit notes that if Hannaford’s products are truly traceable, then it would be aware of some of these “destructive” practices. If not, “their sustainability promises were nevertheless empty and false” when it comes to those products, the complaint says.
The plaintiff is seeking a jury trial and monetary relief.

title: Special education aide accused of punching 6-year-old autistic student, telling witness ‘you did not see that’
text:
HORRY COUNTY, S.C. (WMBF/Gray News) — A special education aide is accused of punching a nonverbal student with autism and then telling a witness, “You did not see that.”
The alleged incident happened at Pee Dee Elementary School in South Carolina.
Horry County police charged Kristin Daly, 57, with unlawfully placing a child at risk of or causing harm.
Horry County police were notified on Sept. 26 about an assault that happened the day before at Pee Dee Elementary School.
A witness told police they saw Daly punch a 6-year-old nonverbal, autistic student with a closed fist, causing the student to stumble backward, according to arrest warrants.
Daly then looked at the witness and said, “You did not see that,” according to a police report.
Police said the student was not seriously injured.
The student is known to run toward people while swinging his arms, which can result in him hitting teachers and other staff members, the police report stated.
Daly began working for Horry County Schools full-time in 2022. District spokesperson Lisa Bourcier said Daly has been on administrative leave since Sept. 28.
Jail records show Daly was released from jail Monday afternoon on a $10,000 bond.
