title: Isolation is one of the hardest battles for caregivers. It doesn’t have to be.
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
When Cathyann Adams called the Aroostook Area Agency on Aging last winter, she was fast approaching her breaking point.
Her husband, Chris, was in the advanced stages of Lewy body dementia and declining fast. As his full-time caretaker, Adams felt herself slipping, too. She was desperate for a break.
The couple had moved from Vermont to Caribou a few years prior — a homecoming for Chris, who grew up in Fort Fairfield, and a new adventure for Adams.
But Chris’s diagnosis, which came shortly after their move, and his ensuing decline soon became the center of their lives, leaving little room for making friends and building a support system.
“I was alone,” said Adams, 67. “I didn’t know how I was going to go forward.”
In a rural state like Maine, the emotional and physical toll of caregiving — known as caregiver fatigue — is compounded by an isolation that aging experts say is all too common, placing both the caregivers and the people they’re caring for at greater risk of depression, illness and death.
Maine has the nation’s highest median age (44.9 years) and the highest proportion of residents ages 65 and older (24.6%), according to the U.S. Census Bureau.
Maine also is the second most rural state — 61.5% of residents live outside designated urban areas — a fact that, coupled with harsh winter weather and a lack of public transportation, makes it harder to access services and foster connection.
But aging experts also say there are ways to minimize isolation and caregiver fatigue.
Making a plan early, leaning on your community, and taking advantage of services like respite care, companionship programs, support groups and classes can all help alleviate the pressure.
RESPITE DAY PROGRAMS
Ruth White has heard many pleas for help like Adams’.
“You have such an array of emotions,” she said, ranging from happiness and pride to frustration, resentment and anger. The emotional whiplash and constant stress are exhausting.
“You don’t want to be in your head. You have to be loving and caring (but) you’re just dying,” said White, family caregiver program coordinator for the Aroostook Agency on Aging. “That’s usually the point when we start to get the people to come in.”
She often suggests they take advantage of the agency’s adult day respite center, where caregivers can leave their loved one for a few hours and step away from the demands of the job. There are similar centers across the state.
Older adult service providers say respite care is one of the most impactful resources for caregivers struggling with burnout.
“It’s so important for them to have that ability to walk away from that caregiving for a little while and get back out into the world and sort of regain a little bit of the life that they put so much thought and effort into,” said Ashley Butterfield, executive director of Bath-Brunswick Respite Care.
The Bath-based center is the only respite day program in the region, Butterfield said. They served about 40 families last year.
“I think every caregiver, no matter what stage they’re in, understands everything that they’re giving up. They understand that they do need to socialize more, they understand that they need to maintain connections, but it’s really hard,” Butterfield said. “And I think that’s really where so much of the social isolation stems from. It’s just easier to not go out into the world.”
DON’T WAIT
Jess Maurer’s No. 1 piece of advice for new caregivers is “make a plan early.”
Do not wait. Figure out now who you can lean on, and how you can get a break. The longer you wait, the harder it will be to see a way out, said Maurer, executive director of the Maine Council on Aging.
Start talking to your friends about what you might need.
Who can make a meal once a week that you can divvy up for your person throughout the week? Who can come sit with them or take them to a doctor’s appointment?
Or, if you’re dealing with more challenging behaviors, who can do your grocery shopping or take your car in for an oil change?
Ask for help with “the basic things of life that get lost,” Maurer said.
“It feels really awkward, because it feels very much like ‘This is my responsibility. I have to take care of my parent. I have to take care of myself. I shouldn’t be asking other people,'” she said. “We really have to get past that in a big way because there are so many people who are really struggling.”
Butterfield, at Bath-Brunswick Respite Care, said caregivers often put off seeking help out of a misplaced sense of guilt: It’s too early to need more solo time; it’s not that bad yet; it’s going to be much worse.
“It doesn’t need to be bad in order for a caregiver to need to maintain their own sense of self,” she said. “No caregiver should need to wait until they’re burnt out.”
A LIFESAVER
The Southern Maine Agency on Aging’s adult day program in Springvale has been a “lifesaver” for Terry Turner.
Her husband, Jack Turner, 75, was diagnosed with dementia three years ago and has been attending the day program three days a week for the last two.
He has been thriving.
“With the dementia scale, I have not seen him go down much,” said Terry Turner, 71. “He thinks he works there. That’s the only thing that gets him going is ‘OK, I gotta go to my job.’ He’s so funny. ‘I’m still waiting on a paycheck,’ he says.”
Turner, meanwhile packs as much as she can into that time.
“I don’t just sit and do nothing,” she said. “I literally use up that time for something that I would really enjoy,” like cardmaking and Bible study with her ladies group.
“I have to socialize myself with my girlfriends, in order to enjoy life, you know?” she said.
The Turners also recently converted their Springvale home into a duplex, where their daughter, 40, lives and can help out.
On days when Jack isn’t at the center, they spend time outside. Jack mows the lawn, Turner tends to her garden, a newer hobby. They dote on their three dogs, who Turner said give Jack purpose. He feeds them carrots.
If she needs to pop to the store, her neighbors or daughter might keep an eye on Jack. For now, things are manageable. She’s happy.
Turner is used to caregiving. She took care of her father, who also had dementia, years before.
“I’m OK with it, because maybe that’s what God wants me to do,” she said. “There are some tough days, and if there are, I might have a cry or whatever, and that’s OK, too.”
RESPITE POP-UPS AND COMPANIONSHIP
Six of Maine’s 16 counties don’t offer day programs. And even in counties where there are programs, some communities are simply too far away to make the trip worthwhile.
The Southern Maine Agency on Aging is trying to fill some of the gaps with a new 12-week pilot “pop-up” respite care program.
Thanks to a nearly $100,000 grant from the Alzheimer’s Association, the agency launched “Dementia Respite Without Walls” last month at the Casco Community Center.
Casco is central to areas like Bridgton, Raymond, Windham and Harrison — communities whose residents are less likely to visit the agency’s centers in Springvale, Biddeford or Portland.
Other families may feel that a day program is not the right fit.
In 2022, the state launched a two-year pilot program called Respite for ME, funded with about $5.1 million in American Rescue Plan funds.
The program, overseen by the Department of Health and Human Services and administered by the local agencies on aging, offered grants up to $2,000 in the first year and just over $5,000 in the second to people providing care to an older adult at home.
The money paid for temporary caregivers to come for a few hours of respite, including in-home care, center visits and overnight stays in a facility. The money could also be used for counseling, training, financial guidance and assistive technology.
The results were promising. While caregiver burden and stress remained at medium or high levels for most caregivers, for people participating in the second year, high stress decreased by 10% and high depression decreased by 14%, according to the pilot’s evaluation. Caregivers reported better relationships with their loved ones and less financial strain and worry.
The state Legislature made the program permanent in July 2025 (with a $2,000 limit on grants) but only allocated $100,000, leaving it effectively unfunded.
Maurer, at the Council on Aging, said advocates will be pushing for full funding for the program next year and encouraging the new governor to make it a budget priority.
A break from isolation doesn’t have to come from dedicated respite care, either.
The University of Maine’s Senior Companion Program, a partnership between the university’s Center on Aging and AmeriCorp, matches homebound, isolated older adults with volunteers ages 55 and older.
There’s also a southern Maine chapter through AmeriCorp and the Opportunity Alliance.
Jennifer Jain, director of the university program, said that while the volunteer program is centered on companionship for older adults, the benefits extend to caregivers by giving them a break.
The pairings are intended to be long-term relationships, not just one-and-done visits, Jain said, and by matching older adults with peers around their own age, they are able to relate to each other on a deeper level.
“I don’t want to say it’s a best kept secret, but it’s something that people do not see us as a program to tap into … but respite is up and rising as more of a need in our state,” she said.
‘A DIVINE APPOINTMENT’
Adams, in Caribou, credits the Aroostook agency with helping her get through the last months of her husband’s disease, which she said was like “being on a very violent rollercoaster.”
She tapped into whatever resources were available.
While he was still well enough to go, she brought Chris to the day program.
For a few hours each week, she had time to do whatever she wanted, not just what needed to be done around the house. She’d get her hair done, go for a long walk, sit and cry when she needed to.
She took their Savvy Caregiver class to learn more about what to expect as Chris’ illness progressed. She took a yoga class and found an online caregiver support group.
White also found her a volunteer with shared interests in music and fellowship who could visit with Chris while Adams worked around the house or ran to the grocery store.
For a few months, she could breathe again. And it allowed her enough room to still find “something joyful to share (with Chris) every day.”
Chris Adams, 71, died on July 23.
“I don’t believe that things happen by accident, so I would say it was a divine appointment when I called that number, and Ruth (White) answered the phone,” Adams said. “In a rural area … you need a community. That’s what the Agency on Aging gave me.”

title: Rick Bennett, Bobby Charles and Hannah Pingree take part in Maine gubernatorial debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WESTBROOK, Maine (WABI/WMTW) - WABI’s media partner WMTW held a gubernatorial debate Wednesday night with independent State Sen. Rick Bennett, Republican candidate Bobby Charles and Democratic candidate Hannah Pingree.
Rick Bennett
Bennett, a longtime Republican, served in the Maine House of Representatives (1990-94) and has had two separate stints serving Oxford County in the Maine Senate (1996-2004, 2020-present). The former State Senate president (2001-02) left the GOP last year.
In a conversation with WABI, he talked about seeing a gap form between parties in recent years. It ultimately led him to run as a third party candidate.
We asked him, if elected, what his priorities would be in year one.
“People have lost trust in government and we need to get that back. It’s critically important, people lost trust in their tax dollars being spent wisely. That’s why I will put forward on day one, I will create an office of inspector general working directly in my office with if ever there is a hint of fraud or miss spending Whistleblower complaint. My team will be there in real time immediately just to study at investigate and report back and will make that transparent. People need to trust their government again, so, with me you’ll get that. But you know the parties have failed. The two party system is not working. They’re more interested in fighting than getting results and we need to move past that and that’s what my candidacy represents an opportunity for people to take control of their government again and to bring cost down to restore trust in government and get our economy moving,” Bennett said.
Bobby Charles
Charles was a former assistant U.S. secretary of state under Colin Powell. In an interview with WABI, he said integrity in government and affordability are two of the biggest challenges Mainers face right now.
Charles says if elected, he would tackle those issues by addressing property taxes, including a homestead exemption, income taxes, especially to encourage young Mainers to stay, live and work in Maine, as well as high energy costs.
Charles also says dealing with addiction in Maine is a major reason he decided to run for office for the first time.
He hopes every Mainer gets out and votes in November.
“This is our one chance. And, when I say one chance, Maine absolutely, unequivocally needs change. If we do not get change now, we’re in a tailspin in all these areas we’ve talked about. We are in a tailspin. I don’t wanna auger in. I don’t wanna see people losing their homes. I don’t want to see people dying because they can’t get into the healthcare they need. I don’t wanna see people paying taxes that they just can’t afford. I don’t want your grandchildren or your children to be leaving the state. I don’t want you to have to leave the state. I want you to feel so good about Maine that you say, ‘God, I not only love the state cause it’s naturally beautiful but I finally trust my governor and my legislature and I know they’re working for me and they’re working hard and I don’t have to look. When the lights go out they’re still in there thinking about how can we possibly help the average Mainer,” Charles said.
Hannah Pingree
Pingree served in the Maine House from 2002 and 2010, and she was elected House Majority Leader (2006-08) and Speaker of the House (2008-10). In January 2019, Gov. Janet Mills appointed Pingree as director of the Office and Policy Innovation and the Future. Pingree held that role until she resigned from the position in May 2025. She then announced her gubernatorial campaign a month later.
Pingree cites housing and health care as her top priorities as well as providing immediate winter relief for Mainers facing high home heating costs.
In an interview with WABI, we asked why voters seem willing to give the Democratic Party another chance at the governorship given headwinds the state faces, Pingree said:
“I’m running as a mom, as somebody who spent 25 years in public service, I’m a lifelong Mainer, I think people want a hopeful vision the future. And I’ve been out there talking about how we improve education for our kids, how we build the housing we need, how we ensure that Maine people have the health care they can afford. And I think Mainers, they believe in their neighbors, they want to take care of each other. I’ve been running a positive campaign. I’ll just say my opponents, especially Bobby Charles, has not. And I think people are sick of, you know, the negativity. And they do want somebody who cares about our state and wants to move it forward. At the same time, I will also say, I think people are worried about this president, about the impacts he has on women’s reproductive rights, on the price of heating oil, on our ability to actually feed kids. And I think that certainly the president has put headwinds for the Republican Party right now. And I think people want a governor who can stand up to him at a critical time.”
Write-in candidates
The Maine Secretary of State’s Office previously announced that there are two declared write-in candidates in the governor’s race: independent Jon Glowa and Republican Randy Wilcox.

title: Old Town Public Library Offers Ghost Hunting Kits Alongside Kayaks And Crochet Supplies
text:
Feel Like Doing A Little Ghost Hunting? You Can Check Out A “Paranormal Investigation Kit” Right From The Old Town Library!
You know that you can check out books, games, and even videos at most libraries. But did you know that in one library in Penobscot County, you can also check out experiences?!
Read More: 10 Terrifying Ghost Stories That Are Uniquely Maine
The Old Town Public Library has a special section where folks can check out more than just books, but items and kits. It's called The Library of Things.
The Library of Things
We're told the Library of Things is located next to the Boo-tique, just past the circulation desk.
Beyond costumes, crochet kits, kayaks, and post hole diggers, you can also check out specific adventure kits.
Codi Badger, Circulation Desk Manager at the library, says it's a fun way to get hands-on and try out new things.
"Our Ghost Hunting Kit is available through our Library of Things, located in the room right next to our circulation desk. It's a fun way for curious patrons to try their hand at paranormal investigating, especially during spooky season!"
Folks can borrow these kits and "things" for up to one week.
Ever feel like doing a little ghost hunting? This fall, the Old Town Public Library has a Ghost Hunting Kit you can try out!
What Is It?
According to their Facebook page, the Old Town Public Library has everything you could need to take a deeper dive into the unknown!
"Our new Ghost Hunting Kit is here! Whether you’re a skeptic or a believer, check it out and add a little mystery to your next adventure."
What's in this kit, you might ask?
We're told this particular parcel contains items that might come in handy for those looking into the shadows and around those dark corners for signs of the spooky or supernatural!
What Does This Kit Come With?
One UV flashlight to spot unexplained glowing fingerprints or interruptions in beams of light.
One EMF detector to measure invisible energy waves (or electromagnetic fields) and detect sudden, unexplained spikes in their surroundings.
One EVP recorder to capture the whispers of spirits and other electronic voice phenomena.
One infrared thermometer to hunt for spots that have dipped in temperature, possibly indicating the presence of evil or ghosts.
One FM radio and a Y7 Portable speaker. Why a radio and speakers? Well, it's believed that spirits can manipulate radio waves and white noise. They often use those avenues to communicate with people, or so the pros say. That's why they call radios spirit boxes or ghost boxes. The speaker helps to amplify the faint sounds that might come through.
A pair of motion-activated light-up cat balls. According to the experts at Ghost Stop,
paranormal investigators often place the balls in quiet, dark rooms on hard surfaces and ask spirits to touch, roll, or light up a specific ball as a "yes/no" or presence sign.
A pair of brass detection rods (you might know them as dowsing rods) that are believed to react when they encounter disturbances in the electromagnetic fields produced by spiritual energy or entities.
And finally, a carrying case for all this cool gear and an information card with details on how to use everything.
Other Things You Might Want To Explore
The Ghost Hunter kit is certainly a really neat idea, but it's not the only fun thing available through the library, Badger says.
"...while the Ghost Hunting Kit might be one of our more unusual items, it's certainly not the only surprise in our Library of Things! Patrons can also borrow kayaks, a lawn mower, a Nut Weasel (for collecting fallen nuts and other yard debris), board games, Tonies kits for kids, nature exploration backpacks, a DVD player, and even a monitor to measure household electricity usage.
Since Halloween is right around the corner, we're also hosting our Boo-tique Halloween Costume Swap throughout October! Families are welcome to donate gently used Halloween costumes or stop by to pick out a costume to take home, completely free. "
Read More: Bucksport, Maine, Is Home to a Spooky Cursed Tomb Legend
"Beyond our Library of Things, we offer free and discounted experiences through our library passes and ticket programs, including tickets to Penobscot Theatre, which is presenting Broomsticks this season, and passes to The Children's Museum, State Park Passes, and other local attractions."
For more information, ask the librarian directly.
The Old Town Public Library is located at 46 Middle Street and is open on Mondays 10 AM to 7 PM, Tuesday through Friday 10 AM to 5 PM, and Saturdays 10 AM to 1 PM.

title: Death Notice: Lisa Ann Higgins
Woman accused of burying cats alive in yard because she thought they were demons
text:
MARTIN COUNTY, Fla. (Gray News) – A 37-year-old Florida woman has been arrested for allegedly burying cats in her yard while they were still alive.
Martin County deputies and animal services officers responded to a residence last week at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park on Southeast Federal Highway to investigate an animal cruelty case.
Investigators spoke with the homeowner, Alba Chavez, who said she buried at least four cats alive in her yard because she believed they were demons, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office.
Deputies began digging up the property, but were only able to save two of the cats. Two other cats were found dead.
“You don’t treat an animal that way and expect to get away with it,” Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said during a briefing last week.
Chavez was booked at the Martin County Jail in multiple counts of aggravated animal cruelty.

title: Sanitation worker dies following road rage shootout while driving garbage truck
text:
PRICHARD, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) - A sanitation worker in Alabama has died after being injured in a road rage shooting in August.
The Mobile County Sheriff’s Office confirmed that Clifton Eugene DuBose Jr., 54, died this week after being hospitalized following a shooting on Aug. 4.
Investigators said DuBose got into a confrontation that day with those in another car on Jarrett Road while he was driving a garbage truck.
According to authorities, DuBose and the driver of the other vehicle’s argument escalated, with both of them stopping their cars and pulling out a gun.
The man’s wife in the other vehicle ended up shooting DuBose in the abdomen, while DuBose fired into the car, the sheriff’s office said.
Sheriff Paul Burch said the shooting was particularly dangerous as children were in the other vehicle.
“The sanitation worker brandished a weapon, as did the other occupants of the vehicle,” Burch said. “Rounds were fired by both parties, and eventually, they drove off. Both called police to report the incident.”
DuBose was described as the aggressor in the altercation and was charged with five counts of shooting into an occupied vehicle. The Mobile County Sheriff’s Office said that he also had an active warrant on a domestic violence charge and was driving on a suspended or revoked license.
Burch said at that time it was unclear how a city employee could be driving a garbage truck without a valid license.
The sheriff also urged residents not to take the law into their own hands.
“Anytime there’s an issue being run off the road by, you know, any government vehicle or any, just report it to law enforcement,” Burch said. “Don’t get into a confrontation. That’s never gonna end well.”

title: OPINION: Election Day: November 2026
text:
COMMUNITY COMMENTARY
by Sheldon Goodine, China
A very large number of folks do not know when Election Day really is. Election Day is the first Tuesday following the first Monday in November.
Why Tuesday? Why November?
The answer lies with America’s 19th century farmers. In 1845 Congress passed a federal law designating the first Tuesday following the first Monday in November as Election Day. Previously, states were allowed to hold elections any time they pleased within a 34-day period before the first Wednesday in December. This system had several flaws, however, including the potential for early voting results to affect turnout and sway opinion in states that held last elections, and those some last-minute voters could potentially decide the outcome of the entire election. Faced with these issues, Congress created the current election day in the hope of streamlining the voting process.
But why a Tuesday in November? In the 1800s most citizens worked as farmers and lived far from their polling places. Since people often traveled for at least a day to vote, lawmakers needed to allow a two-day window for election day. Weekends were impractical, since most people spent Sundays in church and Wednesday was market day for farmers. With this in mind, Tuesday was selected as the first and most convenience day of the week to hold elections.
Farm culture also explains why election day always falls in November. Spring and early summer elections were thought to interfere with the planting season and late summer and early fall elections overlapped with the harvest. That left the late fall month of November, after the harvest was complete, but before the arrival of harsh winter weather as the best choice.
So, there you have it. When you get your calendar in January for the next year, you know exactly when election day will be and you can make your plans to vote.
With early voting and mail in votes, our founding fathers would be appalled at what is happening today. The opportunity for being able to cheat is highly possible as there is no way to verify who the vote belongs to. With 10 months of lead time, municipalities should be able to make arrangements for everyone to cast a vote on election day. The old and trusted method of casting absentee ballots should continue with the same safeguards in place. These ballots, like all other ballots, must be in-house before the close of polls on election day.
Boxes of votes unloaded from a personal vehicle two or three days after election day are just fuel for the incinerator and should not be counted. Let’s get back to doing the right thing and vote on election day. The first Tuesday following the first Monday in November.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: Former Cumberland County district attorney outraises incumbent in campaign contributions
text:
Stephanie Anderson has outraised incumbent Jacqueline Sartoris in campaign contributions, as both vie to be elected district attorney in Cumberland County.
A quarter of Anderson’s donors are attorneys, records show.
Sartoris, a Democrat from Brunswick, was elected in 2022 and recently won her party’s nomination in a June primary against one of her former prosecutors. As of Sept. 1, Sartoris had raised $35,000, including $15,000 in loans, according to campaign finance records. Most of that was received before June 9 and roughly $4,500 came from eight contributors after the primary election.
Anderson, who was district attorney for 28 years before retiring in 2018, had raised more than $69,000 as of Sept. 14. At least 40 contributions came from practicing and retired Maine attorneys, according to an analysis of campaign finance records and a directory run by the Maine Board of Overseers of the Bar.
“I think that really tells you a lot,” said Jennifer Ackerman, a long-time Cumberland County prosecutor who worked under Anderson for 16 years, including seven years as her deputy.
Publicly, the two candidates have sparred about who is most qualified to prosecute what are known as “quality of life crimes,” like public drug use and disorderly conduct, and about the implementation of progressive reforms.
Inside the courthouse, attorneys who have donated to Anderson’s campaign have complained about Sartoris’ leadership. Anderson said she was approached by prosecutors and defense attorneys, “across the political spectrum,” asking her to run. Anderson is running as an unenrolled candidate.
“I mean, I go by yards with my sign beside Troy Jackson signs,” said Anderson, who was reelected seven times as a Republican. “This is an elected position, but it’s not partisan and it should not be politicized.”
Sartoris has said she is aware of discontent among defense attorneys and several prosecutors who have left the office and spoken out publicly, including Ackerman and Valerie Adams, who lost to Sartoris in the Democratic primary.
Sartoris has said it’s proof that she’s making the changes that she promised voters in 2022. In debates and forums, she’s highlighted her recent efforts through a federal grant to inventory untested rape kits, and a recent revamp of the county’s existing restorative justice options.
“This is not a popularity contest for lawyers, who usually want to preserve the status quo,” Sartoris said in a statement. “I ran to bring long-needed change to the people of Cumberland County. I have more regular people on my side, with more donors and more small dollar donations than Anderson. Soliciting money from defense attorneys seems like a conflict of interest.”
Sartoris’ primary campaign four years ago drew an unprecedented $300,000 from an out-of-state political action committee funded by Democratic donor George Soros. The candidates still have another week before they file their newest campaign finance reports. Anderson said on Thursday she has raised another $14,000 in individual contributions since mid-September.
Anderson also serves and is running for another term on the Cape Elizabeth Town Council. She says she has not fundraised for that race.
ENDORSEMENTS
At least eight individuals who have contributed to Sartoris’ campaign this year are attorneys, according to records from the bar and campaign finance reports.
John Kaminski, who donated to her campaign in September and is an attorney focused on affordable housing, praised Sartoris for her work on homelessness and for directing police to share evidence from bike and pedestrian crashes.
“I think she’s had a solid four years in office and will continue to move things forward when she’s reelected,” Kaminski said.
Rep. Grayson Lookner, a Democrat in Portland, said Sartoris has been supportive of his legislative proposals to improve public safety, particularly for diverting at-risk youth from the criminal justice system. House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, a Democrat in Biddeford, said he endorsed Sartoris because of her opponent’s Republican history.
“We’re seeing this across the state that the Republican brand is so bad, that they’ve decided to put a cloak over that label and have ‘unenrolled’ candidates,” Fecteau said. “Voters should know that we have a very strong Democratic district attorney in Jackie.”
Anderson says she believes Sartoris is using the Democratic nomination to her advantage because she doesn’t have enough to highlight from her four years in office. Anderson also accused Sartoris of distorting her remarks.
At a forum hosted by Scarborough town leaders in September, Sartoris accused Anderson of having expressed a desire to work with federal immigration officials.
“I never said that local law enforcement should cooperate with ICE,” Anderson said in an interview, noting that state law restricts police from working with federal immigration officials. “I think I said there’s been a lot of injustices with ICE and it’s been pretty horrific. And why is that a big campaign issue?”
Sartoris previously stated her intent to prosecute agents who commit violent offenses without cause in her district. She has not charged any agents to date.
Anderson suggested the attorneys supporting her campaign “are the people that are paying attention to what’s going on to the DA’s office and what’s going on in the community regarding public safety.” She also highlighted endorsements from three police unions as evidence of her ability to work with law enforcement on prosecuting cases.
Scot Mattox, an attorney who was a Portland police officer for more than 20 years, said he probably arrested more than 1,000 people whose cases Anderson prosecuted.
“Stephanie recognized that a district attorney’s duty is not merely to secure convictions, but to administer justice fairly,” Mattox said in an email.
Former employees who spoke to the Portland Press Herald said they appreciated Anderson’s mentorship and her knowledge of criminal law.
“We can all agree, despite our different professional experiences, that when people like where they work, they care, they work harder, and the morale is stronger,” said defense attorney Kate Marshall, who interned for Anderson and later returned to the office as an assistant district attorney. “This can only benefit the community to which the office serves.”
CRITICISMS
Ackerman said she resigned less than a year after Sartoris took over. Ackerman, who now works for the state, said she was speaking only on her own behalf.
Adams worked in the district attorney’s office for about nine months. Adams was fired by Sartoris after she and a defense attorney asked Sartoris to consider not running.
Adams and Ackerman have both likened Sartoris’ office to a “ship without a captain.”
“She was very much focused on saying what she wanted to do in terms of policies, but the day-to-day work, and the day-to-day policies that our prosecutors needed, we weren’t getting answers,” Ackerman said.
Others have criticized Sartoris’ work in court, saying criminal cases are languishing and that she has at times gone beyond what they believe to be appropriate for her role.
“For me, that makes life for defendants and people who are caught up in the criminal justice system harder,” said defense attorney Rob Andrews.
On the mental health docket, Sartoris said she has dedicated much of her focus on defendants whose mental health might lead them to be found incompetent to stand trial, or not criminally responsible. Attorney Alison Brauner said Sartoris has pushed for forcible medication and the disclosure of clients’ sensitive health information.
“A criminal defendant doesn’t lose their right to privacy around their medical care,” Brauner said.
In a statement, Sartoris said she “will not apologize for asking a judge to medicate people, always at the request of an expert, when their untreated psychotic disorders are causing repeated criminal conduct.”

title: Letter: Be sure to vote for what you believe in
text:
I am writing to encourage all voters to make their voices heard in this midterm election. Early voting is open in Maine, mail-in ballots are available, Election Day is Nov. 3. A non-partisan rally for election education and protection will be held Saturday, Oct. 17, at 10 a.m. on the North Road (across from Marden’s) in Houlton, in conjunction with voting support efforts across the country; all are welcome to participate.
My votes are going to Hannah Pingree, Matt Rush, Janel Underwood-Charette, Matt Dunlap and Troy Jackson. They best reflect my values and positions, including affordability of health care, housing, food and fuel; immigrant rights and protection; LGBTQ equality; Indigenous justice and sovereignty recognition; protection of the environment; and renewal of our country’s generosity and peaceful leadership in the world.
My beliefs and preferred candidates may or may not be the same as yours. But all of us have a right and responsibility to educate ourselves, and to vote for what we believe in. Free, fair and safe elections are a cornerstone of our democracy, to be guarded and celebrated.
Join us for the Oct. 17 rally, make sure you are registered to vote, and cast your ballot in this election. Our communities and our country depend on us all.
Mary Miller
Oakfield

title: A new Republican ad twists Troy Jackson’s old votes on sex offenders
text:
Quick Check is a Bangor Daily News election feature that fact-checks political ads in 400 words or less. We have partnered with The Maine Monitor on a subscription to AdImpact, an ad-tracking platform that powers this feature.
A new Republican ad says Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson went easy on child sex offenders as a state lawmaker, citing votes on sentences and where offenders can live.
The sentencing charge is misleading. The residency charge is closer to true, though one of three votes it cites put Jackson on the side of tougher limits.
The claim
“Troy Jackson voted to let child sex offenders live near playgrounds and schools. Jackson also voted for shorter prison sentences for repeat child sex offenders,” a narrator says.
The context
Saying Jackson voted for “shorter prison sentences” suggests they were being cut. They weren’t.
In 2005, Jackson, then a state representative, joined a 105-33 House majority, including most Republicans, to kill a bill setting new mandatory minimums of 10 years for gross sexual assault and sexual abuse of a minor, and 20 years for repeat offenses. Gov. Janet Mills, then a state representative, also opposed it, arguing it covered too wide a range of cases.
The next year, Jackson was one of five House Democrats who backed a failed amendment for a 25-year mandatory minimum for gross sexual assault of a child under 12, and life in prison for repeat offenders. He backed a version that became law requiring judges to start at 20 years or more.
On residency, Jackson voted in 2005 against a version of a bill barring some offenders from living near schools. It covered only offenders against children under 12 within 500 feet of elementary schools. It narrowly failed.
As a senator in 2011, he voted against a scaled-back Republican bill that would have let some towns expand buffer zones from 750 to 2,500 feet. The opposition was bipartisan. The Republican-led House killed it 93-56.
The ad also gets a 2009 vote backward. Jackson opposed a version that capped local limits at 750 feet and barred stricter ordinances. It put him on the side of 12 of 15 Senate Republicans, including one who warned it would preempt 2,500-foot ordinances in Lyman and Waterboro. It advanced 18-17 and eventually became law with Jackson absent for the final vote.
Who’s behind the ad
The Maine Standard is a super PAC that registered with the Federal Election Commission on Sept. 11. It has booked about $8.7 million in ads, per AdImpact, but hasn’t had to disclose donors. Its first fundraising report is due this week.

text:
Social Security benefits are rising in 2027. Calculate how much more you’ll get
The new COLA for 2027 could add roughly $75 a month to the average retired worker's benefit.
Social Security benefits are rising in 2027. Calculate how much more you’ll get
The new COLA for 2027 could add roughly $75 a month to the average retired worker's benefit.
Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6% in 2027, based on the new cost-of-living adjustment released by the Social Security Administration.
Related video above: How much your Social Security benefits could be cut without action from Congress
Nearly 72 million Americans will see a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment beginning in January 2027.
Social Security said retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month on average starting in January.
Calculate your estimated monthly benefit in 2027
The Social Security Administration recalculates benefits annually by factoring in what's called the cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA. This is to ensure that the purchasing power of benefits does not fall behind the current cost of goods.
COLA is computed by comparing the current year's third-quarter inflation average, July through September, against the prior year's third-quarter average.
This year's COLA is higher than the initial estimates by advocacy groups. The Senior Citizens League initially predicted a 3.5% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027.


title: Police lieutenant indicted after allegedly using Flock cameras to track person for personal reasons
text:
SHARONVILLE, Ohio (WXIX/Gray News) - A police lieutenant was indicted Tuesday after he allegedly used Flock camera systems to track a person for personal reasons.
Sharonville Police Lt. Walter Cordes, 48, was charged with unauthorized use of a computer, cable, or telecommunications property after he used the Flock camera system 29 times between Dec. 19, 2024, and April 20, 2026, to track a person’s whereabouts for “reasons unrelated to law enforcement,” according to Hamilton County Prosecutor Connie Pillich.
“When technology is misused, it undermines public trust and the important work being done by law enforcement officers every day,” Pillich said.
In June, prosecutors said Cordes self-reported during a department audit of the system and admitted to conducting the searches.
The Sharonville Police Department said on social media that Cordes was placed on administrative leave while the department conducted an investigation. After the investigation, Cordes was charged and faces up to a year in prison.
The Hamilton County Fraternal Order of Police said its members were surprised by the indictment.
“He is a member of our lodge. Many of the people I have spoken to since say they’re shocked by this indictment and that it happened, but at the same time, that’s why we have checks and balances,” said Rich Krummen, president of FOP Lodge 74.
Sharonville Police Department is now requiring additional training for every officer on the use of law enforcement databases and technology.

title: New research on psychedelics could have big impact on mental health patients
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (InvestigateTV) - Millions of Americans take prescription medications for mental health conditions, but those might not be enough for people with severe depression or post-traumatic stress disorder.
Relief for some can be found in treatments that use drugs that produce psychedelic-like effects. After President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at speeding up research on several psychedelic drugs, it could open the door to similar therapies.
For 25 years, Logan Curtis says he struggled with anxiety, depression and panic attacks tied to childhood abuse.
“I carry a lot of these deep wounds with me,” Curtis said.
Curtis said he tried talk therapy and spent years on antidepressants, including SSRIs, but wanted more than simply managing symptoms.
“I don’t want to just exist,” Curtis said.
Three months ago, Curtis said he watched a documentary that opened his eyes to different treatments. It led him to Derive Health in Charlotte’s Dilworth neighborhood for ketamine treatments. Ketamine is currently the only legal psychedelic medicine in North Carolina and is used in clinical settings for conditions including treatment-resistant depression.
“Ketamine itself is a very safe medication, but it does do best with some medical monitoring or support,” said Dr. Jonathan Leake, who has treated patients with ketamine for a decade.
Leake said ketamine is administered by prescription through an IV over a series of sessions, with medical supervision and therapeutic support.
“You really are seeing people that have suffered, and then over six weeks, they’re kind of transforming before your eyes,” Leake said.
The FDA is now fast-tracking review of three other psychedelic drugs for PTSD, major depressive disorder and treatment-resistant depression, according to advocates tracking the federal actions. The president’s order would loosen research restrictions on psychedelics, including ibogaine.
Both ketamine and ibogaine can produce psychedelic experiences, but the drugs are used very differently.
Ketamine is a type of anesthetic used in small doses that can give you an “out of body” experience. Treatments last around an hour and done in a series over several weeks.
Ibogaine is often used a single, intense all-day session. Researchers also say it carries more serious heart risks with it.
Most psychedelics are illegal on a federal level, but states like Oregon and Colorado have legalized certain therapies. Several of the psychedelic drugs are being studied in trials for mental health conditions.
Gina Giorgio, with the North Carolina Psychedelic Coalition, said the federal push could move approvals faster, but states will play a major role in how research and treatment are carried out.
“This expedites approval through the federal government, but it’s really the states that will be carrying out this type of research and this type of treatment,” Giorgio said. She added that building training protocols for therapists would be essential.
Giorgio said more study is still needed on safety and effectiveness, but she believes the policy shift broadens what could become available for patients who have not found relief through other treatments.
“We’re not saying that this is for everyone,” she said. “But we’re saying it should at least be an option if people are not experiencing relief elsewhere.”
If the drugs are found safe and effective, some approvals could come later this year. Any treatments would be administered in a clinical setting under medical supervision, not taken at home.

title: Police investigate fight at youth football game in Livermore Falls
text:
Livermore Falls police are reviewing a recording and interviews related to a fight that occurred Saturday between parents and a coach at Griffin Field in Livermore Falls.
Video of the altercation, which took place on the sidelines of an Area Youth Sports football game, was disseminated widely on social media.
Once the police investigation is concluded, police Chief Abe Haroon said, the report will be given to the Androscoggin County district attorney for review to determine if any charges will be lodged against participants.
No summonses have been issued and no arrests have been made, he said.
One of the men involved is Cpl. Dylan Rider, an Androscoggin County Sheriff’s deputy, an Area Youth Sports football coach and a county commissioner. Rider was off duty.
In accordance with the organization’s bylaws and code of conduct, the AYS board of directors has initiated a formal review of the incident, AYS President Nixon Ortiz wrote in an email.
“Area Youth Sports (AYS) is aware of the recent incident and video circulating on social media,” Ortiz wrote. “The safety, well-being, and sportsmanship of our youth, families, and community are our highest priorities.”
“Pending the outcome of this thorough investigation, all involved parties have been asked not to attend any practices, games, or AYS events for the balance of this season,” Ortiz wrote. “This interim measure ensures a fair and complete investigative process can play out so that the Board can make informed, appropriate final determinations.”
William Gagne, chief deputy of the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office, said Tuesday that his office is aware of the situation. “It was brought to our attention and we are actively looking into the matter internally,” he said.
A short video recording of the altercation was posted on Facebook by Donna Jewell, who accuses Rider of assaulting her and her husband.
The video shows Jewell going up to Rider with a puppy in her arms. It appears she makes contact with Rider, who turns toward her as her hands go up toward Rider’s face. He grabs Jewell’s arms and pushes her to the ground as he makes his way toward a fight between two men. One of those men was Rider’s father.
Rider’s son also plays on the youth football team. Jewell is the parent of an athlete as well.
Rider wrote on his Facebook post that he was punched and scratched by Jewell, and that his father was allegedly punched in the stomach by the other man.
Jewell, whose post of the video has more than 1,300 comments, did not return a request for comment. In a Facebook post, she said an attorney had advised her and her husband to not discuss the issue in public anymore.
Rider’s attorney, Andre “AJ” Hungerford, wrote in an email, “Because there is an investigation of events on Saturday, October 10, 2026 involving various parties, including Dylan Rider, I am withholding comment until a more appropriate time.”

title: Obituary: Donald William Reny
text:
WINSLOW – It is with heavy hearts that we announce the peaceful passing of Donald William Reny on Friday, Oct. 2, 2026, surrounded by his loving family. Don was 89 years old.
Don was born on Oct. 31, 1936, in North Vassalboro, the son of Arthur and Dorothy (Lizotte) Reny and the third of eight children. He graduated from Winslow High School in 1955 and proudly served four years in the United States Air Force, stationed at Loring Air Force Base in Limestone.
On Nov. 23, 1957, Don married Lorraine Duguay, beginning a life together that would span nearly 69 years. They were blessed with three children: Stephen, Margaret “Peggy,” and Kelly. In 1967, the family moved from Winslow to Yarmouth, where Don built a successful career as a building contractor for more than 30 years.
Following his retirement, Don devoted much of his time to helping others. While spending winters in Kissimmee, Florida, he volunteered for many years at Give Kids the World. Back home in Maine, he volunteered at Notre Dame’s soup kitchen and the Muskie Center. Cooking and preparing meals for those in need brought him tremendous joy and reflected his generous spirit.
Don had many interests throughout his life, including woodworking, hunting, fishing, boating, and reading, but few things brought him more enjoyment than a good game of cribbage. He loved organizing cribbage tournaments and sharing a game with family and friends.
Above all, Don cherished time spent with the people he loved. Whether enjoying a quiet one-on-one visit, gathering with a small group of friends, or hosting a crowd at the family’s summer lake house, Don was happiest when surrounded by others. He was well known for his lobster bakes, pig roasts, and famous “bean hole beans,” which became treasured traditions for family and friends.
Don will also be remembered for his wonderful sense of humor. He loved telling jokes, playing pranks, and finding ways to make those around him smile and laugh. Bringing joy to others was truly one of his greatest gifts.
Don was predeceased by his parents, Arthur and Dorothy Reny; his brother, Robert; his sisters, Pauline Daniels, Lillian Richards, Mary Thorne, and Arlene Mayhugh; and his beloved daughter, Peggy.
He is survived by his loving wife, Lorraine Reny of Winslow; his son, Stephen Reny and his wife, Kathleen Kerr, of Yarmouth; and his daughter, Kelly Williams and her husband, Rod Williams, of Yarmouth.
He is also survived by his grandchildren: Sam Reny and her husband, Joshua McDougall, of North Yarmouth; Alison Thomas and her husband, Luke Thomas, of Thompson’s Station, Tennessee; Patrick Vigue and his wife, Afton Vigue, of Gardiner, Maine; Delia Williams and her fiancé, Mark Matheson, of Franklin, North Carolina; and Madeline Kerr of Yarmouth.
Don was especially proud of his great-grandchildren: Ben, Sunny, Gus, and Levi of Thompson’s Station, Tennessee, and Ambrose and Sawyer McDougall of North Yarmouth.
He is also survived by his brother, Peter Reny of North Vassalboro, and his sister, Priscilla Perry of Holden, along with many extended family members and dear friends.
A Funeral Mass will be celebrated on Saturday, November 14, at 11 a.m., at St. John the Baptist Church in Winslow, followed by a Celebration of Life at the Waterville Elks Lodge. A private inurnment will take place at the Maine Veteran’s Memorial Cemetery at a later date.
Don’s generous heart, quick wit, love of family, and ability to bring laughter into a room will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered by all who knew him.
In lieu of flowers, the family invites those wishing to honor Don’s memory to consider making a donation to Spectrum Generations at http://www.spectrumgenerations.org.

You can now buy a silencer over the counter in Maine. Here’s what you need to know.
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
On Oct. 9, the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives issued a press release detailing new guidance regarding the making and transfer of certain firearms and devices regulated under the National Firearms Act of 1934.
An open letter to federal firearms licensees and the public, signed by ATF Director Robert Cekada, appeared on the bureau’s website the same day.
The letter explains how certain provisions of the NFA and their enforcement apply to firearms no longer subject to the $200 “tax stamp” — silencers, short-barreled rifles and shotguns and “any other weapons” as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 5845(e).
What does it mean?
In a nutshell, it means that as of Oct. 9, 2026, people who are not prohibited from owning or possessing a firearm under the Gun Control Act of 1968 may make, buy and transfer suppressors, short-barreled rifles, short-barreled shotguns and “any other weapons” under the revised federal requirements.
Gone is the $200 special tax, along with certain paperwork requirements and the notoriously long wait times associated with obtaining approval for firearms regulated under the NFA, commonly known as Class III items.
Your gun cabinet is going to get a little more exciting.
What firearms are affected?
Only firearms and items defined as firearms under ATF rules and covered by the tax repeal under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act are affected. This includes rifles with barrels shorter than 16 inches and shotguns with barrels shorter than 18 inches, as well as certain firearms with an overall length of less than 26 inches.
Suppressors, also known as silencers, are included because the ATF defines them as firearms for regulatory purposes.
The “any other weapon” classification applies to certain concealable firearms and devices, including disguised firearms such as cane guns, umbrella guns, pen guns and flashlight guns. It can also include certain wallet holsters and pistols equipped with vertical foregrips, depending on their design and classification.
All these categories are addressed in the ATF guidance letter.
What hasn’t changed?
It is important to note that not all firearms regulated under the NFA are affected by the new ATF guidance. Machine guns and destructive devices remain subject to applicable federal taxes, forms and registration requirements under the National Firearms Act.
Specific parts that convert semiautomatic firearms into fully automatic firearms are also defined as “machine guns” under current federal law. That has not changed, and the regular NFA process still applies.
State specific rules
While the ATF sets federal firearm rules under the National Firearms Act and Gun Control Act, individual states have their own firearm laws.
Across the nation, states have myriad differences in what is legal within their borders. Examples include waiting periods, concealed carry, allowable firearm designs and magazine capacity.
Ownership and possession of suppressors, short-barreled firearms and “any other weapons” also fall under state law.
Read the ATF open letter on ATF.gov

title: Aroostook County heating assistance waitlist grows as funding gap continues
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - Aroostook County residents needing help with heating systems may have to wait longer for assistance. AVEC Community Action held a virtual meeting to discuss heating assistance and the challenges facing local households.
About 100 people, including state representatives, health facility managers and oil company employees, joined the meeting to hear about efforts to keep people warm this winter. One program discussed was the Central Heating Improvement Program, which helps with heating system repairs. 155 households in Aroostook County are currently on the waiting list.
Heidi Rackliffe, chief program officer at AVEC, said the focus is on households with no heat at all.
“So we have to focus on those with absolutely no heat first... Obviously right now we have 155 households in Aroostook County that have a half functioning or no functioning furnace at all. It’s getting cold,” Rackliffe said.
Rackliffe said AVEC is currently between contracts and does not have funding available for the program. She said they expect new funding within about a week that will allow them to begin working on the waitlist.
Residents can apply for AVEC’s heating assistance programs online at avecmaine.org/energy-housing.

title: Special education aide accused of punching 6-year-old autistic student, telling witness ‘you did not see that’
text:
HORRY COUNTY, S.C. (WMBF/Gray News) — A special education aide is accused of punching a nonverbal student with autism and then telling a witness, “You did not see that.”
The alleged incident happened at Pee Dee Elementary School in South Carolina.
Horry County police charged Kristin Daly, 57, with unlawfully placing a child at risk of or causing harm.
Horry County police were notified on Sept. 26 about an assault that happened the day before at Pee Dee Elementary School.
A witness told police they saw Daly punch a 6-year-old nonverbal, autistic student with a closed fist, causing the student to stumble backward, according to arrest warrants.
Daly then looked at the witness and said, “You did not see that,” according to a police report.
Police said the student was not seriously injured.
The student is known to run toward people while swinging his arms, which can result in him hitting teachers and other staff members, the police report stated.
Daly began working for Horry County Schools full-time in 2022. District spokesperson Lisa Bourcier said Daly has been on administrative leave since Sept. 28.
Jail records show Daly was released from jail Monday afternoon on a $10,000 bond.

title: One dead, two hospitalized in Bangor house fire
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - One person is dead and two others are hospitalized following a fire at a home in Bangor early Wednesday morning.
Fire crews were called to the home at the corner of Cedar and Second streets just after 6:30 a.m., where authorities say five people reside.
Person found inside home
Officials say when crews arrived, three people in the street told them someone may still be inside.
Bangor Fire Chief Eric Pelletier said despite the crew’s efforts, that person did not make it out.
Neighbor describes scene
A neighbor who spoke with WABI described the scene.
“Flames were coming out the attic and the firefighters were having a hard time fighting it and shortly after I arrived, the family was notified they had lost their loved one. I’m just in shock. You know it’s sad when tragedy hits so close to home like this and you know when you see these people day after day and everything, knowing that they’re dealing with this pain and this loss, it’s truly heartbreaking,” said Joshua Hutchins.
The neighbor said shortly after he got home, he saw a family member from the home searching for their dog and he helped look.
Pets rescued, others killed
The dog was found, and one cat was rescued. Authorities say another cat and a dog died in the fire.
The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

title: Oakland Lions to donate $10,000 to fire department
text:
With lawn sales and Christmas trees, the Oakland Lions Club aims to raise $20,000 for community causes every year.
But when the club’s fiscal year ended on June 30, the club members realized they had a surplus. They could make an extra donation, and the Searsmont explosion served as their inspiration.
Helping out Oakland’s firefighters had been on the club members’ minds since the lumber mill disaster killed three, including two firefighters.
“We thought we’d protect those that protect us,” Prudy Marcoux, a Lion Club member, said. “Other Lions Clubs in the state are donating to Searsmont and Belmont, but we try to do things for people in our own community. We try to make the money that we’ve made here stay here.”
When Lions Club members asked fire Chief Dave Coughlin what the department needed, he told them about turnout gear — the protective equipment firefighters wear when responding to fires.
The Oakland fire department has added six firefighters to its workforce in the last year, and while they can train in old turnout gear, sometimes past its 10-year life expectancy, the firemen need new gear to fight fires.
Turnout gear is custom made and can cost around $3,000 for just a coat and pants.
Coughlin said the department normally budgets for two new sets every year, and relies on donations, grants and other outside funding for additional gear needed. When the Lions told Coughlin about the donation, he expected to be able to buy one new set of turnout gear.
He was very grateful — and very surprised — to learn the club would cover three sets of gear, with $1,000 left over to go toward helmets, boots and gloves.
Coughlin said Oakland’s Lions have a long history of supporting the fire department, starting with a fire truck they donated in the 1950s. Since then, Coughlin said the club has spearheaded fundraising efforts for the department, and donated things like air packs and rescue saws.
“It’s a really good local cause,” Coughlin said. “We’re really excited to have them.”
Marcoux is thrilled about the donation, and she said it’s all thanks to the community. When the Lions Club collects items for its lawn sales, she said around 20% of the items they receive are new, and people are always helpful when they’re clearing out their houses. The Lions even had a walk-in donation of $1,000 last year.
This kind of support means that in addition to supporting the library reading program, donating to the backpack program and buying shoes and warm coats for children in need, the club get to support the fire department.
“All of our members are excited about this,” Marcoux said. “We know that it’s going to be used and used in our community, and for a good purpose.”
Oakland’s Town Council is expected to accept the donation on behalf of the fire department at 6 p.m. Wednesday at the fire department at 15 Fairfield St.

title: Cheverus field hockey shows poise in comeback win over Biddeford
text:
BIDDEFORD — For a squad that never loses, the Cheverus field hockey team sure knows what to do when it looks like it may be about to happen.
Ava Martin tipped in Mary McCartney’s shot with 1:53 left in the game, and the Stags scored two fourth-quarter goals to beat Biddeford, 2-1, in a showdown between Class A South favorites.
Avery Tinker also scored for Cheverus (12-0), which has now won 29 straight games and has gone unbeaten in its last 86 regular-season games going back to 2021.
Biddeford, which got a goal from Mia Mariello, fell to 10-2 with its fifth straight one-goal loss to the Stags. Biddeford’s last eight losses, dating back to 2023, have all been against Cheverus.
“It’s just a great showing of what we can do,” said Martin, one of the team’s captains along with Sydney Brunelle, who helped set up her winner. “These are high-pressure games, and going into playoff season, we’re ready to go. We know we can dig ourselves out of anything that we put ourselves in.”
Coming up clutch
• With 11 minutes to go and the score tied, McCartney had the ball on her stick alone in front of the net but pulled the shot wide left.
Soon, she got another chance. With just under two minutes to go, Martin inserted a corner to Brunelle, who quickly passed left to McCartney. The senior’s shot was quick and true, and was likely heading in even without Martin making the tip.
“It felt great. Anything you can do for your team, it’s going to be great,” McCartney said. “I was pretty sure it was coming (to me). In that moment, the adrenaline kind of kicks in.”
• Cheverus got two corners in the fourth quarter and converted on both. It wasn’t an accident.
“We plan everything out, exactly where we want to put it,” Martin said. “Sometimes Sydney or Brooke (Brunelle) reads it at the top, but most of the time it’s planned.”
Playing with poise
• Close calls are nothing new for Cheverus, which erased fourth-quarter deficits twice against Biddeford last year. Even this year, Cheverus scored two goals in the final five minutes, including the winner with no time left, in a 4-3 win over Sanford/Kennebunk.
• When the Stags went down 1-0 on Mariello’s goal off an Aubrey Forcier assist with 4:40 left in the third quarter, they again knew what to do. Early in the fourth, Sydney Brunelle got the insert on a corner, hesitated, then ripped a shot that Tinker redirected into the goal with 13:33 remaining.
“I do think experience (helps),” coach Andrea Musante said. “We’ve been in this situation multiple times, so I think when you don’t fold under the pressure and you know that you can do it, it’s built that confidence to do it again.”
Unsung hero
• Biddeford’s pressure throughout the game forced the Cheverus defense to step up, and sophomore Julia Blais found herself in the middle of multiple key stops. In the first quarter, she broke up a Mariello pass into the circle to derail a threat.
She broke up another feed in the second quarter, preventing Addison Barrs from getting the ball in scoring position.
“When it comes her way, I don’t get nervous,” Musante said. “I feel a little bit of relief, because I know she’s going to smoothly shoot the ball (or) get it out wide.”
Coming close
• While her team fell just short, Tigers coach Caitlin Tremberth took a complimentary approach, saying her team played better and more composed than it did in a 3-2 loss to Cheverus earlier in the year.
“They played amazing,” she said. “Each one gave everything they’ve got, and the only difference that’s really separating us and them is that they have that experience in these tough moments.
“We have the heart, we have the hustle, we have all those things, and we have the skill. It’s just a matter of finishing and capitalizing. That’s the final piece. We’ve got to be all gamers.”

title: Sheriff King deserves to be reelected in York County
text:
Sheriff Bill King’s depth of experience in municipal, federal and county law enforcement are unparalleled in Maine. His expertise has been demonstrated by the many improvements at the sheriff’s office since his initial election in 2014.
The York County Sheriff’s Office was the first sheriff’s office in Maine to be accredited by the Maine Law Enforcement Accreditation Program. In its most recent Maine Department of Corrections inspection, the York County Jail received a 100% compliance rating — a rare achievement.
Sheriff King provides inmates with opportunities for self-improvement, facilitating their productive reentry into the community. During his 12 years in office, he has updated all aspects of departmental operations to align with current best practices. The York County Jail’s body scanner intercepts contraband; cruisers have video systems; and deputies have body-worn cameras, all of which improve both citizen and officer safety.
Sheriff Bill King deserves our vote.
Karen B. Lovell
Saco

title: Police investigate report of sexual assault at a fraternity party near the University of Chicago
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Police are investigating a woman’s report that she was sexually assaulted during a fraternity party near the University of Chicago campus, an allegation that comes at a time of heightened awareness of sexual violence on college campuses.
Chicago police said no one had been charged Wednesday, a day after university officials posted an alert saying that a person of interest had been identified.
The Chicago case comes amid an uproar over Cornell University ‘s handling of a woman’s allegations that she was drugged and gang raped by fraternity members in 2024. A campus investigation led to internal disciplinary action by the university, but no criminal charges were ever filed.
The University of Chicago, a top-ranked U.S. research school with an enrollment of 18,000 students, said in a statement that a woman reported being sexually assaulted early Sunday during a party at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house.
The university said the perpetrator fled the house after being confronted by another person.
The 21-year-old woman reported the assault to police and went to a hospital for treatment, according to Chicago police. The university said she is not a student.
Chicago police did not immediately provide a copy of the incident report on the alleged attack when The Associated Press requested it Wednesday.
The Chicago Sun-Times, citing the police report, said the woman told police she had been drinking and dancing at the party before she began feeling unwell. The Sun-Times said the report stated two of the woman’s friends then found her “not fully conscious” in a bathroom with a man and that both were partially undressed.
The friends told police that to get into the bathroom, they had to force their way through several men who were “cheering and appearing to encourage the activity inside,” the Sun-Times reported.
Alpha Epsilon Pi said no fraternity members took part in the alleged attack or encouraged it. The fraternity’s University of Chicago chapter said in a statement that its members rushed to help the woman after being alerted by one of her friends and ended the party immediately.
“There is no evidence at all that any AEPi members participated in this assault or were aware of it while it was transpiring,” Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity’s national organization, said in a statement Wednesday.
The fraternity said the perpetrator was chased out of the house and was recorded by cameras while fleeing.
University officials said the person of interest who has been identified is not a student or otherwise affiliated with the school.
The Cornell case came to light last month after a woman filed a lawsuit against the university and seven fraternity members, saying she was repeatedly assaulted at a fraternity house in October 2024. She went to campus police three weeks later and gave a detailed interview, but local prosecutors never pursued charges. The men she accused have denied wrongdoing.
Cornell announced Tuesday it’s banning parties at fraternity houses until next year. The university said it will include New York State Police in investigations of campus sexual assaults.
Fraternities have also been under scrutiny at the University of Arizona, which suspended fraternity activities earlier this month following multiple reports of assault, hazing and other misconduct.
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia.

title: University of New England offers professional network to help students find careers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The University of New England in Biddeford is launching a professional network designed to connect students with alumni, employers, faculty, professional staff and other professionals and support career development.
The Nor’easter Global Network aims to help students build the relationships, skills and industry knowledge as part of an expanded approach to career readiness that extends beyond preparing students for their first jobs. The goal is to support students and alumni across career stages through professional connections, mentorship, shared expertise and access to opportunities.
“Preparing students for successful careers means giving them more than a strong education: It means connecting them with the people, experiences, and opportunities that will help them put that education to work,” said James Herbert, UNE’s president. “The workforce is changing rapidly, and universities have an important role to play in ensuring graduates are prepared to adapt and succeed.”
UNE introduced the network at its Industry Exploration Day this week.
Digital hub
At the center of the network is UNE CareerConnect, a new digital hub designed to facilitate connections and share knowledge, expertise and opportunities. More than 17,000 student, alumni, faculty, professional staff and employer accounts were imported into CareerConnect ahead of its launch.
Students who draw on the network while at UNE can remain engaged after graduation, sharing their own experiences with future students while continuing to benefit from connections throughout their careers.
The network is led by UNE’s office of career readiness and workforce development, established in 2025 to integrate career development across academic programs, strengthen connections with employers and professional networks and prepare graduates to adapt to a rapidly changing economy.
“By building a culture of professional trust and reciprocity, the network creates pathways for lifelong mobility,” said Ashley Bigda, the office’s director.
The University of New England has campuses in Biddeford and Portland, which house Maine’s only medical school, as well as Tangier, Morocco.
UNE ranked No. 7 among Maine’s largest universities and colleges in the 2026 Mainebiz Book of Lists, with 2,082 undergraduate students. Rankings were based on undergraduate full-time enrollment in fall 2025.

title: MAINE-LY GARDENING: Great pumpkins
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Botanists trace the roots of our Halloween Jack O’Lanterns and Thanksgiving pumpkin pies back to Central and South America where wild bitter gourd-like fruits were eaten by large extinct animals like mastodons that ate them, spreading the seeds. Some 10,000 years ago, the indigenous peoples of the Western Hemisphere domesticated these plants, around the same time that other humans were developing their own agricultural methods in the Fertile Crescent of the Middle East.
Pumpkins were among crops introduced to Europe 500 years ago. At first people were skeptical about some of the new foods, especially tomatoes and potatoes, because the flowers of these plants show they are related to nightshades which can be poisonous, But the pumpkins and other members of the cucurbit family, which includes cucumbers and melons, were enjoyed immediately. Within 100 years these plants were being grown across Europe and Asia. Pumpkins in particular, were so common that they became part of European folklore, seeming to have been with us forever.
Cucurbits are known to cross pollinate very easily. Many gardeners discover oddities in their gardens that result from planting several varieties close to one another. That small plot of butternut squash may surprise you with a few weird, but delicious surprises. Farmers have taken advantage of this trait and now supply us with green, yellow, tan, orange, red, and white squashes and pumpkins, carefully separating the different types.
The type of pumpkins most widely grown for Jack O’Lanterns are the Connecticut Field Pumpkins, consistently large and round, good for carving. Better for cooking are smaller types, often called “sugar pumpkins.” Highmoor Farm, in Monmouth, is one of five research farms operated by the University of Maine to develop and trial crops for Maine farmers and gardeners. It was once an orchard with 5,000 apple trees but has grown a wide variety of vegetables and fruits since its acquisition by the University in 1909. The University recommends several varieties of pumpkins that are particularly suited to our climate.
There are pumpkins for every taste and use at our farm stands and grocery stores. The many shapes and sizes inspire creative carving for outdoor Halloween displays and holiday table settings.
Some people aren’t content with carving a jolly or frightening face for the front steps. They have bigger plans in mind. From the little gourds that have been part of the South American landscape for many thousands of years, pumpkins have been bred to larger, and more recently, gigantic monster plants. More people have joined the giant pumpkin race. The largest now reach close to 3,000 pounds.
Henry David Thoreau recorded in noted for his unfinished work Wild Fruits that he grew a 123-pound pumpkin in 1857. Forty years later, folks were growing pumpkins twice or three times that size. Now commonly exhibited at fairs, the competitors carefully save, and sell, the seeds, after making time all summer to nurture their big babies. Then what? Even Peter Piper’s wife refuses to live in a pumpkin shell. Giant pumpkins aren’t good eating, so why not carve them into boats for one more competition?
 © Judith Chute Hsiang
Jude Hsiang is a retired University Extension Master Gardener Program instructor and a member of the China Community Garden.
