title: Donald Trump’s Russian diesel deal won’t help the US and must be stopped
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Editorial Board operates independently from the newsroom, and does not set policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com.
President Donald Trump recently announced he’d reached an unexpected agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia, which runs counter to long-standing sanctions aimed at stopping Putin’s attacks on Ukraine.
This deal is horrible for many reasons, and Sen. Susan Collins, Sen. Angus King and other senators are right to oppose it. Collins and a bipartisan group of a dozen senators, who sent a letter to the president on Tuesday raising their objections, are looking into ways to block the president’s move. They must act quickly to ensure it is.
“This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded,” the senators said bluntly in the letter.
Diesel prices have soared to over $6 a gallon in part because of Trump’s war with Iran, which has disrupted fuel shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump announced Friday that Russia would immediately supply 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons next month, and another 1 million tons in December.
That sounds like a lot. It is not.
The first shipment of 300,000 tons equals a little over 2 million barrels of diesel. The U.S. uses about 3.6 million barrels of diesel per day. So, the fuel Trump touts from Russia would last less than a day. In terms of global supply, it would last 11 minutes, according to Forbes.
That will do nothing to bring down global prices.
For a virtually meaningless amount of diesel, Trump is allowing Russia to raise money and to be treated like a reasonable global partner. This is counterproductive to U.S. and global interests.
Worse, Trump attacked Ukraine and its leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Trump ludicrously said that Zelenskyy could end Russia’s attacks against Ukraine. To be clear, Russia is the one doing the attacking, and it must be the one to stop its war of aggression.
Trump even suggested that Zelenskyy, who has bravely led Ukraine against relentless Russian attacks, should be replaced.
Trump’s surprise announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that sought to stop the flow of money from fuel sales that Russia is using to finance its war against Ukraine. It directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas. Trump did the opposite.
Collins, who was a co-sponsor of the sanctions law along with King, was among a bipartisan group of six senators who called on Trump to immediately reverse course.
“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine. Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the group said in a press release.
“President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law,” the senators added. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The administration must immediately reverse course.”
A larger group signed on to the Oct. 13 letter to the president.
King, who is not part of the group, also had strong objections to the deal, calling it “illegal, immoral and wrong.”
“Instead of pursuing solutions that are consistent with America’s values, President Trump has decided to ease energy sanctions on Russia. In doing so, he chose Putin over the American people, which will ultimately help fuel that autocracy’s bloody, unprovoked war of aggression on Ukraine,” King said in a statement on Saturday.
“At the end of the day, this deal from the White House is an attempt to boost their short-term political prospects at the true cost of the American people,” he added. “This deal comforts our enemies and will do little for Americans. It’s a fraud.”
Americans need relief from high fuel prices, including the cost of heating oil, which has nearly doubled in recent months.
That relief needs to be real, and it can’t come at the expense of allowing Russia to continue to brutalize Ukraine, or any other country.

title: Whitewashing history is no path to peace
text:
It is hard to imagine a more vacuous and willfully one-sided column than Douglas Rooks’ Oct. 8 piece (“‘Genocide’ or not, US must seek an end to the suffering in Gaza”). In more than 760 words ostensibly offering a solution to Gazan suffering, Rooks places blame entirely on Israel — by my count, he mentions either Israel or Netanyahu by name 24 times while mentioning Hamas but twice.
Whitewashing history provides a weak foundation for peace; serious problems require acknowledging inconvenient facts. It was Hamas that militarized Gaza’s civilian infrastructure and embedded its war-making apparatus among the people it purported to represent. It was Hamas that initiated this war with its murderous Oct. 7 attack, then sheltered its fighters in tunnels while leaving Gazan civilians above ground to endure the foreseeable Israeli response. And, it was Hamas’ continued captivity of Israeli hostages that prolonged the conflict, compounding Gazans’ suffering.
Exploiting civilians — Gazan and Israeli — is integral to Hamas’ strategy. Yet the column never confronts Hamas as an obstacle to resolution. It contemplates Netanyahu’s removal through Israeli democratic elections without considering whether Hamas’ removal from power would advance the cause of peace. Wouldn’t an honest assessment of peace prospects examine the governing entities on both sides?
Lasting relief requires an honest and serious reckoning with the conduct and responsibilities of all parties to the conflict. Ignoring Hamas while focusing solely on Israel is neither honest nor serious and provides no path to peace.
Daniel Kagan
Lewiston

title: Bobby Charles levels unfounded corruption claims at Hannah Pingree in final debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Maine — Republican Bobby Charles accused Democrat Hannah Pingree without evidence of using her state job to enrich her family in Wednesday’s final gubernatorial debate.
He opened the WMTW debate with the charge and came back to versions of it more later in the debate, including during a question about electricity rates.
“She boldly violated the public trust, conspiring with Janet Mills to enrich her family,” Charles said.
The attack dominated an hour of bitter exchanges that showed where each campaign stands three weeks before the Nov. 3 election. Pingree, a former Maine House speaker and top Mills adviser, has led every public poll since the June primary. Charles has gotten almost no help from national Republicans, and he made the debate a test of her character.
The underdog’s attack rests on two allegations he first made at a Sept. 30 news conference in Rockland. Both involve films made by Pingree’s husband, filmmaker Jason Mann, and neither is supported by the public record, according to the Midcoast Villager.
The first, which Charles repeated Wednesday, involves North Haven Sustainable Housing, a nonprofit on Pingree’s home island that Mann now leads. It received an $840,000 forgivable loan from MaineHousing for rental units, and around the same time Mann co-directed and produced a film for the group. Pingree said she was not involved in the award.
The second claim was that Pingree’s former office gave nearly $38,000 to the Island Institute, a Rockland-based nonprofit group, and that the money paid for a climate film produced by Mann. The institute called that “false” and said none of the grant went to his film.
Pingree predicted in her first answer that Charles would spend the night attacking her, and she cast it as a repeat of his primary campaign.
“This is how he won his Republican primary with lies, AI memes, [President] Donald Trump 2.0,” Pingree said. “I think Maine people want a positive campaign where we talk about how we solve the issues.”
Pingree’s strategy has been to tie Charles firmly to Trump, who is unpopular in Maine. She called Charles a “25-year lobbyist.” She also raised his past support for Trump’s Iran war, his opposition to MaineCare expansion and his remarks in August, obtained by the BDN, that he would ask for “ICE and marshals to be at our voting booths.”
Charles has softened his tone on Trump since the primary, and on Wednesday he said he has never met the president. He also defended a scaled-back version of his pledge to cut $4 billion from the state budget. To do it, he cited a $15.9 billion budget figure that includes nearly $6 billion in federal money.
The third candidate, independent state Sen. Rick Bennett, a former Maine Republican Party chair polling in the single digits, cast himself as the alternative to both. He struggled at times to get words in.
“It’s not really a debate. It’s more like who can outshout each other,” Bennett said.

title: Chicago Catholics rally for prayer in Pope Leo’s hometown after his lung cancer diagnosis
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Gail Spreen goes most days to Mass just a few blocks from her home in Chicago, but the service at Holy Name Cathedral on Wednesday — dedicated to Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV — felt different.
“Knowing that everybody is behind him, it was very special to be there today,” Spreen said. “The church was full and everybody was praying. You could just see all those prayers going up and being received.”
Catholics in Chicago and around the world met the news of Leo’s lung cancer diagnosis with shock, concern and support for the 71-year-old, whose candor around his health broke with the Vatican’s tendency to be tight-lipped around papal health. Leo himself announced that he had a nodule and was undergoing surgery, which confirmed that he has lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Surgeons on Tuesday removed the lower lobe of his right lung.
Spreen, whose husband died from cancer, said the pope going public with his diagnosis can “wake up the whole world” to the importance of early detection.
“If the pope can have cancer, anybody can,” she said.
The first American-born pope, Leo undertook his ministry in Peru, but he was born in 1955 in the south side Chicago neighborhood of Bronzeville and grew up in suburban Dolton, near St. Mary of the Assumption, where he attended Mass and elementary school.
He later studied theology at the Catholic Theological Union of Chicago in Hyde Park and taught in local Catholic schools, including at St. Rita High School. Leo is also a White Sox fan, a fact embraced by the team.
Cardinal Blase J. Cupich, the archbishop of Chicago, encouraged fellow Chicagoans and people worldwide to “join me in asking the Lord to return this son of Chicago to wellness.”
“He has much more good work to do, many more wise words to preach and many more ways to inspire others,” Cupich said in a statement.
Earlier Wednesday, students at Our Lady of Mount Carmel Academy made get-well cards and a care package, complete with a White Sox blanket, to send to the Vatican. The Rev. Charles Rubey, a retired priest, planned to offer a Sunday Mass in the apartment where he lives in the suburbs of Chicago.
“I’m praying very hard, asking God to spare him illness, so he’ll be successful in the treatment,” he said.
“I think he’s a hero,” Rubey said of Pope Leo. “He’s highly revered here, highly loved.”
The Vatican said late Wednesday that the pope had celebrated Mass with his secretaries in the afternoon in a special chapel set up for him on the 10th floor of the hospital. He had also resumed his regular diet and begun walking.
For Katrina Coker, Leo has been an authentic embodiment of true Catholicism, which she said should be open and welcoming and loving. Coker of Johns Creek, Georgia, said it was meaningful to her that she happened to be in Chicago this week and she wanted to attend Mass in his hometown to pray for Leo’s recovery.
“I feel somewhat of a kindred spirit, and hopefully he can get a little bit of healing from home,” she said. “I think there’s just so much more that he can do, and I pray that he gets well soon.”
___
Henao reported from Princeton, New Jersey.

title: Police investigate fight at youth football game in Livermore Falls
text:
Livermore Falls police are reviewing a recording and interviews related to a fight that occurred Saturday between parents and a coach at Griffin Field in Livermore Falls.
Video of the altercation, which took place on the sidelines of an Area Youth Sports football game, was disseminated widely on social media.
Once the police investigation is concluded, police Chief Abe Haroon said, the report will be given to the Androscoggin County district attorney for review to determine if any charges will be lodged against participants.
No summonses have been issued and no arrests have been made, he said.
One of the men involved is Cpl. Dylan Rider, an Androscoggin County Sheriff’s deputy, an Area Youth Sports football coach and a county commissioner. Rider was off duty.
In accordance with the organization’s bylaws and code of conduct, the AYS board of directors has initiated a formal review of the incident, AYS President Nixon Ortiz wrote in an email.
“Area Youth Sports (AYS) is aware of the recent incident and video circulating on social media,” Ortiz wrote. “The safety, well-being, and sportsmanship of our youth, families, and community are our highest priorities.”
“Pending the outcome of this thorough investigation, all involved parties have been asked not to attend any practices, games, or AYS events for the balance of this season,” Ortiz wrote. “This interim measure ensures a fair and complete investigative process can play out so that the Board can make informed, appropriate final determinations.”
William Gagne, chief deputy of the Androscoggin County Sheriff’s Office, said Tuesday that his office is aware of the situation. “It was brought to our attention and we are actively looking into the matter internally,” he said.
A short video recording of the altercation was posted on Facebook by Donna Jewell, who accuses Rider of assaulting her and her husband.
The video shows Jewell going up to Rider with a puppy in her arms. It appears she makes contact with Rider, who turns toward her as her hands go up toward Rider’s face. He grabs Jewell’s arms and pushes her to the ground as he makes his way toward a fight between two men. One of those men was Rider’s father.
Rider’s son also plays on the youth football team. Jewell is the parent of an athlete as well.
Rider wrote on his Facebook post that he was punched and scratched by Jewell, and that his father was allegedly punched in the stomach by the other man.
Jewell, whose post of the video has more than 1,300 comments, did not return a request for comment. In a Facebook post, she said an attorney had advised her and her husband to not discuss the issue in public anymore.
Rider’s attorney, Andre “AJ” Hungerford, wrote in an email, “Because there is an investigation of events on Saturday, October 10, 2026 involving various parties, including Dylan Rider, I am withholding comment until a more appropriate time.”

title: Last foliage report issued: Many inland areas past peak, coast and south at peak
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The likely last foliage report of the season was issued Wednesday afternoon. Most places especially inland are now past peak colors.
We have had several storms in the past weeks too that have knocked down a large number of leaves as well. We also saw out first snowfall, while only a dusting at most for many, the snow knocked down more leaves.
The fact is we are nearing the end of the season especially inland.
Color is at peak levels along the coast and down in the southern portion of the state and will likely stay that way into early next week.
This weekend will be windy and chilly which will likely end most of the foliage season even for the coast. Sunday may be the last day to really get a good look at some color before the season really starts to wrap up everywhere.

title: Father creates nation’s only child safety demonstration house after death of son
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (Aging Untold) — A father who lost his 2-year-old son to a furniture tip-over has built the only child-safety demonstration house in the United States to prevent similar tragedies.
Brett Horn founded Charlie’s House in Kansas City, Missouri, after his son Charlie died when a 30-inch dresser fell on him in 2007. The interactive home teaches parents about hidden dangers that experts say cause 90% of childhood accidents.
“My wife and I had no idea that our home wasn’t completely safe, and we wanted to ensure that this type of accident didn’t happen to anyone else,” Horn said.
Furniture tip-overs kill hundreds of children
Between 2000 and 2018, more than 450 children in the United States were killed by furniture tip-overs.
“The dresser that fell on him didn’t even make a sound because unfortunately Charlie’s body was trapped between the dresser and the floor,” Horn said.
Interactive house highlights hidden dangers
The demonstration house includes a living room, bathroom, nursery and kitchen with a working stove, but no one lives there.
Stacy Winkler, the assistant to the director of Charlie’s House, guides visitors through potential hazards.
“This is a pretend home. The stairs over there don’t go anywhere, they just go up to a landing,” Winkler said.
The house demonstrates dangers including cabinet corners, electric appliances, vitamin overdoses and toilet-drowning risks.
Winkler said most people don’t know that children can drown in toilets.
“Ninety percent of all accidents to children happened in the home and 90% of those are preventable,” Winkler said.
Free safety supplies and virtual tours available
Charlie’s House provides free or discounted childproofing supplies to families nationwide who cannot afford safety equipment.
“Cost is an issue for parents who are wanting to properly childproof their home,” Horn said.
For families who cannot visit in person, the organization offers a Charlie’s Safety House app, which provides virtual tours of the demonstration house on mobile devices.
Safety standards change frequently, and cribs used for older children may no longer meet current requirements for younger siblings, according to Charlie’s House.

title: ‘The Vote is Sacred’ bus tour stops in Lewiston
text:
LEWISTON — The way the Rev. Jodi Hayashida sees it, the right to vote in Maine is, for some, constantly under attack.
Why, just on Wednesday, Hayashida said, a far-right group had attempted to harass immigrant voters at Lewiston’s City Hall.
As far as she’s concerned, that harassment is a perfect illustration on why protecting the right to vote is sacred, no matter what the faith of the voter.
“The Vote Is Sacred” bus tour stopped in Lewiston early Wednesday evening to spread that message.
“We are not grounded in the same religious beliefs,” said Hayashida, an organizer at Multifaith Justice Maine and former leader of Auburn’s First Universalist Church. “We don’t use the same language, we don’t worship in the same ways, and we don’t always vote the same way. But our differences don’t frighten us; they delight us. Because we know we share a belief that every life is sacred and should be treated as such.
“And we trust that shared belief is so expansive,” Hayashida said, “that it turns our theological differences into collective strength.”
The Interfaith Alliance, described as a national leader in defending religious freedom and multi-faith democracy, has been leading the bus tour, which will ultimately cover 9,000 miles across the U.S.
In partnership with Multi-Faith Justice Maine and the Maine Council of Churches, the group made a stop Wednesday with a news conference in Kennedy Park next to Bates Street.
“We may worship differently, we may come from different backgrounds, we may not agree on every issue,” said state Rep. Mana Abdi, who represents Lewiston in the Maine House, “but our differences should never prevent us from recognizing our shared humanity, or defending one another’s right.
“Our right to vote is not something we should ever take for granted,” Abdi said. “Generations before us fought and sacrificed to make that right possible. Today, we have responsibility to protect it, and it is, friends, it is very much in danger.”
The event featured a few speakers, who addressed an audience of about two dozen.
“We’re here to say, loud and clear, in one voice, that the vote is sacred,” said the Rev. Allen Ewing-Merrill, director of the BTS Center in Portland. “The vote is sacred and voting is more than just a civic duty. It’s an expression of our hopes, our values, our commitment to one another. Voting is how we shape the world we want to live in. And not only for ourselves, but for our children, our grandchildren, our neighbors, our other-than-human kin and future generations.
“Every ballot we cast is a statement of hope,” Ewing-Merrill said. “Every person who registers, every person who shows up at the polls, every person who delivers a ballot to the drop box, every person who makes their voice heard is offering a prayer for the kind of world we desire for ourselves and our children. And every vote is helping to build a future rooted in dignity, justice, compassion and possibility.”

title: Overboard cruise ship passenger rescued after 20 hours in the water, officials say
text:
(Gray News) – A woman who went overboard from a cruise ship was rescued after 20 hours in the water, Greek authorities said in a press release.
The news release states the woman fell into the water early Friday. A “local emergency plan” was activated and searches began with the help from the Hellenic Coast Guard.
A video shared by the Hellenic Coast Guard shows the moments leading up to the 44-year-old Salvadoran woman’s rescue.
You can see the woman floating in the water inside a lifebuoy and hear someone say, “Are you OK?”
A rope was thrown to the woman and she pulled herself toward the rescue vessel. She received first aid once she was pulled onto the ship, according to the press release.
While the press release did not identify which cruise ship the woman was aboard, USA Today reported she was on Royal Caribbean’s Odyssey of the Seas.
CruiseMapper shows the ship was on a weeklong cruise that departed from Civitavecchia, Italy on Oct. 4. It was scheduled to return on Oct. 11.

title: Up and Down the Kennebec Valley: Medical history in central Kennebec Valley (Windsor)
text:
Windsor
Linwood Lowden’s 1993 history of Windsor has a short chapter on 19th-century medical care, which he titled “An Apple a Day.” He named four doctors known to have practiced or lived in Windsor before 1850: Stephen Barton, James Merrill, Daniel Quimby and Isaac Randall.
Dr. Barton was the earliest to arrive, Lowden said, but died soon afterward. Your writer provided information on his life, including from Lowden’s history, in the Oct. 1 issue of The Town Line.
Dr. Randall’s service in Vassalboro was summarized in the Oct. 8 issue. Lowden added his gruesome testimony in court after he treated Paul Chadwick, the surveyor shot in 1809 during disputes over land. Your writer told the story of the so-called Malta War in the March 7, 2024, article in this historical series.
Below, your writer will share what information – perhaps more than usually contradictory and confusing – she found on Dr. Merrill and Dr. Quimby, plus another doctor who might have been an early Windsor landowner.
* * * * * *
Dr. James Merrill, Lowden said, was born Aug. 26, 1783, in Hebron, Maine. The doctor’s Feb.18, 1870, Portland Daily Press obituary, found on his Find a Grave website, says he was educated at Hebron Academy; got his medical training from “Dr. Chandler, of Portland”; and in 1818 moved to Vassalboro and then to Windsor.
Lowden wrote that when Merrill moved to Windsor about 1820, he bought a farm on Doyle Road (which runs south and a bit east from Hunts Meadow Road, south of Route 17, across the town line to Vigue Road in Whitefield).
By 1822, Lowden wrote, he had apparently moved to the Coopers Mills Road, “on the east side of the West Branch” of the Sheepscot River. This road runs from Route 105 southish to the Whitefield town line; Merrill had moved east, and perhaps north.)
The obituary says that after Merrill moved to Windsor, “he had in the town and vicinity an extensive practice of medicine for nearly forty years.”
Lowden quoted two examples of Merrill’s practice, from Whitefield town records. In 1819, the doctor “provided medical care” to a Whitefield man, charging him 47 cents. Another resident got “nearly a month of care” in the winter of 1820-21, for $17.93.
Merrill lived in China for an unspecified while and “was instrumental in founding the Baptist Church at Weeks Mills” in the southern part of that town, Lowden said.
The China bicentennial history offers two evidences that he was an active China resident in 1830. He is listed among the “founding group” that in January of that year organized the South China Social Library Society, now the South China Library Association.
And Merrill is named (citing Henry Kingsbury’s Kennebec County history) as the initial vice-president of the South China Temperance Society, founded April 28, 1830.
Find a Grave named Merrill’s wife as Lydia N. Merrill (your writer thinks her maiden name is not known), born around 1805 and died March 18, 1877. Merrill died Jan. 22, 1870. Both are buried in Windsor’s Resthaven Cemetery, with 13 other Merrills; one is their daughter Chloe, born in 1843 and died in her early teens, on Aug. 23, 1856.
Find a Grave lists on Dr. Merrill’s page three other children, whose birth dates cannot be right if their mother’s is: Barbara, 1808 -1833; Maria, 1810 – 1895; and Charles, 1811 – 1849. Lydia Merrill’s Find a Grave page lists only Chloe; Chloe’s page lists the same three alleged older siblings.
Neither of the alleged older daughters is buried in Resthaven. The Charles Merrill buried there was born in 1854; Find a Grave does not name his parents.
* * * * * *
Dr. Daniel Quimby, Lowden said, was born June 25, 1796, in Sandwich, New Hampshire. In 1824 in Windsor he married Nancy L. LeBallister. Sometime after 1830 he moved to Calais, where, according to Lowden, he died in June, 1842.
The website FamilySearch adds more information. It says Nancy, born in 1801, was one of a dozen children of Thomas and Hannah (Keene) LeBallister (Thomas LeBallister, from Bristol, bought his first Windsor land in May, 1798, making him one of the early settlers). She was the second Nancy; the first one, born in 1796, died in 1797.
Nancy had two older brothers, born in 1797 and 1799. Her next younger brother, Charles, was born in 1805 and died in 1816, age 10. Six more younger siblings, three brothers and three sisters, were born between 1807 and 1816.
FamilySearch says Daniel and Nancy had at least one son and one daughter, identified as Dr. Lloyd Quimby (1828 – 1913) and Ann Elizabeth Quimby (1831 – 1881). Lloyd was born March 9, 1828, in Calais (suggesting the family moved there before, not after, 1830); he died and is buried in Houston, Texas.
According to this site, Lloyd’s father, Dr. Daniel Quimby, was at an undated time the coroner in Montgomery, Texas; and he died there in 1838, not in Calais in 1842.
* * * * * *
Lowden’s history raises the intriguing possibility that one more Maine doctor might have had a connection with Windsor. He wrote that after a survey done in the fall of 1803, 10 newly-created lots were assigned to 10 settlers, beginning with number one, which went to Daniel Rose.
People soon started arguing over who owned which lot, and in the next paragraph Lowden quoted an 1806 letter from one claimant talking about various lots, starting with “Theirs the Lot No 1 –Dr. Rowes Lott the first Lot in the Plantation….”
If the doctor who owned a Windsor lot in 1803 was indeed Dr. Daniel Rose, not a Dr. Rowe, he was a prominent early Mainer.
His Wikipedia page calls him a politician and physician. It says he was born July 31, 1772 (WikiTree says also Jan. 31, 1772, both dates on the same page), in “the Connecticut Colony” (other sources say Branford, Connecticut) and graduated from Yale – no field of study mentioned – in 1791.
Rose settled in Alna, on the Sheepscot River about 20 miles south of Windsor (the Town of Whitefield separates Alna and Windsor), where, the Wikipedia writer said, he “studied and practiced medicine in nearby Boothbay.”
His obituary, published in Portland’s Eastern Argus on Nov. 11, 1833, and reproduced on a Find a Grave page, says after Yale, he “devoted himself for many years in the practice of Medicine, in which profession he maintained a high rank.”
He was either a private or a captain of engineers in the War of 1812 – the obituary says an engineer, “distinguished for his skill and the accuracy of his judgment.” A war record donated to this Find a Grave site says he enlisted June 29, 1814, and on that same date was in a “skirmish at Bristol.” Discharged July 1, 1814, he re-enlisted Sept. 7 and was again discharged on Sept. 23.
The obituary is the only source that says Rose served in the Massachusetts legislature before Maine became a separate state on March 15, 1820, and was a member of the convention that prepared Maine’s state constitution.
Rose was in the Maine Senate from 1820 to 1824, serving as president in 1822 and 1823. From Jan. 2 to Jan. 5, 1822, the Wikipedia writer said, his Senate presidency meant that he “served as the fourth governor of Maine…, filling an unexpired term between the administrations of Benjamin Ames and Albion K. Parris.”
After his 1824 Senate term, Rose moved to Thomaston to become the first warden of the state prison, “which he helped design.” He resigned in 1828 and became a “Land Agent” for the state, serving until 1831.
Find a Grave says Rose married twice, to “Miss Hammond” and to Olive Peaseley. WikiTree agrees, and adds that he fathered seven children.
His obituary praises his public service and his character, calling him “capable, faithful and honest”; a “kind, faithful, and indulgent” husband and father; and a “warm hearted and confiding” friend.
“The poor, especially, within the circle of his practice as a physician, will remember him with gratitude,” the writer of the obituary said.
Rose died in Thomaston on Oct. 25, 1833. Find a Grave says he is buried in Thomaston’s Elm Grove Cemetery, and shows the small, partly lichen-covered gravestone of Dr. Daniel Rose.
The Find a Grave page with his war record and obituary features Hon. Daniel Rose, buried in Thomaston Village Cemetery. This page says he was born in 1770 (not 1772); it shows a contributed photo of a well-maintained tombstone with his name, date of death and age and also “Olive Rose Wife of D. Rose Died Sep 12, 1845, aged 65 years.”
This wife was the former Olive Peasley, born in 1780, married in 1807 and died in 1845. The Find a Grave page names only one child, Olive Rose (1812 -1875); the article cited immediately below says there were seven children.
The younger Olive Rose, according to an on-line article about a new – 2025 –shop in Rockland named Olive Rose, might have been “the first woman elected to public office in the United States.” Later, the statement is qualified: she was “almost certainly” the first elected woman in Maine, and “perhaps” in the country.
This article says Lincoln County voters – all men, of course — elected her Register (or Recorder – both titles are used) of Deeds in 1853, after she had served as assistant to the previous holder of the office. In the town of Warren, she got 73 votes; her male opponent got four votes.
Rose held the office until 1857, when her older brother Edwin succeeded her. She earned $300 to $400 a year, the website says.
This wife was the former Olive Peasley, born in 1780, married in 1807 and died in 1845. The Find a Grave page names only one child, Olive Rose (1812 -1875).
Main sources
Grow, Mary M., China Maine Bicentennial History including 1984 revisions (1984)
Lowden, Linwood H., good Land & fine Contrey but Poor roads a history of Windsor, Maine (1993)
Websites, miscellaneous.

title: A.J. Brown returns to Patriots practice after high ankle sprain
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown is a step closer to returning to game action.
Brown was back on the practice field on Wednesday for the first time since being placed on injured reserve last month because of a high ankle sprain.
He became eligible to return after missing the last four games. He now must be activated within 21 days or placed on season-ending IR.
Cornerback Christian Gonzalez also practiced after missing the last two games because of a shoulder issue. In addition, offensive lineman Marcus Bryant (ankle) returned after being placed on injured reserve during the preseason.
Brown was injured in the second half of New England’s season-opening 13-10 loss at Seattle on Sept. 9. He left the game early in the third quarter following an incomplete pass from quarterback Drake Maye. He was falling to the turf as he tried to make the catch, and Seahawks cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett’s knee made contact with Brown’s ankle, pushing it against the ground. Brown had three catches for 26 yards before the injury.
“I think he’s stayed engaged,” coach Mike Vrabel said. “I think it’s difficult sometimes to stay engaged. I think his routine was really good, his ability to be around guys in the meetings and then also focus on rehab. He’s just treating everything as a pro, being where he’s supposed to be and working hard to get back.”
During the portion of practice open to the media Wednesday, Brown could be seen smiling at times as he went through some light drills with his right ankle heavily wrapped with tape.
“It’s a warm welcome in the huddle to have him back in there,” Maye said. “You can see how closely he’s been watching the games. Little things he picks up on, you can tell he really watching and really cares. …There’s not many like him that are around here in this league.”
Patriots safety Kevin Byard said Brown’s return brings instant energy to the sideline.
“Huge boost. He’s a receiver (No. 1),” Byard said. “Very talented guy as far as the pass game. Obviously, the last couple of weeks our pass game has been playing really well. So, he’s obviously just going to add another dynamic to that. And hopefully we’ll continue to have a good passing game with A.J. in there.”
Brown’s fellow receivers – Mack Hollins, Romeo Doubs, Pop Douglas, Kyle Williams and Efton Chism – have stepped up without him, accounting for six touchdown catches in his absence, and the Patriots have gone 3-1 with Brown on the shelf. Maye is coming off passing for a season-high 374 yards and four touchdowns last week against the Las Vegas Raiders.
Brown’s potential return to the lineup is perfect timing, with Hollins going on injured reserve last week because of a calf injury.
But Maye said Brown returning to the mix gives him another option to spread the ball around in the passing game.
“We have a lot of guys that can make plays. So it’s going to be tough on defenses,” Maye said.

title: Troy Jackson said he’d detail campaign funding Wednesday morning. He didn’t.
text:
In the heat of the moment during a Tuesday Senate debate, Democrat Troy Jackson offered to send his Republican rival the details of his campaign fundraising and spending a day before the deadline to file it with the Federal Election Commission.
But as of 1 p.m., Jackson had not followed through on his promise, a spokesperson for Sen. Susan Collins said.
The seemingly spontaneous offer came after the 73-year-old Collins parried an attack about her billionaire supporters by noting that Jackson has not yet filed any campaign finance reports.
“I would point out that we have no idea who is financing Troy’s campaign,” Collins said. “He promised to be completely transparent, yet he has not filed a single report.”
An irritated Jackson shot back, saying he would release his report on Wednesday morning.
“I’ll give you the report tomorrow morning,” he said. “How about that? Is that enough? Because we see yours and I know that there’s no billionaires funding me…I’ll give you the report tomorrow and then we’ll talk about it on Thursday.”
Jackson’s campaign did not respond to questions about his comments at the debate.
The 58-year-old former logger and state Senate president is not breaking any campaign finance laws by not releasing the report early. But his failure to follow through on his televised offer could give Collins another line of attack when they face off in their fourth and final debate on Thursday.
The reason Jackson’s campaign funding and spending remain a mystery so late in the cycle is a matter of timing.
Jackson was named the Democratic nominee to replace Graham Platner after the oyster farmer dropped out on July 25. That was well after the previous campaign finance reporting period closed on June 30.
The next round of reports aren’t due until midnight on Thursday, at which point they will become public.
Although no report has been filed, Jackson doesn’t appear to have had much trouble raising money.
In July, he was the third-highest fundraiser on the Democrats’ ActBlue platform, raising $5.3 million despite being a candidate for only a few days.
And his campaign has spent, or reserved, at least $20 million in advertisements, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

title: Franklin Towers Residents Must Relocate During Renovations
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Franklin Towers residents must relocate while Portland apartment building undergoes renovations
The approximately 200 people who live at Franklin Towers in Portland, most of whom are elderly or disabled, will have to relocate while the 16-story apartment building undergoes major renovations.
Franklin Towers has been plagued by bedbugs, cockroaches, mold, asbestos and other toxins, so the Portland Housing Authority is conducting a multi-million-dollar renovation project.
"Tearing down the walls and all that stuff and tearing up all the tiles, and if there's asbestos in the tiles, then, yeah, that's a big problem," said Franklin Towers resident David Caston.
The Portland Housing Authority, which operates Franklin Towers, sent letters out to residents that told them it will be safer to have everybody out of the building while work is being done.
According to the residents, the original plan was to do the work in phases, allowing residents to live in areas of the building that were not undergoing renovation work.
"We're all worried and, like, what are they going to do with us next? They say one thing and change it, and they've done that multiple times now," said resident Samantha Hashey.
Caston has lived at Franklin Towers for 17 years. He likes it there, but said he does not like they way the housing authority is promising different things.
"I'm pretty shaken up about it. I don't know where the hell I'm going to go," Caston said.
Other residents shared their displeasure about moving somewhere else.
"I would have to be on the bus route because I have doctor's appointments," said resident Wesley Ward.
The Portland Housing Authority released a statement on Wednesday from its director of real estate development, Jay Waterman.
“We are working closely with each household to ensure comprehensive relocation support, assisting residents with temporary housing placements tailored to their individual needs and accessibility requirements," Waterman said in the statement. "We have two relocation coordinators on staff. We have had a great response to our outreach to many of our affordable housing colleagues in the Greater Portland area and are hopeful we will find temporary homes for all the residents in the coming months."
Residents said the Portland Housing Authority has called a meeting for 5 p.m. Thursday in the Franklin Towers common room to discuss next steps.

title: ‘Curative’ blood cancer therapy coming to Westbrook cancer clinic
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After Yoni Resnick and Stephen Rolfe opened the canister, thin white vapor wafted out — a reaction caused by the liquid nitrogen inside meeting the warm air in the pharmacy at New England Cancer Specialists in Westbrook.
The canister contained a solution used for a life-saving cancer therapy that is increasingly employed to treat certain blood cancers. The treatment, called chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, or CAR T, will be available for the first time at the Westbrook clinic.
New England Cancer Specialists expects to give the therapy to its first patient in November.
Obtaining the liquid nitrogen canister, which stores the T-cells at minus 200 degrees Celsius, was one of the key steps to making the treatment more accessible in Maine, officials with the cancer clinic said.
Resnick and Rolfe manage the pharmacy and must test the liquid nitrogen canister, which arrived at the pharmacy this week, to make sure it’s maintaining its temperature, and conduct other tests to ensure it can safely transport the T-cells and the solution they are stored in. The canister passed the first test during the initial opening on Wednesday.
Dr. John Winters, director of the CAR T program at the clinic said patients will soon be able to receive the infusion treatment at their offices and recover at home. Winters said patients previously had to travel to Boston for the therapy. The process takes about three weeks, and patients need to stay near where they received the infusion in case complications arise, he said.
“This harnesses the patient’s own immune cells to kill the cancer,” Winters said. The treatment can be “curative” for certain types of lymphoma and put multiple myeloma in “durable remission,” he said.
Winters said only about 20% of patients in Maine were able to access CAR T, because of the logistical difficulties of traveling to Boston.
Resnick, vice president of pharmacy at New England Cancer Specialists, said having only one in five patients in Maine able to access CAR T is “dismal” and having a location in the state will improve access. He said barriers to access include not only the travel time to Boston, but needing a caregiver while recovering from the infusion, and also the financial costs of traveling and lodging.
Winters said the way the therapy works is patients have blood removed, the T-cells are extracted from the blood, and the blood is returned to the patient. The harvested T-cells are shipped to a lab in California in the liquid nitrogen canister, and then returned to Maine a few weeks later.
Then the patient comes back to the office, and the engineered T-cells, designed to fight their cancer, are infused into their blood, he said.
“This is curative for patients who before had no hope,” Winters said.
Patients with late-stage lymphoma or multiple myeloma would typically have about a year or less to live without the CAR T treatments, he said.
Winters said CAR T has been available for about a decade, and is increasingly used earlier as a treatment option as outcomes from the therapy prove to work. In the future, he said, the therapy will likely become a frontline treatment for certain blood cancers, reducing reliance on chemotherapy.
He said initially it will be used on one patient at the clinic per month, but they expect usage will expand as the CAR T program at New England Cancer Specialists ramps up.
According to the American Cancer Society, CAR T is also used for certain types of leukemia, and is being researched for its effectiveness on other cancers.
According to the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention, Maine has about 400 new cases of non-Hodgkin lymphoma per year. CAR T can treat certain types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Multiple myeloma is a rarer cancer, at about 1.7% of all cancer diagnoses, according to the National Cancer Institute.
Deborah Cote, 69, of Dresden, said she was diagnosed with lymphoma in 2015, and was selected for CAR T therapy last year. Cote said she traveled to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston in March for the treatment, and had to stay in Boston for about three weeks. She said she was fortunate to have a friend willing to stay with her.
“If I could have stayed in Maine, that would have been unbelievable,” Cote said. “I have a support group here, and I missed that support group in Boston.”
Cote said the treatment has improved her life, and doctors “can’t find a wisp of cancer cells in me.”
“I feel better than I’ve felt in many years,” Cote said.

title: Social Security recipients to get 3.6% cost of living boost, an average of $75 per month
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, with some recipients complaining that is not enough to offset soaring prices.
The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month for the 73 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and nearly 7.5 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
The announcement comes as inflation adds pressure on household budgets and businesses and as midterm elections are weeks away.
The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
The agency’s commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.”
Older adults feel the bite of rising costs
Some older adults feel the increase is a drop in the bucket as inflation has eaten away at monthly savings. The government reported last month that inflation accelerated in August as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA will not put a dent in her healthcare costs, which are set to increase after the Trump administration concludes at year’s end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin said that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people.
The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press.
She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans’ healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.”
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.
Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance,” given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he said.
Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.
Social Security faces a looming funding shortfall
The Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
While a permanent solution for shoring up the benefits program has not been passed into law, lawmakers on the Hill have called for new measures to replenish the trust funds.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. Treating all income the same “would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” they wrote in The New York Times.
The move is controversial because Republicans have traditionally criticized calls to raise taxes on the wealthy.
The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the payroll tax cap would add roughly $3 trillion into the program over the next 10 years.
Both the Trump and Biden administrations signed into law new benefits for retirees, which boosted their finances, but simultaneously accelerated the insolvency of the old-age benefits program.
The Trump administration, as part of Republicans’ tax and spending bill, gave a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and over, which applies to all income — not just Social Security. But those who aren’t able to claim the deduction include the lowest-income older adults who already don’t pay taxes on Social Security, those who choose to claim their benefits before they reach 65 and those above a defined income threshold.
Additionally, Democratic President Joe Biden in 2024 repealed two federal policies — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that previously limited Social Security payouts for roughly 2.8 million people, including largely former public workers.

title: Farmington-area school district technology specialist earns state award
text:
FARMINGTON — Nicole Lesperance, technology integration specialist and training coordinator for Regional School Unit 9, has received the 2026 ACHIEVE Award from the Association of Computer Technology Educators of Maine, recognizing her leadership in helping teachers use technology to improve classroom instruction.
Lesperance, who spent nearly 20 years in the classroom before moving into educational technology, has helped transform the district’s Summer Tech Institute from a small professional development event into a regional gathering for educators. Attendance grew from 27 participants in 2023 to 80 in 2025, according to district presentation materials.
“I have a lot of passion for my job, so personally it feels amazing to see that it shines through and is noticed,” Lesperance said. “Professionally, it is an absolute honor to be amongst the amazing educators that have received this award before me.”
The ACHIEVE Award recognizes educators who use technology in innovative and meaningful ways to strengthen teaching and learning. Lesperance is one of two Maine educators selected for the award this year, along with Keith Kelley, an integrated technology teacher at Nokomis Middle School in RSU 19.
Lesperance and Kelley are scheduled to be recognized in connection with ACTEM’s Fall Conference, set for Oct. 15-16 at the Augusta Civic Center.
For Lesperance, the Summer Tech Institute represents both a professional accomplishment and a reflection of her years working directly with students.
Four years ago, she moved from teaching first grade into her current technology integration role. She said she and her supervisor envisioned reviving the institute while expanding its reach beyond RSU 9.
“We started small that first year, but with the vision to eventually open it up to all in education,” she said. “I have strived to do just that.”
The institute is held annually at Mt. Blue High School on the second Wednesday and Thursday of August, shortly before the start of the school year. The timing is intentional, allowing educators to return from summer break and prepare for the coming academic year.
Lesperance said she wanted the event to offer something different from traditional professional development, particularly because attendance falls during educators’ summer vacations.
“With almost 20 years in the classroom, I wanted to ‘hit this one out of the park’ for them,” she said. “With it being in the summer, I wanted this event to be something that was optional but so fun, engaging, enjoyable and fulfilling that educators wanted to be there.”
The institute’s growth reflects that effort. In 2023, the event drew 27 attendees and featured 12 presenters offering 22 sessions. Attendance increased to 39 in 2024 and reached 80 in 2025, when 24 presenters participated.
The program has also evolved in how sessions are organized and delivered. Earlier versions relied on Apple educators and district technology coaches to provide instruction. Sessions are now developed through an open proposal process, allowing educators to contribute presentations across a range of subjects and skill levels.
The 2026 institute, held Aug. 12-13, included an escape room and interactive art gallery organized by the WorkForce Ready 2030 Partnership, an initiative supporting computer science education.
Participant feedback included praise for the event’s organization, practical classroom applications and opportunities to collaborate with colleagues from other schools.
One attendee described the institute as the most organized and effective of five professional development events the person had attended that summer. Others highlighted the variety of sessions, enthusiastic presenters and welcoming atmosphere.
While the Summer Tech Institute has become one of her most visible projects, Lesperance said the district’s commitment to maintaining a dedicated technology integration position is equally significant.
“Not every district understands or sees the importance of it,” she said. “Just because we live in a technological age doesn’t mean that we know best educational technology practices, the options out there, or how best to apply them.”
Her approach emphasizes what students learn through technology rather than the equipment or applications they use.
“The device and software shouldn’t matter because those are always changing,” Lesperance said. “What should matter is the computational thinking that is at the base of everything.”
Computational thinking involves approaching problems systematically, recognizing patterns and developing logical solutions. Lesperance sees those skills as more lasting than familiarity with any particular technology.
“I truly believe in the process over the product, and not just using technology as a replacement, but as a way to elevate learning, abilities, and understanding,” she said. That philosophy also shapes her work with educators as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly common in classrooms.
Lesperance said AI has changed conversations with teachers and students, particularly as schools consider how to use the technology responsibly and effectively.
For her, the most important question is not whether AI can complete an assignment, but whether it can help students better understand the material.
“For me, the important conversation to be having, and am having, is how artificial intelligence can be used to deepen understanding of a concept, topic, and more,” she said. “Yes, it can be used to complete a task, but there is so much more to it, and that is what we need to be teaching so it can be leveraged.”
Beyond individual classrooms, Lesperance said RSU 9 is working to expand computer science integration through its participation in the WorkForce Ready 2030 Partnership. The initiative complements her broader goal of helping teachers identify effective instructional practices while preparing students for a world in which technology continues to evolve.
Lesperance said she hopes people outside the school system recognize the work taking place throughout the district, including efforts that may not always be visible to the public.
“I am so proud of the work we do here,” she said. “Like so many educators I know, we don’t settle. We constantly strive to be the best we can, deliver the best we can, support the best we can.”
The Summer Tech Institute is scheduled to return Aug. 11-12, 2027, continuing a program Lesperance helped rebuild with the goal of making professional development accessible, engaging and useful to educators across the region.

title: Dolly Parton’s nephew denies threatening to harm her estate, pushes back against restraining order
text:
(AP) - Dolly Parton’s nephew and longtime head of security said in a Tennessee court filing Tuesday that he was a close friend and ally of Parton’s longtime manager Danny Nozell before Nozell took out a restraining order accusing him of threatening to do violence and destroy Parton’s legacy and business empire.
In an affidavit opposing the temporary order becoming permanent, Bryan Seaver said text messages Nozell cited as evidence against him were a “private conversation between two friends who were both frustrated, grieving and discussing strategy.” The text messages were sent shortly before and after Parton’s Aug. 25 death.
Seaver said he never sent threatening messages to any of Parton’s businesses or business partners or their employees.
The filings represent Seaver’s first public defense of himself since a serious rift opened up in the country music legend’s circle and spilled into public view shortly after her death, with Nozell and Seaver on opposing sides.
Seaver’s court filing says Nozell did not react with alarm to his text messages at the time and that he agreed with or reacted positively to some of them. Seaver says Nozell encouraged him to publicly tout the military and arms aspect of his security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, as a smart business-promotion move, then turned around and used them as evidence of Seaver’s capacity for dangerous violence.
She’s Alive, an entity run by Nozell and founded to manage and protect Parton’s estate, terminated Seaver and SAPS in early September, and the following week petitioned for the restraining order against him, arguing that his“terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable.”
In granting the temporary restraining order, Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles, cited Seaver’s “claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate.”
The two sides will make their cases to Myles at a hearing on Oct. 20. Emails seeking comment were sent to lawyers for She’s Alive and Nozell.
Seaver said he was blindsided by the order, which was granted while he was doing contract security work in Haiti.
Seaver and SAPS must refrain from entering any She’s Alive property or talking with or being within 1,000 feet (about 300 meters) of She’s Alive employees and business partners. The order is also meant to keep Seaver from interfering with its business relationships.
Seaver argued in his response that the order is so broad, and Parton’s business reach so great, that much of Nashville and even his own relatives are off limits to him.
In one message written Sept. 1 that was cited by She’s Alive, Seaver said: “I’m going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or f——— pay me.”
Seaver said his anger and the demand were only over more than $250,000 that his company was owed for completed work by Herschend Family Entertainment, which operates Parton’s amusement park Dollywood and her Songteller Hotel, which opened after her death.
Seaver acknowledged being overly crude and profane in his messages to Nozell. He said allegations that he had “menaced and intimidated” HFE employees were simply false.
He included as an exhibit a 2024 letter from Parton praising him and his company. Parton had handpicked Seaver to announce her death once she succumbed to cancer.
Parton was a widely beloved country music giant, philanthropist and cultural icon who wrote hundreds of songs, including classics such as “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors” and “I Will Always Love You.” Her music earned a total of more than 100 million worldwide sales and more than 1 billion online streams.

title: Ahead of 3rd anniversary, survivors of Lewiston mass shootings call for accountability
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- Mass shooting survivors and victims’ family members gathered Wednesday in front of the media nearly three years after the Oct. 25, 2023, tragedy.
- Some survivors continue to call into question how $1.9 million of the $6.6 million raised in the aftermath of the shooting reached area nonprofits instead of victims’ families and survivors.
- They say they have been denied an audience with the Legislature’s Government Oversight Committee.
LEWISTON — With the anniversary of the Oct. 25, 2023, mass shooting approaching, some victims, survivors and their families gathered at Veterans Memorial Park on Main Street to hold a news conference.
Standing in front of the cameras, Amy Sussman read the names of the 18 people killed at Just-In-Time Recreation and Schemengees Bar and Grille: Ronald Morin, Peyton Brewer-Ross, Joshua Seal, Bryan MacFarlane, Joseph Walker, Arthur Strout, Maxx Hathaway, Stephen Vozzella, Thomas Conrad, Michael Deslauriers II, Jason Walker, Tricia Asselin, William Young, Aaron Young, Robert Violette, Lucille Violette, William Brackett and Keith Macneir.
Sussman, who is Hathaway’s aunt, said the grieving families and survivors are still seeking answers on how the Maine Community Foundation handled collecting and disbursing the $6.6 million Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund.
What they are looking for, she said, is accountability, transparency and fairness.
Some $4.7 million of the Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund was granted to victims’ families and survivors; $1.9 million went to 29 area nonprofits.
Speaking at the news conference were survivors Jennifer Zanca, Destiny Johnson, Danielle Chabot and Strout’s father, Arthur Barnard.
Zanca, who was shot at Schemengees Bar and Grille, learned a year later she would need more surgery and, by the end of it, owed $93,000 in hospital bills that she said her insurance company denied.
“The FBI, Homeland Security came to my home and told me I would never have to worry about hospital bills,” Zanca said. “Except I did.”
Zanca said it was a year later that she learned about the distribution of funds occurring in the months following the shooting.
“You mean to tell me that 29 nonprofits received $65,000 each, that only a few had anything to do with the shooting, while victims that were shot received less than half that amount from the Maine Community Foundation?” Zanca asked. “Some nonprofits received nine times the amount than victims that fled from flying bullets, while others saved lives and witnessed the carnage that is forever embedded in their memories.”
Nearly three years after the shootings, some victims and survivors are still asking the Maine Attorney General’s Office and the Legislature’s Government Oversight Committee to hear their side of the story. Sussman said survivors have also tried unsuccessfully to meet with Gov. Janet Mills.
Attorney General Aaron Frey sat before the Government Oversight Committee on Sept. 16 and told legislators that the Office of Program Evaluation and Government Accountability cannot investigate the handling of funds because the funds were not handled by a government entity.
Frey also told legislators the only recourse for an investigation would be through the Maine Charitable Solicitations Act; however, he said, no complaints have been filed through that act.
The Maine Community Foundation has publicly defended its handling of the donations since as early as 2024, saying families and survivors were notified that the Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund would be two separate funds: one for victims and another for nonprofit organizations, as suggested by nationally recognized victims’ advocate, Jeff Dion.
The foundation said it did not take administrative fees so all donations could go to families and community recovery efforts.
Maine Community Foundation said the Attorney General’s Office found that donor intent had been followed and that there were no concerns about how the funds were collected and distributed.
Sussman said victims’ families and survivors feel as though they have been silenced by the Government Oversight Committee from giving their own account of what they were initially told by the Maine Community Foundation.
“The Maine Community Foundation gave us this document on their own letterhead,” Sussman said, holding up a binder and pointing to a page, “saying that 100% of the Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund was for the victims’ families and survivors. We were sent emails saying (the same).
“What we didn’t know was that the Maine Community Foundation was collecting money for nonprofits on the backs of the 18 people who were murdered and the 118 who survived … in the worst mass violence event in the state’s history.”
Victims’ families and survivors learned a week ago that the Government Oversight Committee will not hear from groups of victims and survivors in a meeting after having several requests ignored, Sussman said.
“We recently learned that one of the co-chairs and members of the committee work for or are on the boards of nonprofits that received grants from the Maine Community Foundation,” Sussman said. “This conflict of interest is prominent in the ruling party of the state Legislature.”
In April, some 57 victims’ family members and survivors sent a complaint, accompanied by new documents, to the Maine Office of the Attorney General to reopen its investigation. They declined, Sussman said.
“True accountability means that no other family or individual will have to go through what we have in the aftermath of a tragedy at the hands of an unethical nonprofit. … That no other family or individual will have to get up off their knees from grief and suffering to fight for what is right because the ruling party in this state of Maine will not help us.”
Sussman said she recently learned of two new complaints being filed with the Attorney General’s Office.
“We are continuing to demand accountability. … It is being swept under the rug by the governor, the attorney general, the Government Oversight Committee and the city of Lewiston,” Sussman said. “The actions of the Maine Community Foundation have hurt not only us, but all nonprofits.”
“We are on the right side of this,” Sussman said. “We’re not giving up and we’re not going away.”

title: ‘Images: Real and Whimsical’ exhibition on display at Damariscotta gallery
text:
River Arts in Damariscotta is pleased to announce “Images: Real and Whimsical,” an exhibition featuring the work of artists Stephanie Muri and Chris Lawrence. The exhibition brings together two distinct approaches to art, from Muri’s whimsical and experimental mixed-media work to Lawrence’s colorful and expressive paintings inspired by the Maine coast.
Stephanie Muri came to art later in life, following decades as a psychotherapist and instructor of clinical social work. Her earlier work continues to influence her creative practice, bringing curiosity, compassion, humor, and a belief in the healing power of small moments to her artwork. Working primarily in mixed media, collage, printmaking, and found materials, Muri embraces experimentation, intuition, color, and texture. Her whimsical, abstract pieces celebrate surprise, transformation, and the simple joy of creative discovery.
Chris Lawrence describes his work as “representative of a moment; a memory of a place and time.” His paintings are inspired by the sensory experiences associated with a particular scene — the vibrant sky of a sunrise, the crash of surf on the rocks, the lazy bump of a skiff against a dock, or the bitter sting of cold air. Inspired by the magic of the Maine coast, Lawrence moves from wide-open seascapes to narrow vignettes of the world around him. He uses bold colors and contrast in acrylic and oil paintings to recreate these remembered moments.
Together, Muri and Lawrence offer viewers an engaging look at two different artistic visions. “Images: Real and Whimsical” invites visitors to appreciate the contrast between Lawrence’s recognizable coastal scenes and Muri’s imaginative explorations of color, texture, and form.
The public is invited to meet the artists at the opening reception on Saturday, Oct. 17, from 2–4 p.m. The exhibition will be on view through Oct. 28.
River Arts is located at 36 Elm St. in Damariscotta and is open Tuesday through Saturday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. For more information, visit riverartsme.org or call 207-563-6868.

title: Knox County courts will close during transition to electronic filing system
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine — The Knox County courts will be transitioning to a new computer docketing system on Dec. 7, which will require a two-week closure for staff training and installation of the new equipment.
Knox County is one of the last courts in the state to undergo the transition.
The court will reopen at noon on Dec. 7. That week will be an administrative week in which the court is open to the public only from noon to 4 p.m.
Normal business hours will return Dec. 14.
The state courts in Waldo, Lincoln and Sagadahoc counties also will transition to electronic filing on Dec. 7.
There will be Zoom training for attorneys on how to file paperwork prior to the transition.
The Maine Judicial Branch remains on track to have all courts on the new system by February 2027.
Supreme Judicial Court Chief Justice Valerie Stanfill noted in a news release: “We are pleased that the transition from paper filing to eFiling has proceeded so smoothly this year, a testament to the hard work and dedication of all Judicial Branch staff. The eCourts project implementation and project support teams have traveled all over the state to make the transition successful, and they certainly deserve special acknowledgement.”
This story appears through a media partnership with Midcoast Villager.

title: What you need to know about the flu shot as flu season picks up in Maine
text:
What you need to know about the flu shot as flu season picks up in Maine
Flu season has begun in Maine and medical experts are urging people across the state to get a flu shot.
For the week ending Oct. 10, the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention listed influenza activity in Maine as low with 15 people admitted to the hospital with the flu over the previous week. That was one more than the week before. Only five were hospitalized during the week before that.
The Maine CDC said that, for the week ending Oct. 10, 0.44% of all visits to Emergency Departments in Maine indicated the flu, up from 0.41%, 0.27% and 0.24% the previous three weeks.
Activity of COVID-19 was considered very low in Maine for the week ending Oct. 10, with four people hospitalized, though the state did report one person died from COVID-19 that week.
On Tuesday, Adam Jordan, a pharmacist for Northern Light Health, spoke with Maine's Total Coverage about flu season and flu shots.
What is a common myth that you hear about flu shots?
One of the most common myths that we hear is it "gives you the flu." All flu shots are inactive—meaning there are no live, active virus parts in them. If people feel sick or off after getting the shot, what they are feeling is usually a reaction from their body fighting the inactive virus.
When you say reaction, what does that mean?
When we say that your immune system responds to the flu shot, we mean that it responds to inactivate virus parts or proteins in the vaccine. This gives your body the information it needs to train your immune system to recognize and fight off the virus if you become infected with it later in the season. It takes your immune system about two weeks from the time you are vaccinated until you develop that protection, so it is recommended to get vaccinated in September or October, before peak flu season develops.
What do you say to people who claim the flu isn't that serious?
Certain people are at higher risk of developing a serious illness and complications if they become infected with the flu. This demographic includes children, those over 65 years old, those with respiratory conditions (like asthma), diabetes, heart disease or other health conditions. Those with a weakened immune system, like patients with cancer, are also at higher risk.
Getting vaccinated helps decrease the odds of you passing it off to any friends or family who do fit those demographics.
How effective is the flu vaccination each year?
Flu vaccines are designed to defend you against three different strains of influenza that are suspected to be in high circulation during a given season. It saves anywhere from 40% to 60% of people from needing an outpatient provider visit, or hospitalization in more serious cases. Vaccination can reduce the severity of illness, even if you do become infected.
You can learn more or schedule a flu shot with Northern Light Health online.
