title: Here’s how much more Social Security recipients will get from a cost-of-living boost
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, with some recipients complaining that is not enough to offset soaring prices.
The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month for the nearly 72 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and about 7.3 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
The announcement comes as inflation adds pressure on household budgets and businesses and as midterm elections are weeks away.
The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
The agency’s commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.”
Older adults feel the bite of rising costs
Some older adults feel the increase is a drop in the bucket as inflation has eaten away at monthly savings. The government reported Wednesday that inflation accelerated in September, with the consumer price index rising 3.7% in September compared with a year ago and gas prices have spiked in the wake of renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.
Nancy Altman, president of the Social Security Works advocacy group, said the latest inflation data shows that “as important as the Social Security COLA is, it is not keeping up with prices.”
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA will not put a dent in her healthcare costs, which are set to increase after the Trump administration concludes at year’s end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin said that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people.
The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press.
She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans’ healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.”
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.
Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance,” given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he said.
Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.
Social Security faces a looming funding shortfall
The Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
While a permanent solution for shoring up the benefits program has not been passed into law, lawmakers on the Hill have called for new measures to replenish the trust funds.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. Treating all income the same “would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” they wrote in The New York Times.
The move is controversial because Republicans have traditionally criticized calls to raise taxes on the wealthy.
The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the payroll tax cap would add roughly $3 trillion into the program over the next 10 years.
Both the Trump and Biden administrations signed into law new benefits for retirees, which boosted their finances, but simultaneously accelerated the insolvency of the old-age benefits program.
The Trump administration, as part of Republicans’ tax and spending bill, gave a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and over, which applies to all income — not just Social Security. But those who aren’t able to claim the deduction include the lowest-income older adults who already don’t pay taxes on Social Security, those who choose to claim their benefits before they reach 65 and those above a defined income threshold.
Additionally, Democratic President Joe Biden in 2024 repealed two federal policies — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that previously limited Social Security payouts for roughly 2.8 million people, including largely former public workers.

Meanwhile, House Democrats revealed a policy plan for the first 100 days after the midterms if they regain control of the House for the first time since 2023. Their agenda includes making life more affordable, conducting oversight of the Trump administration, and reversing Medicaid cuts.

title: DOJ threatens California with legal action over alleged noncitizens on voter rolls
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice has threatened California with possible legal action over what it says are noncitizens believed to have received mail ballots for next month’s midterm elections.
A letter sent Tuesday to Secretary of State Shirley Weber from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy U.S. attorney general, says the department has provided officials in Los Angeles County with a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of names the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election.
California mails ballots to all registered voters.
The letter obtained by The Associated Press gives the state 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are included on the list. For individuals whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received it. The letters warns that legal action may follow if the state does not meet the 48-hour deadline to review the list.
“If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief,” the letter states.
Weber’s office issued a statement late Wednesday saying the Justice Department gave it 48 hours to obtain the list from Los Angeles, investigate it and take action, noting the demand was being made just three weeks before Election Day.
It also said that over the summer, the Department of Homeland Security claimed that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls, but refused to provide the methodology or data sources when the office asked for them.
“Now the USDOJ, under threat of ‘emergency’ litigation, demands that California blindly trust this administration without any evidence or legal authority to justify its request,” Weber said in the statement.
She said California requires that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that those who are not eligible are removed from the voter rolls.
Unclear how many names DOJ flagged
A separate, similar letter was sent to the registrar’s office in Los Angeles County, which the U.S. attorney’s office had investigated during the state’s June primary.
Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan said in a statement that his office also received a thumb drive, along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls. The secretary of state’s office said the password was written “on a sticky note.”
Logan said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device and hasn’t yet accessed any files. The letter, which Logan made public, does not specify the number of individuals flagged by the federal government.
Logan said his office is working with the secretary of state and attorney general’s offices to decide how to proceed.
“Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established,” Logan wrote. “And any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”
California Attorney General Rob Bonta slammed the letter in an unrelated press conference on Wednesday, calling it another example of President Donald Trump spreading “absolutely false conspiracy theories that there is widespread voter fraud when there is not.”
Bonta did not say how the secretary of state’s office would respond to the Justice Department, but said: “Will we be engaging in conspiracy theories? We will not.”
Nationwide search for alleged noncitizen voters
The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.
In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state.
“I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official,” Weber said in response.
That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero.
As part of its project to find noncitizens on the voter rolls, the Justice Department has been seeking detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. Some Republican-led states have turned over the information, which has been run through a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database that has been criticized as inaccurately flagging U.S. citizens.
The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for that information, but so far has lost those cases in court. California is among the states that successfully sued, in part by arguing that turning over the data would violate state privacy laws.
Election official calls 48 hour deadline “unreasonable”
Santa Cruz County Clerk Tricia Webber, who is president of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, said she had not seen the letters but said the 48-hour deadline to vet voters flagged by the federal government was “completely unreasonable.”
She said when there is a report of an ineligible voter incorrectly on the rolls, her office does due diligence to investigate. That involves looking at the voter’s registration history, identifying whether that person had voted before and, most importantly, reaching out to the voter, she said.
“It would take more than 48 hours to even begin to get the full picture,” Webber said. She also questioned how the federal government came up with a list of alleged noncitizen voters since it doesn’t have access to the state’s detailed voter information.
Webber added that throughout the course of her decades-long career working for local election agencies, she has “never seen anything that would make me believe that our voter records are filled with fraudulent voters.”
___
Associated Press writer Sophie Austin in Sacramento contributed to this report.

title: Maine home prices rose in September despite sales slump
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine saw home prices rise in September despite a continued sales slump.
Buyers closed deals on 1,526 homes last month, down 4.2% from 1,592 in September 2025, according to the Maine Association of Realtors.
Meanwhile, the median sales price for a Maine home rose 2.6% year over year to $415,000.
That sales decline came after a 10% year-over-year slump in August and after a stellar July that saw home listings exceed 6,200 for the first time since December 2019 and 77 daily sales, making it the eighth best July for home sales since 2000.
Judy Oberg, the president of the Maine Association of Realtors and an associate broker at family-owned Oberg Insurance & Real Estate Agency in Bridgton, on Tuesday attributed the slowdown to a seasonal adjustment, as well as inflation and mortgage rates at a three-year high that are squeezing out less monied buyers.
“With more homes for sale, the upside for buyers is that … they have more choices, more time, less competition, and more advantage to negotiate a purchase price that matches the current demand,” Oberg said.
Maine isn’t alone in seeing a sales slump. Nationally, home sales fell 1.9% in September, while the median sales price nudged up 1.2% to $422,700, according to the National Association of Realtors.
In the Northeast, sales dropped 4.1% year over year, but the median sales price jumped 4.7% to $523,600.
On the county level in Maine, the most significant increase in median home prices for the three-month period ending Sept. 30 was in Hancock County, where it rose 18.4% to $527,962, compared with the same time last year. Lincoln (8.2%), Franklin (7.6%%), Sagadahoc (6%) and Somerset (5.4%) counties also saw notable increases in sale prices for that three-month period. The highest median home price during that period was in Cumberland County, where it reached $614,950, up about 1.6% from the same time a year ago.
The median home price fell most sharply in Washington (5.4%), Oxford (3.7%) and Androscoggin (2.8%) counties for that three-month period. Aroostook had the lowest median home price overall ($174,900).
On the sales front, Hancock County saw the largest sales bump for the three-month period ending Sept. 30, increasing about 16%. It was followed by Lincoln (15%), Waldo (6.4%) and Washington (4.2%) counties. Sales fell most sharply in York (9.2%), Piscataquis (8.2%), Franklin (6.8%), Knox (5.7%) and Somerset (4.8%) counties during that period.

title: Troy Jackson said he’d detail campaign funding Wednesday morning. He didn’t.
text:
In the heat of the moment during a Tuesday Senate debate, Democrat Troy Jackson offered to send his Republican rival the details of his campaign fundraising and spending a day before the deadline to file it with the Federal Election Commission.
But as of 1 p.m., Jackson had not followed through on his promise, a spokesperson for Sen. Susan Collins said.
The seemingly spontaneous offer came after the 73-year-old Collins parried an attack about her billionaire supporters by noting that Jackson has not yet filed any campaign finance reports.
“I would point out that we have no idea who is financing Troy’s campaign,” Collins said. “He promised to be completely transparent, yet he has not filed a single report.”
An irritated Jackson shot back, saying he would release his report on Wednesday morning.
“I’ll give you the report tomorrow morning,” he said. “How about that? Is that enough? Because we see yours and I know that there’s no billionaires funding me…I’ll give you the report tomorrow and then we’ll talk about it on Thursday.”
Jackson’s campaign did not respond to questions about his comments at the debate.
The 58-year-old former logger and state Senate president is not breaking any campaign finance laws by not releasing the report early. But his failure to follow through on his televised offer could give Collins another line of attack when they face off in their fourth and final debate on Thursday.
The reason Jackson’s campaign funding and spending remain a mystery so late in the cycle is a matter of timing.
Jackson was named the Democratic nominee to replace Graham Platner after the oyster farmer dropped out on July 25. That was well after the previous campaign finance reporting period closed on June 30.
The next round of reports aren’t due until midnight on Thursday, at which point they will become public.
Although no report has been filed, Jackson doesn’t appear to have had much trouble raising money.
In July, he was the third-highest fundraiser on the Democrats’ ActBlue platform, raising $5.3 million despite being a candidate for only a few days.
And his campaign has spent, or reserved, at least $20 million in advertisements, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

Edgecomb Fire and Rescue report
text:
Edgecomb Fire and Rescue responded to 10 calls in August, compared with 22 calls in July. August calls included one fire, one fire alarm, two medical emergencies (MEs), and six motor vehicle accidents (MVAs). For the year-to-date, we have responded to 177 calls, slightly fewer than 198 calls at the same time last year.
Trainings during September included Mutual Aid Training and Extraction Training. Other training included our monthly “Truck Check” of all apparatus and equipment. The department was the grateful recipient of some new equipment graciously donated by the Gavin Martin Foundation on Sept. 26. The Gavin Martin Foundation is dedicated to honoring the legacy of Gavin Martin, a 21-year-old Edgecomb firefighter who died in a car crash in December 2025. Ongoing training and proper equipment are critical in maintaining our readiness to respond to any call.
September call report
Following is a list of our September calls in chronological date order:
Sept. 1, 9:23 a.m.: ME for an 80-year-old male, fallen and requesting a lift assist; 3:56 p.m.: MVA at U.S. Route 1 and Station/Dodge Roads for a four-car accident with possible personal injuries.
Sept. 3, 8:06 a.m.: MVA at McKay Road and River Road, for a single vehicle with unknown personal injuries; noon: MVA at Route 27 near Mason Road, for a car versus pole with unknown personal injuries; 8:30 p.m.: ME for a 30-year-old male with chest pains, not breathing normally.
Sept. 15, 5:39 p.m.: MVA at U.S. Route 1 at the Abenaki Trading Post for a 2-car accident with a large fuel spill.
Sept. 16, 5:09 a.m.: MVA at Route 27 and Eddy Road for a 2-car accident with possible personal injuries.

Sept. 25, 1:24 p.m.: MVA Route 1, property damage only.
Annual Fish Fry, Nov. 7
Please save the date, Nov. 7, for the EFD Auxiliary’s annual fish fry. This community event features fried fish or fried chicken tenders with all the trimmings and is a meaningful way to honor veterans on Veterans Day. The fish fry is our biggest fundraiser of the year, and all proceeds are used to supplement our budget, which helps reduce the town’s taxes.
Weekly meetings
The department meets every Wednesday at 6:30 p.m. at the fire station. Anyone interested in learning more about the department is welcome to attend. We are always looking for more volunteers. No experience necessary!

title: Lauren Marie Mitchell Spargo (1955-2026)
A.J. Brown returns to Patriots practice after high ankle sprain
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown is a step closer to returning to game action.
Brown was back on the practice field on Wednesday for the first time since being placed on injured reserve last month because of a high ankle sprain.
He became eligible to return after missing the last four games. He now must be activated within 21 days or placed on season-ending IR.
Cornerback Christian Gonzalez also practiced after missing the last two games because of a shoulder issue. In addition, offensive lineman Marcus Bryant (ankle) returned after being placed on injured reserve during the preseason.
Brown was injured in the second half of New England’s season-opening 13-10 loss at Seattle on Sept. 9. He left the game early in the third quarter following an incomplete pass from quarterback Drake Maye. He was falling to the turf as he tried to make the catch, and Seahawks cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett’s knee made contact with Brown’s ankle, pushing it against the ground. Brown had three catches for 26 yards before the injury.
“I think he’s stayed engaged,” coach Mike Vrabel said. “I think it’s difficult sometimes to stay engaged. I think his routine was really good, his ability to be around guys in the meetings and then also focus on rehab. He’s just treating everything as a pro, being where he’s supposed to be and working hard to get back.”
During the portion of practice open to the media Wednesday, Brown could be seen smiling at times as he went through some light drills with his right ankle heavily wrapped with tape.
“It’s a warm welcome in the huddle to have him back in there,” Maye said. “You can see how closely he’s been watching the games. Little things he picks up on, you can tell he really watching and really cares. …There’s not many like him that are around here in this league.”
Patriots safety Kevin Byard said Brown’s return brings instant energy to the sideline.
“Huge boost. He’s a receiver (No. 1),” Byard said. “Very talented guy as far as the pass game. Obviously, the last couple of weeks our pass game has been playing really well. So, he’s obviously just going to add another dynamic to that. And hopefully we’ll continue to have a good passing game with A.J. in there.”
Brown’s fellow receivers – Mack Hollins, Romeo Doubs, Pop Douglas, Kyle Williams and Efton Chism – have stepped up without him, accounting for six touchdown catches in his absence, and the Patriots have gone 3-1 with Brown on the shelf. Maye is coming off passing for a season-high 374 yards and four touchdowns last week against the Las Vegas Raiders.
Brown’s potential return to the lineup is perfect timing, with Hollins going on injured reserve last week because of a calf injury.
But Maye said Brown returning to the mix gives him another option to spread the ball around in the passing game.
“We have a lot of guys that can make plays. So it’s going to be tough on defenses,” Maye said.

title: Brothers, 3 and 5, found dead in pond after sneaking out of apartment while mom napped
text:
DAYTONA BEACH, Fla. (WKMG) - Police in Florida say the bodies of two young brothers who snuck out of their apartment while their mother was taking a nap were found in a pond nearby.
Two brothers – 3-year-old Kashh and 5-year-old Elijah – were reported missing Saturday before their bodies were discovered in a pond near their Daytona Beach apartment complex. Police say Elijah had autism and noted that many children with autism are drawn to water.
Daytona Beach Police Chief Jakari Young said investigators believe the boys’ deaths were accidental and that there is no indication of foul play.
“This is your greatest nightmare – to lose both of your children in that fashion,” Young said.
According to Young, the brothers’ single mother fed them about 5 p.m. Saturday before lying down for a short nap. When she woke up about 15 minutes later, both boys – along with the family dog – had gotten out of the apartment.
“She does have a child safety lock on the door, so apparently, they figured out how to navigate that child safety lock, and they exited the apartment,” Young said.
Police say surveillance video shows the kids running around then going into the pond. Moments later, their mother is seen on the video coming outside.
“She was trying to do her due diligence to see if she could locate the children before calling 911,” Young said. “But by then, based on what we can see now on the surveillance video, they were already submerged in the water.”
While Young believes the deaths were accidental, the case has been handed over to the State Attorney’s Office, which will decide whether the mother will face any charges.
Neighbors say they hope the apartment complex will put up fencing or other protections at the pond.

title: Obituary: Kenneth P. Tardiff
text:
MANCHESTER – Kenneth P. Tardiff, 64, died unexpectedly Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026, at his home. He was born in Augusta, on June 21, 1962 a son of Roger K. and Luella E. (Bumford) Tardiff.
Mr. Tardiff attended Augusta schools and had been employed for many years in construction, operating heavy equipment and also as a mechanic.
He was an avid hunter, fisherman and general outdoorsman. In 2007, Ken experienced a trifecta shooting a moose, buck and doe, an achievement he was most proud of.
Ken was an automotive enthusiast with a passion for hot rods and engines. In recent years, he rebuilt his 1969 Chevy El Camino known as “Elky69” with a 454 big block, and a sharp looking 1997 Jeep Wrangler. There wasn’t anything he couldn’t fix or troubleshoot.
Ken enjoyed traveling. He and Tamara vacationed at several destination throughout the Caribbean and Mexico, Nascar races, and camping trips to OOB. They enjoyed their time at the family camp on Ward Pond hosting many lobster feeds. He was a great host and cook.
Mr. Tardiff was pre-deceased by his daughters: Kayla A. and Natasha R. Tardiff; his parents: Roger K. Tardiff and Luella E. (Bumford) Rouillard and his father and mother in-law, Frank & Valerie Hillman.
He is survived by his wife, Tamara R. Hillman-Tardiff of Manchester; two sisters: Suzanne M. Stitham and her husband Michael of Mars Hill and Nancy A. Wagstaff and her husband James of Trenton as well as two nieces: Emilie and Jessica Hillman; a brother-in-law Tom Hillman and his wife Lisa and many cousins and friends. He will truly be missed by all!
There will be no public visiting hours. A funeral service will be held on Tuesday, October 20, at 10 a.m., at Plummer Funeral Home, 16 Pleasant St., Augusta. Burial and committal will be later that day in Snows Corner Cemetery, Herman.

title: Norway Savings Bank contributes $2,500 to the Center for Grieving Children
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — Grief is a natural response to loss, and the only way out is through it.
It’s a sentiment that guides the life-changing work of the Center for Grieving Children as it accompanies Maine children, teens and families on journeys of hope and recovery at no cost. Last year alone, the organization served nearly 4,000 individuals through their peer support groups, grief education, and community outreach.
The impact of the Center inspired Norway Savings Bank to continue its longtime support with a recent $2,500 donation to the organization. NSB has contributed more than $15,000 to the Center over the last five years. NSB also worked with the Center to produce a series of videos it could use to recruit potential facilitators to help with a wide range of groups, including children ages 3-18 and their parents and caregivers, young adults ages 19-30 and bereaved parents and young widowers/partners. The videos have been successfully employed to explain the Center’s volunteer training process as well as display how people from all walks of life have contributed their time and talents to the Center’s mission.
“Norway Savings made the video project so easy and enjoyable. They came to the Center and then delivered these beautiful videos that explain how people can volunteer at the Center, the training we provide, and how rewarding being a Center facilitator truly is,” Emma Walker, director of philanthropy for the Center for Grieving Children, said. “This idea and project are already making an incredible impact on our work. We’re so grateful for NSB’s financial contributions, of course, but also for going the extra mile to capture the stories of our facilitators and bringing them to the community.”
“We our genuinely thankful for the contributions of NSB and their staunch belief in our mission of providing a safe space, loving peer support, outreach, and education to grieving children, teens, families, and the community,” Gretchen Johnson, executive director of the Center, said. “Norway Savings’ contributions make our work possible and helps to sustain our future of providing loving care to Mainers.”
To donate, volunteer or discover other ways to offer support for the Center, visit www.cgcmaine.org/get-involved. To learn more about the Center’s services and how to receive assistance, call 207-775-5216 or email cgc@cgcmaine.org.

title: Family settles lawsuit for nearly $50 million over teen’s alleged starvation death
text:
VANCOUVER, Wash. (KING) — A lawsuit over the starvation-related death of a 15-year-old boy has ended with a nearly $50 million settlement.
The case centers on a family that lived in Washington state, just over the border from Portland, Oregon.
The lawsuit named the Washington State Department of Children, Youth and Families, the Department of Social and Health Services, and Evergreen Public Schools in Vancouver, Washington, as defendants.
The settlement came just before the case was set to go to trial this month.
The state and Evergreen Public Schools are paying $49.33 million to the family of Karreon Adams-Franks. The lawsuit alleged the defendants missed years of chances to save him.
Chris Davis, the family’s attorney, said Karreon was 15, autistic, nonverbal and legally blind.
Allegations of abuse
The lawsuit said Karreon’s adoptive parents, his biological aunt and her husband, starved and abused the teen and his two brothers. In 2023, they were convicted in connection with his death and the abuse of all three brothers.
“This case is incredibly unusual just by the egregious facts and how many times the state and the school district had to prevent it and save these boys, and they failed miserably,” Davis said.
Felicia Adams was sentenced to 35 years in prison. Jesse Franks was sentenced to 30 years.
“The boys were beaten with paddles and extension cords. One of the boys was choked out by an extension cord. The boys were locked in their bedroom for days at a time,” Davis said.
State response
The lawsuit alleged state agencies failed to act on years of warning signs. It said a child protective services worker visited the home six days before Karreon died in November 2020 but took no action.
“I can say they dropped the ball, but it’s more egregious than that. They simply ignored their legal obligation to investigate complaints when they were made and then to report ongoing signs of abuse and neglect,” Davis said.
Davis said he believes the school district is at fault as well.
Evergreen Public Schools said, in part, in a statement that it hopes the settlement will allow Karreon’s brothers to continue healing without the burden of enduring a trial.
Evergreen Public Schools maintained throughout the litigation that none of its staff failed to make a mandatory report to DCYF or law enforcement.
The state agencies involved declined to comment on the settlement.

BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - $1 million is going to five Maine communities to benefit Maine fishermen and improve seafood infrastructure.
Rockland is getting $300,000 to plan — and eventually make — improvements to the commercial fishing pier, benefiting about 100 commercial fishing and seafood operations working off the pier.
Tremont is getting more than $161,000 dollars to upgrade their cold storage facility with heat pumps, insulation, and weather-tight windows.
Nearly $127,000 dollars will go to Swan’s Island to add a cold storage facility and heat pumps to a vacant area near Burnt Coat Harbor.
Additionally, Freeport is getting over $218,000 to replace aging docks at three different locations and Boothbay Harbor is receiving over $193,000 to modernize a bait-salter and an ice making machine at the Boothbay Fish Pier.
The money is from the Seafood Infrastructure Adaptation Fund from the Seafood Economic Accelerator in Maine.

title: Maine can no longer justify Susan Collins
text:
In some other time, the reelection of Sen. Susan Collins might be justifiable. These are not ordinary times. Now we need to recall what we learned in our elementary classrooms: The United States is a democracy protected by three branches of government to ensure adequate checks and balances; that way, no one branch harms its citizens’ freedoms and security.
Susan Collins has failed to safeguard our country against an executive branch run amok. She expresses “concern” when she needs to act — against a president who wages war and kills children; violates established civil rights; enriches himself while working Americans struggle to buy food, fill their gas tanks and provide for their children; and who damages the environment endangering future generations.
Collins has failed her responsibility to stop this man’s terrifying destruction. All we can do is vote for Troy Jackson.
Ellen McQuiston
Anson

title: This 78-year-old Vermont logger is also a lawmaker, polo umpire and former pilot
text:
MIDDLESEX, Vt. (Aging Untold) — Jed Lipsky, 78, still works alone cutting down pine trees, a job he has done for 55 years.
A logging career that started young
Lipsky started cutting trees at age 15 in his native Massachusetts, where he also built ski trails.
“So I started cutting when I was 15 and loved it,” Lipsky said. “Very challenging.”
Lipsky uses cutting and wedging techniques to control where a tree falls.
Asked where his crew is, Lipsky said, “You’re looking at him.”
Logging is considered the most dangerous profession in North America, Lipsky said. He has had multiple surgeries and broken bones during his 55 years in the profession.
From skiing to polo
Lipsky has also worked as a competitive skier, a pilot and a professional polo player.
“I’ve had a pretty complex life. Pretty wonderful life,” Lipsky said.
Lipsky now serves as the sole umpire for the Sugarbush Polo Club in Shelburne.
In his early 30s, Lipsky played professional polo, including in the All-Ireland Championships, the Dominican Republic, Hawaii and Texas. During that time, his logging business and his marriage suffered.
“I consider it a quest for glory,” Lipsky said. “And it was a false quest.”
Logger turned legislator
Lipsky, now 78, said working alone gives him time to reflect.
“Every single day you learn, and you generally learn the most from your mistakes,” Lipsky said.
He now serves in the Vermont Legislature as an independent representing Stowe.
“I’m definitely the only logger in the Vermont Legislature,” Lipsky said. “I feel very fortunate.”

title: These trading posts swap plants and produce to help the community
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (InvestigateTV) - Producing fresh food in cities from coast to coast, urban farming is taking root across the country.
Today’s urban farmers are reviving the idea of families growing a big share of the nation’s fruits and vegetables.
By transforming spaces not typically used for agriculture, these efforts are helping to increase food security.
Noah Curtis is enthusiastic about gardening. He loves what he does and wants to share it with others.
“I think it’s just good for you. I think humans are supposed to be at least somewhat in nature,” Curtis said.
Curtis started gardening when he was a kid, thanks to his dad, who inspired him to grow food.
“Just eating fresh food from your garden is way healthier than the stuff that we get at the store. Tastes better, it’s more sustainable,” Curtis said.
Now at 28 years old, Curtis noticed something missing in his generation.
“I feel like in my generation has kind of been shot. People just don’t talk anymore, which is really weird. It’s not good,” he said.
The concept
Three years ago, Curtis started a project called Pineal Trade Stations.
“The concept is take a plant, leave a plant,” Curtis said.
People build their own Pineal Trade Station and then get uploaded to the Pineal map by purchasing the activation kit.
The trade stations are community-run hubs where neighbors can trade and share plants, seeds, houseplants and other urban homesteading goods.
“There is so much extras if you’re growing a garden, like you have to thin out your plants all the time,” Cutirs explained. “And most of the time it just goes in the trash or the compost pile. But somebody could just have it and it, you know, saves people money, but it also kind of just brings that human back to community. Like people are actually real people.”
Community response
Deanna O’Connell saw Curtis on Facebook and called him up. This will be her third summer to host a station.
“I saw Noah on Facebook, called him up, thought it’s a great idea,” O’Connell said.
“With gardening, you always have extra zucchini, tomatoes, all that stuff,” she said.
“Some of our neighbors have even put extra groceries in it at times, and the neighborhood has utilized that also,” O’Connell said.
Instead of a price tag, the stations run on trust. Take what you need. Leave what you can.
Curtis said the project addresses a larger need in 2026.
“I think everybody kind of feels it in 2026 that everybody just hates each other. And that’s crazy. I think, yeah, it’s like, you know, if half the country hates half the country, it’s not going to end well, like for anybody,” he said.
The stations offer a reason to slow down and show up.
“Cycle of good that you can put yourself in,” Curtis said.
“It’s a little goodness in the world, you know, to give back, and without expecting anything in return,” O’Connell said.
Curtis chose the name Pineal Gardens for a reason. Pineal is not a plant but a gland deep in the middle of the brain. Its job is to secrete the hormone melatonin, which helps regulate the body’s sleep-wake cycles.
There are about 100 Pineal Trade stations across 15 states. For more information click here.

title: Dolly Parton’s nephew denies threatening to harm her estate, pushes back against restraining order
text:
(AP) - Dolly Parton’s nephew and longtime head of security said in a Tennessee court filing Tuesday that he was a close friend and ally of Parton’s longtime manager Danny Nozell before Nozell took out a restraining order accusing him of threatening to do violence and destroy Parton’s legacy and business empire.
In an affidavit opposing the temporary order becoming permanent, Bryan Seaver said text messages Nozell cited as evidence against him were a “private conversation between two friends who were both frustrated, grieving and discussing strategy.” The text messages were sent shortly before and after Parton’s Aug. 25 death.
Seaver said he never sent threatening messages to any of Parton’s businesses or business partners or their employees.
The filings represent Seaver’s first public defense of himself since a serious rift opened up in the country music legend’s circle and spilled into public view shortly after her death, with Nozell and Seaver on opposing sides.
Seaver’s court filing says Nozell did not react with alarm to his text messages at the time and that he agreed with or reacted positively to some of them. Seaver says Nozell encouraged him to publicly tout the military and arms aspect of his security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, as a smart business-promotion move, then turned around and used them as evidence of Seaver’s capacity for dangerous violence.
She’s Alive, an entity run by Nozell and founded to manage and protect Parton’s estate, terminated Seaver and SAPS in early September, and the following week petitioned for the restraining order against him, arguing that his“terrorizing conduct made their continued retention untenable.”
In granting the temporary restraining order, Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles, cited Seaver’s “claimed access to weapons, experience with violence, and intention to retaliate.”
The two sides will make their cases to Myles at a hearing on Oct. 20. Emails seeking comment were sent to lawyers for She’s Alive and Nozell.
Seaver said he was blindsided by the order, which was granted while he was doing contract security work in Haiti.
Seaver and SAPS must refrain from entering any She’s Alive property or talking with or being within 1,000 feet (about 300 meters) of She’s Alive employees and business partners. The order is also meant to keep Seaver from interfering with its business relationships.
Seaver argued in his response that the order is so broad, and Parton’s business reach so great, that much of Nashville and even his own relatives are off limits to him.
In one message written Sept. 1 that was cited by She’s Alive, Seaver said: “I’m going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly’s brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It’s going to be great. Or f——— pay me.”
Seaver said his anger and the demand were only over more than $250,000 that his company was owed for completed work by Herschend Family Entertainment, which operates Parton’s amusement park Dollywood and her Songteller Hotel, which opened after her death.
Seaver acknowledged being overly crude and profane in his messages to Nozell. He said allegations that he had “menaced and intimidated” HFE employees were simply false.
He included as an exhibit a 2024 letter from Parton praising him and his company. Parton had handpicked Seaver to announce her death once she succumbed to cancer.
Parton was a widely beloved country music giant, philanthropist and cultural icon who wrote hundreds of songs, including classics such as “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors” and “I Will Always Love You.” Her music earned a total of more than 100 million worldwide sales and more than 1 billion online streams.

title: Sea lion swarm: Hundreds of sea lions take over California roadway
text:
Sea lion swarm: Hundreds of sea lions take over California roadway, closing traffic to one lane
Hundreds of sea lions have invaded a roadway near a harbor bridge in a California town, reducing traffic to one lane and raising safety concerns for drivers and visitors.
The sea lions have been appearing in greater numbers, taking over more of the roadway in Moss Landing.
"I hate to see it, but also they're well-protected, and that might be part of the problem," Ed Wright said.
One woman, Taniell Liepner, added, "We were talking to the marine wildlife folks, the volunteers and such, and they were saying they're very social creatures. So two of them started, and now all of a sudden there's like two to three hundred of them."
On Monday, county crews briefly cleared the road by cleaning and washing it down, but the sea lions quickly returned.
"They used a shovel to make noise and push them to the other side, and then I come back a half hour later, and here they come again," Wright said.
California Highway Patrol officers have increased patrols in the area, using sirens to force the sea lions off the road and back into the water. However, the animals continue to return, leading to traffic and safety concerns.
"Keep your distance. Like you were saying, it's obviously not safe to try to get too close and personal with them, but enjoy them from afar and drive slow as if you're coming out this way. Just be safe," Liepner said.
Marine biologists believe the abundance of food in the bay is attracting the sea lions, and the thinking is that the animals will move on when their food source diminishes.
"So that allows business to continue to flow across that bridge. That's something that would be a really great thing moving forward with kind of an unknown timetable of how long they'll be in the area," said Giancarlo Rulli, with the Marine Mammal Center.
Sea lions are federally protected mammals, making it illegal to kill, harass or feed them.

title: Who's behind The Maine Independent?
text:
Less than a month before the midterms, a large dark money group is sending copies of a partisan newspaper to thousands of Maine voters.
The Maine Independent is nondescript. Its masthead is plain in black and white. It includes crosswords and recipes among its 12 pages. But the paper has no explanation of who’s behind it, no statements about its mission, and no reason why it wound up on voters’ doorsteps.
Despite its moniker, it is far from an independent local news organization, both in its funding and its politics.
The paper is one of about 20 nearly identical publications created in swing states across the country over the last decade by American Independent Media, a subsidiary of a similarly named, large dark money group closely tied to Democratic super PACs, politicians and campaign operatives.
From Alaska to Florida, the American Independent Foundation has propped up outlets created to boost Democrats ahead of crucial state and federal elections. They present themselves as independent local news organizations, mailing 12 pages of ideologically slanted stories to voters who never subscribed to the outlet.
Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson “will fight for universal healthcare and lower drug prices,” one Maine Independent headline reads. “Susan Collins says she’s pro-choice, but her Senate votes helped end Roe,” says another.
In addition to its printed paper, the outlet has reached hundreds of thousands of people through more than $47,000 worth of social media ads, according to the Meta Ad Library.
None of The Maine Independent’s content is flatly untrue or blatantly misleading. But all of their stories omit important nuance in support of Democratic politicians.
“It’s an attempt to mimic journalism by providing information that might, in fact, be accurate, but is framed in a partisan manner,” said Michael Socolow, a journalism professor at the University of Maine and board member of the Maine Press Association.
The Maine Independent is one of many so-called “pink slime” news outlets established in Maine by both liberal and conservative dark money groups in the lead up to the 2026 midterm elections. The term, an allusion to ultra-processed meat products, is used in a news context to refer to outlets run by partisan interests posing as local and independent news.
NewsGuard, an organization that tracks misinformation and rates news outlets’ credibility, said American Independent Media and its local sites “generally fail to maintain basic standards of accuracy and accountability” by infusing opinion into their reporting and failing to disclose the partisan interests behind the operation.
“That’s what makes these publications so pernicious,” said Sam Howard, politics editor at NewsGuard. “They threaten to undermine what’s left of the trust that news consumers have in the media, particularly local media. Because these publications are framed as local, seemingly independent, seemingly nonpartisan publications.”
Joe Conason, the Independent’s editor-in-chief, did not respond to interview requests or questions about their reach and operations in Maine.
SLIME-SWAMPED MAILBOXES
Mailing newspapers to voters en masse has been a hallmark of American Independent Media’s operation for years.
In 2021, the organization mailed papers to Virginia voters ahead of a tightly contested gubernatorial election. In the run up to the 2022 midterms, the Independent mailed faux-local papers to more than 2.5 million people in Wisconsin, Michigan and Pennsylvania, The Washington Post reported.
Ahead of this year’s midterms, they have has expanded to at least five more battleground states with pivotal Senate races: Florida, North Carolina, Iowa, Alaska and Maine.
Those state branches have each spent tens of thousands of dollars on social media ads, according to the Meta Ad Library. But their main business is still sending physical papers through the mail, according to Chiara Vercellone, a senior analyst at NewsGuard.
“They’re trying to prove their credibility, and we know that there’s a lot of junk out on the internet or on social media,” she said. “Creating a seemingly innocent-looking newspaper that people receive in their mails touts their supposed credibility.”
American Independent Media micro-targets its print papers toward moderates and women in swing states, The Washington Post reported in 2022. At that time, the organization mailed monthly copies to some 3.2 million voters nationwide, making it one of the country’s largest print media operations.
Spreading pink slime through the mail could prove more effective in Maine than elsewhere, said Socolow. The state’s population of only 1.3 million residents is comparatively small and skews older, on average, than anywhere else in the country.
“People still read the newspapers that pop into their mailboxes,” Socolow said. “I think it’s a smart strategy to reach older people.”
THE OPERATION
The American Independent Foundation describes its mission in business and tax filings as spreading “increased public awareness of progressive values.”
Among the foundation’s owners are Conason, a longtime journalist and liberal commentator, and Matt Fuehrmeyer, former director of research for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. Its media arm similarly has been run by Jessica Floyd, a longtime operative for Democratic campaigns and super PACs, and Ari Rabin-Havt, deputy director of Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders’ 2020 presidential campaign.
Both organizations are tax-exempt nonprofits. The foundation is a 501(c)(3) organization, which are prohibited from political activity by law. American Independent Media, however, is a 501(c)(4) — meaning it has legal leeway to be more political.
Neither group is required to disclose its donors or financial backers, placing them each in the realm of so-called dark money groups that are dumping tens of millions of dollars into Maine’s Senate race.
Together, they operate The American Independent News, which acts as a national news source and syndicate for its local outlets’ content.
Both the foundation and its media arm have contracted with a number of progressive consulting firms and media groups, their tax filings show, including a marketing firm called Mission Control, which describes itself as “the most successful direct mail firm working in Democratic politics today” — hinting at the Independent’s mailing strategy.
Unlike many other pink slime outlets, The Maine Independent’s articles include real people’s bylines on their stories, many of whom were reporters at traditional newspapers prior to joining the partisan outlet.
But despite the dozens of Maine-centric stories the outlet has published, none of its staff appear to be based in the state.
Only a few of The American Independent’s reporters and editors have publicly available contact information. Neither they nor the publication’s general contact lines responded to questions about The Maine Independent or its parent organization.
A GROWING ECOSYSTEM
The Maine Independent is not the only pink slime site created here by national partisan groups in the months prior to this November’s pivotal midterm elections.
Conservative dark money groups and super PACs have similarly established several outlets masquerading as local Maine news sources ahead of the November elections.
Those operations have primarily used social media as a means to spread their message. The Independent, however, is taking a markedly different approach by mailing printed copies directly to voters.
It’s not uncommon for swing states to be inundated with political ads ahead of important elections. But Socolow, the UMaine professor, said the influx of misleading news outlets in Maine highlights how much stake national interests have in winning the state’s U.S. Senate race — and how they can use a shifting media ecosystem to do so.
“You would think you would see this kind of proliferation in a much larger audience area,” Socolow said. “But I think the reason that so many of them are here is that it’s cheap. We’re a small and easily influenced voter base, through social media and micro-targeting.”
Partisan news isn’t a new phenomenon, Socolow noted. Prior to the last hundred years or so, political parties often sponsored newspapers to toe the party line. Even today, local outlets like the Maine Beacon and Maine Wire are run with the stated goal of pushing particular political agendas.
What is new is national groups seeding swing states with slanted faux-local news, Socolow said. And with the advent of social media, those efforts have become more widespread than ever.
What remains to be seen, however, is how effective the strategy will be.

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar's phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal probe, AP source says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal authorities investigating Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar seized the Democratic lawmaker’s phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the probe.
The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence in Minnesota as federal authorities probe potential fraud in Omar’s immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar’s Washington, D.C. home on Monday just weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.
On Tuesday, Washington D.C. U.S Attorney Jeanine Pirro said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and that her office is also probing issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures.
“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.
The search of Omar’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests that will determine control of the House and the Senate was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the Democrat for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.”
“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”
A phone message seeking comment was left Wednesday with a representative for Omar.
Though the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking reelection. The Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.

title: The cruelty of cutting MaineCare
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
On Thursday, Oct. 1, over 1,000 immigrants across the state lost their MaineCare (Medicaid) coverage due to H.R.1 — the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Those losing access to healthcare include victims of sex trafficking and abuse, and U.S. military veterans — all of whom are in the U.S. with permission from the federal government. People have already had medically necessary procedures like transplants canceled because they cannot pay for the necessary follow-up care. These draconian cuts to coverage for immigrants also prevent them from purchasing plans on the health insurance marketplace.
When health insurance is stripped away from high-needs populations, research repeatedly shows that they put off timely care, instead waiting until their condition becomes severe. This puts unnecessary and increasing pressure on Maine’s emergency services, where, as we all know, healthcare infrastructure is already under enormous strain. These healthcare cuts hurt our neighbors, our coworkers, and our friends, and they have the potential to hurt each of us, when we need access to care in an emergency.
Maine Equal Justice has been calling attention to these changes, and Alex Carter, MEJ’s senior policy advocate stated “I think one of the greatest myths about so many of these changes is that it’s about saving money, but when people go without necessary healthcare and treatment, the long-term effects of that are much higher, healthcare costs and a much higher burden on our healthcare system … There is no good rationale other than cruelty.”
These are only the first wave of cuts to health insurance coverage, with many cuts scheduled to take place after the midterm elections, at the beginning of 2027. Beginning in January, tens of thousands more Mainers will lose health insurance to pay for tax cuts for the wealthy, almost all of whom are U.S. citizens. The Maine Center for Economic Policy estimates around 29,000 Mainers will lose MaineCare in 2027. They estimate 5,966 people in Cumberland County, 4,088 in York County, 1,922 in Androscoggin County, and 441 in Sagadohoc County. Rural areas will be hit the hardest across the state. Thirty-four to 44% of all Mainers receiving MaineCare in our other 12 counties are estimated to lose coverage. The state of Maine’s own estimates are even higher, stating that over 31,000 people across the state will lose their health insurance in 2027.
The changes in H.R.1 that cut access to essential food and medical assistance also shift costs to the states. The state of Maine’s Department of Health and Human Services estimates that the increased cost to Maine for MaineCare will exceed $5 billion over the next 10 years.
Maine families are already under incredible financial stress from existing healthcare costs, and do not need to further bear the costs of tax cuts for the wealthy by paying higher taxes. According to Consumers for Affordable Health Care’s 2026 statewide survey:
• Two out of three Maine households reported adverse financial impacts because of medical bills, including struggling to pay for basic necessities such as food, heat, or housing, needing to take on additional debt, or having to rely upon savings.
• Six out of 10 households stated a major medical event would be a financial disaster.
• Four out of 10 households reported they have lost sleep worrying about medical costs.
The robber barons responsible for the Big Beautiful Bill are creating a future financial crisis for our state and they are burying working families, it is as simple and as cruel as that.
It can be incredibly maddening and frustrating to watch the intentional dismantling of systems designed to take care of those who are most vulnerable and most in need. Those who work in healthcare, or those who are sick, or are taking care of a sick loved one, must face these frustrations every day.
There are things that can be done by each of us. We need to take collective care of each other while holding those in power accountable. Before and after the upcoming elections, Oasis Free Clinics will continue to provide no-cost, patient-centered care to adults in Maine. We continue to need clinical and administrative volunteers. To meet the growing needs, we hope you can learn more about what we do at Oasis Free Clinics and why we do it: We believe healthcare is a human right. Support for Oasis, and for Maine’s other free safety net clinics, is increasingly needed. We hope you can consider adding your support at this critical moment.
You can find out about our Brunswick clinic, at 331 Maine St., by visiting oasisfreeclinics.org, or contacting me at [email protected].
Danny Muller is the executive director of Oasis Free Clinics.

title: Collins, Jackson spar over energy costs, health care in third Maine Senate debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) -For the third time, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins met challenger Troy Jackson on the debate stage Tuesday night.
Hosted by WABI and WAGM, the incumbent Republican and her Democratic challenger went head-to-head on affordability, energy, health care and tariffs.
The candidates also addressed immigration enforcement and the recent ICE-involved shooting in Biddeford, Maine — a flashpoint in the race over federal enforcement tactics and community safety.
Data centers and their impact on Maine’s electric grid and rates also came up, as large-scale projects raise questions about energy demand, costs for ratepayers, and local oversight.
Here are the key takeaways:
Heating, energy costs lead off
The debate opened with affordability, as Maine households brace for a sharp rise in heating fuel costs this winter.
Collins blamed state policies under Jackson’s leadership in Augusta for Maine having the fourth-highest electricity rates in the country, despite increased heat pump use.
Jackson countered that federal LIHEAP funding only helps temporarily, asking what happens “on the back end when that money is all spent.”
Jackson said the No. 1 driver of higher electric rates is the war in Ukraine, while energy experts also point to global oil disruptions tied to the war in Iran and problems in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran war funding sparks clash
Jackson attacked Collins’ record on the Iran war, noting she chairs the Appropriations Committee:
“She talks about how she voted nine times against the war... she’s the chair of Appropriations. If she wants to stop the war, she can cut the funding off.”
Collins has said she voted nine times against authorizing the war. Jackson claimed she first voted five times to enable it before opposing it.
Health care, fraud accusations
The candidates then debated health care quality and costs for Mainers.
Collins said nothing was done in Augusta under Jackson’s leadership to better detect fraud in Medicare and Medicaid.
Jackson fired back, referencing a ProPublica article from last week:
“I’m shocked that you’re talking about fraud because there’s only one person up here that’s been accused of that by the FBI.”
Campaign money, transparency
Collins accused Jackson of failing to file Federal Election Commission reports disclosing his contributors and expenditures, despite promising transparency.
“We have no idea who is financing Troy’s campaign because he has yet to file a single FEC report,” Collins said.
Jackson responded:
“She didn’t deny that 90 billionaires are funding her... I’ll give you the report tomorrow morning.”
Canadian tariffs close debate
Both candidates said they opposed Canadian import tariffs, but differed on effectiveness.
“Troy and I both would have voted against the Canadian tariffs... I’ve been able to negotiate and get certain items removed from the tariff list. Troy would’ve gotten nothing,” Collins said.
Jackson said he works regularly with the Canadian ambassador and the consulate in Boston and is “100 percent against” tariffs, arguing Collins failed to stop a trade war she could have prevented in Congress.

title: Maine offers $42M in home heating assistance for eligible households
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
As temperatures start to drop across Maine, qualifying households can access $42 million in home heating assistance to help offset this season’s historically high fuel prices.
Heating oil in Maine cost an average of $5.97 a gallon as of Oct. 5, up from $5.49 a gallon a month earlier, according to data from the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
To help low-income Maine households and seniors with limited incomes cover their energy bills this winter, the federal Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Community Services announced the release of $38 million in annual Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program funding.
Additionally, Augusta-based MaineHousing issued nearly $4 million in Home Energy Assistance Program payments to fuel vendors for homeowners facing concerns over potentially limited supply.
That funding is being carried over from the 2025-26 heating season. It had been targeted for home weatherization projects, but MaineHousing wanted to enable vendors to begin deliveries now to help ensure these households enter winter with heating fuel available.
MaineHousing estimates the money will help close to 4,400 of Maine’s most vulnerable households. Priority households include those with older adults, young children and people with disabilities.
“By putting these carryover funds to work now, we hope to ease some of the financial pressure that extraordinarily high heating fuel prices are placing on Maine’s lowest-income households,” said MaineHousing Director Dan Brennan.
Maine historically receives approximately $38 million annually in federal fuel assistance funding, with about $26 million going to direct heating assistance distributed through local community action agencies statewide. The rest is used for energy-related programs including central heating improvements, emergency fuel intervention and weatherization.
Households can apply through the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance program, administered by MaineHousing.
Eligibility information and the application are available on MaineHousing’s website by clicking on the thermostat image. Mainers can also contact their local community action agency or call 211 Maine for help.
Recent changes to Maine’s Low Income Assistance Program will also make it easier for eligible households and others to receive an automatic discount on their electricity bills.
MaineHousing is a quasi-state agency that annually helps more than 90,000 Maine households pay for heat, rent and home repairs, while investing more than $750 million in the state economy.

title: Lawmakers warn Aroostook residents a proposed wind farm will do more harm than good
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
State and county lawmakers shared financial and environmental concerns about the proposed County Line wind farm with concerned Haynesville residents.
Maine Rep. Tracy Quint, R-Hodgdon, and Aroostook County Commissioner William Dobbins pointed to misleading promises by regulators and developers about jobs and financial rewards for people living along the expansive wind farm route.
The lawmakers’ comments further affirmed Haynesville residents’ fears that their quality of life will be affected by the project. In this Aroostook County town of 97, there are no stores and no gas stations — and residents said they like it that way.
“They can all talk about how they are all into the climate, climate efficient, and they can destroy all of northern Maine in order to reach those goals,” Quint said during a packed Tuesday Select Board meeting. “It was never about the rural areas and keeping things beautiful. They want to be carbon neutral and however they have to do that, they are willing to do so as long as it’s up here.”
The wind project, slated to install 150 to 200 turbines along thousands of acres of commercial timberland, is part of the planned Northern Maine Renewable Energy Development Program.
The exact location has not been publicly released, but residents and the lawmakers speculate, based on previous mapping, that the turbines will be installed from Glenwood Plantation in the Unorganized Territory near Wytopitlok Lake to Island Falls.
In August, the Maine Public Utilities Commission chose Clearway Energy Group LLC, headquartered in San Francisco, for an 800-megawatt onshore wind project that will generate electricity for transmission to the New England grid.
Clearway officials did not respond to the Bangor Daily News request for comment.
The regulators also selected Central Maine Power/Avangrid to develop a 1,200-megawatt transmission line for the generated wind power that will connect northern Maine to the regional grid through substations in Haynesville and Pittsfield.
The 108-mile transmission route’s Haynesville substation and the County Line wind farm already had residents’ attention following the PUCs August bid award.
Subsequently, several Haynesville residents formed the Haynesville Maine Residents MPUC-Avangrid Substation Awareness Group. In a September meeting at resident Alan Trudeau’s home, they signed a petition to temporarily halt new power generation and transmission projects.
During Tuesday’s meeting, Haynesville Town Clerk Aaron Zufelt read the town attorney’s response to the legality of the proposed temporary hold on the project, which Trudeau wrote. According to town attorney Jacob Flewelling, provisions dealing with electrical substations and new transmission lines are unenforceable because the state’s control through the PUC preempts the town’s ability to enact an ordinance.
Nonetheless, provisions dealing with utility-scale solar or wind energy facilities and large-scale data centers are likely enforceable, he said.
“I believe the town has the authority to do so,” Flewelling said.
Flewelling recommended the town develop separate ordinances: one for utility-scale solar and wind energy facilities and the other for large data centers, giving the town more flexibility in responding to such issues.
“Without windmills, they don’t need the corridor,” Quint said. “The whole linchpin here is the windmills and that’s where the fight is. If they can’t do the windmills, they have no need for this project.”
“Why don’t they build their clean energy down in the Berkshires?” one resident asked.
Quint agreed.
“Funny thing is, they are not volunteering for that. It’s definitely for us. We’re a cheap date, unfortunately,” she said. “They have no problem using and abusing that, so talk to your neighbors. A lot of people don’t realize what’s going on.”
According to Dobbins, 11% of the project will be billed to Aroostook County government.
“We’re paying for them to destroy our area and then send that power somewhere else,” Quint said. “That infuriates me, truthfully.”
Several residents asked how the project will benefit the town.
Both lawmakers said power bills will not go down and that promises of 2,500 jobs are not realistic because such projects require skilled technicians.
Zufelt said there will likely be property tax relief similar to the existing Oakfield project.
Oakfield residents who qualify for a homestead exemption receive about $2,000 a year for 20 years toward property tax bills, according to Town Manager Dale Morris.
The County commissioners need to sit down and renegotiate the contract, if the project goes through, so the community gets something from it, Dobbins said.
“We’re not getting a thing out of it at this point,” he said. “The majority of [the public utilities commission] are from southern Maine and they are not interested in us, to tell you the truth.”
During the discussion, a resident asked if the temporary pause the residents are working on will help when negotiating with Clearway.
“If that moratorium goes in and says ‘you can’t do this’ they have to deal with the town at that point, correct?” he asked.
Quint said that the temporary pause would tell the developer that the town is “a little bit hostile” toward the project’s development.
“They prefer to go to places that don’t have moratoriums,” she said. “You can be working on an ordinance while you have the moratorium. It’s giving you time and you’re less than a cheap date that way.”
The Select Board will begin drafting documents to temporarily halt a wind project while they research and develop their own town ordinance related to such projects, Selectman Craig Clifford said.

title: Bright and breezy Thursday
text:
Bright and breezy Thursday
Bright and breezy Thursday
A chilly breeze from the northwest continues Wednesday night into Thursday morning, gusting to 25 to 30 mph. Sunshine is expected from start to finish on Thursday, with temperatures running near average: highs in the 50s and low 60s.
Clouds will roll in Thursday night as the next storm approaches. A strengthening low-pressure system passing to the north brings another widespread, needed rainfall to Maine starting Friday morning.
Showers continue Friday evening before wrapping up in the early morning hours on Saturday. Expect a blustery first half of the weekend with northerly winds gusting to around 40 mph. Temperatures struggle to climb into the 40s and low 50s Saturday afternoon, and feels-like temperatures will remain in the 30s.
Snow showers are likely in the mountains on Saturday, and we can't rule out a few flurries spilling further south. Clouds and spotty showers may try to linger along the coast in the morning, giving way to a partly to mostly sunny afternoon.

title: Maine can no longer justify Susan Collins
text:
In some other time, the reelection of Sen. Susan Collins might be justifiable. These are not ordinary times. Now we need to recall what we learned in our elementary classrooms: The United States is a democracy protected by three branches of government to ensure adequate checks and balances; that way, no one branch harms its citizens’ freedoms and security.
Susan Collins has failed to safeguard our country against an executive branch run amok. She expresses “concern” when she needs to act — against a president who wages war and kills children; violates established civil rights; enriches himself while working Americans struggle to buy food, fill their gas tanks and provide for their children; and who damages the environment endangering future generations.
Collins has failed her responsibility to stop this man’s terrifying destruction. All we can do is vote for Troy Jackson.
Ellen McQuiston
Anson

title: REVIEW POTPOURRI: Remembering Margot Kidder and musical greats
text:
Margot Kidder
Actress Margot Kidder (1948-2018) guest starred in 1973 on the season 25th episode, Trial Run for Death, of Buddy Ebsen’s highly successful TV series Barnaby Jones. She portrays the romantically involved mistress of a very popular NASCAR-type race car driver who’s already married to the filthy rich boss’ daughter.
Clu Gulager’s redundantly characterized car driver obviously considers his mistress a temporary thrill and, of course, makes promises of commitment for later which he does not plan to keep, even resorting to murdering a brother-in-law who catches the couple smooching at the race track maintenance shed.
Meanwhile, the mistress exerts increasing pressure to make later in less than five minutes, so the boyfriend attempts to murder her.
While I initially found the mistress both dangerous and naive, Ms. Kidder developed a characterization that, just in her facial expressions of torment and loneliness, climaxes into a rude awakening when she realizes lover boy is going to kill her and is rescued in the nick of time by the shrewd investigator Barnaby. And the genuine relief and gratitude she conveys is endearing.
This actress did good work in the late ‘70s Superman as Lois Lane and in Amityville Horror.
In 2018 at the age of 69, Margot Kidder committed suicide via an overdose of pills, having struggled with depression for decades.
Music Masterpieces
Collector’s Library of the World’s Musical Masterpieces. Murray Hill S-2169, 16 LPs, recorded 1950s-’60s.
The mail order Murray Hill often merchandised these sets 50 years ago for $10 and consigned them in college bookstores or through Publishers Clearing House listings. And, as inexpensive and tantalizing as these albums were, we collecting youngsters had very, very tight budgets in which $10 was a lot of money.
About two years ago, I bought this set at a Waterville vendor’s for one buck, not bothering to count them first. Three being missing, I still decided not to press for a credit or refund.
The works – Bach’s 3 Concertos for Violin, Brahms 3rd and 4th Symphonies, Beethoven Woodwind Octet, Egmont Overture and 5th Symphony, Dvorak New World Symphony, Tchaikovsky Nutcracker Suite, 5th and Pathetique Symphonies, Strauss Waltzes, Schubert Unfinished Symphony and Trout Quintet, Mozart 11th Piano Sonata, Eine Kleine Nachtmusik, 40th and Jupiter Symphonies, Chopin Piano Encores, Rimsky-Korsakov Scheherazade and the infamous Stravinsky Rite of Spring.
The best performances were the Scheherazade and the Rite of Spring conducted by Sir Eugene Goossens (1893-1962) whose fabled career I wrote about months ago; the Tchaikovsky 5th Symphony conducted in a very poetic manner by Sir Malcolm Sargent (1895-1967) whose affection for colorful suits, ties and gossip earned him the nickname of Flash Harry; the Tchaikovsky Pathetique in an understated, eloquent interpretation by the African-American conductor Dean Dixon (1915-1976) who moved to Europe after World War II to pursue a career there because of the racism here.
Stravinsky’s Rite received its choreographed world premiere in Paris in 1913 and was conducted then by Hancock Maine’s summer resident Pierre Monteux (1875-1964) – during the premiere, a riot broke out during the production with fiss fights, thrown chairs, etc.
Other performances of note in the set – the Leopold Stokowski/Houston Symphony Brahms 3rd, the William Steinberg/Pittsburgh Symphony Brahms 4th, the propulsive yet elegant Josef Krips Beethoven 5th Symphony and Egmont Overture, the underrated violinist Charles Cyrolink playing the three Bach Concertos, pianist Frank Glazer with the Fine Arts Quartet doing Schubert’s Trout Quintet (cellist George Sopkin retired to near Blue Hill after the Quartet disbanded), and Leopold Ludwig conducting the Schubert Unfinished and Dvorak New World.
* * * * * *
Nathaniel Hawthorne – “The Sabbath eve is the eve of love.”
Moby Dick‘s Herman Melville in a funky mood – “All my books are botches.”
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!
