title: County budget review off to a tense start
text:
ELLSWORTH — As the Hancock County Budget Advisory Committee launched its work on the upcoming annual budget Oct. 7, one member voted in opposition to nearly every vote. Paul Bissonnette said he couldn’t “in good conscience” vote for a proposed budget with a potential 13.6% increase.
Bissonnette is chairman of the Bucksport Town Council. The town has had budget challenges in recent years, and the town manager did not take any increase last year.

title: Series of suspicious deaths along river trail sparks serial killer fears
text:
LANSING, Mich. (CNN) - A series of suspicious deaths along a Michigan river trail is stoking public fears of a possible serial killer.
Five suspicious deaths have happened along a river trail in Lansing, Michigan, since last October. Four of them were between July and September of this year, all within weeks of each other. The victims were men, ranging in age from 22 to 70 years old.
“One question that we are being asked. Do we have a serial killer in Lansing?” Lansing Police Chief Robert Backus said. “We are looking at the idea or the possibility that these may be related cases.”
Backus says one link is that the victims were all homeless, possibly sleeping outside. The attacks appeared to take place in the early morning hours, roughly 3 to 4 a.m.
A suspect has been arrested and charged in connection with one of the homicides, which took place in late August. He remains in custody without bond and is expected to undergo a mental health evaluation, according to court records.
“Is this a suspect for all the incidents? That is a challenging question to answer,” Backus said.
As the investigation continues, police are stepping up patrols in the area, adding more security cameras and working with local homeless groups to spread awareness.

title: Isolation is one of the hardest battles for caregivers. It doesn’t have to be.
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
When Cathyann Adams called the Aroostook Area Agency on Aging last winter, she was fast approaching her breaking point.
Her husband, Chris, was in the advanced stages of Lewy body dementia and declining fast. As his full-time caretaker, Adams felt herself slipping, too. She was desperate for a break.
The couple had moved from Vermont to Caribou a few years prior — a homecoming for Chris, who grew up in Fort Fairfield, and a new adventure for Adams.
But Chris’s diagnosis, which came shortly after their move, and his ensuing decline soon became the center of their lives, leaving little room for making friends and building a support system.
“I was alone,” said Adams, 67. “I didn’t know how I was going to go forward.”
In a rural state like Maine, the emotional and physical toll of caregiving — known as caregiver fatigue — is compounded by an isolation that aging experts say is all too common, placing both the caregivers and the people they’re caring for at greater risk of depression, illness and death.
Maine has the nation’s highest median age (44.9 years) and the highest proportion of residents ages 65 and older (24.6%), according to the U.S. Census Bureau.
Maine also is the second most rural state — 61.5% of residents live outside designated urban areas — a fact that, coupled with harsh winter weather and a lack of public transportation, makes it harder to access services and foster connection.
But aging experts also say there are ways to minimize isolation and caregiver fatigue.
Making a plan early, leaning on your community, and taking advantage of services like respite care, companionship programs, support groups and classes can all help alleviate the pressure.
RESPITE DAY PROGRAMS
Ruth White has heard many pleas for help like Adams’.
“You have such an array of emotions,” she said, ranging from happiness and pride to frustration, resentment and anger. The emotional whiplash and constant stress are exhausting.
“You don’t want to be in your head. You have to be loving and caring (but) you’re just dying,” said White, family caregiver program coordinator for the Aroostook Agency on Aging. “That’s usually the point when we start to get the people to come in.”
She often suggests they take advantage of the agency’s adult day respite center, where caregivers can leave their loved one for a few hours and step away from the demands of the job. There are similar centers across the state.
Older adult service providers say respite care is one of the most impactful resources for caregivers struggling with burnout.
“It’s so important for them to have that ability to walk away from that caregiving for a little while and get back out into the world and sort of regain a little bit of the life that they put so much thought and effort into,” said Ashley Butterfield, executive director of Bath-Brunswick Respite Care.
The Bath-based center is the only respite day program in the region, Butterfield said. They served about 40 families last year.
“I think every caregiver, no matter what stage they’re in, understands everything that they’re giving up. They understand that they do need to socialize more, they understand that they need to maintain connections, but it’s really hard,” Butterfield said. “And I think that’s really where so much of the social isolation stems from. It’s just easier to not go out into the world.”
DON’T WAIT
Jess Maurer’s No. 1 piece of advice for new caregivers is “make a plan early.”
Do not wait. Figure out now who you can lean on, and how you can get a break. The longer you wait, the harder it will be to see a way out, said Maurer, executive director of the Maine Council on Aging.
Start talking to your friends about what you might need.
Who can make a meal once a week that you can divvy up for your person throughout the week? Who can come sit with them or take them to a doctor’s appointment?
Or, if you’re dealing with more challenging behaviors, who can do your grocery shopping or take your car in for an oil change?
Ask for help with “the basic things of life that get lost,” Maurer said.
“It feels really awkward, because it feels very much like ‘This is my responsibility. I have to take care of my parent. I have to take care of myself. I shouldn’t be asking other people,'” she said. “We really have to get past that in a big way because there are so many people who are really struggling.”
Butterfield, at Bath-Brunswick Respite Care, said caregivers often put off seeking help out of a misplaced sense of guilt: It’s too early to need more solo time; it’s not that bad yet; it’s going to be much worse.
“It doesn’t need to be bad in order for a caregiver to need to maintain their own sense of self,” she said. “No caregiver should need to wait until they’re burnt out.”
A LIFESAVER
The Southern Maine Agency on Aging’s adult day program in Springvale has been a “lifesaver” for Terry Turner.
Her husband, Jack Turner, 75, was diagnosed with dementia three years ago and has been attending the day program three days a week for the last two.
He has been thriving.
“With the dementia scale, I have not seen him go down much,” said Terry Turner, 71. “He thinks he works there. That’s the only thing that gets him going is ‘OK, I gotta go to my job.’ He’s so funny. ‘I’m still waiting on a paycheck,’ he says.”
Turner, meanwhile packs as much as she can into that time.
“I don’t just sit and do nothing,” she said. “I literally use up that time for something that I would really enjoy,” like cardmaking and Bible study with her ladies group.
“I have to socialize myself with my girlfriends, in order to enjoy life, you know?” she said.
The Turners also recently converted their Springvale home into a duplex, where their daughter, 40, lives and can help out.
On days when Jack isn’t at the center, they spend time outside. Jack mows the lawn, Turner tends to her garden, a newer hobby. They dote on their three dogs, who Turner said give Jack purpose. He feeds them carrots.
If she needs to pop to the store, her neighbors or daughter might keep an eye on Jack. For now, things are manageable. She’s happy.
Turner is used to caregiving. She took care of her father, who also had dementia, years before.
“I’m OK with it, because maybe that’s what God wants me to do,” she said. “There are some tough days, and if there are, I might have a cry or whatever, and that’s OK, too.”
RESPITE POP-UPS AND COMPANIONSHIP
Six of Maine’s 16 counties don’t offer day programs. And even in counties where there are programs, some communities are simply too far away to make the trip worthwhile.
The Southern Maine Agency on Aging is trying to fill some of the gaps with a new 12-week pilot “pop-up” respite care program.
Thanks to a nearly $100,000 grant from the Alzheimer’s Association, the agency launched “Dementia Respite Without Walls” last month at the Casco Community Center.
Casco is central to areas like Bridgton, Raymond, Windham and Harrison — communities whose residents are less likely to visit the agency’s centers in Springvale, Biddeford or Portland.
Other families may feel that a day program is not the right fit.
In 2022, the state launched a two-year pilot program called Respite for ME, funded with about $5.1 million in American Rescue Plan funds.
The program, overseen by the Department of Health and Human Services and administered by the local agencies on aging, offered grants up to $2,000 in the first year and just over $5,000 in the second to people providing care to an older adult at home.
The money paid for temporary caregivers to come for a few hours of respite, including in-home care, center visits and overnight stays in a facility. The money could also be used for counseling, training, financial guidance and assistive technology.
The results were promising. While caregiver burden and stress remained at medium or high levels for most caregivers, for people participating in the second year, high stress decreased by 10% and high depression decreased by 14%, according to the pilot’s evaluation. Caregivers reported better relationships with their loved ones and less financial strain and worry.
The state Legislature made the program permanent in July 2025 (with a $2,000 limit on grants) but only allocated $100,000, leaving it effectively unfunded.
Maurer, at the Council on Aging, said advocates will be pushing for full funding for the program next year and encouraging the new governor to make it a budget priority.
A break from isolation doesn’t have to come from dedicated respite care, either.
The University of Maine’s Senior Companion Program, a partnership between the university’s Center on Aging and AmeriCorp, matches homebound, isolated older adults with volunteers ages 55 and older.
There’s also a southern Maine chapter through AmeriCorp and the Opportunity Alliance.
Jennifer Jain, director of the university program, said that while the volunteer program is centered on companionship for older adults, the benefits extend to caregivers by giving them a break.
The pairings are intended to be long-term relationships, not just one-and-done visits, Jain said, and by matching older adults with peers around their own age, they are able to relate to each other on a deeper level.
“I don’t want to say it’s a best kept secret, but it’s something that people do not see us as a program to tap into … but respite is up and rising as more of a need in our state,” she said.
‘A DIVINE APPOINTMENT’
Adams, in Caribou, credits the Aroostook agency with helping her get through the last months of her husband’s disease, which she said was like “being on a very violent rollercoaster.”
She tapped into whatever resources were available.
While he was still well enough to go, she brought Chris to the day program.
For a few hours each week, she had time to do whatever she wanted, not just what needed to be done around the house. She’d get her hair done, go for a long walk, sit and cry when she needed to.
She took their Savvy Caregiver class to learn more about what to expect as Chris’ illness progressed. She took a yoga class and found an online caregiver support group.
White also found her a volunteer with shared interests in music and fellowship who could visit with Chris while Adams worked around the house or ran to the grocery store.
For a few months, she could breathe again. And it allowed her enough room to still find “something joyful to share (with Chris) every day.”
Chris Adams, 71, died on July 23.
“I don’t believe that things happen by accident, so I would say it was a divine appointment when I called that number, and Ruth (White) answered the phone,” Adams said. “In a rural area … you need a community. That’s what the Agency on Aging gave me.”

title: Spruce Mountain field hockey rolls past Gray-New Gloucester/NYA
text:
YARMOUTH — Late arrivals are becoming the norm for the Spruce Mountain field hockey team.
After arriving late to a game against Lisbon last week, the Phoenix showed up only 25 minutes before the scheduled start of Wednesday’s game against Gray-New Gloucester/North Yarmouth Academy.
The fashionably late Phoenix were undeterred and earned a 5-1 victory over the Patriots.
“I think that we play better when we have that happen to us,” Spruce Mountain midfielder Maddie Gramaldi said. “It’s happened a couple of times, and our warm-ups were quick, but we just got the main stuff we needed to do done.”
Fast off the bus
Spruce Mountain (11-2), ranked second in the Class C South Heal point standings, started fast and scored twice in the first quarter. First, Malaire Richards deflected a ball past Patriots keeper Mallory Kulas. Aisla Armandi knocked in the second goal.
“We recognized that we were going to have a quick start,” Armandi said. “We realized we needed to bring our energy and be really intense because we knew they were a very talented team.”
The Phoenix spent most of the contest on offense. Neither team scored in the second quarter, but Spruce Mountain capitalized on its penalty-corner chances with goals by Grimaldi and Linda Lake to extend the lead to 4-0 in the third.
“We were in the 25 most of the game,” Spruce Mountain coach Alex Bessey said. “I think we talked a lot about (at) halftime, just finishing.”
Armandi scored her second goal early in the fourth quarter.
Patriots don’t quit
Gray-New Gloucester/NYA (3-8) started getting the ball in its offensive zone after Spruce Mountain made mass substitutions in the final quarter.
The Patriots got their first shot on goal with a minute remaining, then Emma Elgee scored on the second shot with 50 seconds left.
“She just recently started getting quite a bit of playing time for us,” Patriots coach Julia Leary said. “The last couple of games, went into a starting position. She’s a fantastic forward. She’s incredibly conditioned. … She’s been a huge asset for us offensively this year.”
Unsung hero
Maddie Grimaldi set the tone for the Phoenix by controlling the middle of the field. That allowed Spruce Mountain to keep the Patriots on their heels and in the defensive end of the field.
“Her communication was good, her energy was good,” Bessey said. “Then (she was) working well with her teammates and making the right passes.”
Statistical leaders
Spruce Mountain: Aisla Armandi (2 goals), Linda Lake (goal, assist), Maddie Grimaldi (goal), Malaire Richards (goal), Kyleigh Marcotte (one save)
Gray-New Gloucester/NYA: Emma Elgee (goal), Layla Whitman (assist), Mallory Kulas (11 saves).

title: After final debate, here’s where things stand in the race to become Maine’s next governor
text:
The fourth and final gubernatorial debate saw no huge fireworks Wednesday evening while covering largely familiar ground.
That means the race to succeed Gov. Janet Mills remains Democrat Hannah Pingree’s race to lose.
Pingree, a 49-year-old former Maine House speaker from North Haven who led Mills’ policy office, has consistently led polling of the contest by double digits and made no huge stumbles in the debates, though she was light on specifics at times.
Republican Bobby Charles, a 66-year-old Leeds lawyer who has led a lobbying and consulting firm and previously worked in drug and domestic policy roles under former Republican Presidents Ronald Reagan, George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush, expectedly and repeatedly sought to go after Pingree and link her with Mills in order to blame the two for rising energy and housing costs in Maine.
Independent Rick Bennett, a 63-year-old former state senator from Oxford who previously chaired the Maine Republican Party before leaving the GOP last year, reiterated that he is an experienced option for those tired of the two-party system, but his path to victory still looks very narrow.
If Charles surges past Pingree on Election Day, or if Bennett surpasses Charles on Election Day and competes with Pingree for the top spot, then it will be a massive surprise and a sign that the polls completely missed the mark. Here are a few quick notes on the race after the last debate.
No national Republican money for Charles?
It did not arise during Wednesday evening’s debate hosted by WMTW, but it matters for whether any sudden developments will grip the race in the home stretch.
Charles told reporters in July that he had met earlier that month with the Republican Governors Association and several Republican governors who planned to support him financially to the tune of “likely millions, and they are very committed to the idea that Maine is a pickup for them.”
If that money suddenly appears for Charles, then it will arrive with fewer than three weeks until Election Day. The Republican Governors Association did not respond to requests for comment after Charles made those comments earlier in the year, and the national support has not materialized for his campaign. Charles reported raising more than $1.8 million in his last campaign finance report, while Pingree had raised more than $4.2 million and Bennett raised about $923,000.
A political action committee with well-heeled Republican donors that was set up over the summer to support Charles has instead spent $70,000 to boost Bennett.
A rare moment of Pingree-Bennett bickering
Pingree may have heard about that infusion of pro-Bennett cash from the No Nonsense PAC, as she briefly went after Bennett during Wednesday’s debate, calling him “a lifelong Republican” and noting he chaired the state Republican Party from 2013 to 2017. That coincided with the party supporting President Donald Trump and former Gov. Paul LePage in their elections.
“He didn’t leave the party until he decided to run for governor because he knew he couldn’t beat Bobby Charles because the party has gone MAGA,” Pingree said. “And again, I have respect for Rick, but I don’t think it’s fair to say that he has been independent-minded.”
Bennett replied by alluding to how he voted against Republican proposals in the state Senate and was the chamber’s “most independent member.” Charles chimed in by noting Bennett decided to cast a Democratic ballot in the June primary.
Pingree made her rare attack on Bennett, whom she has otherwise referred to as “my friend,” after Bennett gave a line he has given in several debates about what he represents.
“We need to get back to a politics of compromise and collaboration. The party candidates can’t do that,” Bennett said. “Hannah Pingree has a D on her jersey. Bobby Charles has an R on his jersey. My jersey says Maine.”
Who gets to work in the next administration?
The brief amount of bickering between Pingree and Bennett was an exception to what has otherwise been a peaceful, drama-free set of interactions during each debate. Charles has notably gone after the two by calling them “insiders” for their years of legislative service in Augusta.
If the polls turn out to be fairly accurate, then Pingree will succeed Mills. The talk will quickly turn next month to who may join the next governor’s administration. Bennett is one name to watch if he loses the race and Pingree wins it, given their mostly amicable interactions.
But it is still far too early to say who will serve under the next governor. Campaigns are careful to not look too far ahead and publicly discuss any plans beyond Nov. 3.

title: Maine Named One of the Worst States for a Fall Move in New Study
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Named One of the Worst States for a Fall Move in New Study
While we may be known as Vacationland, a recent report suggests Maine is among the more challenging states for a fall move.
👇 KEEP READING: 30 Restaurants to Try Outside of Portland, Maine 👇
My Baggage compared all 50 states using five equally weighted measures: median asking rent, average fall temperature, rainfall, flight cancellations and storm-related property damage.
Using rental market data and federal weather and transportation records, the company ranked states on each measure and averaged those rankings, favoring lower costs, less rain, fewer cancellations, less storm damage, and warmer temperatures.
Maine ranked as the seventh-worst state for a fall move, despite having one of the lower median asking rents among the bottom 10 states at $1,694.
Among those 10 states, Maine had the second-lowest average fall temperature at 46.8 degrees, behind Alaska, and averaged 11.66 inches of rainfall during the season.
For anyone planning a fall move to Maine, cooler temperatures and rain can mean taking extra steps to keep furniture, boxes, and other belongings dry during loading and unloading.
Shorter daylight hours also leave less time to complete an outdoor move before dark.
The ranking focuses on costs, weather, and travel conditions associated with a fall move, rather than Maine’s overall appeal as a place to live.
Factors such as job opportunities, schools, and proximity to family were not among the five measures used.
And there you have it! According to this report, settling into Vacationland during the fall may require a little extra planning.

title: In the middle of fast food life, a homeless couple hope for better days in Lewiston
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
For days, a man named Frank wondered about the Subaru wagon parked in the lot at the Burger King near his home.
The wagon, stuffed to the roof in the rear portion of the car, never seemed to move. A couple and small dog could be seen in the front seats but they just mostly sat there, staring off into the vast space of Gendron Place, formerly the Promenade Mall.
Frank finally went out to investigate, and when he did, he found what he feared he might.
Living in the cram-packed Subaru, enduring frigid nights and running out of just about everything, was a couple living in desperate conditions.
Inside the car, crumpled on one side after it was struck by a van last week, was a 59-year-old woman named Kathy and her lifelong companion, Patrick.
As far as Kathy is concerned, that spot at the very edge of the Burger King lot marks the couple’s last stand. Since they were kicked out of their apartment at River Valley Village in June, the couple has been moving from parking lot to parking lot, just trying to scrape by.
Now, there’s no place left for them to go.
Patrick gets $500 a month for a disability, but that money has to come through a relative. Kathy has no income. Though the couple is not married, they’ve been together essentially all their lives; since they were children.
Now, they’re running out of gas. Patrick can’t drive anymore because his driver’s license was suspended. Reaching out to family has produced no help so now it’s just a matter of night-by-night survival, huddled up in the crowded Subaru with their 13-year-old Yorkshire Terrier named Lucky while nighttime temperatures dip down close to freezing.
“It’s hard on the body,” says Kathy, of her monthslong homeless ordeal. “All we do is sit here day after day, looking out into that parking lot. It’s not very exciting.”
Both Kathy and Patrick, who is 54, have health problems. Both have trouble walking, so most of their time is spent sitting and staring and musing over the series of events that brought them to this ultimate dead-end.
Asked why they were kicked out of their apartment at River Valley Village, Kathy says only that it was for “something stupid.” Most of their belongings, she said, got left behind at their home of 10 years on June 4.
What meager possessions they have left are balled up as efficiently as possible and stuffed in the back of the car. Lucky sleeps on a pile of blankets and a pillow. Patrick and Kathy, they sit slumped in the front seats with the glow of city lights shining down upon them.
It’s been uncomfortable living since summer gave way to fall.
“Some nights,” Kathy says, “we get really cold.”
In spite of her struggles, Kathy is a spunky woman. She hobbles when she walks, talks fast and manages self-effacing humor at times — if she spends too much time thinking about the pickle she’s in, Kathy says, it would overwhelm her.
“You’re lucky,” she says. “This is the first time I’ve been able to talk about this without bursting out crying.”
Patrick, he doesn’t talk much. His health problems prohibit him from joining Kathy in her grim, vivid descriptions of the situation. He just stares forlornly into the bland parking lot that is his only view. He looks like a man who is still coming to grips with the dire straits in which he finds himself.
And just when they think they’ve sunk their lowest, Kathy says, life finds a way to make things even worse.
On the night of Oct. 9, as the Subaru they call home was parked in its usual spot next to the Burger King, a woman driving a cargo van backed into them. The collision shoved the car into a storage container sitting at the edge of the lot and mangled the side of the Subaru.
“I was sitting in the front,” Kathy says. “I bent right over to cover the dog as much as I can so he wouldn’t get hurt.”
When police came to investigate, Patrick couldn’t produce his insurance card and a cop told him he could no longer drive. The woman in the van was sent on her way and never said a word to the couple inside the Subaru.
Since then, the couple hasn’t moved from that spot. Day after day, hour after hour, they sit, watching their supplies dwindle and wondering if there is any light at the end of this terrible tunnel.
Kathy doesn’t like to think about what might happen if not for help they’ve received from strangers. Workers from two nearby fast food restaurants have come by to check on them, she says. A manager from Popeye’s Chicken said he wants to help the couple any way he can.
Other businesses have allowed the couple to use their restrooms and a few folks have brought by food and blankets.
For a couple who has next to nothing, all of those gestures mean a lot.
But when she gets talking about the heroes they rely on so much, it’s Frank who causes her eyes to twinkle.
“That gentleman on the porch,” she calls him. “He’s been helping us a lot.”
Frank has brought the couple bottles of water and canned food for Lucky, even though Patrick and Kathy have never asked him for anything. He keeps an eye on them and keeps hoping for some miracle to help the couple along.
“I’ve been doing what I can,” says Frank, who initially didn’t want to be recognized at all for his role in the matter. “There are people who are asking for things and there are people who aren’t asking, but they do have a need. I watch these guys and they’re just sitting in this same spot day after day.”
Every day, Frank sees people parking next to the Subaru in the Burger King lot. Those people get out of their own cars, fetch their food and drive away, never sparing a glance at the couple inside the crowded wagon they call home.
He sees people walking dogs in the area, but those people, too, just move right past the Subaru with no inkling of the desperate battles going on inside it.
Surely some of those people might be willing to help, Frank muses, if only they were made aware of the situation.
“I think people care,” he says, “but they don’t know this is happening.”
After all, Frank says, most people are aware of the homeless who stand on street corners with signs asking for help. People know all about those unhoused men and women who set up tents in Kennedy Park because those homeless souls are in full view.
He worries in particular about people like Kathy and Patrick, who keep a lower profile and don’t tend to outright ask for help.
And so Frank has been trying to let people know about the couple’s plight, on the logic that the more people there are who know about it, the more chances there are that help will be forthcoming.
“Maybe something positive can come of it,” Frank says.
Meanwhile, Kathy and Patrick sit and wait and hope for that miracle to get them off this dead end on which they find themselves. They make phone calls when they can and reach out to family who might be able to help, but so far, none of that has gotten them anywhere.
And so they bundle up for one more night and try to get comfortable in those bucket seats. They hunker down as night falls and the temperature drops, with the sounds of the city serenading them to a troubled sleep.
They have their dog, they have help from a few strangers and they have each other.
The question is whether any of that will be enough.
People in Maine in need of assistance can call 211 to be connected with health, educational and financial services.

title: Parents charged after 8-year-old girl living in ‘squalid’ home dies from asthma attack
text:
SAN JOSE, Calif. (KGO) - The mother and stepfather of an 8-year-old California girl who suffered a fatal asthma attack are facing charges after her death was ruled a homicide.
Gabrielle Hanson, 32, and Jacob Randolph, 39, the mother and stepfather of 8-year-old Aurora Williams, made their first court appearance Tuesday. Prosecutors charged the couple with felony child neglect in connection with Aurora’s death following a severe asthma attack in May.
The Santa Clara District Attorney’s Office says Aurora was in serious distress for eight hours before her parents sought medical help. She was eventually taken to the hospital but died four days later.
“Why does this keep happening? This little asthmatic girl and her brothers and sisters were living in a home filled with roaches, mold, animal feces and two parents who were not providing enough care or food for their children,” District Attorney Jeff Rosen said.
Rosen says the family’s San Jose home was “squalid,” infested with cockroaches and mold and littered with garbage and pet feces. Thirteen people, seven of whom were children, and at least eight animals lived there.
Rosen says Aurora’s cause of death was lack of oxygen from severe asthma with lung injury and an infection. He says medical neglect was a significant factor in her death, which was ruled a homicide by the medical examiner.
“When she was finally brought to a hospital, staff found that she was below 1% of her expected body weight and had roaches on her emaciated body. Do you know what Aurora’s answer was when the hospital staff asked her about the vermin? The little girl said, ‘Oh yeah, bugs just crawl on me,’” Rosen said.
Authorities say the home was later deemed unlivable after conditions there contributed to Aurora’s death. The six other children in the household, ages 2 months to 17 years, were placed in foster care.
The Santa Clara County Department of Family and Children’s Services had frequent involvement with the family. In a statement, spokesperson Peter Gallota said the county was aware of the charges but could not comment further because the matter is ongoing litigation.
Rosen is now criticizing the county’s child welfare system and calling for reforms. He says his office will form a team to examine issues within the welfare system.
“Somewhere in our county right now, there are children who are in danger. Can we help them? I believe that we can. I believe that we must,” Rosen said.
Hanson and Randolph are scheduled to return to court Nov. 20.

title: Woman accused of burying cats alive in yard because she thought they were demons
text:
MARTIN COUNTY, Fla. (Gray News) – A 37-year-old Florida woman has been arrested for allegedly burying cats in her yard while they were still alive.
Martin County deputies and animal services officers responded to a residence last week at the Hobe Sound Mobile Home Park on Southeast Federal Highway to investigate an animal cruelty case.
Investigators spoke with the homeowner, Alba Chavez, who said she buried at least four cats alive in her yard because she believed they were demons, according to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office.
Deputies began digging up the property, but were only able to save two of the cats. Two other cats were found dead.
“You don’t treat an animal that way and expect to get away with it,” Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said during a briefing last week.
Chavez was booked at the Martin County Jail in multiple counts of aggravated animal cruelty.

title: Federal judge orders Trump administration to halt work on historic DC golf course until Oct. 26
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes on Tuesday ordered a halt to tree-cutting at the East Potomac Golf Course until Oct. 26, putting a further pause on work at the historic D.C. course that has been part of President Donald Trump’s plans to remake the city.
Reyes issued the order one day after a tense three-hour hearing in which she harshly criticized the government for having deceived her with its actions over the holiday weekend.
At the Monday hearing, Reyes ordered a 24-hour pause that could be extended to 14 days if necessary. It was limited to one day while the government tried to find a key Trump administration official to discuss why a massive tree-cutting at the park needed to occur over the holiday weekend, with little notification to plaintiffs in a lawsuit trying to halt renovation plans or the judge.
The judge also ordered during that period the government “must provide the court and plaintiffs three business days’ written advance notice prior to making any irreparable modification to any permanent form or feature of the East Potomac Golf Course.”
The DC Preservation League and two local golfers are the plaintiffs in the lawsuit.
The co-counsel in the case, Democracy Forward, thanked Reyes for stepping in and halting what the group called the “mad rush” to turn the public recreation space into a high-end golf course. “We are pleased that the court intervened and will prevent additional work while we seek more lasting relief,” the group said in a statement.
The Monday hearing and Tuesday order were prompted by the National Park Service ordering the cutting of hundreds of trees at the golf course after filing the court notification only minutes before the close of business on Oct. 9 on a holiday weekend, giving the plaintiffs little time to respond. At least 400 trees were cut down over the weekend with plans for several hundred more.
In explaining her order, Reyes said the court, based on limited information so far, concluded that government officials raced to undertake a tree management plan at the park “because President Trump demands haste on his redesign, and not because of some newfound zeal to implement a small part” of a 2019 National Park Service Cultural Landscape Report that suggested work was needed at the district’s public golf courses.
The historic park, especially the golf course, caught the eye of Trump, who wants to turn it into a world-class golf venue. It’s part of his grand vision for Washington, D.C., where he has multiple projects underway, including a $400 million White House ballroom and the soon-to-begin construction of his triumphal arch. He began talking about the city’s public courses in late 2025.
“When completed, this Course will have the ability to host Major Golf Tournaments, including The U.S. Open, The Ryder Cup, The PGA Championship, and other top PGA Tour events,” Trump posted on social media in June.
The course has been the subject of multiple emergency hearings, including one in May in which Reyes was out of the country, because of concerns from the plaintiffs that the administration would move ahead with work despite the pending lawsuit. In each instance Reyes declined issuing temporary stop orders out of trust for the government’s attorney in the case.
“Every single time I have given the government the benefit of the doubt and every single time I made absolutely clear that I want notice,” Reyes said at Monday’s hearing. “What has happened has cost the government all credibility with me.”

title: The first new sunscreen type in 25 years has arrived on US store shelves
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — For the first time in more than a quarter-century, Americans have a new option when shopping for sunscreen: a skin-protecting chemical that’s long been a go-to option in Europe and other parts of the world.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved bemotrizinol — sometimes called BEMT — in June. The first sunscreens containing it are now hitting U.S. store shelves, including formulas from Neutrogena and other manufacturers.
Dermatologists say the chemical fills an important market gap by offering broad protection, like the most well-established sunscreen ingredients, but without their cosmetic downsides, including white streaking.
BEMT has decades of safety data behind it, including studies showing it has minimal absorption into the skin. That’s been a concern with some older sun-blocking chemicals.
“It’s not a brand-new ingredient that you’re going to be the first person to try,” said Dr. Jennifer Stein, a dermatologist at NYU Langone Health.
Here’s what to know:
New ingredient offers broad protection without streaks
To be effective, sunscreens must protect against both forms of ultraviolet light that can damage the skin — UVB rays, which cause most sunburn, and UVA rays that pose the greatest risk of skin cancer and wrinkles.
Sunscreens that block both forms are labeled “broad spectrum protection.” Those that don’t must carry an FDA warning label.
BEMT is the first chemical-based sunscreen in the U.S. that offers this dual protection. Previously, manufacturers had to mix multiple ingredients to protect against both UVA and UVB light.
“This ingredient provides a solution for what is currently a big gap with respect to providing strong UVA protection,” said David Andrews, chief science officer of the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit that advocates for higher sunscreen standards.
A different class of sunscreens, using minerals such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, has long been shown to offer strong protection against both forms of ultraviolet light. These mineral-based formulas work by physically blocking harmful rays from the skin.
But some people — particularly those with darker complexions — tend to avoid them because they cause white streaking and discoloration. In other cases, people don’t like their texture or consistency.
“Those are good sunscreens,” Stein said. “But for people who aren’t so inclined to use them — maybe they don’t like how it feels on their skin — this is a nice option.”
There’s less skin penetration with the new formula
The fact that chemical-based sunscreens are absorbed into the skin means they have to be carefully studied to make sure they aren’t building up in the body at unsafe levels.
Last month, the FDA revoked approval of an older chemical ingredient, oxybenzone, after determining it was “absorbed through the skin to a greater extent than previously understood.”
That’s not a problem with BEMT.
“It’s a molecule that’s too big to really penetrate through the skin and get absorbed into the bloodstream,” Stein said. “The older chemical sunscreens had small molecules.”
As part of its safety review, the FDA reviewed studies of BEMT in more than 500 patients conducted by Dutch manufacturer DSM Nutritional Products. Levels of the chemical absorbed into the skin were nearly undetectable, the studies found.
Agency reviewers said research in people who used the sunscreen daily for up to three weeks showed that BEMT “did not cause irritation” or allergic reactions. As a result, the FDA designated the ingredient as “generally recognized as safe and effective,” alongside the older mineral ingredients zinc oxide and titanium dioxide.
More than a dozen other ingredients are currently used in U.S. sunscreens, but the FDA has said they will require additional evidence to support their safety and effectiveness. The FDA review is part of an ongoing effort to overhaul U.S. sunscreen ingredients that kicked off in 2019.
More evidence is needed about the impact on coral reefs
Scientists have shown that some sunscreen ingredients can trigger bleaching and damage coral reefs. That’s led to bans on two chemical ingredients — oxybenzone, the ingredient recently targeted by the FDA, and octinoxate — in Hawaii and parts of Florida. It’s estimated about 25% of the sunscreen people apply to their skin washes off while swimming or wading in the ocean.
The U.S. government doesn’t classify the environmental impact of sunscreens, and marketing claims like “reef safe” or “reef friendly” have no standard definition or requirements. The European Union’s environmental agency has found “limited evidence of environmental toxicity” with BEMT, but longer-term research is needed.
Mineral ingredients like zinc oxide are generally considered safer for the environment, although some experts recommend staying away from so-called nano formulations. Those products are made with tiny particles that are more likely to be inhaled or absorbed by marine organisms.
Older chemicals were often unstable
Experts say BEMT has one other key advantage, in that it doesn’t quickly break down in the sun. That’s been a particular issue for avobenzone, the only other chemical-based ingredient that filters UVA light.
“Avobenzone has been known to be particularly unstable on its own, and a lot of work and reformulation efforts have gone into trying to find ways to stabilize it,” said Andrews. “BEMT is significantly more stable.”
As with all sunscreens, dermatologists say it’s important to reapply every few hours — more frequently if you’re swimming or sweating a lot.
Also, people shouldn’t rely on sunscreen alone when spending time outside, Stein said. Taking breaks in the shade, wearing a hat and sun-protective clothing are all important protections.
“Sunscreen is just one part of an overall sun-protection plan,” Stein said. “Clothing is even better.”
Story by Matthew Perrone, AP health writer.

title: A look at what’s on the ballot in Gorham
text:
Absentee voting is underway in Gorham ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3. On their ballots, Gorham residents will see Town Council and school committee races, a referendum to borrow money for high school renovations, and notable races for Maine House, Senate, governor and federal positions.
Where you’ll vote on Election Day in Gorham depends on where you live. Voters in the northern parts of town will vote at Great Falls Elementary School, voters in the western and southern parts will vote at the Shaw Gym by the Gorham Municipal Center and voters in the eastern parts will head to Gorham Middle School. Election Day voting hours are 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., and a list of addresses in each ward and a map is available on the town’s website.
In-person absentee voting is held in the town clerk’s office until Oct. 15 and will move to the council chambers of the Gorham Municipal Center from Oct. 19-29. There will be special absentee voting hours from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Oct. 27, and regular hours are 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. Mondays, Wednesdays and Thursdays and 7 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. Tuesdays.
TOWN COUNCIL
Two Gorham town councilors — four-term Chair Suzanne Phillips and one-term Councilor Lou Simms — are up for reelection. Newcomers Sam Purinton and Roger Kramer are running for the open seats.
In her responses to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Phillips said her priorities include affordability, planning ahead in development and strengthening the town’s tax base, as well as making Gorham a friendlier place for businesses. She emphasized the importance of managing the large housing projects in the pipeline and making sure businesses have room to grow, and improving communication between the town and residents.
Simms wrote in his responses that he is focused on supporting schools and considering the costs and benefits of prospective developments. He said he wants the Town Council to prioritize the input of residents and quality of life over corporate interests, and emphasized that mixed-use development generates significant property tax revenue without adding kids to schools, and provides gathering spaces for community.
Purinton said his priorities are ensuring schools are funded while keeping property taxes to a minimum by focusing development pressure on land that is already developed. He added that he wants to bring more transparency to the Town Council, as he believes it should not have discussed its purchase-and-sale agreement with Amazon in executive session before voting to sell land to the corporation in August 2025.
Simms and Purinton are campaigning together.
Kramer did not respond to the Voter Guide Survey.
SCHOOL COMMITTEE
Three seats are open on the seven-person Gorham School Committee. Incumbent Michelle Littlefield is up for reelection, and five newcomer candidates — Nancy Flagg, Sheldon Jones, Karl Krebs, Michael Lund Ziegler and Matthew Steinback — are seeking seats.
In her responses to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Littlefield said she wants to ensure children receive the best education possible, support educators and their expertise and identify solutions to reduce burdens on local taxpayers.
Flagg wrote that her priorities are fostering a healthy community, supporting diverse types of achievement and managing technological changes available to students and schools.
Jones said he is focused on supporting the resources teachers and students need, balancing school spending with what Gorham families can afford and listening to parents, educators and residents in decision making.
Krebs said he wants to make sure schools in Gorham have resources for students that perform better in alternative learning environments, center diversity and support community engagement opportunities for students.
Lund Ziegler said he intends to support teachers and families with thoughtful long-term strategies.
Steinback explained that he will prioritize ensuring that Gorham schools are safe, supportive and academically strong, strengthen mental health resources and substance-use prevention, and guide responsible and transparent budgeting.
$6.7M HIGH SCHOOL RENOVATIONS BOND
A referendum on the Gorham ballot will ask voters to borrow nearly $6.7 million to finance capital improvement projects at Gorham High School.
The projects include improving the parking lot, sidewalks, ADA access and drainage for $763,000, replacing six old portable classrooms for $4.6 million, and replacing windows, doors and brick veneer work for $1.3 million.
The bond is part of Gorham Schools’ 10-year plan for capital improvements after the district learned it wouldn’t receive state funding for renovations for at least 10-15 years, according to Superintendent Heather Perry.
“This is looking for some of those larger ticket items, those bigger projects that go out 15, 20-plus years that could be bonded as a way to move these projects forward and get the necessary changes made for our schools,” Perry said at the Aug. 4 Town Council meeting.
The last large renovation at the school was completed in 1992, Perry said.
The Gorham Town Council voted 7-0 to send the bond question to voters. If voters approve, the council will decide the bond period.
MAINE SENATE & HOUSE
In Maine Senate District 30, which covers Gorham and part of Scarborough, voters will decide between Republican Thad Moody and current Maine House District 124 Rep. and Democrat Sophie Warren.
Gorham Town Councilor and Republican candidate Kelly Dearborn is up against one-term Democrat incumbent Parnell Terry for Maine House District 108, which covers the west part of Gorham.
In Maine House District 109, covering the east part of Gorham, Republican Diana Kushnar is facing Gorham Town Councilor and Democrat Seven Siegel.
CUMBERLAND COUNTY RACES
Democrat Paul Aranson is running uncontested for Cumberland County judge of probate, as is incumbent Democrat Kevin Joyce for Cumberland County sheriff.
Incumbent Jacqueline Sartoris and challenger Stephanie Anderson are facing off for the District 2 attorney seat.
Read more about candidates’ campaign goals on the Press Herald Voter Guide.

title: Pope Leo spent 'a tranquil night' in the hospital after cancer surgery, Vatican says
text:
Pope Leo shares first message after lung cancer diagnosis
Pope Leo XIV thanked fellow Catholics for their prayers on Wednesday in his first message since he underwent surgery for lung cancer in Rome.
"As you know, I have been unable to be among you during these days," Leo wrote in a statement to Catholics participating in a symposium for the 10th anniversary of Amoris laetitia, a document written by his predecessor, Pope Francis.
Related video above: Pope Leo XIV diagnosed with cancer
"I thank you warmly for your prayers and for the work you have done together. Your sharing of experiences and attentive listening are indeed a gift to the whole Church," he said. "I ask you please to pray for me, as I pray for you."
Leo was diagnosed with pulmonary adenocarcinoma, a common type of lung cancer, during a 90-minute surgery in Rome yesterday wherein doctors removed the lower lobe of one of his lungs, according to medical staff who treated the pontiff.
The pope announced his planned surgery in a speech over the weekend to the faithful in St. Peter’s Square, saying that the "growth" on his lung was found at an early stage.
The pope isn’t known to be a smoker and has made efforts to have a healthy lifestyle, but there is a history of cancer in his immediate family. His older brother Louis Prevost is currently in treatment for cancer, and their parents died of the disease in the 1990s.
Pope Leo has canceled all his public appearances until Oct. 20 in light of his treatment, though he is due to embark on a long trip to South America next month.
Earlier on Wednesday, the Vatican said that Pope Leo is eating regularly and has begun walking and doing respiratory exercises, and his post-operative tests are normal following surgery to remove a cancerous mass from his lung, the Vatican said Wednesday.
Leo's two doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, provided a medical update on Wednesday. Blood tests and a chest X-ray confirmed a normal post-operative recovery, with levels within the norm, they said.
"The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room. He resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch," they reported. "Recovery is proceeding as planned."
No word yet on whether the pope's cancer had spread
Experts said some of Leo’s lymph nodes would also have been removed and tested to determine whether the cancer had spread. Those results have not so far been made public.
If the cancer has spread, test results will guide treatment, said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted therapy, which uses pills to treat cancers with specific characteristics.
Liu, who is not involved in the pope's care, said that, of the different types of lung cancers, adenocarcinoma has the most favorable prognosis.
“While we know the diagnosis, we now need to know the stage,” Liu said. “We now need to know how big it is, how many spots in the lung are involved. Is it just one nodule, or more than one, and the lymph nodes, are they cancerous?”
Dr. PierCarlo Gentile, head of radiation oncology at Rome’s San Pietro Fatebenefratelli Hospital, said the minimally invasive, video-assisted chest surgery the pope underwent typically requires 15 to 20 days of recovery. Postoperative complications, including infections, are rare, he said.
The pope is breaking with a tradition of secrecy surrounding health issues
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the nodule, or growth, on his lung during his Sunday noon prayer, announcing it to the world on live television almost as an aside at the end of his blessing.
“That was truly a revolution. It was like he was reading a medical bulletin himself,” said Giovanni Maria Vian, a church historian and the former editor-in-chief of the Vatican newspaper L'Osservatore Romano.
The Vatican has long been secretive about the health of popes and tightly controlled any such information — a practice encapsulated in the popular Italian saying, “ The pope is fine until he’s dead.”
St. John XXIII died in 1963, nearly a year after doctors diagnosed stomach cancer that was kept hidden at the time. St. John Paul II died in 2005 after suffering for years from the obvious effects of Parkinson's disease that the Vatican only confirmed after he died.
Pope Francis seemed more up front about his health problems, giving an Argentine doctor a tell-all interview for a book about his physical and mental health. But in the end, Francis, too, tightly controlled the information that was released in his dying months.
Vian, who was part of the Vatican communications team from 2007 to 2018, said the Vatican's obsession with secrecy about the pope's health was due to both practical and cultural considerations. He noted the Vatican is a 2,000-year-old institution that is culturally European — and Europeans tend to be more guarded about health problems than people in the United States.
“In theory, the pope has an absolute power, so you can understand that there are many people who would aspire to that absolute power," he said. Secrecy about a pope's health, therefore "is a legitimate defense of both the pope in question and the institution itself.”
He attributed Leo's decision to reveal his health condition to his American outlook and serenity, and said he hoped it would extend to other aspects of Vatican communications.
That said, Leo didn't share everything he knew Sunday when he announced the existence of the nodule: Tuesday's medical bulletin said doctors had suspected cancer based on tests, a suspicion that was confirmed in surgery.
The pope has a trip to South America planned for November
The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20. But there was no word on whether he would be able to keep his planned trip to South America next month.
Oncology surgeons often advise patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery — which would give the pope just enough time to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. But whether he can go will depend on his recovery.
The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 19,000 miles on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
“If it is stage 1, he can complete these trips. If more treatment is needed, I would likely advise against the trips,” said Liu.

title: Judge sides with CNN, MS NOW, Politico in White House showdown
text:
(AP) - A federal judge has extended an order blocking President Donald Trump’s administration from banning reporters for three news outlets from the White House, broadening his support for the journalists by arguing that the restriction violates their constitutional rights to free speech and due process.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that CNN, MS NOW and Politico are likely to succeed in the extraordinary case pitting the president against the news outlets that cover him. In a victory for the journalists, Kelly expanded a previous, temporary ruling that the administration had violated the news outlets’ Fifth Amendment right to due process.
In a late-night ruling Tuesday, he also sided with a second argument by the outlets: that Trump’s ban breached their First Amendment right to free speech.
Kelly rejected Trump’s reasoning that the ban was driven by policy goals, such as protecting national security. He argued the ban was the result of Trump’s stated belief that the outlets’ reporting was inaccurate and biased.
“Simply put,” Kelly wrote, “That is unlawful viewpoint discrimination” — the government taking action against types of speech or coverage it does not like.
“Still,” he added in his late-night order, “no one should interpret the Court’s decision to suggest that President Trump’s concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media’s reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed.”
The White House called the decision “misguided” and said it plans to appeal.
“The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President’s Oval Office,” the statement said. “The lies they smear are a disservice to the American public and tear at the very fabric of our Democracy. They’re completely capable of reporting from directly outside.”
Trump’s standoff with the press is far from over. Kelly’s order did not address whether Trump can ban the three outlets from the rotating pool of broadcast networks that cover the president in tight spaces and share the reporting.
Stepped-up disputes between the president and the press
The fight reflects Trump’s increasing combativeness against news outlets and reporters whose content he does not like — including sharply curtailing Pentagon access for the press corps that covers the Defense Department. Trump or other parts of the executive branch have also, in policy and in the courts, grappled with The Wall Street Journal, The Associated Press and The New York Times — in addition to using the FCC to target broadcast networks.
The case of the three news outlets is increasingly messy and expensive. After the five-outlet rotating pool stood by CNN and canceled its coverage of Trump, the Justice Department over the weekend announced it was investigating whether those five companies violated antitrust laws in doing so.
Kelly’s ruling stood largely by the news outlets. He wrote that without a preliminary injunction blocking Trump’s ban, the outlets “are likely to suffer irreparable harm, and that the balance of the equities and the public interest tip in their favor.”
An email to the Justice Department, which is arguing the case for the administration, was not immediately returned.
Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the three media organizations, hailed the judge’s ruling.
“When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment,” Boutrous said in a statement. “The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound. The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future.”
Judge says no warning given before banishment
Kelly, who was nominated to the bench by Trump, previously ordered the White House to restore the reporters’ “hard pass” press credentials while he weighed their claims. With that temporary order expiring Tuesday, the judge issued a preliminary injunction that preserves the status quo indefinitely while the case is pending.
Kelly said that, “to put it mildly,” the White House didn’t give the plaintiffs any warning that they were in danger of losing their hard passes before Trump’s Sept. 18 social media post about their bans.
The judge also said the impact of the White House ban goes far beyond a single reporter’s ability to do their job.
“The ban threatens to cut off all Plaintiffs’ access to the White House press area—a space open to many of their competitors—thereby restricting their ability to observe happenings there firsthand, immediately report on those activities, and try to engage with government officials,” the judge wrote.
Hard passes give journalists who regularly cover the White House longer term access to its campus without having to get permission ahead of time.
The government asked Kelly to suspend his own decision pending an appeal, but the judge said it didn’t justify that request. Kelly said the bans impacted a total of 78 reporters at the three news organizations.
Earlier judicial action against White House had been only temporary
Trump provided no notice before announcing the bans in a Sept. 18 social media post, which criticized the outlets’ reporting as “fake news.” Kelly temporarily blocked the bans on Sept. 24 at the request of the news outlets, which jointly filed a lawsuit in Washington, D.C.
Attorneys for the outlets have described Trump’s move as “unprecedented and blatantly unconstitutional” under the First and Fifth amendments. They argued that it’s illegal for Trump to punish the journalists because he doesn’t like the content of their reporting.
“The ban also inflicts an injury on all news media organizations — which now risk a similar fate if they engage in fact-based, independent reporting the President deems insufficiently favorable,” plaintiffs’ lawyers wrote.
Government lawyers argued that access to the White House is a privilege — not a right — and said the president can impose the bans to protect national security and to stem the spread of misinformation.
“The White House is the official residence and workplace of the President,” Justice Department attorneys wrote. “Presidents have had a relationship with the press since the beginning. They have long decided which journalists should receive privileged access, which has varied substantially from administration to administration.”
___

title: Several St. John Valley Schools Plan Consolidation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ST. JOHN VALLEY, Maine (WAGM) - Two Saint John Valley school districts are exploring a major change. The Madawaska School District and MSAD33 are planning to consolidate in one regional school. NewsSource8’s Karri Triplett gives a look at what this would mean for families in the area.
In the Saint John Valley, school officials from Madawaska and MSAD33 are looking at bringing students from pre-K through 12th grade under one roof. We spoke with the superintendent about how the project is coming along. “We’d have to merge to one district. So, that’s going on right now. We have what’s called a reorganization committee and they’ve been meeting regularly and they’ve finally last night finalized a plan that’s going to be given to the commissioner for approval and then we hope to take that to the voters of Madawaska, and Frenchville, and St. Agatha in January and February. At the same time, we’ve already started working with an engineering firm for the new school. We are currently in the site selection phase. So, narrowing down properties around the area.”
Sirois says the consolidation is needed for several reasons. “We’re putting a lot of money into these old building and having a new building that’s going to have a longer time frame to not put money into it is going to be promising as well. So, we’re excited about that. The future of rural schools is going to have to be regionalization in order to offer programming that’s competitive with larger schools. As we get smaller, we can offer less and less to our students. You know, higher electives and different programs that you just can’t offer when you have such small numbers. By consolidating we can bring some of that back and have more robust curriculum and programs.”
Sirois says they won’t have this opportunity again. “One thing that I want the residents to understand is that the school construction rules are changing for the state of Maine. This project will be the last project that’s fully funded by the state of Maine. So, any thought of consolidation or building a school in the future is gonna come at a larger local tax cost. So, this is a golden opportunity for us to at least get a base model school for essentially free and then add any local monies we want to make it bigger and better when the time comes.”
The districts will hold public meetings on the consolidation throughout the next two months. They hope to have a site selected between June and November of next year and the construction completed in 2032. Anyone with questions about the consolidation plan can email Superintendent Sirois at bsirois@vuesc.org.

title: Medomak Valley High students told not to drink school's water
text:
Medomak Valley High students told not to drink school's water due to recent lead testing results
Students at Medomak Valley High School in Waldoboro have been told not to drink water from the school's system following an "abnormal" change in testing results.
Medomak Valley High facilities director Brian Race informed students, parents and staff members that the "do not drink" order was issued due to recent lead testing results.
"We're conducting additional testing to determine the cause for such an abnormal change compared to past test results," Race said. "I will keep you informed as I receive additional information."
The school will provide bottled water for all students and staff in the meantime.

title: Letter: Troy Jackson needed in Senate to challenge Donald Trump
text:
While I have the utmost respect for William Cohen as a politician, was an ardent supporter of him while he was in the U.S. House and Senate, and was his classmate at Bowdoin College, I disagree with his thesis in his recent column in the BDN, which is that replacing Sen. Susan Collins “would be bad for Maine.” Rather, I believe Maine voters would make a major mistake in reelecting Collins. I think the best thing Maine voters can do is to elect Troy Jackson, and deny Collins yet another six-year term.
I admit that the senator has voted against President Donald Trump’s legislative agenda slightly more than her Republican colleagues. However, 90% of the time in Trump’s first term, and 92% during his current administration, Collins has supported the president’s disastrous agenda. I ask: How can this be good for Mainers?
This is a critical election, and the Democrats have a very good chance to regain control of the Senate, and rein in the president’s destructive legislation. With several key senatorial races up for grabs, a Jackson victory at the polls is very critical for the Democratic Party to gain control of the Senate.
Unfortunately, Collins and the Republican Senate majority have generally lacked the conscience and fortitude to oppose and defeat Trump’s legislative proposals. The time for change is now. Elect Troy Jackson for U.S. Senate.
Rich Stuart
Thomaston

title: Rams' Alaric Jackson suspended 2 games for striking Bills LB Bradley Chubb after Monday night game
text:
Rams' Alaric Jackson suspended 2 games for striking Bills LB Bradley Chubb after Monday night game
Rams starting left tackle Alaric Jackson has been suspended for two games without pay for striking Buffalo linebacker Bradley Chubb in the face after their teams' overtime game Monday night.
The NFL announced the suspension Tuesday for Jackson, who is slated to miss Los Angeles' games against Arizona and Las Vegas, pending a potential appeal. In a press release, the league called Jackson's blow "an act of unsportsmanlike conduct."
Jackson struck Chubb after the two exchanged words following the Bills' 37-34 overtime victory over the Rams at SoFi Stadium.
Jackson was doing a jersey swap with another Bills player when Chubb had words with him and walked away. Jackson followed and confronted Chubb before throwing a strike that knocked Chubb's hat off his head.
Teammates quickly separated the two, but Jackson was already in trouble yet again.
Jackson was arrested on June 9 on suspicion of felony domestic violence after a confrontation with a woman at his home in the San Fernando Valley. His case was assigned for a prefiling diversion that likely allows him to avoid criminal charges, but the NFL has yet to announce a decision on possible league discipline for that incident.
He was sued in 2025 by a woman who alleged he recorded sexual acts with her on his phone without her consent. The incident, which wasn't publicly revealed until the lawsuit was filed, led to Jackson being suspended for the first two games of the 2024 season for an undisclosed violation of the NFL's personal conduct policy.
Jackson, a Canadian-American dual citizen, is one of the Rams' longest-tenured players. He won a Super Bowl ring as a backup lineman in February 2022.
The former undrafted free agent out of Iowa is in his fourth season as the Rams' starting left tackle and the protector of Matthew Stafford's blind side. The Rams re-signed Jackson to a three-year, $57 million deal in February 2025.
Jackson's absence is potentially serious for the Rams because they don't have a trusted backup at the most important position on their offensive line.
David Quessenberry is listed as their backup left tackle, but the 36-year-old veteran has played just 128 offensive snaps over the past two seasons, including only 10 last year. When Jackson missed one game last season, the Rams played relatively new signee DJ Humphries instead of Quessenberry.
Rookie lineman Keagen Trost, another potential backup, has been on injured reserve all season with a hamstring problem.

title: Parents charged after 8-year-old girl living in ‘squalid’ home dies from asthma attack
text:
SAN JOSE, Calif. (KGO) - The mother and stepfather of an 8-year-old California girl who suffered a fatal asthma attack are facing charges after her death was ruled a homicide.
Gabrielle Hanson, 32, and Jacob Randolph, 39, the mother and stepfather of 8-year-old Aurora Williams, made their first court appearance Tuesday. Prosecutors charged the couple with felony child neglect in connection with Aurora’s death following a severe asthma attack in May.
The Santa Clara District Attorney’s Office says Aurora was in serious distress for eight hours before her parents sought medical help. She was eventually taken to the hospital but died four days later.
“Why does this keep happening? This little asthmatic girl and her brothers and sisters were living in a home filled with roaches, mold, animal feces and two parents who were not providing enough care or food for their children,” District Attorney Jeff Rosen said.
Rosen says the family’s San Jose home was “squalid,” infested with cockroaches and mold and littered with garbage and pet feces. Thirteen people, seven of whom were children, and at least eight animals lived there.
Rosen says Aurora’s cause of death was lack of oxygen from severe asthma with lung injury and an infection. He says medical neglect was a significant factor in her death, which was ruled a homicide by the medical examiner.
“When she was finally brought to a hospital, staff found that she was below 1% of her expected body weight and had roaches on her emaciated body. Do you know what Aurora’s answer was when the hospital staff asked her about the vermin? The little girl said, ‘Oh yeah, bugs just crawl on me,’” Rosen said.
Authorities say the home was later deemed unlivable after conditions there contributed to Aurora’s death. The six other children in the household, ages 2 months to 17 years, were placed in foster care.
The Santa Clara County Department of Family and Children’s Services had frequent involvement with the family. In a statement, spokesperson Peter Gallota said the county was aware of the charges but could not comment further because the matter is ongoing litigation.
Rosen is now criticizing the county’s child welfare system and calling for reforms. He says his office will form a team to examine issues within the welfare system.
“Somewhere in our county right now, there are children who are in danger. Can we help them? I believe that we can. I believe that we must,” Rosen said.
Hanson and Randolph are scheduled to return to court Nov. 20.

title: 1 dead and 2 hospitalized after Bangor fire
text:
One person died and two people were hospitalized Wednesday morning after a Bangor house fire.
The fire broke out at the home divided into two apartments at the intersection of Cedar and Second streets at 6:36 a.m., Bangor Fire Chief Eric Pelletier said. It took two minutes for firefighters to arrive on scene, because it’s near the Bangor Fire Department’s Central Station on Main Street.
Three people were outside the house when firefighters arrived, and they said one person was still inside, Pelletier said. Two of the people outside were taken to the hospital with smoke inhalation that’s not considered life-threatening, Pelletier said.
Firefighters found one person deceased, he said. A dog also died in the fire.
It appears the fire started on the first floor and spread through all three floors, Pelletier said. Firefighters encountered cluttered conditions inside the house that made it difficult to maneuver, he said.
The cause of the fire is not yet known, he said.
Firefighters didn’t hear any smoke detectors when they entered the house, Pelletier said. He stressed the importance of working smoke detectors.
The Red Cross is expected to be called to the scene to assist people who were displaced, Pelletier said.
The state fire marshal’s office and Bangor police were on scene.

title: An AI chatbot tipped off police about an unsolved murder, but the tip wasn’t real
text:
