title: Terry Bradshaw gives health update, says he's nearing retirement from broadcasting
text:
Terry Bradshaw gives health update, announces he's nearing retirement from broadcasting
Four-time Super Bowl champion Terry Bradshaw has announced that he is now cancer-free after receiving two separate cancer diagnoses in 2022.
The 78-year-old two-time Super Bowl MVP gave his health update in a recent interview with "Good Morning America" co-host Michael Strahan to promote his new memoir and talked about both his double cancer diagnosis in 2022 and his struggles with mental health and depression.
Bradshaw was diagnosed with bladder cancer in November 2021 and had a tumor in his neck from a rare form of skin cancer in March 2022.
Related video above: Pope Leo XIV diagnosed with cancer
"You've been through a lot, two types of cancer, but you're good now?" Strahan asked.
"Yes, I am. I'm cancer-free, Mike," Bradshaw said.
The two co-hosts of "FOX NFL Sunday" also discussed Bradshaw's struggles with depression, with Bradshaw highlighting why it was particularly tough for him.
"Men are the worst about knowing they have a problem, not wanting to seek they have a problem because they don't want anybody to know they have a weakness," Bradshaw said when asked about his own struggles with depression. "And as a football player, it's even worse, the macho thing."
Bradshaw emphasized how difficult a journey it can be for someone to find the right help for them.
"It took me three different doctors, three progressions, to finally get to the point where they diagnosed me clinically depressed," Bradshaw said. "The key to it for me was No. 1: acknowledging I had a problem; No. 2: accepting that it was depression; and then No. 3: working my life to try to do everything I can to not bring it up because it's an ugly little monster."
Bradshaw finished with a message to all men going through similar struggles:
"I just want men to know: You got to seek help. It's an ugly monster," Bradshaw said.
This call to action is joined by comments the longtime sports correspondent made in a separate interview with "NBC News Daily" on the future of his broadcasting career.
"I realize my time on television as a sports broadcaster is coming to an end," Bradshaw said. "I just love life. Billy Graham said, and I never forgot this quote, he said, 'The day you retire is the day you start dying.'"
He added, "I'm a workaholic; I love to work," before he said he knew he was nearing the end of his broadcasting career.

title: 6 dead, including a child, in small plane crash near Wisconsin Dells
text:
DELLONA, Wis. (AP) — Six people, including one child, were killed Tuesday night in a plane crash near Wisconsin Dells, the Sauk County Sheriff’s Department said.
The six-seat, single-engine plane was traveling from Kenosha to Menomonie when it crashed in a wooded area near Mirror Lake State Park in the Town of Dellona shortly before 10 p.m., authorities said. Rain was falling as a thunderstorm moved through the area.
The National Transportation Safety Board said Wednesday that the plane was flying at 24,000 feet (7,315 meters) when the pilot reported icing and requested to descend. Air traffic control approved the descent, and the plane began a right descending turn that increased in rate until communications and data tracking were lost, the NTSB said.
The sheriff’s department said it received multiple reports of a downed aircraft around 9:30 p.m. Five adults and one child who were traveling in the plane were found dead, the sheriff’s department said.
Police said the fixed-wing Piper PA-46 airplane contacted a nearby air traffic control tower before the crash. Investigators were reviewing those transmissions and whether weather played a role in the crash, the sheriff’s department and the Federal Aviation Administration said.
Police said there wasn’t any damage to structures or anyone on the ground. The names of those killed were not immediately released.
The FAA and NTSB are investigating.

title: You can see the history of PEZ as it celebrates 100 years
text:
ORANGE, Conn. (InvestigateTV) - For 100 years, tiny candy bricks have been hiding inside some of the most famous faces in American history.
PEZ, the iconic candy, is made and packaged at the company’s factory in Connecticut, the only PEZ manufacturing facility in the United States.
“It’s part pop culture; it’s become an American icon, essentially. Everybody knows PEZ,” said Shawn Peterson, direct-to-consumer business manager at PEZ Candy, Inc.
At the PEZ Visitor Center in Orange, the company’s history fills every shelf and even the floor.
Peterson, who also serves as the company historian, has contributed much of what’s inside from his personal collection of about 5,000 dispensers.
“I lost track of that a long time ago,” Peterson said.
The history of PEZ is well documented. The witch or Halloween dispenser came out in the mid-1950s. The first licensed character was Popeye, followed by Mickey Mouse in 1961.
The brand started in Austria as a peppermint candy marketed to adults as an alternative to smoking. PEZ arrived in the United States in the 1950s and eventually made Connecticut its American home.
Twelve million pieces of PEZ roll off the line each day at the Orange facility. Everything made there is shipped from the location.
The recipe is simple — sugar, flavoring and pressure. The little brick shape has not changed in more than 90 years.
Workers make the candy in 600-pound batches. Every roll is sorted, lined and packaged to ship. The factory’s see-through windows give about 80,000 global fans a year a chance to see how their favorite candy is made.
“We get people from all over, not just here in the U.S. or the East Coast, but globally. I’ve got people from probably 80 different countries,” Peterson told us.
As America celebrates its 250th anniversary, PEZ is celebrating its centennial. For the one-hundred-year-old brand, half of its history has been in the United States.
PEZ is rolling out an entire year of plans to celebrate, just as they did during America’s bicentennial in 1976 with Uncle Sam, Betsy Ross and a little colonial soldier dispensers.
“They all say made in the USA,” Peterson said.

title: Maine Named One of the Worst States for a Fall Move in New Study
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Named One of the Worst States for a Fall Move in New Study
While we may be known as Vacationland, a recent report suggests Maine is among the more challenging states for a fall move.
👇 KEEP READING: 30 Restaurants to Try Outside of Portland, Maine 👇
My Baggage compared all 50 states using five equally weighted measures: median asking rent, average fall temperature, rainfall, flight cancellations and storm-related property damage.
Using rental market data and federal weather and transportation records, the company ranked states on each measure and averaged those rankings, favoring lower costs, less rain, fewer cancellations, less storm damage, and warmer temperatures.
Maine ranked as the seventh-worst state for a fall move, despite having one of the lower median asking rents among the bottom 10 states at $1,694.
Among those 10 states, Maine had the second-lowest average fall temperature at 46.8 degrees, behind Alaska, and averaged 11.66 inches of rainfall during the season.
For anyone planning a fall move to Maine, cooler temperatures and rain can mean taking extra steps to keep furniture, boxes, and other belongings dry during loading and unloading.
Shorter daylight hours also leave less time to complete an outdoor move before dark.
The ranking focuses on costs, weather, and travel conditions associated with a fall move, rather than Maine’s overall appeal as a place to live.
Factors such as job opportunities, schools, and proximity to family were not among the five measures used.
And there you have it! According to this report, settling into Vacationland during the fall may require a little extra planning.
What are your thoughts on these findings? We’d love to hear from you! Feel free to join the conversation by messaging us on the app.

title: Inflation worsened last month in sign that prices remain high as midterms near
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Prices remain elevated ahead of midterms after inflation reportedly worsened last month
U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes, and air fares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before the midterm elections that have focused heavily on issues related to affordability.
Related video: President Trump heading to Arizona and Montana today to speak with voters ahead of the midterms
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month.
The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but this year has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn't all linked to gas prices, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that also use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed's 2% target.
Ongoing inflation has taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living issue. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn't moving quickly enough back to the central bank's target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9%.
Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year.
By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war's disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can't address those bottlenecks.
Warsh has said his goal is to keep the gas price spike from seeping into more areas of the economy. It's already pushed up the price of air fares about 22% from a year ago.
Gas prices jumped more than 9% from August to September, Wednesday's report said. Rising gas costs are a highly visible sign of inflation and often drive down measures of consumer sentiment about the economy.
Prices at the pump have ticked lower in the past two weeks to a nationwide average of $4.33 a gallon, according to AAA, though they remain higher than a month ago.
Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients.
The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones.
Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed's preferred inflation gauge.
On Sept. 1, Nintendo increased the price for its Switch 2 gaming system by 11% to $499.99. And Apple's newest iPhone, the iPhone 17, cost about 10% more than its previous upgrade, though some of that likely reflects greater capabilities.

title: Trump says ‘massive’ oil, gas and mineral exploration in ‘beautiful’ Greenland is set to begin
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - U.S. President Donald Trump said that “massive” oil, gas and mineral exploration is set to begin in “our new and beautiful Greenland,” though it wasn’t clear what developments he was referring to on an island where resource extraction has stymied companies for decades.
Despite Trump’s optimism, the harsh climate of Greenland — a self-governing territory of Denmark, rather than a part of the United States — as well as a lack of infrastructure have foiled all previous attempts to extract so-called rare earth minerals, as well as oil and gas. No efforts have ever progressed beyond the exploratory stage, and a moratorium on new gas and oil permits has been in place for several years.
“Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform following a campaign event Tuesday in Wasilla, Alaska.
Trump was stumping for Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is seeking a third term to represent the state in an election against Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola.
Rising energy prices — a direct result of the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28 after the U.S. and Israel launched joint strikes — are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for working class Americans before the midterm elections next month. Trump’s comments are likely aimed at addressing voters’ concerns before Election Day on Nov. 3.
Recent deal paved way for more US bases but no exploration rights
Last month, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, following months of tensions with NATO allies over the U.S. president’s repeated demands to take control of the semiautonomous Danish territory. It doesn’t grant the U.S. any special exploration rights, but does place some limits on investments by non-NATO countries in strategic sectors.
The deal also paved the way for more U.S. bases in Greenland and eased tensions over Trump’s repeated calls for Greenland to become part of the United States. The agreement would still apply if Greenland eventually chooses independence.
Trump has expressed his desire to acquire Greenland since 2019 and, during his second term, issued threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a NATO ally.
Naaja H. Nathanielsen, who represents Greenland in Denmark’s parliament, told The Associated Press on Wednesday that she wasn’t very surprised — or concerned — following Trump’s post.
“This is just the way the president decides to engage,” she said. “I think we have all come to expect something like that.”
Nathanielsen said that any current projects regarding resource extraction were still years away from potential success. She said that she believes Americans worried about the price of gas were the post’s intended audience, rather than Greenlanders, before the upcoming election.
“I recognize the worry in the U.S., but I think it’s not a quick fix,” she told the AP. “There’s no Greenlandic barrels of oil on ground in any near future.”
Nathanielsen also said that she wasn’t upset by Trump calling the island “our Greenland.”
“I think, of course, it’s somewhat disrespectful,” she said. “But you can also see it as a term of endearment if you wanted to be very generous. Right now, I don’t think much of it.”
Representatives from Denmark’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as from Greenland’s prime minister and the island’s mining ministry, did not immediately return requests for comment Wednesday.
Greenland has valuable resources
Greenland has large deposits of the rare earth minerals that are needed to make everything from computers and smartphones to the batteries, solar and wind technologies that will power the transition away from fossil fuels. China currently dominates the world’s supply of these critical minerals and the Trump administration is seeking to break Beijing’s chokehold on them.
The U.S. Geological Survey has also identified major potential offshore deposits of oil and natural gas.
But tapping these resources could be prohibitively difficult: The rare earth minerals are encased in rock, and the offshore oil and natural gas deposits are covered by Arctic ice. And in 2021, Greenlandic lawmakers said the island would not issue any new oil and gas permits because of the environmental impacts of oil extraction, and a desire to avoid further worsening of the global climate crisis.
Trump boasts about Greenland’s strategic spot in the Arctic
Trump’s Truth Social post also touted Greenland’s strategic location, saying that “from a Security Purpose in the Defense and Offense of both the United States of America, and Europe,” the island is “second to none.”
“Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived,” he wrote. “It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!”
The United States was prominent in Greenland for decades but, since 1945, the U.S. military presence in Greenland has decreased from thousands of soldiers on 17 bases and installations to roughly 200 soldiers on the remote Pituffik Space Base in the northwest. The base supports missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance operations for the U.S. and NATO.
Trump said last month that the U.S. would “immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” including “building two very major military bases.”

title: Mother accused of driving off cliff with her 2 children in car, authorities say
text:
CHATTANOOGA, Tenn. (WVLT/Gray News) - A woman in Tennessee is facing several charges after she allegedly drove off a cliff with children inside the car.
According to an affidavit obtained by WVLT News, authorities responded to a crash around 8:30 p.m. on Sept. 7.
Officers found 30-year-old Chase Klinedinst had been driving on Stuart Street and, upon reaching the dead end of the road, continued onto a dirt path leading to Coffey’s Cliff, which is about 20 to 25 feet above a train yard.
Police said she drove around a bend and made a left turn before “driving over the edge of the cliff and falling.”
The car came to rest upside down adjacent to railroad tracks, prompting railroad operations to be suspended on one of the rail lines.
Investigators learned Klinedinst also had her two children in the car.
While both children were in child restraint seats, one of them was taken to the emergency room for treatment and was found to have a fractured forearm and pulmonary contusions.
While first responders were removing Klinedinst from the car and helping her to the top of the cliff, she was allegedly “very combative with the medics” and had “very slurred” speech.
Officers also said they could smell a “very strong odor of an intoxicating beverage” from about 5 feet away, and investigators found an empty bottle of wine and another unopened bottle that “was still cold and covered in condensation.”
Klinedinst was charged with two counts of child neglect, driving under the influence and vehicular assault. Her next scheduled court appearance is set for Nov. 17.

title: Lawrence rolls to first place in Class B North football
text:
FAIRFIELD, Maine (WABI) - Lawrence has brought its brand of football to a 6-0 start this season.
“Man, we’re just smash mouth football. We’re just trying to run it down the opponent’s throat and on defense we push them back,” said Keegan Littlefield, senior running back, defensive back.
“The coaching staff, the bond, the locker room, we just get along so well, and we call it really a brotherhood around here,” said Brady Richards, senior offensive, defensive lineman.
The players entered the season with high expectations.
“We were expecting good things, but we knew it wasn’t going to be easy, and we knew it was going to be a fight,” said Jaiden Hebert, junior running back, linebacker.
“As much as we like to say humble, we’ve really kind of known since we were younger. The personnel we have this year is huge. We’ve had guys who have been playing varsity for four years now. Our junior class is very strong. They combine well with our seniors,” said Jackson Dangler, junior quarterback, defensive back.
The Bulldogs aren’t satisfied with what they’ve accomplished. They’ve got a bigger goal.
“We want to go as far as we can, hopefully reach that state game. We haven’t really earned anything yet,” said Richards.
“I told them that Monday after the Cony game. That was a big win for us. I told them, ‘I don’t know about you guys, but I didn’t walk off the field with a trophy.’ So, if we want the trophy, we’ve got to continue getting better every day,” said Pete Curtis, first-year head coach.
Lawrence’s last state football championship came in 2006. They’ve won four regional titles since.
The Bulldogs go to Camden Hills on Saturday at 1 p.m. before hosting Messalonskee on Fri. Oct. 23 at 7 p.m. to finish the regular season.

title: Edgecomb Fire and Rescue report
text:
Edgecomb Fire and Rescue responded to 10 calls in August, compared with 22 calls in July. August calls included one fire, one fire alarm, two medical emergencies (MEs), and six motor vehicle accidents (MVAs). For the year-to-date, we have responded to 177 calls, slightly fewer than 198 calls at the same time last year.
Trainings during September included Mutual Aid Training and Extraction Training. Other training included our monthly “Truck Check” of all apparatus and equipment. The department was the grateful recipient of some new equipment graciously donated by the Gavin Martin Foundation on Sept. 26. The Gavin Martin Foundation is dedicated to honoring the legacy of Gavin Martin, a 21-year-old Edgecomb firefighter who died in a car crash in December 2025. Ongoing training and proper equipment are critical in maintaining our readiness to respond to any call.
September call report
Following is a list of our September calls in chronological date order:
Sept. 1, 9:23 a.m.: ME for an 80-year-old male, fallen and requesting a lift assist; 3:56 p.m.: MVA at U.S. Route 1 and Station/Dodge Roads for a four-car accident with possible personal injuries.
Sept. 3, 8:06 a.m.: MVA at McKay Road and River Road, for a single vehicle with unknown personal injuries; noon: MVA at Route 27 near Mason Road, for a car versus pole with unknown personal injuries; 8:30 p.m.: ME for a 30-year-old male with chest pains, not breathing normally.
Sept. 15, 5:39 p.m.: MVA at U.S. Route 1 at the Abenaki Trading Post for a 2-car accident with a large fuel spill.
Sept. 16, 5:09 a.m.: MVA at Route 27 and Eddy Road for a 2-car accident with possible personal injuries.
Sept. 17, 11:40 a.m.: Fire alarm at 747 River Road from a commercial alarm company.
Sept. 23, 3:26 p.m.: Boat fire on the Sheepscot River, near 121 Shore Road, for a 33-foot cabin cruiser boat with an engine on fire. Firefighter Bill Witzell responded in his personal boat and rescued the four boat passengers in life jackets, secured the boat, and waited until the Wiscasset Fire rescue boat, the Marine Patrol, and the Coast Guard all responded and extinguished the fire.
Sept. 25, 1:24 p.m.: MVA Route 1, property damage only.
Annual Fish Fry, Nov. 7
Please save the date, Nov. 7, for the EFD Auxiliary’s annual fish fry. This community event features fried fish or fried chicken tenders with all the trimmings and is a meaningful way to honor veterans on Veterans Day. The fish fry is our biggest fundraiser of the year, and all proceeds are used to supplement our budget, which helps reduce the town’s taxes.
Weekly meetings
The department meets every Wednesday at 6:30 p.m. at the fire station. Anyone interested in learning more about the department is welcome to attend. We are always looking for more volunteers. No experience necessary!

title: Yarmouth dominating, and other Maine high school football storylines for Week 7
text:
As we head into Week 7 and creep toward the end of the Maine high school football regular season, some teams have emerged as state title contenders, while others still have work to do.
Thornton Academy (6-0) and Bonny Eagle (6-0) have all but secured Class A South postseason berths, but can a team like Noble, which is currently on the outside of the playoff picture, find a way to win out and make a postseason run? To do so, the first step for the Knights is getting past South Portland on Friday.
Lawrence and Cony appear to be the favorites in Class B North, but can Skowhegan and Messalonskee make some headway in the division in their final two weeks of the regular season?
Here are three storylines to follow heading into Week 7:
DOMINATION STATION IN YARMOUTH
Yarmouth has been nothing short of dominant this season.
The Clippers (6-0) have outscored their opponents 354-54, tallying 60 points exactly in their last three games and averaging 59 points per game.
They’re first in the Large School South eight-man Crabtree standings and have trounced the other top contenders in the division — Spruce Mountain (4-2), whom they defeated 48-0 on Sept. 12, and Cape Elizabeth (4-2), whom they defeated 82-40 on Sept. 19.
“We’re super excited about this group,” said coach Nick Orsi. “We knew coming into the season it was going to be pretty special. We had a lot of players returning on the offensive side of the ball, including our quarterback, all our wide receivers. We added our running back, Stephen Connolly (54 carries, 940 yards, 14 touchdowns), to the mix this year. He’s a junior from NYA. He’s part of our co-op.”
The Clippers’ passing game is especially prolific, led by senior quarterback Iggy McGrath, who has thrown for 1,227 yards and 21 TDs and has yet to have a pass intercepted.
Even with such a high-performing offense, Orsi believes Yarmouth’s defense is the biggest difference-maker this year. Taking away the game against Cape Elizabeth, the Clippers have only allowed 14 points. Three of their games have been shutouts.
“We’re actually holding opponents to about 150 yards a game in total offense,” Orsi said. “That’s pretty remarkable in eight-man football — there’s so much space on the field, it typically tends to be higher-scoring games. We had a really rough first half against Cape Elizabeth and we gave up an opening-drive touchdown against Lake Region, but outside of that, the starting defense has been virtually flawless.”
On both sides of the ball, Yarmouth has proven itself a contender to win the eight-man Large School state championship for the first time since 2022.
Before then, the Clippers will close out their regular season with games against Orono (3-3) on Friday and Gray-New Gloucester (4-1) on Oct. 23.
HAS WELLS TURNED THE CORNER?
After Leavitt defeated Wells 42-0 on Sept. 26, coach Tim Roche knew his team was at a crossroads, sitting at 2-2 in a competitive Class C division.
“I just said to them, ‘We either step up to this challenge in the next five games, or we just say, ‘Oh … we’re not very good,’” Roche said. “I think we’re good.”
The Warriors (4-2) have won their last two games, defeating Gardiner 47-31 on Oct. 2 and Freeport 28-24 on Oct. 8. With three games remaining, Wells may be on its way to rejoining the field of Class C contenders alongside Leavitt, Greely, Foxcroft Academy and Hermon. Eight teams make the Class C postseason, and the top four host quarterfinals. Wells is currently ranked fifth but could move up if it wins its next three. The Warriors finish the regular season with games against York (2-4) on Saturday, Nokomis (2-4) on Oct. 24 and Hampden Academy (0-6) on Oct. 30.
HIGH-OCTANE HORNETS
Leavitt coach Michael Hathaway said it best after his team’s season-opening 39-8 win over Medomak Valley on Sept. 4: The Hornets don’t want to be reliant on only one component of their offense.
“Really, we just want to spread the ball around,” Hathaway said. “Whether it’s run or pass or whatever, we don’t want to be relying on any one thing. So I think you saw it tonight … a lot of different guys touching the ball.”
With three games to go in the Class C regular season, it’s safe to say Hathaway’s vision for the season has been realized. Leavitt (6-0), No. 1 in the Crabtree standings, is averaging 42 points per game and has had different players step up to play leading roles.
Darren Flagg, for example, scored five touchdowns across the team’s first two games against Medomak Valley and Greely. Then, Landen Reny and Jeremiah McKenzie combined for five touchdowns in a Week 4 win against Wells.
Against Gardiner last week, Flagg was back at the forefront, reaching the end zone five times while exemplifying Leavitt’s quest for versatility: he scored twice on runs, twice on receptions and once on an interception return.
Leavitt plays Nokomis at 7 p.m. Thursday.

title: South Portland police investigating embezzlement allegations related to Strikers youth soccer club
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - South Portland Police Chief Dan Ahern confirmed that the police department is investigating allegations of embezzlement related to the South Portland Strikers, a popular youth soccer club.
Hundreds of local children are involved with the Strikers, who play home games at the Wainwright Recreation Complex.
The president of the club, Gabe Harp, sent an email to parents Monday night, saying: “The South Portland Strikers Board of Directors is aware of an ongoing matter that involves the potential unauthorized use of club funds in 2025 and 2026 by a former member of our board.”
Ahern would not provide any additional information about the case, including who is being investigated or the amount of money that was embezzled.
“We take our fiduciary responsibilities seriously, have engaged an external financial professional, and are implementing improved financial controls and governance practices,” Harp said in his email to parents.
Harp’s email to parents went on to say that because this is an active legal matter, the organization will not share specifics, and the priority is to cooperate with law enforcement.
The Cumberland County District Attorney’s Office said it could be two to three weeks before the case ends up in the DA’s office and charges are filed.

title: Charlie McAvoy scores in return to help the Bruins beat the Sharks
text:
SAN JOSE, Calif. — Charlie McAvoy scored in his season debut after serving a six-game suspension and the Boston Bruins beat the San Jose Sharks 6-3 on Tuesday night.
McAvoy missed the first six games of the season as punishment for slashing Buffalo’s Zach Benson late in Game 6 of the first round of the playoffs last season when the Bruins got eliminated.
He didn’t take long to make an impact as he got in front of the crease and knocked in a pass from JJ Peterka late in the first period to give Boston a 2-1 lead.
Fraser Minten scored two goals and Matthew Poitras and Pavel Zacha also scored for the Bruins, who have won three straight games. Will Borgen added an empty-net goal.
Jeremy Swayman made 35 saves.
Ivar Stenberg scored his first career goal for San Jose. Macklin Celebrini and Jacob Trouba also scored for the Sharks. Yaroslav Askarov made 20 saves.
Stenberg, the No. 2 overall pick in the draft in June, tied the game at 2 early in the second period when he tapped in a perfect back-door pass from Celebrini on the power play.
Poitras put Boston back in front midway through the second when he got the puck alone in front of the net and beat Askarov. The Bruins extended the lead when Zacha scored with 3 seconds remaining in the period when he finished a two-on-one with Morgan Geekie.
Celebrini scored on the power play early in the third to make it a one-goal game but Minten’s second goal of the game midway through the period restored the two-goal lead.
Up next
Bruins: Visit Anaheim on Friday night.
Sharks: Visit Nashville on Thursday night.

title: Multi-agency Operation On Waldo Street Ends With Suspect Still At Large
text:
Maine Authorities Seeking Lewiston Man Who Is Possibly Armed & Dangerous Following Shelter-In-Place Order
What began as an investigation into suspected drug trafficking and reports of gunfire at an apartment in Rumford Wednesday afternoon resulted in a statewide search for an individual from Lewiston who authorities say could be armed and dangerous.
How did it all begin?
The Rumford Police Department says they started their investigation after receiving tips this past weekend of suspected drug trafficking and weapons being discharged in the area of 209 Waldo Street in Rumford.
Read More: Bangor, Maine House Fire Kills 1 Person, Hospitalizes 2
They were told that both individuals who lived in town and some who did not reside in the area were believed to be involved in this activity. After receiving a search warrant and upon getting another report of gunfire in the area, officers arrived in that neighborhood early Wednesday morning, before dawn.
What happened next?
Things became intense when it was thought that the suspects allegedly involved in the illicit activities might still be armed and inside the first-floor apartment. As a precaution, the Rumford PD, the Oxford County Sheriff's Office, and the Maine State Police Tactical Team worked together to establish a safe perimeter around the building.
About noon, the Rumford Police issued a 'Shelter In Place' order for folks living in the area, asking them to remain inside while they "dealt with an incident."
Read More: Stolen Vehicle Chase Ends In Fatal Medway Collision
Once the court gave the go-ahead, late Wednesday morning, authorities closed off the roads to the area and staged first responders nearby, in case the exchange with the suspects became violent.
What was the result?
At 1:20 PM, the Rumford Police Department said authorities lifted the order after determining the suspects were no longer in the building and had fled the area earlier. In its place, law enforcement is asking people to keep a lookout for one individual in particular.
"The subsequent search of the apartment, along with information developed during the ongoing investigation, has yielded additional evidence supporting the reports received from members of the public...Rumford Police are actively seeking BLAKE LACHANCE, age 21, of Lewiston, who is wanted in connection with the following felony charges: [Aggravated Assault with a Dangerous Weapon, Criminal Threatening with a Dangerous Weapon, and Reckless Conduct with a Dangerous Weapon]...LACHANCE should be considered potentially armed and dangerous."
The Rumford PD says anyone who sees Lachance should avoid contact and call the police immediately.

title: Bangor advances homelessness strategy as winter approaches
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Bangor’s fight against homelessness continues, with winter fast approaching.
The Homeless Advisory Committee met Tuesday to work on its strategic plan, with updates on warming centers and Project Hope.
Shelter expansion plans
The city plans to expand by five beds at the Bangor Area Homeless Shelter, 25 at Mansion Church, and 65 at the Brick Church.
Last year, shelters averaged 85 people a night, jumping to 125 on the coldest nights.
A City Council workshop tomorrow will discuss using Together Place for overflow.
Project Hope funding setback
The committee had backed Project Hope, pairing $300,000 from MaineHousing with a $126,000 city match, but the council voted it down after public opposition.
This week, city officials will meet with MaineHousing, Preble Street and Community Care to explore other funding options.

title: Here’s how much more Social Security recipients will get from a cost-of-living boost
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Social Security Administration projected Wednesday that the annual cost-of-living adjustment for older adults and people with disabilities will go up by 3.6% beginning in 2027, with some recipients complaining that is not enough to offset soaring prices.
The adjustment translates to $75 extra per month for the nearly 72 million people who receive monthly Social Security benefits and about 7.3 million beneficiaries who get Supplemental Security Income.
The announcement comes as inflation adds pressure on household budgets and businesses and as midterm elections are weeks away.
The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for retirees and disabled beneficiaries is financed by payroll taxes collected from workers and their employers, up to a certain annual salary. That is set to increase to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 in 2026.
The agency’s commissioner, Frank Bisignano, said in a statement that the adjustment will give recipients “greater financial stability.”
Older adults feel the bite of rising costs
Some older adults feel the increase is a drop in the bucket as inflation has eaten away at monthly savings. The government reported Wednesday that inflation accelerated in September, with the consumer price index rising 3.7% in September compared with a year ago and gas prices have spiked in the wake of renewed fighting between the United States and Iran.
Nancy Altman, president of the Social Security Works advocacy group, said the latest inflation data shows that “as important as the Social Security COLA is, it is not keeping up with prices.”
Lorrie Ufkin, a 71-year-old retiree who lives outside Rochester, Minnesota, said the COLA will not put a dent in her healthcare costs, which are set to increase after the Trump administration concludes at year’s end a temporary Medicare Part D subsidy program that has helped offset premiums. Ufkin said that her premiums and drug cost are expected to rise, although the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services has projected a modest increase for most people.
The COLA “doesn’t even meet what they’re going to do for changes to Medicare,” she told The Associated Press.
She said one of the medications both she and her husband take will go from $11 per month for each prescription, to $200 per month, after Republican administration changes made to older Americans’ healthcare programs. She said that was “catastrophic.”
Senior advocacy groups say the COLA is a strong reminder of the financial straits of many older people.
“There’s a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans — one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last. That makes Social Security’s cost-of-living adjustment critically important,” said AARP CEO Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan.
Jaime Jakubczak, a 68-year-old resident of Buffalo, New York who retired early at 55, has recently gone back to work to make ends meet, specifically to afford rising property taxes. He said the COLA is insufficient because it is offset by high inflation and a proposed 3.9% property tax increase in his town.
Jakubczak called the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment “a pittance,” given how high food, healthcare and gasoline prices have become across the country.
“We were getting ahead a little bit with the COLA based on inflation, but the inflation is so high that it doesn’t offset what our COLA allowance is,” he said.
Most older adults believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5% COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.
Social Security faces a looming funding shortfall
The Social Security Administration faces a looming bankruptcy date if a funding shortfall is not addressed by Congress.
The June 2026 Social Security and Medicare trustees’ report states that Social Security’s combined trust funds — which cover old age and disability recipients — will be unable to pay full benefits beginning in 2034. After that, incoming revenue would cover about 83% of scheduled benefits.
While a permanent solution for shoring up the benefits program has not been passed into law, lawmakers on the Hill have called for new measures to replenish the trust funds.
Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, in June proposed lifting the Social Security payroll tax cap, which is a maximum amount of earnings taxable. Treating all income the same “would generate substantial revenue that would extend the solvency of Social Security for another generation,” they wrote in The New York Times.
The move is controversial because Republicans have traditionally criticized calls to raise taxes on the wealthy.
The Peterson Foundation estimates that lifting the payroll tax cap would add roughly $3 trillion into the program over the next 10 years.
Both the Trump and Biden administrations signed into law new benefits for retirees, which boosted their finances, but simultaneously accelerated the insolvency of the old-age benefits program.
The Trump administration, as part of Republicans’ tax and spending bill, gave a temporary tax deduction for people 65 and over, which applies to all income — not just Social Security. But those who aren’t able to claim the deduction include the lowest-income older adults who already don’t pay taxes on Social Security, those who choose to claim their benefits before they reach 65 and those above a defined income threshold.
Additionally, Democratic President Joe Biden in 2024 repealed two federal policies — the Windfall Elimination Provision and the Government Pension Offset — that previously limited Social Security payouts for roughly 2.8 million people, including largely former public workers.

title: What to know about Pope Leo’s lung cancer diagnosis
text:
ROME (AP) - Pope Leo XIV spent a peaceful night in Rome’s Gemelli hospital after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung and confirmed he has cancer, the Vatican said Wednesday.
The surgery confirmed that the pope has the most common type of lung cancer, known as lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin late Tuesday.
The Vatican said doctors were waiting for the results of further tests before deciding on a course of treatment. The press office pointed to the medical statement’s mention of the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors took out all suspect tissue in hopes of removing any lingering traces of the cancer.
Experts said some of Leo’s lymph nodes also would have been removed and tested to determine if the cancer had spread. There was no word yet on those test results.
If the cancer has spread, more tests will be needed to determine what kind of therapy to pursue, said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy or targeted therapy, which involves oral pills for specific cancers.
“Adenocarcinoma is the most common (type of lung cancer), also with the most favorable prognosis,” said Liu, who is not involved in the pope’s care. “While we know the diagnosis, we now need to know the stage.”
He added: “We now need to know how big it is, how many spots in the lung are involved. Is it just one nodule, or more than one, and the lymph nodes, are they cancerous?”
For now, the implications for the pope’s long-term health remain unclear. The Vatican said more information would be provided later in the day.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the nodule, or growth, on his lung during his Sunday noon prayer.
The Vatican says the surgery was successful
The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about three hours, the Vatican statement said Tuesday. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes.
“The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said, adding that the pope later returned to his room.
The right lung has three sections or lobes while the left has two. After one lobe is removed, the rest of the lung can gradually compensate, especially in otherwise healthy and physically active people. Leo is known to be sporty, with weekly tennis games and swimming.
Before the surgery, Leo walked into the Gemelli hospital through the main entrance and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery was performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
Oncologists said prior to the operation that even if the nodule turned out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis would be “excellent” since it would have been removed at an early stage.
While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo is staying in a nearby room since the apartment is undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
The pope has a trip to South America planned for November
The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20. But there was no word on whether he would be able to keep his planned trip to South America next month.
Oncology surgeons often advise patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery — which would give the pope just enough time to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. But whether he can go will depend on his recovery.
The current itinerary for the trip is ambitious and the longest of his papacy to date, calling for Leo to clock just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles) on a dozen flights and two helicopter rides, and a significant altitude change in Peru.
“If it is stage 1, he can complete these trips. If more treatment is needed, I would likely advise against the trips,” said Liu.
___
Barry reported from Milan. Associated Press writer Lauran Neergaard in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Portland Water District expands assistance for low-income customers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland Water District expands assistance for low-income customers
In a new partnership with Maine DHHS, the Portland Water District will allow eligible customers to receive water bill credits without applying
Portland Water District expands assistance for low-income customers
In a new partnership with Maine DHHS, the Portland Water District will allow eligible customers to receive water bill credits without applying
The Portland Water District announced Wednesday that it is expanding its financial assistance program to help more low-income customers pay their water bills.
The district's Board of Trustees approved an expansion of its Lifeline Water Rates program, which provides assistance to eligible customers.
Through a partnership with the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, eligible customers will automatically be included in the program without having to apply or take any other steps.
The district says customers will be notified when the credit is applied to their accounts.
Officials say that the goal of the expansion is to make financial assistance more accessible to households struggling with utility costs.
The program builds on the district's low-income assistance programs.
More information is available on the Portland Water District website.

title: South Portland chooses private developer partner for Mahoney
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
South Portland will team up with a private developer to transform the old Mahoney Middle School.
The City Council voted unanimously to move forward with a partnership with Developers Collaborative, a Portland-based firm, per the Mahoney City Center Committee’s unanimous recommendation. The developer will work for the city for free for six months while figuring out the feasibility of the project, creating a plan, collecting more community input and crafting a legal agreement.
The city decided to pursue a partnership with a private developer to shrink the price tag, which many residents and council members viewed as too steep. A private developer would be able to benefit from federal and state historic tax credit programs, which could cover about a third of the total project cost.
When the original conceptual design for the civic hub came in with a price tag of $193.8 million in December — $120 million more than preliminary estimates — councilors said they couldn’t imagine residents voting for something that expensive. The plans were scaled back, with a renovation option estimated to cost $70 million to $76 million and leave 25% to 35% of the building unoccupied.
But councilors were discouraged, believing that the proposal had lost sight of the original goal of creating a community hub. They postponed the referendum vote, and the Mahoney committee went back to the drawing board.
Since July, the committee has evaluated proposals from three developers, prioritizing the teams’ experience with adaptive reuse and historical preservation and collaborating with municipalities. Developers Collaborative’s proposal scored the highest.
The firm has completed more than 20 redevelopment projects in the state that involved historic tax credits, including schools, churches, municipal buildings, mills and other properties, including the Rumery Lofts in Portland, an auto dealership converted into a mixed-use residential building, and Johnson Hall, a theater in Gardiner.
Developers Collaborative has redeveloped more than 12 former schools, so they have familiarity with floor plans, corridor widths and other structural elements of those buildings.
The firm also has experience designing community-centered spaces. They converted the former Motherhouse convent and created the Stevens Square Campus in Portland, transforming the space into nearly 200 homes, a community pool, gymnasium and a new home for Portland’s Good Theater. The project, which cost slightly more than $100 million, involved multiple historic tax credits and phases.
Kevin Bunker, a founder of the firm, said he’s been excited about the potential of the Mahoney building for decades, saying he used to drive by it with his mentor, Richard Berman, who would point it out and say, “Someday that’s going to be a project of yours.”
He said he is excited to find ways to incorporate uses for residents of all ages.
“No one’s going to be excited about ‘here’s a great, shiny new place to come and pay your taxes,’” Bunker said. “But people will get excited if they can check out a book there or use the open space and maybe see a show at a community theater or get a bite to eat.”

title: After final debate, here’s where things stand in the race to become Maine’s next governor
text:
The fourth and final gubernatorial debate saw no huge fireworks Wednesday evening while covering largely familiar ground.
That means the race to succeed Gov. Janet Mills remains Democrat Hannah Pingree’s race to lose.
Pingree, a 49-year-old former Maine House speaker from North Haven who led Mills’ policy office, has consistently led polling of the contest by double digits and made no huge stumbles in the debates, though she was light on specifics at times.
Republican Bobby Charles, a 66-year-old Leeds lawyer who has led a lobbying and consulting firm and previously worked in drug and domestic policy roles under former Republican Presidents Ronald Reagan, George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush, expectedly and repeatedly sought to go after Pingree and link her with Mills in order to blame the two for rising energy and housing costs in Maine.
Independent Rick Bennett, a 63-year-old former state senator from Oxford who previously chaired the Maine Republican Party before leaving the GOP last year, reiterated that he is an experienced option for those tired of the two-party system, but his path to victory still looks very narrow.
If Charles surges past Pingree on Election Day, or if Bennett surpasses Charles on Election Day and competes with Pingree for the top spot, then it will be a massive surprise and a sign that the polls completely missed the mark. Here are a few quick notes on the race after the last debate.
No national Republican money for Charles?
It did not arise during Wednesday evening’s debate hosted by WMTW, but it matters for whether any sudden developments will grip the race in the home stretch.
Charles told reporters in July that he had met earlier that month with the Republican Governors Association and several Republican governors who planned to support him financially to the tune of “likely millions, and they are very committed to the idea that Maine is a pickup for them.”
If that money suddenly appears for Charles, then it will arrive with fewer than three weeks until Election Day. The Republican Governors Association did not respond to requests for comment after Charles made those comments earlier in the year, and the national support has not materialized for his campaign. Charles reported raising more than $1.8 million in his last campaign finance report, while Pingree had raised more than $4.2 million and Bennett raised about $923,000.
A political action committee with well-heeled Republican donors that was set up over the summer to support Charles has instead spent $70,000 to boost Bennett.
A rare moment of Pingree-Bennett bickering
Pingree may have heard about that infusion of pro-Bennett cash from the No Nonsense PAC, as she briefly went after Bennett during Wednesday’s debate, calling him “a lifelong Republican” and noting he chaired the state Republican Party from 2013 to 2017. That coincided with the party supporting President Donald Trump and former Gov. Paul LePage in their elections.
“He didn’t leave the party until he decided to run for governor because he knew he couldn’t beat Bobby Charles because the party has gone MAGA,” Pingree said. “And again, I have respect for Rick, but I don’t think it’s fair to say that he has been independent-minded.”
Bennett replied by alluding to how he voted against Republican proposals in the state Senate and was the chamber’s “most independent member.” Charles chimed in by noting Bennett decided to cast a Democratic ballot in the June primary.
Pingree made her rare attack on Bennett, whom she has otherwise referred to as “my friend,” after Bennett gave a line he has given in several debates about what he represents.
“We need to get back to a politics of compromise and collaboration. The party candidates can’t do that,” Bennett said. “Hannah Pingree has a D on her jersey. Bobby Charles has an R on his jersey. My jersey says Maine.”
Who gets to work in the next administration?
The brief amount of bickering between Pingree and Bennett was an exception to what has otherwise been a peaceful, drama-free set of interactions during each debate. Charles has notably gone after the two by calling them “insiders” for their years of legislative service in Augusta.
If the polls turn out to be fairly accurate, then Pingree will succeed Mills. The talk will quickly turn next month to who may join the next governor’s administration. Bennett is one name to watch if he loses the race and Pingree wins it, given their mostly amicable interactions.
But it is still far too early to say who will serve under the next governor. Campaigns are careful to not look too far ahead and publicly discuss any plans beyond Nov. 3.

title: ‘Curative’ blood cancer therapy coming to Westbrook cancer clinic
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After Yoni Resnick and Stephen Rolfe opened the canister, thin white vapor wafted out — a reaction caused by the liquid nitrogen inside meeting the warm air in the pharmacy at New England Cancer Specialists in Westbrook.
The canister contained a solution used for a life-saving cancer therapy that is increasingly employed to treat certain blood cancers. The treatment, called chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, or CAR T, will be available for the first time at the Westbrook clinic.
New England Cancer Specialists expects to give the therapy to its first patient in November.
Obtaining the liquid nitrogen canister, which stores the T-cells at minus 200 degrees Celsius, was one of the key steps to making the treatment more accessible in Maine, officials with the cancer clinic said.
Resnick and Rolfe manage the pharmacy and must test the liquid nitrogen canister, which arrived at the pharmacy this week, to make sure it’s maintaining its temperature, and conduct other tests to ensure it can safely transport the T-cells and the solution they are stored in. The canister passed the first test during the initial opening on Wednesday.
Dr. John Winters, director of the CAR T program at the clinic said patients will soon be able to receive the infusion treatment at their offices and recover at home. Winters said patients previously had to travel to Boston for the therapy. The process takes about three weeks, and patients need to stay near where they received the infusion in case complications arise, he said.
“This harnesses the patient’s own immune cells to kill the cancer,” Winters said. The treatment can be “curative” for certain types of lymphoma and put multiple myeloma in “durable remission,” he said.
Winters said only about 20% of patients in Maine were able to access CAR T, because of the logistical difficulties of traveling to Boston.
Resnick, vice president of pharmacy at New England Cancer Specialists, said having only one in five patients in Maine able to access CAR T is “dismal” and having a location in the state will improve access. He said barriers to access include not only the travel time to Boston, but needing a caregiver while recovering from the infusion, and also the financial costs of traveling and lodging.
Winters said the way the therapy works is patients have blood removed, the T-cells are extracted from the blood, and the blood is returned to the patient. The harvested T-cells are shipped to a lab in California in the liquid nitrogen canister, and then returned to Maine a few weeks later.
Then the patient comes back to the office, and the engineered T-cells, designed to fight their cancer, are infused into their blood, he said.
“This is curative for patients who before had no hope,” Winters said.
Patients with late-stage lymphoma or multiple myeloma would typically have about a year or less to live without the CAR T treatments, he said.
Winters said CAR T has been available for about a decade, and is increasingly used earlier as a treatment option as outcomes from the therapy prove to work. In the future, he said, the therapy will likely become a frontline treatment for certain blood cancers, reducing reliance on chemotherapy.
He said initially it will be used on one patient at the clinic per month, but they expect usage will expand as the CAR T program at New England Cancer Specialists ramps up.
According to the American Cancer Society, CAR T is also used for certain types of leukemia, and is being researched for its effectiveness on other cancers.
According to the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention, Maine has about 400 new cases of non-Hodgkin lymphoma per year. CAR T can treat certain types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Multiple myeloma is a rarer cancer, at about 1.7% of all cancer diagnoses, according to the National Cancer Institute.
Deborah Cote, 69, of Dresden, said she was diagnosed with lymphoma in 2015, and was selected for CAR T therapy last year. Cote said she traveled to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston in March for the treatment, and had to stay in Boston for about three weeks. She said she was fortunate to have a friend willing to stay with her.
“If I could have stayed in Maine, that would have been unbelievable,” Cote said. “I have a support group here, and I missed that support group in Boston.”
Cote said the treatment has improved her life, and doctors “can’t find a wisp of cancer cells in me.”
“I feel better than I’ve felt in many years,” Cote said.

title: Ahead of 3rd anniversary, survivors of Lewiston mass shootings call for accountability
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- Mass shooting survivors and victims’ family members gathered Wednesday in front of the media nearly three years after the Oct. 25, 2023, tragedy.
- Some survivors continue to call into question how $1.9 million of the $6.6 million raised in the aftermath of the shooting reached area nonprofits instead of victims’ families and survivors.
- They say they have been denied an audience with the Legislature’s Government Oversight Committee.
LEWISTON — With the anniversary of the Oct. 25, 2023, mass shooting approaching, some victims, survivors and their families gathered at Veterans Memorial Park on Main Street to hold a news conference.
Standing in front of the cameras, Amy Sussman read the names of the 18 people killed at Just-In-Time Recreation and Schemengees Bar and Grille: Ronald Morin, Peyton Brewer-Ross, Joshua Seal, Bryan MacFarlane, Joseph Walker, Arthur Strout, Maxx Hathaway, Stephen Vozzella, Thomas Conrad, Michael Deslauriers II, Jason Walker, Tricia Asselin, William Young, Aaron Young, Robert Violette, Lucille Violette, William Brackett and Keith Macneir.
Sussman, who is Hathaway’s aunt, said the grieving families and survivors are still seeking answers on how the Maine Community Foundation handled collecting and disbursing the $6.6 million Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund.
What they are looking for, she said, is accountability, transparency and fairness.
Some $4.7 million of the Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund was granted to victims’ families and survivors; $1.9 million went to 29 area nonprofits.
Speaking at the news conference were survivors Jennifer Zanca, Destiny Johnson, Danielle Chabot and Strout’s father, Arthur Barnard.
Zanca, who was shot at Schemengees Bar and Grille, learned a year later she would need more surgery and, by the end of it, owed $93,000 in hospital bills that she said her insurance company denied.
“The FBI, Homeland Security came to my home and told me I would never have to worry about hospital bills,” Zanca said. “Except I did.”
Zanca said it was a year later that she learned about the distribution of funds occurring in the months following the shooting.
“You mean to tell me that 29 nonprofits received $65,000 each, that only a few had anything to do with the shooting, while victims that were shot received less than half that amount from the Maine Community Foundation?” Zanca asked. “Some nonprofits received nine times the amount than victims that fled from flying bullets, while others saved lives and witnessed the carnage that is forever embedded in their memories.”
Nearly three years after the shootings, some victims and survivors are still asking the Maine Attorney General’s Office and the Legislature’s Government Oversight Committee to hear their side of the story. Sussman said survivors have also tried unsuccessfully to meet with Gov. Janet Mills.
Attorney General Aaron Frey sat before the Government Oversight Committee on Sept. 16 and told legislators that the Office of Program Evaluation and Government Accountability cannot investigate the handling of funds because the funds were not handled by a government entity.
Frey also told legislators the only recourse for an investigation would be through the Maine Charitable Solicitations Act; however, he said, no complaints have been filed through that act.
The Maine Community Foundation has publicly defended its handling of the donations since as early as 2024, saying families and survivors were notified that the Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund would be two separate funds: one for victims and another for nonprofit organizations, as suggested by nationally recognized victims’ advocate, Jeff Dion.
The foundation said it did not take administrative fees so all donations could go to families and community recovery efforts.
Maine Community Foundation said the Attorney General’s Office found that donor intent had been followed and that there were no concerns about how the funds were collected and distributed.
Sussman said victims’ families and survivors feel as though they have been silenced by the Government Oversight Committee from giving their own account of what they were initially told by the Maine Community Foundation.
“The Maine Community Foundation gave us this document on their own letterhead,” Sussman said, holding up a binder and pointing to a page, “saying that 100% of the Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund was for the victims’ families and survivors. We were sent emails saying (the same).
“What we didn’t know was that the Maine Community Foundation was collecting money for nonprofits on the backs of the 18 people who were murdered and the 118 who survived … in the worst mass violence event in the state’s history.”
Victims’ families and survivors learned a week ago that the Government Oversight Committee will not hear from groups of victims and survivors in a meeting after having several requests ignored, Sussman said.
“We recently learned that one of the co-chairs and members of the committee work for or are on the boards of nonprofits that received grants from the Maine Community Foundation,” Sussman said. “This conflict of interest is prominent in the ruling party of the state Legislature.”
In April, some 57 victims’ family members and survivors sent a complaint, accompanied by new documents, to the Maine Office of the Attorney General to reopen its investigation. They declined, Sussman said.
“True accountability means that no other family or individual will have to go through what we have in the aftermath of a tragedy at the hands of an unethical nonprofit. … That no other family or individual will have to get up off their knees from grief and suffering to fight for what is right because the ruling party in this state of Maine will not help us.”
Sussman said she recently learned of two new complaints being filed with the Attorney General’s Office.
“We are continuing to demand accountability. … It is being swept under the rug by the governor, the attorney general, the Government Oversight Committee and the city of Lewiston,” Sussman said. “The actions of the Maine Community Foundation have hurt not only us, but all nonprofits.”
“We are on the right side of this,” Sussman said. “We’re not giving up and we’re not going away.”

title: Augusta voters face ballot question to approve $7.3 million bond
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Augusta voters face ballot question to approve $7.3 million bond that includes investment in Augusta Civic Center
The first question on Augusta residents' ballots in November will be whether to approve the city taking out a bond of more than $7 million.
The money, which will be paid off over the course of 30 years, will go toward roads, a fire engine, the completion of a community pool and the Augusta Civic Center.
According to City Manager Jared Mills, bond approval has been on Augusta ballots each of the last three years.
"If we were to just try to pay out of the tax base for that, that would be a lot of money and a lot of tax increase," Mills said. "
Mills said that $1.8 million of the total bond will go towards the Civic Center. The money will go toward bleachers on the lower level of the basketball court and switchgear engineering.
According to a Mainebiz report, the Civic Center held the second-highest attendance out of all the state's entertainment venues.
"The Civic Center's bread and butter is not these large shows, it's not these large concerts, and things like that, that Portland and Bangor have. It's the day-to-day," Mills said.
Mills added the facility holds an economic impact not only on those who host events at the space, but on the city as a whole. He stated investment now, paid over the course of several years, will hold a lighter load than down the road.
"The cost of construction is going up," Mills said. "So if we don't stay up on this and what they call defer maintenance or defer any of these things over the years, the cost is just going to significantly go up, or you don't do that service anymore."
The second question on Augusta ballots relates to an expansion of the Farrington Elementary School as the Lillian P. Hussey Elementary School is aging. It would close if the second question is passed.
It would be a more than $53 million project. According to Mills, the state would be responsible for the funding.
This year, the only polling place in Augusta is the Civic Center.

title: Family settles lawsuit for nearly $50 million over teen’s alleged starvation death
text:
VANCOUVER, Wash. (KING) — A lawsuit over the starvation-related death of a 15-year-old boy has ended with a nearly $50 million settlement.
The case centers on a family that lived in Washington state, just over the border from Portland, Oregon.
The lawsuit named the Washington State Department of Children, Youth and Families, the Department of Social and Health Services, and Evergreen Public Schools in Vancouver, Washington, as defendants.
The settlement came just before the case was set to go to trial this month.
The state and Evergreen Public Schools are paying $49.33 million to the family of Karreon Adams-Franks. The lawsuit alleged the defendants missed years of chances to save him.
Chris Davis, the family’s attorney, said Karreon was 15, autistic, nonverbal and legally blind.
Allegations of abuse
The lawsuit said Karreon’s adoptive parents, his biological aunt and her husband, starved and abused the teen and his two brothers. In 2023, they were convicted in connection with his death and the abuse of all three brothers.
“This case is incredibly unusual just by the egregious facts and how many times the state and the school district had to prevent it and save these boys, and they failed miserably,” Davis said.
Felicia Adams was sentenced to 35 years in prison. Jesse Franks was sentenced to 30 years.
“The boys were beaten with paddles and extension cords. One of the boys was choked out by an extension cord. The boys were locked in their bedroom for days at a time,” Davis said.
State response
The lawsuit alleged state agencies failed to act on years of warning signs. It said a child protective services worker visited the home six days before Karreon died in November 2020 but took no action.
“I can say they dropped the ball, but it’s more egregious than that. They simply ignored their legal obligation to investigate complaints when they were made and then to report ongoing signs of abuse and neglect,” Davis said.
Davis said he believes the school district is at fault as well.
Evergreen Public Schools said, in part, in a statement that it hopes the settlement will allow Karreon’s brothers to continue healing without the burden of enduring a trial.
Evergreen Public Schools maintained throughout the litigation that none of its staff failed to make a mandatory report to DCYF or law enforcement.
The state agencies involved declined to comment on the settlement.

title: Bangor advances homelessness strategy as winter approaches
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Bangor’s fight against homelessness continues, with winter fast approaching.
The Homeless Advisory Committee met Tuesday to work on its strategic plan, with updates on warming centers and Project Hope.
Shelter expansion plans
The city plans to expand by five beds at the Bangor Area Homeless Shelter, 25 at Mansion Church, and 65 at the Brick Church.
Last year, shelters averaged 85 people a night, jumping to 125 on the coldest nights.
A City Council workshop tomorrow will discuss using Together Place for overflow.
Project Hope funding setback
The committee had backed Project Hope, pairing $300,000 from MaineHousing with a $126,000 city match, but the council voted it down after public opposition.
This week, city officials will meet with MaineHousing, Preble Street and Community Care to explore other funding options.
