title: Matt Dunlap stands up and delivers for Mainers, even when he has to oppose his own party
text:
Alan Cobo-Lewis lives in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District.
In 2003 my twin children were toddlers attending an integrated preschool in Milford — integrated meaning it supported children without disabilities and also supported children with significant disabilities with intensive early intervention. The school was caught in a nasty dispute with the local special education director, putting at risk the early intervention and early childhood special education of dozens of children, about half of whom had disabilities. And the bureaucrats in Augusta barely seemed to care.
A bipartisan group of legislators — with deep participation by then-state Rep. Matt Dunlap — supported parents like us when we invited the commissioner of education, an assistant attorney general, and the statewide director of the early intervention/early childhood special education system to meet with parents at the school about this crisis. The pressure from families and from legislators eventually led to a resolution that saved the school and the children’s placements. We were forever grateful to legislators, including people like Matt who had to stand up to a cabinet officer from his own party, for their support.
Not long after, Matt co-sponsored a bill to give parents of children with disabilities the same rights as parents of any other child to decide when their child was ready to enter kindergarten, without losing the early childhood special education to which children with disabilities were entitled. Even though this bill enjoyed unanimous bipartisan support in committee (it was a money-saver for the state and for local school districts and was good for kids and families), it was surprisingly and vociferously opposed by the Maine Department of Education, apparently because they had the misguided impression that it stood in opposition to universal pre-kindergarten, which the department was championing at the time (and which still hasn’t been achieved more than two decades later).
Every step of the way, the executive branch opposed parents of young children with disabilities, and every step of the way, Matt helped us overcome. The bill was eventually signed by the governor — but only after Matt helped organize the Legislature to be ready to override a threatened veto from a governor of his own party.
Then, in 2007, as secretary of state, Matt accompanied activist Mary Adams in court as an ally in her quest to keep the “Taxpayer Bill of Rights” citizen initiative on the ballot, even though he opposed the bill’s policy. Matt showed right then and there that he believed deeply in the right of the people to rule themselves and that he would defend the people’s rights.
Later, in 2020, when President Donald Trump appointed Matt to the federal Election Integrity Commission, friends and colleagues of mine from out of state expressed concern about who this Democrat was who was being appointed. I assured them that I trusted Matt implicitly. Indeed, Matt became famous enough to land coverage in Rolling Stone magazine when he sued to demand access to information that he was legally entitled to as a member of the commission.
Matt is unafraid to stand up to any executive from either party.
In 2007, I was honored to serve with Matt when he chaired Maine’s Special Task Force on Improving Public Understanding and Participation in the Rulemaking Process. State rules are so opaque, but have such deep impact on people who live in Maine, and Matt was determined to get the public better access to the process so that bureaucrats and bad actors couldn’t run roughshod over the people’s rights. And he delivered.
Throughout his career, I have seen Matt listen carefully to what the people of Maine go through and then move — with caring, with an understanding of how government actually works, and with a determination that government must work for the people — to ensure that people get what they need even when they are opposed by powerful forces from within his own party or from the other party.
This is why I am proud to support Matt Dunlap for Congress.

title: Portland District 4 and 5 City Council candidates discuss housing, public safety and more
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — Candidates and community members gathered at The Light Church on Brentwood Street for back-to-back forums Wednesday night so constituents could get to know who is running to represent them on the Portland City Council this November.
Running for the District 4 seat, which represents East Deering and parts of the Back Cove, Deering Center and North Deering neighborhoods, are incumbent Anna Bullett and challenger Jacob Viola.
The race for the District 5 seat, which includes Riverton and portions of North Deering, is a bit more crowded: Michael Todd Chretien, Jakobi Delgado, Kevin Gardella and Ilma López are looking to replace Councilor Kate Sykes, who did not seek reelection.
The Deering Center Neighborhood Association hosted the consecutive debate-style forums and posed a wide range of questions, but housing and public safety were among the most extensively covered issues Wednesday night.
DISTRICT 4
One of the first questions posed to candidates in both of Wednesday evening’s forums was how they would work to address the housing crisis.
In the District 4 debate, Bullett leaned heavily into her experience on the council to date and the work she hopes to build on. That includes the city’s work with a Social Housing Task Force and working with the permitting and inspections office on a performance improvement plan.
Viola said he believes the city is “under-building” and “over-regulating” and, along the same vein as Bullett, said he wants to bring people together across departments to figure out a better process. He noted it’s simply too expensive to build in the city for many developers.
When asked for their stance, both candidates said they’d support changing the city’s inclusionary zoning policies, which require large developments to have at least 25% of their housing units be affordable.
The candidates were also asked how they would address the police department’s recruiting challenges.
Bullett said part of the department’s staffing struggle is that recruits need to wait and enroll in one of the state’s training academy sessions, which can be months apart. She said she would like to see the city find a way to have the department do its own training, which could speed up the onboarding process.
Viola said the city needs to find a way to hire more officers, and that social workers could be brought on to help ease the inundation of calls related to drug use and mental health. He said he’s heard from many residents who want more enforcement, but the department doesn’t have the resources.
When asked how they’d address recent pedestrian fatalities and biking safety concerns, both candidates leaned into the city’s Vision Zero plan. They both noted the work done so far on speed tables and other crash-mitigation infrastructure, and that more are needed.
Viola added that he’s spoken with traffic engineers on the campaign trail who have advised him that “novelty” along roads — such as flashing lights and rearranging signage — can have a slowing effect on drivers.
Bullett said she’d like to see a better pedestrian and biking “after-crash protocol” for the council, which she said right now doesn’t go far beyond councilors being notified by police of incidents.
DISTRICT 5
On how they’d address the housing crisis, the four candidates for District 5 showed a lot of overlap, such as wanting to improve the city’s permitting process and changing its inclusionary zoning policies. However, they did find chances to differentiate themselves.
Chretien highlighted his goal of building 5,000 units in the next five years, while also appointing a city “housing czar.” While also mentioned by others, Delgado leaned heavily into existing policies that pose challenges for smaller developers.
López said the city needs to work to “define” what affordable housing really means, noting some people she’s spoken to on the campaign trail say they can’t afford their “affordable” unit. Gardella emphasized that the city needs to do a better job of including nearby residents when large housing projects are proposed.
Chretien, López and Gardella all said they support the current rent control ordinance, with some tweaking to accommodate smaller landlords. Delgado was a bit more hesitant, saying he supports it in the short term, but that it’s “a band-aid” for a bigger problem: a lack of housing supply.
All candidates agreed it will take a multi-pronged approach to tackle public drug use, mental health, and other issues often associated with homelessness.
Gardella noted “trained medical experts” or “street doctors” could take some of the brunt off public safety personnel. Delgado was adamant that the county must reopen treatment facilities, and he would work with the county to do so.
López and Chretien both emphasized the need for institutions to work more collaboratively on the issue. López said the city needs more “in between” services and Chretien said it needs more “wraparound” services.
The candidates were split on expanding the police department, despite staffing level concerns.
Delgado and Gardella said the department needs to hire more constables. Gardella added that he’d like to expand mobile healthcare programming, while Delgado said law enforcement needs more services for their own mental health.
López said the police department may not need to hire more personnel if other sectors of the city can do more to help curb issues stemming from homelessness. Chretien said the department is an appropriate size for the city, and while hiring more officers isn’t realistic, looking at how the department can “reallocate” its current staff is.
The District 4 and 5 candidates also touched on a variety of other topics at the forum, including taxes, climate change, communication with constituents and some issues specific to Deering Center.
Members of the Deering Center Neighborhood Association say they plan to share footage of the forums ahead of Election Day. For more information and updates from the association, visit deeringcenter.me.

title: Losses mounted for Hearts of Pine this season, but fans never wavered
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
There will be no well-attended watch parties in the coming weeks. The State Theater and the Portland Zoo won’t be packed to the rafters with Hearts of Pine fans, completely absorbed by the Hearts competing in a playoff match.
The Hearts of Pine were eliminated from USL League One playoff contention last week, and now there are two games remaining in the season. Portland plays at Forward Madison FC on Saturday and hosts Charlotte Independence on Oct. 24 to wrap up the 2026 campaign.
While the team didn’t come close to matching the on-field success of its inaugural season, things are as good as ever off the field. The Hearts are second in USL League One in average attendance, trailing only Boise. Portland’s average attendance at Fitzpatrick Stadium is 6,235, which is around 1,000 fewer than Boise but about 2,200 more than the Richmond Kickers, who rank third in the league in average attendance.
The Hearts have played 38 consecutive sellouts at Fitzpatrick, and it’s pretty much a lock to be 39 after the final game of the season. Tickets for the season finale on Oct. 24 against Charlotte are still scarce and expensive. A Wednesday morning glance at StubHub showed tickets going for $104 to $140 each for a pair of seats together, while a single could be had for $63.
The average face value of a Hearts ticket is a modest $27. With no postseason on the horizon, it’s a little surprising to see the secondary market remain so robust. If the team has another down season, is this demand sustainable?
Dirigo Union, the team’s enthusiastic supporters group, will always be there, singing throughout the match and bringing the noise. The question is, if there’s another season of frustrating play on the pitch, will the casual fans still drive up ticket prices and make Hearts of Pine games EVENTS?
Right now, that’s a question without an answer, unless you have a crystal ball. The best we can do is a qualified probably.
Remember, the Hearts have a waiting list for season tickets that runs 8,000 names deep. Even if half the season ticket holders suddenly pull the chute, there’s more than enough fans eager to take their place.
Bass Pettitt is co-chair of Dirigo United. Admittedly, he sees the future of Hearts fandom through the optimistic eyes of a superfan. He can only go by what he’s seen so far and conversations with casual fans he meets through his job at Bayside Bowl. What he hears from them makes him bullish that the current trend of ticket scarcity will continue, at least through next season.
“I talk to my friends who are league bowlers who have never been into soccer in their life, and they’re like, ‘Man, I went for the first time and I had so much fun,’ and they tell me about three things that aren’t anything that happened on the field,” Pettitt said. “And then I ask them about the game and they’re like, ‘Yeah, I’m learning about soccer and I’m excited to be there and be a part of it.’ There’s a lot of people like that. I’m sure the idea of losing consistently will run dry on them.”
The way the Hearts have lost so many games this season is what frustrates fans new and old. The team has allowed a late goal a dozen times, turning a win into a loss or tie, or a tie into a loss. Ten times in 30 matches, the team surrendered a goal in stoppage time at the end of a game.
That frustration hasn’t resulted in fans staying away. Hearts of Pine management has done an amazing job making games a family-friendly experience that goes beyond the results on the field. In that regard, the Hearts are like Portland’s other three pro franchises, the Portland Sea Dogs, Maine Mariners and Maine Celtics.
Where those clubs hold an edge, though, is affiliation. If they don’t win, fans can go to games knowing they could be watching a future member of the Boston Red Sox, Boston Bruins or Boston Celtics. The Hearts are their own thing. Players move on to higher leagues, but there’s not a common final team that’s the goal at the top of the pyramid.
Reaching the USL League One semifinals last year, being a penalty kick from the championship game, was more than anyone could have expected from a club in its first season of play. That alone is reason enough to think the crowds will continue to fill Fitzpatrick Stadium over the next few seasons, and then a possible new stadium on the waterfront in 2029.
“We’re in the growth stage. We’re toddlers,” Pettitt said.
That growth comes with pains on the field. Right now, there’s no indication those will become aches at the turnstiles.

title: Let’s give Troy Jackson a chance
text:
I am not interested in the Senate campaign ads costing millions of dollars, money that would be better spent helping those in need of food or fuel for the winter. However, I am very interested in how the candidates will vote in the Senate.
How our senators vote has a huge impact on the lives of us in Maine as well as the nation as a whole. How will they vote on support of President Trump’s agenda, selection of judges, support for the war in Iran, taxes, environment and medical care — just to mention a few.
I have been unhappy how Sen. Collins has voted on many of these issues. I believe it is time to give Troy Jackson a chance.
David Juers
Cape Elizabeth

title: Cornell president admits he never followed up on gang rape allegation ahead of no-confidence debate
text:
Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff knew in 2024 that a student had reported being gang raped at a fraternity house, but never followed up to learn what had happened to her or whether any of the accused students had been punished.
In an interview with The New York Times published Tuesday, a day before Cornell’s Faculty Senate was set to begin debating a no-confidence resolution in his administration, Kotlikoff acknowledged that he did not know until recently that the woman had dropped out of Cornell or that students had been expelled or suspended over the incident.
Kotlikoff publicly addressed what he called “deeply disturbing” allegations involving drug use and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house in a November 2024 message to the Cornell community, saying criminal and university investigations were underway.
He subsequently convened a presidential task force to examine how Cornell handles sexual assault, but said this week that he never followed up to learn the outcomes of the criminal or Title IX investigations into the woman’s allegations.
Case has drawn national attention, roiled campus
The case has drawn national attention since the woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints.
On Tuesday, Kotlikoff announced a ban on fraternity parties through the end of the academic year and plans to give state police a role in investigating sexual assault reports.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten initially declined to pursue charges after reviewing a summary prepared by Cornell University Police, but later said it omitted key details. He reopened the investigation after the lawsuit was filed. Gov. Kathy Hochul subsequently removed him from the case, appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor and ordered an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the allegations.
The Cornell Faculty Senate’s proposed resolution, declaring no confidence in the administration’s ability to handle reports of sexual assault on campus, reflects growing concerns among some faculty members that people who report sexual misconduct face institutional barriers and fear retaliation. Some have called for Kotlikoff’s resignation, while others have urged patience as independent investigations proceed.
Kotlikoff was scheduled to address the Faculty Senate on Wednesday before members begin debating the resolution. Debate was expected to continue Oct. 28, followed by electronic voting by the Faculty Senate, which has approximately 130 voting members. A simple majority is required for passage.
Professor who reported harassment says it nearly cost her career
For Ariana Kim, an associate music professor at Cornell and co-sponsor of the resolution, Kotlikoff’s acknowledgment that he had not followed up on the woman’s case was deeply troubling.
“I mean, that’s appalling in and of itself, right?” Kim said. “That you don’t know about a student who faced an alleged horrific crime, that you don’t think to check in.”
Kim, a Grammy-nominated violinist, said she was motivated to take action after being struck by Jane Doe’s story, as well as her own personal experiences on campus since she started at Cornell a decade ago as a young academic in her 20s. She said when she experienced bullying and sexual harassment by senior colleagues, Cornell failed to properly document her complaints and that she was never clearly informed what disciplinary action, if any, had been taken.
“I was asked what I had done to provoke the situation,” she said.
Kim said she continued to be expected to work alongside colleagues involved in the dispute. She believes reporting the misconduct later affected her tenure review.
She spent 18 months appealing an adverse tenure decision, a process during which she lost 20 pounds (9 kilograms) and struggled to eat or sleep. A university appeals board ultimately overturned the original decision, and she secured tenure.
Now seeking promotion to full professor, Kim said she recognizes that publicly criticizing university leaders could again jeopardize her career.
“I’m speaking out publicly against this administration that may very well deny my promotion,” she said.
Kim said she has considered leaving Cornell many times over the years but is determined to stay and make the university safer for those who come after her.
“If by me fighting, it helps move the needle a little bit so that my female students aren’t going through this in 10 years or my female colleagues aren’t going through this in five years, then maybe it’s worth it.”
Faculty members question whether Cornell can investigate itself
Anne Marie Brady, a senior extension associate at Cornell’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations and another co-sponsor of the resolution, questioned whether Cornell University Police can independently investigate serious allegations of sexual misconduct.
“There doesn’t seem to be independence between the administration and the Cornell Police Department,” Brady said. She pointed to its handling of campus protests as one reason for her concerns and said serious criminal allegations should be investigated by outside law enforcement agencies.
Brady welcomed Kotlikoff’s announcement that state police would take on a role in sexual assault investigations, saying it showed the administration was listening to faculty concerns. But she questioned the timing, a day before the Senate was scheduled to begin debating the no-confidence resolution.
“I’m happy that they are listening — we need a dialogue,” she said. “We need to debate and discuss this. But I also feel it’s a bit disingenuous that it comes out just before the resolution.”

title: Ex-fiance of US Rep. Nancy Mace and 2 others charged with sex crimes
text:
Ex-fiance of US Rep. Nancy Mace and 2 others charged with sex crimes she detailed in House speech
U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace's former fiance and two of his business associates were charged with sex crimes and voyeurism on Wednesday over an episode the South Carolina congresswoman described in detail during a speech last year on the House floor about how crimes against women are not investigated thoroughly.
Video above: Congresswoman Nancy Mace says she won't run for South Carolina Senate
John Douglas Osborne committed sex acts on a 23-year-old incapacitated and intoxicated woman while Mace's ex-fiance Patrick Bryant and Eric Bernard Bowman watched, according to sworn statements by agents from the State Law Enforcement Division, which brought the charges.
The men talked about who would assault the woman beforehand, took photos and recorded the assault, which was also seen on a security system feed at the home in Sullivan's Island, an affluent suburb of Charleston, state agents said. The woman had fallen into a pool and was passed out on a couch covering herself with a pillow, agents said.
Another woman who happened to be watching the feed saw the assault and took pictures and wrote about it in a journal, police said. Mace and Bryant were not yet engaged at the time of the October 2018 assault.
Osborne, 46, is charged with first-degree assault and battery and two counts of third-degree criminal sexual conduct. Bryant, 53, and Bowman, 46, are each charged with voyeurism.
Along with the voyeurism charge, Bowman was also charged with obstruction of justice after agents said he did a factory reset on a cellphone he knew investigators were seeking in a search warrant, and with publishing the name of a victim of criminal sexual conduct after posting the victim’s name and a video of her on X.
Bryant didn't return a message seeking comment on Wednesday, and attorneys who have been listed as representing Bowman and Osborne in other cases did not immediately return messages.
Mace, a Republican, described the assault at length in a nearly hourlong speech in February 2025 that named the men and described other photos and videos found when she looked at Bryant's cellphone when they were still together.
Mace said she “accidentally uncovered some of the most heinous crimes against women imaginable. We’re talking about rape, non-consensual photos, non-consensual videos of women and underage girls, and the premeditated, calculated exploitation of women and girls in my district.”
At the time, Bryant completely denied the allegations. “I take this matter seriously and will cooperate fully with any necessary legal processes to clear my name,” he told The Associated Press.
The State Law Enforcement Division didn't say if their investigation into any of the men is continuing.
After the arrests, Mace released a statement detailing the 25 bills she says will protect victims of sexual assault, harassment or discrimination, including in retaliatory defamation and libel lawsuits that may result from allegations they bring to light.
The Republican, who is leaving the House this term after losing her bid to be South Carolina governor, introduced a proposal this week to require that anyone who brings such a case and loses must pay attorney fees for the defendant.
“Protecting women and holding predators accountable isn’t a slogan. It’s been one of my top priorities in Congress. For too long, survivors have faced broken systems while predators exploited loopholes and walked free,” Mace said in her statement.

title: InvestigateTV+: Mother’s journey to forgive
text:
(InvestigateTV) — One mother faces her son’s killer after decades of harboring hate. InvestigateTV+ shows you how they’re now working to heal together.
Then, doctors explain how they’re safely using drugs with psychedelic-like effects to help patients struggling with certain mental health conditions and how a move by the federal government could open the door to similar therapies.
Plus, celebrate a century of Pez as we get an up-close look at how the candy is made.
Forgiving the man who killed her son
Forgiveness is easily said, but often rarely given, just like second chances.
For one Nashville mother, however, forgiveness and a second chance for a career criminal were on a collision course.
Clemmie Greenlee’s lesson in forgiveness came after years of tears, hatred and anger aimed at Kim Birdsong. Then decades later, in a move that’s shocked family and friends, Greenlee found peace after the unthinkable.
New research on psychedelics
Millions of Americans take prescription medications for mental health conditions, but those might not be enough for people with severe depression or post-traumatic stress disorder.
Relief for some can be found in treatments that use drugs that produce psychedelic-like effects. After President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at speeding up research on several psychedelic drugs, it could open the door to similar therapies.
Trading plants and produce
Producing fresh food in cities from coast to coast, urban farming is taking root across the country.
Today’s urban farmers are reviving the idea of families growing a big share of the nation’s fruits and vegetables.
By transforming spaces not typically used for agriculture, these efforts are helping to increase food security.
Noah Curtis is enthusiastic about gardening. He loves what he does and wants to share it with others.
The history of PEZ
For 100 years, tiny candy bricks have been hiding inside some of the most famous faces in American history.
PEZ, the iconic candy, is made and packaged at the company’s factory in Connecticut, the only PEZ manufacturing facility in the United States.

title: Collins, Jackson spar over energy costs, health care in third Maine Senate debate
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) -For the third time, U.S. Sen. Susan Collins met challenger Troy Jackson on the debate stage Tuesday night.
Hosted by WABI and WAGM, the incumbent Republican and her Democratic challenger went head-to-head on affordability, energy, health care and tariffs.
The candidates also addressed immigration enforcement and the recent ICE-involved shooting in Biddeford, Maine — a flashpoint in the race over federal enforcement tactics and community safety.
Data centers and their impact on Maine’s electric grid and rates also came up, as large-scale projects raise questions about energy demand, costs for ratepayers, and local oversight.
Here are the key takeaways:
Heating, energy costs lead off
The debate opened with affordability, as Maine households brace for a sharp rise in heating fuel costs this winter.
Collins blamed state policies under Jackson’s leadership in Augusta for Maine having the fourth-highest electricity rates in the country, despite increased heat pump use.
Jackson countered that federal LIHEAP funding only helps temporarily, asking what happens “on the back end when that money is all spent.”
Jackson said the No. 1 driver of higher electric rates is the war in Ukraine, while energy experts also point to global oil disruptions tied to the war in Iran and problems in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran war funding sparks clash
Jackson attacked Collins’ record on the Iran war, noting she chairs the Appropriations Committee:
“She talks about how she voted nine times against the war... she’s the chair of Appropriations. If she wants to stop the war, she can cut the funding off.”
Collins has said she voted nine times against authorizing the war. Jackson claimed she first voted five times to enable it before opposing it.
Health care, fraud accusations
The candidates then debated health care quality and costs for Mainers.
Collins said nothing was done in Augusta under Jackson’s leadership to better detect fraud in Medicare and Medicaid.
Jackson fired back, referencing a ProPublica article from last week:
“I’m shocked that you’re talking about fraud because there’s only one person up here that’s been accused of that by the FBI.”
Campaign money, transparency
Collins accused Jackson of failing to file Federal Election Commission reports disclosing his contributors and expenditures, despite promising transparency.
“We have no idea who is financing Troy’s campaign because he has yet to file a single FEC report,” Collins said.
Jackson responded:
“She didn’t deny that 90 billionaires are funding her... I’ll give you the report tomorrow morning.”
Canadian tariffs close debate
Both candidates said they opposed Canadian import tariffs, but differed on effectiveness.
“Troy and I both would have voted against the Canadian tariffs... I’ve been able to negotiate and get certain items removed from the tariff list. Troy would’ve gotten nothing,” Collins said.
Jackson said he works regularly with the Canadian ambassador and the consulate in Boston and is “100 percent against” tariffs, arguing Collins failed to stop a trade war she could have prevented in Congress.

title: A stellar young doctor left Maine. Blame ICE and Susan Collins.
text:
Tim Sample is a Maine humorist, writer and illustrator.
A couple of years ago, a close family member had a sudden, life-threatening medical emergency. To say that it was a frightening and confusing experience for all concerned is an understatement. We felt extremely fortunate to be living in Portland, a five-minute ambulance ride from some of the best medical care in New England. Although it was touch and go for the first 36 hours or so, it’s no exaggeration to say that the compassionate and highly skilled staff at Maine Medical Center saved my family member’s life.
The months following her release from the hospital featured many complicated tests, screenings, diagnostics and follow-up office visits with a variety of medical specialists in an effort to ensure that the life-threatening event would not recur.
One physician in particular emerged as by far the most helpful of these specialists. He was a young, handsome, articulate, highly educated, deeply compassionate and empathetic doctor who, along with his wife and two young daughters, had emigrated to the U.S. from a Middle Eastern country.
Over the course of the next 18 months or so, we looked forward to office visits with “Dr. X” and came to rely on his ability to effectively navigate the often-confusing world of the U.S. health care system. We were therefore shocked and saddened to learn, during a follow-up visit last spring, that our favorite doctor would soon be leaving the practice.
Although disappointed, we were certainly not surprised. After all, it had been obvious to us from our first meeting that this young and gifted physician was on his way up. His next stop? Who knows. Maybe the Mayo Clinic or perhaps some other world-renowned top-tier medical facility.
When we visited the practice this past week for an appointment with our new physician, we were shocked to learn that “Dr. X” had in fact not moved on to a better position in this country. He had simply packed up his young family and moved back to the Middle East.
What? Why would he do that when he had such a bright future ahead of him here in the U.S.? The nurse practitioner checking us in gave us a terse one-word answer, as chilling as the word itself. “ICE,” she muttered.
Then I remembered an encounter with the doctor, his wife and their two lovely young daughters at an ice cream parlor in Portland last summer and recalled that the wife had been wearing the hajib, the traditional garment often worn by Muslim women. That’s when the scales finally fell from my eyes.
Why would a man like this, arguably among the best and the brightest in his chosen field, even consider raising his family in a country where armed gangs of government-funded thugs routinely harass, abduct and murder innocent civilians based solely on race, ethnicity, religion or country of origin with little or no oversight or genuine legal justification? Instead, he chose to take his chances in a Middle Eastern culture, which, let’s just say it, is not known for strong support of women’s rights.
So, where does Sen. Susan Collins come into this story? It’s clear to me that despite what I consider her tiresome and redundant “concerns,” Collins supports the Republican view that ICE is actually some sort of legitimate “law enforcement” agency that deserves billions of dollars of federal funding in order to continue its unchecked, lawless rampage both here in our beloved State of Maine and elsewhere across the country.
The bottom line? We can and must do better! I believe it’s time to retire Susan Collins and uphold the rule of law with strong Democratic leadership in the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives.

title: China select board holds two public hearings before regular meeting
text:
The two public hearings that preceded the Oct. 5 China select board meeting both drew comments from their very small audience.
The first hearing was on proposed amendments to the General Assistance Ordinance’s appendices, the annual revisions to the maximum allowable assistance amounts.
Town Manager Rebecca Hapgood shared state information on the increases, about which Joann Austin had several questions that Hapgood answered.
The second hearing was on the Nov. 3 local ballot, an oversize document that has election of select board members and one referendum question on one side and three more questions on the other side.
Austin wanted to know what changes are in the revised solid waste ordinance voters are asked to approve or reject. Hapgood replied the ordinance is completely rewritten, mostly updates and reordering to make it easier to find information.
After the public hearings, select board members unanimously approved both the revised state aid amounts and the Nov. 3 ballot.
The ballot, and related documents, are available on the China website, www.chinamaine.org., under the Elections tab in the green box on the right-hand side of the main page.
The website also announces that China registered voters may vote early in person in the town office beginning Monday, Oct. 5. Hapgood said there had been a “flood” of voters.
Delta exec explains effects of Fairfield & Benton withdrawal
At the Oct. 5 China select board meeting, Chris Mitchell, executive director of Delta Ambulance, explained effects of the expected withdrawal of Fairfield and Benton from the service’s clients.
In summary, he said fewer towns – 11 instead of 13 – mean fewer calls and therefore less revenue from transporting patients.
Delta, like other regional ambulance services, cannot support itself only by what its patients pay. Costs are much too high, and insurance does not cover them. Delta has therefore billed its member towns.
The budget was balanced with 13 towns, Mitchell said, and he had not planned to ask towns to pay more next year than this. If Fairfield and Benton leave, he will have to consider whether he can cut services, for example by having fewer ambulances, or whether he will need to raise towns’ fees.
Before Fairfield can apply for its own ambulance license, Mitchell said, Maine Emergency Medical Services will hold a 30-day public comment period. He urged China residents to watch for a notice of the public comment period and to submit comments on the effect the change might have.
The address he provided is: Maine Emergency Medical Services, Attn Licensing/Transport Application Comments, 152 State House Station, Augusta ME 04333-0152; or email maine.ems@maine.gov; or Fax 207-287-6251.
With Chris Hahn, chairman of China’s Tax Increment Financing (TIF) Committee, in the audience, board members approved the committee’s recommendation to hire a consultant. They invited Raegan LaRochelle, a consultant who specializes in TIFs, to submit a proposal to work with the committee.
Select Board Chairman Brent Chesley said LaRochelle’s fee will come from TIF funds.
Resident Sheldon Goodine wants a job with the town, too, but he offered to work for free. Goodine has in his head a five-year plan to site, design and fund a community center; he wants approval to collect information for Hapgood and the select board to turn his vision into a building.
Board members had no objections.
In other business Oct. 5, board members:
— Accepted Hapgood’s recommendation to change the town website to Catalis, which she said is far superior to the present one.
— Adopted a policy for naming town-owned lands, trails, recreational areas and facilities, and approved several Thurston Park trail names, after discussion with Thurston Park Committee Chairman Jeanette Smith. Trail number one became Nelson Family Trail; trail number two became Chamberlain Trail; and the upper and lower ridge trails were renamed Birch Breeze and Dragonfly Drift.
— Renewed the liquor license for Nash’s Café, in South China, on a 4-0-1 vote, with café owner and board member Natasha Littlefield abstaining.
Hapgood’s list of announcements from the town office included:
— All town departments will be closed Monday, Oct. 12, in observance of Indigenous Peoples Day.
— On Oct. 15, dog licenses for 2027 will be available.
— The next regular select board meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m. Monday, Oct. 19.

‘VisionQuest’ Episode 2 Is a Huge Turning Point in the MCU
text:
‘VisionQuest’ Episode 2 Is a Huge Turning Point in the Marvel Cinematic Universe
The following post contains minor SPOILERS for VisionQuest. If you’re concerned about spoilers and don’t have a good Vision handy to touch you on the forehead and mess with your brain while telling the story of the Ship of Theseus, I’d avoid reading further.
Marvel has already announced the cast and creative team of their first X-Men movie, but the official introduction of mutants to the Marvel Cinematic Universe still resembles a leaky faucet. Drip ... drip ... drip.
The latest droplet with potentially major ramifications for the future of the MCU happens in Episode 2 of VisionQuest. In a broad sense, the show has nothing to do with the X-Men; it follows Paul Bettany’s Vision, who is a psychological mess following the events of WandaVision. He’s trying to piece together who or what he is at this point, after his body was reassembled by scientists at S.W.O.R.D. and his old memories were re-implanted in his robot brain by the artificial Vision created by his love and Avengers teammate, Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen).
Meanwhile, Vision is being pursued by a ruthless bounty hunter named Paladin (Todd Stashwick) who kidnaps a young man named Thomas he claims is actually Vision’s son Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) from Vision and Wanda Maximoff sitcom existence in WandaVision.
READ MORE: 15 Actors Who Have Played Multiple Superheroes
Vision insists Thomas is not his kid — and even if he was the old Vision’s son he’s not his son — but he still goes to rescue him anyway. He arrives at the sanitarium where Paladin is holding Thomas and a fierce firefight breaks out. With his super-strength and forehead-mounted death laser, Vision makes quick work of Paladin’s henchmen.
Then Paladin himself appears, and blasts multiple holes through the normally invulnerable Vision. How is that even possible?
“The bastard’s using adamantium rounds!” says one of Vision’s A.I. allies, F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady)
This detail builds off the events of the largely not-great 2025 MCU movie Captain America: Brave New World. Its core conflict centered around the battle for control of “Celestial Island,” the remains of an ancient alien that was nearly born during the events of the even-worse 2021 MCU movie Eternals. Those remains contained a brand-new substance called “adamantium,” which is supposedly harder than any other element on the planet.
Naturally, every country on Earth wants the stuff for itself; the United States and Japan nearly go to war over control of adamantium, even though Celestial Island is bigger than Bermuda and the whole thing is made of this mineral or metal or whatever, so there should be plenty of it to go around. (Also: How do you mine something that’s harder than anything you could make a drill out of? Would a vibranium drill work? I have so many questions.) Just one year later in VisionQuest, we see that adamantium is already starting to make its way out into the world in the form of Paladin’s adamantium-tipped bullets.
Adamantium is best known as the stuff coating Wolverine’s claws and skeleton. So it’s primarily here as yet another teeny tiny tease of the X-Men}s future in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. (The announced X-Men cast does not include Wolverine, although it seems likely Hugh Jackman’s Wolverine could show up somewhere in Avengers: Doomsday or Secret Wars.)
Maybe more importantly than its connection to the X-Men, though, is the fact that the addition of adamantium to the MCU also adds a new level of threat for the Avengers. The first two episodes of VisionQuest showed the title character shrugging off dozens of bullets and knives and other conventional weapons. He tears through bad guys like a forehead-mounted death laser through human flesh. It seems like nothing can stop him — until he’s shot a couple times with these adamantium rounds. Suddenly, Vision’s near death and needs a timely rescue from Thomas to escape from Paladin.
It’s tough to tell a suspenseful story about a character who can’t be killed. (Lest we forget, Vision has already died twice in the Marvel Cinematic Universe.) That makes the addition of adamantium is even more important, because this stuff is so deadly it poses a danger to Marvel’s strongest characters. Granted, half of the entire universe was snapped out of existence by Thanos and then resurrected by the Avengers, so maybe death is meaningless in the MCU at this point anyway. But it’s still nice to be able to emotionally invest in the idea that there’s something at stake for these heroes. Otherwise, what are we watching for?

title: Joyce A. Davis
text:
Joyce Ann Davis, 81, joined her husband in death on Oct. 10, 2026, having been surrounded by family in her home.
Joyce was born in Montgomery, Alabama, to Myron and Charlotte Reynolds. She grew up in Brooks, Maine where she met the love of her life, Erving Davis Jr. She then became a telephone operator and worked at the Rockland telephone office until it closed. Together, Joyce and Erving shared a passion for classic cars and created many cherished memories throughout their years together traveling to countless car shows.
Joyce will be remembered for her loving free spirit, summers at camp, wild bingo games and late nights of running a Scrabble board or building puzzles.
Joyce is survived by her three daughters, Michelle Davis, Jennifer Kuhn (Clayton) and Valicia Kuhn (Wade); her siblings Joette Fields (Ralph) and Myron Reynolds Jr.; her grandchildren Maxine Hynes (Kenneth), James Kuhn, Corinne Coopshaw, Erving Pierce, Myron Hahn (Emily), Meradith Roy, Della Hahn and her four-legged companion Hazel, great-grandchildren Casen, Lane, Lunetta, Slate, Anita-Joyce, Asharah and Venora with another due to arrive in December.
Joyce was preceded in death by her parents Myron Sr. and Charlotte Reynolds, her husband Erving Davis Jr, her sister Joalene Reynolds, her sons-in-law, Dale Hahn and James Roy, and her grandson-in-law, Stephen Coopshaw.
There will be a private graveside service at a later date.
In lieu of flowers the family welcomes donations to Four Paws at Little River Vet in memory of Joyce. 1447 Atlantic Highway, Northport, ME 04849.
Memories and condolences may be shared with the family at www.ripostafh.com

title: Mary Shannon Lindstrom for State House District 124
text:
During my term as the chair of the Scarborough Town Council, we were on the heels of a new school referendum defeat. Mary Shannon Lindstrom was chair of the Scarborough Board of Education, and we immediately got to work on a new process in pursuit of a solution that the community could embrace.
She was integral in implementing a process our community members had faith in — that government and its representatives will listen to the people. With those tireless efforts and with the help of volunteer community members, Scarborough successfully passed a new school bond last year.
Shannon personifies all that we would want in a political leader. She is caring, thoughtful, engaged and driven. She understands the impact our decisions have on our seniors, business leaders, parents and children alike. I have full confidence that Scarborough will be best represented in Augusta with Shannon representing District 124.
Nicholas McGee
Scarborough

title: House Democrats plan a first 100-days agenda if they sweep to power in midterm elections
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats are preparing an ambitious 100-days agenda focused on delivering their campaign promises — making life more affordable and conducting vast oversight of the Trump administration — if the party seizes majority control in next month’s elections.
Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is in line to become House speaker if the party wins power, said the Democrats will be united “right out of the gate” on reinstating Affordable Care Act tax breaks, reversing Republican Medicaid cuts, holding votes against the Iran war and undoing President Donald Trump’s tariff regime.
They expect to launch the agenda in the first 100 hours, once the new Congress is seated in January.
“Fighting for an affordable America — that’s what unites Democrats all across the country,” Jeffries said recently at the party campaign headquarters in Washington.
“That’s our commitment to the American people, because the cost of living is way too high and far too many people who are working hard, playing by the rules, can’t thrive and can barely survive — and are drowning — in the Trump economy.”
It’s a hyper-focused agenda tapping into the voter sentiment that is driving much of the midterm election as Americans wrestle with affordability concerns and inflationary costs from the Iran war and other policies.
The undertaking will also test the ability of the sprawling House Democrats to work together and avoid the chaotic divisions and disruptions that have hobbled Republicans under Speaker Mike Johnson’s leadership.
Democrats have been out of power in the House since 2023. If Jeffries takes the helm, he would be the first Democratic speaker since Nancy Pelosi, leading a new generation of lawmakers that includes a handful of far-left candidates who are aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America.
“The antidote to that is getting things done,” said Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski, who is poised to become chair of the New Democrat Coalition, the largest caucus within the House Democrats. She said the party is determined to show the American people that “Democrats know how to govern.”
A Freedom Caucus of the far-left?
Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chairman of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said he is often asked if Democrats will be confronting their own version of the Freedom Caucus, referring to the far-right Republicans who often grind the House agenda to a halt.
“It doesn’t work that way,” Casar told The Associated Press in an interview. “The Freedom Caucus breaks things. But if you’re a progressive, you want to pass things.”
Leader Jeffries, Casar and other Democrats have been in touch with the progressive candidates, many of whom are backed by the DSA as the party focuses on shared priorities.
“This notion that because we’ll have new members somehow we’re going to be disjointed — not so,” said Louisiana Rep. Troy Carter, who hopes to become chair of the Congressional Black Caucus. “All those banking on that, save the popcorn for another day.”
The Republicans, who are confronting an increasingly difficult election-year climate to hold onto their majority, portray Democrats as beholden to a far-left socialist agenda.
If Republicans retain power, Johnson has said they would press on with what they have already accomplished alongside Trump, which has been an agenda focused on cutting taxes and federal spending.
“What we would do in the next two years is exactly what we have been doing already,” Johnson said on CNBC’s Squawk Box, “and that is putting the conditions in place for a strong America again.”
Fix healthcare, stop the war, end the tariffs – and investigate Trump
Months ago, Jeffries launched five working groups to tackle the affordability agenda focused on healthcare, housing, groceries and goods, gas and utilities, and care-giving.
Each group is headed by a progressive and a centrist Democrat — the healthcare working group, for example, is run by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Rep. Terri Sewell of Alabama — with the goal of striking common ground on draft policies that all House Democrats can support.
At the same time, Jeffries has tasked the ranking Democrats on the House Oversight and Judiciary committees with preparing investigations. They are focused on Trump, his family and his administration, as part of a sweeping anti-corruption agenda. Impeachment, Jeffries has said, is neither on nor off the table.
“We need to lower the cost of groceries and gas. Two, we need to make healthcare affordable for every single American. Three, we’re going to hold the crooks accountable who’ve visited unprecedented corruption on the American people,” Jeffries said. “Beginning on day one.”
Democrats plan to vote quickly to reinstate the health care tax credits for the Affordable Care Act, which expired in 2025, leaving millions of Americans confronting higher health insurance costs.
Proposals are also ready to reverse the Medicaid cuts that Republicans put in place as part of their “One Big Beautiful Bill” of tax breaks and program cuts, including new work requirements for recipients.
There are measures to reverse Trump’s tariffs as Congress works to claw back power from the White House.
And Democrats, who have forced multiple votes on ending the Iran conflict, plan to pressure the Trump administration to end the military action by pushing forward more war powers resolutions.
Much of the House Democrats’ agenda, if they regain power, would depend on the size of the majority. Details also depend on the Senate, and whether it flips to Democrats.
“We cannot simply go back to the status quo,” said Usamah Andrabi, a spokesman for Justice Democrats, an outside group that supports the far-left progressives.
And Trump, at the White House, has ultimate say, with veto power at the stroke of a pen.
“We’re going to do a lot and we’re going to be very busy,” Carter said. “We will not be able to fix everything overnight.”

title: Multi-agency Operation On Waldo Street Ends With Suspect Still At Large
text:
Maine Authorities Seeking Lewiston Man Who Is Possibly Armed & Dangerous Following Shelter-In-Place Order
What began as an investigation into suspected drug trafficking and reports of gunfire at an apartment in Rumford Wednesday afternoon resulted in a statewide search for an individual from Lewiston who authorities say could be armed and dangerous.
How did it all begin?
The Rumford Police Department says they started their investigation after receiving tips this past weekend of suspected drug trafficking and weapons being discharged in the area of 209 Waldo Street in Rumford.
Read More: Bangor, Maine House Fire Kills 1 Person, Hospitalizes 2
They were told that both individuals who lived in town and some who did not reside in the area were believed to be involved in this activity. After receiving a search warrant and upon getting another report of gunfire in the area, officers arrived in that neighborhood early Wednesday morning, before dawn.
What happened next?
Things became intense when it was thought that the suspects allegedly involved in the illicit activities might still be armed and inside the first-floor apartment. As a precaution, the Rumford PD, the Oxford County Sheriff's Office, and the Maine State Police Tactical Team worked together to establish a safe perimeter around the building.
About noon, the Rumford Police issued a 'Shelter In Place' order for folks living in the area, asking them to remain inside while they "dealt with an incident."
Read More: Stolen Vehicle Chase Ends In Fatal Medway Collision
Once the court gave the go-ahead, late Wednesday morning, authorities closed off the roads to the area and staged first responders nearby, in case the exchange with the suspects became violent.
What was the result?
At 1:20 PM, the Rumford Police Department said authorities lifted the order after determining the suspects were no longer in the building and had fled the area earlier. In its place, law enforcement is asking people to keep a lookout for one individual in particular.
"The subsequent search of the apartment, along with information developed during the ongoing investigation, has yielded additional evidence supporting the reports received from members of the public...Rumford Police are actively seeking BLAKE LACHANCE, age 21, of Lewiston, who is wanted in connection with the following felony charges: [Aggravated Assault with a Dangerous Weapon, Criminal Threatening with a Dangerous Weapon, and Reckless Conduct with a Dangerous Weapon]...LACHANCE should be considered potentially armed and dangerous."
The Rumford PD says anyone who sees Lachance should avoid contact and call the police immediately.

title: Construction worker injured by flying barrel on I-95
text:
PITTSFIELD, Maine (WABI) - A construction worker was seriously injured Wednesday morning when he was hit by a barrel after a truck crashed into it.
It happened around 8:15 AM Wednesday on I-95 in Pittsfield.
Police said a silver pickup truck hauling a black dump trailer hit a concrete barrier and a barrel while driving through a single-lane construction zone.
The orange construction barrel was then propelled into an employee of Northeast Construction, who was seriously injured, according to police.
Police say eyewitnesses reported seeing the driver turn around as the crash happened before speeding away.
Authorities say the 56-year-old worker’s injuries are not life threatening, and he was taken to the hospital for treatment.
State Police are now trying to identify the driver of the pickup truck.
Anyone with information is asked to call the Bangor Regional Communications Center.

title: Troy Jackson said he’d detail campaign funding Wednesday morning. He didn’t.
text:
In the heat of the moment during a Tuesday Senate debate, Democrat Troy Jackson offered to send his Republican rival the details of his campaign fundraising and spending a day before the deadline to file it with the Federal Election Commission.
But as of 1 p.m., Jackson had not followed through on his promise, a spokesperson for Sen. Susan Collins said.
The seemingly spontaneous offer came after the 73-year-old Collins parried an attack about her billionaire supporters by noting that Jackson has not yet filed any campaign finance reports.
“I would point out that we have no idea who is financing Troy’s campaign,” Collins said. “He promised to be completely transparent, yet he has not filed a single report.”
An irritated Jackson shot back, saying he would release his report on Wednesday morning.
“I’ll give you the report tomorrow morning,” he said. “How about that? Is that enough? Because we see yours and I know that there’s no billionaires funding me…I’ll give you the report tomorrow and then we’ll talk about it on Thursday.”
Jackson’s campaign did not respond to questions about his comments at the debate.
The 58-year-old former logger and state Senate president is not breaking any campaign finance laws by not releasing the report early. But his failure to follow through on his televised offer could give Collins another line of attack when they face off in their fourth and final debate on Thursday.
The reason Jackson’s campaign funding and spending remain a mystery so late in the cycle is a matter of timing.
Jackson was named the Democratic nominee to replace Graham Platner after the oyster farmer dropped out on July 25. That was well after the previous campaign finance reporting period closed on June 30.
The next round of reports aren’t due until midnight on Thursday, at which point they will become public.
Although no report has been filed, Jackson doesn’t appear to have had much trouble raising money.
In July, he was the third-highest fundraiser on the Democrats’ ActBlue platform, raising $5.3 million despite being a candidate for only a few days.
And his campaign has spent, or reserved, at least $20 million in advertisements, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

title: What to know about Pope Leo’s lung cancer diagnosis
text:
ROME (AP) - Pope Leo XIV spent a peaceful night in Rome’s Gemelli hospital after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung and confirmed he has cancer, the Vatican said Wednesday.
The surgery confirmed that the pope has the most common type of lung cancer, known as lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin late Tuesday.
The Vatican said doctors were waiting for the results of further tests before deciding on a course of treatment. The press office pointed to the medical statement’s mention of the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors took out all suspect tissue in hopes of removing any lingering traces of the cancer.
Experts said some of Leo’s lymph nodes also would have been removed and tested to determine if the cancer had spread. There was no word yet on those test results.
If the cancer has spread, more tests will be needed to determine what kind of therapy to pursue, said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy or targeted therapy, which involves oral pills for specific cancers.
“Adenocarcinoma is the most common (type of lung cancer), also with the most favorable prognosis,” said Liu, who is not involved in the pope’s care. “While we know the diagnosis, we now need to know the stage.”
He added: “We now need to know how big it is, how many spots in the lung are involved. Is it just one nodule, or more than one, and the lymph nodes, are they cancerous?”
For now, the implications for the pope’s long-term health remain unclear. The Vatican said more information would be provided later in the day.
The American pontiff has offered a rare level of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy. He revealed the discovery of the nodule, or growth, on his lung during his Sunday noon prayer.
The Vatican says the surgery was successful
The 71-year-old was in the operating room for about three hours, the Vatican statement said Tuesday. The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes.
The right lung has three sections or lobes while the left has two. After one lobe is removed, the rest of the lung can gradually compensate, especially in otherwise healthy and physically active people. Leo is known to be sporty, with weekly tennis games and swimming.
Before the surgery, Leo walked into the Gemelli hospital through the main entrance and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. The Vatican said the surgery was performed by a team led by Gemelli’s chief thoracic surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora.
While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo is staying in a nearby room since the apartment is undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
The pope has a trip to South America planned for November
The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo’s audiences through Oct. 20. But there was no word on whether he would be able to keep his planned trip to South America next month.
Oncology surgeons often advise patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery — which would give the pope just enough time to make his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. But whether he can go will depend on his recovery.
“If it is stage 1, he can complete these trips. If more treatment is needed, I would likely advise against the trips,” said Liu.

title: Father creates nation’s only child safety demonstration house after death of son
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (Aging Untold) — A father who lost his 2-year-old son to a furniture tip-over has built the only child-safety demonstration house in the United States to prevent similar tragedies.
Brett Horn founded Charlie’s House in Kansas City, Missouri, after his son Charlie died when a 30-inch dresser fell on him in 2007. The interactive home teaches parents about hidden dangers that experts say cause 90% of childhood accidents.
“My wife and I had no idea that our home wasn’t completely safe, and we wanted to ensure that this type of accident didn’t happen to anyone else,” Horn said.
Furniture tip-overs kill hundreds of children
Between 2000 and 2018, more than 450 children in the United States were killed by furniture tip-overs.
“The dresser that fell on him didn’t even make a sound because unfortunately Charlie’s body was trapped between the dresser and the floor,” Horn said.
Interactive house highlights hidden dangers
The demonstration house includes a living room, bathroom, nursery and kitchen with a working stove, but no one lives there.
Stacy Winkler, the assistant to the director of Charlie’s House, guides visitors through potential hazards.
“This is a pretend home. The stairs over there don’t go anywhere, they just go up to a landing,” Winkler said.
The house demonstrates dangers including cabinet corners, electric appliances, vitamin overdoses and toilet-drowning risks.
Winkler said most people don’t know that children can drown in toilets.
“Ninety percent of all accidents to children happened in the home and 90% of those are preventable,” Winkler said.
Free safety supplies and virtual tours available
Charlie’s House provides free or discounted childproofing supplies to families nationwide who cannot afford safety equipment.
“Cost is an issue for parents who are wanting to properly childproof their home,” Horn said.
For families who cannot visit in person, the organization offers a Charlie’s Safety House app, which provides virtual tours of the demonstration house on mobile devices.
Safety standards change frequently, and cribs used for older children may no longer meet current requirements for younger siblings, according to Charlie’s House.
“I want Charlie’s legacy to be that other children are not harmed from simple things in their own home,” Horn said. “And I believe we’re accomplishing that.”
