title: Losses mounted for Hearts of Pine this season, but fans never wavered
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
There will be no well-attended watch parties in the coming weeks. The State Theater and the Portland Zoo won’t be packed to the rafters with Hearts of Pine fans, completely absorbed by the Hearts competing in a playoff match.
The Hearts of Pine were eliminated from USL League One playoff contention last week, and now there are two games remaining in the season. Portland plays at Forward Madison FC on Saturday and hosts Charlotte Independence on Oct. 24 to wrap up the 2026 campaign.
While the team didn’t come close to matching the on-field success of its inaugural season, things are as good as ever off the field. The Hearts are second in USL League One in average attendance, trailing only Boise. Portland’s average attendance at Fitzpatrick Stadium is 6,235, which is around 1,000 fewer than Boise but about 2,200 more than the Richmond Kickers, who rank third in the league in average attendance.
The Hearts have played 38 consecutive sellouts at Fitzpatrick, and it’s pretty much a lock to be 39 after the final game of the season. Tickets for the season finale on Oct. 24 against Charlotte are still scarce and expensive. A Wednesday morning glance at StubHub showed tickets going for $104 to $140 each for a pair of seats together, while a single could be had for $63.
The average face value of a Hearts ticket is a modest $27. With no postseason on the horizon, it’s a little surprising to see the secondary market remain so robust. If the team has another down season, is this demand sustainable?
Dirigo Union, the team’s enthusiastic supporters group, will always be there, singing throughout the match and bringing the noise. The question is, if there’s another season of frustrating play on the pitch, will the casual fans still drive up ticket prices and make Hearts of Pine games EVENTS?
Right now, that’s a question without an answer, unless you have a crystal ball. The best we can do is a qualified probably.
Remember, the Hearts have a waiting list for season tickets that runs 8,000 names deep. Even if half the season ticket holders suddenly pull the chute, there’s more than enough fans eager to take their place.
Bass Pettitt is co-chair of Dirigo United. Admittedly, he sees the future of Hearts fandom through the optimistic eyes of a superfan. He can only go by what he’s seen so far and conversations with casual fans he meets through his job at Bayside Bowl. What he hears from them makes him bullish that the current trend of ticket scarcity will continue, at least through next season.
“I talk to my friends who are league bowlers who have never been into soccer in their life, and they’re like, ‘Man, I went for the first time and I had so much fun,’ and they tell me about three things that aren’t anything that happened on the field,” Pettitt said. “And then I ask them about the game and they’re like, ‘Yeah, I’m learning about soccer and I’m excited to be there and be a part of it.’ There’s a lot of people like that. I’m sure the idea of losing consistently will run dry on them.”
The way the Hearts have lost so many games this season is what frustrates fans new and old. The team has allowed a late goal a dozen times, turning a win into a loss or tie, or a tie into a loss. Ten times in 30 matches, the team surrendered a goal in stoppage time at the end of a game.
That frustration hasn’t resulted in fans staying away. Hearts of Pine management has done an amazing job making games a family-friendly experience that goes beyond the results on the field. In that regard, the Hearts are like Portland’s other three pro franchises, the Portland Sea Dogs, Maine Mariners and Maine Celtics.
Where those clubs hold an edge, though, is affiliation. If they don’t win, fans can go to games knowing they could be watching a future member of the Boston Red Sox, Boston Bruins or Boston Celtics. The Hearts are their own thing. Players move on to higher leagues, but there’s not a common final team that’s the goal at the top of the pyramid.
Reaching the USL League One semifinals last year, being a penalty kick from the championship game, was more than anyone could have expected from a club in its first season of play. That alone is reason enough to think the crowds will continue to fill Fitzpatrick Stadium over the next few seasons, and then a possible new stadium on the waterfront in 2029.
“We’re in the growth stage. We’re toddlers,” Pettitt said.
That growth comes with pains on the field. Right now, there’s no indication those will become aches at the turnstiles.

title: Bangor may fund an additional emergency warming center this winter
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bangor City Council is considering using city funding to support an emergency warming center that would expand overnight shelter space on the coldest nights throughout the winter.
That would likely cost just over $100,000, with the majority of those funds coming out of the federal Community Development Block Grant program.
The added capacity would provide needed beds after two existing warming centers were denied funding requests by MaineHousing. Without these extra beds, warming center leaders have worried that the city won’t have enough space to bring people inside, which could be life-threatening for homeless community members.
The city’s public health department has proposed allocating funds to the Together Place Peer Run Recovery Center so it can open a warming center on nights when temperatures drop below 15 degrees.
City councilors expressed support for the proposal during a workshop Wednesday evening but are awaiting more information on how that would affect the Community Development Block Grant budget and plan to return for more discussion on the matter at a committee meeting on Monday.
The city stepped in to provide emergency funding for the Brick Church and the Together Place during a similar scramble last year after the Brick Church’s funding request was denied by MaineHousing.
This year, the Together Place was denied state funding to reopen, as was the Mansion Church, although the latter plans to open anyway. MaineHousing awarded funding for 65 warming center beds at the Brick Church and five at the Bangor Area Homeless Shelter. The Brick Church is getting $427,65, far more than in years past, but it can’t shoulder the burden of sheltering everyone living on Bangor’s streets alone.
Between the three overnight warming centers that operated last year, 85 people visited per night on average, according to a memo from Jennifer Gunderman, the city’s public health director, summarizing a partial sample of data from last year. On 20 nights, more than 90 people visited one of the centers, and on 11 nights, more than 100 visited.
The maximum number of people who went to a warming center on a single night was between 120 and 125, Gunderman added during Wednesday’s workshop.
The Bangor Area Homeless Shelter, the Brick Church and the Mansion Church can offer about 95 warming center beds combined, Gunderman said, meaning more beds are needed for the coldest nights.
She estimated there will be between 50 to 60 nights when temperatures in Bangor fall below 15 degrees, which is also the cutoff for Portland’s city-run emergency warming center. The southern Maine city has faced some criticism from advocates who think the threshold should be higher.
That would add up to about $106,000 to open more beds on the coldest nights, according to Gunderman. She suggested allocating $5,000 of the city’s heating assistance funds, about $11,000 in general assistance funds and $90,000 in Community Development Block Grant funds to the Together Place.
“I think Director Gunderman has an excellent handle on the situation,” Shea Mullaney, board president of the Together Place, said after the workshop, adding that his organization is prepared to provide 40 warming center beds as soon as the council gives the green light.
That would put the city’s overall capacity at around 135 beds on the coldest nights.
“We are always excited to collaborate with the city on proposals that they put forward,” Mullaney said. He also stressed that the council should consider data reported at a committee meeting last month, showing that the majority of Bangor shelter guests are from the city or surrounding area within Penobscot County, when making its decision.
Data supplied by Bangor shelters from the first half of this year shows that 68% of visitors reported Penobscot County as their last place of residence, and roughly half came from Bangor, according to Kelly Watson, MaineHousing’s Director of Homeless Initiatives.
“It is starting to get cold out there,” Gunderman noted, saying the council’s decision will need to be timely.
The council also plans to move forward with smaller funding allocations to The Well and Manna Ministries, which both provide daytime warming center space, pending review of their financial documents.
Gunderman proposed giving $5,000 in heating assistance money and $10,000 in Community Development Block Grant funds to The Well.
Manna also requested $5,000, although it’s unclear if the organization still needs it given private funds the organization has raised since. The city is waiting on clarification, according to City Manager Carollynn Lear.
Councilor Michael Beck suggested that the city itself should apply for warming center funding next year from the state, saying that while he appreciates the work of the independent local warming centers, “this is two years in a row they didn’t have it covered, and then we’re the ones at the table having to scramble.”

title: Exhibits at Maine art galleries are full of tricks and treats
text:
Summer has ended and soon, so will these exhibitions at galleries in Portland, Rockland and Woolwich. At least one is a trickster, while the others are clearly treats. See them before they come down.
“The Darkroom,” through Oct. 24, 82 Parris St., Portland; 248-974-5738, 82paris.com
You have less than a week to experience this entrancing two-channel video by Portland artist Olivia Maday. And since 82Parris is an artist-run affair, hours on not regular (usually 11 a.m.-2 p.m. Saturday and Sunday, but Maday is filling out gallery-sitting time on Thursday and Friday; call before). For this project, Maday indulged her love of Victorian cabinet cards, a kind of photograph mounted on cardboard that was developed in the 1870s.
The installation consists of two “screens” composed from 270 of these cards — all of women — that have been grommeted and joined together with metal loops into two grids, then suspended from the ceiling. Projected onto them are shadowy video images of Maday seen through a scrim as she dances, accompanied by a soundtrack of chimes, humming, wind and whispering. We get the sense that inside all these somber-faced ladies lived a joyous, sensual spirit that is embodied here by Maday’s lithe movements. That spirit is celebrated, revived and activated by Maday’s dance, bringing to life a freer self that they were forced to repress.
The light of the video also casts shadows behind the screen, which are their own interesting element. They can appear as architecture supporting and housing these women, or just as easily suggest bars in a jail cell that confines them. We know not who any of these women are, something also emphasized by the shadow projection, where their faces as well as their identities are shorn away so that they become nothing more than black rectangles.
Maday is creating an archive of these cabinet cards and trying to uncover the history of each poser with what little information she can glean from words written on the back, records kept by the studios that produced them, and so on. It is an effort to resuscitate these women’s narratives and reconnect them to their lives.
“Dominique Ostuni: Would an Angel Apologize for Spilling Champagne?” through Oct. 31, 357 Main St., Rockland. 207-596-0084, dowlingwalsh.com
In Friedrich Nietzsche’s “The Birth of Tragedy,” the philosopher muses on how our search for balance between order and chaos generates art. Certainly countless works of art have manifested this way, but few as excessively or ebulliently as Dominique Ostuni’s immersive installation at Dowling Walsh.
The chaos the young Bowdoinham-based Ostuni was responding to (she’s 28) is genuinely heartbreaking. Raised in an Italian Catholic family, they were socially snubbed by their church when her parents divorced. The artist’s father had cancer, but rather than reform himself to aid his body in healing, he refused to deny himself his habits. So, one day, he got drunk and expressed his anger at the institution’s religious hegemony by driving his car through the doors of the church (The church did not prosecute because they took pity on his illness).
Ostuni could have responded darkly and mournfully to this outlandish, yet sad, event. Instead, she created an installation that casts a sardonic eye toward the Christian view of angels as helpful guides, adopting a more profane interpretation of them as mischievous tricksters from Greek mythology that more than matches the outlandishness of her father’s act.
When we begin to examine more microscopically the laboriously and obsessively produced elements that comprise Ostuni’s lamps, chandeliers, figurines, vases, a mirror and other objects — as well as queries and phrases scrawled on the walls of the gallery — we come face to face with questions of taste, value and so-called “bad” behavior.
A wall scrawl reads “Mirror, mirror on the wall, who is the most in need of confession of them all?” One of the luminous porcelain tiles of the hundreds that make up a floor-to-ceiling chandelier is a list: “Can an angel be: A trickster? A liar? A thief? A jester? A king? A drunk? A glutton? A collector? A late sleeper? A nepo-baby? A tastemaker? A spender? The splendor!”
Beyond the many words on the many objects in the exhibition, some of these questions are simply inherent in the techniques and visual language of the objects themselves. Ostuni’s liberal use of gold glazing connects them to Meissen and Nymphenburg porcelain figurines, at one time the height of fashion but in contemporary aesthetics a bit dated and borderline kitsch (one could also draw allusions to the bad taste of Trump’s gilding of the White House).
While interrogating subjective notions of taste, Ostuni’s execution of these legendary porcelain techniques is also masterful, especially in the way she varies the translucence and opacity of her material to achieve a desired effect. The tile on which the list mentioned above appears is so thin that the writing lives almost as if it is on a lightbox, while other tiles are thicker and glazed so heavily that you cannot see beyond the surface design. All this requires tremendous skill and nuance.
The show’s over-the-top quality may at first feel overwhelming, but I encourage deep looking to see how much substance (and humor) is there beyond the decorative façade of the works. That humor and wit, as Nietzsche postulated, create equanimity amidst the chaos and disorder of an intense event, resulting in singular works of art.
“Interwoven,” through Oct. 31, 8 Elm St., Rockland. 207-593-8300, trianglegallery8elm.com
Every piece in this fiber arts show is exquisite, as well as exquisitely crafted. Felt, metallic threads, handmade papers, sweetgrass and other materials emanate an alluring textural quality that makes the experience multi-sensorial — visual, tactile, emotional — sensual as well as sculptural.
The six artists participating are Judith Daniels (felt vessels), Nancy Giesberger and Sarah Haskell (embroideries and weavings), Eric Stark (sweetgrass basketry techniques), Karen Olson (various handmade papers) and Daphne Taylor (quilting). The works marry materials-based techniques with a wide variety of thematic concerns.
Haskell’s weavings and embroideries, for instance, explore liminal states of being. “The Space Between” and “Beyond Gravity” invite us into mystical, non-concretized dimensions of the mind or of existence, or into emotional states of longing and loss. Here, thematic substance and technical precision carry equal weight. Giesberger’s weavings use computer modeling, generative code linking and a jacquard loom to innovate traditional weave structures. We sense the underlying mathematics, but we actually feel the hypnotic, wavy movements and become mesmerized with the catching and refracting of light.
Stark employs basketry techniques to weave directly onto found objects (here stones) in service of exploring organic form. Each work is a play between spontaneous intuition and the shaping possibilities offered by basketry. Daniels, primarily a felt maker, also incorporates other techniques such as shibori dying to create vessels that feel nourishing in their sense of holding and interiority, but also proffer a vividly alive experience of color.
Taylor’s work uses stitching as a kind of line with which she “draws.” The embroidered imagery is often nature-derived (leaf and planet shapes, or perhaps pebbles dropped in the water, inciting concentric ripples). But though imagery may be simple, the stitching is anything but — at once meticulous and fluid. Finally, Olson’s sculptures feel fragile and delicate. Constructed from handmade papers, linen thread, photographic fragments and wax, they look as if you could blow them over. That is, until we realize that integral to their making is tremendous resilience that comes from living and expressing from late-diagnosed autism. Their very making feels miraculous, a process not only of creating an object, but of creating a self.
“Jennifer Brou: Somewhere Still,” through Nov. 7, Woolwich. 207-809-9670, sarahbouchardgallery.com
No, you are not looking at black and white large-format photographs of the woods in Jennifer Brou’s astounding exhibition. You are gazing at graphite drawings so fastidiously rendered that they look like photographs. This would be an accomplishment in itself at a small scale — 8 by 10 inches, say. But Brou’s works are 33 by 24.5 inches, at which size they become, frankly, mindboggling.
However, beyond the technical mastery of these graphite drawings, there is the palpable stillness and profound silence one senses in the works. It is a quality that can only come from long hours spent observing phenomena: The way snow mounds around tree trunks like small craters and puffy, fast-moving clouds filter light that creates shadows (“Long Shadows”). The way the sun, low on the horizon, burns through the tracery of trees (“Late Afternoon” and “Winter Sunset”). The way single leaves have clung onto their branches though the long winter, refusing to fall (“April”). Or the way a ray of light lands softly on a tiny leaf cluster in the lower left-hand corner of “Midsummer,” a drawing that took Brou four months to complete.
In order to depict the subtlety and delicacy of these little miracles of nature, an artist must understand them thoroughly and intimately, from the inside out — something that comes only after many hours of observation and of revisiting a spot again and again. Brou sketches and photographs, completing the bulk of the work on these in her studio. But this must be preceded by close and contemplative looking.
We can get right up to the surface of a work and scrutinize it long enough to see that the groundcover and understory of “Midsummer” is so lifelike that we swear it is real, while we can also notice how in another drawing such as “Altar” the forest floor is almost blurry, as if soft-focused by a camera setting.
Finally, to see them in Bouchard’s treehouse-like gallery is pure magic. It’s like Dorothy waking up in Oz — the works inside in moody monochrome, while outside everything is crisp, shimmering and bright.
“Richard Keen: Downeast with Love,” through Dec. 5, 100 Fore St., Suite B, Portland. 207-804-0459, elizabethmossgalleries.com
OK, this one doesn’t end in October, but while you’re up…
There’s often been something about Richard Keen’s paintings that have been problematic for me. It’s had partly to do with the way the uber-simplified forms and DayGlo colors flirt with abstraction but stay, in my experience of them, safely on the side of representation. Their flatness — everything pushed right up against the picture plane — their graphic quality, and a brief (unfortunate) tryst with spray glitter have in the past come off as more decorative than, as the title of the show indicates, deeply connected to a landscape that is purportedly meaningful for Keen.
But this is changing in very encouraging ways. I still view the artist’s “Blue Trees” paintings in this exhibition, along with works like “Purple Trees No. 14” through my old lens. Especially in a show about Maine landscape painting, Keen’s typical visual language can feel contradictory in that it seems to deracinate those landscapes of place; though we know it is supposed to be Maine, they felt like they could be anywhere. By loosening up the angular geometries and flatness in works such as two “Rockweed” paintings, “Asters and Rocks” and “Union River Bay,” something comes alive in them — an organic fluidity that evokes coastal topographies that are constantly shifting, ebbing and flowing.
Were it not for our knowledge of the centrality of Keen’s love of the Maine landscapes, we might take “Rockweed No. 17” as pure abstraction sans content. And it would be a good abstraction. While this might seem to counter the above comment about deracinating place, the effect is to actually transmit the sense of the ever-morphing movement and mutability of the aquatic plant of the title and the conditions in which it exists. It gets at a more essential truth of his subject and the particularity of its locale.
This feels like an exciting development and a huge leap forward. “Rockweed No. 20” and “Asters and Rocks” convey site-specificity in ways that “Purple Trees No. 14,” rigidly locked in its one-point perspective, does not. Organic form goes a long way toward transmitting the ephemerality of currents, weather patterns, light effects and so on that we experience in our state. This looseness also softens the stubborn insistence of Keen’s contrived geometries, which are valuable only up to a point when you are trying to convey nature. It would be different if his earlier work explored the fractals of nature, but that oeuvre felt more like an arbitrary geometry imposed upon nature.
Also welcome is a more complex compositional impulse that adds depth to the paintings, defying the former flatness, especially in works such as “Flat Rock No. 4 (Dresden)” and “Green Trees No. 2 (Surry).” Gone in these paintings is that sense of the entire phenomena as occurring front and center — nothing before it or behind it. Instead, we can travel into and out of these works, rather than merely spectating.
There are other experiments here that feel inchoate, such as “Supermoon Horse Dreams” and “Strawberry Horse Moon.” These seem to be striving a little too hard for something mythic. But that’s OK. The most salient fact is that Keen is clearly breaking free from self-imposed parameters that might have felt fresh at one time but were no longer serving him. Liberation is always cause for celebration in my book.
Jorge S. Arango has written about art, design and architecture for over 35 years. He lives in Portland and can be reached at [email protected]. This column is free to access through support by The Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation.

title: ‘Curative’ blood cancer therapy coming to Westbrook cancer clinic
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
After Yoni Resnick and Stephen Rolfe opened the canister, thin white vapor wafted out — a reaction caused by the liquid nitrogen inside meeting the warm air in the pharmacy at New England Cancer Specialists in Westbrook.
The canister contained a solution used for a life-saving cancer therapy that is increasingly employed to treat certain blood cancers. The treatment, called chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, or CAR T, will be available for the first time at the Westbrook clinic.
New England Cancer Specialists expects to give the therapy to its first patient in November.
Obtaining the liquid nitrogen canister, which stores the T-cells at minus 200 degrees Celsius, was one of the key steps to making the treatment more accessible in Maine, officials with the cancer clinic said.
Resnick and Rolfe manage the pharmacy and must test the liquid nitrogen canister, which arrived at the pharmacy this week, to make sure it’s maintaining its temperature, and conduct other tests to ensure it can safely transport the T-cells and the solution they are stored in. The canister passed the first test during the initial opening on Wednesday.
Dr. John Winters, director of the CAR T program at the clinic said patients will soon be able to receive the infusion treatment at their offices and recover at home. Winters said patients previously had to travel to Boston for the therapy. The process takes about three weeks, and patients need to stay near where they received the infusion in case complications arise, he said.
“This harnesses the patient’s own immune cells to kill the cancer,” Winters said. The treatment can be “curative” for certain types of lymphoma and put multiple myeloma in “durable remission,” he said.
Winters said only about 20% of patients in Maine were able to access CAR T, because of the logistical difficulties of traveling to Boston.
Resnick, vice president of pharmacy at New England Cancer Specialists, said having only one in five patients in Maine able to access CAR T is “dismal” and having a location in the state will improve access. He said barriers to access include not only the travel time to Boston, but needing a caregiver while recovering from the infusion, and also the financial costs of traveling and lodging.
Winters said the way the therapy works is patients have blood removed, the T-cells are extracted from the blood, and the blood is returned to the patient. The harvested T-cells are shipped to a lab in California in the liquid nitrogen canister, and then returned to Maine a few weeks later.
Then the patient comes back to the office, and the engineered T-cells, designed to fight their cancer, are infused into their blood, he said.
“This is curative for patients who before had no hope,” Winters said.
Patients with late-stage lymphoma or multiple myeloma would typically have about a year or less to live without the CAR T treatments, he said.
Winters said CAR T has been available for about a decade, and is increasingly used earlier as a treatment option as outcomes from the therapy prove to work. In the future, he said, the therapy will likely become a frontline treatment for certain blood cancers, reducing reliance on chemotherapy.
He said initially it will be used on one patient at the clinic per month, but they expect usage will expand as the CAR T program at New England Cancer Specialists ramps up.
According to the American Cancer Society, CAR T is also used for certain types of leukemia, and is being researched for its effectiveness on other cancers.
According to the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention, Maine has about 400 new cases of non-Hodgkin lymphoma per year. CAR T can treat certain types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Multiple myeloma is a rarer cancer, at about 1.7% of all cancer diagnoses, according to the National Cancer Institute.
Deborah Cote, 69, of Dresden, said she was diagnosed with lymphoma in 2015, and was selected for CAR T therapy last year. Cote said she traveled to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston in March for the treatment, and had to stay in Boston for about three weeks. She said she was fortunate to have a friend willing to stay with her.
“If I could have stayed in Maine, that would have been unbelievable,” Cote said. “I have a support group here, and I missed that support group in Boston.”
Cote said the treatment has improved her life, and doctors “can’t find a wisp of cancer cells in me.”
“I feel better than I’ve felt in many years,” Cote said.

title: I see Maine’s Bill Green as a red flag
text:
Bringing Bill Green and his endorsement out for the last 30 days shows us how desperate Sen. Susan Collins is. She did the same thing when Sara Gideon was ahead of her in the polls.
Bill Green should be embarrassed. Don’t be fooled again, Maine. When Collins voiced support for the SAVE America Act, she showed who she works for — and it isn’t us.
Wayne Elliot
West Bath

title: Maine town has 100 cemeteries but nowhere to bury its dead
text:
Residents of the town of Penobscot who haven’t already bought a cemetery plot currently can’t be buried in the Hancock County town when they die.
That’s because its only two active cemeteries — the town-owned Bay Cemetery behind its post office and the association-run Hillside Cemetery at the intersection of routes 15 and 199 — are out of room.
In response, residents have voted to explore taking ownership of one of the town’s many small, private old burial grounds, the former Hatch-Hutchings Cemetery just west of Hillside on Route 15. It’s one of dozens of historic family cemeteries across the small town and hasn’t had a known owner for 136 years.
“People live in Penobscot their whole life, and when it’s time that they be laid to rest, right now we don’t have that to offer them,” Select Board Chair Harold Hatch said.
The proposal is an example of potentially reclaiming and continuing to use one of Maine’s many old cemeteries, an idea that comes as some other municipalities in the state are approaching the limits of their current burying places and looking for solutions.
Having a local cemetery available is important for people who have spent their whole lives in the town and want to be laid to rest there, according to Hatch, who would like to be buried in Penobscot himself.
Some of his own ancestors are in the Civil War-era cemetery the town is now eyeing, which he and his wife, Penny, reclaimed from the woods decades ago and have maintained for 35-plus years.
Thirty residents voted at a special town meeting Saturday to use surplus funds for the cost of taking ownership of the cemetery, according to the town clerk, Rita Martynowski. No attendees opposed it.
Hatch described the vote as authorizing the Select Board to start exploring the process with its attorney. He said it’s not likely to be costly.
Research would probably involve using a title service. If it can’t find an owner on record — which he suspects it won’t, based on his deed research — Penobscot likely would pursue taking the property by eminent domain, if voters approve the move at a future town meeting, he said.
He didn’t know how long the town has owned the Bay Cemetery or how many people are buried there, but it’s been in use since the 19th century and expanded decades ago with the purchase of more acreage from the adjoining landowners.
The abutters weren’t willing to split off more land to help grow the cemetery again, he said, leading Penobscot to look at other options.
The Hatch-Hutchings cemetery isn’t big — somewhere around 2 acres — but owning it would give the town time to figure out if any other properties it owns could become a larger cemetery, according to Hatch.
Penobscot has 73 known cemeteries, according to local research posted on the town website, about half of them found long abandoned. Hatch estimates there are about 100, either forgotten or cared for by individuals.
The Hatch-Hutchings Cemetery, too, was once overgrown and barely visible from the road decades ago when Penny Hatch noticed grave markers through the trees and thought they should clean it up, he said.
They cut down trees and cleared out brush with local helpers over a few evenings, and have continued to work on it in the following years out of respect for veterans buried there, he said. The parcel is now neatly mowed, and contains more land that hasn’t been cleared.
Its last recorded owner — also a Hatch — was in 1890. The property is not on tax rolls because cemeteries are tax-exempt.
Town records list nine known burials in the plot, including at least one Civil War veteran, between 1862 and 1894. Most are members of the Hatch and Hutchings families.
The Hatches tried to figure out how to make it an active cemetery again so they and others of their generation could be buried there, Harold Hatch said.
His mother-in-law’s headstone was recently placed on the property underneath an American flag on a flagpole with a solar-powered light, but the family hasn’t put her ashes there because the future of the property is uncertain.
Renewing it as a privately owned cemetery would require creating a nonprofit organization and other steps, he said, so town ownership seemed like a better alternative when they recently learned no more public lots were available.
“There’s like 98 other cemeteries in town, but none of them are active,” Hatch said. “We need to do something for the town, and we thought that this would probably be a good opportunity.”
A previous version of this story had a reference that incorrectly flipped the names of the Hatch-Hutchings Cemetery.

title: Cony girls soccer surges past Lincoln in second half
text:
AUGUSTA — It was a situation that might have caused concern for the Cony girls soccer team if it had happened a month ago.
Instead, the Rams responded with a flourish.
After falling behind in the second half, Cony scored two goals in the final 20 minutes to beat Lincoln Academy, 2-1, in a Class B game Wednesday afternoon at Fuller Field.
The Rams (8-4-1) are in a title battle with Hermon, Skowhegan and Belfast for fourth place in the Class B North Heal points standings as they continue their climb after starting the season with three losses in their first four games.
“That was huge, that was a really big game for us,” said Cony junior forward Kya Douin, who had a goal and an assist. “We knew (Lincoln Academy) was a really good team and we had to work hard in the last few practices and just grind it out.”
Here are some other takeaways from Wednesday’s game:
How did it happen?
After a scoreless first half, Lincoln (8-4) took the lead when sophomore Dory Westhaver pushed the ball into the net from a scrum in front of Cony senior keeper Charlotte Gearhart off a corner kick.
Cony responded less than four minutes later when Douin sent a kick from 17 yards that bent to the left and over the head of Eagles keeper Natalie Hanna.
“You could see, from that moment, we felt like we were going to win,” said Cony coach Michael Sweeting.
Four minutes later, Douin sent a perfectly placed ball up the middle of the field to junior forward Riley Miller, who took off on a breakaway and knocked a low shot past Hanna.
What does it mean?
After a 3-7-4 record a season ago, Cony has already secured its best season under Sweeting. In the last two weeks, the Rams have a victory over Class B North rival Erskine Academy and a tie against Class C South contender Hall-Dale.
“We’re not just a boot-it-and-run team anymore,” Sweeting said. “We still play forward fast, we still try to be aggressive, but it’s with a purpose now.”
Not only will the Rams be in the playoffs, but with Wednesday’s win, they’ll likely host a preliminary-round game.
“This team has really done a good job of getting together and playing for each other,” said Sweeting, who is in his third year leading the program. “It’s been a little bit of a journey for this team … It looks like we’re going to have a home playoff game next week, and it’s been a minimum of 16 years since (the program) has had that.”
Lincoln entered the match ranked No. 5 in Class B South, with a season sweep over Erskine on its record.
Unsung hero
Playing in her final regular-season game at Fuller Field, Gearhart made six saves for the Rams and was a vocal leader for a defense that allowed just three shots in the second half.
“Our defense is our rock right now,” Douin said. “We have so much faith in them in the back. I don’t worry about them at all.”
Gearhart was one of the two Cony seniors honored before the game, with midfielder Kelsie Huard.
“They really deserve (this win),” Sweeting said of his two seniors.
Statistical leaders
Cony: Kya Douin (1 goal, 1 assist), Riley Miller (1 goal), Charlotte Gearhart (6 saves)
Lincoln Academy: Dory Westhaver (1 goal), Natalie Hanna (7 saves)

title: Candidates for district attorney, at-large councilor make cases at Portland forum
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — With just over two weeks until Election Day, candidates seeking votes for Cumberland County district attorney and Portland’s councilor at-large seat attempted at a downtown forum Wednesday to separate themselves on how they would tackle public safety in Maine’s largest city.
The forum, organized by the Bayside Neighborhood Association and Portland Downtown, was recorded in front of a studio audience at the Portland Media Center, where candidates faced a series of questions squeezed into half-hour segments.
CUMBERLAND COUNTY DISTRICT ATTORNEY
The candidates for Cumberland County district attorney — Stephanie Anderson and incumbent Jacqueline Sartoris — largely picked up where they had left off during recent public appearances, trading jabs regarding each other’s record and how the prosecutor’s office should be handled moving forward.
Sartoris, elected in 2023, has been on the defensive as Anderson continues to claim that the district attorney’s office has been in disarray under Sartoris, and that it’s led to a loss of accountability that’s now reflected on Portland streets.
“People are getting away with too much,” Anderson said.
Sartoris responded that under her tenure, there’s been a drop in the crime rate, and that cases are up 44% compared to when she took office. But, she said, she’s also followed through on reform-minded work regarding sexual assault cases and plans to expand that work to domestic violence.
While Anderson said Sartoris was elected as the result of partisan politics, Sartoris continued to cite Anderson’s ties to the Republican Party.
Anderson, first elected in 1990 and reelected six times, was a registered Republican throughout her tenure. After stepping down in 2018, she served as chair of the Cumberland County Republican Committee, and has continued to receive support from Maine conservatives.
Democrats have criticized Anderson for running as an unenrolled candidate, calling it an attempt to distance herself from the Republican Party in a deeply Democratic county.
Anderson responded Wednesday that she unenrolled from the Republican Party when she stepped down as district attorney, not when she decided to run for the office.
“There’s a lot about both parties I do not like,” she said.
Anderson, 73, has garnered support from police unions and a number of attorneys. So far, she’s also outraised Sartoris in campaign contributions.
Anderson said she was “happily” retired when approached by people across the political spectrum to come back.
“Public safety has been shattered, morale destroyed,” she said during her opening statement.
Sartoris said she has emphasized “a return to charging” following a pandemic-era dip, and that the county has also seen a decrease in the “return to jail rate,” or people returning to jail within 30 days.
She also defended the office’s current relationship with law enforcement agencies. Anderson said that if she’s elected, the relationship would improve “the minute I get elected,” and she claimed police are not bringing cases because they don’t think they’ll be prosecuted.
Sartoris said “the numbers show otherwise,” but that reform also means change, including her recent push for agencies to take a harder line on bicycle and pedestrian-related crashes, calling it “a shift for local departments.”
Both also said changes are needed in the approach to mental health to address public safety in Portland. In line with Mayor Mark Dion, Anderson said the county should establish a secure treatment center at the Cumberland County Jail.
The pair also had a rare agreement on another topic: state legislators need to take action to get more prosecutors on the job in Maine to address the backlogged caseload.
COUNCILOR AT-LARGE
The candidates for Portland’s councilor at-large seat provided a slightly calmer view of the issues at play for one of the three City Council seats up for grabs Nov. 3.
Each candidate attempted to showcase a brand: Atiim Boykin as the social worker and artist who will keep working class people in Portland; Joey Brunelle as a progressive organizer who can expand democracy in the city and get more minds together to solve problems; and Kate Snyder as the civil servant who has the experience and credentials the city needs right now.
The questions offered were related to the Bayside Neighborhood Association’s goals, and ranged from public safety and social services to greenspace and tree canopy.
When asked how Portland could share the social service burden across the city, Brunelle said locating the Homeless Services Center on Riverside Street has made it more difficult for people to access services, and that Portland needs smaller scale services in more locations so that a single neighborhood doesn’t see the “full brunt of helping those in need.”
Snyder, the former mayor, said the council previously looked at that idea but it didn’t gain traction due to the cost.
Boykin, who works in behavioral health, is proposing a collaboration among city nonprofits that streamlines services.
The candidates were also asked about the city’s inclusionary zoning policy and housing production. All candidates said some form of change is needed to unlock more development to address housing affordability.
Snyder said she’s in favor of reverting to the previous policy, which required that large developments include 10% affordable units (the current policy requires 25%).
“We were never meant to have static policy,” she said.
Boykin said the city should “experiment” with the model, perhaps having zones where the policy doesn’t apply. Brunelle would form a task force to look at not just inclusionary zoning, but also permitting and other policies that play a role in housing production.
“Let the experts tell us,” he said. “Expand the circle of voices.”
The candidates also debated pedestrian safety, how the city could empower neighborhood associations and how they would support equity with greenspace across the city.
The vacant “Midtown” properties in Bayside also came up during the discussion, with Snyder stating that any housing built there should also include greenspace and connectivity to Deering Oaks and other parks.
Brunelle said residents need to “take matters into our own hands” to replicate programs that are working and get city committees to be better utilized. He said in the current era, we need to “go back to a barn-raising form of government.”
In a final plea to voters, Boykin said he’s part of the class of people that are the first to get pushed out when a city gets attractive. He said he wants Portland to be a safe place where the working class can continue to live.
“I’m not running to do the same job, but just a little bit better,” Brunelle said. “I offer a new way of approaching problems, by bringing more people into the process.”
Snyder said the current times call for a candidate who isn’t about politics, and is “serious about serving the community.”
“I’m ready to do that,” she said.

title: South Portland will vote on emergency ICE ordinance
text:
South Portland may soon restrict city employees from cooperating with federal immigration enforcement through a city ordinance.
The City Council said at Tuesday’s meeting that it will bring forth an emergency ordinance at its next meeting on Oct. 27 to get a firmer statute on the books before election day. South Portland would join other cities like Portland, Lewiston, Rockland, Waterville (and potentially Biddeford on Oct. 20) in officially restricting staff cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
“If it gives people in our community 1% less fear and 1% more hope, we absolutely should move it forward as quickly as we can,” Councilor Carter Scott said.
No city employee would be able to voluntarily work with immigration enforcement, nor could any municipal funds or resources be used to facilitate enforcement, per the draft ordinance’s language.
City employees would not be able to allow ICE officers to use city-owned properties for staging or processing, nor could they provide those federal agents with special access to nonpublic areas.
The ordinance would stipulate that city employees, including police officers, would not participate in stops, arrests or detentions on behalf of ICE, nor would they be able to share addresses, contact information or immigration status beyond what is required by law.
All city staff would be trained about the specifics of the policies, and any suspicious activity would be directed to the city manager’s office, who would then report aggregate information to the council and through an annual report.
Right now, school employees are not included within the language of the ordinance, but if School Board members and the school district’s lawyers agree they should be included, the council could amend the language to include these staff members.
To pass an emergency ordinance, the council will need to unanimously vote on the language and a preamble explaining why the urgent matter should bypass the typical ordinance process (which would take several weeks, including two readings and a waiting period).
City employees are currently unable to cooperate with immigration enforcement officers, so the policy wouldn’t necessarily change the status quo, according to City Manager Scott Morelli.
That stance has been in place since 2017, when the city passed a principle that it would not cooperate with federal immigration enforcement or use city resources to support surveillance based on race, ethnicity or national origin.
The city passed a resolution in early February, following the surge of immigration enforcement, that expanded upon that charge. It was mostly symbolic, acknowledging the fear and disruption caused by federal agents’ presence in the city.
Since then, residents have continued to call on the city to do more, out of concern about the safety of immigrant neighbors.
There has been an ongoing ICE presence in Greater Portland. Members of immigrant communities have continued to be detained in the street, at work, at home and at the ICE processing facility in Scarborough.
ICE has arrested more people in Maine this year than in the previous two years combined, according to data from Jan 1. Through July 31 analyzed by the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition. South Portland tied with Lewiston for the highest number of detentions in the state, at 64 people.
City staff and leaders can’t control ICE’s activity in the area, nor will this ordinance deter detainments, Morelli said.
“We do have authority over what our own city government does,” Mayor Elyse Tipton said.

title: Maine can no longer justify Susan Collins
text:
In some other time, the reelection of Sen. Susan Collins might be justifiable. These are not ordinary times. Now we need to recall what we learned in our elementary classrooms: The United States is a democracy protected by three branches of government to ensure adequate checks and balances; that way, no one branch harms its citizens’ freedoms and security.
Susan Collins has failed to safeguard our country against an executive branch run amok. She expresses “concern” when she needs to act — against a president who wages war and kills children; violates established civil rights; enriches himself while working Americans struggle to buy food, fill their gas tanks and provide for their children; and who damages the environment endangering future generations.
Collins has failed her responsibility to stop this man’s terrifying destruction. All we can do is vote for Troy Jackson.
Ellen McQuiston
Anson

title: New York to ban horse-drawn carriage rides in Central Park
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New York City lawmakers plan to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park, ending their more than 150-year run as an iconic, old-timey tourist attraction, following decades of opposition from animal welfare activists and the death of a teenage tourist last spring.
The City Council is expected to approve a bill next week that would end the rides by 2028. Three consecutive mayors had called for an end to the carriage rides because of safety concerns, only to have lawmakers yank back the reins.
A spokesperson for Julie Menin, the council speaker, confirmed the incoming vote and said the proposal had enough support to pass. Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office said he had reached a deal with the speaker on the legislation.
“The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City,” Mamdani said in a social media post.
Teen’s death reignited debate over carriage rides
The latest push for a ban started in June, when 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, visiting the city from India, died after jumping from a runaway horse carriage during a ride with family members. His death, which appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park, reignited the debate over whether carriages, a romantic throwback to the city’s past, have a place in a modern metropolis.
Mahajan’s family has appeared at City Hall, in person and through videoconference calls from India, begging the city to finally end the rides.
“We are shattered, our whole family shattered. The pain does not go away,” his father, Deepak Mahajan, told city council members via a videocall during a hearing for the bill last summer, saying his son leapt from the carriage to try and help his mother, who was flung from her seat, after the horse bolted. “Every morning we wake up and think of nothing but the loss of our son.”
For decades, animal welfare activists and other critics have decried the carriage industry, arguing horses shouldn’t be hauling tourists around busy streets and Central Park while having to navigate bustling traffic and gawking passersby. In the past, horses have collapsed, gotten startled and run off, hitting cars or other objects, with each accident resulting in fresh calls for a ban.
“The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable. Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City’s history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability,” Menin said in a statement.
The industry and its supporters have long cast the rides as a way for visitors to experience the New York they know from classic movies and television.
Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse danced into one of the carriages in “The Band Wagon.” Robert Redford and Jane Fonda rode one in “Barefoot in the Park.” Macaulay Culkin escaped bandits in a carriage in “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.”
“Taking a horse and carriage ride in New York City is one of the most iconic things to do in New York City and people from all over the world know about us and travel to New York to go to a carriage ride in New York,” Conor McHugh, a longtime carriage driver, told the Council earlier this year.
Mayors have faced pushback in efforts to ban rides
Efforts to close down the industry have been met with pushback from unions and influential supporters, often resulting in tiresome political fights that have seen mayors throw up their hands over nagging worries about putting carriage drivers out of work and what to do with the horses if they can no longer work.
Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen said the Council’s bill has “no meaningful economic relief for workers” and that Menin “used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis.”
“This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families’ livelihoods are being destroyed. This entire situation is reprehensible,” he said in a statement.
The proposal as written would require the mayor’s office to develop a workforce transition plan for drivers, and includes a measure that would allow the city to consider some kind of compensation for industry workers. Carriage owners could not sell their horses off for slaughter, according to the bill’s language, which requires that horses be disposed of in a “humane manner.”
“I think we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry,” Mamdani told reporters Wednesday.
The mayor’s predecessor, Eric Adams, called for ending the industry during the waning days of his administration, but the proposal went nowhere. The mayor before that, Bill de Blasio, had pledged to eliminate the rides on day one of his administration but abandoned the crusade after heavy opposition from unions and a media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson.
Over the years, the city has placed various safety regulations around the industry, including a requirement that the horses get at least five weeks of vacation a year outside of city limits with daily access to a pasture. The horses are inspected by a veterinarian twice a year, and the maximum age they can work at is 26, according to city regulations. And they don’t work when it is hotter than 89 degrees.

title: ERIC’S TECH TALK: Simulated not Super, Mr. President
text:
President Trump wants to rename artificial intelligence. From now on, he says, it should be called “Super Intelligence,” or SI for short. He explained why at the United Nations General Assembly in September. “The use of the word ‘artificial’ makes intelligence fake,” he said. “It makes it sound fake and it is not fake.”
He’s right about one thing. The word “artificial” does make it sound fake.
That’s exactly why we should keep it.
I’ll give the president this much: names matter. What we call a thing shapes how we see it. That’s why he wants to change the name, and it’s why I’d rather we didn’t.
We usually worry that AI will one day outsmart us. The more immediate danger is that we’ll mistake a convincing performance of intelligence for the real thing.
I felt that pull the first time I used AI. As a writer, one of the first things I tried was giving it a character profile from one of my novels and asking it to play that character in a conversation with me. There was a moment of unreality. It felt like my character had come to life and was talking to me through the screen.
But the longer I experimented, the more the spell wore off. I noticed how easily I could reshape the performance. Change the profile and I got a different character, just as convincing as the last. It was a good trick. A very useful and entertaining trick, but a trick nonetheless.
And like any trick, it loses its power once you see how it’s done. People who walk away convinced AI is truly intelligent are like the person who leaves a magic show sure that magic is real.
So how is it done? Pour water into a glass bottle and it takes the shape of the bottle. But the water never becomes the bottle. AI does the same thing with language. It takes on the shape of whatever context you pour into it.
But AI writes code and passes exams, you might say. Isn’t that intelligence? It’s useful, and often impressive. But a performance of understanding isn’t proof of understanding.
AI resembles the human mind because it was built to. Its designers borrowed from what we’ve learned about the brain and trained it on mountains of human language. We shouldn’t be surprised when it sounds like us. But sounding like us doesn’t establish that it thinks like us, too.
I’m not saying we’ll never build a truly intelligent machine. A future technology might be different. But we should be certain before we accept that a machine truly thinks, because so much follows from it. In fact, whether AI is truly intelligent may matter less than whether we believe it is.
Belief alone is enough to do harm. If we trust a machine’s judgment and act on it, the consequences are real, whether its intelligence is real or simulated.
Sociologists call this the Thomas theorem: “If men define situations as real, they are real in their consequences.” A healthy bank can fail because enough depositors believe it’s failing. There were no witches in Salem, but enough people believed there were, and more than 20 people died.
AI is a tool to enhance our own abilities. But start treating its judgment as superior to our own and the roles flip. We stop using it to help us think and start letting it decide for us.
So who benefits if we believe this is real intelligence? Look at who’s telling the story, and who’s selling it. Calling a product “intelligent” is a marketing claim, like the promise that social media would connect us all. (Mostly, it just ate our time and divided us.)
Calling it “Super Intelligence” is the same pitch, turned up. “Super” invites us to believe the machine knows better than we do. That’s a useful belief for anyone selling it.
When we believe a machine knows better, we trust its answers, defer to its judgment, and stop checking its work. And when something goes wrong, treating the machine as an independent decision-maker gives people somewhere to hide.
In the classic 1939 movie The Wizard of Oz, the Wizard calls himself “the Great and Powerful Oz.” He was the original super intelligence, but he turned out to be just a man running a show. Caught out, he booms, “Pay no attention to that man behind the curtain!” I’d say pay every attention to him. These days, he likely works for a tech company.
When an AI chatbot sounds warm or wise, ask what context you gave it. Enjoy the trick, but know it’s a trick. Keep a human in charge of the decisions that matter. And when something goes wrong, blame the people behind it, not the machine.
We already have a name that reminds us, every single day, that a convincing performance can still be a simulation. If it has to change, make it Simulated instead of Super.
If the president wants to call it SI, I’m happy to oblige. Just remember what the S stands for.
Eric W. Austin lives in China and writes about technology and community issues. He can be reached by email at ericwaustin@gmail.com.

title: Midcoast businesses and individuals having real conversations with future leaders
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This week is a direct reflection of my recent activities, as I have been meeting with students about paid internships and I have been interviewing candidates for statehouse offices. They are very different conversations, but both relevant for the businesses in our region.
Let’s start with the students, as “I believe that children are our future, teach them well and let them lead the way” (cite your sources: Whitney Houston). But seriously, our students are literally our future. We are amidst the greatest generational employee shift of this century, and potentially of the last 45 years. We haven’t seen this amount of new employee onboarding since the mid-1970s/early ’80s when many baby boomer kids turned working age and flooded the economy with troves of new workers. The tail end of those boomer workers are retiring after four-plus decades of a career, and for the last eight years, we’ve been replacing employees with great institutional knowledge, with those who need training to get up to that same level of understanding.
Our chamber has been helping these transitions through our ChamberWorks 2030 workforce programs which began in 2021. That has evolved into our current partnership with United Way of Mid Coast Maine, where together we recruit students to engage with local businesses through internships, and other programming. The umbrella for this work is called Connecting To Tomorrow, and it’s now in its third year.
The program is essentially recruiting businesses to be internship host sites and then connecting students from Morse, Brunswick, Richmond, and Mt. Ararat high schools with 20-40-hour paid internships in the industries they want to explore. Additionally, the United Way and I go into the classrooms at least twice per school year to get the students excited and educated about the program, and those presentations have been happening for a couple of weeks now.
The students we meet are incredible, engaged, and nervously excited to pursue these opportunities. Sure, getting paid from the grant is nice, but they truly want the experiences. When we take questions from them, it becomes evident why they want these experiences (and this is where you come in) — because they don’t have the same advantages we did.
When I was their age, I routinely had to call friends’ houses and talk to their parents before talking to my friends. These students don’t have that opportunity, so they are worse at cold calling and speaking to strangers.
When I was their age, everything was in-person, so you learned to read body language. You had in-person moments of connection outside the confines of online screen — they have less and less of that.
When I was their age, if I wanted to date, I’d have to have an awkward conversation — I couldn’t send a text message to avoid the messy stuff. No wonder they struggle with any awkward conversations now.
Which is all to say, beyond what they will learn about a specific industry, these internships also give essential life skill opportunities. Negotiating your work schedule; communicating about being late; asking questions when you are unsure; expectation setting so the employer knows what you are good at, and what you may need help with. All of these are essential workplace skills, that these students haven’t dealt with. Please, take a moment to consider being an internship host site, so that together we can shape these students into the leaders of tomorrow (e-mail [email protected]).
Speaking of leaders, I am nearly halfway through the 23 interviews that I am trying to complete by Friday, Oct. 23, with the candidates for the statehouse who represent all, or even a portion, of our 16-community chamber region. These 10-12-minute videos give you a great flavor of the candidates and their views. As an update: All confirmed videos will be released on Oct. 23 or earlier. You will find those links on our chamber social media channels, including Facebook, and on our chamber website.
The big takeaway thus far is this: These are normal citizens who strive to do their best. Yet the only way they can do their best is to hear from you, their constituents.
Maine is a part-time legislature, and these candidates run for office out of a sense of service, but also out of the sense that they can help create the solutions. I have spoken about a variety of needs in these interviews thus far, with heating oil, housing, and overall affordability being the most frequent topics. However, each legislator has a topic or two beyond that which they are passionate and knowledgeable about too.
Bottom line: these candidates are extremely approachable — so approach them. Push back if you disagree — they love to talk through it. A great example was in a data privacy conversation I had with one legislator which is a topic likely to come up again. The candidate mentioned how the issue gets confused and citizens don’t know what the bill will do, and I echoed that from a business leader standpoint. We talked about creating a simple T-bar to help communicate the issue, where on one side it says “Here’s what you can do now online,” and on the other side, “Here’s what you can do if the bill passes.” We identified the problem, talked about the issue, and came up with a solution — that’s how this is supposed to work!
So don’t get tied to partisan bickering — ain’t nobody got time for that. Regardless of their party, on Nov. 4 we will have a slate of legislators who are there to represent you.
So, if they come to your door before Election Day, talk to them, or shoot them a message. Because at the end of the day, they want to do what’s right, regardless of party. At the very least, watch our videos to get a good sense of them — I think you will be impressed with their insights.
Cory King is executive director of the Bath-Brunswick-Topsham Regional Chamber of Commerce.

title: House Speaker Mike Johnson campaigns for Paul LePage in Bangor
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Speaker of the House Mike Johnson (R-LA) made a stop in Bangor Wednesday to speak to Paul LePage supporters.
Johnson said Maine’s Second District race is one of the most important in the country for the Republican Party.
He stressed the importance of getting out to vote on Election Day, noting midterms typically have lower voter turnout.
The Speaker says LePage is the kind of person the Republican Party needs in Congress.
“On the 250th anniversary of the greatest nation in the history of the world, we are fighting to literally save the Republic. Exactly. And to do that, I gotta have patriots and experienced, thoughtful guys like Paul LePage, okay? He is overqualified to be in Congress, and I’m so glad you’re willing to do it,” said Speaker Johnson.
LePage faces Democratic nominee Matt Dunlap in the midterm election.
WABI will host a debate between the candidates Thursday evening.

title: UUCB partners with Portland church for concert benefitting Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project
text:
The Unitarian Universalist Church of Brunswick and Woodfords Congregational Church of Portland will host a concert to benefit the Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project at 7 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 24, at Woodfords Church. The concert will feature a wide variety of music, poetry and dance presented by Maine artists from a diversity of cultural backgrounds and life experiences.
Musical artists include Madeleine Hanna and the four-person Jawahir Arabic Music Ensemble performing song and dance primarily from Lebanon; the Pihcintu Multinational Girls Choir along with the band Akiwacu, featuring the voices of children from 16 different countries impacted by war, famine and turmoil; and Hadithi Abdulle, oud player and singer from Somalia, presenting music on the theme of resiliency and personal testimony. Poetry will be shared by Jeri Thériault, a Franco-American poet from Maine, and Richard Blanco (via video) — selected by President Barack Obama as the fifth inaugural poet in U.S. history. Signed copies of his poetry suitable for framing will be available by donation. The evening will be topped off by the Singing Resistance chapters of both Portland and Brunswick-Topsham who will lead songs developed in 2026 as resistance cries in the face of the Minneapolis ICE occupation. Pulling this all together will be emcee Mohamed Awale, a Brunswick comedian.
Donations will be accepted at the door and go directly to ILAP as well as to presenting artists who have been impacted by recent immigration activity. ILAP is Maine’s only statewide provider of free immigration legal services. ILAP advances justice for Maine’s immigrants through free immigration legal services, community outreach and advocacy.
Doors open for the concert at 6:30 p.m. Woodfords Congregational Church is located ta 202 Woodfords St., Portland.

title: Federal judge orders Trump administration to halt work on historic DC golf course until Oct. 26
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes on Tuesday ordered a halt to tree-cutting at the East Potomac Golf Course until Oct. 26, putting a further pause on work at the historic D.C. course that has been part of President Donald Trump’s plans to remake the city.
Reyes issued the order one day after a tense three-hour hearing in which she harshly criticized the government for having deceived her with its actions over the holiday weekend.
At the Monday hearing, Reyes ordered a 24-hour pause that could be extended to 14 days if necessary. It was limited to one day while the government tried to find a key Trump administration official to discuss why a massive tree-cutting at the park needed to occur over the holiday weekend, with little notification to plaintiffs in a lawsuit trying to halt renovation plans or the judge.
The judge also ordered during that period the government “must provide the court and plaintiffs three business days’ written advance notice prior to making any irreparable modification to any permanent form or feature of the East Potomac Golf Course.”
The DC Preservation League and two local golfers are the plaintiffs in the lawsuit.
The co-counsel in the case, Democracy Forward, thanked Reyes for stepping in and halting what the group called the “mad rush” to turn the public recreation space into a high-end golf course. “We are pleased that the court intervened and will prevent additional work while we seek more lasting relief,” the group said in a statement.
The Monday hearing and Tuesday order were prompted by the National Park Service ordering the cutting of hundreds of trees at the golf course after filing the court notification only minutes before the close of business on Oct. 9 on a holiday weekend, giving the plaintiffs little time to respond. At least 400 trees were cut down over the weekend with plans for several hundred more.
In explaining her order, Reyes said the court, based on limited information so far, concluded that government officials raced to undertake a tree management plan at the park “because President Trump demands haste on his redesign, and not because of some newfound zeal to implement a small part” of a 2019 National Park Service Cultural Landscape Report that suggested work was needed at the district’s public golf courses.
The historic park, especially the golf course, caught the eye of Trump, who wants to turn it into a world-class golf venue. It’s part of his grand vision for Washington, D.C., where he has multiple projects underway, including a $400 million White House ballroom and the soon-to-begin construction of his triumphal arch. He began talking about the city’s public courses in late 2025.
“When completed, this Course will have the ability to host Major Golf Tournaments, including The U.S. Open, The Ryder Cup, The PGA Championship, and other top PGA Tour events,” Trump posted on social media in June.
The course has been the subject of multiple emergency hearings, including one in May in which Reyes was out of the country, because of concerns from the plaintiffs that the administration would move ahead with work despite the pending lawsuit. In each instance Reyes declined issuing temporary stop orders out of trust for the government’s attorney in the case.
“Every single time I have given the government the benefit of the doubt and every single time I made absolutely clear that I want notice,” Reyes said at Monday’s hearing. “What has happened has cost the government all credibility with me.”

title: You can see the history of PEZ as it celebrates 100 years
text:
ORANGE, Conn. (InvestigateTV) - For 100 years, tiny candy bricks have been hiding inside some of the most famous faces in American history.
PEZ, the iconic candy, is made and packaged at the company’s factory in Connecticut, the only PEZ manufacturing facility in the United States.
“It’s part pop culture; it’s become an American icon, essentially. Everybody knows PEZ,” said Shawn Peterson, direct-to-consumer business manager at PEZ Candy, Inc.
At the PEZ Visitor Center in Orange, the company’s history fills every shelf and even the floor.
Peterson, who also serves as the company historian, has contributed much of what’s inside from his personal collection of about 5,000 dispensers.
“I lost track of that a long time ago,” Peterson said.
The history of PEZ is well documented. The witch or Halloween dispenser came out in the mid-1950s. The first licensed character was Popeye, followed by Mickey Mouse in 1961.
The brand started in Austria as a peppermint candy marketed to adults as an alternative to smoking. PEZ arrived in the United States in the 1950s and eventually made Connecticut its American home.
Twelve million pieces of PEZ roll off the line each day at the Orange facility. Everything made there is shipped from the location.
The recipe is simple — sugar, flavoring and pressure. The little brick shape has not changed in more than 90 years.
Workers make the candy in 600-pound batches. Every roll is sorted, lined and packaged to ship. The factory’s see-through windows give about 80,000 global fans a year a chance to see how their favorite candy is made.
“We get people from all over, not just here in the U.S. or the East Coast, but globally. I’ve got people from probably 80 different countries,” Peterson told us.
As America celebrates its 250th anniversary, PEZ is celebrating its centennial. For the one-hundred-year-old brand, half of its history has been in the United States.
PEZ is rolling out an entire year of plans to celebrate, just as they did during America’s bicentennial in 1976 with Uncle Sam, Betsy Ross and a little colonial soldier dispensers.
“They all say made in the USA,” Peterson said.

title: Aging Untold: How to support aging parents through loss of a child
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we navigate the unimaginable grief of losing a child and discuss where parents and families can find meaningful support.
We also break down what causes involuntary tremors, how to distinguish them from conditions like Parkinson’s and when to consult a physician.
Finally, we introduce you to a 78-year-old logger, polo umpire and state lawmaker proving it is never too late to reinvent yourself.
No parent expects to lose a child. When an older adult suffers the unimaginable loss, their grief is often overlooked, but there are things families and caregivers can do to help.
The Aging Untold hosts say that acceptance — not resolution — is the realistic goal, and staying connected with loved ones can help with healing.
For friends and family who aren’t sure how to support a grieving parent, Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, said they don’t need the right words — just their presence.
If you have experienced a new tremor, it can be unsettling.
Essential tremor and tremors associated with Parkinson’s are not the same, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
An essential tremor is a movement disorder that causes parts of your body to shake, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
Some causes behind a new tremor can be treated and reversed.
Rogers recommends sitting down with a physician to rule out underlying causes before assuming a tremor is benign.
Brett Horn has created the only child safety demonstration house in the United States in the hopes that it will prevent the type of tragedy that happened in his own family.
Horn and his wife lost their 2-year-old son, Charlie, when a 30-inch dresser fell on him in 2007.
“I want Charlie’s legacy to be that other children are not harmed from simple things in their own home,” Horn said. “And I believe we’re accomplishing that.”
He founded Charlie’s House in Kansas City, Missouri. It is an interactive home that teaches parents about hidden dangers that experts say cause 90% of childhood accidents.
Read the full article here to get a look inside Charlie’s House and learn about the dangers you can prevent.
At 78, Jed Lipsky works alone cutting down pine trees in Vermont.
He said logging is considered the most dangerous profession in North America, and he has had multiple surgeries and broken bones during his 55 years in the profession.
During his “pretty complex life,” Lipsky has been a competitive skier, a pilot and a professional polo player. He also now serves in the Vermont Legislature.
“I’m definitely the only logger in the Vermont Legislature,” Lipsky said. “I feel very fortunate.”

title: Six Flags Over Georgia set to reopen on Friday after deadly roller coaster accident
text:
ATLANTA (ANF/Gray News) — Six Flags Over Georgia is set to reopen on Friday, just four days after a man was killed when he fell off a roller coaster.
Six Flags Over Georgia’s website shows the park will reopen Friday.
In a statement, the park’s management called safety its “highest priority.”
“While we are unable to comment on specifics related to the incident or currently closed rides at this time, we are committed to rigorous ride inspection, maintenance and safety procedures that meet or exceed industry standards,” officials added.
PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Six Flags Over Georgia roller coaster death: Everything we know
On Monday, 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem was ejected from the Goliath roller coaster, hitting other patrons on the ride, according to Cobb County police. His body was found underneath the attraction, and the park was evacuated.
The death is still under investigation, with no official cause given yet.
In the wake of the accident, Six Flags temporarily shut down nine rides across six parks that were similar to Goliath. The coaster — which goes up to 70 mph, has a maximum elevation of 200 feet and drops twice — uses clamshell lap restraints to secure passengers.
Kariem was a beloved teacher at Wesley International Academy, a K-8 charter school in Atlanta. Soledad Gomez, one of his former students, described him as a joyful man.
“I always just remember his smile and his glasses, and it’s just like, he never got mad at us. He was always patient with us. He would joke with us,” Gomez said.
In a statement, Six Flags said it’s cooperating with the police investigation.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends, and loved ones. We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected,” a Six Flags spokesperson said. “The park team and local authorities responded immediately, and we are cooperating fully with local authorities as they complete their investigation. Out of respect for the family’s privacy, we will not be sharing additional details at this time.”
Since Kariem’s death, Six Flags has temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six parks “out of an abundance of caution.” Officials said the affected attractions are similar to Goliath, which only uses a lap bar to secure riders.
Though Six Flags Over Georgia will reopen Friday, Goliath will remain temporarily closed. In a statement, the park’s president said Goliath does not have an anticipated reopening date yet.
