title: Here are the 3 candidates running unopposed for Bangor School Committee
text:
Three parents are running for three open seats on the Bangor School Committee, meaning all will automatically win a seat.
We asked them about their plans for the role and their stances on the big decisions facing Bangor’s school department, including how the district may reorganize in the face of aging facilities.
All three agreed that it’s not financially feasible to continue maintaining 10 schools, but there were differences in their proposed solutions.
The uncontested election contrasts with the 12-candidate City Council race, which is the largest pool in at least four decades.
Only one School Committee candidate, Katie Brydon, is running for reelection, while current chair Timothy Surrette and member Shelly Okere are stepping down. Surrette is term-limited.
Election Day is Nov. 3 and voters can request an absentee ballot through Oct. 29.
School Committee candidates are listed below in the order they appear on the ballot.
Jamie Beck
Jamie Beck, 40, grew up in Bangor and returned 11 years ago. She works as a lecturer and graduate assistant at the University of Maine while she’s pursuing a master’s degree in business administration, and previously worked as a speech language pathologist in public schools.
Beck, a Democrat, has three children in Bangor schools and said she volunteers regularly with her children’s schools and the parent teacher organization. She decided to run for School Committee after one of her children was affected by the relocation of Fairmount School this year into a wing of the high school due to asbestos and other repair needs.
She said her top priority would be to implement strong communication from the school department as it works through the upcoming decisions regarding facilities and possible school consolidation.
“Fear bubbles up in a vacuum,” she said. “I can be a voice for frequent, clear, honest and complete communication between everyone involved.”
Beck said she’d like to encourage schools to expand nature-based learning programs, and to work on leveling the playing field for students by examining disparities in outcomes, test scores and student experiences between schools.
“I would love to see how we can, in all of the strategic planning conversations, ensure that all of our students have what they need so that we do have much more consistent outcomes,” she said.
She noted that while Bangor’s neighborhood schools are really important for younger students, she thinks the district is “doing them a disservice” by waiting until high school to combine students from the east and west sides of the city. She’d like to see schools consolidate at the middle school level, and then later at the upper elementary level while maintaining neighborhood schools for the youngest students.
At the outset of the election, it was unclear whether Beck would be able to be sworn in because her husband, Michael Beck, is a city councilor. The city later clarified that she would be allowed to serve due to new evidence establishing that the School Committee is excluded from a nepotism rule barring immediate family members of councilors from serving on council-appointed boards.
Katie Brydon
Brydon, 42, grew up in the Bangor area and has lived in the city since 2013. She has three children in Bangor schools and is the executive director of Nature Links, a Blue Hill-based nonprofit that teaches adults with disabilities. Her previous experience includes working in schools and writing disability education policy.
Brydon is a Democrat and the only candidate who has already served on the School Board after being elected in 2023. She said her three years on the committee have given her a better understanding of the major gaps in the school system, like aging infrastructure, behavioral challenges driven by factors ranging from technology to the opioid epidemic to COVID-19, and more support for teachers.
She said her top priority would be to address Bangor’s aging school facilities by balancing what the city can afford with the ethos of the school district and the community, making the upcoming changes “as palatable and thoughtful and inclusive of this vibrant community as possible.”
For Brydon, that means avoiding the elimination of neighborhood schools — a message she heard loud and clear in the backlash to the department’s quick response to facilities issues at Fairmount last year. At the same time, she said that she sees reducing the number of schools in the district as the fiscally responsible choice.
“Having 10 schools across 3,400 students no longer makes sense,” she said.
Similarly to Beck, Brydon also added that consolidating students before they reach high school could also help ensure that their experiences are more similar, acknowledging that many residents see disparities between schools on the east and west sides.
“What I want to continue to do is to challenge every student to reach their full potential,” she said.
Brydon ran for state legislature this spring with the goal of advocating for better school funding at the state level. She lost her primary but said she still sees working more closely with state legislators as an important tool for securing more funding and support for Bangor’s teachers.
Emily Tilton
Emily Tilton, 37, grew up in Bangor and moved back to the city after attending college and post-graduate training to be a pharmacist. She said she’s always enjoyed serving children, both in her job working in pediatrics and during a several-month stint in her last year of pharmacy school when she worked as a substitute teacher in Bangor and Brewer.
She has two children in Bangor schools and volunteers as a coach for her daughter’s soccer team in the city’s parks and recreation department.
Tilton, a Republican, said she decided to run for School Committee after seeing how technology was being used in her son’s classroom. Her top priority is to ensure that all technology use in the school department is evaluated for learning outcomes, effects on students and whether it aligns with data-driven best practices. She said she’d like to see a full audit of technology use in the district.
“I think that really, technology should be used for its true intent, which is as a tool, and I do not think that technology should be used as a form of teaching or a form of learning,” Tilton said, pointing to the risk of harms associated with constant distractions and lost opportunities to build communication skills. She’d especially like to minimize technology use between pre-k and fifth grade and implement rules around artificial intelligence use.
Tilton also said she wants to “bring back the conversation of academic achievement” that she experienced as a student in Bangor schools by encouraging more public discussion and support around programs that drive academic excellence.
“It’s not going to look the same for every student, but every student is capable of achieving,” she said.
She also thinks there are opportunities for parents to help support Bangor teachers more, such as by volunteering and running storytimes in classrooms.
On the issue of aging facilities, Tilton said she’d like to preserve the feeling of neighborhood schools, which are “really woven into the fabric of our community” and offer benefits like walkability, smaller class sizes and close relationships with school administrators, while also being mindful of the tax burden imposed by expensive school repairs.
She said she wouldn’t support consolidation into large citywide schools and wants to keep schools to 400 students or fewer, but suggested a middle ground like expanding the neighborhood schools to include fourth graders and moving fifth graders up to the district’s middle schools.

title: One dead, two hospitalized in Bangor house fire
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - One person is dead and two others are hospitalized following a fire at a home in Bangor early Wednesday morning.
Fire crews were called to the home at the corner of Cedar and Second streets just after 6:30 a.m., where authorities say five people reside.
Person found inside home
Officials say when crews arrived, three people in the street told them someone may still be inside.
Bangor Fire Chief Eric Pelletier said despite the crew’s efforts, that person did not make it out.
Neighbor describes scene
A neighbor who spoke with WABI described the scene.
“Flames were coming out the attic and the firefighters were having a hard time fighting it and shortly after I arrived, the family was notified they had lost their loved one. I’m just in shock. You know it’s sad when tragedy hits so close to home like this and you know when you see these people day after day and everything, knowing that they’re dealing with this pain and this loss, it’s truly heartbreaking,” said Joshua Hutchins.
The neighbor said shortly after he got home, he saw a family member from the home searching for their dog and he helped look.
Pets rescued, others killed
The dog was found, and one cat was rescued. Authorities say another cat and a dog died in the fire.
The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

title: DOJ threatens California with legal action over alleged noncitizens on voter rolls
text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice has threatened California with possible legal action over what it says are noncitizens believed to have received mail ballots for next month’s midterm elections.
A letter sent Tuesday to Secretary of State Shirley Weber from Trent McCotter, the acting deputy U.S. attorney general, says the department has provided officials in Los Angeles County with a password-protected thumb drive that contains a list of names the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent ballots to participate in the Nov. 3 election.
California mails ballots to all registered voters.
The letter obtained by The Associated Press gives the state 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are included on the list. For individuals whose citizenship cannot be independently verified, the state is to instruct local election officials to segregate their mail-in ballots until their status can be determined, and to not provide a ballot to anyone who has not yet received it. The letters warns that legal action may follow if the state does not meet the 48-hour deadline to review the list.
“If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief,” the letter states.
Weber’s office issued a statement late Wednesday saying the Justice Department gave it 48 hours to obtain the list from Los Angeles, investigate it and take action, noting the demand was being made just three weeks before Election Day.
It also said that over the summer, the Department of Homeland Security claimed that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls, but refused to provide the methodology or data sources when the office asked for them.
“Now the USDOJ, under threat of ‘emergency’ litigation, demands that California blindly trust this administration without any evidence or legal authority to justify its request,” Weber said in the statement.
She said California requires that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that those who are not eligible are removed from the voter rolls.
Unclear how many names DOJ flagged
A separate, similar letter was sent to the registrar’s office in Los Angeles County, which the U.S. attorney’s office had investigated during the state’s June primary.
Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan said in a statement that his office also received a thumb drive, along with a “hand written note providing a password” to access the list of alleged noncitizens on the voter rolls. The secretary of state’s office said the password was written “on a sticky note.”
Logan said he did not consider the thumb drive a secure device and hasn’t yet accessed any files. The letter, which Logan made public, does not specify the number of individuals flagged by the federal government.
Logan said his office is working with the secretary of state and attorney general’s offices to decide how to proceed.
“Federal and state laws are clear on how voter eligibility is established,” Logan wrote. “And any action to remove a voter from eligibility must be based on verifiable information, not assertions of unconfirmed data matching.”
California Attorney General Rob Bonta slammed the letter in an unrelated press conference on Wednesday, calling it another example of President Donald Trump spreading “absolutely false conspiracy theories that there is widespread voter fraud when there is not.”
Bonta did not say how the secretary of state’s office would respond to the Justice Department, but said: “Will we be engaging in conspiracy theories? We will not.”
Nationwide search for alleged noncitizen voters
The Trump administration has made the hunt for noncitizen voters a priority this year, even though the problem is exceptionally rare. The Justice Department has charged about 90 people for various types of election misconduct so far this year, including 50 who are alleged to have voted as noncitizens. There were more than 227 million registered voters in the United States during the 2024 presidential election.
In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to California, Nevada, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, alleging that as many as 250,000 noncitizens were registered in those states. Election officials there were skeptical of the claim, including Weber, the California secretary of state.
“I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official,” Weber said in response.
That same month, the Republican administration claimed Nevada had 1,500 noncitizen voters on its voter rolls. But after the federal government identified them to the state, the number of actual registered noncitizens turned out to be zero.
As part of its project to find noncitizens on the voter rolls, the Justice Department has been seeking detailed voter information — including dates of birth, addresses, driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers — from the states. Some Republican-led states have turned over the information, which has been run through a U.S. Department of Homeland Security database that has been criticized as inaccurately flagging U.S. citizens.
The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for that information, but so far has lost those cases in court. California is among the states that successfully sued, in part by arguing that turning over the data would violate state privacy laws.
Election official calls 48 hour deadline “unreasonable”
Santa Cruz County Clerk Tricia Webber, who is president of the California Association of Clerks and Election Officials, said she had not seen the letters but said the 48-hour deadline to vet voters flagged by the federal government was “completely unreasonable.”
She said when there is a report of an ineligible voter incorrectly on the rolls, her office does due diligence to investigate. That involves looking at the voter’s registration history, identifying whether that person had voted before and, most importantly, reaching out to the voter, she said.
“It would take more than 48 hours to even begin to get the full picture,” Webber said. She also questioned how the federal government came up with a list of alleged noncitizen voters since it doesn’t have access to the state’s detailed voter information.
Webber added that throughout the course of her decades-long career working for local election agencies, she has “never seen anything that would make me believe that our voter records are filled with fraudulent voters.”
___
Associated Press writer Sophie Austin in Sacramento contributed to this report.

title: Here are this week’s 3 Maine high school football games to watch
text:
This season, Varsity Maine reporters will offer up suggestions each week for three games that are worth a drive to watch in person, with a brief explanation of why we think these games are worth a fan’s time.
With just two weeks to go in the regular season for most Maine football teams, and three remaining for some, there are several season-defining matchups.
And for some teams, this is the second week in a row in which that’s the case.
Here are three Week 7 games to keep on your radar:
Hermon (6-0) at Greely (5-1), 7 p.m. Friday
Still undefeated, Hermon has made light work of its opponents, outscoring them 258-32. The Hawks have yet to face their first true test, which should come against the defending state champion.
Greely had a 21-game winning streak broken by Leavitt in its second game of the season — a rematch of the 2025 state final. Since then, the Rangers have won four in a row. They defeated Oceanside 35-8 last week behind four touchdowns from quarterback Luke Piper.
Could Greely be the team that finally knocks off Hermon, or will the Hawks affirm their status as a title contender?
South Portland (4-2) at Noble (2-4), 7 p.m. Friday
South Portland and Noble were dealt two of the state’s most difficult schedules this fall.
The Red Riots and Knights have both had to face Class A South juggernauts Bonny Eagle and Thornton Academy — the top two teams in the Varsity Maine 11-man football poll — and Noble also has played fourth-ranked Marshwood.
South Portland got the best of another strong A South team in Massabesic last week, while Noble lost to the Mustangs on Oct. 2.
Currently sitting in fourth place in the A South Heal point standings, the Red Riots could essentially clinch a playoff spot by defeating Noble, which is fifth and one spot out of the postseason.
The Knights prevailed when the two teams faced off last year. After such a topsy-turvy first six games of the season, Noble badly needs a win to realistically keep its playoff hopes alive.
Portland (5-1) at Oxford Hills (4-1), noon Saturday
Through the first six weeks of the season, Portland and Oxford Hills have emerged as the front-runners in Class A North, so this game could be a regional final preview.
Both teams were undefeated until recently. Portland lost to Thornton Academy, 43-13, on Oct. 2, and the Vikings lost to Bonny Eagle, 45-6, on Oct. 9.
Portland won last year’s regular-season meeting, and Oxford Hills never got a chance to avenge that loss, as Bangor knocked off the Vikings in the semifinals.
The Bulldogs will have to be on the lookout for a rushing attack spearheaded by junior Keegan Ridley and quarterback Toby Oufiero, the latter of which tallied four touchdowns against Lewiston on Oct. 2, while the Vikings will have to be wary of Portland’s Alex Martin, who rushed for two touchdowns against Bangor last weekend and gained 219 yards against Thornton.

title: Former Cumberland County district attorney outraises incumbent in campaign contributions
text:
Stephanie Anderson has outraised incumbent Jacqueline Sartoris in campaign contributions, as both vie to be elected district attorney in Cumberland County.
A quarter of Anderson’s donors are attorneys, records show.
Sartoris, a Democrat from Brunswick, was elected in 2022 and recently won her party’s nomination in a June primary against one of her former prosecutors. As of Sept. 1, Sartoris had raised $35,000, including $15,000 in loans, according to campaign finance records. Most of that was received before June 9 and roughly $4,500 came from eight contributors after the primary election.
Anderson, who was district attorney for 28 years before retiring in 2018, had raised more than $69,000 as of Sept. 14. At least 40 contributions came from practicing and retired Maine attorneys, according to an analysis of campaign finance records and a directory run by the Maine Board of Overseers of the Bar.
“I think that really tells you a lot,” said Jennifer Ackerman, a long-time Cumberland County prosecutor who worked under Anderson for 16 years, including seven years as her deputy.
Publicly, the two candidates have sparred about who is most qualified to prosecute what are known as “quality of life crimes,” like public drug use and disorderly conduct, and about the implementation of progressive reforms.
Inside the courthouse, attorneys who have donated to Anderson’s campaign have complained about Sartoris’ leadership. Anderson said she was approached by prosecutors and defense attorneys, “across the political spectrum,” asking her to run. Anderson is running as an unenrolled candidate.
“I mean, I go by yards with my sign beside Troy Jackson signs,” said Anderson, who was reelected seven times as a Republican. “This is an elected position, but it’s not partisan and it should not be politicized.”
Sartoris has said she is aware of discontent among defense attorneys and several prosecutors who have left the office and spoken out publicly, including Ackerman and Valerie Adams, who lost to Sartoris in the Democratic primary.
Sartoris has said it’s proof that she’s making the changes that she promised voters in 2022. In debates and forums, she’s highlighted her recent efforts through a federal grant to inventory untested rape kits, and a recent revamp of the county’s existing restorative justice options.
“This is not a popularity contest for lawyers, who usually want to preserve the status quo,” Sartoris said in a statement. “I ran to bring long-needed change to the people of Cumberland County. I have more regular people on my side, with more donors and more small dollar donations than Anderson. Soliciting money from defense attorneys seems like a conflict of interest.”
Sartoris’ primary campaign four years ago drew an unprecedented $300,000 from an out-of-state political action committee funded by Democratic donor George Soros. The candidates still have another week before they file their newest campaign finance reports. Anderson said on Thursday she has raised another $14,000 in individual contributions since mid-September.
Anderson also serves and is running for another term on the Cape Elizabeth Town Council. She says she has not fundraised for that race.
ENDORSEMENTS
At least eight individuals who have contributed to Sartoris’ campaign this year are attorneys, according to records from the bar and campaign finance reports.
John Kaminski, who donated to her campaign in September and is an attorney focused on affordable housing, praised Sartoris for her work on homelessness and for directing police to share evidence from bike and pedestrian crashes.
“I think she’s had a solid four years in office and will continue to move things forward when she’s reelected,” Kaminski said.
Rep. Grayson Lookner, a Democrat in Portland, said Sartoris has been supportive of his legislative proposals to improve public safety, particularly for diverting at-risk youth from the criminal justice system. House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, a Democrat in Biddeford, said he endorsed Sartoris because of her opponent’s Republican history.
“We’re seeing this across the state that the Republican brand is so bad, that they’ve decided to put a cloak over that label and have ‘unenrolled’ candidates,” Fecteau said. “Voters should know that we have a very strong Democratic district attorney in Jackie.”
Anderson says she believes Sartoris is using the Democratic nomination to her advantage because she doesn’t have enough to highlight from her four years in office. Anderson also accused Sartoris of distorting her remarks.
At a forum hosted by Scarborough town leaders in September, Sartoris accused Anderson of having expressed a desire to work with federal immigration officials.
“I never said that local law enforcement should cooperate with ICE,” Anderson said in an interview, noting that state law restricts police from working with federal immigration officials. “I think I said there’s been a lot of injustices with ICE and it’s been pretty horrific. And why is that a big campaign issue?”
Sartoris previously stated her intent to prosecute agents who commit violent offenses without cause in her district. She has not charged any agents to date.
Anderson suggested the attorneys supporting her campaign “are the people that are paying attention to what’s going on to the DA’s office and what’s going on in the community regarding public safety.” She also highlighted endorsements from three police unions as evidence of her ability to work with law enforcement on prosecuting cases.
Scot Mattox, an attorney who was a Portland police officer for more than 20 years, said he probably arrested more than 1,000 people whose cases Anderson prosecuted.
“Stephanie recognized that a district attorney’s duty is not merely to secure convictions, but to administer justice fairly,” Mattox said in an email.
Former employees who spoke to the Portland Press Herald said they appreciated Anderson’s mentorship and her knowledge of criminal law.
“We can all agree, despite our different professional experiences, that when people like where they work, they care, they work harder, and the morale is stronger,” said defense attorney Kate Marshall, who interned for Anderson and later returned to the office as an assistant district attorney. “This can only benefit the community to which the office serves.”
CRITICISMS
Ackerman said she resigned less than a year after Sartoris took over. Ackerman, who now works for the state, said she was speaking only on her own behalf.
Adams worked in the district attorney’s office for about nine months. Adams was fired by Sartoris after she and a defense attorney asked Sartoris to consider not running.
Adams and Ackerman have both likened Sartoris’ office to a “ship without a captain.”
“She was very much focused on saying what she wanted to do in terms of policies, but the day-to-day work, and the day-to-day policies that our prosecutors needed, we weren’t getting answers,” Ackerman said.
Others have criticized Sartoris’ work in court, saying criminal cases are languishing and that she has at times gone beyond what they believe to be appropriate for her role.
“For me, that makes life for defendants and people who are caught up in the criminal justice system harder,” said defense attorney Rob Andrews.
On the mental health docket, Sartoris said she has dedicated much of her focus on defendants whose mental health might lead them to be found incompetent to stand trial, or not criminally responsible. Attorney Alison Brauner said Sartoris has pushed for forcible medication and the disclosure of clients’ sensitive health information.
“A criminal defendant doesn’t lose their right to privacy around their medical care,” Brauner said.
In a statement, Sartoris said she “will not apologize for asking a judge to medicate people, always at the request of an expert, when their untreated psychotic disorders are causing repeated criminal conduct.”

title: Death Notice: Cynthia “Cindy” Anne Chapman
Grad student who allegedly poisoned a colleague has been arrested fleeing to China
text:
CHEYENNE, Wyo. (AP) — A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she didn’t get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested Oct. 6 at Los Angeles International Airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment — research similar to work she’d done in China.
Wang remained jailed without bail Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.
U.S. officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.
The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.
“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your student’s life is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told The Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”
Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.
Amateur sleuthing helps campus cops develop case
The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “K.T.,” began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.
Wang allegedly was recorded Sept. 27 going through the alleged victim’s desk. On Oct. 1, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.
Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.
During an interview by campus police on Oct. 5, Wang allegedly said she “had not used acrylamide in years.” A day later she was taken into custody in Los Angeles while in possession of “multiple laptops, multiple portable external digital storage devices, related accessories, physical records and written materials,” according to a request by Wyoming prosecutors to “significantly increase” her $200,000 bond upon extradition.
Wang had no reason to go through the desk of the other student whose federally funded, patent-pending research involved “new technology for cancer, neurological and genetic disease treatment,” according to the affidavit.
Wang “was reportedly working on similar research in China before coming to the U.S.,” the affidavit alleges.
A high-achieving student from Vietnam
Gomelsky described the alleged victim as a highly successful student from Vietnam.
Wang failed her first attempt to defend her dissertation and became envious of her colleague’s success in discovering how to deliver RNA to human cells using bacteria, Gomelsky told The Associated Press.
The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.
He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.
Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.
Wang had not been doing lab work since June while she worked on her dissertation, he said.
Suspect faces return to Wyoming to face charges
Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.
It’s not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany County Circuit Court Judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5 million cash-only.
Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.
Best known as a carcinogenic byproduct of cooking starchy food and burning tobacco, acrylamide can be acutely toxic in high doses. It’s used in microbiology research involving proteins or DNA.
Discovery of the substance immediately made Tak Sumaya, an assistant professor who helped identify it in the coffee maker water, suspicious. Acrylamide is “not something you would find in that kind of quantity anywhere,” Sumaya said.
The alleged victim was working on “a pretty promising cancer therapy method,” Sumaya said. Wang, Sumaya added, took photos of every page of a notebook the alleged victim left on his desk.
“You wouldn’t do that with like your office or lab mate’s notebook unless there’s a really good reason, and there wasn’t,” Sumaya said.
Professor says the victim is still experiencing symptoms
The alleged victim went to the campus health clinic in August with worsening finger tingling and numbness, and leg weakness. Suspicion led his wife and others to boil away coffee maker water from the shared office to isolate 63 milligrams of white powder that tested positive for acrylamide, according to the affidavit.
The amateur investigators turned the sample over to university police.
The alleged victim continues to experience symptoms from the poisoning, including not being able to focus, tiring easily and a loss of sensation in his left hand, Gomelsky said.
“Acrylamide is a neurotoxin that cannot be neutralized so it stays in neurons and basically kills them. So it’s unclear if he’ll fully recover or not,” the professor said.
___
Brown reported from Billings, Montana, and Riddle from Los Angeles.

title: Whitewashing history is no path to peace
text:
It is hard to imagine a more vacuous and willfully one-sided column than Douglas Rooks’ Oct. 8 piece (“‘Genocide’ or not, US must seek an end to the suffering in Gaza”). In more than 760 words ostensibly offering a solution to Gazan suffering, Rooks places blame entirely on Israel — by my count, he mentions either Israel or Netanyahu by name 24 times while mentioning Hamas but twice.
Whitewashing history provides a weak foundation for peace; serious problems require acknowledging inconvenient facts. It was Hamas that militarized Gaza’s civilian infrastructure and embedded its war-making apparatus among the people it purported to represent. It was Hamas that initiated this war with its murderous Oct. 7 attack, then sheltered its fighters in tunnels while leaving Gazan civilians above ground to endure the foreseeable Israeli response. And, it was Hamas’ continued captivity of Israeli hostages that prolonged the conflict, compounding Gazans’ suffering.
Exploiting civilians — Gazan and Israeli — is integral to Hamas’ strategy. Yet the column never confronts Hamas as an obstacle to resolution. It contemplates Netanyahu’s removal through Israeli democratic elections without considering whether Hamas’ removal from power would advance the cause of peace. Wouldn’t an honest assessment of peace prospects examine the governing entities on both sides?
Lasting relief requires an honest and serious reckoning with the conduct and responsibilities of all parties to the conflict. Ignoring Hamas while focusing solely on Israel is neither honest nor serious and provides no path to peace.
Daniel Kagan
Lewiston

title: Worried on behalf of heating oil customers in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Department of Energy’s statistical arm, the Energy Information Administration, announced that total winter heating bills, for households using heating oil, are projected to be 21% higher on average this winter compared to last winter.
The price of heating oil is forecast to average $5.26 per gallon, a 34% increase nationwide. A slightly milder winter in the Northeast is going to slightly lower consumption by about 9%, which will help to soften the total bill increase down to 21%.
I attended college in Maine and lived in Portland and Gorham in the mid-’90s. I have friends in Maine who have been struggling over high energy prices. This winter’s heating bill will require them to make difficult budgetary sacrifices elsewhere.
George Albrecht
Warwick, R.I.

title: Trump may scrap plan to livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution, sources say
text:
FORT HOOD, Texas (CNN) - President Donald Trump and his advisors are debating whether to call off plans to livestream the execution of the Fort Hood shooter, according to sources.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hassan last week.
Democrats and some Republicans raised objections about the idea.
Trump’s position
Sources say the president was not initially aware of Hegseth’s plan but firmly backs the idea of using a firing squad to kill Hassan.
Hassan was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding dozens of others at Fort Hood in 2009.
Law enforcement responded to the attack and shot Hassan in the back. He has been paralyzed from the waist down ever since.
Sources say Trump does not necessarily like the optics of livestreaming the execution of a man in a wheelchair.
Hassan is set to die on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood.

title: Maine man wanted after police search Rumford apartment following reports of gunfire
text:
RUMFORD, Maine (WMTW) — Authorities are searching for a Maine man who is wanted on several felony charges connected to an incident that prompted a shelter-in-place advisory in the town of Rumford on Wednesday.
Blake Lachance, 21, of Lewiston, is wanted on one count each of aggravated assault with a dangerous weapon, criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon and reckless conduct with a dangerous weapon.
The Rumford Police Department said officers and members of the Maine State Police Tactical Team executed a search warrant at a first-floor apartment at 209 Waldo St. following an investigation into reports of gunfire and suspected drug trafficking at the home.
Rumford police said that over the weekend, they received information concerning suspected drug trafficking involving locals and people from out of town at the Waldo Street apartment. Police said they also received reports from concerned residents, who told police that people associated with the apartment were armed and had been periodically firing guns in the surrounding neighborhood.
Before sunrise Wednesday morning, Rumford police responded to a report of gunfire in the Waldo Street area. Responding officers determined that the people believed to be involved had been inside the apartment and were potentially still there.
Given the possibility of encountering armed suspects, officers from the Rumford Police Department and Oxford County Sheriff’s Office established a perimeter around 209 Waldo St. while investigators prepared applications for search and arrest warrants.
The Maine State Police Tactical Team was called in to help secure the area and execute the search warrant, which was authorized by a court late Wednesday morning.
Police said that as officers prepared to search the apartment, Rumford Public Works crews established temporary road closures and traffic detours in the surrounding neighborhood. MedCare Ambulance paramedics were also staged nearby as a precaution.
In a Facebook post shared shortly before 12:15 p.m. Wednesday, Rumford police said people near the intersection of Waldo Street and Maine Avenue were advised to shelter in place and stay inside.
Rumford police said the Maine State Police Tactical Team entered the apartment shortly before 1 p.m. and determined the suspects were no longer inside. Investigators believe the suspects had fled the apartment several hours earlier, around the time police initially responded to the report of gunfire Wednesday morning.
At 1:20 p.m., Rumford police announced that the shelter-in-place advisory had been lifted and that roads that were closed were being reopened.
According to officials, a subsequent search of the apartment, coupled with information developed during the ongoing investigation, yielded additional evidence supporting the reports that police received from members of the public.
Police said Lachance should be considered potentially armed and dangerous, so members of the public should not approach or attempt to confront him.
Authorities are asking anyone who has information regarding his whereabouts to immediately contact law enforcement.
The investigation in Rumford remains active, and police said more people are expected to face criminal charges as investigators continue to develop evidence and identify those involved.

title: Iowa faces a reckoning over water quality and cancer rates in midterm campaigns
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Iowa is facing a budget deficit, high costs and economic strain from trade disputes that have squeezed farmers.
But problems that have simmered for decades — water quality and cancer rates — have been forced to the forefront of state politics this year. They are the focus of debate questions, roundtable events and campaign advertisements for candidates from both parties, up and down the ballot.
The issue has historically been politically taboo to avoid pointing fingers at the powerful agricultural industry in Iowa, one of the country’s top producers of corn, soybeans and hogs. Chemical fertilizers and animal waste contain nitrates and phosphorus that can get washed with rain or snowmelt into the state’s web of rivers.
The problem has long caused tension between Iowa’s more liberal urban centers, which rely on rivers and lakes for drinking water, and mostly conservative stewards of its rich farmland. Farmers are increasingly participating in practices to prevent runoff, although critics say the lack of regulation forces downstream Iowans to pay for the pollution.
The spotlight has grown — and the political calculus has shifted — after back-to-back years of restrictions on water use in the Des Moines area coupled with a burgeoning “Make America Healthy Again” movement in Iowa’s small town and rural communities.
Cancer rates are a growing problem in Iowa
Iowa has the second highest rate of newly diagnosed cancers in the country. Specific diagnoses, like prostate, breast and lung cancer, are increasing in Iowa faster than in the U.S. overall. It’s affecting urban and rural parts of the state.
New state-funded research at the University of Iowa shows most — but not all — of Iowa’s above-normal rates for five cancers can be explained by demographic and behavioral factors, such as smoking and binge drinking. Researchers next assess environmental factors, including nitrate levels.
“The real issue is the water and the nitrates,” said Democrat Josh Turek, who is running for U.S. Senate, as he talked with cancer patients last week. “Every Iowan deserves when they turn on the tap to ensure that their water is clean and not giving them cancer.”
Some studies have found a link between nitrates in drinking water and certain diseases, but it remains an area of debate. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency does not currently classify nitrates as a cancer risk. The agency initiated a plan to review that assessment in 2017, but it’s been stalled, revived and stalled again under different White House administrations.
The Republican congresswoman running against Turek, Ashley Hinson, recently gathered farmers, researchers and local officials to discuss Iowa’s water problems. She said there is an ongoing need for investments in infrastructure, water quality monitoring and conservation programs but also said that Iowans can feel safe because tap water meets federal regulations.
“We all know that we have some challenges here in Iowa,” she said. “I don’t think water quality is a partisan issue.”
Farm runoff is a key contributor to river pollution — and political tensions
It’s been more than a decade since the Des Moines area’s water utility, fed up with paying roughly $16,000 per day to remove nitrates from water, sued counties further upstream to get them to help cover the cost. The complaint was ultimately dismissed, and Iowa’s Republican leaders celebrated the ruling.
Last year, Central Iowa Water Works issued its first-ever ban on lawn watering to reduce demand on its nitrate removal facilities, and state politicians rejected any suggestion of a “blame game” that would implicate farmers. Iowa had been investing nearly $100 million annually in its nutrient reduction strategy in recent years.
In May, though, Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds and lawmakers committed an additional $320 million for water infrastructure, conservation initiative incentives and other projects, including millions to Central Iowa Water Works to update equipment.
“Water quality isn’t a farm issue. It isn’t a city issue, and it isn’t a political issue,” Reynolds said. “But it absolutely is non-negotiable.”
Still, criticism of slow progress has continued, including from candidates running to replace Reynolds.
Governor candidates make the issue central
Republican Zach Lahn and Democrat Rob Sand both emphasize that the state needs to better prioritize the water problem, though neither have called for mandating farming conservation practices that reduce runoff.
Lahn, who was endorsed early in his primary by political committee MAHA Action, has diverged from many of his Republican peers in directly linking polluted water and agrochemicals to Iowa’s cancer crisis.
At Lahn’s agriculture-focused town hall in northeast Iowa in August, one attendee raised the issue.
“Right now the farmers, I would say, are really getting blamed for the high cancer rate in Iowa,” she said. “Even our daughter calls from Des Moines and says: ‘Should we be drinking this water?’”
Lahn said he knows certain agrochemicals are important “tools in the tool chest.”
“We’re not here to ban products,” he said, “but we do have to address the water quality issue.”
Federal regulations say drinking water is safe with a maximum nitrate level of 10 milligrams per liter. That threshold was set to prevent what’s known as blue baby syndrome, a condition when an infant’s blood doesn’t have enough oxygen, but more scientific studies are now analyzing the relationship between nitrate-laden water below that threshold and certain cancers.
Lahn said he tested the nitrate levels from his well water and creek in rural east-central Iowa, finding both well above the federal limit.
Central Iowa Water Works ran its nitrate removal treatment for a record 193 days straight earlier this year, and the treated water’s nitrate levels hovered around eight to nine milligrams per liter in the heart of summer.
Sand usually references water early in his stump speech, naming one reason he initially registered as a Democrat is the party’s advocacy for clean water because he likes to fish. He said Tuesday after meeting with cancer survivors and parents of children with cancer that he’s seen the topic rise in the public consciousness over the past few years.
“I hear from people regularly who are so concerned about it that they wonder whether or not they want to be in Iowa,” Sand said.
Iowa’s race for agriculture secretary illustrates the tension
Twenty years ago, research scientist Chris Jones said he’d give his boss at Des Moines’ water utility updates on the rivers’ nitrate levels.
“He’d say to me, ‘Where’s the outrage?’” Jones recalled. “Now, the outrage has arrived.”
Jones, who later worked on water quality monitors at the University of Iowa, says it’s a huge failure of the state for Iowans to lose faith in drinking water.
Jones is a Democrat running in the election to be Iowa’s secretary of agriculture, trying to unseat incumbent Republican Mike Naig.
Chief among their differences is whether conservation solutions should be mandatory. In a debate, Naig said Jones is an outlier in demanding farmers be required to adopt conservation practices. Iowa’s agricultural industry resists mandates, in part because not all farmers own the land they farm and some conservation efforts might lead to profit loss, at least initially.
Naig, who previously worked for chemical manufacturer Monsanto, highlighted the records that his department has set under Reynolds’ leadership and said conservation work is being scaled up to accelerate progress.
“It’s been a hot topic on the campaign trail,” Naig said, but “we have to have a long view of these things, and we’re making progress.”

Aging Untold: How to support aging parents through loss of a child
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we navigate the unimaginable grief of losing a child and discuss where parents and families can find meaningful support.
We also break down what causes involuntary tremors, how to distinguish them from conditions like Parkinson’s and when to consult a physician.
Finally, we introduce you to a 78-year-old logger, polo umpire and state lawmaker proving it is never too late to reinvent yourself.
No parent expects to lose a child. When an older adult suffers the unimaginable loss, their grief is often overlooked, but there are things families and caregivers can do to help.
The Aging Untold hosts say that acceptance — not resolution — is the realistic goal, and staying connected with loved ones can help with healing.
For friends and family who aren’t sure how to support a grieving parent, Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, said they don’t need the right words — just their presence.
If you have experienced a new tremor, it can be unsettling.
Essential tremor and tremors associated with Parkinson’s are not the same, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
An essential tremor is a movement disorder that causes parts of your body to shake, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
Some causes behind a new tremor can be treated and reversed.
Rogers recommends sitting down with a physician to rule out underlying causes before assuming a tremor is benign.
Brett Horn has created the only child safety demonstration house in the United States in the hopes that it will prevent the type of tragedy that happened in his own family.
Horn and his wife lost their 2-year-old son, Charlie, when a 30-inch dresser fell on him in 2007.
“I want Charlie’s legacy to be that other children are not harmed from simple things in their own home,” Horn said. “And I believe we’re accomplishing that.”
He founded Charlie’s House in Kansas City, Missouri. It is an interactive home that teaches parents about hidden dangers that experts say cause 90% of childhood accidents.
Read the full article here to get a look inside Charlie’s House and learn about the dangers you can prevent.
At 78, Jed Lipsky works alone cutting down pine trees in Vermont.
He said logging is considered the most dangerous profession in North America, and he has had multiple surgeries and broken bones during his 55 years in the profession.
During his “pretty complex life,” Lipsky has been a competitive skier, a pilot and a professional polo player. He also now serves in the Vermont Legislature.
“I’m definitely the only logger in the Vermont Legislature,” Lipsky said. “I feel very fortunate.”

title: Katie Zacharia’s White House debut raises new questions about the press secretary’s job
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump’s new press secretary stepped to the podium, the eyes of a packed room of journalists — and many in their audiences — upon her. She smiled broadly at the sea of faces both probing and friendly. With that, Katie Zacharia went live and became the official voice of the world’s most powerful person.
Fourteen minutes and just three questioners later, she was done. In the aftermath, it was clear that the former Newsmax commentator accomplished at least one thing: She put the “brief” back in briefing.
In her debut Tuesday, Zacharia looked downward and often read directly from a script. She paused and grinned when she uttered the words “Department of War.” She stumbled on a question about her background and mixed up the words “husband” and “president.” The few questions she took were nonconfrontational and from media outlets that have been sympathetic to the Republican president. In short: She made no memorable impression — or at least, to hear some tell it, not the one she likely wanted.
This would not be an easy job under any circumstances. Trump most frequently serves as his own spokesman. And his antagonism toward the media has created a new layer of tension. Zacharia is finding out on day one that she, too, will be under constant watch. Some — including a few of those who have stood in her shoes — didn’t think it went all that well.
In fractured times, in a national media scrum unimaginable just a few decades ago, what is the proper way to approach a job like this? How do you speak effectively when your boss speaks for himself so often that he commandeers the news cycle multiple times a day — and sometimes late into the night — with remarks provocative, unexpected and sometimes incendiary?
For one, you realize for whom you work: not your audience of millions but your audience of one, and the absolute need for his approval.
“I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people,” Zacharia said. Nowhere did she mention the task of disseminating accurate information to Americans.
The press secretary role has been many things
Over the nearly 10 decades since former journalist George E. Akerson made his and the office’s debut as Herbert Hoover’s press secretary in 1929, the job has served many purposes: deliverer of information, amplifier of policy, jouster with journalists, protector of the presidential reputation and, sometimes, overlord of obfuscation.
Under Trump and his second-term press secretary so far — Karoline Leavitt, who resigned in August — the job has been primarily one of acting as the immovable object against an irresistible, and in Trump’s eyes sometimes treasonous, force.
Leavitt got to know this terrain well in her 17-month tenure. She took a smiling but combative stance against a press that was increasingly coming under Trump’s criticism for coverage — and was named in at least one lawsuit about White House media access. She was not shy about interdicting what she considered media bias. “What a stupid question,” she said to one reporter at a briefing last year.
Trump, outside the White House on Tuesday shortly after Zacharia’s briefing, praised her debut as “excellent.” She was standing behind him at the time.
Other early reviews were more critical. MS NOW quoted one unnamed White House official as saying of the performance: “She needs to get much better fast, otherwise she’ll break Scaramucci’s record.” Anthony Scaramucci, an early White House communications director for first-term Trump, lasted 11 days in 2017. Said Scaramucci on X Tuesday afternoon: “I hope she makes it.”
Joe Biden’s former press secretary, Jen Psaki, now the host of a show on MS NOW, put it more succinctly, posting on X: “Well that briefing was basically an SNL skit….except it wasnt.”
Talking up Trump but taking few questions
While Zacharia’s performance — and of course, that’s what every briefing is — may have been bumpy to some, it was also mostly content-free except for news she broke about the White House asking U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to quit, which she immediately did.
Predictably, also like Leavitt before her, Zacharia spent a great part of her opening monologue praising Trump and giving an “up ‘til now”-style update on his second term’s priorities and accomplishments so far. Talking points included a “booming economy,” “his historic boom in energy production” and “a great relationship with Venezuela.”
She was also fond of superlatives, a trait that likely will resonate with a president whose remarks are often equally if not more expansive: “President Trump is working to secure the Western Hemisphere for centuries to come.”
When it came to questions, though, she was downright parsimonious. She allowed three questioners, then answered an additional one as she prepared to depart. The three called on during the briefing were Breitbart, Fox News and the Daily Mail, all of which have been friendly to Trump in varying degrees during periods of his two terms. And she said she would continue Leavitt’s policy of bringing “new media” in — which has often meant outlets more sympathetic to Trump.
“We love new media and we want to be able to embrace it,” she said. Currently, three major outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — are fighting to regain White House access after Trump banished them last month, saying he didn’t like their coverage and calling it “fake news.”
How will Zacharia fare in coming days and weeks and, if it lasts, months? That, like so much else, depends on one thing: Donald Trump.
The late U.S. Sen. Howard Baker once famously said that, when being asked difficult things, handle it something like this: If you don’t like the question being asked, just answer a different question. On Tuesday, a half-century later, Katie Zacharia found a different way in — pick three nonconfrontational questioners, then defer to your boss and say: The End.

title: Father sentenced for killing 9-year-old daughter after claiming she was abducted while on vacation
text:
ELIZABETHTOWN, N.Y. (WCAX/Gray News) - A Montreal man was sentenced Wednesday to 25 years to life in prison for killing his 9-year-old daughter and concealing her body in New York.
Luciano Frattolin, 45, was convicted by a jury in August for killing his 9-year-old daughter, Melina, in Ticonderoga on their way back from vacation in July 2025.
New York State Police said Warren County 911 received a call from Frattolin reporting that his 9-year-old daughter was missing in a possible abduction, which led to an AMBER Alert being issued.
Hours after the alert was issued, Melina was found dead. Her body was found north of Lake George Village, near the state border with Vermont.
Investigators said the pair had been traveling through parts of the Northeast together for the last week and were headed back to Canada when Frattolin allegedly killed his daughter and dumped her body.
“You tried to show her how much fun you could have with her, and something happened, and no one other than you will be able to tell us what happened. Like everyone that has heard of this story, everyone wants to know why,” the judge said.
During the trial, prosecutors said cellphone and car data placed Frattolin in the Ticonderoga area the night Melina was killed, even as he insisted she was kidnapped and denied being there.
The district attorney also pointed to notes Frattolin wrote mentioning “ending the madness” and making a decision about Melina, who he claimed was mentally ill.
The judge handed down a sentence of 25 years to life for second-degree murder and a consecutive sentence of one to three years for hiding Melina’s body.
“We continue to suffer deeply since the day Melina was brutally murdered. Nothing can bring Melina back, but we are relieved that this chapter is over,” said Essex County District Attorney Michael Langey.
Despite being satisfied with the sentence, Langey said he’d like to see changes in the state’s criminal justice system regarding who can be charged with first-degree murder, which carries the potential for longer sentences and no eligibility for parole.

title: Ahead of 3rd anniversary, survivors of Lewiston mass shootings call for accountability
text:
Key Takeaways Key Takeaways are written by Maine Trust staff and highlight the most important points of this article so you can get the gist at a glance.
- Mass shooting survivors and victims’ family members gathered Wednesday in front of the media nearly three years after the Oct. 25, 2023, tragedy.
- Some survivors continue to call into question how $1.9 million of the $6.6 million raised in the aftermath of the shooting reached area nonprofits instead of victims’ families and survivors.
- They say they have been denied an audience with the Legislature’s Government Oversight Committee.
LEWISTON — With the anniversary of the Oct. 25, 2023, mass shooting approaching, some victims, survivors and their families gathered at Veterans Memorial Park on Main Street to hold a news conference.
Standing in front of the cameras, Amy Sussman read the names of the 18 people killed at Just-In-Time Recreation and Schemengees Bar and Grille: Ronald Morin, Peyton Brewer-Ross, Joshua Seal, Bryan MacFarlane, Joseph Walker, Arthur Strout, Maxx Hathaway, Stephen Vozzella, Thomas Conrad, Michael Deslauriers II, Jason Walker, Tricia Asselin, William Young, Aaron Young, Robert Violette, Lucille Violette, William Brackett and Keith Macneir.
Sussman, who is Hathaway’s aunt, said the grieving families and survivors are still seeking answers on how the Maine Community Foundation handled collecting and disbursing the $6.6 million Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund.
What they are looking for, she said, is accountability, transparency and fairness.
Some $4.7 million of the Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund was granted to victims’ families and survivors; $1.9 million went to 29 area nonprofits.
Speaking at the news conference were survivors Jennifer Zanca, Destiny Johnson, Danielle Chabot and Strout’s father, Arthur Barnard.
Zanca, who was shot at Schemengees Bar and Grille, learned a year later she would need more surgery and, by the end of it, owed $93,000 in hospital bills that she said her insurance company denied.
“The FBI, Homeland Security came to my home and told me I would never have to worry about hospital bills,” Zanca said. “Except I did.”
Zanca said it was a year later that she learned about the distribution of funds occurring in the months following the shooting.
“You mean to tell me that 29 nonprofits received $65,000 each, that only a few had anything to do with the shooting, while victims that were shot received less than half that amount from the Maine Community Foundation?” Zanca asked. “Some nonprofits received nine times the amount than victims that fled from flying bullets, while others saved lives and witnessed the carnage that is forever embedded in their memories.”
Nearly three years after the shootings, some victims and survivors are still asking the Maine Attorney General’s Office and the Legislature’s Government Oversight Committee to hear their side of the story. Sussman said survivors have also tried unsuccessfully to meet with Gov. Janet Mills.
Attorney General Aaron Frey sat before the Government Oversight Committee on Sept. 16 and told legislators that the Office of Program Evaluation and Government Accountability cannot investigate the handling of funds because the funds were not handled by a government entity.
Frey also told legislators the only recourse for an investigation would be through the Maine Charitable Solicitations Act; however, he said, no complaints have been filed through that act.
The Maine Community Foundation has publicly defended its handling of the donations since as early as 2024, saying families and survivors were notified that the Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund would be two separate funds: one for victims and another for nonprofit organizations, as suggested by nationally recognized victims’ advocate, Jeff Dion.
The foundation said it did not take administrative fees so all donations could go to families and community recovery efforts.
Maine Community Foundation said the Attorney General’s Office found that donor intent had been followed and that there were no concerns about how the funds were collected and distributed.
Sussman said victims’ families and survivors feel as though they have been silenced by the Government Oversight Committee from giving their own account of what they were initially told by the Maine Community Foundation.
“The Maine Community Foundation gave us this document on their own letterhead,” Sussman said, holding up a binder and pointing to a page, “saying that 100% of the Lewiston-Auburn Area Response Fund was for the victims’ families and survivors. We were sent emails saying (the same).
“What we didn’t know was that the Maine Community Foundation was collecting money for nonprofits on the backs of the 18 people who were murdered and the 118 who survived … in the worst mass violence event in the state’s history.”
Victims’ families and survivors learned a week ago that the Government Oversight Committee will not hear from groups of victims and survivors in a meeting after having several requests ignored, Sussman said.
“We recently learned that one of the co-chairs and members of the committee work for or are on the boards of nonprofits that received grants from the Maine Community Foundation,” Sussman said. “This conflict of interest is prominent in the ruling party of the state Legislature.”
In April, some 57 victims’ family members and survivors sent a complaint, accompanied by new documents, to the Maine Office of the Attorney General to reopen its investigation. They declined, Sussman said.
“True accountability means that no other family or individual will have to go through what we have in the aftermath of a tragedy at the hands of an unethical nonprofit. … That no other family or individual will have to get up off their knees from grief and suffering to fight for what is right because the ruling party in this state of Maine will not help us.”
Sussman said she recently learned of two new complaints being filed with the Attorney General’s Office.
“We are continuing to demand accountability. … It is being swept under the rug by the governor, the attorney general, the Government Oversight Committee and the city of Lewiston,” Sussman said. “The actions of the Maine Community Foundation have hurt not only us, but all nonprofits.”
“We are on the right side of this,” Sussman said. “We’re not giving up and we’re not going away.”

title: Texas prosecutor says ICE agent appeared to intentionally strike man with vehicle in Houston
text:
HOUSTON (AP) — A Texas prosecutor says a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent appeared to use a vehicle to intentionally strike a man who took off running in Houston and that an investigation opened by his office could result in criminal charges.
Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, needed surgery for a broken leg after being hit by a car Saturday, said Cesar Espinosa, executive director of FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights organization that is helping the man’s family.
The encounter has set off new criticism over immigration enforcement in Houston, where local prosecutors have also investigated a July fatal shooting by a federal immigration officer.
Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare, a Democrat, expressed concern over surveillance footage that shows Parra Hernandez and another person jumping out of a white truck and running as a dark SUV pursues them. A vehicle strikes Parra Hernandez, who is seen on the ground seconds later.
“In a case like this, the most obvious criminal charge is aggravated assault with a deadly weapon,” Teare told FOX 26 Houston. “Meaning the car was used as a deadly weapon. And it certainly is what appears to have happened based on the surveillance footage.”
Tim Oberle, a spokesperson for ICE in Houston, said in a statement sent to The Texas Tribune on Saturday that “As ICE officers attempted to apprehend the illegal aliens, Miguel Parra-Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”
Spokespersons for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Tuesday.
Parra Hernandez has been in the U.S. for 34 years and was on his way to work when the encounter began, according to Espinosa. Espinosa declined to share Parra Hernandez’s status.
He said he saw two ICE agents in Parra Hernandez’s room while visiting him at the hospital.
“He already had a surgery for the injury under his knee and now we’re waiting for swelling to go down in his ankle to be able to have a reconstructive surgery on his ankle,” Espinosa said.
Teare said ICE and DHS have not cooperated with his office during its investigation.
In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his request for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. The shooting was one of at least 10 deaths involving encounters with immigration officers since the start of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

title: Bar Harbor resident seeks recall of elected officials
text:
BAR HARBOR — Resident Charles Sidman, originator of the citizen’s initiative that established the town’s current cruise ship regulations, has filed three new initiatives with Town Clerk Liz Graves ahead of election day on Nov. 3. Sidman plans to gather signatures in support of the efforts at the polls.
