title: After final debate, here’s where things stand in the race to become Maine’s next governor
text:
The fourth and final gubernatorial debate saw no huge fireworks Wednesday evening while covering largely familiar ground.
That means the race to succeed Gov. Janet Mills remains Democrat Hannah Pingree’s race to lose.
Pingree, a 49-year-old former Maine House speaker from North Haven who led Mills’ policy office, has consistently led polling of the contest by double digits and made no huge stumbles in the debates, though she was light on specifics at times.
Republican Bobby Charles, a 66-year-old Leeds lawyer who has led a lobbying and consulting firm and previously worked in drug and domestic policy roles under former Republican Presidents Ronald Reagan, George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush, expectedly and repeatedly sought to go after Pingree and link her with Mills in order to blame the two for rising energy and housing costs in Maine.
Independent Rick Bennett, a 63-year-old former state senator from Oxford who previously chaired the Maine Republican Party before leaving the GOP last year, reiterated that he is an experienced option for those tired of the two-party system, but his path to victory still looks very narrow.
If Charles surges past Pingree on Election Day, or if Bennett surpasses Charles on Election Day and competes with Pingree for the top spot, then it will be a massive surprise and a sign that the polls completely missed the mark. Here are a few quick notes on the race after the last debate.
No national Republican money for Charles?
It did not arise during Wednesday evening’s debate hosted by WMTW, but it matters for whether any sudden developments will grip the race in the home stretch.
Charles told reporters in July that he had met earlier that month with the Republican Governors Association and several Republican governors who planned to support him financially to the tune of “likely millions, and they are very committed to the idea that Maine is a pickup for them.”
If that money suddenly appears for Charles, then it will arrive with fewer than three weeks until Election Day. The Republican Governors Association did not respond to requests for comment after Charles made those comments earlier in the year, and the national support has not materialized for his campaign. Charles reported raising more than $1.8 million in his last campaign finance report, while Pingree had raised more than $4.2 million and Bennett raised about $923,000.
A political action committee with well-heeled Republican donors that was set up over the summer to support Charles has instead spent $70,000 to boost Bennett.
A rare moment of Pingree-Bennett bickering
Pingree may have heard about that infusion of pro-Bennett cash from the No Nonsense PAC, as she briefly went after Bennett during Wednesday’s debate, calling him “a lifelong Republican” and noting he chaired the state Republican Party from 2013 to 2017. That coincided with the party supporting President Donald Trump and former Gov. Paul LePage in their elections.
“He didn’t leave the party until he decided to run for governor because he knew he couldn’t beat Bobby Charles because the party has gone MAGA,” Pingree said. “And again, I have respect for Rick, but I don’t think it’s fair to say that he has been independent-minded.”
Bennett replied by alluding to how he voted against Republican proposals in the state Senate and was the chamber’s “most independent member.” Charles chimed in by noting Bennett decided to cast a Democratic ballot in the June primary.
Pingree made her rare attack on Bennett, whom she has otherwise referred to as “my friend,” after Bennett gave a line he has given in several debates about what he represents.
“We need to get back to a politics of compromise and collaboration. The party candidates can’t do that,” Bennett said. “Hannah Pingree has a D on her jersey. Bobby Charles has an R on his jersey. My jersey says Maine.”
Who gets to work in the next administration?
The brief amount of bickering between Pingree and Bennett was an exception to what has otherwise been a peaceful, drama-free set of interactions during each debate. Charles has notably gone after the two by calling them “insiders” for their years of legislative service in Augusta.
If the polls turn out to be fairly accurate, then Pingree will succeed Mills. The talk will quickly turn next month to who may join the next governor’s administration. Bennett is one name to watch if he loses the race and Pingree wins it, given their mostly amicable interactions.
But it is still far too early to say who will serve under the next governor. Campaigns are careful to not look too far ahead and publicly discuss any plans beyond Nov. 3.

title: Documents: Ousted Georgia police officer gave ICE agent husband access to Flock system
text:
Documents: Ousted Georgia police officer gave ICE agent husband access to Flock system
A now-former Georgia police officer gave her husband, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent, access to the police department’s Flock license plate reader system, which he used to conduct hundreds of searches tied to ICE investigations, according to newly obtained documents reviewed by sister station WJCL.
The records show Amber Harpe's husband did not have his own Flock account through the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. Harpe acknowledged giving him her Savannah Police Department username and password.
Her husband told investigators he used the account to locate ICE targets who had active arrest warrants. He said every search was related to his federal law enforcement work and denied using the system for personal reasons.
The Savannah Police Department fired Harpe after concluding that she knowingly gave an unauthorized person access to a sensitive police system, violated department policy and compromised safeguards designed to track who was using law enforcement data.
Nearly 1,000 searches across six states
The investigation began after an internal audit flagged an unusually high volume of searches through Harpe’s account between January and July 2026.
The audit identified 983 search entries involving 97 identifiable license plates from Georgia, New Jersey, Maryland, Florida, South Carolina and North Carolina.
South Carolina plates represented most of the activity. Forty-eight South Carolina plates accounted for 788 search entries, according to the records. Department documents also noted that most registered vehicle owners identified in the audit were Hispanic.
During a July 27 administrative interview, Harpe told investigators she did not recognize the names connected to many of the searches. She said her husband performed most of them.
Harpe attributed the searches involving Maryland and South Carolina plates, along with most of those involving Georgia vehicles, to her husband.
She said she rarely used Flock herself and generally accessed it to help investigate missing-person cases involving behavioral health patients.
Harpe acknowledged that she allowed her husband to use her credentials and understood she was not permitted to share her access.
Husband said searches targeted wanted people
Harpe’s husband’s name is redacted in the documents obtained by WJCL 22 News.
During an Aug. 3 interview with Savannah police investigators, he confirmed that he asked Harpe for her login information because he did not have Flock access through his federal job.
He said ICE had already developed “target packages” for the people he searched and that those people had active arrest warrants. The Flock information allowed him to try to locate them while working in the field, according to the investigative report.
Harpe’s husband estimated that he used the account for about four months. He said he stopped roughly three weeks before his interview because the agency no longer conducted vehicle stops and he no longer needed the system.
Harpe gave investigators a slightly different timeline, saying her husband stopped about a week before her interview because he was concerned she could face discipline.
He denied searching for relatives, former romantic partners or anyone for personal reasons. He maintained that every person he searched was an ICE target and said the Flock information helped his agency locate wanted people with criminal histories.
He also acknowledged that using another officer’s account could violate policy.
“The investigation established that Amber Harpe provided her Flock Safety credentials to her husband,” the final report said. “Both provided consistent statements that the searches involved ICE targets and were conducted for law-enforcement purposes.”
SPD raised concerns about immigration enforcement
In the documents, Maj. Michelle Halford wrote that SPD does not participate in federal immigration enforcement. She said the demographic pattern identified in the audit, combined with Harpe’s husband’s role as an ICE agent, raised concerns that department resources had been used without authorization to further immigration enforcement.
Harpe’s decision gave her husband the ability to search for and track people through a Savannah police system even though he did not have independent access through his federal employment, Halford wrote.
She said the arrangement exposed the police department to legal and reputational risks.
“Public trust is non-negotiable,” Halford wrote. “These tools exist to keep our community safe, not for personal or unauthorized use.”
The investigation did not find that Harpe violated Georgia’s law governing automated license plate readers. The disciplinary case instead centered on an SPD information-management policy prohibiting employees from allowing unauthorized people to access city or department software.
Supervisors disagreed over punishment
Department leaders agreed that Harpe violated policy, but they initially disagreed over whether she should be fired.
Interim Maj. Max Nowinsky sustained the allegation and recommended an eight-hour suspension.
Nowinsky wrote that Harpe showed poor judgment by providing direct access to her husband. However, he also emphasized that investigators found no evidence the searches were conducted for personal reasons or personal gain.
He cited Georgia law allowing law enforcement agencies, including federal agencies, to exchange captured license plate data for legitimate law enforcement purposes.
Nowinsky also considered Harpe’s work history. She joined SPD in March 2020, served in the Behavioral Health Unit and had no prior disciplinary record. Department documents described her as a well-respected employee.
Halford rejected the proposed one-day suspension and recommended termination, citing the intentional sharing of credentials, recurring unauthorized access and scale of the activity.
Assistant Police Chief Robert Gavin agreed that Harpe should be fired.
Gavin acknowledged that state law permits law enforcement agencies to share license plate information for legitimate purposes. He said that authority did not allow Harpe to share her personal login information or let another person access the system under her identity.
“Credentials are assigned to one authorized user to ensure accountability, audit integrity, and system security,” Gavin wrote.
Because the searches were recorded under Harpe’s account, the system’s audit trail identified her — not her husband — as the user.
Gavin concluded that Harpe knowingly allowed her husband to bypass SPD’s security protocols and undermined the department’s ability to oversee the use of sensitive information.
Harpe said she was helping another agency
Harpe accepted responsibility for sharing her credentials but argued that firing her was excessive.
In her appeal, Harpe said her husband was a certified federal law enforcement officer and that every search was conducted for law enforcement purposes.
“The violation occurred because I gave my husband, who is a certified law enforcement officer with the Department of Homeland Security, access to my Flock account,” Harpe wrote. “Every search he conducted was for law enforcement use only and not for personal gain.”
Harpe said she was trying to assist another agency in the same way she would expect another agency to help Savannah police.
She also argued that the result would have been no different if she had personally conducted each search at her husband’s request and then provided him with the information.
“There was no malicious intent, no personal gain, and no intent to harm the Department or undermine public trust,” Harpe wrote.
She asked department leaders to consider her clean disciplinary history, years of service and the investigation’s finding that the searches were related to law enforcement work. She requested a written reprimand or, at most, the one-day suspension Nowinsky recommended.
Gavin denied her appeal Aug. 11, and the police chief’s office agreed with the termination recommendation two days later.
Civil Service Board appeal withdrawn
Harpe requested a hearing before Savannah’s Civil Service Board on Aug. 19. City records show her termination took effect Sept. 26.
She withdrew the appeal around Sept. 28, and her Oct. 13 Civil Service Board hearing was canceled.
The newly obtained documents do not explain why she withdrew the appeal.
Harpe’s case was part of a wider SPD investigation into alleged Flock misuse. Several other former employees were accused of searching for romantic partners, former partners or other people for personal reasons.

title: Maine governor candidate profile: Rick Bennett
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - As part of WABI’s candidate profile series, we had independent candidate for governor Rick Bennett in our studio recently.
A longtime Republican, he’s running for Governor as an independent this year.
During our conversation he talked about seeing a gap form between parties in recent years.
It ultimately led him to run as a third party candidate.
We asked him, if elected, what his priorities would be in year one.
“People have lost trust in government and we need to get that back. It’s critically important, people lost trust in their tax dollars being spent wisely. That’s why I will put forward on day one, I will create an office of inspector general working directly in my office with if ever there is a hint of fraud or miss spending Whistleblower complaint. My team will be there in real time immediately just to study at investigate and report back and will make that transparent. People need to trust their government again, so, with me you’ll get that. But you know the parties have failed. The two party system is not working. They’re more interested in fighting than getting results and we need to move past that and that’s what my candidacy represents an opportunity for people to take control of their government again and to bring cost down to restore trust in government and get our economy moving,” Bennett said.
Full interviews with Democratic nominee Hannah Pingree and Republican nominee Bobby Charles are available on our website, streaming apps and YouTube page.

title: Worried on behalf of heating oil customers in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The U.S. Department of Energy’s statistical arm, the Energy Information Administration, announced that total winter heating bills, for households using heating oil, are projected to be 21% higher on average this winter compared to last winter.
The price of heating oil is forecast to average $5.26 per gallon, a 34% increase nationwide. A slightly milder winter in the Northeast is going to slightly lower consumption by about 9%, which will help to soften the total bill increase down to 21%.
I attended college in Maine and lived in Portland and Gorham in the mid-’90s. I have friends in Maine who have been struggling over high energy prices. This winter’s heating bill will require them to make difficult budgetary sacrifices elsewhere.
George Albrecht
Warwick, R.I.

title: Pres. Trump urges Alaskans to vote for the real Dan Sullivan
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Gray Media’s White House correspondent Jon Decker interviewed President Donald Trump in Wasilla, Alaska, as the US Senate race between Republican Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola comes down to the wire.
Jon Decker:
Mr. President, welcome to Alaska. You have done exceptionally well in Alaska, won the state three times. You won by 13.5 points in 2024. And yet in this Senate race, it’s exceptionally close. Why do you suppose that is and why did you travel seven hours for this campaign event?
President Donald Trump:
Well, I think maybe the people don’t know what a great job Dan Sullivan does. Senator Sullivan is a great senator, respected by everybody. And I think I have to tell the people I did 1 to 3 times the fact I got the highest vote in the history of Alaska. So I said, I better come out here and explain, because Dan Sullivan is great and they have a fake Sullivan in here. They put the Democrats, put a guy named Sullivan who never did anything only because of his name, hoping to confuse people, which I thought was disgraceful. So I came out here for that too. We can’t let them get away with that.
Jon Decker:
It is so expensive to live in Alaska. You know that, Mr. President. Gas is so expensive here. Going going to the grocery store. Also very expensive is affordability. Whatever you want to call a cost of living. A big issue as to why. Dan Sullivan, Senator Sullivan is not performing as well as he’d like to right now.
President Donald Trump:
Well, affordability is big, but it was caused by the Biden administration. We’re bringing it down. I’ve only been here a little more than a year and a half, and we’re bringing it way down. Groceries have come way down. Everything is coming down, and all will be coming down as soon as I finish with Iran, which is going to be very soon. They’re defeated in every way. Their military is gone. Their navy, their air force, everything’s gone. They have the highest inflation of any country in the world. They have no money. They have no leadership. Their leadership was gone. The second phase is gone. They have some people we don’t even know. I mean, frankly, who are we dealing with? Nobody’s exactly sure. Nobody wants to be the leader. So Iran is in is going to fail very shortly. And when they do. Gasoline is going to be tumbling down and other costs are going to be tumbling down. But affordability is a nice word. But as everyone knows, and really, Jon, you know, we inherited that from the Biden administration. He had the worst inflation in the history of our country. And we took it over and we brought everything down. And last for the last three months, we’ve been at 1.7% inflation.
Jon Decker:
You and Senator Sullivan, you see eye to eye on virtually everything, almost to 100% voting record that Senator Sullivan has with you. You don’t see eye to eye on one issue in particular. Mr.. Mr. president, and that is the issue of Russia and President Putin. Senator Sullivan is called President Putin a dictator, an authoritarian, a mafia regime leader. He’s against that diesel deal that you announced last week. Why, Mr. President, are you right? And Senator Sullivan is wrong on this. Well, look, I have to make deals with people so I don’t go around calling them names. I’m a deal maker. I’ve always been a very good deal maker. I became very rich because of deals. So I don’t go around mocking people. You know, part of the reason you have that war in the first place is Biden went around mocking Russia and mocking everybody else and didn’t know what he was doing. That was a war that should have never started. If I were president, if that election wasn’t rigged and it was rigged, you wouldn’t have had a war with Ukraine and with Russia. So I also feel it’s not all coming to us and it’s diesel. What you need. I feel that it’s great because it’s it’s released to the world. title: High schools Wednesday: Lisbon boys soccer blanks Sacopee Valley
text:
Keegan Schmoll led Lisbon with a goal and an assist in its 3-0 boys soccer victory over Sacopee Valley on Wednesday in Lisbon.
Cooper Story and Jake Baird also scored for the Greyhounds (6-4-3), while Nolan Parker and Kael Richards each had an assist.
Lisbon finished with a 9-4 advantage over the Hawks (2-8-1) in shots on goal.
BUCKFIELD 2, MT. ABRAM 1: Nate Thomas stood tall in goal with 22 saves for the Bucks (6-5-2) in their win over the Roadrunners (6-5-2) in Salem Township.
Nolan Litchfield and Evan St. Pierre provided a goal apiece for Buckfield.
Brennan Mitchell scored for Mt. Abram off an assist by Will Swain. Goalie Ben Beaulier made two saves.
LEAVITT 3, MORSE 1: Avery Schlobohm assisted on all three goals as the Hornets (7-2-3) defeated the Shipbuilders (3-7-2) in Turner.
Tyler Mates and Carter Berube each netted first-half goals and Angelo Toscano scored in the second half for Leavitt. Goalkeeper Luke Horn made three saves.
Thomas McKenzie scored an unassisted goal for Morse with 2:40 left in the game.
HALL-DALE 3, MOUNTAIN VALLEY 0: The Bulldogs (12-1) defeated the pesky Falcons (5-5-2) to earn their 12th straight victory in a Class C South matchup in Rumford.
Hall-Dale broke through 20 minutes into the game when Davis Madore sent a nice through ball to Kayden Reith for the first goal. Kayden Ferguson added another first-half goal, poking in a cross by Collin McArthur. McArthur finished the scoring by heading in a cross from Colby Keene with six minutes remaining in the game.
Mountain Valley goalie Gabe Hall finished with 14 saves, while Hall-Dale’s Landon Gilbert stopped two shots.
MONMOUTH ACADEMY 7, WINTHROP 0: Zane Foyt and Bryce Fletcher scored in each half, leading the Mustangs (11-0) to a win over the Ramblers (3-8-2) in Winthrop.
Jake Harmon and Noah Schultz added to Monmouth’s lead during a five-goal second half that included an own goal.
FIELD HOCKEY
WINTHROP/MARANACOOK 5, OAK HILL 1: Evelyn Mortimer scored three goals to pace the Ramblers (12-1) to a win over the Raiders (4-8) in Wales.
Natalie Irwin and Ella Giles each chipped in with a goal and an assist. The Ramblers broke the game open with three goals in the third quarter after leading 1-0 at halftime.
Madalyn Sikora scored for Oak Hill.
MOUNTAIN VALLEY 8, TELSTAR 0: Addie Libby and Melina Byam each scored three goals to pace the Falcons (9-3) past the Rebels (1-11) in Rumford.
Ava Tidswell and Emma Williamson also scored for Mountain Valley. Libby and Williamson assisted on two goals apiece, while Byam, Tidswell and Layla Buotte had one assist each.
Telstar goalie Madelyn Cooley made 25 saves.
GIRLS SOCCER
POLAND 3, OLD ORCHARD BEACH 0: Three second-half goals boosted the Knights (9-1-2) past the Seagulls (5-6) in a Western Maine Conference tilt in Old Orchard Beach.
Payton Rose opened the scoring for Poland midway through the second half. Julia Paradis added a goal from the top of the 18-yard box, and Regan Wakem scored off a pass from Leksi Langevin.
Knights goalie Payton black stopped three shots, while Old Orchard Beach’s Amelia Gervais made 13 saves.
MOUNTAIN VALLEY 2, DIRIGO 2: Annabel Taylor struck twice in the second half as Mountain Valley (4-6-2) erased a two-goal deficit and salvaged a tie against Dirigo (6-4-1) in Dixfield.
Xandria Libby scored on a breakaway and Abby Luczynski put in a direct kick in the first half, staking the host Cougars to a 2-0 lead.
Ella Aasen and Mackenzie Gammon assisted on Taylor’s goals.
Dirigo keeper Lilly Knowlton finished with 13 saves. Mountain Valley’s Violet Simmons stopped eight shots.

title: Spruce Mountain field hockey rolls past Gray-New Gloucester/NYA
text:
YARMOUTH — Late arrivals are becoming the norm for the Spruce Mountain field hockey team.
After arriving late to a game against Lisbon last week, the Phoenix showed up only 25 minutes before the scheduled start of Wednesday’s game against Gray-New Gloucester/North Yarmouth Academy.
The fashionably late Phoenix were undeterred and earned a 5-1 victory over the Patriots.
“I think that we play better when we have that happen to us,” Spruce Mountain midfielder Maddie Gramaldi said. “It’s happened a couple of times, and our warm-ups were quick, but we just got the main stuff we needed to do done.”
Fast off the bus
Spruce Mountain (11-2), ranked second in the Class C South Heal point standings, started fast and scored twice in the first quarter. First, Malaire Richards deflected a ball past Patriots keeper Mallory Kulas. Aisla Armandi knocked in the second goal.
“We recognized that we were going to have a quick start,” Armandi said. “We realized we needed to bring our energy and be really intense because we knew they were a very talented team.”
The Phoenix spent most of the contest on offense. Neither team scored in the second quarter, but Spruce Mountain capitalized on its penalty-corner chances with goals by Grimaldi and Linda Lake to extend the lead to 4-0 in the third.
“We were in the 25 most of the game,” Spruce Mountain coach Alex Bessey said. “I think we talked a lot about (at) halftime, just finishing.”
Armandi scored her second goal early in the fourth quarter.
Patriots don’t quit
Gray-New Gloucester/NYA (3-8) started getting the ball in its offensive zone after Spruce Mountain made mass substitutions in the final quarter.
The Patriots got their first shot on goal with a minute remaining, then Emma Elgee scored on the second shot with 50 seconds left.
“She just recently started getting quite a bit of playing time for us,” Patriots coach Julia Leary said. “The last couple of games, went into a starting position. She’s a fantastic forward. She’s incredibly conditioned. … She’s been a huge asset for us offensively this year.”
Unsung hero
Maddie Grimaldi set the tone for the Phoenix by controlling the middle of the field. That allowed Spruce Mountain to keep the Patriots on their heels and in the defensive end of the field.
“Her communication was good, her energy was good,” Bessey said. “Then (she was) working well with her teammates and making the right passes.”
Statistical leaders
Spruce Mountain: Aisla Armandi (2 goals), Linda Lake (goal, assist), Maddie Grimaldi (goal), Malaire Richards (goal), Kyleigh Marcotte (one save)
Gray-New Gloucester/NYA: Emma Elgee (goal), Layla Whitman (assist), Mallory Kulas (11 saves).

title: Losses mounted for Hearts of Pine this season, but fans never wavered
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
There will be no well-attended watch parties in the coming weeks. The State Theater and the Portland Zoo won’t be packed to the rafters with Hearts of Pine fans, completely absorbed by the Hearts competing in a playoff match.
The Hearts of Pine were eliminated from USL League One playoff contention last week, and now there are two games remaining in the season. Portland plays at Forward Madison FC on Saturday and hosts Charlotte Independence on Oct. 24 to wrap up the 2026 campaign.
While the team didn’t come close to matching the on-field success of its inaugural season, things are as good as ever off the field. The Hearts are second in USL League One in average attendance, trailing only Boise. Portland’s average attendance at Fitzpatrick Stadium is 6,235, which is around 1,000 fewer than Boise but about 2,200 more than the Richmond Kickers, who rank third in the league in average attendance.
The Hearts have played 38 consecutive sellouts at Fitzpatrick, and it’s pretty much a lock to be 39 after the final game of the season. Tickets for the season finale on Oct. 24 against Charlotte are still scarce and expensive. A Wednesday morning glance at StubHub showed tickets going for $104 to $140 each for a pair of seats together, while a single could be had for $63.
The average face value of a Hearts ticket is a modest $27. With no postseason on the horizon, it’s a little surprising to see the secondary market remain so robust. If the team has another down season, is this demand sustainable?
Dirigo Union, the team’s enthusiastic supporters group, will always be there, singing throughout the match and bringing the noise. The question is, if there’s another season of frustrating play on the pitch, will the casual fans still drive up ticket prices and make Hearts of Pine games EVENTS?
Right now, that’s a question without an answer, unless you have a crystal ball. The best we can do is a qualified probably.
Remember, the Hearts have a waiting list for season tickets that runs 8,000 names deep. Even if half the season ticket holders suddenly pull the chute, there’s more than enough fans eager to take their place.
Bass Pettitt is co-chair of Dirigo United. Admittedly, he sees the future of Hearts fandom through the optimistic eyes of a superfan. He can only go by what he’s seen so far and conversations with casual fans he meets through his job at Bayside Bowl. What he hears from them makes him bullish that the current trend of ticket scarcity will continue, at least through next season.
“I talk to my friends who are league bowlers who have never been into soccer in their life, and they’re like, ‘Man, I went for the first time and I had so much fun,’ and they tell me about three things that aren’t anything that happened on the field,” Pettitt said. “And then I ask them about the game and they’re like, ‘Yeah, I’m learning about soccer and I’m excited to be there and be a part of it.’ There’s a lot of people like that. I’m sure the idea of losing consistently will run dry on them.”
The way the Hearts have lost so many games this season is what frustrates fans new and old. The team has allowed a late goal a dozen times, turning a win into a loss or tie, or a tie into a loss. Ten times in 30 matches, the team surrendered a goal in stoppage time at the end of a game.
That frustration hasn’t resulted in fans staying away. Hearts of Pine management has done an amazing job making games a family-friendly experience that goes beyond the results on the field. In that regard, the Hearts are like Portland’s other three pro franchises, the Portland Sea Dogs, Maine Mariners and Maine Celtics.
Where those clubs hold an edge, though, is affiliation. If they don’t win, fans can go to games knowing they could be watching a future member of the Boston Red Sox, Boston Bruins or Boston Celtics. The Hearts are their own thing. Players move on to higher leagues, but there’s not a common final team that’s the goal at the top of the pyramid.
Reaching the USL League One semifinals last year, being a penalty kick from the championship game, was more than anyone could have expected from a club in its first season of play. That alone is reason enough to think the crowds will continue to fill Fitzpatrick Stadium over the next few seasons, and then a possible new stadium on the waterfront in 2029.
“We’re in the growth stage. We’re toddlers,” Pettitt said.
That growth comes with pains on the field. Right now, there’s no indication those will become aches at the turnstiles.

title: Death Notice: Pauline Alice Allen
‘Friday the 13th’s Jason Voorhees Is 80 Years Old
text:
‘Friday the 13th’s Jason Voorhees Is 80 Years Old
From 1980 to 2009, New Line Cinema released 12 Friday the 13th movies. For a six-year period in the ’80s, New Line pumped out a new installment every single year. Say what you will about Jason Voorhees’ hostile attitude toward camp counselors, his tendency to solve interpersonal disputes with violence, his drab sense of personal style: The dude does work hard.
Or at least he did work hard. Since 2009, Friday the 13th has been like Jason lying at the bottom of Crystal Lake between sequels: Totally dormant. That finally changes with the new Peacock and A24 streaming series Crystal Lake. But while Jason is a character on the show, he’s not the dude impaling horny teenagers while wearing a hockey mask and coveralls anymore. He’s not even the show’s central antagonist.
That would be Jason’s mom, Pamela Voorhees, played by Linda Cardellini. As all Friday the 13th fans, while Jason became the big bad of this franchise starting with its sequel, the original movie’s villain was Mrs. Voorhees, who was driven mad by her son’s death and began killing counselors at the camp where he drowned. Crystal Lake is a prequel, focusing on good ol’ Pammy at the start of her rampage in the picturesque locale of the title.
Especially after a 17-year absence, a Friday the 13th reboot/prequel makes a certain amount of sense. (It had only been nine years since Rob Zombie’s Halloween II when Blumhouse made their Halloween legacyquel starring Jamie Lee Curtis as Laurie Strode. Younger fans of A24’s might not know Jason Voorhees or his mother at all at this point.
But there’s another reason why Peacock and A24 may have chosen the prequel route: Jason Voorhees is now 80 years old.
At least, he would be if any new film carried forward the continuity established by that first Friday the 13th from 1980. Those movies established that Jason was born in 1946 and then drowned in Crystal Lake 11 years later. That timeframe lines up with the age of Betsy Palmer, the actress who played Mrs Voorhees in Friday the 13th, who was born in 1926. That would have made her roughly 20 when she had Jason, and in her mid-50s during the events of that film.
READ MORE: 12 Forgotten Movie Prequels
Granted, the standard rules of aging and a body’s physical decay may not apply to an undead zombie monster man like Jason Voorhees, who has died at least a couple times already. But still: 80 years old! Jason has lived through 14 different American Presidents. Alaska didn’t become a U.S. state until Jason Voorhees was 13. He’s four years older than George Cukor’s Born Yesterday — which he certainly was not.
So now we know why Jason keeps wearing that hockey mask. He doesn’t want people to know his age. That thing’s like serial killer Botox. Covers up the wrinkles.
I think the rights holders are trying to cover up Jason’s age too. Horror movies in general, and slasher movies in particular, are predominantly targeted at young audiences. Trying to convince a 22 year old to buy a ticket for a film about a serial killer who predates the microwave oven would be a tough sell. Instead of promoting an octogenarian with a pitchfork, you do Crystal Lake.
I have a real soft-spot in my heart for some of those old Friday the 13th sequels, and I hope Crystal Lake is goo. But I really hope its success finally opens the door to a 13th Friday the 13th movie — which has to be called Friday, the 13th with a comma — and that it stars Old Jason.
Seriously, let Jason be old. He already walks slowly. Let him walk really slowly. Let him occasionally complain about his back. Let him get distracted and screw up a kill because he’s busy looking at AI slop on Facebook he thinks is real. Let him get stabbed in the back while he struggles to open a bottle of Motrin. Let him bludgeon some horny camp counselor with a VCR that’s flashing “12:00 AM” over and over. Let him fall down after the final girl ties together the laces of his Hokas that he wears because his podiatrist told them they would give him better arch support.
Old Jason. Let’s go.

title: Obituary: Cynthia “Cindy” Anne Chapman

title: New York to ban horse-drawn carriage rides in Central Park
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New York City lawmakers plan to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park, ending their more than 150-year run as an iconic, old-timey tourist attraction, following decades of opposition from animal welfare activists and the death of a teenage tourist last spring.
The City Council is expected to approve a bill next week that would end the rides by 2028. Three consecutive mayors had called for an end to the carriage rides because of safety concerns, only to have lawmakers yank back the reins.
A spokesperson for Julie Menin, the council speaker, confirmed the incoming vote and said the proposal had enough support to pass. Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s office said he had reached a deal with the speaker on the legislation.
“The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City,” Mamdani said in a social media post.
Teen’s death reignited debate over carriage rides
The latest push for a ban started in June, when 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, visiting the city from India, died after jumping from a runaway horse carriage during a ride with family members. His death, which appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park, reignited the debate over whether carriages, a romantic throwback to the city’s past, have a place in a modern metropolis.
Mahajan’s family has appeared at City Hall, in person and through videoconference calls from India, begging the city to finally end the rides.
“We are shattered, our whole family shattered. The pain does not go away,” his father, Deepak Mahajan, told city council members via a videocall during a hearing for the bill last summer, saying his son leapt from the carriage to try and help his mother, who was flung from her seat, after the horse bolted. “Every morning we wake up and think of nothing but the loss of our son.”
For decades, animal welfare activists and other critics have decried the carriage industry, arguing horses shouldn’t be hauling tourists around busy streets and Central Park while having to navigate bustling traffic and gawking passersby. In the past, horses have collapsed, gotten startled and run off, hitting cars or other objects, with each accident resulting in fresh calls for a ban.
“The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable. Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City’s history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability,” Menin said in a statement.
The industry and its supporters have long cast the rides as a way for visitors to experience the New York they know from classic movies and television.
Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse danced into one of the carriages in “The Band Wagon.” Robert Redford and Jane Fonda rode one in “Barefoot in the Park.” Macaulay Culkin escaped bandits in a carriage in “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.”
“Taking a horse and carriage ride in New York City is one of the most iconic things to do in New York City and people from all over the world know about us and travel to New York to go to a carriage ride in New York,” Conor McHugh, a longtime carriage driver, told the Council earlier this year.
Mayors have faced pushback in efforts to ban rides
Efforts to close down the industry have been met with pushback from unions and influential supporters, often resulting in tiresome political fights that have seen mayors throw up their hands over nagging worries about putting carriage drivers out of work and what to do with the horses if they can no longer work.
Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen said the Council’s bill has “no meaningful economic relief for workers” and that Menin “used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis.”
“This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families’ livelihoods are being destroyed. This entire situation is reprehensible,” he said in a statement.
The proposal as written would require the mayor’s office to develop a workforce transition plan for drivers, and includes a measure that would allow the city to consider some kind of compensation for industry workers. Carriage owners could not sell their horses off for slaughter, according to the bill’s language, which requires that horses be disposed of in a “humane manner.”
“I think we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry,” Mamdani told reporters Wednesday.
The mayor’s predecessor, Eric Adams, called for ending the industry during the waning days of his administration, but the proposal went nowhere. The mayor before that, Bill de Blasio, had pledged to eliminate the rides on day one of his administration but abandoned the crusade after heavy opposition from unions and a media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson.
Over the years, the city has placed various safety regulations around the industry, including a requirement that the horses get at least five weeks of vacation a year outside of city limits with daily access to a pasture. The horses are inspected by a veterinarian twice a year, and the maximum age they can work at is 26, according to city regulations. And they don’t work when it is hotter than 89 degrees.

title: Old Town Public Library Offers Ghost Hunting Kits Alongside Kayaks And Crochet Supplies
text:
Feel Like Doing A Little Ghost Hunting? You Can Check Out A “Paranormal Investigation Kit” Right From The Old Town Library!
You know that you can check out books, games, and even videos at most libraries. But did you know that in one library in Penobscot County, you can also check out experiences?!
Read More: 10 Terrifying Ghost Stories That Are Uniquely Maine
The Old Town Public Library has a special section where folks can check out more than just books, but items and kits. It's called The Library of Things.
The Library of Things
We're told the Library of Things is located next to the Boo-tique, just past the circulation desk.
Beyond costumes, crochet kits, kayaks, and post hole diggers, you can also check out specific adventure kits.
Codi Badger, Circulation Desk Manager at the library, says it's a fun way to get hands-on and try out new things.
"Our Ghost Hunting Kit is available through our Library of Things, located in the room right next to our circulation desk. It's a fun way for curious patrons to try their hand at paranormal investigating, especially during spooky season!"
Folks can borrow these kits and "things" for up to one week.
Ever feel like doing a little ghost hunting? This fall, the Old Town Public Library has a Ghost Hunting Kit you can try out!
What Is It?
According to their Facebook page, the Old Town Public Library has everything you could need to take a deeper dive into the unknown!
"Our new Ghost Hunting Kit is here! Whether you’re a skeptic or a believer, check it out and add a little mystery to your next adventure."
What's in this kit, you might ask?
We're told this particular parcel contains items that might come in handy for those looking into the shadows and around those dark corners for signs of the spooky or supernatural!
What Does This Kit Come With?
One UV flashlight to spot unexplained glowing fingerprints or interruptions in beams of light.
One EMF detector to measure invisible energy waves (or electromagnetic fields) and detect sudden, unexplained spikes in their surroundings.
One EVP recorder to capture the whispers of spirits and other electronic voice phenomena.
One infrared thermometer to hunt for spots that have dipped in temperature, possibly indicating the presence of evil or ghosts.
One FM radio and a Y7 Portable speaker. Why a radio and speakers? Well, it's believed that spirits can manipulate radio waves and white noise. They often use those avenues to communicate with people, or so the pros say. That's why they call radios spirit boxes or ghost boxes. The speaker helps to amplify the faint sounds that might come through.
A pair of motion-activated light-up cat balls. According to the experts at Ghost Stop,
paranormal investigators often place the balls in quiet, dark rooms on hard surfaces and ask spirits to touch, roll, or light up a specific ball as a "yes/no" or presence sign.
A pair of brass detection rods (you might know them as dowsing rods) that are believed to react when they encounter disturbances in the electromagnetic fields produced by spiritual energy or entities.
And finally, a carrying case for all this cool gear and an information card with details on how to use everything.
Other Things You Might Want To Explore
The Ghost Hunter kit is certainly a really neat idea, but it's not the only fun thing available through the library, Badger says.
"...while the Ghost Hunting Kit might be one of our more unusual items, it's certainly not the only surprise in our Library of Things! Patrons can also borrow kayaks, a lawn mower, a Nut Weasel (for collecting fallen nuts and other yard debris), board games, Tonies kits for kids, nature exploration backpacks, a DVD player, and even a monitor to measure household electricity usage.
Since Halloween is right around the corner, we're also hosting our Boo-tique Halloween Costume Swap throughout October! Families are welcome to donate gently used Halloween costumes or stop by to pick out a costume to take home, completely free. "
Read More: Bucksport, Maine, Is Home to a Spooky Cursed Tomb Legend
"Beyond our Library of Things, we offer free and discounted experiences through our library passes and ticket programs, including tickets to Penobscot Theatre, which is presenting Broomsticks this season, and passes to The Children's Museum, State Park Passes, and other local attractions."
For more information, ask the librarian directly.
The Old Town Public Library is located at 46 Middle Street and is open on Mondays 10 AM to 7 PM, Tuesday through Friday 10 AM to 5 PM, and Saturdays 10 AM to 1 PM.

title: Vatican releases update on Pope Leo XIV following his surgery, lung cancer diagnosis
text:
ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV resumed his regular diet, began walking and celebrated Mass in the hospital Wednesday as he recovered from surgery to remove a cancerous mass from his lung, the Vatican said. Questions remained about whether the cancer had spread, while Peru’s president suggested Leo might have to alter his planned visit to Latin America next month.
Blood tests and a chest X-ray showed the 71-year-old pope was recovering normally, his two doctors said.
“The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room. He resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the pope’s personal doctor, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the head thoracic surgeon at Gemelli hospital. “Recovery is proceeding as planned.”
Tuesday’s surgery confirmed that Leo has lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung.
The right lung has three lobes and the left has two. After one lobe is removed, the remaining lung tissue can gradually compensate, especially in otherwise healthy, physically active people. Leo is known for his interest in sports, including weekly tennis games and swimming.
The Vatican said late Wednesday that the pope had celebrated Mass with his secretaries in the afternoon in a special chapel set up for him on the 10th floor of the hospital.
No word yet on whether the pope’s cancer had spread
Experts said some of Leo’s lymph nodes would also have been removed and tested to determine whether the cancer had spread. Those results have not so far been made public.
If the cancer has spread, test results will guide treatment, said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown’s Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted therapy, which uses pills to treat cancers with specific characteristics.
Liu, who is not involved in the pope’s care, said that, of the different types of lung cancers, adenocarcinoma has the most favorable prognosis.
“While we know the diagnosis, we now need to know the stage,” Liu said. “We now need to know how big it is, how many spots in the lung are involved. Is it just one nodule, or more than one, and the lymph nodes, are they cancerous?”
Dr. PierCarlo Gentile, head of radiation oncology at Rome’s San Pietro Fatebenefratelli Hospital, said the minimally invasive, video-assisted chest surgery the pope underwent typically requires 15 to 20 days of recovery. Postoperative complications, including infections, are rare, he said.
Doubts over Latin America trip
The Vatican hasn’t announced any changes to Leo’s planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6-17.
But Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori said Wednesday that the pope’s diagnosis and recovery could affect the visit, even as she expressed hope it would go ahead. Leo spent two decades as a missionary in Peru, holds Peruvian citizenship and is beloved by his flock there.
“We understand that this recovery will take several weeks, longer than expected,” Fujimori told reporters. “We also understand that there could be some changes to the schedule of his visit.”
The ambitious itinerary for the longest trip of his papacy covers just over 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles), with a dozen flights and two helicopter rides across the three countries, as well as a significant change in altitude in Peru.
Fujimori said millions of Peruvians were praying for the pontiff’s recovery and awaiting further announcements from the Vatican.
“We hope his recovery will be swift and that his visit can go ahead, but we will also understand if that is not possible,” she said. “What matters most is that His Holiness regains his health.”
Oncology surgeons often advise patients not to fly for three weeks after surgery.
“If it is Stage 1, he can complete these trips. If more treatment is needed, I would likely advise against the trips,” said Liu.
Doctors took tissue samples before surgery
The pontiff has offered a rare degree of transparency about the first publicly disclosed major health problem of his 17-month papacy.
He revealed the discovery of a nodule, or growth, on his lung during his Sunday noon prayer, announcing it on live television. But Leo did not disclose everything he knew Sunday.
Tuesday’s medical bulletin said preoperative tests had led doctors to suspect cancer, which surgery confirmed. Leo did not use the word cancer in his announcement, though he described the nodule as being at an “early stage” and “circumscribed.”
The Vatican has now said that those tests included a robotic bronchoscopic biopsy, known as an ION broncoscopy, meaning doctors had already taken tissue samples to assess whether the mass was cancerous.
The procedure requires general anesthesia and must be performed in a hospital equipped with one of the advanced machines, said Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, chief thoracic surgeon at the European Institute of Oncology in Milan. He said Gemelli hospital had had one for about a year.
The Vatican did not say when Leo underwent the diagnostic tests, which also included a chest CT scan with contrast and a PET scan.
A PET scan can be used to make sure that the disease has not traveled to other places in the body, said Dr. Brendon Stiles, chief of surgical oncology at Montefiore Einstein in New York. Between the scan and the biopsy, Stiles said, “we can be hopefully reassured that this should be a stage-one cancer.”
Pope breaks with a tradition of secrecy surrounding health issues
The Vatican has long been secretive about the health of popes and tightly controlled any such information — a practice encapsulated in the popular Italian saying, “ The pope is fine until he’s dead.”
St. John XXIII died in 1963, nearly a year after doctors diagnosed stomach cancer that was kept hidden at the time. St. John Paul II died in 2005 after suffering for years from the obvious effects of Parkinson’s disease that the Vatican only confirmed after he died.
Pope Francis seemed more up front about his health problems, giving an Argentine doctor a tell-all interview for a book about his physical and mental health. But in the end Francis, too, tightly controlled the information that was released in his dying months.
As a result, Leo’s decision to announce himself that he had a nodule and was undergoing surgery was significant.
“That was truly a revolution. It was like he was reading a medical bulletin himself,” said Giovanni Maria Vian, a church historian and the former editor-in-chief of the Vatican newspaper L’Osservatore Romano.
Vian, who was part of the Vatican communications team from 2007 to 2018, said the Vatican’s obsession with secrecy was due to both practical and cultural considerations. He noted the Vatican is a 2,000-year-old institution that is culturally European — and Europeans tend to be more guarded about health problems than people in the United States.
___
Barry reported from Milan. Associated Press video producer Paolo Santalucia in Rome and Associated Press writer Lauran Neergaard in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Kerrieann Harrison (1969-2026)
‘It’s a forever change’: supporting aging parents through loss of a child
text:
(Aging Untold) — Losing a child is something no parent expects to face, no matter their age.
The Aging Untold experts are talking candidly about why this grief is so often overlooked in older adults and how families and caregivers can help.
An “unnatural” loss, no matter your age
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, pointed out a troubling pattern she’s seen in her work with older adults.
“One of the saddest things I see is when we have our aged community and they lose their child, and it’s not treated the same,” Cradduck said. “If you’re my age and you lose a child, everybody rallies around and they’re there for you. But when an aged person loses their child, it’s like, ‘Well, you’re old. What do you expect?’ ... I think that is such an unfairness that we have allowed ourselves to do.”
A story from the nursing home
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, shared a personal memory from her time as a nursing home administrator that illustrates how older adults’ grief could go unacknowledged.
“I greeted a new resident, went into the room, sat at the bedside and we were just talking, and all of a sudden she started telling me about her daughter who had died of cancer. It broke my heart,” O’Rourke said.
O’Rourke described how her team responded.
“We got activities, we got social services, we got the chaplain, got everybody together, and I said we’re going to keep an eye on her. Let her talk, let her grieve. Let her say her daughter’s name. Let her share the memories, look at the photos and remember her so you can create some history with her,” O’Rourke said.
A grief that never fully resolves
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said there is a prolonged grieving process for a parent mourning the death of a child.
“I’ve had a couple of friends and colleagues and your heart just hurts for them. But to see how they can sometimes get stalled is very hard to get over,” Rogers said.
A shift in perspective helped Rogers’ friends and colleagues while navigating loss.
“I listened to them and they said, ‘You know, hey, I had to remember the time that they were here and concentrate on the good, not look at this loss, and celebrate the life,” Rogers said.
She said that helped the people she knows stay intact physically, emotionally and spiritually.
Cradduck added that acceptance — not resolution — is the realistic goal.
“I think you have to assume that you’re always going to grieve this loss,” Cradduck said. “You can make it to acceptance, which is the goal. But I don’t think you ever will ever not be grieving that child. I believe that’s just something that’s significant and it stays forever. And I think you have to go into it knowing that this is a forever change.”
Staying connected helps everyone heal
O’Rourke shared an example from a neighbor who lost her daughter but chose to stay close to her son-in-law and grandchildren.
“She faced the fear of being there without her daughter, but she said it was one of the best things that she did, because when they talked about the daughter, it helped her heal,” O’Rourke said.
Cradduck noted the ripple effect of that choice.
“It helped her son-in-law, and it helps those grandchildren to keep that memory alive and keep that person alive,” Cradduck said.
You don’t need the right words — just presence
Katherine Ambrose, an aging-well coach, offered guidance for friends and family who aren’t sure how to support a grieving parent.
“Don’t feel like you need to have the right words — just your presence is enough, just being there,” Ambrose said. “Also giving people permission to not be OK, and that there’s no time limit, there’s no comparison on how long you feel a certain way. People can grieve for the rest of their lives.”
Finding purpose in the pain
Several hosts pointed to purpose and legacy as paths toward healing.
Rogers observed that many grieving parents find a way to honor their child by helping others.
“When they have a loss of a child, they find another purpose to help you maintain the memory of that person,” Rogers said. “That’s a healthy way of doing it.”
Cradduck shared a personal connection to this idea, describing a close friend whose son was an organ donor.
“She knows where some of his organs went to,” Cradduck said. “I’ve watched the change in her, and I know that it’s a forever change for her, as it is for her entire family. But there is a peace that can come, and I think that has to be recognized. There can be a peace that comes in finding the purpose for that pain and doing something with it.”
Cradduck closed with a message for anyone going through this kind of loss.
“If you’re going through it, please find a way to make that pain purposeful and let that legacy live on,” Cradduck said.

title: Obituary: Mary Frances Maschino
text:
GARDINER – Mary Frances Maschino, 88, died peacefully on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, at the Balsam House in Readfield.
She was born in Gardiner, on Dec. 12, 1937, to Joseph B. and Dorothy M. (Austin) McNamara.
Mary grew up in Gardiner, enjoying Girl Scouts, reading, working at the Gardiner Public Library, visiting with friends and relatives, playing the piano, and playing the cornet in the high school band – where she met her future husband, Jerry.
She graduated from Gardiner High School, attended University of Maine in Orono before transferring to Simmons College in Boston, earning a degree in Library Science. After marrying Jerry in 1963, they moved to Dorchester, Massachusetts; Stratham, New Hampshire; East Greenwich, Rhode Island; Townsend, Massachusetts; Waverly, Pennsylvania; and Indianapolis, Indiana, before retiring to her family home in Gardiner, becoming snowbirds, spending winters in Florida. As a stay-at-home mom, Mary volunteered at local libraries, the kids’ schools, scouts, and community organizations. For many years she served as the crossing guard at the Community House in Waverly and she worked at the Abington Community Library. In Indianapolis, she studied for two years at the Indianapolis Museum of Art and became a docent, giving tours and sharing her knowledge and love of art while she was working at Girls, Inc. as their research librarian. She decided to go back to college and earned her Master of Library Science at Indiana University, the year she turned 60. During retirement, she enjoyed attending programs at the Kennebec Historical Society, working at the election polls, and attending a variety of cultural events in Maine and Florida. She shared her love of ice cream, reading, art, and music with her family.
She was predeceased by her parents and husband, Jerry Maschino.
Mary is survived by her three children: Sara Maschino of Gardiner, Anna Bragdon (Tarren) of Ave Maria, Florida, and Karl Maschino (Anne) of Fairfax, Virginia; eight grandchildren: Isabelle and Sebastian Jadik (Deanna); Wyatt, Waverly, Asher, and Jude Bragdon, and Hannah and Ryan Maschino; one great-grandchild, Oella May (Sebastian); and many friends.
Family and friends are invited to attend visitation on Friday, October 16, from 4-6 p.m., at Staples Funeral Home, 53 Brunswick Avenue, Gardiner. A graveside service will be held on Saturday, October 17, at 10 a.m. at St. Joseph Cemetery in Gardiner. A celebration of Mary’s life will follow from 2-4 p.m. at Staples Funeral Home in Gardiner.
Arrangements and guidance are in the care of Staple Funeral Home and Cremation Care, 53 Brunswick Avenue, Gardiner, Maine.
Condolences, memories, and photos may be shared with the family on the obituary page of the Staples Funeral Home website, http://www.staplesfuneralhome.com.
The family requests that, in lieu of flowers, those who wish may make a gift in Mary’s name to the Gardiner Public Library, https://gardinerpubliclibrary.org/support/ or the Kennebec Historical Society, https://www.kennebechistorical.org/ or a charity of your choice.

title: Lone Pine Brewing plans to open bigger tasting room in downtown Portland
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Lone Pine Brewing Company aims to expand its retail presence in Maine, and plans to launch a much larger tasting room in downtown Portland next spring, according to a company spokesperson.
Lone Pine temporarily closed its Anderson Street tasting room about a month ago.
“Anderson Street is small, and it’s not in an ideal location. We’re trying to establish a much bigger, better flagship location for Lone Pine in downtown Portland,” said Simon Thorpe, who sits on the board of directors for Lord Hobo Brewing Company and Lone Pine. Massachusetts-based Lord Hobo and Lone Pine announced their merger about two years ago.
Thorpe said the company has been looking at a couple of potential Portland locations in the past six months or so. “The aim is to have a much bigger presence in Portland than we do at the moment.”
The company is also considering tasting rooms in additional Maine locations like Bangor and Lewiston, Thorpe said.
A new brewery is opening in Lone Pine’s former location in Old Orchard Beach, which closed in late September. “Someone looking from the outside might say, ‘They’re retrenching away from retail in Maine,'” Thorpe said. “Nothing could be further from the truth.”
Thorpe explained that because the Old Orchard Beach space was highly seasonal, it was difficult to staff and attract customers year round.
Lone Pine first opened its Anderson Street tasting room in 2016. The facility doesn’t serve food, and seats 70 people outside, but only about 24 inside. Thorpe said the plan is for the new downtown Portland tasting room to seat 250 inside, another 100 outside, and have a kitchen and food menu.
Thorpe said the company is also looking to “expand capabilities” at Lone Pine’s Gorham brewery, possibly including adding a tasting room.
Lone Pine quadrupled its production in both 2017 and 2018, becoming one of Maine’s 10 largest breweries.

title: 6 people killed, including child, in plane crash in Wisconsin, authorities say
text:
6 people killed, including child, in plane crash in Wisconsin, authorities say
Six people, including a child, were killed Tuesday night when a small plane crashed in Wisconsin, according to the Sauk County Sheriff's Office.
The crash happened around 9:30 p.m. near Wisconsin Dells. Five adults and one child were killed.
Nobody on the ground was hurt, according to officials.
FlightAware data indicates the single-engine plane took off from Kenosha Regional Airport shortly before 9 p.m., less than an hour before the crash.
Authorities have not released the identities of the victims or confirmed what caused the plane to crash.
The crash scene, about 50 miles northwest of Madison, remains secured as investigators work to determine the cause.
The Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board have been notified and will assist in the investigation.

title: Sanitation worker dies following road rage shootout while driving garbage truck
text:
PRICHARD, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) - A sanitation worker in Alabama has died after being injured in a road rage shooting in August.
The Mobile County Sheriff’s Office confirmed that Clifton Eugene DuBose Jr., 54, died this week after being hospitalized following a shooting on Aug. 4.
Investigators said DuBose got into a confrontation that day with those in another car on Jarrett Road while he was driving a garbage truck.
According to authorities, DuBose and the driver of the other vehicle’s argument escalated, with both of them stopping their cars and pulling out a gun.
The man’s wife in the other vehicle ended up shooting DuBose in the abdomen, while DuBose fired into the car, the sheriff’s office said.
Sheriff Paul Burch said the shooting was particularly dangerous as children were in the other vehicle.
“The sanitation worker brandished a weapon, as did the other occupants of the vehicle,” Burch said. “Rounds were fired by both parties, and eventually, they drove off. Both called police to report the incident.”
DuBose was described as the aggressor in the altercation and was charged with five counts of shooting into an occupied vehicle. The Mobile County Sheriff’s Office said that he also had an active warrant on a domestic violence charge and was driving on a suspended or revoked license.
Burch said at that time it was unclear how a city employee could be driving a garbage truck without a valid license.
The sheriff also urged residents not to take the law into their own hands.
“Anytime there’s an issue being run off the road by, you know, any government vehicle or any, just report it to law enforcement,” Burch said. “Don’t get into a confrontation. That’s never gonna end well.”

title: South Portland has 43 new affordable housing units
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Landry Woods, a three-story, 43-unit apartment community for adults 55 and older, is now complete.
The apartment complex is an addition to Landry Village, a neighborhood of one-story buildings that includes 50 one- and two-bedroom apartments for older Mainers and those with disabilities. The area is a hub of affordable housing where such options can be hard to come by.
The South Portland Housing Authority began construction of Landry Woods last year, providing affordable, one-bedroom units for older residents who earn 60% or less than the area median income.
The housing authority has another expansion planned for Landry Village — Landry Heights, a 38-unit, low-income housing project.
South Portland needs more housing for all income levels, according to the 2022 city assessment. Housing demand averages 54 year-round units per year. That’s double the average number of vacant units per year.
The cost of housing is also increasing. The median home price rose 56% from 2015 to 2021, from $256,704 to $400,000, adjusting for inflation, according to MaineHousing data. Rental costs have also increased: In 2012, the median gross rent was $980. In 2021, it was $1,465, a 49% increase.
Within the past few years, the housing authority has opened multiple affordable housing developments in the city: Betsy Ross Crossing (a 52-unit development for seniors) in 2025, Jocelyn Place (60 income-limited, one-bedroom apartments for seniors) in 2024, and Thornton Heights Commons (42 units for residential and commercial use) in 2023.

title: ‘Helping Hands, Heating Homes’ event to raise funds for Midcoast heating assistance
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Midcoast churches are banding together for the second time to raise funds for heating assistance for local families. The public event, “Helping Hands, Heating Homes,” is at 5:30 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 24, at St. Patrick’s Catholic Church on Academy Hill Road in Newcastle. The event will include a spaghetti dinner, silent auction and concert.
The cost to attend all events of the evening is $25 per person, or a maximum of $60 per family. All proceeds will be divided equally between the Ecumenical Council on Homeless Prevention and the Community Housing Improvement Project. The first dinner/auction raised over $8,000.
The music will begin at 6:30 p.m. The concert will feature Echoes of Faith Trio, Faith Baptist Church Choir and local musician Sean Fleming.
The evening will be hosted by local celebrity and longtime WCSH6 personality Don Carrigan. The auction will run throughout the evening and will include mostly silent auction items, with a few live auction items and at least one raffle.
“There are many families struggling to heat their homes right now,” said Don Sproul, chairperson of the event and president of the Water of Life Lutheran Church. “This is a great opportunity for the community to come together. Our goal is to raise $10,000 to help local families this year.”
According to Steve Ward, co-coordinator at ECHP, the need for heating assistance is historically high this year. ECHP once served nine families; now the need is for over 60 families.
Sproul said there are three ways people can help:
• Donate items to the silent auction. You may do so by emailing Kim Tolley at [email protected].
• Purchase tickets at zeffy.com/en-US/ticketing/2nd-annual-helping-hands-heating-homes-fundraiser.
• If you cannot attend but wish to donate to the heating assistance fund, you may do so through the ticket link or by contacting Sproul at 207-441-7778.
Volunteers from Water of Life Lutheran Church, St. Patrick’s Catholic Church, St. Andrew’s Episcopal Church, Wiscasset United Church of Christ and Faith Baptist Church have been involved in the planning of this event. Representatives from CHiP, ECHP, Stepping Stones and the Central Lincoln County YMCA have also assisted.

title: Eleanor Yesmentes
text:
Eleanor Yesmentes, formerly of East Boothbay died peacefully at her home in Milford, MA on October 5th just days away from her 89th birthday.
Eleanor was beautiful inside and out. She was funny, sweet and had an incredible sense of humor. She loved people and was a natural performer. Piano was her passion and she'd play classical music from memory for all who wanted to listen as well as for the church.
Over the years she was a Welcome Wagon hostess, animal control officer and choir director but being a school bus driver brought her the most joy.
With a great sense of adventure, Eleanor loved to travel both near and far and was often seen around town in her convertible corvette with her big poodle in the passenger seat, usually on their way for an ice cream. Her motto was, "Life is short, eat dessert first!"
Eleanor was predeceased by her husband Pete and survived by her son Peter of Winchendon, Massachusetts, a daughter Katie Daley and her husband Dan of Mendon, Massachusetts and was predeceased by her youngest child, Sarah Plummer, wife of Todd Plummer of Boothbay. Eleanor is also survived by six grandsons, Evan and Peter Yesmentes, Alden and Austin Daley and Troy and Jay Plummer.
While in East Boothbay Eleanor was active in the Boothbay Shores Association, the Down East Yacht Club and St. Columba's Church.
As her struggles with dementia became overwhelming for her, she moved closer to her daughter where she became a much loved member of the community. She remained playful, funny and sweet right up until the end. She lived an amazing life filled with love, laughter and music. We should all be so lucky.
Eleanor loved the ocean with the sound of the foghorn and the pounding waves so while there will be no calling hours, there will be a private service aboard her grandson's boat on a day when the sun is shining and seas are calm.
